abducens-nucleus.name: Abducens nucleus
abducens-nucleus.summary: The abducens nucleus lies under the facial colliculus in the caudal pons and is the horizontal gaze center's output stage: its motor neurons supply the ipsilateral lateral rectus, and its internuclear neurons cross in the MLF to drive the contralateral medial rectus. Because both cell types live together, a nuclear lesion causes a conjugate gaze palsy toward the side of the lesion, not an isolated lateral rectus palsy. The facial nerve fibers loop around it, so a nuclear lesion often adds an ipsilateral facial palsy.

anatomy.location: Dorsal caudal pons beneath the facial colliculus of the fourth ventricular floor, paramedian, with the PPRF just anterior and lateral to it and the MLF medial to it.

abducens-nucleus.function: Abduction of the ipsilateral eye and, through internuclear neurons, conjugate horizontal gaze to the ipsilateral side; final common pathway for saccades, pursuit and the vestibulo-ocular reflex in the horizontal plane.

bestView.label: facial colliculus level of the caudal pons
floor of the fourth ventricle at the facial colliculus

imaging.normalAppearance: Not resolved on routine MRI; the facial colliculus is the paramedian bump on the floor of the fourth ventricle at the caudal pons. Small lesions here are best seen on thin axial FLAIR or DWI.

pathology.pathology: Pontine tegmental infarct or demyelination at the facial colliculus
pathology.finding: Small paramedian dorsal pontine lesion with ipsilateral gaze palsy and lower motor neuron facial weakness.
Mass in the dorsal pons displacing the ventricular floor; sixth nerve and gaze palsies are early signs.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: Thin FLAIR/DWI through the pons

lesionEffects.deficit: Conjugate horizontal gaze palsy toward the side of the lesion
lesionEffects.mechanism: Loss of both motor and internuclear neurons

lesionEffects.deficit: Ipsilateral lower motor neuron facial palsy
lesionEffects.mechanism: Facial nerve genu looping over the nucleus
Abducens fascicle or nerve, not the nucleus

examination: Ask the patient to follow a target to each side: nuclear lesions stop both eyes at the midline
Test the vestibulo-ocular reflex (doll's eyes) — absent toward the lesion side in nuclear lesions, preserved in PPRF lesions
Facial movement including the forehead
pearls: A gaze palsy that cannot be overcome by the oculocephalic reflex is nuclear; one that can is supranuclear (PPRF or cortex)
Gaze palsy plus peripheral facial palsy equals the facial colliculus

amygdala.name: Amygdala
amygdala.summary: An almond-shaped group of nuclei in the anteromedial temporal lobe, in front of the hippocampal head and beneath the uncus, at the tip of the temporal horn. It attaches emotional significance to sensory input: the lateral and basolateral nuclei receive highly processed sensory and prefrontal input, the central nucleus sends output to the hypothalamus and brainstem for autonomic and behavioral fear responses, and the corticomedial group receives olfactory input. It drives fear conditioning, threat detection and emotional memory, and its bilateral loss produces the placidity, hyperorality and hypersexuality of the Klüver–Bucy syndrome.

anatomy.location: Anteromedial temporal lobe at the anterior end of the temporal horn, in front of and partly above the hippocampal head, below the lentiform nucleus (with which it is continuous through the substantia innominata) and medial to the temporal pole white matter; its output pathways are the stria terminalis and the ventral amygdalofugal pathway.

subdivisions.name: Basolateral group (lateral, basal, accessory basal nuclei)
subdivisions.note: sensory and prefrontal input; emotional learning

subdivisions.name: Central nucleus
subdivisions.note: output to hypothalamus, periaqueductal gray, brainstem autonomic nuclei: fear expression

subdivisions.name: Corticomedial group and medial nucleus
subdivisions.note: olfactory and pheromonal input

subdivisions.name: Bed nucleus of the stria terminalis (extended amygdala)
subdivisions.note: anxiety and stress responses

efferents.via: stria terminalis and ventral amygdalofugal pathway

amygdala.function: Fear and threat processing, emotional conditioning, assignment of emotional value to stimuli and memories, autonomic and endocrine responses to emotion, social recognition of facial expression, olfactory-emotional integration.

bestView.label: amygdala in front of the hippocampal head under the uncus
anteromedial temporal lobe at the tip of the temporal horn

imaging.normalAppearance: Homogeneous gray matter at the anterior tip of the temporal horn on coronal T1, above and in front of the hippocampal head and beneath the uncus; the MASSP mesh in this atlas outlines it. Involved together with the hippocampus in encephalitis and sclerosis.

pathology.finding: FLAIR hyperintensity and swelling of the amygdala and hippocampus.

pathology.pathology: Amygdala enlargement in temporal lobe epilepsy
pathology.finding: Enlarged, mildly T2-bright amygdala on the side of seizure onset.
Bilateral symmetrical amygdala calcification with absent fear responses.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: Coronal T2/FLAIR

lesionEffects.deficit: Klüver–Bucy syndrome: placidity, hyperorality, hypersexuality, visual agnosia, hypermetamorphosis
lesionEffects.mechanism: Bilateral amygdala and anterior temporal destruction

lesionEffects.deficit: Loss of fear and impaired recognition of fearful faces
lesionEffects.mechanism: Bilateral amygdala lesions

lesionEffects.deficit: Seizures with fear aura and autonomic features
lesionEffects.mechanism: Amygdala involvement in temporal lobe epilepsy
Hyperactivity of the amygdala in anxiety and PTSD

examination: Recognition of emotional facial expressions
Ask about ictal fear, palpitations or gastric sensations
Behavioral observation: placidity, oral exploration
pearls: A temporal lobe seizure that begins with intense fear and a rising epigastric sensation points to the amygdala and hippocampus
The Klüver–Bucy syndrome after herpes encephalitis or bilateral temporal surgery is the human evidence for amygdala function

anterior-commissure.name: Anterior commissure
anterior-commissure.summary: The anterior commissure is a compact bundle of crossing fibers in the front wall of the third ventricle, in front of the columns of the fornix and below the rostrum of the corpus callosum, connecting the two temporal lobes, the amygdalae and the olfactory regions. It is the second largest forebrain commissure and the fixed landmark of stereotactic neurosurgery: the line from the anterior to the posterior commissure defines the axis of the Talairach and MNI coordinate systems used throughout this atlas. It is displaced by third ventricular and suprasellar masses, spared or enlarged in callosal agenesis, and it carries the interhemispheric transfer that persists after callosotomy, explaining why some information still crosses in split-brain patients.

anatomy.location: Midline bundle crossing the lamina terminalis at the front of the third ventricle just in front of the fornix columns, whose lateral limbs sweep back beneath the anterior limb of the internal capsule and the pallidum into the temporal lobes; the smaller anterior limb passes forward to the olfactory tracts.

afferents.from: Anterior and inferior temporal cortex, amygdala
Olfactory bulb and anterior olfactory nucleus

anterior-commissure.function: The posterior limb connects the anterior and inferior temporal cortex, the amygdala and the temporal pole of the two sides and carries visual, auditory and olfactory memory representations between the hemispheres, complementing the corpus callosum; the anterior limb links the olfactory bulbs and the anterior olfactory nuclei so that odor information is shared. The commissure also contributes fibers from the nucleus accumbens and the bed nucleus. Its clinical use is anatomical: as the origin of the AC-PC coordinate system it locates thalamic and subthalamic targets for deep brain stimulation, and its position is a check on midline shift and third ventricular distortion.

bestView.label: anterior commissure in the front wall of the third ventricle
commissural fibers crossing beneath the fornix columns

imaging.normalAppearance: A small round dark bundle on midline sagittal T1 images in front of the fornix columns and below the rostrum, marking the front of the third ventricle; on axial images its posterior limbs arc laterally beneath the pallidum into the temporal stems.

pathology.finding: Upward and forward displacement or thinning of the anterior commissure by a colloid cyst, craniopharyngioma or giant aneurysm; distortion of the AC-PC line invalidates stereotactic coordinates.
Absent corpus callosum with a preserved or enlarged anterior commissure and Probst bundles running parallel to the interhemispheric fissure.
Focal FLAIR lesion in the commissure in multiple sclerosis, usually asymptomatic.

lesionEffects.deficit: Reduced interhemispheric transfer of visual and olfactory information
lesionEffects.mechanism: Loss of temporal and olfactory commissural fibers, evident mainly after callosotomy
Distortion of the anterior commissure shifts the AC-PC coordinate frame used for deep brain stimulation targeting

lesionEffects.deficit: Usually no deficit from an isolated lesion
lesionEffects.mechanism: Function is duplicated by the corpus callosum

examination: Identify the commissure on the midline sagittal image and check the AC-PC line before any stereotactic planning
Interhemispheric transfer tests (cross-localization of touch, naming objects in the left hand) after callosal surgery
Smell testing when both olfactory pathways may be involved
pearls: The AC-PC line is the equator of stereotactic space; MNI coordinates in this atlas are measured from the anterior commissure
In callosal agenesis the anterior commissure often grows to compensate
Split-brain patients still share smells and some emotions across the anterior commissure

pitfalls: A commissure displaced by a mass makes atlas-based coordinates wrong; always plan stereotactic targets on the patient's own AC-PC line

anterior-spinal-artery.name: Anterior spinal artery
anterior-spinal-artery.summary: A single midline artery formed by the union of a branch from each vertebral artery that descends along the whole length of the cord in the anterior median fissure. Its sulcal branches feed the anterior two-thirds of the cord: anterior horns, corticospinal and spinothalamic tracts. It depends on segmental radicular feeders, especially the artery of Adamkiewicz, so aortic disease or surgery can infarct the mid-thoracic cord while sparing the posterior columns.

anatomy.location: Formed on the ventral medulla by two contributory branches from the intracranial vertebral arteries, runs caudally in the pia of the anterior median fissure to the conus, reinforced at intervals by anterior radicular arteries entering with the ventral roots, chiefly at C5–C6, T4–T6 and T9–L2.

subdivisions.name: Cervical segment
subdivisions.note: reinforced by radicular branches from the vertebral, deep cervical and ascending cervical arteries

subdivisions.name: Mid-thoracic watershed (about T4–T8)
subdivisions.note: the least reinforced, most vulnerable segment

subdivisions.name: Thoracolumbar segment
subdivisions.note: reinforced by the artery of Adamkiewicz, usually from a left T9–T12 intercostal artery

anterior-spinal-artery.function: Perfuses the anterior two-thirds of the spinal cord through sulcal (central) branches: anterior and lateral gray horns, the lateral and anterior corticospinal tracts, the spinothalamic tracts and the autonomic pathways; the posterior columns are supplied separately.

bestView.label: ventral medulla where the two contributory branches unite
descending on the anterior surface of the medulla and cervical cord

imaging.normalAppearance: A fine midline flow void on the anterior surface of the cord on high-resolution axial T2; better shown on spinal CTA or MRA with contrast. The intracranial origin is seen anterior to the medulla just below the vertebrobasilar junction.

pathology.finding: T2 hyperintensity of the anterior two-thirds of the cord over several segments with 'owl's eye' bright anterior horns on axial images and restricted diffusion acutely; the posterior columns are spared.
pathology.timing: T2 change may take 12–24 h to appear; DWI is positive earlier

pathology.finding: Restricted diffusion in the paramedian ventral medulla involving the pyramid, medial lemniscus and hypoglossal fibers.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: Sagittal and axial T2 plus DWI of the cord; CTA/aortic imaging to find dissection or aneurysm

lesionEffects.deficit: Flaccid then spastic paraparesis or quadriparesis
lesionEffects.mechanism: Anterior horns and corticospinal tracts

lesionEffects.deficit: Loss of pain and temperature below the level with preserved vibration and proprioception
lesionEffects.mechanism: Spinothalamic tracts infarcted, posterior columns spared
Descending autonomic pathways and intermediolateral column
Occlusion of the rostral anterior spinal artery

examination: Sensory level to pin-prick with preserved vibration at the same dermatomes
Reflexes: initially absent (spinal shock), later brisk with extensor plantars
Bladder scan for retention

html.summary: A single midline artery formed by the union of a branch from each vertebral artery that descends along the whole length of the cord in the anterior median fissure. Its sulcal branches feed the anterior two-thirds of the cord: anterior horns, corticospinal and spinothalamic tracts. It depends on segmental radicular feeders, especially the artery of Adamkiewicz, so aortic disease or surgery can infarct the mid-thoracic cord while sparing the posterior columns.

html.anatomy.location: Formed on the ventral medulla by two contributory branches from the intracranial vertebral arteries, runs caudally in the pia of the anterior median fissure to the conus, reinforced at intervals by anterior radicular arteries entering with the ventral roots, chiefly at C5–C6, T4–T6 and T9–L2.

html.imaging.sequenceOfChoice: Sagittal and axial T2 plus DWI of the cord; CTA/aortic imaging to find dissection or aneurysm

arachnoid-granulations.name: Arachnoid granulations
arachnoid-granulations.summary: Tufts of arachnoid that push through the dura into the venous sinuses, chiefly the superior sagittal sinus and its lateral lacunae, and act as one-way valves returning CSF to the blood when CSF pressure exceeds venous pressure by a few centimetres of water. Their scarring after subarachnoid hemorrhage or meningitis is the classical cause of communicating hydrocephalus, and raised venous pressure from sinus thrombosis backs up CSF absorption to produce intracranial hypertension. Large granulations are a common incidental finding that can mimic sinus thrombosis or a mass on imaging.

anatomy.location: Along the superior sagittal sinus and its lateral lacunae in the parasagittal dura, also in the transverse and sigmoid sinuses and around spinal nerve roots; they enlarge and calcify with age and can erode the inner table of the skull.

arachnoid-granulations.function: Bulk resorption of CSF into the venous system, pressure-dependent and valve-like; supplemented by lymphatic and perineural drainage routes.

bestView.label: superior sagittal sinus and lateral lacunae at the vertex
granulations projecting into the transverse sinus

imaging.normalAppearance: Round CSF-signal filling defects within the dural sinuses on contrast MR venography or CTV, following CSF on all sequences, often with a small vessel entering them; they should not be mistaken for thrombus, which is denser on CT and has a different signal on T1/T2.

pathology.finding: Dilatation of all four ventricles including the fourth, with transependymal edema, after subarachnoid hemorrhage, meningitis or carcinomatosis.
Well-defined CSF-signal filling defect in the transverse sinus, with no restriction and no expansion of the sinus.
pathology.pitfalls: Do not diagnose sinus thrombosis from a granulation: check T1 signal and the shape on MR venography

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: MR venography or CT venography

lesionEffects.deficit: Communicating hydrocephalus after subarachnoid hemorrhage or meningitis
lesionEffects.mechanism: Blocked absorption at the granulations

lesionEffects.deficit: Raised intracranial pressure with sinus thrombosis
lesionEffects.mechanism: Venous hypertension impeding CSF absorption

Gait and cognition in the weeks after subarachnoid hemorrhage
Headache features and visual obscurations
pearls: Hydrocephalus in which all four ventricles are enlarged is communicating: the problem is absorption, not obstruction

arachnoid-mater.name: Arachnoid mater
arachnoid-mater.summary: The delicate, avascular middle meninx that lines the dura and bridges the sulci and fissures, leaving the CSF-filled subarachnoid space between itself and the pia. Its trabeculae cross that space like a spider's web, its granulations push through the dura into the venous sinuses to absorb CSF, and its cells form the barrier that keeps CSF separate from the dural blood supply. It is the origin of meningiomas (arachnoid cap cells) and of arachnoid cysts, and infection of the subarachnoid space beneath it is meningitis.

anatomy.location: Inner surface of the dura from the vault to the sacrum, separated from it by the potential subdural space and from the pia by the subarachnoid space; it does not follow the brain into the sulci, hence the cisterns.

arachnoid-mater.function: Contains the CSF, absorbs it into the venous sinuses through the granulations, forms the blood–CSF barrier at the dural interface, and gives origin to meningiomas.

bestView.label: basal subarachnoid cisterns beneath the arachnoid
subarachnoid space over the convexity

imaging.normalAppearance: Not visible as a membrane; recognized through the subarachnoid space it encloses and by its lesions: arachnoid cysts are sharply defined CSF-signal extra-axial collections following CSF on every sequence, and leptomeningeal enhancement follows the sulci in meningitis.

pathology.finding: Well-defined extra-axial CSF-signal cyst, most often in the middle cranial fossa, suppressing on FLAIR and not restricting on DWI; remodels bone.
Sulcal FLAIR hyperintensity with leptomeningeal enhancement following the sulci and cisterns.
Dural-based enhancing mass arising from arachnoid cap cells.
Clumped, adherent cauda equina roots displaced to the periphery of the thecal sac (empty sac sign) after surgery, hemorrhage or infection, with chronic radicular pain.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: FLAIR and T1+Gd; lumbar puncture for CSF

lesionEffects.mechanism: Inflammation of the subarachnoid space
Blockage of the granulations by blood or exudate

lesionEffects.deficit: Cranial nerve palsies in basal meningitis
lesionEffects.mechanism: Nerves crossing the inflamed basal cisterns

lesionEffects.deficit: Mass effect from a large arachnoid cyst
lesionEffects.mechanism: Expanding CSF collection

examination: Neck stiffness, Kernig and Brudzinski signs
Fundoscopy
Cranial nerves
Fever and rash
pearls: An arachnoid cyst that follows CSF on every sequence and suppresses on FLAIR is benign and usually needs nothing

area-broca.name: Broca's area
area-broca.summary: The posterior part of the inferior frontal gyrus of the dominant (usually left) hemisphere, the pars opercularis and pars triangularis. It assembles the motor programs of speech and sentence structure and passes them to the adjacent face and mouth area of the motor cortex, receiving input from Wernicke's area through the arcuate fasciculus. Its damage produces non-fluent, effortful, agrammatic speech with relatively preserved comprehension, typically with right face and arm weakness because the same MCA superior division supplies both.

anatomy.location: Inferior frontal gyrus just in front of the lower precentral gyrus and above the Sylvian fissure, in the dominant hemisphere; the frontal operculum covering the insula.

area-broca.function: Speech production: articulatory planning, grammar and syntax; also contributes to verbal working memory and to comprehension of complex syntax.

bestView.label: posterior inferior frontal gyrus above the Sylvian fissure
pars opercularis and triangularis in front of the precentral gyrus

imaging.normalAppearance: The pars triangularis and opercularis are seen on sagittal images 45–55 mm left of the midline as the two gyri in front of the lower precentral gyrus; fMRI language mapping localizes it before surgery.

pathology.finding: Restricted diffusion in the left inferior frontal gyrus and adjacent opercular cortex.
Left inferior frontal and insular atrophy in the agrammatic variant of primary progressive aphasia.
Left frontal opercular glioma; awake mapping required for resection.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: DWI; T1 for atrophy; fMRI/awake mapping before surgery

lesionEffects.deficit: Non-fluent aphasia: effortful, telegraphic speech, agrammatism, impaired repetition, preserved comprehension
lesionEffects.mechanism: Loss of articulatory and syntactic programming

lesionEffects.deficit: Apraxia of speech and buccofacial apraxia
lesionEffects.mechanism: Motor programming of oral movements

area-postrema.name: Area postrema
area-postrema.summary: The area postrema is a small, highly vascular strip of tissue on each side of the caudal floor of the fourth ventricle, at the obex, lacking a blood–brain barrier so that its neurons sample the blood and CSF directly. It is the chemoreceptor trigger zone for vomiting: circulating toxins, drugs, hormones and metabolic signals excite it, and it drives the adjacent nucleus of the solitary tract and the medullary vomiting pattern generator. It also senses osmolality, glucose and gut peptides and participates in fluid balance and feeding. Clinically it is the target of antiemetic dopamine and serotonin antagonists, the site of the intractable hiccups and vomiting that herald neuromyelitis optica, and the reason that medullary lesions near the obex present with vomiting before any classical neurological sign.

anatomy.location: Paired circumventricular organs on the lateral walls of the caudal fourth ventricle at the obex, immediately dorsal to the nucleus of the solitary tract and the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus, with fenestrated capillaries and specialized ependyma.

afferents.from: Blood and CSF (no barrier): toxins, drugs, hormones

efferents.to: Nucleus of the solitary tract and the ventrolateral medullary vomiting center
Dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus

area-postrema.function: Its neurons carry receptors for dopamine, serotonin, substance P, opioids, glucagon-like peptide 1 and amylin, and are excited by emetic drugs such as apomorphine, chemotherapy agents and digoxin, by uremia and ketoacidosis, and by vestibular input in motion sickness. They project to the nucleus of the solitary tract, the parabrachial nucleus and the vomiting center in the ventrolateral medulla, which coordinates the retching sequence of gastric relaxation, retrograde intestinal contraction, glottic closure and abdominal contraction. Through solitary and hypothalamic connections the area postrema also mediates satiety from gut hormones, the pressor response to angiotensin and the aversion learned after nausea.

bestView.label: obex at the caudal tip of the fourth ventricle
dorsal medulla at the obex, lateral to the midline

imaging.normalAppearance: Not resolved as a distinct structure on routine MRI; it lies at the posterior surface of the medulla at the obex, where the fourth ventricle narrows into the central canal. Because it lacks a barrier, it can enhance faintly after gadolinium as a normal finding.

pathology.finding: T2 and FLAIR hyperintensity of the dorsal medulla at the obex, often extending into the upper cervical cord, in a patient with intractable vomiting and hiccups; aquaporin-4 antibodies positive.
Lesion of the caudal floor of the fourth ventricle (PICA infarct, ependymoma, hemangioblastoma) presenting with vomiting and hiccups.

lesionEffects.mechanism: Direct excitation or irritation of the chemoreceptor trigger zone and its solitary connections

lesionEffects.deficit: Loss of the emetic response to toxins
lesionEffects.mechanism: Ablation of the trigger zone, as in experimental lesions
Loss of the sensing of osmolality, angiotensin and gut peptides

examination: Unexplained vomiting or hiccups lasting days without a gastrointestinal cause: examine the lower cranial nerves and image the medulla
Ask about optic neuritis and myelitis when an area postrema syndrome is suspected
pearls: Weeks of unexplained hiccups or vomiting can be the first attack of neuromyelitis optica, weeks before the myelitis

pitfalls: Faint enhancement of the area postrema after gadolinium is normal because it has no blood–brain barrier

area-wernicke.name: Wernicke's area
area-wernicke.summary: The posterior part of the superior temporal gyrus and the planum temporale of the dominant hemisphere, wrapping onto the supramarginal gyrus. It converts the sounds processed by the adjacent auditory cortex into words and meaning and sends the plan for spoken output forward to Broca's area through the arcuate fasciculus. Its destruction, usually by an inferior division MCA infarct, produces fluent but empty speech full of paraphasias and neologisms, with impaired comprehension and repetition, and often no weakness, so the patient may be mistaken for confused or psychotic.

anatomy.location: Posterior third of the superior temporal gyrus and the planum temporale of the dominant (usually left) hemisphere, at the posterior end of the Sylvian fissure adjacent to the supramarginal and angular gyri.

area-wernicke.function: Comprehension of spoken and written language, selection of words for speech, and monitoring of one's own output.

bestView.label: posterior superior temporal gyrus at the end of the Sylvian fissure
posterior superior temporal gyrus and planum temporale

imaging.normalAppearance: Located on the left posterior superior temporal gyrus 50–60 mm from the midline, behind Heschl's gyrus and below the supramarginal gyrus; fMRI language mapping identifies it before temporal surgery.

arteries-lenticulostriate.name: Lenticulostriate arteries
arteries-lenticulostriate.summary: A fan of small perforating arteries that rise from the first segment of the middle cerebral artery (lateral lenticulostriates) and from the proximal anterior cerebral artery (medial lenticulostriates, including the recurrent artery of Heubner), pierce the anterior perforated substance and supply the putamen, globus pallidus, caudate and the internal capsule. They are end arteries, so their occlusion produces lacunar infarcts and their rupture under chronic hypertension produces the typical deep putaminal hemorrhage.

anatomy.location: Arise from the superior and posterior wall of the M1 segment (and from A1 for the medial group) in the Sylvian cistern, ascend through the anterior perforated substance, and fan out through the lentiform nucleus toward the body of the caudate and the genu and anterior part of the posterior limb of the internal capsule.

subdivisions.name: Medial lenticulostriates (including Heubner's artery)
subdivisions.note: head of the caudate, anterior limb of the internal capsule, anterior putamen

subdivisions.name: Lateral lenticulostriates
subdivisions.note: putamen, lateral globus pallidus, body of the caudate, genu and superior posterior limb of the internal capsule

bestView.label: perforators rising through the anterior perforated substance into the lentiform nucleus

arteries-mra-atlas.name: Cerebral arteries (MRA atlas iso-surface)
arteries-mra-atlas.summary: This mesh is the intracranial arterial tree extracted from a population magnetic resonance angiography atlas: the iso-surface of the average vessel probability map, thresholded within the brain, so it shows the vessels that are constant across people, the internal carotid siphons, the circle of Willis, the proximal anterior, middle and posterior cerebral arteries with their first cortical branches, the basilar and vertebral arteries and the cerebellar arteries. It is the atlas's imaging-derived counterpart to the named artery meshes registered from the whole-body model: it sits exactly on the MNI template so that it overlays the MRI slices without registration error, and it shows where the arteries really run relative to the brain surface and the cisterns.

anatomy.location: Intracranial arteries from the petrous carotid and the vertebrobasilar junction up to the second- and third-order cortical branches, following the basal cisterns, the Sylvian fissures, the interhemispheric fissure and the ambient cisterns, in MNI space with the brain mask as the limit.

arteries-mra-atlas.function: The tree gives the spatial relation of each artery to the parenchyma it supplies and to the cranial nerves and cisterns it crosses: the M1 segment along the anterior perforated substance where the lenticulostriates leave it, the A1 and anterior communicating complex above the chiasm, the P2 segment around the peduncle beside the third nerve, the basilar trunk in front of the pons, and the vertebral arteries at the medulla. Because it is an average, it is thicker and smoother than any individual's vessels and it omits variants (fetal PCA, hypoplastic A1), but it is the correct reference for locating aneurysm sites, thrombectomy targets and perforator origins on the atlas MRI.

bestView.label: circle of Willis in the suprasellar cistern

arteries-pontine.name: Pontine arteries
arteries-pontine.summary: Numerous small branches leave the basilar artery along its course and enter the pons. The paramedian arteries pierce the ventral pons beside the midline and supply the corticospinal fibers, pontine nuclei, medial lemniscus and the abducens and facial nuclei; the short circumferential branches supply the anterolateral pons and the long circumferential branches (AICA, SCA) the lateral tegmentum. Paramedian branch disease from basilar atheroma is a very common cause of pontine lacunes.

subdivisions.note: anterolateral basis pontis and middle cerebellar peduncle entry zone

subdivisions.name: Long circumferential arteries
subdivisions.note: lateral tegmentum, together with AICA and SCA branches

bestView.label: paramedian basis pontis, the lacunar site
basilar artery on the ventral pons with perforators entering

imaging.normalAppearance: Individual perforators are not resolved on MRI. Their territories are the paramedian wedges of the pons on axial slices, best judged relative to the midline and the ventral surface.

pathology.finding: A wedge of restricted diffusion in one half of the basis pontis extending to the ventral surface (branch atheromatous disease) or a smaller deep lacune; the corticospinal tract is usually involved.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: DWI; CTA of the basilar artery for atheroma or occlusion

lesionEffects.mechanism: Corticospinal fibers in the basis pontis
Corticospinal fibers plus pontocerebellar fibers
Basis pontis at the level of the facial and hypoglossal projections

lesionEffects.deficit: Abducens palsy or horizontal gaze palsy with contralateral hemiparesis
lesionEffects.mechanism: Abducens nucleus/PPRF plus the corticospinal tract (Foville)
Facial fascicle plus the corticospinal tract (Millard–Gubler)
MLF in the paramedian tegmentum

Horizontal eye movements looking for adduction lag or gaze palsy
Facial movement including the forehead
Speech and fine finger movements

A crossed sign (cranial nerve on one side, limbs on the other) means the brainstem: pons if it is VI or VII

arteries-thalamoperforating.name: Thalamoperforating and thalamogeniculate arteries
arteries-thalamoperforating.summary: Small perforating branches from the P1 segment of the posterior cerebral artery and the posterior communicating artery supply the thalamus. The paramedian (posterior thalamoperforating) group from P1 feeds the medial thalamus and rostral midbrain; when a single trunk from one P1 supplies both sides (artery of Percheron), its occlusion causes bilateral paramedian thalamic infarcts with coma-like somnolence and vertical gaze palsy. The thalamogeniculate arteries from P2 supply the lateral thalamus and are the usual cause of the pure sensory stroke and thalamic pain syndrome.

anatomy.location: Arise from the posterior aspect of the P1 segments in the interpeduncular fossa and from the posterior communicating artery (anterior thalamoperforators), entering the posterior perforated substance beside the mammillary bodies; the thalamogeniculates leave the P2 segment in the ambient cistern and enter the thalamus beneath the geniculate bodies.

subdivisions.name: Anterior (tuberothalamic) group
subdivisions.note: from PComm: anterior nuclei, mammillothalamic tract; amnesia and apathy when infarcted

subdivisions.name: Paramedian (posterior thalamoperforating) group
subdivisions.note: from P1: mediodorsal nucleus, intralaminar nuclei, rostral midbrain; artery of Percheron variant

subdivisions.name: Inferolateral (thalamogeniculate) group
subdivisions.note: from P2: ventral posterior nuclei, ventral lateral nucleus; pure sensory stroke

subdivisions.name: Posterior choroidal group
subdivisions.note: pulvinar, lateral geniculate body, medial thalamus

arteries-thalamoperforating.function: Supply the thalamic relay and association nuclei and the paramedian midbrain, including the oculomotor nuclear complex and the reticular activating system at the mesodiencephalic junction.

bestView.label: interpeduncular fossa where the paramedian perforators enter
medial and lateral thalamus, the infarct sites
paramedian thalamus on both sides of the third ventricle

imaging.normalAppearance: Not visible on routine MRI; the territories are the medial thalamus flanking the third ventricle (paramedian) and the lateral thalamus beside the posterior limb of the capsule (inferolateral).

pathology.finding: Symmetrical restricted diffusion in the paramedian thalami, often with a V-shaped lesion in the rostral midbrain along the interpeduncular fossa; CT is frequently normal early.
pathology.pitfalls: Bilateral thalamic swelling on FLAIR can mimic deep venous thrombosis or a glioma; check DWI and the internal cerebral veins

pathology.finding: A small diffusion-restricting lesion in the ventral posterolateral thalamus producing a contralateral pure hemisensory syndrome.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: DWI with thin slices through the thalamus; MRV if bilateral thalamic edema without restriction

lesionEffects.deficit: Hypersomnolence or coma with vertical gaze palsy
lesionEffects.mechanism: Bilateral paramedian thalamic and rostral midbrain infarction (artery of Percheron)
Anterior and mediodorsal nuclei and the mammillothalamic tract

lesionEffects.deficit: Pure hemisensory loss, later central pain
lesionEffects.mechanism: Ventral posterior nuclei (thalamogeniculate territory)

examination: Test vertical saccades and pursuit and look for skew deviation
Bedside memory and attention testing once alert
Pin-prick, temperature and vibration over the face, arm and leg
pearls: Sudden coma with bilateral thalamic infarcts and no other explanation should prompt a search for a basilar tip embolus
All modalities lost on one side of the body including the face, with no weakness, is a thalamic lesion

artery-aca.name: Anterior cerebral artery
artery-aca.summary: The smaller terminal branch of the internal carotid. It runs medially above the optic nerve into the interhemispheric fissure, where the anterior communicating artery links it to its partner, then arches back over the corpus callosum. Its cortical branches supply the medial surface of the frontal and parietal lobes as far as the parieto-occipital sulcus plus a narrow strip of the adjoining convexity, which includes the leg and foot areas of the motor and sensory cortices. Central branches, including the recurrent artery of Heubner, supply the head of the caudate and the anterior limb of the internal capsule.

anatomy.location: From the carotid terminus at the medial end of the lateral sulcus the A1 (precommunicating) segment passes over the optic nerve or chiasm to the anterior communicating artery; the A2 segment ascends in front of the lamina terminalis and genu of the corpus callosum, and the pericallosal artery (A3 onward) runs back in the callosal sulcus giving off callosomarginal and frontopolar branches.

subdivisions.name: A1 (precommunicating)
subdivisions.note: gives medial lenticulostriate perforators and the recurrent artery of Heubner near the AComm

subdivisions.name: A2 (postcommunicating)
subdivisions.note: ascends around the genu; orbitofrontal and frontopolar branches

subdivisions.name: Pericallosal and callosomarginal arteries
subdivisions.note: medial frontal and paracentral lobule, precuneus

artery-aca.function: Supplies the paracentral lobule (motor and sensory cortex of the contralateral leg and foot), the medial prefrontal cortex and supplementary motor area, the anterior cingulate, the anterior four-fifths of the corpus callosum, and via Heubner's artery the head of the caudate and anterior limb of the internal capsule.

bestView.label: pericallosal artery arching over the corpus callosum
paired A2 segments in the interhemispheric fissure
medial frontal cortex and paracentral lobule, the classic infarct site

imaging.normalAppearance: On sagittal T1 the pericallosal artery is a curving flow void just above the corpus callosum; on axial slices the paired A2 segments sit in the midline in front of the genu. CTA and MRA show the A1 segments converging on the anterior communicating complex.

pathology.finding: Restricted diffusion along the medial frontal and parietal cortex from the frontal pole to the paracentral lobule, sometimes involving the caudate head and anterior limb of the capsule when the proximal A1/Heubner is included; bilateral when both A2s arise from one A1 (azygos variant).
pathology.timing: DWI bright within an hour; FLAIR follows by roughly 6 hours

pathology.finding: Saccular aneurysm at the A1–A2 junction; rupture gives blood in the interhemispheric fissure and frontal horns with a gyrus rectus hematoma.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: DWI for infarction; CTA or DSA for aneurysms of the anterior communicating complex

lesionEffects.deficit: Weakness and sensory loss of the leg and foot, arm relatively spared
lesionEffects.mechanism: Paracentral lobule (leg area of the motor and sensory homunculi) on the medial surface
Medial prefrontal and anterior cingulate cortex, especially with bilateral infarcts or a single A1 supplying both A2s
Supplementary motor area and medial frontal cortex
Supplementary motor area and its connections with Broca's area

examination: Test hip flexion and foot dorsiflexion against gravity; compare with shoulder abduction and finger extension
Check sensation on the foot and shin
Ask about bladder control and observe initiative and spontaneous speech
Elicit a grasp reflex by stroking the palm
pearls: Leg-predominant hemiparesis points to the ACA, arm and face-predominant to the MCA
Bilateral leg weakness with incontinence after subarachnoid hemorrhage suggests bilateral ACA vasospasm from an AComm aneurysm

artery-acom.name: Anterior communicating artery
artery-acom.summary: A short midline vessel joining the two anterior cerebral arteries in front of the optic chiasm. It completes the front of the circle of Willis and lets one carotid supply both medial hemispheres. It is the single most common site of intracranial saccular aneurysm, and its small perforators supply the optic chiasm, the hypothalamus, the fornix and the septal region, which explains the amnesia and personality change that can follow aneurysm rupture or repair.

anatomy.location: Lies in the lamina terminalis cistern above the optic chiasm and below the rostrum of the corpus callosum, connecting the A1–A2 junctions of the two anterior cerebral arteries; typically only 2–3 mm long and often fenestrated or duplicated.

artery-acom.function: Collateral channel between the two internal carotid systems; its perforators supply the anterior hypothalamus, the columns of the fornix, the septal nuclei and the optic chiasm.

bestView.label: midline between the A1–A2 junctions above the chiasm
AComm complex in the interhemispheric fissure

imaging.normalAppearance: Not reliably seen on routine MRI; on CTA and MRA it is the short transverse vessel joining the A1–A2 junctions, best appreciated on an anteroposterior projection. Asymmetric A1 segments are common and make one side dominant.

pathology.finding: Subarachnoid blood concentrated in the interhemispheric fissure, suprasellar cistern and frontal horns, often with a gyrus rectus hematoma; CTA shows the sac pointing anteriorly, superiorly or posteriorly.
pathology.timing: Non-contrast CT is most sensitive in the first 6–12 hours; sensitivity falls after a few days as blood is cleared

pathology.pathology: Basal forebrain infarct after clipping or vasospasm
pathology.finding: Small diffusion-restricting lesions in the septal region, columns of the fornix or anterior hypothalamus, presenting as anterograde amnesia and confabulation.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: Non-contrast CT then CTA for suspected subarachnoid hemorrhage; lumbar puncture if CT is negative and suspicion remains

lesionEffects.mechanism: Perforators to the basal forebrain and fornix are lost after rupture, vasospasm or surgery
Vasospasm of both A2 segments after aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage
Direct compression of the chiasm by a large downward-pointing aneurysm

examination: Bedside memory testing with delayed recall after subarachnoid hemorrhage
Leg power and gait once the patient is mobilized
Confrontation visual fields
pearls: Thunderclap headache with blood in the interhemispheric fissure points to an AComm aneurysm

artery-adamkiewicz.name: Artery of Adamkiewicz
artery-adamkiewicz.summary: The largest of the anterior radicular arteries that reinforce the anterior spinal artery. It usually arises from a left intercostal or lumbar artery between T9 and T12, enters with a nerve root, and makes a characteristic hairpin turn as it joins the anterior spinal artery. It is the main supply of the lower thoracic cord, the lumbar enlargement and the conus, so its loss during aortic surgery, dissection or embolization causes paraplegia.

anatomy.location: Arises from a posterior intercostal or lumbar artery (left side in about three-quarters of people, T9–T12 in most), passes through the intervertebral foramen with the ventral root, ascends briefly and then descends in a hairpin loop to join the anterior spinal artery in the anterior median fissure.

artery-adamkiewicz.function: Chief feeder of the anterior spinal artery for the lower two-thirds of the cord; perfuses the anterior horns and lateral tracts of the thoracolumbar cord and the conus medullaris.

bestView.label: not within the MNI brain volume: the artery joins the cord at the lower thoracic level
hairpin loop entering with a left T9–T12 root on spinal CTA

imaging.normalAppearance: Not present in the brain volume. On spinal CTA or contrast MRA the artery is a small vessel with a hairpin configuration on the anterior surface of the lower thoracic cord, mapped before thoracoabdominal aortic surgery.

pathology.pathology: Cord infarct from loss of the Adamkiewicz supply
pathology.finding: Anterior cord T2 hyperintensity from the mid-thoracic level to the conus with acute diffusion restriction after aortic surgery, dissection or hypotension; the posterior columns are spared.
pathology.timing: T2 changes appear over the first day; DWI earlier

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: Sagittal T2 and DWI of the thoracolumbar cord; CTA of the aorta

lesionEffects.deficit: Paraplegia with a thoracic sensory level for pain and temperature
lesionEffects.mechanism: Anterior two-thirds of the thoracolumbar cord

lesionEffects.deficit: Retention of urine, loss of bowel control
lesionEffects.mechanism: Conus and descending autonomic pathways
Posterior columns perfused by the posterior spinal arteries

examination: Sensory level to pin-prick on the trunk
Vibration sense at the malleoli to show sparing
Bladder scan; check anal tone
pearls: Postoperative paraplegia after aortic repair is cord ischemia in the Adamkiewicz territory; a lumbar drain to lower CSF pressure is part of the response
The mid-thoracic cord (T4–T8) is the watershed between the cervical and Adamkiewicz supplies and the commonest site of hypotensive cord infarcts

artery-aica.name: Anterior inferior cerebellar artery
artery-aica.summary: A branch of the lower basilar artery that runs laterally across the pontomedullary junction toward the cerebellopontine angle, usually giving rise to the labyrinthine (internal auditory) artery, and supplies the lateral caudal pons, the middle cerebellar peduncle, the flocculus and the anterior inferior cerebellum. Its occlusion combines a lateral pontine syndrome with ipsilateral deafness, facial palsy and facial sensory loss.

anatomy.location: Leaves the basilar in its lower third, runs posterolaterally near the abducens rootlet, passes in close relation to the facial and vestibulocochlear nerves at the internal acoustic meatus (often looping into it), and reaches the petrosal surface of the cerebellum.

subdivisions.name: Labyrinthine (internal auditory) artery
subdivisions.note: cochlea and vestibular labyrinth; end artery

subdivisions.name: Lateral pontine perforators
subdivisions.note: spinal trigeminal nucleus, facial nucleus, vestibular and cochlear nuclei, spinothalamic tract, middle cerebellar peduncle

subdivisions.name: Cerebellar branches
subdivisions.note: flocculus and anterior inferior hemisphere

artery-aica.function: Supplies the lateral caudal pons, the inner ear, the middle cerebellar peduncle and the anterior inferior cerebellar surface.

bestView.label: cerebellopontine angle with the AICA loop near the internal acoustic meatus
lateral caudal pons and middle cerebellar peduncle, the infarct site

imaging.normalAppearance: Seen on thin axial T2 through the cerebellopontine angle as a loop near the seventh and eighth nerves; on CTA/MRA it is the lateral branch from the lower basilar. Its territory is the lateral inferior pons, the peduncle and the anterior inferior cerebellum.

pathology.pitfalls: Acute vertigo plus hearing loss is easily labeled labyrinthitis; check for facial weakness, crossed sensory loss and ataxia

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: DWI with attention to the pons and peduncle; audiometry; CTA of the basilar

lesionEffects.mechanism: Labyrinthine artery to the inner ear and the cochlear/vestibular nuclei
Facial nucleus or fascicle in the caudal pons

lesionEffects.deficit: Facial pain and temperature loss with contralateral body loss
lesionEffects.mechanism: Spinal trigeminal nucleus and the crossed spinothalamic tract
Middle cerebellar peduncle and cerebellum
Descending sympathetic fibers in the lateral tegmentum

Facial movement including forehead
Corneal reflex and facial pin-prick
Finger-nose and heel-shin testing
pearls: Wallenberg plus deafness and facial palsy means AICA (lateral pons) rather than PICA (lateral medulla)

artery-anterior-choroidal.name: Anterior choroidal artery
artery-anterior-choroidal.summary: A slender but strategically important branch of the internal carotid that arises just before the terminal bifurcation, runs backwards along the optic tract, and ends in the choroid plexus of the temporal horn. On the way it supplies the posterior limb of the internal capsule, the optic tract and lateral geniculate body, the medial temporal lobe and part of the cerebral peduncle, so a tiny vessel can produce a dense hemiplegia with hemianopia.

anatomy.location: Leaves the posterolateral wall of the supraclinoid internal carotid distal to the posterior communicating origin, passes posteromedially beneath the optic tract, then curves laterally around the cerebral peduncle to enter the choroidal fissure and the inferior horn of the lateral ventricle.

subdivisions.name: Cisternal segment
subdivisions.note: runs along the optic tract in the crural and ambient cisterns; branches to the tract, peduncle, uncus and amygdala

subdivisions.name: Plexal segment
subdivisions.note: inside the temporal horn, supplying the choroid plexus and anastomosing with the lateral posterior choroidal artery

artery-anterior-choroidal.function: Supplies the posterior limb of the internal capsule (corticospinal and thalamocortical fibers), the retrolenticular fibers of the optic radiation, the lateral geniculate nucleus, the optic tract, the crus cerebri, the uncus, part of the hippocampus and amygdala, and the globus pallidus.

bestView.label: origin lateral to the optic tract, running back toward the temporal horn
posterior limb of the internal capsule, the classic infarct site

imaging.normalAppearance: Not resolved on routine MRI; on CTA it is a thread-like vessel hugging the optic tract between the carotid terminus and the temporal horn. Its territory appears on axial slices as the posterior limb of the internal capsule and the adjacent medial temporal structures.

pathology.finding: Restricted diffusion in the posterior limb of the internal capsule extending down toward the cerebral peduncle and into the lateral geniculate region, with a variable medial temporal component; usually small-vessel or embolic.
pathology.timing: DWI positive within minutes to hours; ADC pseudonormalizes after ~1–2 weeks

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: DWI with ADC; CTA to exclude a carotid terminus lesion

lesionEffects.deficit: Hemiparesis of face, arm and leg
lesionEffects.mechanism: Corticospinal fibers in the posterior limb of the internal capsule
Thalamocortical fibers passing through the posterior limb

lesionEffects.deficit: Homonymous hemianopia, sometimes sparing a horizontal sector
lesionEffects.mechanism: Optic tract, lateral geniculate body and the origin of the optic radiation

examination: Test face, arm and leg power for a uniform hemiparesis
Visual fields by confrontation for a homonymous defect
Compare pin-prick and vibration on both sides
pearls: The triad hemiplegia, hemianesthesia and hemianopia without cortical signs (no aphasia, no neglect) suggests the anterior choroidal artery
Wedge-shaped sector sparing of the hemianopia reflects the dual supply of the lateral geniculate body by the anterior and lateral posterior choroidal arteries

artery-basilar.name: Basilar artery
artery-basilar.summary: Formed by the union of the vertebral arteries at the lower border of the pons, the basilar artery runs in the midline groove of the pons to its upper border, where it divides into the two posterior cerebral arteries. Along the way it gives the anterior inferior cerebellar, labyrinthine, pontine and superior cerebellar arteries. Because it feeds the whole pons and the midbrain, occlusion is one of the most devastating strokes, ranging from crossed brainstem syndromes to the locked-in state or coma.

anatomy.location: Lies in the prepontine cistern on the anterior surface of the pons, in the basilar sulcus, between the two abducens nerves at its origin and the two oculomotor nerves at its termination in the interpeduncular cistern.

subdivisions.name: Paramedian branches
subdivisions.note: medial pons: corticospinal fibers, pontine nuclei, medial lemniscus, abducens and facial nuclei

subdivisions.name: Short circumferential branches
subdivisions.note: anterolateral pons

subdivisions.name: Long circumferential branches (AICA, SCA)
subdivisions.note: lateral pons and cerebellum

subdivisions.name: Basilar tip
subdivisions.note: P1 segments, thalamoperforators, superior cerebellar arteries

relations.lateral: abducens nerves inferiorly and oculomotor nerves superiorly

artery-basilar.function: Supplies the entire pons, the superior cerebellum, the inner ear (via the labyrinthine artery), and through its terminal branches the midbrain, thalamus and occipital lobes.

bestView.label: basilar trunk on the clivus in front of the pons
midline flow void in the prepontine cistern
basilar tip in the interpeduncular cistern

imaging.normalAppearance: A single midline flow void in front of the pons on every axial T2 slice through the pons and a smooth tube on sagittal T1. On non-contrast CT the artery lies on the clivus; a dense basilar suggests acute thrombus. CTA shows the whole vessel from the vertebral confluence to the tip.

pathology.finding: Absent contrast in a segment of the basilar with bilateral pontine, cerebellar, thalamic and occipital infarcts on DWI depending on the level; the hyperdense basilar sign on plain CT is an early clue.
pathology.timing: Hyperdense basilar visible at once; DWI lesions evolve over hours; recanalisation therapy is time-critical

pathology.finding: A wedge of restricted diffusion in one paramedian half of the pons reaching the ventral surface, from branch atheromatous disease of a paramedian perforator.
Saccular aneurysm at the bifurcation projecting upward into the interpeduncular cistern; may compress the oculomotor nerves or the midbrain.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: CTA immediately when a brainstem stroke is suspected; DWI for extent; DSA for treatment planning

lesionEffects.deficit: Quadriparesis with preserved consciousness and vertical eye movements (locked-in)
lesionEffects.mechanism: Bilateral ventral pontine infarction sparing the tegmentum and midbrain

lesionEffects.deficit: Crossed syndromes: ipsilateral cranial nerve palsy with contralateral hemiparesis
lesionEffects.mechanism: Unilateral paramedian pontine infarct catching the abducens or facial nucleus/fascicle and the corticospinal tract
Pontine tegmentum and reticular activating system

lesionEffects.deficit: Top-of-the-basilar syndrome: somnolence, vertical gaze palsy, hallucinations, hemianopia
lesionEffects.mechanism: Embolus at the bifurcation involving thalamus, midbrain and occipital lobes

examination: Assess consciousness, pupils, corneal reflexes and eye movements in every stuporous patient
Look for bilateral long-tract signs
Ask about preceding vertigo, diplopia, dysarthria and drop attacks (basilar TIAs)
pearls: Bilateral or crossed signs with altered consciousness mean the basilar artery until proven otherwise; call for CTA
Locked-in patients are awake: examine vertical eye movements and blinking before assuming coma

pitfalls: Basilar occlusion may present with fluctuating symptoms or apparent psychiatric change over hours before collapse
A dolichoectatic basilar can compress cranial nerves or cause perforator strokes without occlusion

html.summary: Formed by the union of the vertebral arteries at the lower border of the pons, the basilar artery runs in the midline groove of the pons to its upper border, where it divides into the two posterior cerebral arteries. Along the way it gives the anterior inferior cerebellar, labyrinthine, pontine and superior cerebellar arteries. Because it feeds the whole pons and the midbrain, occlusion is one of the most devastating strokes, ranging from crossed brainstem syndromes to the locked-in state or coma.
html.function: Supplies the entire pons, the superior cerebellum, the inner ear (via the labyrinthine artery), and through its terminal branches the midbrain, thalamus and occipital lobes.
html.anatomy.location: Lies in the prepontine cistern on the anterior surface of the pons, in the basilar sulcus, between the two abducens nerves at its origin and the two oculomotor nerves at its termination in the interpeduncular cistern.
html.imaging.normalAppearance: A single midline flow void in front of the pons on every axial T2 slice through the pons and a smooth tube on sagittal T1. On non-contrast CT the artery lies on the clivus; a dense basilar suggests acute thrombus. CTA shows the whole vessel from the vertebral confluence to the tip.
html.imaging.sequenceOfChoice: CTA immediately when a brainstem stroke is suspected; DWI for extent; DSA for treatment planning

artery-internal-carotid.name: Internal carotid artery
artery-internal-carotid.summary: The internal carotid artery is the main feeder of the anterior circulation. It rises from the common carotid bifurcation, enters the skull through the carotid canal, crosses the cavernous sinus and, after piercing the dura medial to the anterior clinoid process, ends by splitting into the anterior and middle cerebral arteries. Its ophthalmic, posterior communicating and anterior choroidal branches leave in the short subarachnoid segment just before that bifurcation.

anatomy.location: Begins at the level of the upper border of the thyroid cartilage (around C4) as the larger terminal branch of the common carotid; a carotid sinus dilatation marks its origin. The cervical segment gives no branches. The petrous segment turns forward and medially inside the temporal bone, the cavernous segment runs horizontally in the cavernous sinus lateral to the sphenoid body, and the supraclinoid segment lies in the subarachnoid space beside the optic chiasm and terminates at the medial end of the lateral sulcus.

subdivisions.name: Cervical
subdivisions.note: no branches; the carotid sinus and body sit at the origin

subdivisions.name: Petrous
subdivisions.note: in the carotid canal, surrounded by the sympathetic carotid plexus

subdivisions.name: Cavernous
subdivisions.note: S-shaped siphon inside the cavernous sinus; the abducens nerve lies lateral to it

subdivisions.name: Supraclinoid (cerebral)
subdivisions.note: subarachnoid; gives ophthalmic, posterior communicating, anterior choroidal branches, then bifurcates

relations.medial: sphenoid body and pituitary fossa in the cavernous segment
relations.lateral: cranial nerves III, IV, V1 and V2 in the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus; VI lies directly beside the artery inside the sinus
relations.superior: optic nerve and chiasm at the terminal bifurcation

artery-internal-carotid.function: Delivers most of the blood to the cerebral hemispheres: the entire lateral convexity (via the middle cerebral artery), the medial frontal and parietal surfaces (via the anterior cerebral artery), the eye and orbit (ophthalmic artery), and the deep structures supplied by the anterior choroidal and lenticulostriate perforators. Through the posterior communicating artery it can also back-fill the posterior circulation.

bestView.label: cavernous carotid: paired flow voids lateral to the pituitary fossa
carotid siphon in the cavernous sinus
terminal bifurcation into A1 and M1 lateral to the chiasm

imaging.normalAppearance: On T1 and T2 the artery is a round signal void (flow void) because of fast flow: the siphon is easiest to find on axial slices lateral to the sella, and the supraclinoid segment just anterolateral to the optic chiasm. On CT angiography and time-of-flight MRA the vessel is bright, and the siphon calcifies with age on non-contrast CT.

pathology.finding: Focal narrowing of the proximal internal carotid at or just above the bifurcation, measured against the distal normal lumen (NASCET method); an ipsilateral cortical MCA/ACA-territory infarct on DWI is the typical downstream signature.

Crescentic T1-bright intramural hematoma on fat-saturated axial T1 around a narrowed eccentric lumen, usually in the upper cervical or petrous segment; may present with Horner syndrome and ipsilateral embolic infarcts.
pathology.timing: Intramural methemoglobin is brightest from days 3 to ~14 after the tear

pathology.finding: Absent opacification of the distal ICA, A1 and M1 with a large ACA plus MCA territory infarct; on non-contrast CT a hyperdense M1 or carotid terminus may be visible early.
pathology.timing: Hyperdense vessel sign is visible immediately; parenchymal hypodensity develops over hours

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: CTA of the neck and head for stenosis and occlusion; fat-saturated T1 for dissection; DWI for the downstream infarct

lesionEffects.deficit: Contralateral hemiparesis and hemisensory loss with aphasia (dominant) or neglect (non-dominant)
lesionEffects.mechanism: Loss of flow to both ACA and MCA territories when the terminus occludes without adequate collateral supply
Emboli from a carotid plaque pass into the ophthalmic artery and retinal arterioles

lesionEffects.deficit: Partial Horner syndrome (ptosis and miosis without anhidrosis of the face)
lesionEffects.mechanism: The sympathetic plexus travelling on the artery is stretched by a dissection; sweat fibers to the face travel with the external carotid, so sweating is spared

examination: Auscultate the neck for a carotid bruit and compare pulses
Fundoscopy for retinal emboli (Hollenhorst plaques) after monocular visual loss
Look for a small pupil and mild ptosis on the side of neck pain after trauma or chiropractic manipulation
pearls: Retinal symptoms plus contralateral hemispheric symptoms point to the carotid, because the ophthalmic artery is its first intracranial branch
A partial Horner syndrome with neck pain is carotid dissection until proven otherwise
The cavernous segment is why a carotid aneurysm or fistula presents with cranial nerves III, IV, V1, V2 and VI signs

pitfalls: The absence of a carotid bruit does not exclude a tight stenosis; near-occlusion can be silent
Tortuous or kinked cervical carotids in the elderly mimic stenosis on a single projection

artery-labyrinthine.name: Labyrinthine (internal auditory) artery
artery-labyrinthine.summary: The labyrinthine artery is a long, thin end artery, usually a branch of the anterior inferior cerebellar artery and occasionally of the basilar, which enters the internal acoustic meatus with the facial and vestibulocochlear nerves and divides into the cochlear and vestibular branches that supply the inner ear. The cochlea and the labyrinth have no collateral supply, so occlusion, embolism or vasospasm produces sudden unilateral deafness with vertigo, and because the artery arises from AICA, the same event often infarcts the lateral pons and the anterior inferior cerebellum. Sudden hearing loss in a patient with vascular risk factors, or hearing loss accompanying vertigo, should therefore be treated as a posterior circulation event until imaging proves otherwise.

anatomy.location: Arises from the AICA (about 85%) or directly from the basilar artery in the cerebellopontine angle, runs laterally with the seventh and eighth nerves into the internal acoustic meatus, and divides within the meatus into the anterior vestibular artery, the common cochlear artery and its vestibulocochlear branch.

efferents.to: Cochlea, vestibular labyrinth, nerves of the internal acoustic meatus

artery-labyrinthine.function: Supplies the cochlea (through the spiral modiolar artery), the vestibular labyrinth (saccule, utricle and the semicircular canals) and the nerves within the meatus; the anterior vestibular artery supplies the utricle and the superior and horizontal canals, the posterior vestibular branch the saccule and posterior canal, a division that explains partial syndromes such as isolated utricular or canal ischemia. Its stria vascularis territory maintains the endocochlear potential required for hair cell transduction.

bestView.label: internal acoustic meatus and cerebellopontine angle
seventh and eighth nerves with the labyrinthine artery entering the meatus

imaging.normalAppearance: Too small to see on routine MRA; the AICA loop in the cerebellopontine angle and sometimes entering the meatus is visible on high-resolution T2 (CISS/FIESTA) and is a normal finding. The inner ear itself shows as bright fluid signal in the cochlea and canals.

pathology.finding: Loss of the normal bright fluid signal or abnormal enhancement of the cochlea and vestibule on delayed post-contrast 3D-FLAIR, often with an AICA territory infarct in the lateral pons and cerebellum on DWI.
Absent AICA or basilar atheroma at its origin in a patient with sudden deafness and vertigo.
AICA loop deep within the meatus contacting the eighth nerve, of debated relevance to tinnitus and vertigo.

lesionEffects.mechanism: Cochlear ischemia (end artery, no collaterals)

lesionEffects.deficit: Acute vertigo with nystagmus and vomiting
lesionEffects.mechanism: Labyrinthine ischemia, with or without cochlear involvement
Associated AICA occlusion: facial palsy, facial sensory loss, ataxia, Horner

examination: Weber and Rinne tests; sudden sensorineural loss is an emergency
Head impulse test and nystagmus; look for the other AICA signs (facial weakness, corneal reflex, limb ataxia)
Vascular risk factor review and posterior circulation imaging in sudden deafness with vertigo
pearls: Hearing loss with vertigo is the signature of the labyrinthine artery and therefore of AICA; the PICA syndrome spares hearing
The artery is an end artery: the cochlea dies within minutes of occlusion, and steroids are the only treatment for the idiopathic form
An AICA loop in the meatus is a common normal finding on MRI

pitfalls: Isolated labyrinthine infarction has a normal brain MRI; the diagnosis rests on the clinical context and inner ear imaging

artery-mca-inferior-division.name: Middle cerebral artery, inferior division
artery-mca-inferior-division.summary: The inferior trunk of the middle cerebral artery runs backwards across the insula beneath the Sylvian fissure and supplies the lateral temporal lobe, the posterior parietal cortex and the angular region. On the dominant side this is the territory of Wernicke's area, so occlusion causes a fluent aphasia with poor comprehension; on either side it interrupts the optic radiation and produces a contralateral visual field defect, usually with little or no weakness.

anatomy.location: Courses posteroinferiorly over the insula and out of the posterior Sylvian fissure, dividing into temporal (anterior, middle, posterior), temporo-occipital, angular and posterior parietal branches.

subdivisions.name: Temporal branches
subdivisions.note: superior and middle temporal gyri including Heschl's gyrus and Wernicke's area

subdivisions.name: Angular artery
subdivisions.note: angular and supramarginal gyri; often the terminal branch of the MCA

subdivisions.name: Posterior parietal artery
subdivisions.note: posterior supramarginal region and parietal association cortex

subdivisions.name: Temporo-occipital artery
subdivisions.note: posterior temporal cortex bordering the PCA territory

artery-mca-inferior-division.function: Perfuses the lateral temporal cortex including the primary auditory cortex and Wernicke's area, the inferior parietal lobule (supramarginal and angular gyri) and the white matter carrying the optic radiation.

bestView.label: posterior Sylvian region and superior temporal gyrus
angular gyrus and inferior parietal lobule

imaging.normalAppearance: On CTA the inferior trunk is the branch running back and down from the M1 bifurcation; its territory is the cortex behind and below the posterior end of the Sylvian fissure.

pathology.finding: Restricted diffusion in the superior and middle temporal gyri, the angular and supramarginal gyri and the underlying white matter, sparing the frontal lobe; the deep temporal component may cut the optic radiation.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: DWI; CTA of the intracranial circulation

lesionEffects.deficit: Wernicke (fluent) aphasia with impaired comprehension and repetition
lesionEffects.mechanism: Posterior superior temporal gyrus of the dominant hemisphere

lesionEffects.deficit: Contralateral homonymous hemianopia or superior quadrantanopia
lesionEffects.mechanism: Optic radiation fibers in the temporal and parietal white matter
Right inferior parietal lobule
Angular gyrus

examination: Ask the patient to follow multi-step commands and to repeat phrases; note paraphasias and jargon
Visual fields by confrontation in each quadrant
Line bisection and clock drawing for neglect
Finger naming, left-right orientation, calculation and writing
pearls: Fluent nonsense speech without weakness is an inferior division stroke, easily mistaken for delirium or psychosis
A superior quadrantanopia points to the temporal loop of the optic radiation (Meyer's loop)

artery-mca-superior-division.name: Middle cerebral artery, superior division
artery-mca-superior-division.summary: The superior trunk of the middle cerebral artery leaves the bifurcation at the limen insulae and climbs over the frontal operculum. Its branches feed the inferior frontal gyrus (Broca's area on the left), the frontal eye field, the precentral and postcentral gyri for the face, hand and arm, and the anterior parietal cortex. Occlusion produces the classic 'cortical' stroke with face and arm weakness and, on the dominant side, a non-fluent aphasia.

anatomy.location: Runs upward and backward across the insula and around the frontal and anterior parietal opercula in the Sylvian fissure, emerging on the convexity as the orbitofrontal, prefrontal, precentral, central and anterior parietal arteries.

subdivisions.name: Orbitofrontal and prefrontal branches
subdivisions.note: lateral prefrontal cortex and inferior frontal gyrus

subdivisions.name: Precentral (pre-Rolandic) artery
subdivisions.note: premotor cortex, frontal eye field, Broca's area

subdivisions.name: Central (Rolandic) artery
subdivisions.note: face and arm areas of the precentral and postcentral gyri

subdivisions.name: Anterior parietal artery
subdivisions.note: anterior supramarginal region

artery-mca-superior-division.function: Perfuses the frontal and anterior parietal convexity: motor and sensory cortex for the face, hand and arm, the frontal eye field, the premotor cortex and, on the dominant side, Broca's area.

bestView.label: frontal operculum and precentral gyrus
central sulcus region, face and hand areas

imaging.normalAppearance: The superior trunk appears on CTA as the larger of the two M2 branches leaving the bifurcation, arching upward over the insula. Its cortical territory is the frontal and anterior parietal convexity above the Sylvian fissure.

pathology.finding: Restricted diffusion in the inferior and middle frontal gyri, precentral and postcentral gyri and anterior insula, sparing the temporal lobe and the posterior parietal cortex; the basal ganglia are spared because the lenticulostriates arise from M1.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: DWI; CTA to distinguish a branch occlusion from an M1 occlusion (which would add the lenticulostriate territory)

lesionEffects.deficit: Face and arm weakness with relative sparing of the leg
lesionEffects.mechanism: Precentral gyrus opercular and hand areas

lesionEffects.deficit: Cortical sensory loss of the face and arm
lesionEffects.mechanism: Postcentral gyrus
Inferior frontal gyrus of the dominant hemisphere
Frontal eye field
Right frontal-parietal opercular cortex

examination: Test speech output (fluency, naming, repetition) against comprehension of commands
Pronator drift and finger tapping versus hip flexion
Observe conjugate gaze deviation and test saccades to the contralateral side
pearls: Non-fluent aphasia with right face and arm weakness is the left superior division; the leg is spared and visual fields are usually intact
Comprehension is preserved because Wernicke's area belongs to the inferior division

artery-mca.name: Middle cerebral artery
artery-mca.summary: The larger terminal branch of the internal carotid and the artery most often occluded in stroke. The M1 segment runs laterally beneath the anterior perforated substance, giving the lateral lenticulostriate perforators to the basal ganglia and internal capsule, then splits in the Sylvian fissure into superior and inferior divisions whose cortical branches cover almost the entire lateral convexity: motor and sensory cortex for face and arm, Broca's and Wernicke's areas, the frontal eye field, the insula and the parietal association cortex.

anatomy.location: From the carotid terminus the horizontal M1 segment passes laterally in the Sylvian cistern below the anterior perforated substance to the limen insulae, where it divides (M2 segments run over the insula, M3 segments turn around the opercula, M4 branches spread across the convexity).

subdivisions.name: M1 (sphenoidal)
subdivisions.note: lateral lenticulostriate perforators; anterior temporal branch

subdivisions.name: Superior division
subdivisions.note: orbitofrontal, prefrontal, precentral, central and anterior parietal branches: frontal and anterior parietal convexity

subdivisions.name: Inferior division
subdivisions.note: posterior parietal, angular and temporal branches: posterior parietal and lateral temporal cortex

relations.lateral: temporal lobe below and frontal operculum above in the Sylvian fissure
relations.superior: anterior perforated substance, through which the lenticulostriate arteries enter

artery-mca.function: Supplies the lateral surface of the hemisphere except the superior strip taken by the ACA and the occipital pole and inferior temporal surface taken by the PCA. This includes the face, hand and arm areas of the motor and sensory cortices, the frontal eye field, Broca's area, Wernicke's area, the auditory cortex, the insula and, through the lenticulostriates, the putamen, globus pallidus, caudate body and the anterior and superior parts of the internal capsule.

bestView.label: M1 segment in the Sylvian cistern and the bifurcation at the limen insulae
M2 branches over the insula
convexity territory: frontal and parietal opercula

imaging.normalAppearance: M1 is a prominent flow void lateral to the carotid terminus on axial T2; branches in the Sylvian fissure appear as dots within CSF. On non-contrast CT the M1 segment may look denser than other vessels when thrombosed (hyperdense MCA sign).

pathology.finding: Early signs: hyperdense M1, loss of the insular ribbon, obscuration of the lentiform nucleus and sulcal effacement; later a wedge of hypodensity over the lateral convexity with mass effect peaking at 3–5 days.
pathology.timing: Early signs within 1–3 h; hypodensity by 6–12 h; maximal swelling day 3–5

pathology.finding: Restricted diffusion in the insula, opercular cortex and lateral convexity, with a lentiform and capsular component when M1 is occluded proximal to the lenticulostriates; FLAIR vascular hyperintensities mark slow collateral flow.
pathology.timing: DWI positive within minutes; FLAIR after ~6 h (the DWI–FLAIR mismatch estimates onset)

pathology.finding: Saccular aneurysm at the M1 bifurcation in the Sylvian fissure; rupture gives Sylvian and temporal lobe hematoma.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: Non-contrast CT plus CTA in the acute phase to identify a large-vessel occlusion amenable to thrombectomy; DWI/FLAIR for infarct extent and timing

lesionEffects.mechanism: Precentral gyrus face and hand areas on the convexity
Postcentral gyrus and parietal association cortex
Frontal eye field: the intact hemisphere drives the eyes away from itself
Broca's and Wernicke's areas both within the territory
Right parietal association cortex
Optic radiation in the deep parietal and temporal white matter

examination: Compare arm drift with leg drift: MCA infarcts weaken the arm more than the leg
Assess speech fluency, comprehension and repetition
Look for gaze deviation and test for visual and tactile extinction
Visual fields by confrontation
pearls: Face and arm weakness plus aphasia or neglect is the MCA; leg-predominant weakness is the ACA
A dense hemiplegia involving the leg too with an MCA occlusion means the lenticulostriates (internal capsule) are involved, i.e. an M1 occlusion
Malignant MCA infarction in the young can require decompressive craniectomy within 48 hours

pitfalls: Isolated hand weakness can be a small cortical MCA branch infarct and is easily mistaken for a peripheral nerve lesion
Wernicke aphasia without weakness may be labeled confusion or psychosis

artery-ophthalmic.name: Ophthalmic artery
artery-ophthalmic.summary: The ophthalmic artery is the first branch of the intracranial internal carotid, arising as the parent vessel leaves the cavernous sinus. It enters the orbit through the optic canal beneath the optic nerve and supplies the globe, including the central retinal artery, and the extraocular muscles, lacrimal gland, ethmoid sinuses and forehead skin. Because it is the carotid's first branch, retinal ischemia is the classic warning sign of carotid disease.

anatomy.location: Originates from the supraclinoid internal carotid immediately after the artery pierces the dural roof of the cavernous sinus, medial to the anterior clinoid process. It runs anteriorly through the optic canal inferolateral to the optic nerve, crosses over the nerve inside the orbit and ends as supratrochlear and dorsal nasal branches at the medial orbital margin.

subdivisions.name: Central retinal artery
subdivisions.note: enters the optic nerve about 1 cm behind the globe; an end artery for the inner retina

subdivisions.name: Posterior ciliary arteries
subdivisions.note: supply the choroid and the optic nerve head

subdivisions.name: Lacrimal, ethmoidal, supraorbital, supratrochlear, dorsal nasal branches
subdivisions.note: orbit walls, sinuses, forehead and nose; anastomose with external carotid branches

artery-ophthalmic.function: Sole arterial supply of the retina and optic nerve head and the main supply of the orbit. Its anastomoses with the facial and maxillary arteries (external carotid) provide a collateral route into the carotid siphon when the cervical internal carotid is occluded, which is why reversed flow in the ophthalmic artery on Doppler indicates carotid occlusion.

bestView.label: orbital apex: ophthalmic artery crossing the optic nerve

imaging.normalAppearance: Too small to be seen on routine MRI; on CTA or MRA a fine vessel accompanies the optic nerve through the optic canal. Orbital fat gives bright T1 signal around the nerve sheath, which is dark.

pathology.finding: Retinal examination (not imaging) shows a pale retina with a cherry-red macula; the imaging task is finding the embolic source with carotid Doppler or CTA and screening for temporal arteritis.
A saccular outpouching at the ophthalmic origin projecting medially or superiorly under the optic nerve, causing a unilateral nasal or altitudinal field defect from nerve compression.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: Carotid Doppler plus CTA/MRA for embolic sources; fundoscopy is the diagnostic test for the retina itself

lesionEffects.deficit: Transient or permanent monocular visual loss
lesionEffects.mechanism: Embolus or hypoperfusion in the central retinal artery, a functional end artery

lesionEffects.deficit: Altitudinal field loss (upper or lower half)
lesionEffects.mechanism: Ischemia of the optic nerve head supplied by the posterior ciliary arteries (anterior ischemic optic neuropathy)

html.summary: The ophthalmic artery is the first branch of the intracranial internal carotid, arising as the parent vessel leaves the cavernous sinus. It enters the orbit through the optic canal beneath the optic nerve and supplies the globe, including the central retinal artery, and the extraocular muscles, lacrimal gland, ethmoid sinuses and forehead skin.
