artery-pca.name: Posterior cerebral artery
artery-pca.summary: The terminal branches of the basilar artery. Each posterior cerebral artery curves around the midbrain, sending perforators to the thalamus and midbrain and choroidal branches to the ventricles, then spreads over the inferomedial temporal lobe and the whole occipital lobe including the calcarine cortex. Occlusion gives a contralateral homonymous hemianopia, often with macular sparing, and proximal occlusion adds thalamic and midbrain deficits.

anatomy.location: Arises at the basilar bifurcation in the interpeduncular cistern (P1 segment), receives the posterior communicating artery, runs around the cerebral peduncle in the ambient cistern (P2), passes through the quadrigeminal cistern (P3) and ends in calcarine and parieto-occipital branches on the medial occipital surface (P4).

subdivisions.name: P1 (precommunicating)
subdivisions.note: thalamoperforating arteries to the medial thalamus and midbrain; medial posterior choroidal artery

subdivisions.name: P2 (ambient)
subdivisions.note: thalamogeniculate arteries to the lateral thalamus, lateral posterior choroidal artery, anterior and posterior temporal branches

subdivisions.name: P3–P4 (cortical)
subdivisions.note: calcarine, parieto-occipital and posterior temporal arteries

artery-pca.function: Supplies the occipital lobe (primary and association visual cortex), the inferomedial temporal lobe including the hippocampus and parahippocampal gyrus, the splenium of the corpus callosum, the thalamus and the midbrain.

bestView.label: P2 segment in the ambient cistern lateral to the midbrain
calcarine cortex, the cortical infarct site
calcarine sulcus and the medial occipital territory

imaging.normalAppearance: The P1 and P2 segments are paired flow voids wrapping around the midbrain on axial T2 through the interpeduncular and ambient cisterns. Cortical branches lie in the calcarine and parieto-occipital sulci.

pathology.finding: Restricted diffusion in the medial occipital lobe and inferomedial temporal lobe; with proximal occlusion the ipsilateral thalamus and cerebral peduncle are included. Bilateral occipital infarcts follow a basilar tip embolus.
pathology.timing: DWI within minutes; FLAIR after ~6 h

pathology.finding: Symmetrical parieto-occipital vasogenic edema that is bright on FLAIR but not restricted on DWI, mimicking bilateral PCA infarcts but reversible.
pathology.pitfalls: Check ADC: PRES is facilitated diffusion, infarct is restricted

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: DWI with ADC; CTA of the vertebrobasilar system; cardiac evaluation for embolism

lesionEffects.mechanism: Calcarine cortex; the occipital pole has collateral supply from the MCA
Left occipital cortex plus the splenium, disconnecting the right visual cortex from the left language areas
Fusiform and lingual gyri
Thalamogeniculate perforators to the ventral posterior nuclei
Hippocampus and parahippocampal cortex

lesionEffects.deficit: Third nerve palsy with contralateral hemiparesis (Weber) or ataxia (Claude)
lesionEffects.mechanism: P1 perforators to the midbrain

artery-pcom.name: Posterior communicating artery
artery-pcom.summary: A short vessel running backwards from the supraclinoid internal carotid to join the posterior cerebral artery, linking the anterior and posterior circulations on each side. It runs directly above the oculomotor nerve, which is why an aneurysm at its origin produces a painful third nerve palsy with a dilated pupil. Its perforators supply the anterior thalamus, hypothalamus and part of the internal capsule.

anatomy.location: Leaves the posterior wall of the supraclinoid carotid, passes posteromedially in the interpeduncular cistern above the oculomotor nerve and lateral to the mammillary body, and joins the posterior cerebral artery at the P1–P2 junction.

artery-pcom.function: Collateral channel between the carotid and vertebrobasilar systems; in the fetal variant it is the main supply of the posterior cerebral artery. Its thalamic perforators (anterior thalamoperforating branches) supply the anterior thalamus, the hypothalamus and the posterior limb of the internal capsule.

bestView.label: running back from the carotid toward the P1–P2 junction above the oculomotor nerve
relationship to the oculomotor nerve in the interpeduncular cistern

imaging.normalAppearance: Often seen as a small flow void behind the carotid on axial T2 through the suprasellar cistern. On CTA/MRA it is the short vessel between the carotid and the PCA; a fetal-type PComm is as large as the PCA it feeds and the ipsilateral P1 is small.

pathology.pathology: PComm aneurysm with third nerve palsy
pathology.finding: Saccular aneurysm at the carotid–PComm junction projecting posterolaterally toward the oculomotor nerve; subarachnoid blood in the suprasellar and ambient cisterns if ruptured.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: CTA (or catheter angiography) urgently for any painful third nerve palsy with pupil involvement

lesionEffects.deficit: Painful third nerve palsy with a dilated pupil
lesionEffects.mechanism: Compression of the pial surface of the oculomotor nerve, where the parasympathetic pupillary fibers lie superficially

lesionEffects.deficit: Contralateral hemiparesis with amnesia after aneurysm treatment

artery-pica.name: Posterior inferior cerebellar artery
artery-pica.summary: The largest branch of the vertebral artery. It takes a tortuous course between the medulla and the cerebellum, supplying the dorsolateral medulla, the inferior surface of the cerebellar hemisphere and vermis, the cerebellar tonsil and the choroid plexus of the fourth ventricle. Its occlusion (or, more often, occlusion of the parent vertebral artery) produces the lateral medullary syndrome, and a large cerebellar infarct in its territory can swell and compress the brainstem.

anatomy.location: Arises from the intracranial vertebral artery 1–2 cm below the vertebrobasilar junction, loops caudally around the medulla between the rootlets of the glossopharyngeal, vagus and accessory nerves, curves over the cerebellar tonsil (the caudal loop) and then ascends onto the inferior cerebellar surface.

subdivisions.name: Anterior and lateral medullary segments
subdivisions.note: perforators to the dorsolateral medulla: spinothalamic tract, spinal trigeminal nucleus, nucleus ambiguus, vestibular nuclei

subdivisions.name: Tonsillomedullary and telovelotonsillar segments
subdivisions.note: cerebellar tonsil, choroid plexus of the fourth ventricle

subdivisions.name: Cortical segment
subdivisions.note: inferior vermis and inferior hemispheric surface

artery-pica.function: Supplies the dorsolateral medulla and the inferior cerebellum (posterior lobe inferior surface, tonsil, inferior vermis) plus the fourth ventricular choroid plexus.

bestView.label: PICA loop beside the medulla and tonsil
dorsolateral medulla, the Wallenberg site
inferior cerebellar hemisphere

imaging.normalAppearance: A small tortuous flow void beside the medulla on axial T2, seen more consistently on CTA/MRA as a loop around the tonsil. Its cerebellar territory is the inferior and posterior hemispheric surface below the horizontal fissure.

pathology.pitfalls: Lesions are small: use thin-slice DWI and look on coronal reformats; a normal DWI in the first hours does not exclude it

pathology.pathology: PICA cerebellar infarct with mass effect

lesionEffects.deficit: Loss of pain and temperature on the face with loss on the opposite body
lesionEffects.mechanism: Spinal trigeminal tract ipsilaterally and the already-crossed spinothalamic tract
Nucleus ambiguus

artery-sca.name: Superior cerebellar artery
artery-sca.summary: The last branch of the basilar artery before it divides, the superior cerebellar artery winds around the midbrain just below the oculomotor nerve and the tentorium to reach the upper cerebellar surface. It supplies the superior cerebellum, the dentate nucleus, the superior cerebellar peduncle and the dorsolateral upper pons. Infarction causes ipsilateral limb ataxia, sometimes with contralateral pain and temperature loss and a Horner syndrome, and large infarcts can swell against the brainstem.

subdivisions.name: Medial branch
subdivisions.note: superior vermis and the dentate nucleus region

subdivisions.name: Lateral branch
subdivisions.note: superior lateral hemisphere

subdivisions.name: Perforators
subdivisions.note: dorsolateral rostral pons and the superior cerebellar peduncle

bestView.label: SCA in the ambient cistern below the tentorium
superior cerebellar hemisphere, the infarct site

artery-vertebral.name: Vertebral artery
artery-vertebral.summary: The two vertebral arteries carry blood from the subclavian arteries up through the transverse foramina of the cervical vertebrae and the foramen magnum to unite at the pontomedullary junction into the basilar artery. Intracranially each gives the posterior inferior cerebellar artery, the contribution to the anterior spinal artery and small medullary perforators, so vertebral occlusion or dissection presents as a lateral medullary or cerebellar stroke.

subdivisions.name: V1–V3 (extracranial)

subdivisions.name: V4 (intracranial)
subdivisions.note: posterior meningeal, posterior spinal, anterior spinal, PICA and direct medullary branches

autonomic-cranial-parasympathetic.name: Cranial parasympathetic outflow
autonomic-cranial-parasympathetic.latin: Pars parasympathica: nervi craniales III, VII, IX, X
autonomic-cranial-parasympathetic.summary: The craniosacral parasympathetic system leaves the brainstem in four cranial nerves, each with its own brainstem nucleus and peripheral ganglion: the oculomotor nerve (Edinger–Westphal nucleus → ciliary ganglion) constricts the pupil and accommodates; the facial nerve (superior salivatory nucleus → pterygopalatine and submandibular ganglia) drives lacrimation, nasal secretion and submandibular and sublingual salivation; the glossopharyngeal nerve (inferior salivatory nucleus → otic ganglion) drives the parotid; and the vagus (dorsal motor nucleus and nucleus ambiguus → ganglia in the walls of the viscera) slows the heart, constricts the bronchi and drives gut secretion and motility down to the splenic flexure. Long preganglionic and short postganglionic fibers, acetylcholine at both synapses and muscarinic receptors at the target are its pharmacological fingerprints.

anatomy.location: Nuclei in the midbrain (Edinger–Westphal), pons (superior salivatory) and medulla (inferior salivatory, dorsal vagal, ambiguus); preganglionic fibers in CN III, VII, IX and X; ganglia in the orbit (ciliary), pterygopalatine fossa, submandibular region, below the foramen ovale (otic) and within the thoracic and abdominal viscera.

subdivisions.name: Oculomotor (III)
subdivisions.note: Edinger–Westphal → ciliary ganglion → sphincter pupillae, ciliary muscle

subdivisions.name: Facial (VII)
subdivisions.note: superior salivatory nucleus → greater petrosal nerve → pterygopalatine ganglion (lacrimal, nasal, palatine glands); chorda tympani → submandibular ganglion (submandibular, sublingual glands)

subdivisions.name: Glossopharyngeal (IX)
subdivisions.note: inferior salivatory nucleus → tympanic plexus, lesser petrosal nerve → otic ganglion → parotid via the auriculotemporal nerve

subdivisions.name: Vagus (X)
subdivisions.note: dorsal motor nucleus and ambiguus → cardiac, pulmonary, esophageal and abdominal plexuses → intramural ganglia

autonomic-cranial-parasympathetic.function: Rest-and-digest control of the head and thoracoabdominal viscera: pupillary constriction and accommodation, secretion of tears and saliva, cardiac slowing, bronchoconstriction, gut secretion and peristalsis.

bestView.label: Edinger–Westphal region of the midbrain
dorsal vagal nucleus region in the medulla

imaging.normalAppearance: Nuclei and ganglia are not resolved on routine MRI; the relevant imaging is of the nerves along their courses (orbit for the ciliary ganglion region, temporal bone for the facial nerve, skull base for IX and X).

pathology.pathology: Compressive third nerve palsy with pupil involvement
pathology.finding: PComm aneurysm compressing the superficial parasympathetic fibers.

pathology.pathology: Facial nerve lesion proximal to the geniculate ganglion
pathology.finding: Enhancement of the labyrinthine segment with reduced tearing and salivation on that side.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: Imaging of the relevant cranial nerve; pharmacological pupil tests; Schirmer test

lesionEffects.mechanism: Preganglionic fibers in CN III or the ciliary ganglion

lesionEffects.deficit: Dry eye and reduced nasal secretion

Salivary flow

autonomic-sacral-parasympathetic.name: Sacral parasympathetic outflow and bladder control
autonomic-sacral-parasympathetic.summary: The sacral parasympathetic neurons in the S2–S4 segments of the conus send preganglionic fibers through the pelvic splanchnic nerves to ganglia in the walls of the bladder, rectum and genitals, driving detrusor contraction, rectal emptying and erection. Micturition is a reflex coordinated in the pontine micturition center and released or withheld by the frontal lobes: bladder filling is sensed, the pons switches detrusor contraction on and the sphincter (pudendal, Onuf's nucleus) off, and the cortex decides when. Lesions above the sacral cord give a spastic, small, reflexic bladder with urgency; lesions of the conus, cauda equina or pelvic nerves give a flaccid, large, areflexic bladder with retention and overflow.

anatomy.location: Sacral parasympathetic nucleus in the intermediolateral region of S2–S4 in the conus medullaris; pelvic splanchnic nerves joining the inferior hypogastric plexus; intramural ganglia in the pelvic viscera; pudendal nerve (S2–S4, somatic) to the external sphincters and perineum.

subdivisions.name: Sacral parasympathetic nucleus (S2–S4)
subdivisions.note: detrusor contraction, rectal contraction, erection

subdivisions.name: Onuf's nucleus (S2–S4, somatic)
subdivisions.note: external urethral and anal sphincters via the pudendal nerve; spared in ALS, lost in multiple system atrophy

subdivisions.name: Sympathetic (T11–L2) via the hypogastric nerves
subdivisions.note: bladder neck closure, ejaculation, relaxation of the detrusor

subdivisions.name: Pontine micturition center
subdivisions.note: coordinates detrusor and sphincter (detrusor-sphincter synergy)

subdivisions.name: Medial frontal cortex
subdivisions.note: voluntary initiation and inhibition of voiding

autonomic-sacral-parasympathetic.function: Emptying of the bladder and rectum, penile and clitoral erection, and, with the sympathetic and somatic components, continence, ejaculation and coordinated voiding.

bestView.label: cord (the sacral outflow lies in the conus at L1–L2, below the MNI volume)
pontine tegmentum: the micturition center lies dorsally near the locus coeruleus

imaging.normalAppearance: Not imaged directly; the sagittal lumbar MRI shows the conus and cauda equina, and cranial MRI shows the medial frontal and pontine regions. Urodynamics classify the bladder dysfunction.

pathology.finding: Mass, disc or infarct at the conus or compressing the sacral roots with an areflexic bladder.
Cervical or thoracic myelopathy with detrusor overactivity and detrusor-sphincter dyssynergia.

pathology.pathology: Normal pressure hydrocephalus / bilateral medial frontal lesions
pathology.finding: Ventriculomegaly or medial frontal lesions with urge incontinence and gait apraxia.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: Spine MRI; post-void residual; urodynamics

lesionEffects.deficit: Urgency, frequency and reflex incontinence with a small bladder
lesionEffects.mechanism: Suprasacral cord lesion: detrusor overactivity without inhibition, often with dyssynergia

lesionEffects.deficit: Retention with overflow, a large painless bladder, absent anal reflex
lesionEffects.mechanism: Conus, cauda equina or pelvic nerve lesion: detrusor areflexia
Loss of cortical inhibition and awareness
Sacral parasympathetic loss

Post-void residual by bladder scan

basal-forebrain-cholinergic.name: Basal forebrain cholinergic nuclei
basal-forebrain-cholinergic.summary: The basal forebrain cholinergic nuclei are the medial septal nucleus, the vertical and horizontal limbs of the nucleus of the diagonal band and the nucleus basalis of Meynert, a continuous band of large acetylcholine-producing neurons beneath the anterior commissure and the striatum in the substantia innominata and the septal region. They supply nearly all the acetylcholine of the cerebral cortex, hippocampus and amygdala, tuning attention, cortical plasticity and memory encoding, and they degenerate in Alzheimer disease and dementia with Lewy bodies, which is the rationale for cholinesterase inhibitors. They are injured by anterior communicating artery aneurysm rupture and surgery, producing the basal forebrain amnesia with confabulation.

anatomy.location: Ventral forebrain beneath the anterior commissure and the globus pallidus, from the septal area and the diagonal band on the medial surface, through the substantia innominata under the anterior perforated substance, to the nucleus basalis lateral to the hypothalamus and medial to the amygdala.

basal-forebrain-cholinergic.function: The medial septal nucleus and the vertical limb of the diagonal band project through the fornix to the hippocampus and set the theta rhythm that gates memory encoding; the horizontal limb supplies the olfactory bulb and the amygdala; and the nucleus basalis projects diffusely to the whole neocortex, where acetylcholine increases the signal-to-noise ratio of sensory processing, sustains attention and permits experience-dependent cortical reorganization. These neurons are driven by the hypothalamus, the brainstem arousal systems and the amygdala, and they are silent in slow-wave sleep and active in waking and REM. Their loss reduces cortical acetylcholine and produces the attentional and memory deficits of dementia and of anticholinergic delirium.

bestView.label: basal forebrain beneath the anterior commissure
septal region and diagonal band under the rostrum

imaging.normalAppearance: A thin band of gray matter under the anterior commissure and the pallidum on coronal images at the level of the anterior commissure, best seen as the substantia innominata between the optic tract and the ventral pallidum; nucleus basalis volume is measurable only by atlas-based methods.

pathology.pathology: Alzheimer disease and dementia with Lewy bodies
pathology.finding: Reduced basal forebrain volume on atlas-based measurements, preceding cortical atrophy; correlates with cholinergic deficit and response to cholinesterase inhibitors.

pathology.pathology: Anterior communicating artery aneurysm rupture or surgery
pathology.finding: Infarction of the basal forebrain and septal area beneath the rostrum with amnesia, confabulation and personality change.
Diffuse slowing with inattention and hallucinations in a patient on anticholinergic drugs, reversing when the drug is stopped; reflects loss of cholinergic tone rather than a lesion.

lesionEffects.mechanism: Loss of septohippocampal cholinergic drive and theta rhythm
Loss of cortical acetylcholine from the nucleus basalis
Loss of the cholinergic permissive signal for cortical reorganization

examination: Attention testing (months backward, digit span) before memory testing
Delayed recall and confabulation
Medication review for anticholinergic burden in any cognitively impaired patient
pearls: Cholinesterase inhibitors work because the nucleus basalis dies before the cortex does
Anticholinergic drugs are chemical basal forebrain lesions: stop them before diagnosing dementia
Basal forebrain amnesia after aneurysm surgery confabulates; hippocampal amnesia does not

pitfalls: Basal forebrain infarcts are missed on routine axial CT; MRI with coronal DWI through the anterior commissure shows them

bed-nucleus-stria-terminalis.name: Bed nucleus of the stria terminalis
bed-nucleus-stria-terminalis.summary: The bed nucleus of the stria terminalis is a cluster of small nuclei around the stria terminalis where it ends beside the anterior commissure, lateral to the septal area and the fornix column and medial to the head of the caudate and the internal capsule. With the central nucleus of the amygdala it forms the extended amygdala, and it translates sustained threat and stress into hypothalamic, autonomic and behavioral responses: it mediates anxiety to unpredictable threats, the stress response of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis and aspects of social and sexual behavior, and it is sexually dimorphic. It is injured with the septal region in anterior communicating artery aneurysm rupture and is a research target in anxiety, addiction and stress disorders.

anatomy.location: Ventral forebrain beside the anterior commissure and the columns of the fornix, below the lateral ventricle and the caudate head, above the preoptic hypothalamus and lateral to the septal nuclei, where the stria terminalis arrives from the amygdala along the thalamostriate groove.

afferents.via: stria terminalis and ventral amygdalofugal pathway

efferents.to: Ventral tegmental area and periaqueductal gray
Parabrachial nucleus and nucleus of the solitary tract

bed-nucleus-stria-terminalis.function: The bed nucleus receives the amygdala through the stria terminalis and the ventral amygdalofugal pathway, the hippocampus through the fornix and the prefrontal and insular cortex, and it projects to the paraventricular hypothalamus to drive corticotropin-releasing hormone and the stress axis, to the lateral hypothalamus and brainstem for autonomic and defensive responses, and to the ventral tegmental area for the motivational effects of stress; its own corticotropin-releasing hormone neurons sustain the long-lasting anxious state that follows a threat, in contrast to the brief fear of the amygdala. Its sexually dimorphic subnuclei participate in reproductive and parental behavior and are influenced by gonadal hormones.

bestView.label: bed nucleus beside the anterior commissure and the fornix column
ventral forebrain lateral to the septal area

imaging.normalAppearance: Gray matter lateral to the fornix column and medial to the caudate head at the level of the anterior commissure on coronal images; a few millimeters across, identified with atlases rather than by eye.

pathology.finding: Basal forebrain and septal infarcts extending to the bed nucleus region with amnesia and emotional dysregulation.
Increased activity of the bed nucleus during anticipation of unpredictable threat in research studies; no structural lesion.
Mass under the frontal horns involving the septal and bed nucleus region with mood, drive and memory change.

lesionEffects.deficit: Sustained anxiety and exaggerated stress response
lesionEffects.mechanism: Dysregulation of the extended amygdala corticotropin-releasing hormone circuit

lesionEffects.deficit: Blunted stress and autonomic responses after destruction
lesionEffects.mechanism: Loss of the bed nucleus drive to the paraventricular hypothalamus
Damage to the sexually dimorphic subnuclei and their hypothalamic connections

examination: Anxiety and mood assessment after ventral forebrain injury
Autonomic history: sweating, palpitations, stress intolerance
Recent memory, because the septal area is usually involved with it
pearls: The amygdala handles fear of a present threat; the bed nucleus handles anxiety about an uncertain one
The extended amygdala is the anatomy of stress hormone release and of relapse in addiction
Anterior communicating aneurysm patients can be left anxious and disinhibited as well as amnestic

pitfalls: The bed nucleus is too small to see on routine MRI; lesion-symptom claims about it are inferential

bp3d-brain.name: Brain (BodyParts3D)
bp3d-brain.summary: This mesh is the whole brain from the BodyParts3D anatomical model, registered into MNI space with the same transform as the other whole-body structures, and it is provided as a translucent context envelope with the left and right cerebrum meshes from the same source. It shows the gyral surface of a single individual as modeled by anatomists rather than the population-average envelope derived from the MRI template, so its sulci are deeper and its gyri better defined, and it is useful as a visual reference when the atlas-derived cortical parcels are hidden. The registration residual at deep landmarks is a few millimeters, so it should not be used for measurement.

anatomy.location: The whole brain including the cerebral hemispheres, the cerebellum and the brainstem down to the medulla, in MNI space after a landmark affine registration from the BodyParts3D coordinate frame.

bp3d-brain.function: The mesh serves as a visual context for the deep structures: switched on with low opacity it shows where a nucleus or a tract lies relative to the cortical surface and the sulci, and it gives the sense of the gyral pattern that the smooth atlas parcels lack. It also documents the registration quality of the whole-body source: the difference between this surface and the MRI-derived envelope shows the residual misalignment of the BodyParts3D frame, which is largest at the poles and the ventral surface. It has no clinical function of its own beyond orientation.

bestView.label: BodyParts3D whole brain in MNI space
registered brain surface over the MRI template

imaging.normalAppearance: A single-subject polygonal brain surface with modeled sulci and gyri; it overlays the template brain with a few millimeters of mismatch at the surface, most visible at the frontal and occipital poles.

pathology.finding: Where the BodyParts3D surface departs from the template brain surface on the slices, the local registration error of the whole-body sources can be read off directly.
This is a reference mesh; it does not represent a patient and shows no disease.

lesionEffects.mechanism: Context envelope without a lesion syndrome

examination: Use with low opacity to place deep structures against the gyral surface
Compare with the template envelope to judge registration quality
pearls: The BodyParts3D brain is one person's brain; the envelope is everyone's average
Its sulci are deeper than the template's because it was modeled, not averaged
Keep it translucent: it is scenery, not anatomy to measure

brain-envelope.name: Brain surface (template mask)
brain-envelope.summary: This mesh is the outer surface of the MNI152 template brain, generated from the template's brain mask, and it is the translucent shell that the atlas shows by default around every other structure. It represents the pial surface of the population-average brain including the cerebellum and brainstem, smoothed by averaging, so its sulci are shallow; it coincides exactly with the MRI slices and it is the reference against which the registered whole-body meshes are checked. In syndrome mode it stays visible while the parcels are dimmed, giving the lesion marker and the involved structures a frame, and it defines the field of view of the atlas.

anatomy.location: The boundary of the template brain mask: cerebral hemispheres, cerebellum and brainstem to the foramen magnum, in MNI space at 1 mm resolution, closed and smoothed.

brain-envelope.function: The envelope shows the position of any structure relative to the brain surface and the skull base, marks the tentorial and interhemispheric contours, and provides the visual container for the syndrome, pathway and quiz displays; its coincidence with the MRI means that a slice through it always shows brain at the surface, which makes it the natural reference for judging whether a registered mesh sits correctly. It also gives the scale of the atlas, roughly 140 mm wide, 170 mm long and 120 mm high for the average adult brain, and it is the surface used for camera framing.

bestView.label: template brain surface on the midline
brain envelope around the hemispheres

imaging.normalAppearance: The template brain mask boundary follows the pial surface of the average brain on all slices; individual gyri are visible only as shallow undulations because averaging smooths them.

pathology.finding: The envelope is a reference surface without disease; a patient's brain surface departs from it with atrophy (widened sulci, retracted surface) or mass effect (displaced surface).
Registered whole-body meshes that protrude beyond the envelope reveal the residual error of the affine transform.

Check registered meshes against it for alignment
pearls: The envelope is the average brain's skin; everything in the atlas lives inside it
When a registered nerve pokes through the envelope, blame the registration, not the anatomy
The envelope and the MRI are the same data seen two ways

brainstem.name: Brainstem
brainstem.summary: The brainstem is the stalk that joins the cerebral hemispheres to the spinal cord, made of the midbrain, pons and medulla oblongata, lying in the posterior fossa on the clivus and passing through the tentorial notch above and the foramen magnum below. It contains the nuclei of cranial nerves III to XII, the ascending and descending long tracts, the reticular formation that maintains consciousness and controls breathing and circulation, and the crossings that decide on which side a deficit appears. Its compact packing means small lesions produce crossed syndromes that name the level, and its vital centers make brainstem compression, hemorrhage and basilar occlusion the most dangerous events in neurology.

anatomy.location: Posterior cranial fossa in front of the cerebellum, from the diencephalon at the level of the posterior commissure and mammillary bodies to the pyramidal decussation at the foramen magnum, with the fourth ventricle and aqueduct behind it and the basilar and vertebral arteries in front.

afferents.via: spinothalamic, spinocerebellar and dorsal column pathways

efferents.via: medial lemniscus and reticular activating system
reticulospinal, vestibulospinal, rubrospinal and tectospinal tracts

brainstem.function: Ascending pathways (medial lemniscus, spinothalamic tract, lateral lemniscus, cerebellar peduncles) and descending pathways (corticospinal, corticobulbar, rubrospinal, vestibulospinal, reticulospinal) traverse it; cranial nerve nuclei are arranged in longitudinal columns with motor nuclei medial and sensory nuclei lateral; the reticular formation generates the respiratory rhythm, sets blood pressure and heart rate, and its ascending projections keep the thalamus and cortex awake; and the pontine and medullary gaze centers, the vestibular nuclei and the inferior olive coordinate eye movements and posture. The pyramidal, lemniscal and trochlear decussations and the crossing of the superior cerebellar peduncles determine the side of signs. This entry is the container for the level-by-level and nucleus-by-nucleus descriptions elsewhere in the atlas.

bestView.label: brainstem from the midbrain to the cervicomedullary junction
pons in front of the fourth ventricle

imaging.normalAppearance: On midline sagittal T1 images the midbrain, the bulging pons and the tapering medulla lie on the clivus with the aqueduct and fourth ventricle behind; the pontine-midbrain ratio, the medulla area and the midbrain profile are measured in neurodegenerative disease.

pathology.finding: Restricted diffusion in a paramedian or lateral territory; DWI can be falsely negative in the first hours for small pontine and medullary infarcts.
pathology.timing: Repeat DWI at 24-48 hours if the first is negative and the syndrome is convincing

pathology.finding: Effacement of the perimesencephalic cisterns, midbrain distortion by uncal herniation or tonsillar descent, and Duret hemorrhages in the pontine tegmentum.
Midbrain atrophy with a concave upper profile (hummingbird sign) and a reduced midbrain-to-pons ratio.
Diffuse pontine expansion with T2 hyperintensity in children; focal FLAIR lesions of the pons and middle cerebellar peduncle in multiple sclerosis.

lesionEffects.deficit: Crossed cranial nerve and long-tract signs
lesionEffects.mechanism: Cranial nerve nucleus or fascicle on the side of the lesion with crossed corticospinal or sensory tracts
Damage to the reticular activating system of the upper pons and midbrain
Damage to the medullary respiratory and vasomotor centers
Bilateral ventral pontine destruction sparing the tegmentum

examination: Cranial nerves III-XII in order, then long-tract signs and their sides, then level of consciousness and breathing pattern
Brainstem reflexes in coma: pupils, corneals, oculocephalic and cold caloric responses, gag and cough
Blood pressure, heart rate and respiratory pattern as vital-center signs
pearls: The cranial nerve names the level: III midbrain, VI-VII pons, IX-XII medulla
Sensory loss on one side of the face and the other side of the body is the brainstem's signature
A small lesion in the brainstem produces more deficits than a large one in the hemisphere

pitfalls: Early DWI misses up to a third of small brainstem infarcts; the examination outranks the first scan

cauda-equina.name: Cauda equina
cauda-equina.summary: The bundle of lumbar, sacral and coccygeal nerve roots that descends below the conus medullaris inside the lumbar cistern to reach their intervertebral foramina, produced by the differential growth of the vertebral column over the cord. They are peripheral nerve roots, so their compression by a large central disc, tumor or hematoma causes a lower motor neuron syndrome: asymmetric leg weakness, radicular pain, saddle sensory loss and late sphincter failure. It is a surgical emergency, and the roots float in CSF, which is what makes lumbar puncture below L2 safe.

anatomy.location: Lumbar cistern of the subarachnoid space from the conus at L1–L2 down to the end of the dural sac at S2, surrounding the filum terminale; the roots arrange themselves with the lower sacral roots central and the higher lumbar roots lateral.

cauda-equina.function: Conveys motor, sensory and autonomic fibers of the L2–S5 roots to and from the lower limbs, perineum and pelvic organs.

bestView.label: cord (the cauda equina lies in the lumbar canal, below the MNI volume)

imaging.normalAppearance: On sagittal and axial lumbar T2 the roots are dark linear structures within bright CSF, normally lying dependent; clumping, enhancement or compression by a disc or mass are abnormal. Lumbar MRI is the emergency investigation for suspected cauda equina syndrome.

pathology.pathology: Cauda equina syndrome from central disc herniation
pathology.finding: Large L4–L5 or L5–S1 disc filling the canal and compressing the roots.
Enhancement and thickening of the roots after contrast.
Clumped, peripherally displaced roots after surgery or infection.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: Urgent sagittal and axial lumbosacral MRI

lesionEffects.deficit: Asymmetric flaccid leg weakness with absent reflexes
lesionEffects.mechanism: Lower motor neuron roots

lesionEffects.deficit: Radicular (sciatic) pain and asymmetric saddle numbness
lesionEffects.mechanism: Sensory roots

lesionEffects.deficit: Urinary retention with overflow, fecal incontinence, impotence (later and less symmetric than conus lesions)
lesionEffects.mechanism: Sacral roots S2–S4

lesionEffects.deficit: Absent ankle jerks with preserved plantars
lesionEffects.mechanism: Peripheral (root) lesion

examination: Straight-leg raise and dermatomal sensation of the legs
Perianal sensation and anal tone
Ankle and knee reflexes
Post-void residual bladder volume
pearls: Bilateral sciatica with any bladder symptom or perineal numbness needs an MRI the same day
Cauda equina lesions are painful and asymmetric; conus lesions are quiet and symmetric

caudate-nucleus.name: Caudate nucleus
caudate-nucleus.summary: A C-shaped mass of gray matter that follows the lateral ventricle: a bulbous head in the wall of the frontal horn, a body along the floor of the ventricle above the thalamus, and a slender tail curving down into the roof of the temporal horn to end near the amygdala. With the putamen (to which it is joined by gray bridges across the anterior limb of the internal capsule) it forms the striatum, the input stage of the basal ganglia. The head receives prefrontal and association cortex and is the substrate of the cognitive and limbic loops; its atrophy flattens the frontal horns in Huntington disease, and lesions cause abulia, executive dysfunction and sometimes chorea rather than weakness.

cerebellar-cortex-layers.name: Cerebellar cortex: layers and circuit
cerebellar-cortex-layers.summary: The cerebellar cortex is a uniform three-layered sheet folded into thousands of folia: an outer molecular layer of parallel fibers, stellate and basket cells; a single row of Purkinje cells; and an inner granular layer packed with granule cells and Golgi cells. Two afferent systems enter it. Mossy fibers from the pontine nuclei, spinal cord and vestibular nuclei excite granule cells, whose axons rise to the molecular layer and split into parallel fibers that run along the folium and excite the flat dendritic trees of thousands of Purkinje cells. Climbing fibers from the contralateral inferior olive each wrap around a single Purkinje cell and fire a complex spike that teaches it. Purkinje cells are the only output, inhibiting the deep nuclei. The uniformity of this circuit is why the cerebellum applies the same computation to movement, gaze and cognition, and its cell types are the targets of specific diseases: Purkinje cells in alcohol, paraneoplastic and hypoxic injury, granule cells in medulloblastoma.

anatomy.location: The gray matter covering the folia of the whole cerebellum, about 1 mm thick, with the same three layers everywhere; the Purkinje layer separates the outer molecular layer from the inner granular layer, and the white matter core carries the afferent and efferent fibers to the deep nuclei.

subdivisions.name: Molecular layer
subdivisions.note: parallel fibers, Purkinje dendrites, stellate and basket cells

subdivisions.name: Purkinje cell layer

subdivisions.name: Granular layer

afferents.from: Pontine nuclei, spinal cord, vestibular nuclei, reticular formation

cerebellar-cortex-layers.function: Mossy fiber input is expanded by the granule cells into a sparse code carried by the parallel fibers, which Purkinje cells read through about 200,000 synapses each; climbing fiber input signals errors and induces long-term depression at the parallel fiber synapses that were active just before, so that the Purkinje cell learns to predict and correct the error, the basis of motor learning and of the adaptation of the vestibulo-ocular reflex. Basket and stellate cells sharpen the Purkinje output in space and Golgi cells in time. Purkinje cells inhibit the deep nuclei and the vestibular nuclei, sculpting the excitatory signal that collaterals of the mossy and climbing fibers have already delivered there, so that the cerebellum's output is a timed modulation rather than a command.

cerebellar-hemisphere.name: Cerebellar hemispheres (lateral zone)
cerebellar-hemisphere.summary: The lateral zones of the cerebellum, the neocerebellum, expanded enormously with the cerebral cortex and are wired to it: the contralateral motor and association cortices project through the pontine nuclei and middle cerebellar peduncle, and the hemispheres reply through the dentate nucleus, superior cerebellar peduncle and thalamus to the same cortex. They plan and time skilled limb movements, particularly of the hand and of speech, and lesions produce the classic ipsilateral limb signs: dysmetria, intention tremor, dysdiadochokinesia and rebound.

cerebellar-lobule-crus-i.name: Crus I
synonyms: Crus I of the ansiform lobule
cerebellar-lobule-crus-i.summary: Crus I is the upper of the two large hemispheric lobules of the posterior lobe (the superior semilunar lobule), lying between lobule VI above the horizontal fissure and Crus II below, forming the bulk of the posterior lateral hemisphere. It is the cognitive cerebellum: it has no somatotopic body map but is connected through the pontine nuclei and the dentate nucleus to the prefrontal, parietal and temporal association cortex, and it participates in working memory, language, executive function and social cognition. Damage causes the cerebellar cognitive-affective syndrome rather than limb ataxia, it is a common site of cerebellar metastases and of PICA-territory infarcts of the posterolateral hemisphere, and its volume is altered in autism and schizophrenia.

anatomy.location: Posterior lobe of the hemisphere between the superior posterior fissure and the horizontal fissure, lateral to the vermian folium, forming the superior semilunar lobule that wraps around the lateral edge of the hemisphere below the tentorium.

afferents.from: Prefrontal, parietal and temporal association cortex via the pontine nuclei

It is a node of the default mode and frontoparietal networks, and its connections with the prefrontal cortex are the anatomical basis of the executive and affective changes after posterior cerebellar lesions.

synonyms: Crus II of the ansiform lobule
cerebellar-lobule-crus-ii.summary: Crus II is the lower of the two large posterior hemispheric lobules (the inferior semilunar lobule), between the horizontal fissure above and lobule VIIB below, on the posteroinferior surface of the cerebellum in the posterior inferior cerebellar artery territory. It is the region most often involved in cerebellar cognitive-affective syndrome after PICA infarcts and tumor resection, and it swells against the medulla and the fourth ventricle in large infarcts, so its edema is a cause of the delayed deterioration that follows cerebellar stroke.

cerebellar-lobule-i-iv.name: Lobules I–IV
cerebellar-lobule-i-iv.summary: Lobules I to IV form the anterior part of the anterior lobe of the cerebellum, the lingula, central lobule and culmen of the vermis with their small hemispheric wings, tucked under the tentorium in front of the primary fissure and behind the superior medullary velum. They are spinocerebellar cortex receiving the spinocerebellar tracts from the legs and trunk and projecting through the fastigial and interposed nuclei to the vestibulospinal and reticulospinal systems, so they regulate muscle tone, posture and the gait of the lower limbs. Their degeneration in chronic alcoholism produces the classic anterior lobe syndrome of a wide-based ataxic gait with relatively preserved arm coordination, and they are compressed by superior vermian and tentorial masses.

The result is continuous adjustment of limb tone and of the timing of the leg muscles in walking and standing, with a somatotopic map in which the legs are represented anteriorly. Loss produces gait and stance ataxia and hypotonia of the legs.

html.summary: Lobules I to IV form the anterior part of the anterior lobe of the cerebellum, the lingula, central lobule and culmen of the vermis with their small hemispheric wings, tucked under the tentorium in front of the primary fissure and behind the superior medullary velum. They are spinocerebellar cortex receiving the spinocerebellar tracts from the legs and trunk and projecting through the fastigial and interposed nuclei to the vestibulospinal and reticulospinal systems, so they regulate muscle tone, posture and the gait of the lower limbs. Their degeneration in chronic alcoholism produces the classic anterior lobe syndrome of a wide-based ataxic gait with relatively preserved arm coordination, and they are compressed by superior vermian and tentorial masses.
html.function: The anterior lobe cortex receives the dorsal and ventral spinocerebellar tracts (leg and trunk proprioception and copies of spinal interneuron activity) and the cuneocerebellar tract from the arm, together with pontine input from the sensorimotor cortex and olivary climbing fibers; its Purkinje cells inhibit the fastigial and interposed nuclei, which drive the vestibulospinal, reticulospinal and rubrospinal systems and the ventrolateral thalamus. The result is continuous adjustment of limb tone and of the timing of the leg muscles in walking and standing, with a somatotopic map in which the legs are represented anteriorly. Loss produces gait and stance ataxia and hypotonia of the legs.
html.anatomy.location: Anterior lobe of the cerebellum from the superior medullary velum back to the primary fissure, rostral and superior to lobule V, mostly vermian with small hemispheric extensions, lying beneath the tentorium and behind the midbrain and the superior cerebellar peduncles.
html.imaging.normalAppearance: The anterosuperior vermis on midline sagittal images between the fourth ventricle roof and the primary fissure, folded into narrow folia; atrophy widens its fissures before the rest of the cerebellum.

cerebellar-lobule-ix.name: Lobule IX
cerebellar-lobule-ix.summary: Lobule IX is the uvula of the vermis and the cerebellar tonsils of the hemispheres, the most inferior part of the posterior lobe, sitting above the foramen magnum on either side of the medulla. The uvula is vestibulocerebellar cortex with the nodulus, receiving the vestibular nerve and nuclei and controlling vestibulo-ocular and vestibulospinal reflexes and the perception of tilt and self-motion; the tonsils are the parts of the cerebellum that herniate through the foramen magnum in raised intracranial pressure and in Chiari malformation. It is supplied by the posterior inferior cerebellar artery, and its infarction mimics a peripheral vestibular lesion with isolated vertigo.

anatomy.location: Inferior vermis (uvula) and the tonsils of the hemispheres between the secondary fissure above and the posterolateral fissure below, above the foramen magnum and the cisterna magna, beside the medulla and behind the fourth ventricle's inferior medullary velum.

cerebellar-lobule-ix.function: The uvula, with the nodulus, receives primary vestibular afferents and vestibular nuclear input together with visual motion signals from the inferior olive and the pontine nuclei, and its Purkinje cells project to the vestibular and fastigial nuclei to calibrate the vestibulo-ocular reflex, to distinguish tilt from translation and to hold gaze after head movements (velocity storage); it also contributes to the control of head and eye movements during locomotion. The tonsils are hemispheric cortex with sensorimotor and cognitive connections through the dentate nucleus, but their clinical importance is mechanical: their descent compresses the medulla and blocks CSF flow. Uvular and nodular damage produces vertigo, downbeat nystagmus and imbalance without limb ataxia.

cerebellar-lobule-v.name: Lobule V
cerebellar-lobule-v.summary: Lobule V is the posterior part of the anterior lobe, the culmen of the vermis and its hemispheric extension, ending at the primary fissure that separates the anterior from the posterior lobe. It contains the anterior somatotopic map of the body, with the arm and hand lateral and the leg medial, and it works with the primary motor cortex through the pontine nuclei and the dentate-thalamic projection to time and coordinate limb movements, so its lesions produce limb ataxia and dysmetria of the ipsilateral arm and leg. It is in the superior cerebellar artery territory and it is compressed or infarcted with the rest of the superior cerebellum, and it shows early atrophy in the spinocerebellar ataxias.

anatomy.location: Posterior part of the anterior lobe between lobule IV in front and the primary fissure behind, extending from the vermian culmen laterally into the anterior quadrangular lobule of the hemisphere, beneath the tentorium above the superior cerebellar peduncle.

afferents.from: Motor and somatosensory cortex via the pontine nuclei

efferents.to: Motor cortex via the ventrolateral thalamus (from the nuclei)

cerebellar-lobule-v.function: Lobule V receives corticopontine input from the motor and somatosensory cortex through the middle cerebellar peduncle and spinocerebellar input from the limbs, and its Purkinje cells project to the interposed nuclei (intermediate zone) and the dentate nucleus (lateral part), which send the corrected motor signal to the motor cortex through the ventrolateral thalamus and to the red nucleus; this loop predicts the sensory consequences of a movement and corrects it in flight, so that reaching is smooth and rhythmic movements keep time. Climbing fibers from the inferior olive signal errors and drive motor learning. Its lateral part is the cerebellar hand area used in fine finger movements.

pathology.finding: Restricted diffusion of the anterior superior cerebellar hemisphere and vermis with ipsilateral limb ataxia and dysarthria.

cerebellar-lobule-vi.name: Lobule VI
cerebellar-lobule-vi.summary: Lobule VI is the first lobule of the posterior lobe, immediately behind the primary fissure, comprising the declive of the vermis and the posterior quadrangular lobule of the hemisphere, the simplex lobule. It is a transition between the motor cerebellum of the anterior lobe and the cognitive cerebellum of Crus I and II: it holds a second representation of the face, mouth and eye movements, it supports articulation and the timing of speech, and its vermian part with lobule VII is the oculomotor vermis that calibrates saccades. It is a superior cerebellar artery territory, it is involved in the dysarthria of cerebellar strokes, and it is one of the regions most consistently abnormal in the cerebellar cognitive-affective syndrome and in studies of autism.

anatomy.location: Anterior part of the posterior lobe between the primary fissure in front and the superior posterior fissure behind, from the vermian declive laterally into the simplex (posterior quadrangular) lobule of the hemisphere, under the tentorium and above the horizontal fissure.

afferents.from: Premotor, motor and prefrontal cortex via the pontine nuclei

efferents.to: Motor and prefrontal cortex via the thalamus

cerebellar-lobule-vi.function: The hemispheric part of lobule VI receives the ventral premotor, motor and somatosensory cortex through the pontine nuclei and the trigeminal system, and its projection through the dentate nucleus to the motor thalamus times the muscles of the mouth, tongue and larynx, so lesions produce scanning dysarthria; the vermian part receives the superior colliculus, the vestibular nuclei and the nucleus prepositus and projects to the fastigial nucleus to adjust saccade amplitude and pursuit gain, so lesions produce saccadic dysmetria and impaired pursuit. Its lateral parts also participate in working memory and language tasks with Crus I, and it is a station of the cerebellar pain and emotional networks.

cerebellar-lobule-viib.name: Lobule VIIB
synonyms: lobule VIIB with the vermian tuber
cerebellar-lobule-viib.summary: Lobule VIIB is the narrow hemispheric lobule between Crus II above and lobule VIIIA below, the gracile lobule, on the inferior surface of the posterior cerebellum, with the vermian tuber and folium as its midline counterparts. It lies at the boundary between the cognitive cerebellum of the ansiform lobules and the second sensorimotor map of lobule VIII, and it contributes to both: its lateral part joins the prefrontal loops for working memory and its medial part receives spinal and pontine sensorimotor input. It is supplied by the posterior inferior cerebellar artery, is involved in PICA infarcts and in the cerebellar cognitive-affective syndrome, and its vermian part belongs to the oculomotor vermis.

anatomy.location: Inferior surface of the posterior lobe between the ansoparamedian fissure (below Crus II) and the prebiventer fissure (above lobule VIIIA), extending from the tuber of the vermis laterally as the gracile lobule to the lateral margin of the hemisphere.

afferents.from: Prefrontal, parietal and sensorimotor cortex via the pontine nuclei

efferents.to: Dentate and interposed nuclei; fastigial nucleus (vermis)

cerebellar-lobule-viib.function: Lobule VIIB receives corticopontine fibers from the prefrontal and parietal cortex laterally and from the sensorimotor cortex medially, and spinocerebellar input to its paravermian part, projecting to the dentate and interposed nuclei; functionally it takes part in verbal and spatial working memory and in the planning of sequential movements, and the vermian folium and tuber (VIIA) with lobule VI form the oculomotor vermis that calibrates saccades through the fastigial nucleus. It is one of the lobules in which the cerebellum's contribution to attention and to the timing of cognitive operations has been mapped, and its involvement in posterior lobe lesions adds executive symptoms to gait and ocular signs.

cerebellar-lobule-viiia.name: Lobule VIIIA
cerebellar-lobule-viiia.summary: Lobule VIIIA is the upper part of the biventer lobule on the inferior cerebellar surface, between lobule VIIB above and VIIIB below, with the pyramis of the vermis as its midline part. It contains the second, inverted somatotopic map of the body, so it is a sensorimotor lobule like the anterior lobe: it receives spinocerebellar and corticopontine input from the limbs and trunk and projects through the interposed and dentate nuclei to the motor thalamus and the brainstem. Lesions produce ipsilateral limb ataxia and contribute to the gait disorder of PICA infarcts, its vermian part (the pyramis) participates in trunk and posture control, and it is one of the lobules where the cerebellar contribution to motor learning has been mapped.

cerebellar-lobule-viiib.name: Lobule VIIIB
cerebellar-lobule-viiib.summary: Lobule VIIIB is the lower part of the biventer lobule on the inferior cerebellar surface, between lobule VIIIA above and lobule IX (the tonsil) below, completing the second sensorimotor map of the posterior lobe with a representation of the face and the limbs. It receives spinal, trigeminal and pontine sensorimotor input and projects through the interposed and dentate nuclei, contributing to limb coordination, oral movements and the timing of speech, and its vermian part (pyramis and uvula boundary) supports trunk posture. It is in the posterior inferior cerebellar artery territory and is involved in PICA infarcts and in the tonsillar crowding of Chiari malformation, and it is the lobule adjacent to the tonsils that is compressed in tonsillar herniation.

html.summary: Lobule VIIIB is the lower part of the biventer lobule on the inferior cerebellar surface, between lobule VIIIA above and lobule IX (the tonsil) below, completing the second sensorimotor map of the posterior lobe with a representation of the face and the limbs. cerebellar-lobule-x.name: Lobule X (flocculonodular)
cerebellar-lobule-x.summary: Lobule X is the flocculonodular lobe, the nodulus of the vermis and the flocculi of the hemispheres, the oldest part of the cerebellum and the one most directly tied to the vestibular system. The flocculus, tucked beneath the middle cerebellar peduncle in the cerebellopontine angle, adapts the vestibulo-ocular reflex and holds eccentric gaze and smooth pursuit; the nodulus with the uvula controls the vestibulospinal reflexes and the sense of tilt. Lesions cause gaze-evoked and downbeat nystagmus, impaired pursuit and vertigo with imbalance, and this lobe is damaged in medulloblastoma of the fourth ventricle, in PICA and AICA infarcts, in cerebellopontine angle tumors and in Wernicke encephalopathy.

anatomy.location: The nodulus is the most anterior inferior vermian lobule projecting into the fourth ventricle roof below the uvula; each flocculus is a small tufted lobule on the anterior inferior surface of the hemisphere beside the pons and the medulla, under the middle cerebellar peduncle and the vestibulocochlear nerve, joined to the nodulus by the peduncle of the flocculus.

cerebellar-lobule-x.function: The flocculus receives visual motion signals through the inferior olive and the pontine nuclei and vestibular signals from the nerve and nuclei, and its Purkinje cells project directly to the vestibular nuclei to modify the gain and direction of the vestibulo-ocular reflex during learning, to suppress it during fixation and to stabilize gaze in eccentric positions and during pursuit; the nodulus and uvula process otolith and canal signals to separate tilt from translation, limit the duration of post-rotatory nystagmus, and calibrate the vestibulospinal reflexes for stance. Loss of the flocculus produces gaze-evoked nystagmus, downbeat nystagmus, impaired pursuit and inability to suppress the vestibulo-ocular reflex; loss of the nodulus produces vertigo, periodic alternating nystagmus and truncal ataxia.

cerebellar-tonsil.name: Cerebellar tonsil
cerebellar-tonsil.summary: The rounded lobules on the inferomedial surface of each hemisphere that sit directly above the foramen magnum on either side of the medulla. They matter almost entirely because of where they are: raised pressure in the posterior fossa pushes them into the foramen magnum (tonsillar herniation), compressing the medulla and blocking CSF flow, and the Chiari I malformation is defined by their congenital descent below the foramen magnum.

anatomy.location: Inferomedial cerebellar hemisphere adjacent to the vallecula, lateral to the uvula and above the foramen magnum, bounded above by the biventral lobule; normally the tonsillar tips lie at or above the plane of the foramen magnum (McRae line).

cerebellar-tonsil.function: Part of the posterior lobe (hemispheric lobule IX); no unique clinical function, but a critical space-occupying landmark at the craniocervical junction.

bestView.label: tonsil above the foramen magnum on a parasagittal slice

imaging.normalAppearance: On sagittal T1 the tonsillar tip should not lie more than about 5 mm below the line from the basion to the opisthion; peg-like pointed tonsils with obliteration of the cisterna magna indicate Chiari I. Rounded tonsils forced down acutely with effaced CSF indicate herniation.

pathology.finding: Tonsils crowded into the foramen magnum with obliterated basal cisterns and cisterna magna, often with a posterior fossa mass or diffuse swelling; lumbar puncture is contraindicated.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: Sagittal T1/T2 of the craniocervical junction; CT in the emergency setting

cerebellar-vermis.name: Vermis
cerebellar-vermis.summary: The narrow midline ridge joining the two hemispheres, folded into ten lobules from the lingula at the top to the nodule at the bottom. Together with the adjacent paravermis it forms the spinocerebellum, receiving proprioceptive information from the trunk and limbs and vestibular input, and projecting through the fastigial nuclei to the vestibular nuclei and reticular formation. It governs posture, gait, trunk stability and eye movements, which is why midline disease presents with truncal ataxia and nystagmus rather than limb dysmetria. It is also the part most damaged by alcohol and the usual seat of childhood medulloblastoma.

anatomy.location: Midline of the cerebellum between the hemispheres, forming the roof of the fourth ventricle inferiorly; its lobules (I–X) are numbered from the superior surface (lingula) around the posterior surface to the nodule in front of the uvula.

cerebellar-white-matter.name: Cerebellar white matter
cerebellar-white-matter.summary: The cerebellar white matter is the branching core of the cerebellum, the arbor vitae, formed by the afferent fibers arriving through the three peduncles and fanning out to the cortex, the Purkinje cell axons converging on the deep nuclei, and the efferent fibers leaving the nuclei. It contains the dentate, interposed and fastigial nuclei and it is continuous with the peduncles at the hilus of the hemisphere. It is the substrate of the cerebellar signs in multiple sclerosis (the middle cerebellar peduncle and hemispheric white matter are favored sites), of leukodystrophies and of the cerebellar edema that follows infarction, and its atrophy accompanies cortical loss in the spinocerebellar ataxias; hemorrhage and tumors here compress the fourth ventricle.

anatomy.location: The central white matter of each hemisphere and of the vermis, between the folial cortex and the fourth ventricle, continuous laterally and anteriorly with the inferior, middle and superior cerebellar peduncles, and enclosing the dentate nucleus laterally and the interposed and fastigial nuclei near the midline.

efferents.to: Red nucleus and thalamus (from the dentate and interposed nuclei)

efferents.via: inferior cerebellar peduncle and juxtarestiform body

cerebellar-white-matter.function: Mossy fibers from the pontine nuclei, the spinal cord, the vestibular system and the reticular nuclei and climbing fibers from the inferior olive travel through the white matter to the granular and molecular layers of the cortex, while Purkinje axons run inward to inhibit the deep nuclei, whose axons leave through the superior peduncle to the red nucleus and thalamus and through the inferior peduncle to the vestibular nuclei and reticular formation; corticonuclear and nucleocortical loops within the white matter regulate the gain of the circuit. The organization is somatotopic along the peduncles and the medullary laminae of each lobule. Its lesions disconnect cortex from nuclei and produce the same ipsilateral ataxia as cortical lesions, with more dysarthria and tremor when the outflow is involved.

cerebellum.name: Cerebellum
cerebellum.summary: The cerebellum occupies the posterior cranial fossa beneath the tentorium and behind the pons and medulla, attached to the brainstem by three peduncles. It does not initiate movement but calibrates it: it compares intended with actual movement using proprioceptive, vestibular and cortical inputs and corrects timing, force and coordination through the deep nuclei and their projections to the thalamus and brainstem. Because its outflow crosses in the midbrain and the corticospinal tract crosses again in the medulla, each cerebellar hemisphere controls the limbs on its own side, so cerebellar signs are ipsilateral. Midline (vermis) disease affects gait, trunk and eye movements; lateral disease affects limb coordination.

anatomy.location: Posterior cranial fossa below the tentorium cerebelli, separated from the occipital lobes by it; ventrally it forms the roof of the fourth ventricle and is connected to the medulla, pons and midbrain by the inferior, middle and superior cerebellar peduncles.

subdivisions.name: Posterior lobe
subdivisions.note: behind the primary fissure, the bulk of the hemispheres; cortical input, skilled movement and cognition

subdivisions.name: Flocculonodular lobe

html.summary: The cerebellum occupies the posterior cranial fossa beneath the tentorium and behind the pons and medulla, attached to the brainstem by three peduncles. It does not initiate movement but calibrates it: it compares intended with actual movement using proprioceptive, vestibular and cortical inputs and corrects timing, force and coordination through the deep nuclei and their projections to the thalamus and brainstem. Because its outflow crosses in the midbrain and the corticospinal tract crosses again in the medulla, each cerebellar hemisphere controls the limbs on its own side, so cerebellar signs are ipsilateral. Midline (vermis) disease affects gait, trunk and eye movements; lateral disease affects limb coordination.
html.function: Coordination, timing and scaling of voluntary movement; maintenance of posture, gait and muscle tone; control of eye movements; motor learning; and a contribution to language, executive and affective processing (cerebellar cognitive affective syndrome).
html.anatomy.location: Posterior cranial fossa below the tentorium cerebelli, separated from the occipital lobes by it; ventrally it forms the roof of the fourth ventricle and is connected to the medulla, pons and midbrain by the inferior, middle and superior cerebellar peduncles.
html.imaging.normalAppearance: On T1 the folia give the cerebellum a finely striped appearance; the dentate nuclei are visible as wavy dark lines within the hemispheric white matter on T2/SWI. The vermis is best assessed on midline sagittal images and the tonsils on sagittal and coronal images.
html.imaging.sequenceOfChoice: DWI and CT for acute presentations; sagittal T1 for atrophy and tonsillar position

cerebral-aqueduct.name: Cerebral aqueduct
cerebral-aqueduct.summary: A 15 mm canal about 1 mm wide running through the midbrain from the third to the fourth ventricle, surrounded by the periaqueductal gray, with the tectum behind and the tegmentum in front. It is the narrowest point of the ventricular system and the commonest site of obstruction: congenital stenosis, tectal gliomas, pineal masses and post-hemorrhagic gliosis all produce hydrocephalus of the lateral and third ventricles with a normal fourth ventricle, the pattern known as triventricular hydrocephalus.

anatomy.location: Midline midbrain, beginning at the posterior end of the third ventricle below the posterior commissure and opening into the fourth ventricle under the superior medullary velum; slightly kinked at the level of the colliculi.

cerebral-aqueduct.function: Sole CSF passage from the third to the fourth ventricle; CSF pulses through it with each heartbeat, producing a flow void on T2.

bestView.label: aqueduct running through the midbrain between tectum and tegmentum
central dot of CSF in the midbrain

imaging.normalAppearance: A dark flow void on T2 in the midline of the midbrain on sagittal images and a small central dot on axial slices; heavily T2-weighted CISS shows its lumen, and phase-contrast MRI quantifies flow. Absence of the flow void with triventricular dilatation suggests stenosis.

pathology.finding: Dilated lateral and third ventricles with a normal fourth, a narrowed or web-obstructed aqueduct on sagittal CISS and absent flow void; may present in adulthood.
T2-bright bulbous tectum compressing the aqueduct.

pathology.pathology: Aqueductal obstruction after hemorrhage or meningitis
pathology.finding: Gliotic narrowing with the same triventricular pattern.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: Sagittal T2/CISS through the midline; phase-contrast CSF flow study

lesionEffects.deficit: Triventricular hydrocephalus: headache, papilledema, gait disturbance
lesionEffects.mechanism: Obstruction at the aqueduct spares the fourth ventricle
Dilated third ventricle and suprapineal recess or the causative tectal mass pressing on the dorsal midbrain

examination: Papilledema
Up-gaze and pupillary light-near dissociation
Gait and cognition
pearls: Big lateral and third ventricles with a small fourth ventricle mean the block is at the aqueduct
Adult-onset aqueductal stenosis can masquerade as normal pressure hydrocephalus

cerebral-peduncle-crus.name: Crus cerebri (cerebral peduncle)
cerebral-peduncle-crus.summary: The paired ventral pillars of the midbrain, made entirely of descending fibers: corticospinal and corticobulbar fibers occupy the middle three-fifths, flanked by frontopontine fibers medially and parieto-temporo-occipitopontine fibers laterally. The oculomotor nerve emerges from the medial edge into the interpeduncular fossa, and the uncus of the temporal lobe lies against the lateral edge, so a crus lesion produces the Weber syndrome and a herniating uncus produces contralateral hemiparesis or, when it pushes the opposite crus against the tentorium, a falsely localizing ipsilateral hemiparesis (Kernohan notch).

anatomy.location: Ventral midbrain on each side of the interpeduncular fossa, separated from the tegmentum by the substantia nigra, continuous below with the basis pontis and above with the posterior limb of the internal capsule.

subdivisions.name: Medial fifth
subdivisions.note: frontopontine fibers

subdivisions.name: Middle three-fifths
subdivisions.note: corticobulbar (medial) and corticospinal (lateral) fibers, arm medial to leg

subdivisions.name: Lateral fifth
subdivisions.note: parieto-temporo-occipitopontine fibers

cerebral-peduncle-crus.function: Conducts all corticofugal motor traffic from the internal capsule to the pons and spinal cord.

bestView.label: crura as the two anterior bulges of the midbrain flanking the interpeduncular fossa
crus continuing up into the internal capsule

imaging.normalAppearance: The crura are dark compact white matter on T2 forming the anterior contour of the midbrain; the substantia nigra behind them is darker still on T2*. Wallerian degeneration after a hemispheric stroke thins and brightens the ipsilateral crus.

pathology.finding: Paramedian restricted diffusion in the medial crus including the emerging oculomotor fibers.

Medial temporal lobe displaced over the tentorial edge compressing the ipsilateral crus and pushing the midbrain so the contralateral crus is notched by the tentorium; T2 signal in the compressed peduncle.
Atrophy and T2 hyperintensity of the crus months after a large MCA infarct.
pathology.timing: From about 4–10 weeks after the stroke

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: DWI and T2 through the midbrain

lesionEffects.deficit: Contralateral hemiparesis including the lower face and tongue
lesionEffects.mechanism: Corticospinal and corticobulbar fibers in the middle of the crus

lesionEffects.deficit: Ipsilateral third nerve palsy with the hemiparesis (Weber)
lesionEffects.mechanism: Oculomotor fascicle exiting through the medial crus
Contralateral crus compressed against the tentorial edge (Kernohan notch, false localizing)

examination: Limb power, facial and tongue movement on the side opposite the lesion
Pupils and eye movements
In a comatose patient with a dilated pupil, remember the hemiparesis may be on the same side as the pupil
pearls: Third nerve palsy plus contralateral hemiparesis is the crus (Weber)
A dilated pupil with ipsilateral hemiparesis means the herniation is on the side of the pupil, not the weakness

cerebral-white-matter.name: Cerebral white matter
cerebral-white-matter.summary: The cerebral white matter is the mass of myelinated axons beneath the cortex and around the ventricles that connects cortex with cortex (association fibers), the two hemispheres (commissural fibers) and the cortex with the thalamus, brainstem and spinal cord (projection fibers), organized into the centrum semiovale, the corona radiata and the deep bundles of the internal capsule and the long fasciculi. It is supplied by long penetrating medullary arteries from the pial network and by the lenticulostriate and choroidal arteries, which makes its periventricular and deep parts border zones. It is the tissue of small vessel disease, multiple sclerosis, leukodystrophy and diffuse axonal injury, and its disconnection produces the syndromes of the hemisphere without cortical damage.

anatomy.location: All the tissue between the cortical gray matter and the lateral ventricles and deep nuclei: the subcortical U-fibers, the centrum semiovale above the ventricles, the corona radiata fanning into the internal capsule, and the association bundles running beneath the cortex of each lobe and around the ventricles.

efferents.via: corticospinal, corticobulbar and corticopontine fibers via the internal capsule

cerebral-white-matter.function: Short association U-fibers join adjacent gyri, and the long fasciculi (arcuate and superior longitudinal, inferior longitudinal, inferior fronto-occipital, uncinate and cingulum) join the lobes into the language, attention, visual and limbic networks; the corpus callosum and the anterior commissure join the hemispheres; and the projection fibers of the corona radiata carry the corticospinal, corticobulbar, corticopontine and thalamocortical systems through the internal capsule. Oligodendrocyte myelin allows fast conduction, and periventricular regions are perfused by end-arteries so that they suffer first in hypoperfusion and hypertensive small vessel disease. Damage produces disconnection syndromes, slowing and gait and executive decline out of proportion to focal signs.

bestView.label: centrum semiovale above the lateral ventricles
corona radiata converging into the internal capsule

imaging.normalAppearance: Homogeneous bright tissue on T1 and dark on T2 between cortex and ventricles in adults; a thin periventricular FLAIR rim (ependymitis granularis) at the frontal horns is normal, and a few punctate white-matter hyperintensities are common after 60.

pathology.finding: Confluent periventricular and deep white-matter FLAIR hyperintensities with lacunes, microbleeds and enlarged perivascular spaces; correlates with gait and executive decline.
Ovoid periventricular lesions perpendicular to the ventricles (Dawson fingers), juxtacortical and callosal lesions, some enhancing when active.
Punctate microbleeds at the gray-white junction, in the corpus callosum and in the dorsolateral brainstem after acceleration injury, with coma out of proportion to CT findings.

Symmetric confluent white-matter T2 signal change with a pattern that suggests the disorder: parieto-occipital in adrenoleukodystrophy, frontal in Alexander disease, with sparing or involvement of U-fibers.

lesionEffects.deficit: Disconnection syndromes (conduction aphasia, alexia without agraphia, apraxia)
lesionEffects.mechanism: Interruption of association or commissural bundles with intact cortex

lesionEffects.deficit: Subcortical cognitive slowing, gait apraxia and executive dysfunction
lesionEffects.mechanism: Diffuse loss of frontal-subcortical connections in small vessel disease

lesionEffects.deficit: Contralateral hemiparesis or hemianopia from projection fiber lesions
lesionEffects.mechanism: Interruption of the corona radiata or the optic radiation

examination: Gait, speed of processing and executive tests in suspected small vessel disease
Vascular risk factor review
Tests of interhemispheric and intrahemispheric transfer when a disconnection is suspected
pearls: White-matter disease produces slowing and gait failure before any focal sign
Dawson fingers point away from the ventricles along the veins: that is demyelination, not vascular disease
A leukodystrophy is symmetric and confluent; vascular disease is patchy and asymmetric

pitfalls: Age-related white-matter hyperintensities are not multiple sclerosis; shape, location and the corpus callosum decide

cervical-enlargement.name: Cervical and lumbosacral enlargements
cervical-enlargement.summary: The cord is thickest where it supplies the limbs: the cervical enlargement (C5–T1, the brachial plexus segments) and the lumbosacral enlargement (L2–S3, the lumbosacral plexus segments), where the lateral motor columns and the sensory relay for the limbs swell the gray matter. Lesions here combine lower motor neuron signs in the limb at the level with upper motor neuron signs below, and their arterial supply depends on the largest radicular feeders, the C5–C6 radicular arteries above and the artery of Adamkiewicz below.

anatomy.location: Cervical enlargement from C4 to T1 segments, lying opposite the C3–T1 vertebrae; lumbosacral enlargement from L1 to S3 segments, lying opposite the T10–L1 vertebrae just above the conus.

cervical-enlargement.function: Motor and sensory integration for the upper and lower limbs: the largest motor neuron pools and the widest dorsal horns of the cord.

bestView.label: upper cervical cord above the cervical enlargement; the enlargements lie below the MNI volume

imaging.normalAppearance: On sagittal spine MRI the cord widens at C4–T1 and again at T10–L1; a lesion at the cervical enlargement is the commonest site of cervical spondylotic myelopathy, and the lumbosacral enlargement is the target of the anterior spinal artery syndrome after aortic surgery.

pathology.finding: Cord compression at C4–C6 by disc-osteophyte bars and ligamentum flavum with T2 signal change in the cord.

pathology.pathology: Central cord syndrome after hyperextension injury
pathology.finding: Central T2 hyperintensity of the cervical enlargement, arms weaker than legs.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: Sagittal and axial cervical and thoracolumbar T2

lesionEffects.deficit: Lower motor neuron weakness and wasting of the hand or arm with upper motor neuron signs in the legs
lesionEffects.mechanism: Cervical enlargement lesion

lesionEffects.deficit: Arms weaker than legs (central cord syndrome)
lesionEffects.mechanism: Central gray and medial corticospinal fibers of the cervical enlargement

lesionEffects.deficit: Lower motor neuron leg weakness with sphincter failure
lesionEffects.mechanism: Lumbosacral enlargement and conus

examination: Compare hand intrinsic muscle bulk and power with leg tone and reflexes
Reflexes: inverted supinator reflex at C5–C6
Sensory level and sphincters
pearls: Wasted hands with spastic legs: cervical cord at the enlargement (spondylosis, syrinx, MND)
An inverted brachioradialis reflex localizes a cervical lesion to C5–C6
