cervical-sympathetic-chain.name: Cervical sympathetic chain and stellate ganglion
cervical-sympathetic-chain.summary: The head and neck receive their sympathetic supply by a three-neuron chain: first-order neurons in the hypothalamus descend through the brainstem and lateral cervical cord to the ciliospinal center at C8–T2; second-order preganglionic fibers leave in the T1 root, cross the apex of the lung and ascend the cervical chain through the stellate and middle ganglia to the superior cervical ganglion; third-order postganglionic fibers travel on the internal carotid artery to the eye (dilator pupillae, Müller's muscle) and on the external carotid to the facial sweat glands. Interruption anywhere gives Horner syndrome, and the level can be inferred from sweating and from pharmacological pupil tests.

anatomy.location: Superior cervical ganglion at C2–C3 behind the carotid sheath; middle ganglion at C6; stellate ganglion in front of the C7 transverse process and the neck of the first rib, behind the subclavian artery at the apex of the pleura.

subdivisions.name: First-order (central) neuron
subdivisions.note: hypothalamus → brainstem tegmentum → lateral cervical cord; lesions: lateral medullary infarct, cord lesions

subdivisions.name: Second-order (preganglionic) neuron
subdivisions.note: C8–T2 → T1 root → stellate → superior cervical ganglion; lesions: Pancoast tumor, neck and thoracic surgery, trauma

subdivisions.name: Third-order (postganglionic) neuron
subdivisions.note: superior cervical ganglion → internal carotid plexus → cavernous sinus → eye; lesions: carotid dissection, cavernous sinus disease, cluster headache

cervical-sympathetic-chain.function: Pupillary dilation, elevation of the upper lid (Müller's muscle), sweating and vasoconstriction of the face, and sympathetic supply to the salivary glands, thyroid, heart and upper limb (stellate).

bestView.label: upper cervical cord: descending first-order sympathetic fibers in the lateral funiculus
cavernous carotid carrying the third-order fibers

imaging.normalAppearance: The chain is not seen as such; imaging follows the level suggested by the examination: brain and cervical cord MRI for first-order lesions, chest CT of the lung apex for second-order, and carotid CTA/MRI for third-order lesions.

pathology.finding: Apical lung mass invading the stellate ganglion and lower brachial plexus.
Crescentic mural hematoma of the internal carotid with a postganglionic Horner syndrome.
Dorsolateral medullary restriction with a central Horner syndrome.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: Targeted imaging by level: brain/cord MRI, chest CT, carotid CTA

lesionEffects.deficit: Horner syndrome with anhidrosis of the whole ipsilateral face and body side
lesionEffects.mechanism: First-order lesion (brainstem or cord)

lesionEffects.deficit: Horner syndrome with anhidrosis of the face only
lesionEffects.mechanism: Second-order lesion (chest apex, neck)
Third-order lesion beyond the superior cervical ganglion (sweat fibers travel with the external carotid)

lesionEffects.deficit: Harlequin sign: flushing and sweating on one side of the face
lesionEffects.mechanism: Unilateral sympathetic loss revealed on exertion

examination: Pupil inequality greater in the dark; dilation lag
Ptosis of 1–2 mm with 'upside-down' ptosis of the lower lid
Facial sweating after exertion or heat
Apraclonidine test (reverses the anisocoria) and hydroxyamphetamine test (fails to dilate a third-order Horner pupil)
Examine the neck, supraclavicular fossa and hands (T1)
pearls: Painful Horner syndrome is carotid dissection until proven otherwise; Horner with hand weakness is a Pancoast tumor; Horner with crossed brainstem signs is the medulla
Congenital Horner syndrome gives iris heterochromia because pigmentation needs sympathetic input

choroid-plexus.name: Choroid plexus and CSF production
choroid-plexus.summary: Choroid plexus is a frond-like vascular tissue covered by a specialized ependyma that hangs into the lateral, third and fourth ventricles and produces most of the roughly 500 mL of CSF made each day. Its capillaries are fenestrated, but the tight junctions between choroid epithelial cells form the blood–CSF barrier. The plexus of the lateral ventricles is supplied by the anterior and posterior choroidal arteries and is continuous through the foramina of Monro with the roof of the third ventricle; the fourth ventricular plexus protrudes through the foramina of Luschka. It calcifies with age, enhances avidly, and is the seat of choroid plexus papillomas and of xanthogranulomas.

anatomy.location: Body, atrium (glomus) and temporal horn of each lateral ventricle, the roof of the third ventricle, and the lower half of the roof of the fourth ventricle extending into the lateral recesses; absent from the frontal and occipital horns and the aqueduct.

choroid-plexus.function: Secretion of CSF by active transport, maintenance of the blood–CSF barrier, clearance of metabolites, and secretion of growth factors and transthyretin into the CSF.

bestView.label: glomus of the choroid plexus in the atrium
plexus in the roof of the third ventricle and the bodies of the lateral ventricles

imaging.normalAppearance: Enhances strongly after contrast on CT and MRI; the glomus in the atrium is frequently calcified in adults. Cysts (xanthogranulomas) in the glomus are benign and common in the elderly.

pathology.finding: Lobulated, intensely enhancing intraventricular mass, in the atrium in children and the fourth ventricle in adults, with hydrocephalus from CSF overproduction and obstruction.
Enhancing enlarged plexus in cryptococcal or tuberculous infection.
Generalized ventriculomegaly with a papilloma and no obstruction.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: T1+Gd MRI; CT for calcification

lesionEffects.mechanism: Plexus tumor

lesionEffects.deficit: Meningeal signs and altered CSF composition
lesionEffects.mechanism: Inflammation of the plexus in meningitis

examination: Signs of raised intracranial pressure
CSF analysis (protein, cells, glucose) when infection or malignancy is suspected
pearls: Choroid plexus enhancement and calcification are normal; asymmetric enlargement or a mass is not
CSF is produced at about 20 mL per hour, so the whole volume turns over three to four times a day

pitfalls: DERIVED MESH: the fourth-ventricular plexus (choroid-plexus-fourth-ventricle) is constructed, not segmented. It is the posterior (roof) boundary of the caudal half of the aseg fourth-ventricle label dilated by 1 mm, with two short extensions along the lateral recesses towards the foramina of Luschka, so it marks where the plexus lies rather than its fronds. The lateral-ventricle plexus meshes come from Z-Anatomy and are real surfaces.

circle-of-willis.name: Circle of Willis
circle-of-willis.summary: A polygon of arteries on the base of the brain, lying in the subarachnoid space around the optic chiasm, infundibulum and interpeduncular fossa. It is formed by the two internal carotid arteries, the anterior cerebral arteries joined by the anterior communicating artery, and the posterior cerebral arteries joined to the carotids by the posterior communicating arteries. It equalizes pressure and provides collateral flow when one feeding vessel narrows, but it is complete in only a minority of people, which is why the same occlusion causes very different strokes in different patients.

anatomy.location: Lies in the suprasellar, interpeduncular and chiasmatic cisterns around the optic chiasm, the tuber cinereum and the mammillary bodies, above the sella turcica and below the hypothalamus.

subdivisions.name: Anterior part
subdivisions.note: A1 segments and the anterior communicating artery in front of the chiasm

subdivisions.name: Lateral part
subdivisions.note: supraclinoid internal carotids and the posterior communicating arteries

subdivisions.name: Posterior part
subdivisions.note: P1 segments and the basilar bifurcation behind the mammillary bodies

relations.posterior: mammillary bodies and the interpeduncular fossa

circle-of-willis.function: Connects the two carotid systems with each other and with the vertebrobasilar system so that blood can be redistributed across the midline or between the anterior and posterior circulations. Central perforating branches from the circle (medial and lateral striate, anterior and posterior thalamoperforating groups) supply the hypothalamus, optic tract, basal ganglia, internal capsule and thalamus.

bestView.label: suprasellar cistern: the whole circle in one slice on CTA/MRA
carotid termini and A1 segments above the sella

imaging.normalAppearance: On axial T2 through the suprasellar cistern the circle appears as a ring of flow voids around the chiasm and infundibulum. Time-of-flight MRA or CTA displays the complete polygon; asymmetric A1 segments, absent or fetal PComms and duplications are normal variants.

pathology.finding: A round or lobulated outpouching at a branch point of the circle, most often the anterior communicating, posterior communicating and MCA bifurcation sites; a daughter sac and irregular contour suggest rupture risk.
Progressive stenosis of the distal carotids and proximal circle with a 'puff of smoke' cloud of basal collaterals; multiple flow voids in the basal ganglia on T2.
Smooth narrowing of the circle and its branches days 4–14 after aneurysm rupture, with delayed infarcts in the affected territories.
pathology.timing: Peaks around day 7–10

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: CTA or TOF MRA; DSA remains the reference for aneurysm anatomy

lesionEffects.deficit: Variable stroke severity for a given occlusion
lesionEffects.mechanism: Presence or absence of communicating arteries determines collateral flow
Rupture of a saccular aneurysm at a branch point of the circle
Aneurysm compressing the optic chiasm from below or laterally
PComm or basilar tip aneurysm

Neck stiffness and Kernig sign
Serial neurological examination after subarachnoid hemorrhage for delayed ischemia
pearls: Roughly one person in four has a complete, symmetrical circle; most have at least one hypoplastic segment
A carotid occlusion with a good circle may cause no symptoms; with a poor circle it may infarct the whole hemisphere

html.summary: A polygon of arteries on the base of the brain, lying in the subarachnoid space around the optic chiasm, infundibulum and interpeduncular fossa. It is formed by the two internal carotid arteries, the anterior cerebral arteries joined by the anterior communicating artery, and the posterior cerebral arteries joined to the carotids by the posterior communicating arteries. It equalizes pressure and provides collateral flow when one feeding vessel narrows, but it is complete in only a minority of people, which is why the same occlusion causes very different strokes in different patients.
html.function: Connects the two carotid systems with each other and with the vertebrobasilar system so that blood can be redistributed across the midline or between the anterior and posterior circulations. Central perforating branches from the circle (medial and lateral striate, anterior and posterior thalamoperforating groups) supply the hypothalamus, optic tract, basal ganglia, internal capsule and thalamus.
html.anatomy.location: Lies in the suprasellar, interpeduncular and chiasmatic cisterns around the optic chiasm, the tuber cinereum and the mammillary bodies, above the sella turcica and below the hypothalamus.
html.imaging.normalAppearance: On axial T2 through the suprasellar cistern the circle appears as a ring of flow voids around the chiasm and infundibulum. Time-of-flight MRA or CTA displays the complete polygon; asymmetric A1 segments, absent or fetal PComms and duplications are normal variants.
html.imaging.sequenceOfChoice: CTA or TOF MRA; DSA remains the reference for aneurysm anatomy

claustrum.name: Claustrum
claustrum.summary: A thin sheet of gray matter between the putamen and the insular cortex, separated from the putamen by the external capsule and from the insula by the extreme capsule. It is reciprocally connected with almost the entire cortex and has been proposed as a coordinator of cortical activity and of consciousness, but its clinical signature is meagre: it is involved in autoimmune and febrile encephalitides (the claustrum sign) and in some cases of status epilepticus, and its stimulation can suspend consciousness.

anatomy.location: Deep to the insula, lateral to the putamen, a vertical plate of gray matter stretching from the level of the anterior commissure to the posterior end of the lentiform nucleus; the external capsule lies medial, the extreme capsule lateral.

claustrum.function: Widespread reciprocal cortical connections suggesting a role in multisensory integration, attention and the binding of conscious experience; ventral claustrum connects with the amygdala and limbic cortex.

bestView.label: thin gray sheet between the putamen and the insula
claustrum between the external and extreme capsules

imaging.normalAppearance: A thin vertical gray line between the external and extreme capsules on axial T1/T2, easiest to see on high-resolution 3 T images; symmetric FLAIR hyperintensity is the claustrum sign of encephalitis.

pathology.pathology: Febrile infection-related epilepsy syndrome / autoimmune encephalitis
pathology.finding: Bilateral symmetric claustrum FLAIR hyperintensity ('claustrum sign') with refractory status epilepticus.
Restriction of the insula and claustrum in an MCA branch occlusion.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: Axial FLAIR

lesionEffects.deficit: Refractory seizures and altered consciousness with encephalitis
lesionEffects.mechanism: Bilateral claustral inflammation
Diffuse connectivity; deficits attributed to adjacent insula and putamen

examination: Level of consciousness and seizure semiology in encephalitis
Insular signs: taste, autonomic changes
pearls: Bilateral bright claustra on FLAIR in a febrile patient with refractory seizures is a recognized encephalitis pattern
The claustrum is anatomy that outruns clinical knowledge; keep expectations modest

cochlear-nuclei.name: Cochlear nuclei
cochlear-nuclei.summary: The dorsal and ventral cochlear nuclei drape over the inferior cerebellar peduncle at the pontomedullary junction and receive every fiber of the cochlear nerve. From them the auditory pathway becomes bilateral almost at once: second-order axons cross in the trapezoid body to the contralateral superior olive and lateral lemniscus, while others ascend on the same side. This early bilaterality is why a single central lesion above the nuclei never causes deafness in one ear, whereas a lesion of the nerve or nuclei does.

anatomy.location: Lateral surface of the inferior cerebellar peduncle at the lateral recess of the fourth ventricle, where the cochlear nerve enters at the cerebellopontine angle.

cochlear-nuclei.function: First central relay of hearing; begins frequency analysis and the separation of pathways for sound localization (ventral nucleus) and spectral analysis (dorsal nucleus).

bestView.label: lateral recess of the fourth ventricle at the cochlear nerve entry
cerebellopontine angle and internal acoustic meatus

imaging.normalAppearance: Not resolved on routine MRI; the cochlear nerve itself is seen on high-resolution T2 (CISS/FIESTA) entering the brainstem at the lateral recess. AICA infarcts that include the nuclei show lateral pontomedullary restriction.

pathology.finding: Lateral pontomedullary and anterior inferior cerebellar restricted diffusion with acute unilateral hearing loss.
Enhancing mass at the internal acoustic meatus and cerebellopontine angle compressing the nerve before it reaches the nuclei.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: High-resolution T2 of the internal acoustic meatus; DWI for infarct; audiometry

lesionEffects.mechanism: Nerve or cochlear nuclei, before the pathway becomes bilateral
Deafferentation of the nuclei

lesionEffects.deficit: Bilateral mild hearing loss and poor localization from a higher lesion
lesionEffects.mechanism: Lesions above the nuclei affect both ears because of the crossing

examination: Whisper test and finger rub in each ear
Rinne and Weber tuning-fork tests to separate conductive from sensorineural loss
Formal audiometry
pearls: Unilateral deafness is a nerve, cochlear nucleus or cochlear problem, never a hemispheric one

conus-medullaris.name: Conus medullaris
conus-medullaris.summary: The tapered lower end of the spinal cord, containing the sacral segments (S2–S5 and coccygeal), ending at the L1–L2 disc level in most adults, from which the filum terminale continues to the coccyx. It houses the sacral parasympathetic nucleus and Onuf's nucleus, so its lesions produce early, symmetric sphincter failure and saddle anesthesia with relatively little leg weakness, the conus syndrome, which must be distinguished from the asymmetric, painful, lower motor neuron cauda equina syndrome affecting the roots below it.

anatomy.location: Lower border of L1 to the L1–L2 disc in most adults (range T12–L3), surrounded by the emerging lumbar and sacral roots of the cauda equina; the level is fixed by the age of two years.

conus-medullaris.function: Contains the sacral segments: parasympathetic outflow to the bladder, rectum and genitals, motor neurons for the pelvic floor and sphincters, and sensory relay for the perineum.

bestView.label: cord (the conus lies at L1–L2, below the MNI volume)

imaging.normalAppearance: On sagittal lumbar MRI the conus should end at or above L2; a low-lying conus with a thick filum indicates tethering. Conus lesions (ependymoma, infarct, myelitis) appear as focal signal change or expansion of the cone.

pathology.finding: T2 hyperintensity and restricted diffusion of the conus after aortic surgery or in vascular malformations.
Conus below L2 with a thickened filum or lipoma.
Enhancing mass of the conus and filum with hemorrhage.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: Sagittal and axial lumbar T2 and T1+Gd; DWI

lesionEffects.deficit: Early urinary retention and fecal incontinence
lesionEffects.mechanism: Sacral autonomic nuclei
Sacral dermatome relay

lesionEffects.deficit: Mild, symmetric leg weakness with mixed reflexes (brisk knee, absent ankle)
lesionEffects.mechanism: Sacral segments and adjacent lumbar tracts
Sacral parasympathetic outflow

examination: Perianal pin-prick, anal tone and reflex, bulbocavernosus reflex
Bladder scan for retention
Ankle versus knee reflexes
pearls: Sphincters first, symmetric and painless: conus. Legs first, asymmetric and painful: cauda equina

corona-radiata.name: Corona radiata
corona-radiata.summary: The fan of projection fibers that spreads upward and outward from the internal capsule into the centrum semiovale to reach every part of the cortex, interweaving with the callosal and association fibers. It carries the corticospinal, corticobulbar and corticopontine fibers descending from the motor areas and the thalamocortical radiations ascending to the sensory, visual and auditory cortices. Lacunar infarcts and the internal watershed lie here, and subcortical small vessel disease appears in it as the periventricular and deep white matter hyperintensities of ageing.

anatomy.location: Deep white matter of each hemisphere above the internal capsule and lateral to the lateral ventricles, converging downward toward the capsule and fanning upward into the centrum semiovale beneath the cortex.

corona-radiata.function: Conduction of projection fibers between the cortex and the internal capsule: motor outflow and sensory inflow for the whole hemisphere.

bestView.label: corona radiata lateral to the body of the lateral ventricle
fibers fanning from the internal capsule to the cortex

imaging.normalAppearance: Deep white matter lateral to the ventricles on axial FLAIR; punctate and confluent FLAIR hyperintensities here reflect small vessel disease, and a linear chain of DWI lesions parallel to the ventricle marks an internal watershed infarct.

pathology.pathology: Lacunar infarct of the corona radiata
pathology.finding: Small restriction in the deep white matter lateral to the ventricle; pure motor or ataxic hemiparesis.
String of small lesions in the corona radiata on the side of a carotid stenosis.
Confluent periventricular and deep white matter FLAIR hyperintensity with lacunes and microbleeds.
Ovoid periventricular and juxtacortical FLAIR lesions.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: FLAIR and DWI

lesionEffects.mechanism: Corticospinal and corticopontine fibers

lesionEffects.deficit: Gait disturbance, cognitive slowing and pseudobulbar affect with diffuse disease
lesionEffects.mechanism: Bilateral subcortical small vessel disease
Thalamocortical radiation

examination: Power and coordination
Gait (short-stepped, wide-based in small vessel disease)
Cognitive speed and executive testing
Vascular risk factor review

corpus-callosum.name: Corpus callosum
corpus-callosum.summary: The great commissure of about 200 million axons joining homologous areas of the two hemispheres, arching over the lateral ventricles in the floor of the interhemispheric fissure. Its rostrum and genu connect the frontal lobes, the body the motor and parietal regions, and the splenium the occipital and temporal lobes. It lets the hemispheres share information, so its interruption (surgery, infarction, tumor, demyelination) causes disconnection syndromes: alexia without agraphia when the splenium is cut with the left occipital cortex, left-hand apraxia and agraphia when the anterior body is cut. Lesions of the callosum are a hallmark of multiple sclerosis, diffuse axonal injury and butterfly glioma.

anatomy.location: Midline, above the septum pellucidum and fornix and below the cingulate gyrus, from the rostrum beneath the genu in front to the splenium above the pineal region behind; its fibers spread as the radiations into the centrum semiovale and form the forceps minor and major at either end.

subdivisions.name: Rostrum and genu
subdivisions.note: prefrontal and orbitofrontal connections (forceps minor)

subdivisions.name: Body
subdivisions.note: premotor, motor, somatosensory and parietal connections

subdivisions.name: Isthmus
subdivisions.note: pre- and postcentral and auditory connections

subdivisions.name: Splenium
subdivisions.note: posterior parietal, temporal and occipital connections (forceps major)

corpus-callosum.function: Interhemispheric transfer of sensory, motor and cognitive information; coordination of bimanual movements; transfer of visual information from the right hemisphere to left-hemisphere language areas.

bestView.label: rostrum, genu, body and splenium on the midline
body of the callosum forming the roof of the lateral ventricles

imaging.normalAppearance: The bright white arch on midline sagittal T1; thinning of the body or splenium suggests chronic white matter disease or hydrocephalus, and callosal lesions perpendicular to the ventricles (Dawson's fingers) on sagittal FLAIR are characteristic of multiple sclerosis.

pathology.finding: Ovoid FLAIR-bright lesions at the callososeptal interface and perpendicular to the callosum on sagittal FLAIR.
Microhemorrhages in the splenium and body on SWI after rotational trauma; associated with poor outcome.
Enhancing mass crossing the callosum into both hemispheres; lymphoma is homogeneously enhancing and restricts diffusion.
Transient oval restriction in the splenium with encephalitis, antiepileptic withdrawal or metabolic disturbance; reversible.
Absent callosum with parallel lateral ventricles (racing car sign), colpocephaly and radially oriented medial gyri.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: Sagittal FLAIR and T1; SWI for trauma; DWI

lesionEffects.mechanism: Splenium plus left occipital lobe: the seeing right hemisphere cannot reach the left language cortex

lesionEffects.deficit: Left-hand apraxia and agraphia, left tactile anomia
lesionEffects.mechanism: Anterior body: left hemisphere language cannot reach the right motor cortex

lesionEffects.deficit: Alien hand syndrome and intermanual conflict
lesionEffects.mechanism: Anterior callosal disconnection with medial frontal involvement
Loss of interhemispheric motor transfer

Write with the left hand and imitate gestures with each hand
Read words presented briefly in the left visual field
Observe for a hand acting on its own

cortex-calcarine.name: Calcarine (primary visual) cortex
cortex-calcarine.summary: The primary visual cortex lines the walls of the calcarine sulcus on the medial occipital surface and extends around the pole. It receives the optic radiation from the lateral geniculate body and is identified histologically by the stria of Gennari, a band of myelinated fibers in layer IV. Its map is precise: the contralateral hemifield is represented with the macula at the occipital pole occupying half the area, the periphery anteriorly, and the lower field on the upper bank (cuneus) and the upper field on the lower bank (lingual gyrus). Lesions give the most congruous homonymous field defects of any visual pathway lesion.

anatomy.location: Both banks of the calcarine sulcus from the junction with the parieto-occipital sulcus back to the occipital pole, extending slightly onto the lateral surface of the pole.

cortex-calcarine.function: First cortical stage of vision: orientation, edge, spatial frequency, binocular disparity and color contrast analysis of the contralateral hemifield, relayed to extrastriate areas.

bestView.label: calcarine sulcus with cuneus above and lingual gyrus below
striate cortex on the medial occipital surface near the pole

imaging.normalAppearance: Cortex lining the calcarine sulcus on sagittal T1; the stria of Gennari is a fine dark line within the cortex on high-resolution T1 or T2. Calcarine infarcts are wedge-shaped on the medial surface with the pole often intact.

pathology.finding: Restricted diffusion along the calcarine banks, pole spared.
Flow voids in the calcarine region with headache, visual auras and field defect.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: DWI; perimetry

lesionEffects.deficit: Congruous homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing
lesionEffects.mechanism: Whole calcarine cortex with spared pole

Lower bank (lingual gyrus)

cortex-central-operculum.name: Central opercular cortex
cortex-central-operculum.summary: The central operculum is the part of the precentral and postcentral gyri that folds under to form the roof of the middle portion of the lateral sulcus, immediately above the insula. It contains the ventral end of the primary motor and sensory maps, the face, tongue, larynx and pharynx representations, and the secondary somatosensory cortex lies just behind it in the parietal operculum. Lesions produce contralateral lower facial weakness, dysarthria and dysphagia and loss of sensation on the face, and bilateral lesions cause the anarthric opercular syndrome; middle cerebral artery branch infarcts and perisylvian polymicrogyria are the common causes.

anatomy.location: The buried inferior ends of the precentral and postcentral gyri above the insula, between the frontal operculum in front and the parietal operculum behind, forming the upper bank of the posterior Sylvian fissure.

efferents.to: Facial, hypoglossal, ambiguus and trigeminal motor nuclei

cortex-central-operculum.function: The lower end of the motor homunculus here drives the muscles of the face, jaw, tongue, larynx and pharynx through the corticobulbar tract, mostly bilaterally except for the lower face, and the adjacent sensory strip receives touch and proprioception from the face and mouth through the ventral posteromedial thalamus. The region controls the fine sequencing of speech and swallowing, and its secondary somatosensory field integrates pain and touch from both sides of the body. Focal seizures here produce contralateral facial clonic jerking, tongue tingling and drooling that may march to the arm.

bestView.label: central operculum above the posterior insula
buried ends of the central gyri at the Sylvian fissure

imaging.normalAppearance: The lower ends of the precentral and postcentral gyri as they curve into the Sylvian fissure, best seen on coronal images through the posterior insula; the face motor area is at the lateral convexity above the fissure.

pathology.pathology: MCA branch infarct with facial weakness and dysarthria
pathology.finding: Small cortical restricted diffusion at the inferior end of the central gyri; often mistaken clinically for a brainstem or peripheral facial lesion.
Thickened irregular cortex with shallow sulci around the Sylvian fissures, often bilateral, with pseudobulbar palsy and epilepsy from childhood.

pathology.finding: Clonic jerking of the contralateral face with drooling and speech arrest; EEG shows a fronto-central focus.

lesionEffects.deficit: Contralateral lower facial weakness sparing the forehead
lesionEffects.mechanism: Loss of the crossed corticobulbar projection to the lower facial motor nucleus
Weakness and incoordination of the tongue, palate and pharynx from the ventral motor cortex

lesionEffects.deficit: Loss of touch and position sense on the face and in the mouth
lesionEffects.mechanism: Damage to the ventral postcentral gyrus receiving the VPM thalamic projection

examination: Test the lower face: show the teeth, puff the cheeks; forehead sparing points to a supranuclear lesion
Palatal movement, gag, swallowing and tongue power and speed
Facial two-point discrimination and stereognosis of objects in the mouth

cortex-frontal-medial.name: Frontal medial cortex
cortex-frontal-medial.summary: The frontal medial cortex is the medial prefrontal cortex below the anterior cingulate and in front of the subcallosal area, corresponding to the medial part of Brodmann areas 10, 11 and 32 (the ventromedial prefrontal cortex). It integrates the value of choices, regulates emotion through its dense connections with the amygdala and hypothalamus, and forms the anterior hub of the default mode network with the posterior cingulate. It is damaged by anterior cerebral and anterior communicating artery pathology, by subfrontal tumors and by head injury, producing the impulsive, socially inappropriate and poorly regulated behavior classically described after orbitomedial frontal damage.

anatomy.location: Medial surface of the frontal lobe below the cingulate gyrus and anterior to the paraterminal gyrus and the subcallosal area, continuous below with the gyrus rectus and the medial orbital cortex; it faces the falx and the contralateral cortex across the interhemispheric fissure.

afferents.via: uncinate fasciculus and ventral amygdalofugal pathway

cortex-frontal-medial.function: Ventromedial prefrontal neurons encode the expected value and the emotional consequence of an option and pass this to the anterior cingulate, the striatum and the amygdala, so that decisions are guided by anticipated feelings; without it patients choose immediate gains over long-term benefit and cannot learn from social punishment. The region is also the front of the default mode network active in self-reflection and thinking about other minds, it suppresses the amygdala during extinction of fear, and it modulates autonomic tone through the hypothalamus and the periaqueductal gray. Bilateral loss produces apathy, whereas orbital-medial damage sparing the anterior cingulate produces disinhibition.

bestView.label: medial prefrontal cortex below the cingulate gyrus
ventromedial frontal cortex above the gyrus rectus

imaging.normalAppearance: Cortex on the medial surface of the frontal lobe in front of the genu and below the cingulate sulcus; thin, with variable sulcation, best seen on sagittal images a few millimeters off the midline.

pathology.finding: Subarachnoid blood in the interhemispheric fissure and a hematoma in the medial frontal cortex or gyrus rectus; later infarcts of the basal forebrain.
Enhancing dural mass under the medial frontal lobes with edema tracking along the cingulum and personality change.
Medial and orbital frontal atrophy with a widened interhemispheric fissure anterior to the genu.

lesionEffects.deficit: Impulsivity, poor decision making and social disinhibition
lesionEffects.mechanism: Loss of value-based decision signals from the ventromedial prefrontal cortex to the striatum and amygdala
Disconnection of the medial prefrontal cortex from the anterior cingulate and hypothalamus

lesionEffects.deficit: Autonomic dysregulation and altered fear extinction
lesionEffects.mechanism: Loss of prefrontal inhibition of the amygdala and the hypothalamic autonomic outflow

examination: Collateral history of personality change, gambling, tactlessness or new indifference
Bedside social cognition: reading emotion in faces, understanding faux pas
Look for coexisting anosmia and visual field defects when a subfrontal mass is suspected
pearls: The patient with ventromedial frontal damage knows the rules but does not use them; intelligence tests can be normal
Frontal personality change plus anosmia is a subfrontal mass until imaged
Anterior communicating aneurysm patients combine amnesia (basal forebrain) with medial frontal disinhibition

pitfalls: Lesions here can produce a picture indistinguishable from a primary psychiatric illness; a first psychiatric presentation after 40 deserves imaging

html.summary: The frontal medial cortex is the medial prefrontal cortex below the anterior cingulate and in front of the subcallosal area, corresponding to the medial part of Brodmann areas 10, 11 and 32 (the ventromedial prefrontal cortex). It integrates the value of choices, regulates emotion through its dense connections with the amygdala and hypothalamus, and forms the anterior hub of the default mode network with the posterior cingulate. It is damaged by anterior cerebral and anterior communicating artery pathology, by subfrontal tumors and by head injury, producing the impulsive, socially inappropriate and poorly regulated behavior classically described after orbitomedial frontal damage.
html.function: Ventromedial prefrontal neurons encode the expected value and the emotional consequence of an option and pass this to the anterior cingulate, the striatum and the amygdala, so that decisions are guided by anticipated feelings; without it patients choose immediate gains over long-term benefit and cannot learn from social punishment. The region is also the front of the default mode network active in self-reflection and thinking about other minds, it suppresses the amygdala during extinction of fear, and it modulates autonomic tone through the hypothalamus and the periaqueductal gray. Bilateral loss produces apathy, whereas orbital-medial damage sparing the anterior cingulate produces disinhibition.
html.anatomy.location: Medial surface of the frontal lobe below the cingulate gyrus and anterior to the paraterminal gyrus and the subcallosal area, continuous below with the gyrus rectus and the medial orbital cortex; it faces the falx and the contralateral cortex across the interhemispheric fissure.
html.imaging.normalAppearance: Cortex on the medial surface of the frontal lobe in front of the genu and below the cingulate sulcus; thin, with variable sulcation, best seen on sagittal images a few millimeters off the midline.

cortex-frontal-operculum.name: Frontal operculum cortex
cortex-frontal-operculum.summary: The frontal operculum is the lip of frontal cortex that hangs over the anterior part of the insula and forms the upper anterior wall of the lateral sulcus, below the inferior frontal gyrus and in front of the central operculum. It houses ventral premotor cortex, the anterior part of the gustatory cortex and the frontal extension of the language cortex, and it is tightly bound to the insula in function and in disease: middle cerebral artery infarcts, operculo-insular seizures and the opercular (Foix-Chavany-Marie) syndrome all involve it. It is one of the regions where a lesion in either hemisphere produces speech articulation problems.

anatomy.location: Cortex of the lateral frontal surface that folds under to form the roof of the anterior Sylvian fissure, medial to the pars opercularis and triangularis, in contact with the anterior insula; it continues posteriorly as the central operculum.

efferents.to: Cranial nerve motor nuclei (V, VII, IX, X, XII)

cortex-frontal-operculum.function: The frontal operculum coordinates the muscles of the mouth, pharynx and larynx for speech, chewing and swallowing through its projection to the corticobulbar tract, contributes to speech initiation and articulation, and contains part of the gustatory cortex that gives taste its conscious quality. Bilateral damage disconnects the cranial nerve nuclei from voluntary control while automatic emotional movements survive: the patient cannot open the mouth on command but yawns and laughs normally. Seizures beginning here produce salivation, throat sensations, gustatory auras and speech arrest.

bestView.label: frontal operculum over the anterior insula
roof of the anterior Sylvian fissure

imaging.normalAppearance: The frontal operculum is the cortex covering the anterior insula on coronal images, seen as the upper lip of the Sylvian fissure; its gyri are short and curved and continuous with the pars opercularis laterally.

pathology.finding: Bilateral opercular infarcts or perinatal polymicrogyria of the perisylvian cortex in a patient with anarthria and dysphagia but preserved emotional facial movement.
Seizures with throat constriction, salivation, gustatory aura and speech arrest; scalp EEG shows fronto-temporal discharges that are poorly localized.
Restricted diffusion of the frontal operculum and adjacent insula with dysarthria, dysphagia and contralateral lower facial weakness.

lesionEffects.deficit: Anarthria and dysphagia with preserved emotional facial movement
lesionEffects.mechanism: Bilateral loss of voluntary corticobulbar control of the face, tongue and pharynx from the opercular cortex

lesionEffects.deficit: Dysarthria and contralateral lower facial weakness
lesionEffects.mechanism: Unilateral opercular damage to the ventral motor and premotor cortex

lesionEffects.deficit: Gustatory hallucinations and salivation during seizures
lesionEffects.mechanism: Ictal activation of the opercular gustatory cortex

examination: Ask the patient to open the mouth, protrude the tongue and swallow on command, then watch them yawn or smile spontaneously
Assess articulation with repeated syllables (pa-ta-ka)
Taste testing and a seizure history with throat or taste auras
pearls: Automatic-voluntary dissociation of the face means bilateral opercular cortex, not brainstem
Opercular seizures look like panic attacks with a throat sensation and drooling
Both hemispheres contribute to speech articulation; a right opercular stroke can cause dysarthria

pitfalls: Sudden anarthria with a normal brainstem examination should prompt imaging of both opercula, not a diagnosis of conversion

cortex-intracalcarine.name: Intracalcarine cortex
cortex-intracalcarine.summary: The intracalcarine cortex is the primary visual cortex buried in the walls of the calcarine sulcus on the medial occipital surface, the striate cortex of Brodmann area 17 named for the stria of Gennari visible to the naked eye. The upper wall receives the contralateral lower visual field and the lower wall the upper field, with the macula represented at the occipital pole and the far periphery at the anterior end near the parieto-occipital junction. It is supplied by the calcarine branch of the posterior cerebral artery, so a PCA occlusion produces a congruous contralateral homonymous hemianopia, often with macular sparing; bilateral destruction causes cortical blindness and, with unawareness, Anton syndrome.

anatomy.location: Cortex lining the calcarine sulcus from the occipital pole forward to its junction with the parieto-occipital sulcus, between the cuneus above and the lingual gyrus below, facing the falx and the contralateral calcarine cortex.

efferents.to: Cuneus, lingual gyrus and lateral occipital cortex (V2-V5)

cortex-intracalcarine.function: Striate cortex receives the geniculocalcarine radiation in layer IV, where the stria of Gennari marks the dense myelinated input, and analyzes the retinal image into oriented edges, spatial frequencies, binocular disparity and color contrast within a precise retinotopic map in which the central few degrees occupy the posterior half. It sends its output to the surrounding extrastriate areas on the cuneus and lingual gyrus and to the dorsal and ventral streams, and it projects back to the lateral geniculate nucleus and to the superior colliculus. Destructive lesions cause a congruous field defect in the contralateral hemifield, and irritative lesions cause elementary hallucinations of flashes and colored shapes in the corresponding location.

bestView.label: calcarine sulcus on the medial occipital surface
striate cortex within the calcarine fissure

imaging.normalAppearance: The deep horizontal calcarine sulcus on medial sagittal images, running from the occipital pole to the parieto-occipital sulcus; on high-resolution T1 images the stria of Gennari appears as a thin dark line within the gray matter.

pathology.finding: Restricted diffusion of the calcarine cortex and adjacent cuneus and lingual gyrus; the occipital pole is often spared through MCA collaterals.
Bilateral calcarine infarcts, typically from basilar or bilateral PCA occlusion, with blindness that the patient denies.
Elementary visual hallucinations in the contralateral field followed by ictal blindness or eye deviation; occipital spikes accentuated by eye closure.

lesionEffects.mechanism: Destruction of the whole calcarine cortex of one side
Lesion confined to the upper (lower field) or lower (upper field) calcarine bank
Bilateral striate destruction; the pupillary pathway leaves the visual pathway before the cortex

examination: Confrontation fields in all quadrants and formal perimetry
Pupillary light reflexes, which are normal in cortical visual loss
Ask about awareness of the deficit and check for confabulation about what is seen
pearls: A hemianopia with normal pupils and macular sparing is calcarine cortex, not optic tract
Cortical blindness with denial is Anton syndrome; the patient walks into furniture and blames the light
The macula sits at the occipital pole where MCA and PCA branches overlap, which is why it survives a PCA occlusion

pitfalls: Cortical visual loss with a normal fundus and normal pupils is often called functional; perimetry and MRI settle it

cortex-lateral-occipital-inferior.name: Lateral occipital cortex, inferior division
cortex-lateral-occipital-inferior.summary: The inferior lateral occipital cortex is the lower part of the outer surface of the occipital lobe, below the lateral occipital sulcus and above the preoccipital notch, continuous in front with the temporo-occipital cortex. It contains the shape- and object-selective cortex of the lateral occipital complex and part of the extrastriate body area, the beginning of the ventral visual stream that identifies what is seen. It is supplied by the posterior cerebral artery with a middle cerebral artery contribution laterally, and its lesions cause apperceptive agnosia and contralateral upper quadrant defects; the region is a frequent site of visual auras and of the hallucinations of Charles Bonnet syndrome.

anatomy.location: Lower lateral occipital surface between the lateral occipital sulcus above and the inferior margin of the hemisphere at the preoccipital notch, behind the inferior temporal gyrus and lateral to the occipital fusiform gyrus.

afferents.from: Primary visual cortex and lingual gyrus

cortex-lateral-occipital-inferior.function: Neurons of the lateral occipital complex respond to the shape of objects regardless of the cues that define them, whether luminance edges, texture or motion, and represent bodies and body parts in an adjacent patch; this shape information feeds the fusiform and inferior temporal recognition areas. The region is retinotopic for the contralateral upper field and it contributes to the perception of depth and of figure from ground. Damage produces apperceptive agnosia with inability to copy or match shapes despite intact acuity, and release phenomena produce formed hallucinations of objects and figures when the input is lost.

bestView.label: inferior lateral occipital cortex above the preoccipital notch
lower lateral occipital convexity

imaging.normalAppearance: Lateral occipital cortex below the lateral occipital sulcus on axial images through the level of the atria and below, behind the temporo-occipital junction.

pathology.finding: Restricted diffusion of the inferior lateral occipital cortex with a contralateral upper quadrantanopia and impaired shape perception.
Formed visual hallucinations of people or patterns in a patient with visual loss from any cause; imaging excludes a structural occipital lesion.
Focal FLAIR-bright cortex at the lateral occipital surface in a patient with visual seizures.

lesionEffects.mechanism: Loss of shape integration in the lateral occipital complex
Involvement of the ventral extrastriate cortex or the lower optic radiation
Release or ictal activation of object-selective visual cortex

examination: Copy and match simple shapes and letters
Quadrantic visual fields
Ask about hallucinations of people, animals or patterns and whether the patient knows they are unreal
pearls: Charles Bonnet hallucinations are unreal and known to be unreal by the patient; they are a sign of visual loss, not psychosis
An apperceptive agnosic cannot copy a drawing; an associative agnosic copies it slavishly and still cannot recognize it
The lower lateral occipital cortex represents the upper visual field

pitfalls: Hallucinations in a patient with poor vision should prompt an eye examination and an occipital MRI before antipsychotics

cortex-lateral-occipital-superior.name: Lateral occipital cortex, superior division
cortex-lateral-occipital-superior.summary: The superior lateral occipital cortex is the upper part of the convex outer surface of the occipital lobe, above the lateral occipital sulcus and behind the parieto-occipital junction, corresponding to dorsal extrastriate visual areas (V3A, V6 and the lateral occipital complex) that lead into the parietal dorsal stream. It represents where objects are and how they move relative to the observer and guides eye and hand movements toward them, and it is a watershed between the middle and posterior cerebral arteries. Lesions produce optic ataxia, defective motion perception and the simultanagnosia of Balint syndrome when bilateral, and the region is damaged early in posterior cortical atrophy.

anatomy.location: Upper lateral surface of the occipital lobe from the parieto-occipital sulcus and the superior parietal lobule down to the lateral occipital sulcus, and from the occipital pole forward to the angular gyrus.

efferents.to: Superior parietal lobule and intraparietal sulcus

cortex-lateral-occipital-superior.function: Dorsal extrastriate cortex here computes the position of objects in eye- and head-centered coordinates, their motion and the optic flow produced by self-movement, and passes this to the intraparietal cortex for reaching, grasping and shifting attention; it also contains part of the shape-selective lateral occipital complex. It is retinotopic with the contralateral lower field, and it contributes to visually guided saccades and to the perception of depth and of three-dimensional structure from motion. Bilateral damage leaves the patient able to see single objects but unable to perceive the scene as a whole or to reach for what is seen.

bestView.label: superior lateral occipital cortex behind the angular gyrus
dorsolateral occipital convexity

imaging.normalAppearance: Convex lateral occipital cortex above the lateral occipital sulcus on axial images above the atria, behind the angular gyrus and lateral to the parieto-occipital sulcus.

pathology.finding: Symmetric border-zone restricted diffusion in the superior lateral occipital and parietal cortex after hypotension, producing Balint syndrome.
Bilateral dorsal occipito-parietal atrophy with simultanagnosia, optic ataxia and ocular apraxia; hippocampi relatively spared.
Cortical and subcortical vasogenic edema of the occipito-parietal convexity with visual disturbance and seizures.

lesionEffects.deficit: Optic ataxia: misreaching for seen objects
lesionEffects.mechanism: Loss of the dorsal-stream transformation from visual location to hand movement
Loss of the ability to integrate multiple objects into a scene

lesionEffects.deficit: Impaired motion perception and visually guided saccades
lesionEffects.mechanism: Damage to dorsal motion and attention areas

examination: Reaching for a target in the peripheral field while fixating centrally
Describe a complex picture: does the patient report only one item at a time?
Visual fields and pursuit and saccade accuracy
pearls: Balint syndrome is bilateral dorsal occipito-parietal disease: the patient sees but cannot find, reach or take in a scene
The occipito-parietal border zone is the cortex most vulnerable to a drop in perfusion in both hemispheres
Posterior cortical atrophy is Alzheimer disease starting in the dorsal visual stream; memory comes later

pitfalls: Simultanagnosia can pass as poor vision on acuity testing; the patient reads letters but not the scene

cortex-orbitofrontal.name: Frontal orbital cortex
cortex-orbitofrontal.summary: The orbital frontal cortex is the inferior surface of the frontal lobe resting on the orbital roof and the cribriform plate, made of the gyrus rectus medially and the orbital gyri around the H-shaped orbital sulcus laterally (Brodmann areas 11, 12, 13 and 47). It is the cortex of reward, taste and smell integration and of social and emotional behavior, and the region most vulnerable to contusion when the brain slides over the rough anterior fossa floor. Its damage produces the disinhibited, jocular, impulsive patient of the Phineas Gage type, and it atrophies early in behavioral variant frontotemporal dementia.

anatomy.location: Inferior surface of the frontal lobe from the frontal pole back to the anterior perforated substance, with the olfactory sulcus and the olfactory bulb and tract running along the gyrus rectus medially and the orbital gyri lateral to it.

cortex-orbitofrontal.function: The orbitofrontal cortex assigns and updates the reward value of stimuli: it receives taste from the insular gustatory cortex, smell directly from the piriform cortex, and visceral and emotional information from the amygdala and the hypothalamus, and it signals when an expected reward changes so that behavior is reversed. Lateral orbital cortex inhibits inappropriate responses and processes punishment; medial orbital cortex encodes reward and is part of the ventral prefrontal loop with the ventral striatum. It also contributes to olfactory identification and hedonic evaluation, which is why anosmia and altered food preference accompany orbital damage.

bestView.label: orbital gyri on the roof of the orbit
orbital surface of the frontal lobe with the olfactory sulcus

imaging.normalAppearance: Flat gyri on the floor of the anterior cranial fossa above the orbital roofs; the gyrus rectus is the straight medial gyrus beside the olfactory tract, seen best on coronal images through the frontal horns.

pathology.finding: Hemosiderin and gliosis of the inferior frontal surfaces on susceptibility and FLAIR images, often bilateral, months after a head injury.
Extra-axial enhancing midline mass indenting the gyri recti and displacing the olfactory tracts, with anosmia and frontal behavior.
Orbitofrontal and anterior temporal atrophy, often asymmetric, with relative sparing of the posterior cortex.

lesionEffects.mechanism: Loss of orbitofrontal inhibition of limbic and striatal drives

lesionEffects.deficit: Impaired reversal learning and poor judgement
lesionEffects.mechanism: Loss of the value-updating signal from the orbitofrontal cortex to the striatum
Damage to the olfactory tract along the gyrus rectus and to the orbital olfactory cortex

examination: Smell testing with a familiar odor in each nostril
Ask about tact, jokes, spending and eating habits
Go/no-go and Stroop-type tasks for response inhibition
pearls: Orbitofrontal patients pass most cognitive tests and fail at life
The orbital surface is the site of contusion in a fall on the back of the head
Olfactory groove meningioma is the classic subfrontal tumor and presents with personality change and anosmia

pitfalls: Orbitofrontal contusions are invisible on early CT under the bony orbital roof; MRI with susceptibility imaging shows them

cortex-parietal-operculum.name: Parietal operculum cortex
cortex-parietal-operculum.summary: The parietal operculum is the part of the parietal lobe that folds under the posterior lateral sulcus above the posterior insula and the planum temporale, behind the central operculum. It contains the secondary somatosensory cortex (SII) and the parieto-insular vestibular cortex, so it is the cortex of tactile object recognition, of the affective dimension of pain, and of the conscious sense of head motion and verticality. It is a middle cerebral artery territory, and its lesions produce impaired stereognosis and tactile learning, altered pain perception, and vertigo or tilt illusions; seizures here give bilateral tingling, pain or a sense of motion.

anatomy.location: Buried parietal cortex forming the roof of the posterior Sylvian fissure between the central operculum in front and the supramarginal gyrus behind, above the planum temporale and the posterior insula.

afferents.via: short association fibers and corpus callosum

afferents.from: Ventral posterior thalamus and posterior nuclear group

cortex-parietal-operculum.function: SII receives touch and proprioception from both sides of the body through the primary somatosensory cortex and the thalamus, with the two hands represented together, and it integrates them for recognizing objects by touch, learning tactile skills and attending to a stimulus; it also receives nociceptive input and, with the insula and cingulate, gives pain its unpleasant and motivational quality. The adjacent parieto-insular vestibular cortex combines vestibular, visual and neck proprioceptive signals to perceive self-motion and the vertical. Both sides of the body are represented, so a unilateral lesion produces subtler and bilateral tactile deficits than a postcentral lesion.

bestView.label: parietal operculum above the posterior insula
roof of the posterior Sylvian fissure

imaging.normalAppearance: The upper bank of the posterior Sylvian fissure on coronal images through the posterior insula, between the postcentral gyrus above and the planum temporale below.

pathology.finding: Small cortical restricted diffusion at the parietal operculum with impaired stereognosis, tactile extinction and sometimes vertigo.
Bilateral or contralateral tingling, painful auras or a sensation of rotation; scalp EEG shows a centro-parietal focus.
Lesion involving the parietal operculum, insula or thalamus with delayed burning pain and allodynia in the contralateral limbs.

lesionEffects.mechanism: Loss of the SII integration of touch and proprioception

lesionEffects.deficit: Altered pain perception or central pain
lesionEffects.mechanism: Damage to the opercular-insular nociceptive cortex

lesionEffects.deficit: Vertigo, tilt and loss of the subjective vertical
lesionEffects.mechanism: Involvement of the parieto-insular vestibular cortex

examination: Stereognosis: identify coins and keys placed in the hand with eyes closed
Bilateral simultaneous tactile stimulation for extinction
Subjective visual vertical (ask the patient to set a line upright) and a history of tilt illusions
pearls: SII is bilateral: a unilateral lesion impairs tactile recognition subtly, not with anesthesia
Painful seizures are rare and almost always parietal opercular or insular
The vestibular cortex sits here: cortical vertigo exists and is not a brainstem sign

pitfalls: Astereognosis with intact primary sensation is cortical; do not attribute it to a neuropathy

cortex-prefrontal.name: Prefrontal cortex
cortex-prefrontal.summary: The large anterior part of the frontal lobe in front of the premotor areas, comprising dorsolateral, orbitofrontal (ventral) and medial regions. It is the seat of executive function: planning, working memory, cognitive flexibility, judgement, inhibition of inappropriate responses, and the motivation and social calibration of behavior. Its three regions fail in three recognizable ways: the dorsolateral patient cannot plan or shift, the orbitofrontal patient is disinhibited and tactless, and the medial patient is apathetic and mute.

anatomy.location: Frontal pole, superior and middle frontal gyri anterior to the premotor cortex, the orbital surface above the orbital roofs, and the medial surface in front of the cingulate gyrus.

subdivisions.name: Dorsolateral prefrontal cortex
subdivisions.note: working memory, planning, set shifting; connected with the mediodorsal thalamus and dorsal striatum

subdivisions.name: Orbitofrontal cortex
subdivisions.note: reward valuation, impulse control, social behavior; connected with the amygdala and olfactory cortex

subdivisions.name: Ventromedial and medial prefrontal cortex
subdivisions.note: motivation, emotional regulation, decision making

cortex-prefrontal.function: Executive control of thought and action, working memory, emotional and social regulation, and personality.

cortex-premotor-sma.name: Premotor cortex and supplementary motor area
cortex-premotor-sma.summary: Brodmann area 6 in front of the primary motor cortex: the lateral premotor cortex on the convexity and the supplementary motor area on the medial surface of the superior frontal gyrus in front of the paracentral lobule. Both plan and sequence movements and feed the primary motor cortex, the premotor cortex guiding externally cued movements (reaching for what you see) and the SMA organizing internally generated and bimanual sequences. SMA lesions and surgery produce the transient SMA syndrome of contralateral akinesia and mutism, and SMA seizures produce the dramatic fencing posture.

anatomy.location: Convexity in front of the precentral gyrus (premotor) and the medial surface of the superior frontal gyrus above the cingulate sulcus, in front of the paracentral lobule (SMA), both supplied by ACA and MCA branches at the anterior watershed.

cortex-premotor-sma.function: Motor planning, sequencing and initiation; bimanual coordination and postural preparation; contribution to speech initiation on the dominant side.

bestView.label: SMA on the medial superior frontal gyrus in front of the paracentral lobule
premotor cortex in front of the precentral gyrus

imaging.normalAppearance: The SMA occupies the medial superior frontal gyrus between the paracentral lobule and a line dropped from the anterior commissure; it is a classic fMRI landmark for surgical planning. Anterior watershed infarcts involve this region.

pathology.finding: Medial superior frontal lesion with contralateral akinesia and reduced speech that recovers over weeks.
Linear infarct along the superior frontal sulcus between ACA and MCA territories.

cortex-subcallosal.name: Subcallosal cortex
cortex-subcallosal.summary: The subcallosal cortex is the medial frontal cortex beneath the genu and rostrum of the corpus callosum, including the subgenual cingulate (Brodmann area 25), the paraterminal gyrus and the subcallosal area in front of the lamina terminalis. It is the part of the limbic cortex most closely tied to mood: it is overactive in depression, quiet after successful treatment and a target of deep brain stimulation for resistant depression. It connects the medial prefrontal cortex to the hypothalamus, amygdala and brainstem monoamine nuclei, lies against the anterior cerebral and anterior communicating arteries, and is bordered behind by the septal area and the basal forebrain, which is why anterior communicating aneurysm surgery can leave a patient amnestic and apathetic.

anatomy.location: Medial surface of the frontal lobe below the genu of the corpus callosum and in front of the lamina terminalis and the septal area, above the olfactory trigone and the anterior perforated substance, continuous with the gyrus rectus below.

cortex-subcallosal.function: Subgenual cingulate cortex integrates the emotional value assigned by the orbitofrontal cortex with hypothalamic and visceral states and sets the tone of mood and the autonomic response to sadness; it inhibits the amygdala and modulates the raphe and locus coeruleus through descending fibers, and its metabolic activity tracks depressive symptoms. The paraterminal gyrus and subcallosal area belong to the septal region and take part in the reward and memory circuits through the fornix and the medial forebrain bundle. The region also processes olfactory and visceral information reaching it from the anterior perforated substance.

imaging.normalAppearance: Thin cortex under the genu on midline sagittal images, curving down in front of the lamina terminalis and the anterior commissure; the anterior cerebral arteries run immediately in front of it in the interhemispheric fissure.

pathology.finding: Blood in the interhemispheric fissure with a hematoma of the subcallosal and gyrus rectus region; later basal forebrain infarcts with amnesia.
Increased metabolism in the subgenual cingulate that falls with effective treatment; used to plan deep brain stimulation.

pathology.pathology: Low-grade glioma of the gyrus rectus and subcallosal area
pathology.finding: Non-enhancing FLAIR-bright expansion below the genu with mood change and anosmia.

lesionEffects.deficit: Depressed mood, anhedonia and altered autonomic tone
lesionEffects.mechanism: Dysfunction of the subgenual cingulate mood circuit and its hypothalamic and monoaminergic connections

lesionEffects.deficit: Apathy and amnesia after vascular injury
lesionEffects.mechanism: Extension of anterior communicating artery infarction into the septal area and basal forebrain
Involvement of the adjacent olfactory trigone and tract

examination: Mood, anhedonia and sleep history in any patient with a medial frontal lesion
Recent memory and confabulation after anterior communicating artery aneurysm repair
Smell testing
pearls: Area 25 is the hub of the depression circuit and a stimulation target; a lesion here can present as new depression

pitfalls: The subgenual region is small and easily overlooked on axial images; look at midline sagittal views when a mood or memory change follows an anterior circulation event

cortex-supplementary-motor.name: Supplementary motor cortex (juxtapositional lobule)
cortex-supplementary-motor.summary: The supplementary motor area occupies the medial surface of the superior frontal gyrus in front of the paracentral lobule and above the cingulate sulcus, the medial part of Brodmann area 6. It prepares and initiates internally generated, sequenced and bimanual movements and speech, and it contains its own somatotopic map. Its unique clinical picture combines an acute contralateral akinesia with mutism after infarction, seizures that begin with a tonic posture of the arm and vocalization, and, when both sides are damaged, akinetic mutism; it is a territory of the anterior cerebral artery and a frequent site of parasagittal meningioma.

anatomy.location: Medial surface of the hemisphere above the cingulate sulcus and in front of the paracentral lobule, from roughly the level of the anterior commissure back to the precentral sulcus, extending a short way onto the superior convexity.

cortex-supplementary-motor.function: The SMA proper plans movement sequences from memory and initiates them without an external cue, coordinates the two hands, and gates the start of speech; the pre-SMA in front of it selects between competing actions and inhibits unwanted ones. Both receive the ventrolateral thalamus, closing the motor loop of the basal ganglia, and project to the primary motor cortex, the striatum, the pontine nuclei and directly to the spinal cord. Its loss produces reduced spontaneous movement and speech that recover over weeks because the lateral premotor cortex takes over externally cued actions, whereas self-initiated actions remain slow.

pathology.finding: Medial frontal lesion in front of the paracentral lobule; the patient has contralateral akinesia and mutism that resolve over weeks.

cortex-supracalcarine.name: Supracalcarine cortex
cortex-supracalcarine.summary: The supracalcarine cortex is the strip of medial occipital cortex immediately above the calcarine sulcus, on the lower edge of the cuneus, where the primary visual cortex emerges from the sulcus and merges with the surrounding secondary visual cortex (V2). It represents the contralateral lower visual field close to the horizontal meridian, and its retinotopic map continues that of the calcarine cortex. It is supplied by the calcarine branch of the posterior cerebral artery and shares the vulnerability of the cuneus to PCA infarction, posterior reversible encephalopathy and occipital seizures; its lesions produce a contralateral inferior quadrantic defect that respects the horizontal meridian.

anatomy.location: Medial occipital cortex along the upper lip of the calcarine sulcus, between the intracalcarine cortex below and the body of the cuneus above, from the occipital pole to the junction with the parieto-occipital sulcus.

efferents.to: Cuneus and superior lateral occipital cortex (dorsal stream)

cortex-supracalcarine.function: The supracalcarine strip contains the upper-bank continuation of V1 and the neighboring V2, which sharpens edges and combines the orientation, color and disparity signals of the striate cortex into border ownership and texture, feeding both dorsal and ventral streams; the horizontal meridian of the visual field maps to the border between V1 and V2 here, which is why lesions produce field defects with a sharp horizontal edge. The cortex receives callosal fibers from the opposite side that stitch the two hemifields together along the vertical meridian and projects to the parietal and lateral occipital cortex for localization of objects in the lower field.

medial occipital cortex just above the calcarine fissure

imaging.normalAppearance: The medial cortex immediately above the calcarine sulcus on sagittal images, continuous with the cuneus; it is thin and follows the curve of the sulcus to the pole.

pathology.finding: Restricted diffusion along the upper calcarine lip and cuneus with a contralateral lower quadrant defect that stops at the horizontal meridian.
Flow voids on the medial occipital surface with hemosiderin staining, presenting with visual seizures or hemorrhage.
Vasogenic edema of the medial occipital cortex with transient visual loss, headache and seizures.

lesionEffects.deficit: Contralateral inferior quadrantanopia respecting the horizontal meridian
lesionEffects.mechanism: Loss of the upper calcarine bank and V2 representing the lower field

lesionEffects.deficit: Elementary visual hallucinations in the lower contralateral field
lesionEffects.mechanism: Ictal activation of the supracalcarine visual cortex

lesionEffects.deficit: Impaired localization of objects in the lower field
lesionEffects.mechanism: Loss of the projection from this cortex to the dorsal stream

examination: Quadrantic confrontation fields with attention to a horizontal edge of the defect
Perimetry to define the meridian and congruity
Seizure history for brief lower-field flashes
pearls: A field defect with a straight horizontal edge is calcarine: the horizontal meridian is the V1-V2 border on the lips of the sulcus
Occipital AVMs present with seizures and headache and can mimic migraine with aura for years
The supracalcarine and cuneal cortex are one functional unit for the lower field

pitfalls: Small calcarine lesions produce field defects that patients do not notice; a routine field examination after any PCA event is needed

cortex-temporal-fusiform-anterior.name: Temporal fusiform cortex, anterior division
cortex-temporal-fusiform-anterior.summary: The anterior fusiform cortex is the front part of the fusiform (lateral occipitotemporal) gyrus on the inferior surface of the temporal lobe, between the collateral sulcus medially and the occipitotemporal sulcus laterally, beneath the hippocampus and lateral to the parahippocampal gyrus. It is high-order ventral visual cortex that hands object and face identity to the perirhinal cortex and the anterior temporal semantic system, and it is supplied by the posterior cerebral artery through its temporal branches. It atrophies with the temporal pole in semantic dementia, it is the fusiform cortex most often removed in temporal lobectomy, and its lesions contribute to prosopagnosia, associative agnosia and anomia.

anatomy.location: Anterior portion of the fusiform gyrus on the basal temporal surface, medial to the inferior temporal gyrus, lateral to the parahippocampal gyrus and the collateral sulcus, under the anterior hippocampus and amygdala.

afferents.from: Posterior fusiform and inferior temporal cortex

cortex-temporal-fusiform-anterior.function: Anterior fusiform neurons respond to specific familiar objects, faces and written words in a form independent of the image, and their output to the perirhinal and entorhinal cortex allows a seen object to be matched with its memory and its meaning; in the dominant hemisphere it is part of the basal temporal language area that supports naming and reading, and in the right it links a face to the person's identity. It receives the posterior fusiform and inferior temporal cortex through the inferior longitudinal fasciculus and the amygdala, and it projects to the temporal pole and the orbitofrontal cortex. Electrical stimulation here disrupts naming and reading.

bestView.label: anterior fusiform gyrus between the collateral and occipitotemporal sulci
basal temporal surface under the anterior hippocampus

imaging.normalAppearance: The gyrus between the collateral sulcus and the occipitotemporal sulcus on the inferior temporal surface, seen on coronal images through the amygdala and the head of the hippocampus.

pathology.finding: Restricted diffusion of the basal temporal cortex with associative agnosia, anomia or prosopagnosia and often a hemianopia.
Anterior fusiform and inferior temporal atrophy with the temporal pole, asymmetric and progressive, with loss of the meaning of objects and words.
Seizures with ictal anomia, reading arrest or complex visual auras; scalp EEG shows anterior temporal discharges.

lesionEffects.deficit: Associative visual agnosia and anomia for seen objects (left)
lesionEffects.mechanism: Disconnection of fusiform object representations from the semantic and lexical systems
Loss of the face-identity link between the fusiform cortex and the anterior temporal person nodes

lesionEffects.deficit: Loss of object knowledge when combined with polar atrophy
lesionEffects.mechanism: Degeneration of the anterior temporal semantic hub

examination: Naming and identification of objects and famous faces
Reading of words and letters
Recognition by other modalities to prove the deficit is visual
pearls: The basal temporal language area lies on the underside of the dominant temporal lobe; stimulation here stops naming during awake surgery
The anterior fusiform gyrus bridges seeing and knowing: its loss leaves the patient describing an object without recognizing it

cortex-temporal-fusiform-posterior.name: Temporal fusiform cortex, posterior division
cortex-temporal-fusiform-posterior.summary: The posterior temporal fusiform cortex is the middle segment of the fusiform gyrus on the inferior temporal surface, beneath the body of the hippocampus and the atrium, between the collateral sulcus and the occipitotemporal sulcus. It contains the fusiform face area on the right and the visual word form area on the left, the two best-known category-selective regions of the ventral visual stream, and it is supplied by temporal branches of the posterior cerebral artery. Right-sided lesions cause prosopagnosia, left-sided lesions cause pure alexia when the splenial input is also cut, and bilateral disease produces the visual agnosias of posterior cortical atrophy.

anatomy.location: Middle third of the fusiform gyrus, medial to the inferior temporal gyrus and lateral to the parahippocampal gyrus, under the body and tail of the hippocampus at the level of the atrium, in front of the occipital fusiform gyrus.

afferents.from: Occipital fusiform and lateral occipital cortex (V4, LOC)

afferents.via: top-down modulation via the inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus

efferents.to: Angular gyrus and posterior temporal language cortex (left)

cortex-temporal-fusiform-posterior.function: The right posterior fusiform cortex responds preferentially to faces, extracting the configuration of features that identifies an individual, while the left posterior fusiform cortex learns to recognize letter strings and familiar words as visual wholes, allowing fast reading; neighboring patches prefer bodies, places and tools. Both sides receive the occipital form areas and project forward to the anterior fusiform and perirhinal cortex and to the amygdala, and both are modulated by attention from the parietal and frontal cortex. Seizures arising here produce visual auras of faces or letters, and functional imaging of these areas is used to map eloquent cortex before temporo-occipital surgery.

bestView.label: posterior fusiform gyrus under the body of the hippocampus
fusiform face region on the basal temporal surface

imaging.normalAppearance: The fusiform gyrus on coronal images through the atrium, between the collateral and occipitotemporal sulci; the fusiform face area sits at its posterior end on the right and the visual word form area in the corresponding position on the left.

pathology.pathology: Right PCA branch infarct with prosopagnosia
pathology.finding: Restricted diffusion of the right posterior fusiform gyrus, often with a left superior quadrantanopia from the adjacent radiation.
Left occipito-temporal infarct involving the posterior fusiform cortex and the splenial fibers; the patient reads letter by letter but writes normally.
Bilateral fusiform and occipito-parietal atrophy with prosopagnosia, alexia and simultanagnosia; hippocampi preserved.

lesionEffects.mechanism: Loss of the fusiform face area configuration processing
Loss of the visual word form area or its input
Optic radiation fibers in the adjacent white matter

examination: Face recognition of family and famous people; matching faces with different expressions
Reading words of increasing length; letter-by-letter reading is the signature of pure alexia
Quadrantic visual fields
pearls: Reading time that grows with word length is the fingerprint of the visual word form area lesion
The face area is right-sided: a right occipito-temporal stroke makes the patient recognize people by voice and gait

pitfalls: Prosopagnosic patients often deny a problem because they recognize people by other cues; ask whether they recognize themselves in photographs

cortex-temporo-occipital-fusiform.name: Temporal occipital fusiform cortex
cortex-temporo-occipital-fusiform.summary: The temporo-occipital fusiform cortex is the posterior segment of the fusiform gyrus where the temporal lobe meets the occipital lobe on the inferior surface, between the collateral sulcus and the occipitotemporal sulcus behind the level of the atrium. It is ventral extrastriate cortex in which color, texture and shape are combined (the human V4 complex and the posterior parts of the face and word areas) and it feeds the fusiform recognition regions in front of it. It lies squarely in the posterior cerebral artery territory beneath the calcarine cortex, so its infarction accompanies a hemianopia and adds achromatopsia, apperceptive agnosia or alexia; bilateral damage produces cerebral achromatopsia.

anatomy.location: Posterior end of the fusiform gyrus at the temporo-occipital junction, medial to the inferior lateral occipital cortex and lateral to the lingual gyrus and collateral sulcus, on the inferior surface of the hemisphere above the tentorium.

afferents.from: Primary and secondary visual cortex (V1, V2)

efferents.to: Posterior temporal fusiform cortex (face and word areas)

cortex-temporo-occipital-fusiform.function: This ventral occipito-temporal cortex computes the surface color and texture of objects independent of illumination, integrates contours into shapes and begins the category-specific organization that becomes face, word, body and place areas further forward; it is retinotopically organized with the contralateral upper field represented on the lower bank, and the right side dominates for global form and color. It receives the calcarine cortex and V2 through short fibers and projects along the inferior longitudinal fasciculus; the tentorium and the PCA branches lie directly beneath it. Lesions produce contralateral hemiachromatopsia and upper quadrant defects, and ictal activation gives colored visual auras.

bestView.label: temporo-occipital fusiform gyrus above the tentorium
ventral occipito-temporal cortex lateral to the lingual gyrus

imaging.normalAppearance: The fusiform gyrus behind the atrium on coronal images, below the lateral ventricle and above the tentorial surface, with the collateral sulcus separating it from the lingual gyrus medially.

pathology.finding: Restricted diffusion of the ventral occipito-temporal cortex below the calcarine sulcus with loss of color perception in the contralateral hemifield and an upper quadrantanopia.
Bilateral ventral occipito-temporal lesions, typically after sequential PCA strokes or hypotension, with the world seen in shades of gray.
Colored spots or shapes at onset with a posterior temporo-occipital focus; migraine aura is the main mimic.

lesionEffects.mechanism: Loss of the color-constancy cortex of the ventral occipito-temporal region

lesionEffects.deficit: Apperceptive agnosia and impaired shape perception
lesionEffects.mechanism: Loss of ventral extrastriate form processing
Involvement of the lower calcarine bank or the underlying optic radiation

examination: Color naming and matching in each hemifield separately (pseudoisochromatic plates presented to each side)
Copying and matching of shapes
Visual fields by quadrant
pearls: Loss of color in one hemifield with preserved acuity is the ventral occipito-temporal cortex; the patient may say the left side of the room looks washed out
Colored auras are occipital, not migraine, when they last seconds and recur stereotypically
The temporo-occipital fusiform cortex lies on the tentorium: tentorial meningiomas and PCA aneurysm compression present with these deficits

pitfalls: Hemiachromatopsia is never found unless colors are tested in each hemifield; standard color plates presented centrally miss it
