cuneus.name: Cuneus
cuneus.summary: The cuneus is the wedge of medial occipital cortex above the calcarine sulcus and below the parieto-occipital sulcus, the upper bank of the primary visual cortex and its surrounding extrastriate areas (V1 above the sulcus, V2 and V3 on the cuneal surface). It represents the contralateral inferior visual field, so a cuneal lesion produces a contralateral inferior quadrantanopia. It is supplied by the calcarine and parieto-occipital branches of the posterior cerebral artery with a middle cerebral artery contribution at the occipital pole, which explains macular sparing after PCA occlusion, and it is the cortex of the visual auras of occipital epilepsy and migraine.

anatomy.location: Medial occipital surface between the calcarine sulcus below and the parieto-occipital sulcus above, extending from the occipital pole forward to the junction of the two sulci behind the splenium.

efferents.to: Superior parietal and lateral occipital cortex (dorsal stream)

cuneus.function: The cuneal part of the primary visual cortex receives the upper bank of the optic radiation carrying the contralateral lower visual field, with the periphery represented anteriorly and the macula toward the pole, and passes the retinotopic map to the surrounding V2 and V3 on the cuneus and to dorsal-stream areas of the parietal lobe for the localization of objects and the guidance of action. Damage produces a congruous inferior quadrantic field defect, and irritation produces elementary hallucinations of flashes and colored shapes in the lower contralateral field. The cuneus also participates in visual attention and reading, and in the visual imagery that accompanies memory retrieval.

bestView.label: cuneus above the calcarine sulcus
medial occipital cortex between the calcarine and parieto-occipital sulci

imaging.normalAppearance: Triangular medial occipital cortex on sagittal images between the deep calcarine and parieto-occipital sulci; the stria of Gennari is visible as a thin dark line in the calcarine cortex on high-resolution T1 images.

pathology.finding: Restricted diffusion of the cuneus with a contralateral inferior quadrantanopia; macular sparing when the pole is supplied by the MCA.
Brief elementary visual hallucinations of colored circles in the contralateral lower field followed by eye deviation; occipital spikes that increase with eye closure.
Bilateral parieto-occipital vasogenic edema including the cuneus with cortical blindness or visual disturbance.

lesionEffects.mechanism: Loss of the upper calcarine bank representing the lower visual field

lesionEffects.deficit: Elementary visual hallucinations in the lower contralateral field
lesionEffects.mechanism: Ictal activation of the cuneal visual cortex

lesionEffects.deficit: Impaired visually guided reaching and attention to the lower field
lesionEffects.mechanism: Loss of cuneal input to the dorsal visual stream

examination: Confrontation fields by quadrant with finger counting or a red target
Ask about flashes or colored shapes and their duration and side
Reading and scanning of a page for lower-field neglect of text
pearls: Above the calcarine sulcus means below the horizontal meridian: cuneal lesions cut the lower field
Occipital seizure auras last seconds and are colored; migraine auras last minutes and are black and white zigzags
Macular sparing is the fingerprint of a PCA infarct with an intact MCA collateral at the occipital pole

pitfalls: Quadrantic defects are missed by testing hemifields only; count fingers in each of the four quadrants

dentate-gyrus.name: Dentate gyrus
dentate-gyrus.summary: The dentate gyrus is the notched strip of gray matter on the medial surface of the hippocampal formation between the fimbria and the parahippocampal gyrus, interlocking with the cornu ammonis to form the two C-shaped layers of the hippocampus seen on a coronal section. Its granule cells are the first stage of the trisynaptic circuit, receiving the perforant path from the entorhinal cortex and sending mossy fibers to CA3, and they separate similar inputs into distinct memory traces; the dentate gyrus is also one of the two sites of adult neurogenesis. It is involved in mesial temporal sclerosis, where granule cell dispersion and mossy fiber sprouting create a seizure circuit, and its neurogenesis is a target of antidepressant and exercise research.

anatomy.location: Narrow toothed gyrus on the medial aspect of the hippocampus, lying in the concavity of the cornu ammonis, separated from the parahippocampal gyrus by the hippocampal sulcus and from the fimbria by the fimbriodentate sulcus; it continues onto the dorsal surface of the corpus callosum as the indusium griseum.

dentate-gyrus.function: Granule cells of the dentate gyrus receive the perforant path from entorhinal layer II and, through sparse firing and strong lateral inhibition by hilar interneurons, orthogonalize overlapping cortical inputs so that two similar experiences are stored as separable memories (pattern separation); their mossy fibers deliver these codes to CA3. New granule cells are generated throughout adult life in the subgranular zone and are recruited into memory circuits, a process reduced by stress and age and increased by exercise. The hilus contains mossy cells that spread excitation along the gyrus; their loss after injury and the sprouting of mossy fibers back onto granule cells underlie hyperexcitability in temporal lobe epilepsy.

bestView.label: dentate gyrus in the concavity of the cornu ammonis
dentate gyrus along the medial hippocampus

imaging.normalAppearance: On high-resolution coronal T2 images the dentate gyrus is the inner, medial C of the hippocampal double spiral, with the hippocampal sulcus and its vestigial cysts between it and the subiculum; the notched surface faces the ambient cistern.

pathology.finding: Hippocampal atrophy with loss of the internal digitations; pathology shows granule cell dispersion, hilar cell loss and mossy fiber sprouting.
Small CSF-signal cysts between the dentate gyrus and the subiculum, a normal developmental remnant not to be reported as pathology.
Swollen bright hippocampi with subacute amnesia and seizures; dentate involvement contributes to seizure generation.

lesionEffects.mechanism: Loss of dentate pattern separation
Hilar cell loss and mossy fiber sprouting create recurrent excitation
Failure of the first stage of the trisynaptic circuit

examination: Memory tests that use similar lures (recognizing which of two similar pictures was shown)
Seizure history and EEG
Mood and exercise history where neurogenesis is a consideration
pearls: The dentate gyrus keeps similar memories apart; its failure makes one day blur into another
Hippocampal sulcal remnant cysts are normal; report them as such
New neurons are born in the adult dentate gyrus, the exception to the rule that the brain does not regenerate

pitfalls: The dentate gyrus and the dentate nucleus of the cerebellum share a name and nothing else; do not confuse them in reports

dentate-nucleus.name: Dentate nucleus
dentate-nucleus.summary: The largest and most lateral of the deep cerebellar nuclei, a crinkled sheet of neurons within the white matter of each hemisphere that gives the cerebellum its main output. It receives Purkinje cell axons from the lateral hemisphere and collaterals of mossy and climbing fibers, and sends its axons through the superior cerebellar peduncle to cross in the midbrain and reach the contralateral red nucleus and ventral lateral thalamus, from which the motor cortex is informed. It accumulates iron and gadolinium with age, making it conspicuous on SWI and T1.

anatomy.location: Deep in the white matter of each cerebellar hemisphere, lateral to the roof of the fourth ventricle and medial to the hemispheric folia; the emboliform nucleus lies just medial to its hilum.

dentate-nucleus.function: Final relay of the neocerebellar (lateral zone) circuit that times and coordinates skilled limb movement; its output via the thalamus prepares and adjusts cortical motor commands.

bestView.label: dentate nuclei as wavy bands in the hemispheric white matter
dentate lateral to the fourth ventricle roof

imaging.normalAppearance: A crenated dark band on T2* and SWI (iron) and increasingly bright on unenhanced T1 after repeated gadolinium exposure; on routine T1/T2 in the young it is subtle. Symmetrical T2 hyperintensity of the dentate is a metabolic clue.

pathology.finding: Symmetrical bright dentate nuclei on T2/FLAIR in metronidazole toxicity, cerebrotendinous xanthomatosis, Wilson disease, maple syrup urine disease or mitochondrial disease.
Restricted diffusion in the deep hemisphere within an SCA infarct.
Bright dentate on precontrast T1 after many linear-agent doses; no known symptoms.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: Axial T2/FLAIR and SWI

lesionEffects.deficit: Ipsilateral limb ataxia, intention tremor, dysmetria
lesionEffects.mechanism: Loss of hemispheric output before it crosses

lesionEffects.deficit: Holmes tremor after lesions of its outflow
lesionEffects.mechanism: Dentatorubrothalamic fibers after the decussation

lesionEffects.deficit: Palatal tremor after a lesion of the dentate or its outflow
lesionEffects.mechanism: Dentato-rubro-olivary (Guillain–Mollaret) triangle interrupted, with later olivary hypertrophy

examination: Finger-nose and heel-shin
Rebound and rapid alternating movements
Inspect the palate for rhythmic movement in chronic cases
pearls: Bilateral bright dentate nuclei in a patient on metronidazole: stop the drug
Damage to the dentate or the superior peduncle is the usual cause of cerebellar mutism after childhood posterior fossa surgery

dorsal-motor-nucleus-vagus.name: Dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus
dorsal-motor-nucleus-vagus.summary: The largest parasympathetic nucleus of the brainstem, lying beneath the vagal trigone in the floor of the fourth ventricle lateral to the hypoglossal nucleus. Its preganglionic neurons travel in the vagus nerve to the thoracic and abdominal viscera, driving bronchoconstriction, gastric secretion and gut motility. It is functionally paired with the nucleus of the solitary tract just lateral to it, which delivers the visceral afferent information that its reflexes require.

anatomy.location: Dorsal medulla under the vagal trigone of the fourth ventricular floor, lateral to the hypoglossal nucleus and medial to the solitary nucleus, extending from the obex upward through the open medulla.

dorsal-motor-nucleus-vagus.function: Preganglionic parasympathetic outflow to the heart (in part), lungs, esophagus, stomach, small bowel and proximal colon; secretomotor and motor drive to the gut.

bestView.label: dorsal medulla under the floor of the fourth ventricle
vagal trigone in the caudal fourth ventricular floor

imaging.normalAppearance: Not resolved on MRI; the vagal and hypoglossal trigones form the caudal floor of the fourth ventricle. Dorsal medullary lesions here appear as small T2 or DWI lesions beneath the ventricle.

pathology.pathology: Area postrema / dorsal medullary lesion (neuromyelitis optica)
pathology.finding: T2/FLAIR-bright lesion of the dorsal medulla abutting the fourth ventricle, presenting with intractable hiccups and vomiting.
Small restricted-diffusion lesion in the dorsal medulla from PICA or vertebral perforators.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: Axial FLAIR and DWI; aquaporin-4 antibodies if the lesion abuts the fourth ventricle

lesionEffects.deficit: Tachycardia and loss of vagal tone
lesionEffects.mechanism: Loss of parasympathetic drive to the heart (with nucleus ambiguus)
Loss of vagal motor outflow to the stomach and bowel
Involvement of the neighboring area postrema and solitary complex

examination: Heart rate variability and orthostatic responses
Ask about early satiety, nausea and hiccups
Assess the palate and gag for associated ambiguus involvement
pearls: Persistent hiccups and vomiting with a dorsal medullary lesion should raise neuromyelitis optica
Vagal parasympathetic neurons for the heart come mainly from the nucleus ambiguus, not this nucleus

dorsal-root-ganglion.name: Dorsal root ganglion
dorsal-root-ganglion.summary: A swelling on each dorsal root within the intervertebral foramen containing the pseudounipolar cell bodies of all somatic and visceral sensory neurons of that segment. Each neuron sends one process to the periphery in the spinal nerve and one into the cord through the dorsal root. The ganglion lies outside the blood–nerve barrier, which makes it vulnerable to toxins, autoimmune attack and viral latency: herpes zoster reactivates here, and sensory neuronopathies (paraneoplastic, Sjögren, platinum drugs, B6 excess) destroy its cells to produce a non-length-dependent, ataxic sensory loss.

anatomy.location: In the intervertebral foramen (or, for the sacral roots, inside the spinal canal), on the dorsal root just proximal to its union with the ventral root to form the spinal nerve; the trigeminal, geniculate and other cranial sensory ganglia are its cranial equivalents.

dorsal-root-ganglion.function: Houses the first-order sensory neurons for touch, proprioception, pain, temperature and visceral sensation; their central processes form the dorsal root and the posterior columns.

bestView.label: cervicomedullary junction; the ganglia lie in the intervertebral foramina outside the MNI volume

imaging.normalAppearance: Ganglia are seen on axial and coronal T2/T1+Gd of the spine as ovoid enhancing structures in the foramina (normal enhancement, no blood–nerve barrier); enlargement and marked enhancement occur in ganglionopathies and infiltration.

pathology.finding: Posterior column T2 hyperintensity from degeneration of central processes, with normal or enlarged ganglia.
Enhancement of the affected ganglion and root, sometimes with dorsal horn signal change.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: Axial/coronal spine T2 and T1+Gd; nerve conduction studies (absent sensory responses with normal motor)

lesionEffects.deficit: Non-length-dependent sensory loss with severe proprioceptive loss and pseudoathetosis
lesionEffects.mechanism: Loss of large sensory neurons throughout the ganglia
Proprioceptive deafferentation
Reactivation of varicella zoster in one ganglion

lesionEffects.deficit: Absent sensory nerve action potentials with preserved motor studies
lesionEffects.mechanism: Selective sensory neuron loss

examination: Vibration and joint position sense in the arms as well as the legs (non-length-dependent)
Romberg and pseudoathetosis of outstretched fingers
Reflexes (absent)
Look for a dermatomal rash
pearls: Sensory loss that starts in the face, trunk or arms and is worse for proprioception is a ganglionopathy, not a neuropathy: look for cancer (anti-Hu), Sjögren syndrome or drugs
Shingles pain can precede the rash by days: a dermatomal pain with no explanation deserves a second look

pitfalls: The ganglion meshes cover the L1 and L2 ganglia only, because Z-Anatomy models one ganglion per intervertebral foramen from C2 to L2 and no lower.

dura-mater.name: Dura mater
dura-mater.summary: The tough outer meninx. Inside the skull it has two layers: an endosteal layer that is the periosteum of the inner table and a meningeal layer that folds inward as the falx cerebri, tentorium cerebelli, falx cerebelli and diaphragma sellae; where the layers separate they enclose the dural venous sinuses. The meningeal arteries run between dura and bone (epidural hematoma), the bridging veins cross from brain to sinus beneath it (subdural hematoma), and it is the only intracranial structure with pain fibers, so its stretching, inflammation and traction produce headache. It enhances on MRI and thickens in hypotension, inflammation and metastasis.

anatomy.location: Lining the skull from the foramen magnum up, adherent to bone at the sutures and skull base; the meningeal layer continues through the foramen magnum as the spinal dura, which is separated from the vertebral canal by the fat-filled epidural space and ends at S2.

subdivisions.name: Endosteal (periosteal) layer
subdivisions.note: adherent to the skull; site of epidural hematoma when stripped by arterial bleeding

subdivisions.name: Meningeal layer
subdivisions.note: forms the folds and the outer wall of the sinuses; continuous with the spinal dura

subdivisions.name: Dural folds
subdivisions.note: falx cerebri, tentorium cerebelli with its incisura, falx cerebelli, diaphragma sellae

subdivisions.name: Innervation
subdivisions.note: trigeminal (V1 mainly) supratentorially, upper cervical nerves and vagus infratentorially

dura-mater.function: Mechanical protection and partitioning of the brain, formation of the venous sinuses, CSF absorption through the granulations projecting into them, and pain signaling for headache.

bestView.label: convexity dura and falx at the superior sagittal sinus
dura lining the inner table

imaging.normalAppearance: A thin line against the inner table, invisible on CT and faintly enhancing on T1+Gd in short segments; diffuse smooth thick enhancement means intracranial hypotension, pachymeningitis or metastasis. Extra-axial collections are classified by their relation to the dura: lens-shaped epidural (arterial, limited by sutures) versus crescentic subdural (venous, crossing sutures).

pathology.finding: Biconvex hyperdense collection between skull and dura, not crossing sutures, usually temporoparietal from the middle meningeal artery with a skull fracture.
pathology.timing: Classic lucid interval then rapid deterioration over hours

pathology.finding: Crescentic collection over the convexity crossing sutures; hyperdense acute, isodense at 1–3 weeks, hypodense chronic.
Diffuse smooth dural thickening and enhancement, subdural collections, venous engorgement and brain sagging.
Extra-axial, dural-based, homogeneously enhancing mass with a dural tail.
Nodular or thick enhancing dura (IgG4 disease, tuberculosis, breast and prostate cancer).

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: Non-contrast CT for hematomas; T1+Gd for dural disease

lesionEffects.deficit: Headache (worse upright in hypotension, worse lying down in raised pressure)
lesionEffects.mechanism: Traction on or stretching of pain-sensitive dura

lesionEffects.deficit: Focal deficits and coma from expanding hematomas
lesionEffects.mechanism: Compression of the underlying hemisphere and herniation

lesionEffects.deficit: Cranial nerve palsies from dural thickening at the skull base
lesionEffects.mechanism: Entrapment of nerves passing through dural foramina

examination: Postural headache history
Neck stiffness
Pupils and level of consciousness after head injury
Cranial nerves at the skull base
pearls: A lucid interval after head injury followed by decline is an epidural hematoma: get the CT before the second decline
Postural headache that vanishes when lying flat with diffuse dural enhancement is a CSF leak

facial-motor-nucleus.name: Facial motor nucleus
facial-motor-nucleus.summary: The facial motor nucleus sits in the ventrolateral tegmentum of the caudal pons. Its axons take a remarkable detour: they run dorsomedially, loop over the abducens nucleus as the internal genu (raising the facial colliculus), and then pass ventrolaterally to leave the pontomedullary junction. The nucleus supplies all muscles of facial expression plus the stapedius, stylohyoid and posterior belly of the digastric. Its corticobulbar input is bilateral for the upper face but mainly contralateral for the lower face, which is the anatomical basis for distinguishing central from peripheral facial weakness.

anatomy.location: Ventrolateral pontine tegmentum at the level of the facial colliculus, dorsal to the superior olivary complex and ventrolateral to the abducens nucleus; the internal genu lies dorsal to the abducens nucleus.

subdivisions.name: Dorsal (upper face) part
subdivisions.note: frontalis and orbicularis oculi; bilateral cortical input

subdivisions.name: Ventral (lower face) part
subdivisions.note: perioral muscles; contralateral cortical input

subdivisions.name: Medial and intermediate groups
subdivisions.note: stapedius, stylohyoid, posterior digastric, platysma

afferents.note: bilateral to upper face, contralateral to lower face

facial-motor-nucleus.function: Lower motor neurons for facial expression, eye closure, and the stapedius reflex that dampens loud sounds; efferent limb of the corneal and blink reflexes.

bestView.label: ventrolateral caudal pontine tegmentum
internal genu over the abducens nucleus

imaging.normalAppearance: Not resolved on routine MRI. The intrapontine facial fibers and the nerve in the cerebellopontine angle and internal acoustic meatus are seen on high-resolution T2; enhancement of the nerve in the canal is seen in Bell palsy.

pathology.finding: Restricted diffusion in the ventrolateral or paramedian caudal pons; peripheral-type facial weakness with contralateral hemiparesis (Millard–Gubler).
Enhancement of the labyrinthine and geniculate segments of the facial nerve on contrast T1 in the temporal bone; the pons is normal.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: DWI for pontine lesions; T1+Gd of the temporal bone when a peripheral cause is suspected

lesionEffects.deficit: Weakness of the whole ipsilateral face including the forehead
lesionEffects.mechanism: Nucleus or nerve: lower motor neuron lesion

lesionEffects.deficit: Weakness of the lower face only, forehead spared
lesionEffects.mechanism: Supranuclear corticobulbar lesion: the upper face has bilateral cortical input
Loss of stapedius motor neurons

lesionEffects.deficit: Incomplete eye closure with Bell phenomenon
lesionEffects.mechanism: Orbicularis oculi weakness

examination: Raise eyebrows, close eyes tightly, show teeth, puff cheeks; compare the forehead with the mouth
Corneal reflex and blink to threat
Ask about loud-sound intolerance and taste change (taste points to the nerve distal to the pons)
pearls: Forehead involved: nucleus or nerve. Forehead spared: cortex or corticobulbar tract
A peripheral facial palsy with hemiparesis of the opposite limbs is a pontine lesion, not Bell palsy

falx-cerebri.name: Falx cerebri
falx-cerebri.summary: The sickle-shaped fold of meningeal dura that hangs in the interhemispheric fissure from the crista galli in front to the tentorium behind, enclosing the superior sagittal sinus along its attached upper edge and the inferior sagittal sinus in its free lower edge, which lies just above the corpus callosum. It limits side-to-side shift of the hemispheres, which is why supratentorial mass effect produces subfalcine herniation of the cingulate gyrus under its free edge, and it is a favorite site of parasagittal meningiomas that present with leg weakness or seizures.

anatomy.location: Midline between the hemispheres, attached to the frontal crest, the sagittal sulcus of the vault and the tentorium; the free edge lies above the corpus callosum, closer to it posteriorly.

falx-cerebri.function: Partition and support of the hemispheres, housing of the sagittal sinuses, limitation of lateral brain shift.

arteries: anterior ethmoidal branches of the ophthalmic artery

bestView.label: falx between the hemispheres with the superior sagittal sinus at its top
midline line of the falx on axial images

imaging.normalAppearance: A midline line on axial CT, denser when calcified, with the superior sagittal sinus as a triangle at the vertex on coronal images; midline shift of the septum pellucidum under a bowed falx measures subfalcine herniation. Falcine and parasagittal meningiomas are dural-based enhancing masses along it.

pathology.finding: Midline shift of the septum pellucidum with the cingulate gyrus displaced under the falx; may compress the ACA.
Enhancing dural mass with a dural tail, often invading or occluding the superior sagittal sinus.
Blood tracking along the falx after trauma or in non-accidental injury.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: CT for shift; MRI with contrast for masses; MRV for sinus involvement

lesionEffects.deficit: Contralateral leg weakness from ACA compression under the falx
lesionEffects.mechanism: Subfalcine herniation compressing the pericallosal artery

lesionEffects.deficit: Leg weakness or focal motor seizures from a parasagittal mass
lesionEffects.mechanism: Compression of the paracentral lobule

lesionEffects.deficit: Headache and raised pressure from sinus occlusion
lesionEffects.mechanism: Superior sagittal sinus invasion

examination: Leg power and gait
Level of consciousness and headache with mass effect
Seizure history
pearls: Bilateral leg weakness with a midline mass on imaging: a parasagittal meningioma compressing both paracentral lobules
Midline shift on CT is subfalcine herniation; it precedes uncal herniation

fastigial-nucleus.name: Fastigial nucleus
fastigial-nucleus.summary: The most medial deep nucleus, lying in the roof of the fourth ventricle on either side of the midline, is the output of the vermis and flocculonodular lobe. It projects bilaterally to the vestibular nuclei and reticular formation through the juxtarestiform body (partly via the crossed uncinate fasciculus), and to the thalamus, controlling axial and proximal muscles, gait, balance and eye movements. Its rostral part also influences blood pressure and respiration through the medullary reticular formation.

anatomy.location: In the vermian white matter immediately above the fastigium, the apex of the fourth ventricular roof, medial to the globose nucleus.

efferents.via: juxtarestiform body and crossed uncinate fasciculus

fastigial-nucleus.function: Postural and gait control through vestibulospinal and reticulospinal tracts, saccade timing and accuracy (caudal fastigial oculomotor region), and cardiovascular regulation.

bestView.label: midline roof of the fourth ventricle
above the fastigium

imaging.normalAppearance: Not resolved on routine MRI; localized to the vermian white matter just above the peak of the fourth ventricle.

pathology.finding: Vermian mass, infarct or plaque involving the roof of the fourth ventricle with truncal ataxia and saccadic dysmetria.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: Sagittal T2 and FLAIR

lesionEffects.deficit: Truncal ataxia and inability to stand
lesionEffects.mechanism: Loss of vestibulospinal and reticulospinal modulation
Fastigial oculomotor region

lesionEffects.deficit: Gait ataxia with relatively preserved limb coordination
lesionEffects.mechanism: Axial control

examination: Sitting balance, standing and gait
Saccade accuracy to targets
Blood pressure and heart rate variability in bilateral lesions
pearls: Fastigial and vermian lesions cannot sit unsupported: this is the picture of a midline tumor or alcohol
Saccades that overshoot point to the fastigial oculomotor region or the dorsal vermis
Because fastigial output is bilateral, unilateral lesions produce milder, less lateralized deficits than dentate lesions

pitfalls: The fastigial nuclei sit so close to the midline that a single small vermian lesion often damages both, mimicking a diffuse cerebellar disorder

filum-terminale.name: Filum terminale
filum-terminale.summary: A thin, glistening thread of pia mater and residual glial tissue that runs from the tip of the conus medullaris to the back of the first coccygeal segment, anchoring the lower end of the spinal cord inside the thecal sac and then to the coccyx. It contains no functioning cord segments and no roots of its own, but it is the embryological remnant of the caudal cord and it is the structure that gives way in tethered cord syndrome. Two parts are described: the filum terminale internum, about 15 cm long, which lies inside the dural sac surrounded by the roots of the cauda equina, and the filum terminale externum, about 5 cm long, which is invested by the dura it pierces at the S2 level and continues as the coccygeal ligament. Its normal diameter is 2 mm or less, and a filum thicker than that, or one infiltrated by fat, is the commonest anatomical cause of a tethered cord in an adult.

anatomy.location: From the apex of the conus medullaris at the L1–L2 disc in the adult, down through the lumbar cistern in the midline among the descending roots of the cauda equina, to the caudal end of the dural sac at about S2, where it pierces the dura and continues outside it as the coccygeal ligament to the dorsum of the first coccygeal vertebra. In the newborn the conus and therefore the origin of the filum lie two to three vertebral levels lower, and they rise to the adult position by about two years of age as the vertebral column outgrows the cord.
anatomy.boundaries: Above, the tapering tip of the conus medullaris; below, the periosteum of the coccyx. Around it in the lumbar cistern lie the lumbar, sacral and coccygeal roots of the cauda equina; behind it are the laminae and the ligamentum flavum, in front the posterior longitudinal ligament and the lumbar vertebral bodies.

subdivisions.name: Filum terminale internum
subdivisions.note: the intradural part, roughly 15 cm, from the conus to the caudal end of the dural sac at S2, bathed in cerebrospinal fluid and surrounded by the cauda equina

subdivisions.name: Filum terminale externum (coccygeal ligament)
subdivisions.note: the extradural part, roughly 5 cm, ensheathed by dura, fused with the periosteum of the coccyx

relations.anterior: posterior longitudinal ligament and the bodies of L2 to S2
relations.posterior: laminae, ligamenta flava and the epidural fat
relations.lateral: the descending roots of the cauda equina on each side

filum-terminale.function: Mechanical rather than neural: the filum anchors the caudal end of the cord to the coccyx and, together with the denticulate ligaments higher up, limits the excursion of the cord within the vertebral canal during flexion and extension of the trunk. Its elasticity lets the cord move a few millimeters cranially and caudally without traction on the roots. Histologically it holds ependymal cells, glial tissue and occasional nests of neurons that are the remains of the caudal cord segments lost during retrogressive differentiation, which is why tumors of ependymal origin arise here.

bloodSupply.note: A slender continuation of the anterior spinal artery, the artery of the filum terminale, runs on its surface and anastomoses with sacral radicular branches.

bestView.label: cord (the filum runs from L1–L2 to the coccyx, far below the MNI volume)

imaging.normalAppearance: The normal filum is best judged on axial T1 or T2 images of the lumbar cistern at the L5–S1 level, where the cauda equina roots have swept anterolaterally and the filum sits alone in the posterior midline; it should measure 2 mm or less and follow the same signal as a root. On sagittal images it is a fine dark line in bright cerebrospinal fluid and is often invisible. The two observations that matter are the level of the conus tip, which should be at or above the lower border of L2, and the thickness and fat content of the filum. In this atlas the filum is the part of the cord surface below the caudal end of the PAM50 S5 spinal level, so it stands for the whole taper below the conus rather than for a measured thread.

pathology.finding: Conus below the L2 level with a filum thicker than 2 mm, often with a posteriorly displaced conus lying against the laminae.
Linear T1 hyperintensity within the filum that suppresses on fat-saturated images; an incidental finding in some adults and a cause of tethering in others.
Enhancing sausage-shaped mass of the filum and conus in the lumbar cistern, often with hemorrhagic caps.
Thick or fatty filum with a low conus, a dermal sinus or a lipoma, in a child with a cutaneous stigma over the lower back.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: Sagittal and axial lumbar T1 and T2 through to the coccyx, with fat saturation to confirm a fatty filum

lesionEffects.deficit: Progressive back and leg pain worsened by growth, flexion or exercise
lesionEffects.mechanism: Traction on the conus and the sacral roots by a short, inelastic filum

lesionEffects.deficit: Urinary urgency, frequency, incontinence or retention
lesionEffects.mechanism: Stretch injury to the sacral parasympathetic neurons of the conus

lesionEffects.deficit: Foot deformity, leg length or calf asymmetry, and a spastic-ataxic gait
lesionEffects.mechanism: Chronic traction myelopathy of the lower lumbar and sacral segments

lesionEffects.deficit: Saddle sensory loss with absent ankle jerks
lesionEffects.mechanism: Involvement of the sacral segments and the adjacent cauda equina roots

examination: Inspect the lower back for a dimple, sinus, hairy patch, hemangioma or subcutaneous lipoma
Compare foot size, calf circumference and arch shape between the two legs
Ankle jerks, plantar responses and tone in the legs
Perianal sensation, anal tone and the bulbocavernosus reflex
Post-void bladder scan and a formal urodynamic study when tethering is suspected
pearls: A conus tip at or above the lower border of L2 with a filum of 2 mm or less is normal; both have to be checked before tethering is excluded
Tethered cord in an adult usually declares itself after a growth spurt, a fall or a period of heavy lifting rather than at birth
The filum carries no roots, so cutting it at surgery costs nothing neurologically, which is why sectioning a tight filum is a short and effective operation
A cutaneous stigma over the lumbosacral midline in an infant is an indication to image the whole lumbar spine, not to wait for symptoms

pitfalls: DERIVED MESH: this is not a measured filum. It is the part of the Z-Anatomy cord surface that lies below the caudal end of the PAM50 S5 spinal level, cut on a plane normal to the cord centerline, so it shows where the taper below the conus runs but not the true caliber of the thread; use it for orientation, never to judge filum thickness
A fatty filum on its own, with a normal conus level and no symptoms, is a common incidental finding and is not by itself a diagnosis of tethered cord
A low conus can be missed if the sagittal lumbar study stops above the coccyx, because the tethering lesion is often at the very bottom of the sac
The filum is easily mistaken for a nerve root during lumbar puncture and during surgery: intraoperative stimulation, not appearance, tells them apart

PUBLIC EDITION - VERTEBRAL-LANDMARK CUT: the mesh above is cut at a spinal-level boundary of a template whose data may not be redistributed, so the openly shareable build of the atlas cuts the same Z-Anatomy cord surface at a vertebral landmark instead: the conus tip is put at the middle of the model's own L1-L2 intervertebral disc, the classical adult level, and everything below that plane is the filum. That level is a textbook rule applied to one model rather than a measurement, and the two cuts do not fall in the same place -- the vertebral filum is the lower 5 cm or so of the taper, the PAM50-cut one about twice that -- so read either as where the thread runs, never as how long or how thick it is.

flocculonodular-lobe.name: Flocculonodular lobe
flocculonodular-lobe.summary: The oldest part of the cerebellum: the nodule of the vermis and the two flocculi that hang beneath the middle cerebellar peduncles at the cerebellopontine angles. It receives primary vestibular fibers directly from the vestibular nerve and secondary fibers from the vestibular nuclei, plus visual input from the accessory optic system, and projects back to the vestibular nuclei both directly and via the fastigial nucleus. It calibrates the vestibulo-ocular reflex, holds gaze eccentrically and stabilizes balance; lesions produce nystagmus and truncal imbalance without limb ataxia.

anatomy.location: Nodule in the midline in front of the uvula at the caudal end of the vermis, and the flocculus on each side in the cerebellopontine angle behind the cochlear nerve, connected to the nodule by a thin peduncle.

flocculonodular-lobe.function: Vestibulo-ocular reflex gain adaptation, gaze holding, smooth pursuit, and vestibular control of posture and balance.

bestView.label: flocculus in the cerebellopontine angle behind the eighth nerve
nodule at the caudal vermis in front of the uvula

imaging.normalAppearance: The flocculus is a small lobulated structure in the cerebellopontine angle on axial T2 that can be mistaken for a mass; the nodule is seen at the caudal end of the vermis on sagittal images.

pathology.pathology: Flocculus mistaken for a CPA tumor
pathology.finding: Normal folia of the flocculus protruding into the cerebellopontine angle cistern; no enhancement, symmetric with the other side.
pathology.pitfalls: Compare with the opposite side before calling a cerebellopontine angle mass

pathology.finding: Small caudal vermian lesion with positional vertigo and downbeat nystagmus mimicking BPPV.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: Axial and coronal T2; DWI

lesionEffects.deficit: Nystagmus: gaze-evoked, downbeat or periodic alternating
lesionEffects.mechanism: Loss of gaze holding and VOR calibration
Vestibulocerebellar control of posture
Flocculus
Nodulus

examination: Eccentric gaze holding and nystagmus in all directions
Smooth pursuit of a slowly moving target
Romberg and gait; Dix–Hallpike showing atypical (downbeat, non-fatiguing) nystagmus
pearls: Downbeat nystagmus points to the craniocervical junction or the flocculus
Positional vertigo that does not fatigue and is downbeating is central until proven otherwise

pitfalls: In the public edition the flocculonodular lobe is not the non-commercial probabilistic cerebellar atlas but a segmentation of the MNI152NLin2009cAsym template itself, made here with FastSurfer's CerebNet module (Apache-2.0 software; `cerebellar-lobule-x-fs-l`, `-r` and `cerebellar-vermis-x-fs`). Lobule X is the smallest cerebellar parcel — about 950 mm³ per flocculus and 600 mm³ for the nodulus — so it is the one a network places least reliably: Dice against the private-edition lobule is 0.73 left, 0.77 right and 0.69 for the nodulus. Use it to find the flocculus in the cerebellopontine angle, not to measure it.

fornix.name: Fornix
fornix.summary: The main efferent bundle of the hippocampus. The fimbria of each hippocampus gathers into the crus of the fornix, which arches forward under the corpus callosum as the body (the two bodies joining beneath the septum pellucidum) and then splits into the columns that dive in front of the foramen of Monro to end mainly in the mammillary bodies, with fibers to the anterior thalamus, septal nuclei and hypothalamus. It is the second link of the Papez circuit, and bilateral damage (surgery for colloid cysts, tumors of the third ventricle, trauma) produces anterograde amnesia.

anatomy.location: Beneath the corpus callosum and above the third ventricle: crura from the hippocampal tails, body under the septum pellucidum forming the medial wall of the lateral ventricles, columns curving down in front of the foramen of Monro into the hypothalamus behind the anterior commissure.

subdivisions.name: Fimbria and crus
subdivisions.note: hippocampal output fibers

subdivisions.name: Body
subdivisions.note: fused midline bundle with the hippocampal commissure beneath the septum

subdivisions.name: Columns
subdivisions.note: precommissural fibers to the septal area, postcommissural fibers to the mammillary bodies and anterior thalamus

fornix.function: Transmission of hippocampal output to the mammillary bodies, anterior thalamus and septal region for consolidation of episodic memory; also carries cholinergic septal input back to the hippocampus.

bestView.label: body of the fornix under the corpus callosum above the third ventricle
fornix arching from the hippocampus to the mammillary body

imaging.normalAppearance: Thin white matter band under the septum on coronal T1, forming the roof of the third ventricle; the columns are seen in front of the foramen of Monro on sagittal images. Fornix atrophy accompanies hippocampal atrophy in Alzheimer disease and follows temporal lobe surgery.

pathology.pathology: Fornix injury after colloid cyst surgery
pathology.finding: T2 change or discontinuity of the columns with post-operative amnesia.
Colloid cyst, subependymoma or glioma of the third ventricle elevating, splaying or invading the fornices, with memory loss and hydrocephalus.
Thin fornix with enlarged ventricles in Alzheimer disease or after mesial temporal sclerosis.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: Coronal and sagittal T1/T2

lesionEffects.mechanism: Bilateral interruption of the hippocampal-mammillary pathway
Unilateral fornix lesion
Perforators to the fornix columns and septal region

examination: Delayed recall of words and of a figure
Recognition versus free recall
Orientation and confabulation
pearls: Colloid cyst surgery and AComm aneurysm surgery are the two classical iatrogenic causes of fornix amnesia

frontal-eye-field.name: Frontal eye field
frontal-eye-field.summary: A region at the junction of the precentral sulcus and the posterior middle frontal gyrus that drives voluntary saccades to the opposite side. Its output reaches the contralateral paramedian pontine reticular formation (and the superior colliculus), so an irritative lesion drives the eyes away from the lesion and a destructive lesion leaves the eyes deviated toward it. This is the basis of the bedside rule for gaze deviation in acute stroke and seizures.

pathology.finding: Large frontal infarct; the globes are seen deviated toward the side of the lesion on the orbital cuts.

Oculocephalic reflex overcomes a frontal gaze palsy (supranuclear)

frontal-pole.name: Frontal pole
frontal-pole.summary: The frontal pole is the rounded anterior tip of the frontal lobe, the most rostral cortex of the hemisphere, lying against the anterior cranial fossa and the frontal bone. It is granular prefrontal cortex (Brodmann area 10) and belongs to the lateral and medial prefrontal networks that support planning across time, multitasking, prospective memory and the balance between reward and long-term goals. It is the part of the brain most often bruised in head injury, because the anterior fossa floor and the frontal bone stop the moving brain, and bilateral frontopolar contusion produces the apathy, disinhibition and poor judgement that families describe long after the fracture has healed.

anatomy.location: Anterior extremity of the hemisphere, in front of the superior, middle and inferior frontal gyri, curving onto the medial surface above the gyrus rectus and resting on the orbital plate of the frontal bone.

efferents.to: Anterior cingulate and supplementary motor area

frontal-pole.function: Frontopolar cortex sits at the top of the prefrontal hierarchy: it holds a main goal in mind while a subgoal is pursued, chooses between exploring new options and exploiting known ones, and integrates emotional value from the orbitofrontal cortex with the abstract plans of the dorsolateral cortex. It is connected through the frontal aslant, uncinate and cingulum bundles to the anterior cingulate, the temporal pole and the amygdala, and its slow maturation into the third decade explains the immaturity of adolescent judgement. Lesions rarely produce a focal sign; they change the person.

bestView.label: frontal pole against the anterior cranial fossa
anterior tips of both frontal lobes

imaging.normalAppearance: Smooth convex tip of the frontal lobe on all planes; on sagittal images it projects above the orbital roof and in front of the frontal horn. The gyri here are thinner and more variable than the central gyri, so asymmetry of the poles is common and normal.

pathology.finding: Patchy hyperdense hemorrhage and low-density edema at the anterior tips of the frontal lobes, often bilateral and worse on the side opposite the impact; blossoms over the first days.
pathology.timing: Repeat CT at 6-12 hours because contusions enlarge

pathology.finding: Extra-axial enhancing mass on the floor of the anterior fossa displacing both frontal poles upward with edema, presenting late with anosmia and personality change.
Symmetric or asymmetric atrophy of the frontal poles and orbital cortex with knife-edge gyri, out of proportion to the parietal lobes.

lesionEffects.deficit: Apathy, loss of initiative and poor planning
lesionEffects.mechanism: Loss of the frontopolar goal-maintenance and prospective memory network
Disconnection of frontopolar and orbitofrontal cortex from the amygdala and anterior cingulate

lesionEffects.deficit: No focal motor or sensory sign
lesionEffects.mechanism: The pole is prefrontal association cortex remote from the primary areas

ganglion-ciliary.name: Ciliary ganglion
ganglion-ciliary.summary: A parasympathetic ganglion the size of a pinhead in the posterior orbit, lateral to the optic nerve and medial to the lateral rectus, where preganglionic fibers from the Edinger–Westphal nucleus travelling in the inferior division of the oculomotor nerve synapse. Its postganglionic fibers reach the eye in the short ciliary nerves to constrict the pupil and contract the ciliary muscle for accommodation; sympathetic and sensory fibers pass through it without synapsing. Damage to the ganglion or its short ciliary nerves (viral infection, orbital surgery, trauma) produces the Adie tonic pupil, a large pupil that reacts poorly to light but slowly and tonically to near, with denervation supersensitivity to dilute pilocarpine.

anatomy.location: Orbital apex, about 1 cm in front of the superior orbital fissure, between the optic nerve and the lateral rectus, on the lateral side of the ophthalmic artery; connected to the nerve to the inferior oblique (parasympathetic root), the nasociliary nerve (sensory root) and the internal carotid plexus (sympathetic root).

ganglion-ciliary.function: Relay of parasympathetic outflow to the sphincter pupillae and ciliary muscle; passage of sympathetic fibers to the dilator and of sensory fibers from the cornea and iris.

bestView.label: orbital apex lateral to the optic nerve, medial to the lateral rectus

imaging.normalAppearance: Not identifiable on routine orbital MRI; the region is the orbital apex lateral to the optic nerve. Orbital MRI is used to exclude a mass or inflammation when a tonic pupil accompanies other orbital signs.

pathology.finding: Mass or inflammation at the apex affecting the ganglion and the nerves passing through the superior orbital fissure.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: Pharmacological pupil testing (0.1% pilocarpine); orbital MRI only if other signs

lesionEffects.deficit: Adie tonic pupil: large, poorly light-reactive pupil with slow tonic constriction to near and slow redilation
lesionEffects.mechanism: Postganglionic parasympathetic denervation with aberrant regeneration of accommodative fibers into the sphincter

lesionEffects.deficit: Loss of accommodation and blurred near vision
lesionEffects.mechanism: Ciliary muscle denervation

ganglion-geniculate.name: Geniculate ganglion
ganglion-geniculate.summary: The sensory ganglion of the facial nerve, sitting at the sharp bend (genu) of the nerve in the facial canal of the temporal bone where the labyrinthine segment turns into the tympanic segment. It holds the cell bodies for taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue (chorda tympani) and for the small cutaneous area of the external ear and gives off the greater petrosal nerve carrying parasympathetic fibers to the lacrimal gland. Varicella zoster reactivation here produces the Ramsay Hunt syndrome (facial palsy with vesicles in the ear canal), and the ganglion region is where Bell palsy enhances on MRI.

anatomy.location: Anterior genu of the facial nerve in the petrous temporal bone, above the cochlea and medial to the middle ear, at the junction of the labyrinthine and tympanic segments; the hiatus of the greater petrosal nerve opens onto the floor of the middle cranial fossa just in front of it.

ganglion-geniculate.function: First-order neurons for taste from the anterior tongue and palate and for somatic sensation of part of the ear; branch point of the parasympathetic supply to the lacrimal and nasal glands.

bestView.label: genu of the facial nerve in the petrous bone above the cochlea
geniculate ganglion region medial to the middle ear

imaging.normalAppearance: High-resolution temporal bone CT shows the geniculate fossa; MRI shows mild normal enhancement of the ganglion, with asymmetric intense enhancement of the labyrinthine segment and ganglion in Bell palsy and Ramsay Hunt syndrome, and expansion in facial schwannoma or hemangioma.

pathology.finding: Enhancement of the labyrinthine segment, geniculate ganglion and proximal tympanic segment without a mass.
Similar enhancement, sometimes involving the eighth nerve and labyrinth; vesicles in the ear canal clinically.

pathology.pathology: Facial nerve schwannoma or geniculate hemangioma

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: Temporal bone CT and MRI with contrast

lesionEffects.mechanism: Lesion at the ganglion: all facial nerve functions involved

ganglion-otic.name: Otic ganglion
ganglion-otic.summary: A small parasympathetic ganglion lying just below the foramen ovale on the medial side of the mandibular nerve, where preganglionic fibers from the inferior salivatory nucleus arriving by the lesser petrosal nerve (glossopharyngeal nerve, via the tympanic plexus) synapse. The postganglionic fibers join the auriculotemporal nerve to reach the parotid gland. Frey syndrome (gustatory sweating over the parotid after parotidectomy) results from aberrant regeneration of these fibers into the sweat glands of the overlying skin.

ganglion-otic.function: Relay of parasympathetic secretomotor fibers to the parotid gland; passage of sympathetic fibers from the middle meningeal plexus and of motor fibers to tensor tympani and tensor veli palatini.

pathology.finding: Enlarged enhancing mandibular nerve through the foramen ovale with denervation atrophy of the masticatory muscles.

ganglion-pterygopalatine.name: Pterygopalatine ganglion
ganglion-pterygopalatine.summary: The largest parasympathetic ganglion of the head, suspended from the maxillary nerve in the pterygopalatine fossa behind the maxilla. Preganglionic fibers from the superior salivatory nucleus arrive by the greater petrosal nerve (facial nerve) after joining the sympathetic deep petrosal nerve in the nerve of the pterygoid canal (vidian nerve); postganglionic fibers travel with maxillary nerve branches to the lacrimal gland (via the zygomatic and lacrimal nerves) and to the glands of the nose, palate and pharynx. It is a target for blocks in cluster headache and facial pain, and perineural spread of sinonasal cancer passes through it.

anatomy.location: Pterygopalatine fossa, a small space behind the maxillary sinus between the pterygoid process and the maxilla, communicating with the orbit (inferior orbital fissure), the nasal cavity (sphenopalatine foramen), the middle cranial fossa (foramen rotundum) and the pterygoid canal.

afferents.via: greater petrosal nerve → nerve of the pterygoid canal

ganglion-pterygopalatine.function: Secretomotor supply to the lacrimal gland and the mucous glands of the nasal cavity, palate, pharynx and paranasal sinuses; vasomotor control of the nasal mucosa.

bestView.label: pterygopalatine fossa behind the maxillary sinus
fossa medial to the pterygoid process

pathology.finding: Obliteration of the fat in the pterygopalatine fossa with enhancement extending along the vidian nerve or V2 toward Meckel's cave.

ganglion-submandibular.name: Submandibular ganglion
ganglion-submandibular.summary: A small parasympathetic ganglion hanging from the lingual nerve above the deep part of the submandibular gland. Preganglionic fibers from the superior salivatory nucleus travel in the facial nerve, leave it as the chorda tympani in the middle ear, join the lingual nerve in the infratemporal fossa and synapse here; postganglionic fibers supply the submandibular and sublingual glands and the minor glands of the floor of the mouth. The chorda tympani also carries taste from the anterior tongue, so lesions of the facial nerve proximal to it reduce both salivation and taste.

afferents.via: chorda tympani via the lingual nerve

imaging.normalAppearance: Not identifiable; the submandibular gland and lingual nerve region are seen on neck MRI. Denervated glands atrophy and show fatty change.

lesionEffects.mechanism: Chorda tympani or ganglion lesion

ganglion-superior-cervical.name: Superior cervical ganglion
ganglion-superior-cervical.summary: The largest sympathetic ganglion, about 2.5 cm long, lying behind the carotid sheath at the level of C2–C3, where the preganglionic fibers from T1–T3 (having ascended the cervical chain) synapse. Its postganglionic fibers form the internal carotid plexus to the eye, the pupil, the lid, the lacrimal gland and the cavernous sinus region, the external carotid plexus to the facial sweat glands and vessels, gray rami to C1–C4, cardiac nerves, and branches to the pharynx and the pineal gland. It is the third-order relay of the oculosympathetic pathway; lesions distal to it cause Horner syndrome without facial anhidrosis.

anatomy.location: In front of the transverse processes of C2 and C3 (some say C1–C4), behind the internal carotid artery and the carotid sheath, medial to the vagus nerve and in front of longus capitis.

ganglion-superior-cervical.function: Sympathetic supply to the head: pupil dilation, lid elevation (Müller's muscle), vasoconstriction, sweating of the face, and innervation of the pineal gland; contributes to cardiac sympathetic supply.

bestView.label: upper cervical region behind the carotid sheath (outside the brain volume)

imaging.normalAppearance: Seen on neck MRI as a small fusiform structure behind the carotid sheath, easily mistaken for a lymph node; enlargement occurs in schwannoma. Carotid imaging is the key study for postganglionic Horner syndrome.

pathology.finding: Enhancing fusiform mass behind the carotid displacing the vessels anteriorly, sometimes with a Horner syndrome.
Mural hematoma with a postganglionic Horner syndrome (no anhidrosis).

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: Neck MRI; carotid CTA/MRA

lesionEffects.mechanism: Postganglionic fibers on the internal carotid; sweat fibers travel with the external carotid

ganglion-trigeminal.name: Trigeminal ganglion
ganglion-trigeminal.summary: The sensory ganglion of the trigeminal nerve, a crescent of pseudounipolar cell bodies lying in Meckel's cave, a dural pocket on the petrous apex lateral to the cavernous sinus. Its peripheral processes form the ophthalmic, maxillary and mandibular divisions and its central processes form the sensory root entering the pons; the motor root passes beneath it without synapsing. Herpes zoster and herpes simplex lie latent here (zoster ophthalmicus when V1 reactivates), tumors of Meckel's cave (schwannoma, meningioma, perineural spread) produce facial numbness, and the ganglion is the target of radiofrequency and balloon procedures for trigeminal neuralgia.

anatomy.location: Meckel's cave, an evagination of dura and arachnoid on the anterior surface of the petrous temporal bone near its apex, lateral to the cavernous sinus and internal carotid artery, above the foramen ovale, with the temporal lobe above.

ganglion-trigeminal.function: Contains the first-order neurons for touch, pain, temperature and proprioception (except jaw proprioception) of the face, cornea, oral and nasal cavities, teeth, dura and scalp.

html.summary: The sensory ganglion of the trigeminal nerve, a crescent of pseudounipolar cell bodies lying in Meckel's cave, a dural pocket on the petrous apex lateral to the cavernous sinus. Its peripheral processes form the ophthalmic, maxillary and mandibular divisions and its central processes form the sensory root entering the pons; the motor root passes beneath it without synapsing. Herpes zoster and herpes simplex lie latent here (zoster ophthalmicus when V1 reactivates), tumors of Meckel's cave (schwannoma, meningioma, perineural spread) produce facial numbness, and the ganglion is the target of radiofrequency and balloon procedures for trigeminal neuralgia.
html.function: Contains the first-order neurons for touch, pain, temperature and proprioception (except jaw proprioception) of the face, cornea, oral and nasal cavities, teeth, dura and scalp.
html.anatomy.location: Meckel's cave, an evagination of dura and arachnoid on the anterior surface of the petrous temporal bone near its apex, lateral to the cavernous sinus and internal carotid artery, above the foramen ovale, with the temporal lobe above.

globus-pallidus-externus.name: Globus pallidus, external segment
globus-pallidus-externus.summary: The external segment of the globus pallidus is the lateral part of the pallidum, between the putamen and the medial medullary lamina that separates it from the internal segment. It is the relay of the indirect pathway: striatal neurons carrying D2 receptors inhibit it, it in turn inhibits the subthalamic nucleus, and the subthalamic nucleus excites the output nuclei, so activity in this circuit suppresses unwanted movement. Its overactivity or underactivity shapes the balance between akinesia and chorea, and it is the origin of the ansa lenticularis fibers that surround the internal capsule; it is involved in lenticulostriate infarcts and hemorrhages and in the pallidal necrosis of carbon monoxide poisoning.

anatomy.location: Lateral segment of the lentiform nucleus medial to the putamen and the lateral medullary lamina, lateral to the internal segment and the medial medullary lamina, above the anterior commissure and the substantia innominata, medial to the external capsule and lateral to the posterior limb of the internal capsule.

efferents.to: Globus pallidus internus and substantia nigra pars reticulata

globus-pallidus-externus.function: External pallidal neurons fire tonically and are inhibited by the striatal indirect-pathway neurons when dopamine acting on D2 receptors is low; their own inhibitory projection to the subthalamic nucleus then lets the subthalamus excite the internal pallidum and the pars reticulata, which shuts down the thalamus. Reciprocal subthalamo-pallidal connections form a pacemaker whose abnormal synchronization in the beta band underlies parkinsonian bradykinesia. Arkypallidal neurons project back to the striatum to cancel actions in progress, and prototypic neurons also reach the internal pallidum directly. Loss of striatal input to it in Huntington disease removes the brake and produces chorea.

bestView.label: external pallidum between the putamen and the internal segment

imaging.normalAppearance: The lateral, larger part of the pallidum on axial T2 images, darker than the putamen because of its iron and myelin, separated from the internal segment by the thin bright medial medullary lamina.

globus-pallidus-internus.name: Globus pallidus, internal segment
globus-pallidus-internus.summary: The internal segment of the globus pallidus is the medial, smaller part of the pallidum, against the posterior limb of the internal capsule and separated from the external segment by the medial medullary lamina. It is the main output nucleus of the basal ganglia for the limbs: its GABAergic neurons tonically inhibit the ventral anterior and ventrolateral thalamus and the pedunculopontine nucleus through the ansa lenticularis and the lenticular fasciculus, and movement is released when the direct pathway pauses them. It is the target of pallidotomy and of deep brain stimulation for Parkinson disease and dystonia, and it is damaged in kernicterus, in carbon monoxide poisoning and in the pantothenate kinase iron disorder.

anatomy.location: Medial part of the lentiform nucleus between the medial medullary lamina and the posterior limb of the internal capsule, above the optic tract and the substantia innominata, in front of and lateral to the subthalamic nucleus, divided by an accessory lamina into outer and inner portions.

efferents.via: ansa lenticularis and lenticular fasciculus (thalamic fasciculus)

globus-pallidus-internus.function: Internal pallidal neurons discharge continuously to keep the motor thalamus and the brainstem locomotor region suppressed; striatal direct-pathway neurons inhibit them to open a window for the intended movement while subthalamic excitation closes it around competing movements, giving the focused selection the basal ganglia provide. The output leaves through the ansa lenticularis (from the outer portion) and the lenticular fasciculus (from the inner portion), which unite as the thalamic fasciculus in the field H1 of Forel. Excess pallidal output in parkinsonism freezes the thalamus and lesioning or high-frequency stimulation of the nucleus relieves rigidity, bradykinesia and dyskinesia; abnormal patterned output produces dystonia.

bestView.label: internal pallidum against the posterior limb of the internal capsule

globus-pallidus.name: Globus pallidus
globus-pallidus.summary: The medial, wedge-shaped part of the lentiform nucleus, paler than the putamen because of its myelinated fibers, divided by the internal medullary lamina into an external segment (GPe), a relay of the indirect pathway to the subthalamic nucleus, and an internal segment (GPi), the main output nucleus of the basal ganglia. GPi tonically inhibits the ventral anterior and ventral lateral thalamus through the ansa and fasciculus lenticularis; movement is released by pausing that inhibition. Its output is too active in Parkinson disease (hence pallidotomy and GPi stimulation help) and too weak in hemiballismus and chorea. It is rich in iron and is the target of carbon monoxide, hepatic disease and iron-accumulation disorders.

anatomy.location: Medial part of the lentiform nucleus, between the putamen laterally and the posterior limb of the internal capsule medially, above the substantia innominata and anterior commissure; GPi lies medial to GPe.

subdivisions.name: External segment (GPe)
subdivisions.note: receives striatal indirect-pathway input; projects to the subthalamic nucleus

subdivisions.name: Internal segment (GPi)
subdivisions.note: receives direct-pathway striatal input and subthalamic input; tonic GABAergic output to VA/VL thalamus (ansa lenticularis, lenticular fasciculus) and to the pedunculopontine nucleus

globus-pallidus.function: Final output stage of the motor basal ganglia loop: sets the level of thalamocortical facilitation of movement; also part of the limbic loop through the ventral pallidum.

bestView.label: globus pallidus medial to the putamen beside the posterior limb

gyrus-angular.name: Angular gyrus
gyrus-angular.summary: The posterior part of the inferior parietal lobule, arching over the end of the superior temporal sulcus at the meeting point of the parietal, temporal and occipital lobes. It is a multimodal hub: on the dominant side it links written symbols with language (reading, writing), numbers with quantity (calculation) and the body with its labels (finger recognition, right-left), so a left angular lesion yields Gerstmann syndrome and alexia with agraphia. On the right it contributes to spatial attention and self-location, and stimulation here produces out-of-body experiences.

anatomy.location: Behind the supramarginal gyrus at the posterior end of the superior temporal sulcus, bordering the occipital lobe; the angular artery of the MCA reaches it as the artery's terminal branch.

gyrus-angular.function: Reading, writing, calculation, finger gnosis, right-left orientation, semantic integration and, on the right, spatial attention and body awareness.

imaging.normalAppearance: Lies at the posterior end of the superior temporal sulcus, in the MCA–PCA watershed; infarcts and posterior cortical atrophy involve it early.

gyrus-cingulate-anterior.name: Cingulate gyrus, anterior division
gyrus-cingulate-anterior.summary: The anterior cingulate gyrus arches over the genu and the anterior body of the corpus callosum on the medial surface, between the callosal sulcus below and the cingulate sulcus above, Brodmann areas 24, 32 and 33. It is limbic cortex with a motor and a cognitive face: its dorsal part monitors conflict and error and drives effort and vocalization, its ventral (pregenual) part regulates emotion and autonomic tone, and both connect the prefrontal cortex with the amygdala, hypothalamus and striatum. It is supplied by the anterior cerebral artery, and bilateral damage produces apathy and akinetic mutism, whereas seizures beginning here produce fear, hypermotor behavior and autonomic storms.

anatomy.location: Medial frontal surface above the genu and anterior body of the corpus callosum, from the subcallosal region in front to about the level of the central sulcus behind, where the posterior division begins; the cingulum bundle runs in its white matter.

efferents.to: Hypothalamus, periaqueductal gray and facial nucleus

gyrus-cingulate-anterior.function: The anterior cingulate cortex assesses whether the outcome of an action matches its expected value and signals errors and conflicts to the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, weighs the effort a task will cost against its reward and initiates action and speech; it houses cingulate motor areas that project to the spinal cord and the facial nucleus for emotional expression and vocalization. The ventral part integrates emotion with visceral state and inhibits the amygdala, and its projections to the hypothalamus and brainstem change heart rate, blood pressure and respiration with mental effort and pain. It also carries the affective, unpleasant dimension of pain, which is why cingulotomy relieves suffering without removing sensation.

gyrus-cingulate-posterior.name: Cingulate gyrus, posterior division
gyrus-cingulate-posterior.summary: The posterior cingulate gyrus lies above the posterior body and the splenium of the corpus callosum and continues below the splenium as the isthmus, joining the parahippocampal gyrus; it includes the posterior cingulate cortex (areas 23 and 31) and the retrosplenial cortex (areas 29 and 30). It is the posterior hub of the default mode network with the precuneus, essential for episodic memory retrieval, spatial navigation and self-related thought, and it is the first cortex to lose glucose metabolism in Alzheimer disease. It is supplied by the pericallosal branches of the anterior cerebral artery and by the posterior cerebral artery near the isthmus, and its lesions cause topographical disorientation and amnesia.

anatomy.location: Medial surface above the posterior half of the corpus callosum and around the splenium, bounded above by the cingulate sulcus and the subparietal sulcus, continuous in front with the anterior division and below the splenium with the isthmus and the parahippocampal gyrus.

gyrus-cingulate-posterior.function: The posterior cingulate and retrosplenial cortex link the hippocampal memory system with the parietal and prefrontal cortex: the retrosplenial cortex converts egocentric views into the allocentric map used for navigation and recognizes the orientation of familiar scenes, and the posterior cingulate retrieves episodic memories and supports the internally directed thought of the default mode. The region receives the anterior thalamic nuclei and the subiculum and projects through the cingulum to the entorhinal cortex, closing a limb of the Papez circuit. Damage produces an amnesia with prominent loss of direction in familiar places, and metabolic failure here is the earliest imaging sign of Alzheimer disease.

gyrus-cingulate.name: Cingulate gyrus
gyrus-cingulate.summary: The long gyrus arching over the corpus callosum on the medial surface, separated from it by the callosal sulcus and from the frontal and parietal cortex by the cingulate sulcus, and continuous behind the splenium with the parahippocampal gyrus through the isthmus. It is the cortical station of the Papez circuit (receiving the anterior thalamic nuclei) and the cingulum bundle runs in its white matter. The anterior cingulate drives motivation, attention, pain affect and autonomic responses; the posterior cingulate and retrosplenial cortex support episodic memory and spatial orientation and are the earliest hypometabolic regions in Alzheimer disease.

gyrus-heschl.name: Heschl's gyrus (primary auditory cortex)
gyrus-heschl.summary: One or two short gyri running transversely across the upper surface of the superior temporal gyrus, hidden inside the Sylvian fissure. They receive the acoustic radiation from the medial geniculate body and hold a tonotopic map (low frequencies anterolaterally, high frequencies posteromedially). Because the auditory pathway is bilateral from the brainstem up, a unilateral lesion never causes deafness, only subtle deficits in localization and in perceiving speech in noise; bilateral lesions produce cortical deafness or pure word deafness. The planum temporale behind Heschl's gyrus is larger on the left in most people and merges into Wernicke's area.

anatomy.location: On the superior (opercular) surface of the superior temporal gyrus within the depths of the lateral sulcus, running obliquely backward and medially from the lateral surface toward the insula; the planum temporale lies posterior to it.

gyrus-heschl.function: Conscious perception of sound, frequency and intensity analysis, sound localization and the first cortical stage of speech and music perception.

gyrus-inferior-frontal-opercularis.name: Inferior frontal gyrus, pars opercularis
gyrus-inferior-frontal-opercularis.summary: The pars opercularis is the posterior part of the inferior frontal gyrus, between the ascending ramus of the lateral sulcus and the precentral sulcus, forming with the pars triangularis the classical Broca area (Brodmann area 44) in the language-dominant hemisphere. It coordinates the sequencing of articulatory movements and syntax, and it is a core node of the dorsal language stream with the arcuate fasciculus behind it. Infarction of the superior division of the middle cerebral artery here produces non-fluent aphasia with intact comprehension, usually with a right facial and arm weakness because the precentral gyrus lies immediately behind it.

anatomy.location: Posterior division of the inferior frontal gyrus, bounded in front by the ascending ramus of the lateral sulcus, behind by the inferior precentral sulcus and above by the inferior frontal sulcus; it overhangs the insula as part of the frontal operculum.

gyrus-inferior-frontal-opercularis.function: Area 44 translates the phonological plan of an utterance into a motor program for the larynx, tongue and lips through its projection to the ventral precentral gyrus, and it holds the grammatical frame of a sentence, which is why lesions produce agrammatic, telegraphic speech. It receives the posterior temporal language cortex through the arcuate fasciculus and the frontal aslant tract links it to the supplementary motor area for speech initiation. In the non-dominant hemisphere the homologous region contributes to prosody and to response inhibition (stopping an action), and both sides house mirror-neuron-like responses to observed actions.

gyrus-inferior-frontal-triangularis.name: Inferior frontal gyrus, pars triangularis
gyrus-inferior-frontal-triangularis.summary: The pars triangularis is the wedge of the inferior frontal gyrus between the anterior horizontal and the ascending rami of the lateral sulcus, Brodmann area 45. With the pars opercularis behind it, it makes up the Broca region of the dominant hemisphere, but its role is more semantic and selective than motor: it retrieves words among competitors, resolves ambiguity and supports the controlled search of verbal memory. Lesions restricted to it cause word-finding difficulty and reduced fluency without the severe agrammatism and apraxia of speech that follow damage to the pars opercularis, and it is the frontal region that best predicts recovery of naming after stroke.

anatomy.location: Triangular middle division of the inferior frontal gyrus, its apex pointing up toward the inferior frontal sulcus and its base on the lateral sulcus between the horizontal ramus in front and the ascending ramus behind.

afferents.from: Pars opercularis and ventral premotor cortex

gyrus-inferior-frontal-triangularis.function: Area 45 is the frontal end of the ventral language stream: it receives the anterior and middle temporal lobe through the uncinate and inferior fronto-occipital fasciculi and selects among semantic alternatives, generates verbs and category members in fluency tasks, and contributes to syntactic processing of complex sentences. In the right hemisphere its homologue handles emotional prosody and the inhibition of responses. It also participates in verbal working memory, keeping a phonological trace alive by silent rehearsal, and in reading, where it maps letters to sounds.

gyrus-inferior-temporal-anterior.name: Inferior temporal gyrus, anterior division
gyrus-inferior-temporal-anterior.summary: The anterior inferior temporal gyrus forms the lower lateral border of the front of the temporal lobe, between the inferior temporal sulcus and the occipitotemporal sulcus, curving onto the inferior surface toward the fusiform gyrus. It is the end of the ventral visual stream where object and face representations reach the semantic and emotional systems of the anterior temporal lobe, and it is supplied mainly by the posterior cerebral artery with the middle cerebral artery laterally. Its damage contributes to prosopagnosia and object agnosia, to semantic dementia when combined with the temporal pole, and to the visual hallucinations and experiential phenomena of temporal seizures.

anatomy.location: Anterior half of the lowest lateral temporal gyrus, below the inferior temporal sulcus and lateral to the occipitotemporal sulcus and the fusiform gyrus, resting on the floor of the middle cranial fossa.

afferents.from: Posterior inferior temporal and fusiform cortex

gyrus-inferior-temporal-anterior.function: Neurons of the anterior inferior temporal cortex respond to whole objects and faces regardless of their size, position and lighting, and pass these invariant representations to the temporal pole, the perirhinal cortex and the amygdala so that objects can be recognized, named and given emotional meaning. The left side is important for naming objects from vision and for reading words as wholes, the right for recognizing faces and familiar objects and for visual memory. It lies in the posterior cerebral artery territory, and its involvement in a PCA infarct adds visual agnosia or alexia to the hemianopia.

gyrus-inferior-temporal-posterior.name: Inferior temporal gyrus, posterior division
gyrus-inferior-temporal-posterior.summary: The posterior inferior temporal gyrus is the lower lateral temporal cortex behind the level of the posterior insula and in front of the temporo-occipital junction, between the inferior temporal sulcus and the occipitotemporal sulcus. It is high-order visual cortex of the ventral stream that represents object shape, color and category, and in the dominant hemisphere it houses part of the basal temporal language area that supports naming. It receives the posterior cerebral artery below and the middle cerebral artery above and is a typical watershed, so it is affected in hypotensive injury and in posterior cortical atrophy; focal lesions cause object agnosia, color agnosia and anomia, and stimulation here arrests naming during awake surgery.

gyrus-inferior-temporal-posterior.function: Neurons here encode the shape, texture and color of objects and generalize across viewpoints, forming the intermediate stage between the occipital form areas and the invariant object representations of the anterior temporal lobe; the left side also participates in naming from vision and reading, as part of the basal temporal language area with the fusiform gyrus. It projects to the amygdala and perirhinal cortex for object memory and emotional value and to the prefrontal cortex through the inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus for object-based decisions. The right side dominates for global form and face processing and the left for detail and words.

gyrus-inferior-temporal-temporooccipital.name: Inferior temporal gyrus, temporo-occipital part
gyrus-inferior-temporal-temporooccipital.summary: The temporo-occipital part of the inferior temporal gyrus is the most posterior segment of the lower lateral temporal cortex, where it passes into the inferior lateral occipital cortex behind the level of the atrium. It contains shape-selective and object-selective visual cortex (the lateral occipital complex), contributes to the visual word form system in the dominant hemisphere and to face and body perception on the right, and is supplied by the posterior cerebral artery with a middle cerebral artery contribution at its upper edge. Lesions produce apperceptive visual agnosia, alexia and, when the adjacent optic radiation is involved, a contralateral upper quadrant defect.

gyrus-inferior-temporal-temporooccipital.function: This cortex assembles edges, contours and surfaces into whole object shapes and represents them independently of low-level features, the stage at which a drawn outline and a photograph become the same object; the left side contributes to recognizing letter strings as words and the right to recognizing faces and bodies as wholes. It receives the ventral occipital areas and projects forward along the inferior longitudinal fasciculus to the inferior temporal and perirhinal cortex and to the amygdala. Damage produces apperceptive agnosia, in which the patient cannot copy or match shapes, in contrast to the associative agnosia of more anterior lesions where copying is preserved.

gyrus-lingual.name: Lingual gyrus
gyrus-lingual.summary: The lingual gyrus is the tongue-shaped gyrus on the inferomedial occipital surface below the calcarine sulcus, extending forward to the isthmus of the cingulate gyrus and bounded laterally by the collateral sulcus and the fusiform gyrus. It is the lower bank of the primary visual cortex and its surrounding V2, V3 and ventral V4, and it represents the contralateral upper visual field; it also processes color and, together with the parahippocampal cortex in front of it, the recognition of places and landmarks. It is supplied by the posterior cerebral artery, and its lesions produce contralateral superior quadrantanopia, hemiachromatopsia and topographical disorientation.

gyrus-middle-frontal.name: Middle frontal gyrus
gyrus-middle-frontal.summary: The middle frontal gyrus occupies the lateral convexity between the superior and inferior frontal sulci and is the largest territory of dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (Brodmann areas 9 and 46 anteriorly, 8 and 6 posteriorly). Its posterior end holds the frontal eye field, so a destructive lesion turns the eyes toward the lesion and a seizure turns them away. Its anterior two-thirds support working memory, set shifting, planning and the executive functions tested at the bedside by fluency, trail making and the Wisconsin card sort. It is a middle cerebral artery superior division territory and one of the areas that atrophy earliest in behavioral variant frontotemporal dementia.
