gyrus-middle-frontal.function: The dorsolateral prefrontal cortex here holds and manipulates information over seconds (working memory), selects rules and switches them when they fail, and inhibits prepotent responses; it is heavily connected with the parietal attention areas by the superior longitudinal fasciculus and with the mediodorsal thalamus and the caudate in the prefrontal loop of the basal ganglia. The posterior part, the frontal eye field, generates voluntary saccades to the contralateral side and contributes to smooth pursuit. Damage produces the dysexecutive syndrome: poor planning, perseveration, loss of set and impaired fluency with preserved basic language.

gyrus-middle-temporal-anterior.name: Middle temporal gyrus, anterior division
gyrus-middle-temporal-anterior.summary: The anterior middle temporal gyrus lies between the superior and inferior temporal sulci in the front half of the lateral temporal lobe, forward of the level of the posterior insula. It is heteromodal association cortex that stores the meanings of words and the knowledge of objects and people, forming with the temporal pole the semantic system of the ventral language stream. It is supplied by the inferior division of the middle cerebral artery with a contribution from the posterior cerebral artery at its lower border, it atrophies early in semantic dementia and Alzheimer disease, and it is the lateral cortex most often included in an anterior temporal lobectomy for medial temporal epilepsy.

afferents.from: Fusiform and inferior temporal cortex (visual objects)

efferents.via: perforant path input via parahippocampal cortex

gyrus-middle-temporal-anterior.function: The anterior middle temporal cortex links the sound and the written form of a word with its meaning and stores knowledge about objects, animals and famous people in a modality-independent form; on the left it is essential for comprehension of single words and for naming, on the right it contributes to recognizing familiar faces and voices and to understanding social scenes and narratives. It receives the visual object stream from the fusiform and inferior temporal cortex and the auditory identification stream from the superior temporal gyrus and projects to the inferior frontal gyrus through the inferior fronto-occipital and uncinate fasciculi. Seizure spread into this cortex produces the auditory and complex auras of lateral temporal epilepsy.

gyrus-middle-temporal-posterior.name: Middle temporal gyrus, posterior division
gyrus-middle-temporal-posterior.summary: The posterior middle temporal gyrus lies below the posterior superior temporal gyrus and in front of the temporo-occipital junction, at the level of the posterior insula and the atrium of the lateral ventricle. It is a convergence zone where heard, read and seen information meets: in the dominant hemisphere it holds the lexical interface between word forms and meaning and the knowledge of actions and tools, and bilaterally it contains the motion-sensitive cortex at its junction with the occipital lobe. Lesions contribute to fluent aphasia and to verb-naming and action-knowledge deficits, and the underlying white matter carries the optic radiation and the arcuate fasciculus so that infarcts here add a field defect and repetition failure.

gyrus-middle-temporal-posterior.function: This cortex retrieves the meaning of words heard or read and is especially important for verbs, tools and actions, linking the visual form of an action to its motor program and its name; it is part of both the ventral semantic stream and the dorsal stream through the arcuate and middle longitudinal fasciculi. Its posterior end merges with the visual motion area that tracks moving objects and biological motion, and the right side reads intentions from body movement and gaze. Electrical stimulation produces anomia and comprehension failure in the dominant hemisphere, and the cortex is a common site of seizure onset with complex visual and auditory auras.

gyrus-middle-temporal-temporooccipital.name: Middle temporal gyrus, temporo-occipital part
gyrus-middle-temporal-temporooccipital.summary: The temporo-occipital part of the middle temporal gyrus is the posterior end of the gyrus where the temporal lobe merges with the lateral occipital lobe, behind the level of the atrium. It contains the human motion complex (area MT/V5 and its satellites) on its lateral surface and cortex that links visual form with meaning and with reading. It sits at the border of the middle and posterior cerebral artery territories, a watershed, and its damage causes akinetopsia, impaired perception of biological motion and, on the left, difficulties in reading and in retrieving words from pictures; seizures here produce elementary moving visual hallucinations.

Lesions produce loss of motion perception with preserved acuity and form vision, difficulty following moving conversation partners, and in the dominant hemisphere a slowing of reading. The region also guides smooth pursuit eye movements toward the ipsilateral side.

gyrus-occipital-fusiform.name: Occipital fusiform gyrus
gyrus-occipital-fusiform.summary: The occipital fusiform gyrus is the posterior end of the fusiform gyrus on the inferior surface of the occipital lobe, between the collateral sulcus and the lingual gyrus medially and the inferior lateral occipital cortex laterally, behind the temporo-occipital fusiform cortex. It is ventral extrastriate cortex (parts of V2, V3, V4 and the posterior lateral occipital complex) that represents the contralateral upper field and begins the analysis of color, texture and shape that the fusiform recognition areas complete. It is supplied by the posterior cerebral artery, and its lesions add hemiachromatopsia and apperceptive agnosia to a superior quadrantanopia; bilateral lesions give achromatopsia and visual form agnosia.

It projects along the inferior longitudinal fasciculus and receives feedback from the parietal and frontal attention systems. Lesions produce loss of color and shape perception in the contralateral upper field and, with extension medially, a quadrantanopia; seizures here produce colored auras in the upper field.

gyrus-paracingulate.name: Paracingulate gyrus
gyrus-paracingulate.summary: The paracingulate gyrus is a variable gyrus on the medial frontal surface between the cingulate sulcus and the paracingulate sulcus, present in most left hemispheres and fewer right ones, corresponding to the dorsal anterior cingulate and medial prefrontal cortex of Brodmann areas 32 and part of 24. It belongs to the cingulo-opercular control network that monitors performance, detects errors and conflict, and adjusts effort, and it is the medial frontal region most consistently activated by cognitive tasks. Its asymmetry is a normal variant, but reduced paracingulate folding has been linked to schizophrenia, and damage contributes to apathy and to impaired conflict resolution.

Its projections to the striatum and the brainstem autonomic centers couple mental effort to heart rate and blood pressure. Bilateral damage with the neighboring anterior cingulate produces apathy and, when extensive, akinetic mutism.

gyrus-parahippocampal-anterior.name: Parahippocampal gyrus, anterior division
gyrus-parahippocampal-anterior.summary: The anterior parahippocampal gyrus is the medial temporal cortex beneath the hippocampal head and the amygdala, containing the entorhinal cortex (area 28) medially and the perirhinal cortex (areas 35 and 36) along the collateral and rhinal sulci; it bends back on itself medially as the uncus. It is the gateway to the hippocampus: nearly all cortical information enters the hippocampal formation through the entorhinal cortex by the perforant path, and the perirhinal cortex recognizes familiar objects. It is the first cortex to accumulate tau tangles in Alzheimer disease, it is involved in mesial temporal epilepsy, and it is compressed against the tentorium in uncal herniation.

anatomy.location: Anterior part of the parahippocampal gyrus on the inferomedial temporal surface, medial to the collateral and rhinal sulci and the fusiform gyrus, lateral to the ambient cistern and the midbrain, below the amygdala and the hippocampal head, curving into the uncus anteromedially.

afferents.from: Perirhinal and parahippocampal cortex, all association cortices

gyrus-parahippocampal-anterior.function: The entorhinal cortex gathers highly processed sensory and associative input from the whole cortex, especially through the perirhinal (object) and parahippocampal (scene) cortices, and sends it into the dentate gyrus and hippocampus by the perforant path while receiving the hippocampal output from the subiculum and relaying it back to the cortex; its grid cells provide the spatial metric of navigation. The perirhinal cortex signals whether an object has been seen before and links it with its value. Damage here produces anterograde amnesia even with an intact hippocampus, and the region is where Alzheimer tangles and mesial temporal seizures begin.

bestView.label: anterior parahippocampal gyrus beneath the hippocampal head and amygdala

gyrus-parahippocampal-posterior.name: Parahippocampal gyrus, posterior division
gyrus-parahippocampal-posterior.summary: The posterior parahippocampal gyrus is the medial temporal cortex beneath the body and tail of the hippocampus, behind the entorhinal cortex and in front of the isthmus of the cingulate gyrus, bounded laterally by the collateral sulcus and the fusiform gyrus. It contains the parahippocampal cortex proper (areas TH and TF), which houses the parahippocampal place area that recognizes scenes and the spatial layout of the environment, and it relays scene and context information into the entorhinal cortex and the hippocampus. It is supplied by the posterior cerebral artery, its lesions cause landmark and topographical disorientation and context-dependent memory loss, and it atrophies with the rest of the medial temporal lobe in Alzheimer disease.

anatomy.location: Posterior part of the parahippocampal gyrus on the inferomedial temporal surface under the hippocampal body and tail, from the level of the cerebral peduncle back to the splenium where it continues as the isthmus, medial to the collateral sulcus and lateral to the ambient and quadrigeminal cisterns.

afferents.from: Lingual, fusiform and lateral occipital cortex (scenes)
afferents.via: inferior longitudinal fasciculus and short fibers

gyrus-parahippocampal-posterior.function: The posterior parahippocampal cortex receives visual scene information from the lingual and fusiform gyri and the dorsal stream, spatial information from the retrosplenial cortex and the posterior cingulate, and represents places, the arrangement of a room and the context in which an event occurred; it feeds the medial entorhinal cortex, which builds the spatial map of the hippocampus, and it also receives vestibular and auditory input. It is one of the two main channels into the hippocampus, the other being the perirhinal object channel, and its damage produces a memory loss dominated by the where and the when, with impaired navigation and recognition of scenes.

gyrus-parahippocampal-uncus.name: Parahippocampal gyrus and uncus
gyrus-parahippocampal-uncus.summary: The most medial temporal gyrus, running along the medial edge of the temporal lobe from the uncus in front to the isthmus of the cingulate gyrus behind. Its anterior part is entorhinal cortex, the gateway through which cortical information enters the hippocampus (and the first site of Alzheimer tangles); its hook-shaped anterior end, the uncus, carries the primary olfactory cortex and abuts the amygdala. The uncus overhangs the tentorial edge beside the oculomotor nerve and the cerebral peduncle, which is why raised supratentorial pressure produces uncal herniation with a blown pupil.

anatomy.location: Medial temporal lobe between the hippocampal fissure and the collateral sulcus, under the hippocampus; the uncus is its recurved anterior tip lying medial to the temporal horn, above the tentorial incisura, about 2 cm behind the temporal pole.

subdivisions.name: Entorhinal cortex (area 28)
subdivisions.note: anterior parahippocampal gyrus; hippocampal input via the perforant path

subdivisions.name: Uncus

subdivisions.note: scene and spatial memory, continuous with the lingual gyrus and cingulate isthmus

gyrus-postcentral.name: Postcentral gyrus (primary somatosensory cortex)
gyrus-postcentral.summary: The gyrus behind the central sulcus, receiving the thalamocortical projections from the ventral posterior nuclei and mapping the contralateral body in a sensory homunculus that mirrors the motor one: leg and foot on the medial paracentral lobule, hand at the convexity with a large representation, face and tongue lowest. Area 3b in the posterior wall of the central sulcus receives cutaneous touch, area 3a proprioception, and areas 1 and 2 elaborate texture and shape. Its lesions abolish the discriminative aspects of sensation while crude pain and touch survive in the thalamus.

anatomy.location: Between the central sulcus in front and the postcentral sulcus behind, from the lateral sulcus over the vertex to the posterior paracentral lobule on the medial surface; thinner cortex than the precentral gyrus.

afferents.via: posterior limb of the internal capsule

gyrus-postcentral.function: Conscious discriminative touch, proprioception, vibration and localization of pain and temperature for the contralateral body; first stage of tactile object recognition.

bestView.label: postcentral gyrus behind the hand knob
postcentral gyrus behind the central sulcus

gyrus-precentral.name: Precentral gyrus (primary motor cortex)
gyrus-precentral.summary: The gyrus immediately in front of the central sulcus, extending over the vertex onto the medial surface as the anterior part of the paracentral lobule. Its layer V giant pyramidal (Betz) cells and many smaller pyramidal neurons give rise to the corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts. The body is mapped upside down and distorted along it (the motor homunculus): the leg and foot on the medial surface, the trunk and arm over the convexity with a disproportionately large hand area at the hand knob, and the face and tongue lowest, just above the Sylvian fissure. Because the ACA supplies the leg area and the MCA the rest, the pattern of weakness after a stroke tells you which artery is involved.

anatomy.location: Between the precentral sulcus in front and the central sulcus behind, from the lateral sulcus to the superior margin and onto the medial surface; recognized on axial MRI by the omega-shaped hand knob and by the thicker cortex compared with the postcentral gyrus.

gyrus-superior-frontal.name: Superior frontal gyrus
gyrus-superior-frontal.summary: The superior frontal gyrus is the long strip of frontal cortex above the superior frontal sulcus, running from the frontal pole back to the precentral sulcus and folding over the superior margin onto the medial surface, where it is continuous with the paracentral lobule. Laterally and medially it houses parts of the premotor cortex and the supplementary motor area, and its anterior part is dorsolateral prefrontal cortex. It is supplied mainly by the anterior cerebral artery on its medial and upper parts and by the middle cerebral artery laterally, which is why anterior cerebral infarcts produce leg weakness and abulia from this gyrus rather than a face-arm hemiparesis.

anatomy.location: Uppermost of the three frontal convexity gyri, bounded below by the superior frontal sulcus and behind by the precentral sulcus; it wraps over the superomedial border so that its medial part faces the falx above the cingulate sulcus.

efferents.to: Precentral gyrus and spinal cord (leg and trunk)

gyrus-superior-frontal.function: Its posterior part contributes premotor and supplementary motor cortex for the planning and initiation of movement, especially of the legs and trunk and of internally generated, sequenced actions; the frontal eye field lies at its junction with the precentral gyrus. Its anterior part is dorsolateral prefrontal cortex engaged in working memory, self-awareness and the top-down control of attention, and its medial part is part of the default mode network. Seizures beginning here produce abrupt hypermotor or tonic posturing of both limbs with preserved awareness that is often mistaken for a psychogenic attack.

bestView.label: superior frontal gyrus wrapping over the superomedial border

gyrus-superior-temporal-anterior.name: Superior temporal gyrus, anterior division
gyrus-superior-temporal-anterior.summary: The anterior part of the superior temporal gyrus lies below the lateral sulcus in front of Heschl's gyrus, extending forward to the temporal pole. Its upper surface, the planum polare, borders the anterior Sylvian fissure, and its lateral surface is auditory association cortex that processes the identity of sounds, voices and, in the dominant hemisphere, the meaning of spoken words as part of the ventral auditory-language stream. It is supplied by the inferior division of the middle cerebral artery and takes part in the fluent aphasias, in the recognition of voices, and in the auditory hallucinations of temporal lobe seizures and psychosis.

anatomy.location: Anterior half of the uppermost temporal gyrus, bounded above by the lateral sulcus, below by the superior temporal sulcus, in front by the temporal pole and behind by the transverse temporal gyrus of Heschl and the posterior division.

efferents.to: Temporal pole and inferior frontal gyrus

gyrus-superior-temporal-anterior.function: Sound leaves the primary auditory cortex along two streams; the anterior stream through this gyrus identifies what a sound is, recognizing voices, environmental sounds and, on the left, the phonemes and words of speech, and passes them forward to the temporal pole and the inferior frontal gyrus through the uncinate and extreme capsule fibers. The right anterior superior temporal cortex is specialized for the melody and emotional prosody of speech and for voice identity, and both sides respond to music. Lesions here produce word deafness and voice agnosia when the primary cortex is spared, and contribute to the comprehension deficit of Wernicke aphasia.

html.summary: The anterior part of the superior temporal gyrus lies below the lateral sulcus in front of Heschl's gyrus, extending forward to the temporal pole. Its upper surface, the planum polare, borders the anterior Sylvian fissure, and its lateral surface is auditory association cortex that processes the identity of sounds, voices and, in the dominant hemisphere, the meaning of spoken words as part of the ventral auditory-language stream. It is supplied by the inferior division of the middle cerebral artery and takes part in the fluent aphasias, in the recognition of voices, and in the auditory hallucinations of temporal lobe seizures and psychosis.
html.function: Sound leaves the primary auditory cortex along two streams; the anterior stream through this gyrus identifies what a sound is, recognizing voices, environmental sounds and, on the left, the phonemes and words of speech, and passes them forward to the temporal pole and the inferior frontal gyrus through the uncinate and extreme capsule fibers. The right anterior superior temporal cortex is specialized for the melody and emotional prosody of speech and for voice identity, and both sides respond to music. Lesions here produce word deafness and voice agnosia when the primary cortex is spared, and contribute to the comprehension deficit of Wernicke aphasia.
html.anatomy.location: Anterior half of the uppermost temporal gyrus, bounded above by the lateral sulcus, below by the superior temporal sulcus, in front by the temporal pole and behind by the transverse temporal gyrus of Heschl and the posterior division.
html.imaging.normalAppearance: The gyrus that forms the lower lip of the anterior Sylvian fissure on coronal images through the sella and the anterior insula; its flat superior surface, the planum polare, faces the insula.

gyrus-superior-temporal-posterior.name: Superior temporal gyrus, posterior division
gyrus-superior-temporal-posterior.summary: The posterior superior temporal gyrus, behind Heschl's gyrus and beneath the planum temporale, is the core of Wernicke's area in the dominant hemisphere (Brodmann area 22 and the adjoining supramarginal cortex). It maps the sounds of speech onto words and sentences, and through the arcuate fasciculus it feeds the frontal speech area so that heard words can be repeated. Infarction of the inferior division of the middle cerebral artery here produces the fluent, paraphasic, poorly comprehended speech of Wernicke aphasia with a superior quadrantanopia from the adjacent optic radiation, and the right homologue supports the perception of prosody and the spatial localization of sound.

anatomy.location: Posterior half of the superior temporal gyrus, below the posterior Sylvian fissure and above the superior temporal sulcus, from the transverse temporal gyrus back to the point where the gyrus turns up into the supramarginal gyrus.

afferents.from: Primary auditory cortex and planum temporale

efferents.to: Inferior frontal gyrus and premotor cortex

gyrus-superior-temporal-posterior.function: In the dominant hemisphere this cortex converts the acoustic pattern of speech into phonological word forms and matches them against the lexicon, supporting comprehension, and holds the phonological trace needed for repetition and for monitoring one's own output; damage lets the patient speak fluently but with wrong sounds and words they cannot detect. It is the start of the dorsal auditory stream that runs through the arcuate fasciculus to the inferior frontal gyrus and premotor cortex. In the right hemisphere the same region decodes the emotional intonation of speech and the location and movement of sounds, and both sides process the intelligibility of degraded speech.

gyrus-supramarginal-anterior.name: Supramarginal gyrus, anterior division
gyrus-supramarginal-anterior.summary: The anterior supramarginal gyrus caps the upturned end of the lateral sulcus behind the postcentral gyrus, the front part of the inferior parietal lobule (Brodmann area 40). It is where touch, proprioception and hearing meet the motor plans of the frontal lobe: in the dominant hemisphere it stores the spatiotemporal programs of learned skilled movements and the phonological loop used to repeat and to hold speech in mind, and in the right hemisphere it directs attention to the contralateral side of space. It is a middle cerebral artery territory at the junction of the superior and inferior divisions, and its lesions produce ideomotor apraxia, conduction aphasia and neglect.

anatomy.location: Anterior part of the inferior parietal lobule, arching over the posterior end of the lateral sulcus, behind the postcentral sulcus, in front of the posterior division and the angular gyrus, above the planum temporale.

afferents.from: Postcentral gyrus and secondary somatosensory cortex
Planum temporale and posterior superior temporal gyrus

efferents.to: Premotor cortex and inferior frontal gyrus
efferents.via: superior longitudinal fasciculus III / arcuate fasciculus

gyrus-supramarginal-anterior.function: The anterior supramarginal cortex integrates somatosensory and auditory information with body schema and stores, in the left hemisphere, the representations of gestures and tool use that the premotor cortex executes; its loss produces ideomotor apraxia in which the patient knows what to do but cannot perform it to command, on both sides of the body because the right premotor cortex depends on it through the corpus callosum. It also holds the phonological store of verbal working memory and takes part in repetition through the arcuate fasciculus, and on the right it is part of the ventral attention network that reorients attention to unexpected stimuli, whose loss produces neglect and extinction.

gyrus-supramarginal-posterior.name: Supramarginal gyrus, posterior division
gyrus-supramarginal-posterior.summary: The posterior supramarginal gyrus lies between the anterior division and the angular gyrus in the inferior parietal lobule, above the posterior end of the superior temporal sulcus. It is multimodal association cortex that integrates the location of the body and of objects around it and, in the dominant hemisphere, links the sounds of words to their spelling and to the movements of writing; in the right hemisphere it contributes to spatial attention and to the perception of one's own body. It is supplied by parietal branches of the middle cerebral artery, is a watershed with the posterior cerebral artery below, and its lesions add agraphia, spatial disorientation and elements of the Gerstmann syndrome to those of the anterior division.

anatomy.location: Posterior part of the inferior parietal lobule between the anterior supramarginal gyrus in front and the angular gyrus behind, above the superior temporal sulcus and below the intraparietal sulcus.

afferents.from: Superior parietal lobule and intraparietal cortex

gyrus-supramarginal-posterior.function: This cortex represents the position of the limbs and of objects in body-centered coordinates for reaching and grasping, and links auditory word forms with their written form, supporting spelling and writing in the left hemisphere; it is part of the dorsal attention and the sensorimotor integration networks that keep the body schema updated. In the right hemisphere it participates in the sense of ownership of the limbs and in the perception of the contralateral hemispace, and its damage contributes to neglect, asomatognosia and anosognosia. It also receives vestibular input through the parieto-insular vestibular cortex, so lesions can produce a sensation of tilt or of leaving the body.

gyrus-supramarginal.name: Supramarginal gyrus

On the dominant side it belongs to the perisylvian language network: it handles phonological processing and the sensory-motor mapping of speech sounds, and its underlying white matter carries the arcuate fasciculus; lesions here cause conduction aphasia. It also stores the motor engrams for skilled gestures, so dominant lesions cause ideomotor apraxia of both hands. On the right it contributes to spatial attention, and lesions add to neglect.

habenula.name: Habenula
habenula.summary: The habenular nuclei form a small swelling on the dorsomedial surface of the thalamus just in front of the pineal gland, at the caudal end of the stria medullaris thalami, and are joined across the midline by the habenular commissure. They are the epithalamic relay through which the limbic forebrain, the septal area, the lateral hypothalamus and the globus pallidus, reaches the midbrain monoamine nuclei by way of the fasciculus retroflexus to the interpeduncular nucleus, the ventral tegmental area and the raphe. The lateral habenula fires when a reward is smaller than expected and inhibits dopamine neurons, and its overactivity has been linked to depression; it is a target of deep brain stimulation research and a landmark in stereotactic and pineal region surgery.

anatomy.location: Dorsomedial thalamus at the posterior end of the stria medullaris, above and in front of the pineal, forming the habenular trigone on the wall of the third ventricle; the habenular commissure crosses in the pineal stalk.

afferents.from: Septal area, diagonal band, lateral preoptic and hypothalamic areas

efferents.to: Ventral tegmental area and substantia nigra (via the rostromedial tegmental nucleus)

habenula.function: The medial habenula relays septal and diagonal band input to the interpeduncular nucleus and the raphe, using acetylcholine and substance P, and is involved in nicotine responses and aversion. The lateral habenula receives the pallidum, the lateral hypothalamus and the prefrontal cortex and inhibits the dopamine neurons of the ventral tegmental area and the serotonin neurons of the raphe through the rostromedial tegmental nucleus; it encodes negative reward prediction errors and disappointment and suppresses motor and motivational behavior, and it is a node in circadian and sleep regulation through its pineal connections.

hippocampus-ca1.name: Hippocampus CA1
hippocampus-ca1.summary: CA1 is the largest cornu ammonis field of the hippocampus, forming the outer curve of the hippocampal body between CA2 and the subiculum, along the superolateral surface facing the temporal horn. It is the output stage of the trisynaptic circuit: it receives the Schaffer collaterals from CA3 and a direct projection from the entorhinal cortex, compares the two, and sends the result to the subiculum and back to the entorhinal cortex. It is the most vulnerable hippocampal field to anoxia and to seizures (Sommer's sector) and the first to lose neurons in Alzheimer disease, so it is the anatomical substrate of the amnesia after cardiac arrest, of mesial temporal sclerosis and of the earliest Alzheimer memory loss.

anatomy.location: Pyramidal cell field of the hippocampus lying between CA2 near the dentate hilus and the subiculum on the parahippocampal side, occupying the lateral and superior part of the hippocampal body and head under the temporal horn, in front of the tail near the splenium.

hippocampus-ca1.function: CA1 pyramidal cells integrate the pattern-completed memory signal arriving from CA3 through the Schaffer collaterals with the current sensory input arriving directly from entorhinal layer III, and their output through the subiculum and the entorhinal cortex allows a new episode to be stored and a familiar one to be retrieved; their place cells mark the location of the animal in space, and long-term potentiation at the Schaffer synapse is the best-studied cellular model of memory. CA1 neurons have a high metabolic demand and glutamate receptor density, which makes them the first to die in ischemia and in prolonged seizures, and tau pathology spreads into them from the entorhinal cortex.

pathology.timing: Diffusion change appears within 1-3 days; atrophy follows over months

hippocampus-ca23.name: Hippocampus CA2/CA3
hippocampus-ca23.summary: CA2 and CA3 are the inner cornu ammonis fields of the hippocampus, curving into the hilus of the dentate gyrus on the medial side of the hippocampal body. CA3 receives the mossy fibers of the dentate granule cells and, through its dense recurrent collaterals, acts as an autoassociative network that completes a partial cue into a whole memory before passing it to CA1 by the Schaffer collaterals; CA2, a narrow field between them, is specialized for social memory and is relatively resistant to injury. CA3 is the field most prone to generating epileptiform activity, and its mossy fiber synapses are among the largest in the brain.

anatomy.location: Pyramidal cell fields on the inner curve of the hippocampus, medial to CA1, with CA3 extending into the hilus of the dentate gyrus and CA2 forming the short transition to CA1; they lie in the hippocampal body and head under the temporal horn and medial to the parahippocampal gyrus.

hippocampus-ca23.function: CA3 pyramidal cells receive sparse but powerful mossy fiber input from the dentate gyrus, direct perforant path input from the entorhinal cortex and extensive recurrent excitation from each other; this architecture lets them store patterns rapidly and retrieve a complete memory from a fragment, the pattern completion that underlies recollection from a cue. Their recurrent collaterals also make CA3 the most seizure-prone hippocampal field. CA2 neurons receive supramammillary and septal input, resist plasticity at their Schaffer inputs and are necessary for remembering other individuals. Both fields send commissural fibers to the opposite hippocampus and are modulated by cholinergic and serotonergic input.

html.summary: CA2 and CA3 are the inner cornu ammonis fields of the hippocampus, curving into the hilus of the dentate gyrus on the medial side of the hippocampal body. CA3 receives the mossy fibers of the dentate granule cells and, through its dense recurrent collaterals, acts as an autoassociative network that completes a partial cue into a whole memory before passing it to CA1 by the Schaffer collaterals; CA2, a narrow field between them, is specialized for social memory and is relatively resistant to injury. CA3 is the field most prone to generating epileptiform activity, and its mossy fiber synapses are among the largest in the brain.
html.function: CA3 pyramidal cells receive sparse but powerful mossy fiber input from the dentate gyrus, direct perforant path input from the entorhinal cortex and extensive recurrent excitation from each other; this architecture lets them store patterns rapidly and retrieve a complete memory from a fragment, the pattern completion that underlies recollection from a cue. Their recurrent collaterals also make CA3 the most seizure-prone hippocampal field. CA2 neurons receive supramammillary and septal input, resist plasticity at their Schaffer inputs and are necessary for remembering other individuals. Both fields send commissural fibers to the opposite hippocampus and are modulated by cholinergic and serotonergic input.
html.anatomy.location: Pyramidal cell fields on the inner curve of the hippocampus, medial to CA1, with CA3 extending into the hilus of the dentate gyrus and CA2 forming the short transition to CA1; they lie in the hippocampal body and head under the temporal horn and medial to the parahippocampal gyrus.
html.imaging.normalAppearance: On high-resolution coronal T2 images CA3 is the inner gray band of the hippocampal body that turns into the dentate hilus; CA2 is a short segment between CA3 and CA1 that cannot be distinguished without subfield atlases.

hippocampus.name: Hippocampus
hippocampus.summary: A curved ridge of three-layered cortex in the floor of the temporal horn, formed of the dentate gyrus, the cornu ammonis (CA1–CA4) and the subiculum, which together with the entorhinal cortex constitute the hippocampal formation. Information enters from the entorhinal cortex through the perforant path, passes around the trisynaptic circuit (dentate gyrus → CA3 → CA1 → subiculum) and leaves through the fornix. It is essential for forming new declarative memories and for spatial navigation. It is also the most epileptogenic tissue in the brain (mesial temporal sclerosis), the first target of Alzheimer disease, and highly vulnerable to anoxia, herpes encephalitis and limbic encephalitis.

anatomy.location: Medial temporal lobe forming the floor and medial wall of the temporal horn from the amygdala in front to the splenium behind (head, body, tail), covered by the choroid plexus and fimbria, with the parahippocampal gyrus beneath and the ambient cistern medially.

hypoglossal-nucleus.name: Hypoglossal nucleus
hypoglossal-nucleus.summary: A long column of motor neurons in the dorsal paramedian medulla beneath the hypoglossal trigone of the fourth ventricular floor. Its axons run ventrally between the medial lemniscus and the inferior olive and emerge in the preolivary sulcus as the hypoglossal rootlets. It innervates all intrinsic and most extrinsic tongue muscles, and its intramedullary fibers are the reason a medial medullary infarct includes an ipsilateral tongue palsy.

hypoglossal-nucleus.function: Lower motor neurons of the tongue for speech, chewing and swallowing; receives bilateral corticobulbar input with a contralateral predominance for the genioglossus.

hypothalamus-anterior-area.name: Anterior hypothalamic area
hypothalamus-anterior-area.summary: The anterior hypothalamic area is the region between the preoptic area in front and the tuberal hypothalamus behind, above the optic chiasm and around the paraventricular and supraoptic nuclei. It is the heat-loss center: warming of the blood activates its neurons, which drive sweating, cutaneous vasodilatation and panting and inhibit shivering and heat production, and it contains the parasympathetic-leaning autonomic neurons that lower heart rate and blood pressure. Damage produces hyperthermia, whereas irritation produces hypothermia, and the region is injured by suprasellar tumors, anterior communicating aneurysm surgery and hypothalamic hamartomas; it also contributes to sleep induction with the neighboring preoptic nuclei.

anatomy.location: Anterior hypothalamus above the optic chiasm and lateral to the third ventricle, between the medial preoptic nucleus in front and the ventromedial and dorsomedial nuclei behind, surrounding the paraventricular and supraoptic nuclei.

hypothalamus-anterior-area.function: Warm-sensitive neurons here integrate blood temperature with cutaneous thermal input and drive heat loss through sympathetic vasodilatation and sweating, while inhibiting the posterior hypothalamic heat-production pathways; they also generate fever when prostaglandin E2 resets their set point during infection, which is why antipyretics act here. The area contains parasympathetic-promoting autonomic neurons that project to the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus and the nucleus of the solitary tract to slow the heart and lower blood pressure, and with the preoptic sleep-active neurons it promotes non-REM sleep by inhibiting the arousal systems. It also modulates aggression and, through oxytocin and vasopressin neurons nearby, social behavior.

hypothalamus-arcuate.name: Arcuate nucleus
hypothalamus-arcuate.summary: The arcuate nucleus is a curved band of neurons in the floor of the tuberal hypothalamus around the base of the infundibulum, forming the walls of the infundibular recess, outside the blood-brain barrier at the median eminence. It is the interface between the blood and the hypothalamus: its neurons sense leptin, insulin, ghrelin, glucose and gonadal steroids and control appetite, energy expenditure and growth, and its releasing-hormone neurons (growth hormone-releasing hormone, dopamine and kisspeptin-driven gonadotropin-releasing hormone) discharge into the portal capillaries of the median eminence. Its damage produces hyperphagia and obesity, hypogonadism and growth failure, and it is the site of action of dopamine antagonists that raise prolactin and of the appetite drugs that mimic gut hormones.

anatomy.location: Ventral tuberal hypothalamus surrounding the infundibular recess of the third ventricle, at the base of the pituitary stalk, medial to the ventromedial nucleus, behind the optic chiasm and in front of the mammillary bodies, in continuity with the median eminence.

hypothalamus-arcuate.function: Two opposing arcuate populations set energy balance: pro-opiomelanocortin neurons release alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone onto paraventricular melanocortin-4 receptors to suppress feeding and raise expenditure when leptin and insulin are high, whereas agouti-related peptide and neuropeptide Y neurons drive hunger when ghrelin rises and leptin falls. Dopamine neurons of the arcuate (the tuberoinfundibular system) tonically inhibit prolactin secretion, growth hormone-releasing hormone neurons drive the somatotrophs, and kisspeptin neurons pace the gonadotropin-releasing hormone pulses that control reproduction. Because the median eminence lacks a barrier, circulating hormones and toxins reach these neurons directly.

hypothalamus-dorsomedial.name: Dorsomedial nucleus
hypothalamus-dorsomedial.summary: The dorsomedial nucleus lies in the tuberal hypothalamus above the ventromedial nucleus and beside the third ventricle, below the paraventricular nucleus and medial to the fornix and the lateral hypothalamic area. It is a coordinating nucleus that relays circadian information from the suprachiasmatic nucleus to the systems that control sleep and waking, feeding, temperature and corticosteroid secretion, and it drives the cardiovascular and thermogenic components of the stress and fever responses through the sympathetic premotor neurons of the brainstem. It contributes to the food-anticipatory rhythm that wakes animals before an expected meal, and its damage blunts circadian rhythms of activity and feeding and the cardiovascular response to stress.

anatomy.location: Medial tuberal hypothalamus between the paraventricular nucleus above and the ventromedial nucleus below, lateral to the third ventricle and medial to the lateral hypothalamus and the descending column of the fornix, behind the anterior hypothalamic area and in front of the posterior hypothalamus.

hypothalamus-dorsomedial.function: The dorsomedial nucleus receives the subparaventricular zone output of the suprachiasmatic clock and distributes it: to the ventrolateral preoptic and orexin neurons to time sleep and waking, to the paraventricular nucleus to time corticotropin-releasing hormone release, and to the raphe pallidus and the rostral ventrolateral medulla to time thermogenesis and blood pressure. Its excitation by stress produces tachycardia, hypertension and hyperthermia through these same brainstem projections, and it mediates the fever of infection by driving brown fat thermogenesis and cutaneous vasoconstriction when prostaglandin acts on the preoptic area. It also participates in the timing of feeding through leptin-sensitive and ghrelin-sensitive neurons.

hypothalamus-lateral.name: Lateral hypothalamic area
hypothalamus-lateral.summary: The lateral hypothalamic area is the broad zone lateral to the fornix and the medial nuclei, traversed by the medial forebrain bundle, extending the whole length of the hypothalamus from the preoptic area to the mammillary region. It is the feeding and arousal center: its orexin (hypocretin) neurons sustain wakefulness and drive motivated behavior, its melanin-concentrating hormone neurons promote sleep and feeding, and lesions produce aphagia, adipsia and somnolence. Loss of the orexin neurons causes narcolepsy with cataplexy, and the area is damaged by hypothalamic gliomas, which in infants produce the diencephalic syndrome of emaciation with paradoxical alertness.

anatomy.location: Lateral hypothalamus between the fornix and the medial hypothalamic nuclei medially and the internal capsule, the subthalamus and the cerebral peduncle laterally, from the lateral preoptic area in front to the lateral mammillary region behind; the medial forebrain bundle runs through it longitudinally.

hypothalamus-lateral.function: Orexin neurons of the lateral hypothalamus project to the whole brain and especially to the locus coeruleus, the raphe, the tuberomammillary nucleus and the basal forebrain, stabilizing wakefulness and preventing inappropriate transitions into REM sleep; they are activated by hunger, stress and reward and drive food seeking and the motivation to act. Melanin-concentrating hormone neurons have the opposite effect, promoting sleep and energy conservation. The area integrates the medial forebrain bundle traffic between the septal-preoptic region and the brainstem, carrying reward signals from the ventral tegmental area to the accumbens, and it contains glucose-sensitive neurons that trigger feeding when glucose falls. Destruction abolishes eating and drinking and produces stupor.

hypothalamus-medial-preoptic.name: Medial preoptic nucleus
hypothalamus-medial-preoptic.summary: The medial preoptic nucleus lies in the preoptic area at the front of the hypothalamus, in the wall of the third ventricle behind the lamina terminalis and above the optic chiasm, and is developmentally telencephalic though functionally hypothalamic. It regulates reproductive and parental behavior, gonadotropin release through its projections to the arcuate GnRH neurons, thermoregulation and sleep, and it contains the sexually dimorphic nucleus that is larger in males. With the ventrolateral preoptic nucleus beside it, which switches off the arousal systems, it is part of the machinery of sleep onset; lesions produce insomnia, hyperthermia and loss of sexual behavior, and the region is involved in suprasellar tumors and in the anterior communicating artery aneurysm territory.

hypothalamus-paraventricular.name: Paraventricular nucleus
hypothalamus-paraventricular.summary: The paraventricular nucleus is a wedge of neurons in the dorsal anterior hypothalamus against the wall of the third ventricle, the command center of the neuroendocrine and autonomic hypothalamus. Its magnocellular neurons make oxytocin and vasopressin and send them down the infundibulum to the posterior pituitary; its parvocellular neurons release corticotropin-releasing hormone and thyrotropin-releasing hormone into the portal system to drive the pituitary-adrenal and thyroid axes; and a third population projects directly to the brainstem and the spinal intermediolateral column to control sympathetic and parasympathetic outflow. It is the effector of the stress response, of fluid balance and of appetite, and it is damaged by suprasellar tumors, hypothalamic surgery and Wernicke encephalopathy.

anatomy.location: Dorsal part of the anterior hypothalamus lateral to the third ventricle, below the fornix column and the anterior commissure, above the supraoptic nucleus and the optic chiasm, in front of the dorsomedial nucleus.

hypothalamus-paraventricular.function: Magnocellular vasopressin neurons respond to osmoreceptors and to baroreceptor input relayed through the nucleus of the solitary tract, releasing antidiuretic hormone from the posterior pituitary; magnocellular oxytocin neurons drive milk let-down and uterine contraction and modulate social bonding. Descending neurons project to the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus, the ventrolateral medulla and the intermediolateral column to set heart rate, blood pressure, gastric function and thermogenesis, and the nucleus integrates leptin and gut hormone signals from the arcuate nucleus to suppress feeding.

hypothalamus-posterior.name: Posterior hypothalamic nucleus
hypothalamus-posterior.summary: The posterior hypothalamic nucleus occupies the caudal hypothalamus above and behind the mammillary bodies, in front of the periaqueductal gray of the midbrain with which it is continuous. It is the heat-production and sympathetic center: it drives shivering, cutaneous vasoconstriction and brown fat thermogenesis in the cold and raises heart rate and blood pressure in defense and stress, and with the neighboring tuberomammillary and orexin systems it supports arousal. Bilateral lesions produce poikilothermia, in which the patient's temperature drifts with the room, together with somnolence, and stimulation of the region has been used to treat cluster headache, whose attacks are timed by this area.

anatomy.location: Caudal medial hypothalamus dorsal to the mammillary bodies and behind the dorsomedial nucleus, beside the posterior third ventricle beneath the thalamus, continuous behind with the midbrain periaqueductal gray and the ventral tegmental area.

hypothalamus-posterior.function: Posterior hypothalamic neurons receive cold signals from the preoptic area and the spinal cord and drive the sympathetic premotor neurons of the rostral ventrolateral medulla and the raphe pallidus to produce vasoconstriction, piloerection, shivering and thermogenesis; they also raise cardiac output and blood pressure during exercise, stress and the defense reaction and participate in the pressor response to hypoxia. The region is part of the ascending arousal system through its projections to the thalamus and cortex and its interaction with the histaminergic tuberomammillary nucleus and the orexin neurons. It also relays hippocampal and mammillary information to the midbrain and contributes to the timing of cluster headache attacks.

hypothalamus-suprachiasmatic.name: Suprachiasmatic nucleus
hypothalamus-suprachiasmatic.summary: The suprachiasmatic nucleus is a pair of tiny nuclei on the floor of the third ventricle directly above the optic chiasm, the master circadian clock of the body. Its neurons keep a near-24-hour rhythm through a transcriptional feedback loop of clock genes and are reset each day by light reaching them through the retinohypothalamic tract from melanopsin-containing retinal ganglion cells. It times sleep and waking, body temperature, cortisol and melatonin secretion and feeding, and its damage by suprasellar tumors, surgery or stroke produces loss of the sleep-wake rhythm with sleep scattered through day and night; its output is the basis of jet lag, shift-work disorder and the timing of light therapy.

anatomy.location: Floor of the third ventricle immediately above the optic chiasm on each side of the midline, in front of the infundibulum and below the paraventricular nucleus, within the retrochiasmatic hypothalamus.

hypothalamus-suprachiasmatic.function: Suprachiasmatic neurons generate the circadian rhythm autonomously and are entrained by light through the retinohypothalamic tract and by the intergeniculate leaflet of the thalamus and the raphe; they impose the rhythm on the rest of the hypothalamus through projections to the subparaventricular zone and the dorsomedial nucleus, which gate the sleep-wake, feeding and temperature systems, and on the pineal gland through a multisynaptic path via the paraventricular nucleus, the intermediolateral column and the superior cervical ganglion, so that melatonin is secreted only in darkness. Clock output also times cortisol through the paraventricular corticotropin-releasing hormone neurons. With age and in neurodegenerative disease the nucleus loses neurons, contributing to the fragmented sleep and sundowning of dementia.

hypothalamus-supraoptic.name: Supraoptic nucleus
hypothalamus-supraoptic.summary: The supraoptic nucleus is a dense cluster of large neurosecretory neurons straddling the lateral edge of the optic chiasm and the optic tract in the anterior hypothalamus. With the paraventricular nucleus it is the source of the vasopressin and oxytocin stored in the posterior pituitary, and its neurons are osmoreceptors themselves, firing faster as plasma osmolality rises. It is the nucleus of water balance: destruction of its axons in the pituitary stalk or of the neurons themselves causes central diabetes insipidus, and its inappropriate activation causes the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion seen after head injury, subarachnoid hemorrhage and with many drugs and lung diseases.

anatomy.location: Anterior hypothalamus immediately above and lateral to the optic chiasm and the beginning of the optic tract, below the paraventricular nucleus, with a smaller retrochiasmatic part behind the chiasm; its axons run through the infundibulum to the neurohypophysis.

hypothalamus-supraoptic.function: Supraoptic magnocellular neurons synthesize vasopressin (most cells) and oxytocin, transport them down the supraoptico-hypophyseal tract bound to neurophysins and release them from axon terminals in the posterior pituitary into the systemic circulation; their firing is set by intrinsic osmosensitivity, by the osmoreceptors of the organum vasculosum and subfornical organ, by angiotensin II, and by baroreceptor and volume signals relayed from the nucleus of the solitary tract. Vasopressin concentrates the urine through renal V2 receptors and constricts vessels at high concentrations; oxytocin drives labor and lactation. The nucleus also receives inhibitory input from the anterior hypothalamus and is suppressed by alcohol and stimulated by nausea and pain.

hypothalamus-tuberomammillary.name: Tuberomammillary nucleus
hypothalamus-tuberomammillary.summary: The tuberomammillary nucleus is a scattered group of large neurons on the ventral surface of the posterior hypothalamus around the mammillary bodies and the lateral tuberal region, the only source of histamine in the brain. Its axons reach the whole cortex, the thalamus, the basal forebrain and the brainstem and promote wakefulness, attention and appetite suppression; it is silent in sleep, inhibited by the preoptic sleep-active neurons and excited by orexin. It explains the sedation caused by antihistamines that cross the blood-brain barrier, the alerting effect of histamine H3 antagonists used in narcolepsy, and the somnolence of posterior hypothalamic lesions.

hypothalamus-tuberomammillary.function: Histaminergic neurons fire tonically during wakefulness and fastest during attentive waking, releasing histamine onto H1 receptors in the cortex and thalamus to promote arousal and onto the basal forebrain and brainstem arousal nuclei to reinforce them; they are inhibited by GABA and galanin from the ventrolateral preoptic nucleus at sleep onset and excited by orexin from the lateral hypothalamus, forming one arm of the sleep-wake flip-flop switch. Histamine also suppresses appetite, modulates fluid balance and pituitary hormone release, and reduces vestibular signaling, which is the basis of antihistamine treatment of motion sickness. The nucleus receives the prefrontal cortex, the septum and the brainstem.

hypothalamus-ventromedial.name: Ventromedial nucleus
hypothalamus-ventromedial.summary: The ventromedial nucleus is a large, well-defined nucleus in the tuberal hypothalamus lateral to the arcuate nucleus and below the dorsomedial nucleus, classically the satiety center: bilateral lesions in animals produce hyperphagia, obesity and rage, and in humans the same picture follows craniopharyngioma surgery, trauma and hypothalamic gliomas. It integrates leptin and glucose signals with limbic and brainstem input to limit feeding, and it also organizes defensive behavior and female sexual behavior and participates in glucose counter-regulation and in the control of sympathetic tone to fat and muscle. It is supplied by the thalamoperforating and tuberal branches of the posterior circulation.

anatomy.location: Middle of the tuberal hypothalamus, above and lateral to the arcuate nucleus and the infundibular recess, below the dorsomedial nucleus, medial to the lateral hypothalamic area and the fornix, at the level between the chiasm and the mammillary bodies.

hypothalamus-ventromedial.function: Ventromedial neurons express leptin receptors and glucose sensors and, through brain-derived neurotrophic factor and steroidogenic factor 1 populations, drive satiety, energy expenditure and the sympathetic response to hypoglycemia; they project to the paraventricular nucleus, the brainstem feeding centers and the periaqueductal gray. Estrogen-sensitive ventrolateral neurons control lordosis and other aspects of female sexual behavior, and a distinct population drives defensive aggression when the animal is threatened, receiving the amygdala through the stria terminalis. Destruction produces relentless eating and weight gain with irritability, whereas stimulation stops feeding and produces fear-like behavior.

hypothalamus.name: Hypothalamus
hypothalamus.summary: A few grams of tissue forming the floor and lower walls of the third ventricle, from the optic chiasm to the mammillary bodies, that runs the body's internal environment. Its nuclei control the pituitary (releasing hormones to the anterior lobe through the portal vessels; vasopressin and oxytocin from the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei to the posterior lobe), temperature, thirst, hunger, circadian rhythm, sleep–wake state, sexual behavior and the autonomic outflow. Tumors, inflammation, trauma and surgery in this region produce diabetes insipidus, obesity or emaciation, temperature dysregulation, somnolence and endocrine failure.

subdivisions.name: Tuberal (middle) region
subdivisions.note: arcuate nucleus (releasing hormones, appetite), ventromedial (satiety) and dorsomedial nuclei, lateral hypothalamic area (hunger, orexin arousal)

subdivisions.name: Mammillary (posterior) region
subdivisions.note: posterior nucleus (heat conservation, sympathetic), tuberomammillary nucleus (histamine, wakefulness), mammillary bodies (memory)

inferior-cerebellar-peduncle.name: Inferior cerebellar peduncle
inferior-cerebellar-peduncle.summary: The thick bundle that connects the medulla to the cerebellum, forming the posterolateral border of the upper medulla and the lower lateral wall of the fourth ventricle. It carries mostly afferent fibers: the posterior spinocerebellar and cuneocerebellar tracts (unconscious proprioception from the ipsilateral body), the olivocerebellar climbing fibers (from the contralateral inferior olive) and vestibular and reticular inputs; its smaller juxtarestiform part carries fibers between the vestibular nuclei and the cerebellum in both directions.

inferior-colliculus.name: Inferior colliculus
inferior-colliculus.summary: The lower pair of tectal bumps and the obligatory relay of the ascending auditory pathway: every lateral lemniscus fiber ends here before the signal goes on through the brachium of the inferior colliculus to the medial geniculate body and the auditory cortex. Its central nucleus is tonotopically organized, and it also mediates auditory startle and the reflex turning of eyes and head toward a sound through connections with the superior colliculus.

inferior-olivary-nucleus.name: Inferior olivary nucleus
inferior-olivary-nucleus.summary: A crumpled bag of gray matter that produces the olive, the oval bulge on the anterolateral medulla behind the pyramid. It receives input from the cerebral cortex, red nucleus (central tegmental tract) and spinal cord and sends climbing fibers through the contralateral inferior cerebellar peduncle to the cerebellar cortex, where they teach the Purkinje cells during motor learning. Clinically it matters for two reasons: its location defines the level of the lateral medullary syndrome, and interruption of its inputs causes hypertrophic olivary degeneration with palatal tremor.

inferior-olivary-nucleus.function: Source of all climbing fibers to the cerebellum; compares intended and actual movement signals and drives cerebellar motor learning; part of the Guillain–Mollaret triangle with the dentate and red nuclei.

insula.name: Insula
insula.summary: A lobe of cortex buried at the floor of the lateral sulcus, covered by the frontal, parietal and temporal opercula and overlying the claustrum and putamen. Its anterior part is agranular and limbic, processing taste, interoception, autonomic control and the feeling of emotions and disgust; its posterior part is granular and somatosensory, carrying pain, temperature and vestibular representations. It is the first cortex to lose gray–white differentiation in MCA stroke (insular ribbon sign), the site of the cardiac autonomic disturbances after right MCA infarction, and a frequent origin of hard-to-localize focal seizures.

intermediolateral-column.name: Intermediolateral cell column
intermediolateral-column.summary: The lateral horn of gray matter present from T1 to L2, containing the preganglionic sympathetic neurons of the whole body, and its sacral counterpart at S2–S4 containing the preganglionic parasympathetic neurons for the pelvic organs. Its axons leave in the ventral roots (white rami communicantes) to the sympathetic chain. Because all sympathetic outflow to the head passes through the upper thoracic segments and the cervical cord above them, cervical and upper thoracic cord lesions cause Horner syndrome, and lesions above T6 disconnect most of the sympathetic outflow from the brain, producing autonomic dysreflexia.

internal-capsule.name: Internal capsule
internal-capsule.summary: A thick V-shaped band of white matter between the caudate and thalamus medially and the lentiform nucleus laterally, through which almost every fiber connecting the cortex with the brainstem, spinal cord and thalamus must pass. The anterior limb carries frontopontine and anterior thalamic fibers, the genu the corticobulbar fibers, and the posterior limb the corticospinal tract (face to leg, anterior to posterior) with the thalamocortical sensory fibers behind them and the optic and auditory radiations in its retro- and sublenticular parts. Fed by the lenticulostriate and anterior choroidal perforators, it is the classic site of the lacunar pure motor stroke and of hypertensive hemorrhage.

interposed-nucleus.name: Interposed nuclei (emboliform and globose)
interposed-nucleus.summary: The globose and emboliform nuclei lie between the dentate and fastigial nuclei and together form the interposed nucleus, the output of the paravermal (intermediate) zone. They receive Purkinje input from the paravermis and spinocerebellar collaterals and project through the superior cerebellar peduncle to the contralateral red nucleus (rubrospinal tract) and thalamus. They adjust ongoing limb movements and the tone of limb muscles, so their lesions give limb ataxia intermediate in character between the truncal ataxia of fastigial lesions and the dysmetria of dentate lesions.

html.summary: The globose and emboliform nuclei lie between the dentate and fastigial nuclei and together form the interposed nucleus, the output of the paravermal (intermediate) zone. They receive Purkinje input from the paravermis and spinocerebellar collaterals and project through the superior cerebellar peduncle to the contralateral red nucleus (rubrospinal tract) and thalamus. They adjust ongoing limb movements and the tone of limb muscles, so their lesions give limb ataxia intermediate in character between the truncal ataxia of fastigial lesions and the dysmetria of dentate lesions.
html.function: Correction of ongoing limb movement and control of agonist-antagonist balance and limb tone through the rubrospinal and thalamocortical pathways.
html.anatomy.location: In the white matter of each hemisphere medial to the hilum of the dentate nucleus and lateral to the fastigial nucleus, above the roof of the fourth ventricle.

html.imaging.sequenceOfChoice: DWI and SWI

lateral-geniculate-nucleus.name: Lateral geniculate nucleus
lateral-geniculate-nucleus.summary: A small six-layered nucleus under the pulvinar where the optic tract ends. Fibers from the contralateral eye reach layers 1, 4 and 6 and those from the ipsilateral eye layers 2, 3 and 5, so each geniculate maps the contralateral visual hemifield; magnocellular layers 1–2 handle motion and contrast, parvocellular layers 3–6 detail and color. Its axons form the optic radiation to the calcarine cortex. Its dual blood supply from the anterior choroidal and lateral posterior choroidal arteries explains the sector-shaped field defects of geniculate infarcts.

anatomy.location: Ventrolateral to the pulvinar on the inferior surface of the posterior thalamus, lateral to the medial geniculate body and above the hippocampus, at the end of the optic tract; the brachium of the superior colliculus passes medial to it.

lateral-geniculate-nucleus.function: Thalamic relay of the visual pathway; gates and sharpens retinal signals under cortical and brainstem control before they reach the primary visual cortex.

level-medulla-olive.name: Medulla: level of the inferior olive
level-medulla-olive.summary: The open medulla at the level of the inferior olivary nucleus is the most clinically important brainstem section, because it is the site of the lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome and of the medial medullary syndrome. The fourth ventricle roofs the section, and its floor holds the hypoglossal, dorsal vagal and vestibular nuclei. In front lie the pyramids, then the medial lemniscus and the hypoglossal fibers threading between them and the olive; laterally the inferior cerebellar peduncle, spinothalamic tract, spinal trigeminal nucleus, nucleus ambiguus and the descending sympathetic fibers cluster in the wedge that PICA and the vertebral perforators supply.

anatomy.location: Open medulla between the obex and the pontomedullary junction, marked externally by the olive on each side and the inferior cerebellar peduncle behind it; MNI z ≈ −42 to −48.

subdivisions.note: anterior, paramedian; corticospinal tract

subdivisions.name: Medial lemniscus

subdivisions.name: Inferior olivary nucleus

level-medulla-pyramidal-decussation.name: Medulla: level of the pyramidal decussation
level-medulla-pyramidal-decussation.summary: The lowest transverse section of the brainstem, at the junction with the spinal cord, is dominated by the great motor decussation: most corticospinal fibers of each pyramid cross here to form the lateral corticospinal tract of the opposite side. The gray matter still looks spinal, with anterior and posterior horns, but the posterior columns are ending in the gracile and cuneate nuclei and the spinal trigeminal nucleus has replaced the substantia gelatinosa. A lesion here can produce the paradox of an arm weaker than the leg on opposite sides, because arm fibers cross higher than leg fibers.

anatomy.location: Just above the foramen magnum, from the first cervical root down to the point where the pyramids begin to bulge, roughly 35–45 mm below the anterior commissure in MNI coordinates (z ≈ −55 to −60).

subdivisions.name: Pyramidal decussation
subdivisions.note: corticospinal fibers crossing obliquely through the anterior median fissure into the contralateral lateral funiculus

subdivisions.name: Fasciculus gracilis and cuneatus
subdivisions.note: still present, capped by the beginnings of their nuclei

subdivisions.name: Spinal trigeminal nucleus and tract
subdivisions.note: lateral to the posterior horn, continuous with the substantia gelatinosa

subdivisions.name: Spinothalamic tracts
subdivisions.note: anterolateral, unchanged from the cord

subdivisions.name: Anterior horn cells
subdivisions.note: for the first cervical segment and the spinal accessory nucleus

subdivisions.name: Central canal
subdivisions.note: still central; it opens into the fourth ventricle at higher levels

level-medulla-pyramidal-decussation.function: Transition of the cord into the brainstem; the site where upper motor neuron control switches sides, which explains why lesions above this point give contralateral weakness and lesions below give ipsilateral weakness.

bestView.label: cervicomedullary junction: pyramids narrowing, decussating fibers crossing the midline

level-medulla-sensory-decussation.name: Medulla: level of the sensory (lemniscal) decussation
level-medulla-sensory-decussation.summary: A few millimetres above the motor decussation the posterior columns end in the gracile and cuneate nuclei, whose axons sweep forward around the central gray as internal arcuate fibers and cross the midline to form the medial lemniscus. From here upward, fine touch, vibration and proprioception from the body travel on the contralateral side. The pyramids are now large and intact in front, and the spinal trigeminal nucleus, spinothalamic tract and the beginnings of the inferior olive occupy the lateral part.

level-midbrain-inferior-colliculus.name: Midbrain: inferior colliculus level

The trochlear nerve is unique in crossing and leaving dorsally just below the colliculi.

level-midbrain-superior-colliculus.name: Midbrain: superior colliculus level
level-midbrain-superior-colliculus.summary: The upper midbrain, cut through the superior colliculi, contains the oculomotor nuclear complex, the red nucleus and the substantia nigra, and its named syndromes (Weber, Claude, Benedikt, Parinaud) are built from these. The oculomotor fibers descend from the periaqueductal gray through the red nucleus and the medial crus, so a single paramedian lesion combines a third nerve palsy with contralateral hemiparesis (Weber, crus) or contralateral tremor and ataxia (Claude/Benedikt, red nucleus). The pretectal area and the posterior commissure just above control the pupillary light reflex and vertical gaze.

html.summary: The upper midbrain, cut through the superior colliculi, contains the oculomotor nuclear complex, the red nucleus and the substantia nigra, and its named syndromes (Weber, Claude, Benedikt, Parinaud) are built from these. The oculomotor fibers descend from the periaqueductal gray through the red nucleus and the medial crus, so a single paramedian lesion combines a third nerve palsy with contralateral hemiparesis (Weber, crus) or contralateral tremor and ataxia (Claude/Benedikt, red nucleus). The pretectal area and the posterior commissure just above control the pupillary light reflex and vertical gaze.
html.function: Vertical gaze, pupillary constriction, eye movement (oculomotor nucleus), cerebellar-thalamic relay (red nucleus), dopamine supply to the striatum (substantia nigra), and passage of descending motor and ascending sensory tracts.
html.anatomy.location: From the level of the superior colliculi up to the posterior commissure and the junction with the diencephalon; MNI z ≈ −4 to −12.
html.imaging.normalAppearance: On axial T2 the red nuclei are round dark spots either side of the midline and the substantia nigra is a curved dark band behind each crus, both dark because of iron; the superior colliculi form the dorsal surface and the aqueduct is central.
html.imaging.sequenceOfChoice: Axial DWI and T2/SWI through the midbrain; sagittal T2 for the tectum and pineal region

level-pons-caudal.name: Caudal pons (facial colliculus level)
level-pons-caudal.summary: The lower pons is where the abducens and facial nuclei live and where the horizontal gaze machinery sits, so its lesions produce the classic combination of a sixth or seventh nerve palsy on the side of the lesion with hemiparesis of the opposite limbs. The section is divided into a ventral basis pontis, full of pontine nuclei, transverse pontocerebellar fibers and the scattered bundles of the corticospinal tract, and a dorsal tegmentum containing the cranial nerve nuclei, the medial lemniscus (now lying flat), the spinothalamic tract, the MLF and the trapezoid body of the auditory pathway.

anatomy.location: Between the pontomedullary junction and the level of the trigeminal root entry, marked on the floor of the fourth ventricle by the facial colliculus; MNI z ≈ −34 to −40.

level-pons-rostral.name: Rostral pons
level-pons-rostral.summary: The upper pons is the level of the trigeminal nerve: its motor and principal sensory nuclei sit in the lateral tegmentum and the root leaves the lateral surface between the basis and the middle cerebellar peduncle. The basis pontis is at its widest, the superior cerebellar peduncles form the lateral walls of the narrowing fourth ventricle, and the lateral lemniscus carries auditory fibers up toward the inferior colliculus. The locus coeruleus lies in the floor of the ventricle near the upper end of this level.

anatomy.location: From the trigeminal root entry zone up to the isthmus where the pons meets the midbrain; MNI z ≈ −24 to −32.

lobe-frontal.name: Frontal lobe
lobe-frontal.summary: The largest lobe, everything in front of the central sulcus and above the lateral sulcus. From back to front it contains the primary motor cortex on the precentral gyrus, the premotor and supplementary motor areas, the frontal eye field, Broca's area in the dominant inferior frontal gyrus, and the vast prefrontal cortex (dorsolateral, orbitofrontal and medial) that plans, sequences, inhibits and motivates behavior. Its medial surface belongs to the ACA and its lateral surface to the MCA, and its lesions range from contralateral weakness to the personality change, apathy and disinhibition that families notice before doctors do.

anatomy.location: Anterior to the central sulcus and above the lateral sulcus on the convexity; the medial surface extends to the cingulate sulcus and the paracentral lobule; the orbital surface rests on the orbital roofs. The superior, middle and inferior frontal gyri are separated by the superior and inferior frontal sulci; the inferior frontal gyrus is divided into orbital, triangular and opercular parts.

lobe-occipital.name: Occipital lobe
lobe-occipital.summary: The posterior pole of the hemisphere behind the parieto-occipital sulcus, devoted to vision. The primary visual cortex lines the calcarine sulcus on the medial surface, mapping the contralateral hemifield with the macula at the pole and the periphery anteriorly; the surrounding extrastriate areas on the cuneus, lingual gyrus and lateral occipital cortex analyze color, form and motion and feed the ventral (temporal, 'what') and dorsal (parietal, 'where') streams. It is almost entirely PCA territory with MCA collateral at the pole, which is why PCA infarcts spare the macula.

anatomy.location: Behind the parieto-occipital sulcus on the medial surface and behind an imaginary line to the preoccipital notch laterally; the calcarine sulcus divides the medial surface into the cuneus above and the lingual gyrus below; lateral occipital gyri and the occipital pole face the convexity.

lobe-parietal.name: Parietal lobe
lobe-parietal.summary: Behind the central sulcus and above the lateral sulcus, bounded behind by the parieto-occipital sulcus. It receives somatic sensation on the postcentral gyrus and integrates it with vision and hearing in the superior and inferior parietal lobules to build a map of the body and of space. The dominant inferior parietal lobule (supramarginal and angular gyri) supports language, calculation, praxis and reading; the non-dominant lobule supports spatial attention. Lesions produce cortical sensory loss, apraxia, neglect, Gerstmann syndrome and inferior quadrantic field defects from the optic radiation passing beneath.

lobe-temporal.name: Temporal lobe
lobe-temporal.summary: Below the lateral sulcus and in front of the occipital lobe, the temporal lobe carries three quite different functions stacked on top of each other. The superior temporal gyrus holds the primary auditory cortex on Heschl's gyrus and, on the dominant side, Wernicke's area for language comprehension; the middle and inferior temporal and fusiform gyri form the ventral visual stream that recognizes objects, faces and words; and the medial temporal lobe (hippocampus, parahippocampal gyrus, amygdala) makes new memories and colors experience with emotion. The optic radiation loops through its white matter, so temporal lesions cause superior quadrantanopias, and its cortex is the commonest source of focal epilepsy.

html.summary: Below the lateral sulcus and in front of the occipital lobe, the temporal lobe carries three quite different functions stacked on top of each other. The optic radiation loops through its white matter, so temporal lesions cause superior quadrantanopias, and its cortex is the commonest source of focal epilepsy.

lobule-superior-parietal.name: Superior parietal lobule
lobule-superior-parietal.summary: The upper part of the parietal convexity above the intraparietal sulcus, continuous medially with the precuneus. It integrates somatosensory input from the postcentral gyrus with visual information from the occipital lobe to guide reaching, grasping and eye movements in space and to hold a body schema. Bilateral lesions of the superior parietal and adjacent occipital cortex cause Bálint syndrome (optic ataxia, ocular apraxia, simultanagnosia); unilateral lesions cause contralateral tactile agnosia and clumsy visually guided reaching.

lobule-superior-parietal.function: Somatosensory association, visuomotor coordination of reaching and grasping (dorsal 'where/how' visual stream), spatial attention and mental imagery.

locus-coeruleus.name: Locus coeruleus
locus-coeruleus.summary: The locus coeruleus is a compact column of pigmented noradrenergic neurons in the upper pontine tegmentum beneath the floor of the fourth ventricle, at the lateral edge of the periaqueductal gray, whose axons reach almost the entire brain and spinal cord. With only a few tens of thousands of cells it supplies most of the noradrenaline of the cerebral cortex, hippocampus, cerebellum and thalamus and is the engine of arousal, vigilance and the response to novelty and stress. It regulates the sleep–wake cycle, is silent in REM sleep, and modulates pain in the spinal dorsal horn. It degenerates early in Parkinson disease and Alzheimer disease, contributing to the sleep, autonomic and cognitive symptoms that precede the classical signs, and it is the site of the neuromelanin signal that can now be imaged.

anatomy.location: Dorsolateral tegmentum of the rostral pons beneath the lateral floor of the fourth ventricle, medial to the mesencephalic trigeminal nucleus and lateral to the periaqueductal gray, extending into the caudal midbrain; its blue-black pigment is visible to the naked eye on a cut brainstem.

afferents.from: Nucleus paragigantocellularis and the nucleus of the solitary tract

efferents.to: Entire cerebral cortex, hippocampus and thalamus

locus-coeruleus.function: Locus coeruleus neurons fire tonically during waking, phasically to salient stimuli and fall silent in REM sleep; their noradrenaline release through beta and alpha receptors increases the signal-to-noise ratio of cortical processing, focuses attention, promotes memory consolidation in the hippocampus and amygdala, and drives the sympathetic response to stress through the hypothalamus and the medullary pressor centers. Descending fibers to the dorsal horn inhibit pain transmission, and cerebellar fibers modulate Purkinje cell excitability. The nucleus is inhibited by opioids and clonidine and activated by their withdrawal, which produces the sweating, anxiety and tachycardia of the withdrawal syndrome.
