lumbosacral-trunk.name: Lumbosacral trunk
lumbosacral-trunk.summary: The lumbosacral trunk is the thick cord of nerve fibers that carries the lower half of the L4 anterior ramus and the whole of L5 down over the ala of the sacrum to join the S1 ramus, and it is what makes the lumbar and sacral plexuses one continuous lumbosacral plexus. Its fibers travel on into the sciatic, superior gluteal and inferior gluteal nerves, so it carries the L4 and L5 supply of hip abduction, ankle dorsiflexion, foot inversion and great-toe extension. Because it lies directly on the bone at the pelvic brim with nothing between it and the fetal head, it is the nerve injured in maternal obstetric palsy, in which a long labor with a large baby leaves a woman with a unilateral foot drop and weak hip abduction after delivery; it is also compressed by pelvic tumors, by sacral fractures and by badly placed retractors during pelvic surgery.

anatomy.location: The trunk forms at the medial border of psoas major at about the level of the L4-L5 intervertebral disc, where the descending branch of the L4 ramus joins the whole L5 ramus. It then runs downward and backward over the ala of the sacrum, crossing the pelvic brim in front of the sacro-iliac joint, and enters the pelvis to meet the S1 ramus at the upper border of piriformis, where the sacral plexus is formed. It lies deep to the common iliac vessels and directly on the periosteum, covered only by the parietal pelvic fascia.

lumbosacral-trunk.function: The lumbosacral trunk is the conduit through which the L4 and L5 segments reach the sacral plexus, so it supplies no muscle itself but carries the fibers that will run in the superior gluteal nerve to gluteus medius, minimus and tensor fasciae latae, in the inferior gluteal nerve to gluteus maximus, and in the sciatic nerve to the hamstrings and, through the common peroneal division, to the dorsiflexors and evertors of the foot. Its sensory fibers reach the lateral leg and the dorsum of the foot. Damage to it therefore reproduces an L5 pattern that crosses the territory of more than one peripheral nerve: weak hip abduction, weak ankle dorsiflexion and eversion, weak great-toe extension and numbness over the lateral leg, with a preserved ankle jerk. The combination of hip abduction weakness with foot drop is what separates a lumbosacral trunk lesion from a common peroneal nerve palsy at the fibular neck, in which hip abduction is normal.

mammillary-body.name: Mammillary bodies
mammillary-body.summary: Two small rounded nuclei on the undersurface of the hypothalamus behind the tuber cinereum, at the posterior boundary of the third ventricle floor. They receive the fornix from the hippocampus and send the mammillothalamic tract to the anterior thalamic nuclei and the mammillotegmental tract to the brainstem, completing the Papez circuit of memory. They are the most vulnerable structures in thiamine deficiency, shrinking in Wernicke–Korsakoff syndrome, and they serve as a landmark for the basilar tip and the interpeduncular fossa.

anatomy.location: Posterior part of the hypothalamic floor in the interpeduncular cistern, in front of the posterior perforated substance and behind the infundibulum and tuber cinereum; each is about 5 mm across.

mammillary-body.function: Memory relay of the Papez circuit (hippocampus → fornix → mammillary body → anterior thalamus → cingulate); spatial memory and head-direction signals.

bestView.label: mammillary body behind the infundibulum on the floor of the third ventricle

imaging.normalAppearance: Well seen as two small round gray nodules on sagittal and coronal T1 at the posterior floor of the third ventricle; the mammillothalamic tract runs up and back from them. Volume loss and FLAIR hyperintensity are the signs of thiamine deficiency.

mammillothalamic-tract.name: Mammillothalamic tract
mammillothalamic-tract.summary: The mammillothalamic tract is a compact bundle that rises from the mammillary body through the posterior hypothalamus to the anterior nucleus of the thalamus, the diencephalic limb of the Papez memory circuit. It carries hippocampal information that reached the mammillary body through the fornix on to the anterior thalamus, from which the cingulate gyrus and the entorhinal cortex receive it, and interruption of it at any point produces anterograde amnesia. It is a landmark on axial MRI through the midbrain-diencephalic junction, a stereotactic target for epilepsy (anterior thalamic stimulation), and it degenerates with the mammillary bodies in Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome and in thalamic infarcts of the tuberothalamic artery.

anatomy.location: Ascends from the medial mammillary nucleus through the posterior hypothalamus, lateral to the third ventricle and medial to the lateral hypothalamus, to enter the anterior thalamic nuclei; the mammillotegmental tract branches off it to the midbrain.

efferents.to: Cingulate and retrosplenial cortex (via anterior thalamus)

mammillothalamic-tract.function: The tract conveys the output of the medial mammillary nucleus, which itself receives the postcommissural fornix from the subiculum and the theta-modulated input of the supramammillary and tegmental nuclei of Gudden, to the anteroventral and anteromedial thalamic nuclei; the anterior thalamus projects to the cingulate and retrosplenial cortex and the presubiculum, closing the Papez circuit that supports the encoding of new episodic memories and the head-direction signal used in navigation. Lesions of the tract disconnect the hippocampus from the thalamus and produce an amnesia as dense as bilateral hippocampal damage, with confabulation when the frontal connections are also affected.

medial-geniculate-nucleus.name: Medial geniculate nucleus
medial-geniculate-nucleus.summary: The auditory thalamus, a small oval nucleus medial to the lateral geniculate body on the undersurface of the pulvinar. It receives the brachium of the inferior colliculus and projects through the acoustic radiation in the sublenticular internal capsule to Heschl's gyrus. Because the auditory pathway is bilateral from the cochlear nuclei upward, a unilateral geniculate lesion causes only subtle contralateral hearing and localization deficits, never deafness.

anatomy.location: Inferomedial to the lateral geniculate body and lateral to the superior colliculus on the posteroinferior thalamus, receiving the brachium of the inferior colliculus along the lateral midbrain.

medial-geniculate-nucleus.function: Thalamic relay of hearing to the primary auditory cortex, tonotopically organized; also relays auditory information to the amygdala for fear conditioning.

It receives the brachium of the inferior colliculus and projects through the acoustic radiation in the sublenticular internal capsule to Heschl's gyrus. Because the auditory pathway is bilateral from the cochlear nuclei upward, a unilateral geniculate lesion causes only subtle contralateral hearing and localization deficits, never deafness.
html.function: Thalamic relay of hearing to the primary auditory cortex, tonotopically organized; also relays auditory information to the amygdala for fear conditioning.
html.anatomy.location: Inferomedial to the lateral geniculate body and lateral to the superior colliculus on the posteroinferior thalamus, receiving the brachium of the inferior colliculus along the lateral midbrain.
html.imaging.normalAppearance: Small nucleus on thin coronal T2 medial to the lateral geniculate; represented by the MASSP mesh in this atlas.
html.imaging.sequenceOfChoice: DWI; audiometry with central tests

medial-lemniscus.name: Medial lemniscus
medial-lemniscus.summary: The medial lemniscus is the second-order bundle of the dorsal column pathway. It forms in the lower medulla from the internal arcuate fibers of the gracile and cuneate nuclei, crosses immediately in the sensory decussation, and climbs through the medulla, pons and midbrain to the ventral posterolateral nucleus of the thalamus, carrying discriminative touch, vibration and conscious proprioception from the opposite half of the body. Its position rotates as it ascends, which is worth remembering when localizing brainstem infarcts.

anatomy.location: Medulla: a vertical band dorsal to the pyramid on each side of the midline, leg fibers ventral and arm fibers dorsal. Pons: rotated to a horizontal band across the ventral tegmentum behind the trapezoid body, arm medial and leg lateral. Midbrain: the lateral tegmentum, curving dorsolaterally toward the thalamus alongside the spinothalamic tract.

efferents.note: third-order relay to the postcentral gyrus

medial-lemniscus.function: Conveys fine touch, two-point discrimination, vibration and joint position sense from the contralateral body to the thalamus; the trigeminal lemniscus joins it in the pons carrying the same modalities from the face.

bestView.label: medulla: forming behind the pyramids
pons: horizontal band in the ventral tegmentum
midbrain: lateral tegmentum

pathology.finding: Paramedian ventral medullary restriction that includes the lemniscus, giving contralateral loss of vibration and position sense with hemiparesis.
Small tegmental lesion behind the basis pontis causing contralateral hemisensory loss (pure sensory stroke of brainstem origin).

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: DWI and thin T2 through the brainstem

lesionEffects.deficit: Loss of vibration, position sense and discriminative touch on the opposite side of the body
lesionEffects.mechanism: The tract has already crossed in the lower medulla
Loss of proprioceptive feedback to the thalamus and cortex

lesionEffects.deficit: Tingling paresthesias of the opposite face and body
lesionEffects.mechanism: Pontine lesion involving both the medial and trigeminal lemnisci

medial-longitudinal-fasciculus.name: Medial longitudinal fasciculus
medial-longitudinal-fasciculus.summary: A paired paramedian bundle running the length of the brainstem just beneath the aqueduct and the floor of the fourth ventricle. Its clinically decisive contents are the axons of abducens internuclear neurons crossing to the contralateral oculomotor nucleus, which yoke the medial rectus to the opposite lateral rectus for conjugate horizontal gaze; it also carries vestibular fibers to the eye movement nuclei and descends as the medial vestibulospinal tract. A lesion produces internuclear ophthalmoplegia: the eye on the side of the lesion fails to adduct while the other eye abducts with nystagmus.

anatomy.location: Dorsal paramedian tegmentum from the rostral midbrain (interstitial nucleus of Cajal) down through the pons and medulla into the cervical cord, ventral to the periaqueductal gray and the hypoglossal and abducens nuclei.

medial-longitudinal-fasciculus.function: Coordinates conjugate horizontal and vertical eye movements between the III, IV and VI nuclei and links them to the vestibular nuclei; carries the medial vestibulospinal tract for head-eye coordination.

bestView.label: paramedian dorsal pontine tegmentum in front of the fourth ventricle
dorsal paramedian bundle from midbrain to medulla

imaging.normalAppearance: Not resolved on routine MRI; lesions show as small paramedian dorsal tegmental spots. In multiple sclerosis a bilateral INO usually comes with a small FLAIR-bright lesion straddling the midline under the ventricular floor.

pathology.pitfalls: Use thin axial FLAIR or sagittal 3D FLAIR; a normal routine MRI does not exclude a demyelinating INO

pathology.finding: Unilateral paramedian tegmental restricted diffusion from a small perforator in older patients with vascular risk factors.

meningeal-spaces.name: Epidural, subdural and subarachnoid spaces
meningeal-spaces.summary: Three spaces, one real and two potential, separate the meninges and give extra-axial hemorrhages their shapes. The cranial epidural space is potential, opened by arterial bleeding from the meningeal arteries into a lens-shaped hematoma limited by the sutures; the spinal epidural space is real and fat-filled, the site of epidural anesthesia, abscess and hematoma. The subdural space is potential, opened by tearing of bridging veins into a crescent that crosses sutures but not the midline. The subarachnoid space is real, filled with CSF, contains the arteries and cranial nerves, and is where aneurysmal blood and meningitis collect.

anatomy.location: Epidural: between the skull (or vertebral canal) and dura. Subdural: between dura and arachnoid, at the level of the dural border cells. Subarachnoid: between arachnoid and pia, expanded into cisterns at the base and in the lumbar theca.

subdivisions.name: Cranial epidural space
subdivisions.note: middle meningeal artery; lens-shaped hematoma stopped by sutures

subdivisions.name: Spinal epidural space
subdivisions.note: fat and the internal vertebral venous plexus; epidural anesthesia, abscess, hematoma, metastasis

subdivisions.name: Subdural space
subdivisions.note: bridging veins; crescentic hematoma crossing sutures, common in the elderly and anticoagulated

subdivisions.name: Subarachnoid space
subdivisions.note: CSF, arteries of the circle of Willis, cranial nerves; aneurysmal hemorrhage, meningitis, lumbar puncture site

meningeal-spaces.function: The subarachnoid space cushions the brain and circulates CSF; the other two are anatomical planes whose opening defines the extra-axial hemorrhages and infections.

bestView.label: convexity: the planes between skull, dura, arachnoid and brain
subarachnoid basal cisterns
subarachnoid space over the convexity

imaging.normalAppearance: Extra-axial collections are read by shape and density: biconvex epidural (arterial, acute, dense, respects sutures), crescentic subdural (venous, density fading over weeks, crosses sutures), and sulcal or cisternal subarachnoid blood (follows the CSF spaces). Spinal epidural lesions displace the thecal sac.

lesionEffects.mechanism: Arterial expansion with delayed mass effect

lesionEffects.mechanism: Slow venous accumulation

middle-cerebellar-peduncle.name: Middle cerebellar peduncle
middle-cerebellar-peduncle.summary: The largest of the three peduncles, a massive purely afferent bundle carrying the transverse pontine fibers from the contralateral pontine nuclei into the cerebellar hemisphere. It forms the lateral surface of the pons, with the trigeminal root emerging at its junction with the basis pontis. Infarcts here (AICA territory) or demyelination give ipsilateral limb ataxia, and bilateral lesions of the peduncles are a recognized pattern in multiple system atrophy and fragile X-associated tremor/ataxia syndrome.

anatomy.location: Lateral pons, sweeping backward and laterally from the basis pontis into the white matter of the cerebellar hemisphere, lateral to the superior and inferior peduncles.

middle-cerebellar-peduncle.function: Delivers the cortico-ponto-cerebellar input that lets the cerebellar hemispheres coordinate skilled limb movement planned by the contralateral cortex.

bestView.label: lateral pons at the trigeminal root entry, peduncle entering the cerebellum
middle peduncle from pons to hemisphere

imaging.normalAppearance: A thick band of white matter on the lateral pons on axial T2 and FLAIR; symmetrical T2 hyperintensity of both peduncles is a clue to multiple system atrophy (with the pontine 'hot cross bun') or FXTAS.

pathology.finding: Restricted diffusion in the middle cerebellar peduncle and adjacent lateral pons and cerebellum.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: FLAIR and DWI through the pons and cerebellum

motor-unit.name: Motor unit and skeletal muscle
motor-unit.summary: A motor unit is one anterior horn cell, its axon and all the muscle fibers it innervates, from a few fibers in the extraocular muscles to over a thousand in gastrocnemius. Force is graded by recruiting units in order of size and by increasing their firing rate. This is the framework of electromyography: neurogenic disease loses units and enlarges the survivors by collateral reinnervation (large, long, polyphasic potentials with reduced recruitment), while myopathic disease loses fibers within units (small, short, polyphasic potentials with early recruitment). Clinically, the motor unit is the lower motor neuron, and its failure produces weakness with wasting, fasciculations, hypotonia and lost reflexes.

anatomy.location: Anterior horn cell in the spinal gray matter or brainstem motor nucleus, axon in the ventral root and peripheral nerve, terminal branches at the end plates of muscle fibers scattered through the muscle.

subdivisions.name: Type I (slow, oxidative) units
subdivisions.note: small, fatigue-resistant, recruited first; postural muscles

subdivisions.name: Type II (fast) units
subdivisions.note: large, glycolytic, recruited later for power

subdivisions.name: Muscle spindle and Golgi tendon organ
subdivisions.note: sensory feedback that sets tone and the stretch reflex; gamma motor neurons adjust spindle sensitivity

motor-unit.function: Generation of muscle force under voluntary and reflex control; the size principle of recruitment; maintenance of tone through the stretch reflex loop.

bestView.label: cervical cord: anterior horn cells are the motor unit's origin

imaging.normalAppearance: Muscle MRI (T1 for fatty replacement, STIR for edema) shows the pattern of involvement: selective muscles in dystrophies and myopathies, diffuse edema in myositis, denervation edema in the territory of a nerve or root; muscle ultrasound shows increased echogenicity.

pathology.finding: Symmetric STIR-bright edema of proximal muscles, later fatty atrophy; guides biopsy site.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: Muscle MRI; EMG; creatine kinase; biopsy

nerve-axillary.name: Axillary nerve
nerve-axillary.summary: A terminal branch of the posterior cord (C5–C6) that leaves the axilla backward through the quadrangular space with the posterior circumflex humeral artery, winds around the surgical neck of the humerus and supplies deltoid and teres minor and a patch of skin over the deltoid (the regimental badge area). Its fixed course at the surgical neck makes it the nerve most often injured by anterior shoulder dislocation and proximal humeral fracture; the result is a flat shoulder that cannot abduct and numbness over the lateral shoulder.

anatomy.location: From the posterior cord behind the axillary artery, through the quadrangular space (bounded by teres minor, teres major, long head of triceps and the humerus), around the surgical neck of the humerus deep to deltoid.

nerve-axillary.function: Motor supply to deltoid (abduction from 15 to 90 degrees) and teres minor (external rotation); sensory supply to the skin over the lower deltoid (superior lateral cutaneous nerve of the arm).

bestView.label: cervical cord; fibers from C5–C6

imaging.normalAppearance: Peripheral nerves of the limbs are outside the MNI brain volume; no atlas mesh is shown. nerve-common-peroneal.name: Common (and deep/superficial) peroneal nerve
nerve-common-peroneal.summary: The smaller lateral division of the sciatic nerve (L4–S2) runs along the medial border of biceps femoris to the lateral side of the popliteal fossa, winds around the neck of the fibula (where it lies on bone under thin skin) and divides into the deep peroneal nerve, which supplies the anterior compartment (tibialis anterior, extensor digitorum longus, extensor hallucis longus) and the first web space skin, and the superficial peroneal nerve, which supplies the evertors (peroneus longus and brevis) and the dorsum of the foot. Compression at the fibular neck by crossed legs, casts, weight loss or squatting is the commonest cause of foot drop.

anatomy.location: Lateral popliteal fossa along the tendon of biceps femoris, around the neck of the fibula deep to peroneus longus (the fibular tunnel), where it divides; the deep branch runs on the interosseous membrane with the anterior tibial artery, the superficial branch in the lateral compartment.

nerve-dorsal-scapular.name: Dorsal scapular nerve
nerve-dorsal-scapular.summary: The dorsal scapular nerve arises from the C5 root (with a C4 contribution) above the upper trunk, pierces the scalenus medius and descends along the medial border of the scapula deep to the levator scapulae and the rhomboids, which it supplies. Because it leaves the root before the plexus forms, rhomboid weakness distinguishes a C5 root lesion from an upper trunk lesion, and its EMG is one of the tests that places a lesion at the root: a C5 radiculopathy denervates the rhomboids, whereas Erb palsy of the upper trunk spares them. It is entrapped in the scalenus medius, producing interscapular pain and scapular winging in a pattern different from that of the long thoracic nerve.

anatomy.location: Leaves the C5 anterior ramus in the neck, pierces the scalenus medius, runs beneath the levator scapulae along the medial scapular border with the dorsal scapular artery, deep to the rhomboid minor and major, which it supplies together with the levator scapulae.

nerve-dorsal-scapular.function: Motor to the levator scapulae and the rhomboids, it elevates and retracts the scapula and stabilizes it during arm movement; its loss produces mild lateral winging of the scapula with the inferior angle displaced laterally (the opposite direction from serratus anterior weakness), difficulty bracing the shoulders back and a dull interscapular ache. Its origin proximal to the plexus makes it a root marker: rhomboid denervation on EMG with deltoid and biceps weakness means the C5 root or a preganglionic avulsion (a poor prognosis for repair), whereas spared rhomboids mean a postganglionic upper trunk injury that may regenerate. Entrapment in the scalenus medius accompanies neck trauma and thoracic outlet syndromes.

nerve-femoral.name: Femoral nerve
nerve-femoral.summary: The largest branch of the lumbar plexus (L2–L4), the femoral nerve emerges from the lateral border of psoas, passes under the inguinal ligament lateral to the femoral artery (outside the femoral sheath) and divides in the femoral triangle into branches to iliacus, pectineus, sartorius and the four heads of quadriceps and into cutaneous branches for the anterior thigh and, through the saphenous nerve, the medial leg and foot. Its lesions (retroperitoneal hematoma, diabetes, hip surgery, lithotomy position) cause the knee to give way, an absent knee jerk and anteromedial thigh and medial leg numbness.

nerve-genitofemoral.name: Genitofemoral nerve
nerve-genitofemoral.summary: The genitofemoral nerve arises from the L1 and L2 roots within the psoas major, emerges on its anterior surface and descends behind the peritoneum to divide above the inguinal ligament into a genital branch, which enters the inguinal canal to supply the cremaster and the skin of the scrotum or labium, and a femoral branch, which passes under the inguinal ligament to supply the skin of the upper anterior thigh over the femoral triangle. It is the efferent and part of the afferent limb of the cremasteric reflex, it is entrapped after hernia repair and pelvic surgery, and its territory distinguishes L1-L2 lesions from the more lateral femoral cutaneous and ilioinguinal patterns.

anatomy.location: Formed within the psoas from L1 and L2, pierces the anterior surface of the muscle, descends on it beneath the peritoneum and the ureter, crosses the external iliac vessels and divides: the genital branch enters the deep inguinal ring with the spermatic cord (or round ligament) to the cremaster and the scrotal or labial skin; the femoral branch passes lateral to the femoral artery under the inguinal ligament to the skin of the upper thigh.

nerve-genitofemoral.function: Its genital branch is motor to the cremaster and sensory to the anterior scrotum or labium majus, forming the efferent limb of the cremasteric reflex (stroking the medial thigh elevates the testis), whose loss indicates an L1-L2 root, plexus or nerve lesion or a corticospinal lesion above; its femoral branch is sensory to the upper anterior thigh below the inguinal ligament. Entrapment or injury by inguinal hernia mesh, varicocelectomy, appendectomy and psoas abscess produces groin, scrotal and upper thigh pain and numbness that is aggravated by hip extension and relieved by flexion, and its blockade is part of the anesthesia for inguinal surgery.

nerve-iliohypogastric.name: Iliohypogastric nerve
nerve-iliohypogastric.summary: The iliohypogastric nerve is the first branch of the lumbar plexus (L1 with a T12 contribution), emerging from the lateral border of the psoas, crossing the quadratus lumborum and the iliac crest region between the transversus abdominis and the internal oblique, and dividing into a lateral cutaneous branch to the skin of the upper buttock and an anterior cutaneous branch to the skin above the pubis. It supplies the lower abdominal wall muscles with the ilioinguinal nerve, it is injured in appendectomy, hernia repair, iliac crest bone harvest and Pfannenstiel incisions, and its entrapment produces the lower abdominal wall pain that is mistaken for a visceral or spinal cause.

anatomy.location: Leaves the upper lateral border of the psoas, crosses the quadratus lumborum behind the kidney, pierces the transversus abdominis above the iliac crest, runs between it and the internal oblique, gives the lateral cutaneous branch over the iliac crest to the gluteal skin and continues forward to pierce the internal and external obliques above the superficial inguinal ring as the anterior cutaneous branch to the suprapubic skin.

nerve-iliohypogastric.function: Mixed, it supplies the lower fibers of the transversus abdominis and internal oblique that form the conjoint tendon and protect the inguinal region, and sensation to the upper lateral buttock and the hypogastric skin above the pubis; its loss weakens the lower abdominal wall (a factor in direct inguinal hernia) and produces a band of numbness or burning above the groin, and entrapment by sutures, mesh or scar in the abdominal wall produces a chronic pain aggravated by trunk extension and hip extension with a trigger point medial to the anterior superior iliac spine. It shares roots and territory with the ilioinguinal nerve and is blocked together with it for hernia and lower abdominal surgery.

nerve-ilioinguinal.name: Ilioinguinal nerve
nerve-ilioinguinal.summary: The ilioinguinal nerve (L1) runs just below the iliohypogastric nerve, emerging from the lateral border of the psoas, crossing the quadratus lumborum and the iliacus, piercing the transversus abdominis near the iliac crest and passing through the inguinal canal with the spermatic cord or round ligament to emerge through the superficial ring and supply the skin of the upper medial thigh, the root of the penis and anterior scrotum or the mons and labium majus. It is the nerve most often injured in inguinal hernia repair and the commonest cause of chronic postoperative groin pain, and its territory distinguishes it from the genitofemoral nerve (which supplies the femoral triangle and the cremaster) and the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve.

anatomy.location: From the L1 root, along the lateral border of the psoas and across the quadratus lumborum and iliacus below the iliohypogastric nerve, piercing the transversus abdominis near the anterior part of the iliac crest, running between it and the internal oblique, then entering the inguinal canal below the spermatic cord to leave through the superficial inguinal ring to the skin of the upper medial thigh and the external genitalia.

nerve-ilioinguinal.function: Mainly sensory to the upper medial thigh, the root of the penis and anterior scrotum or the mons and labium majus, with motor fibers to the lowest fibers of the internal oblique and transversus abdominis; it provides the sensory afferent of the cremasteric reflex from the medial thigh (the efferent runs in the genitofemoral nerve), and its entrapment by suture, mesh or scar after hernia repair, or by the abdominal wall muscles in athletes, produces a burning groin pain radiating to the genitalia and the medial thigh that is aggravated by walking and hip extension and relieved by flexion, with a trigger point medial to the anterior superior iliac spine. Ilioinguinal block is used for hernia surgery, and neurectomy for refractory neuralgia.

nerve-lateral-antebrachial-cutaneous.name: Lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerve
synonyms: lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm
nerve-lateral-antebrachial-cutaneous.summary: The lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerve is the sensory termination of the musculocutaneous nerve (C5, C6) that emerges lateral to the biceps tendon at the elbow and supplies the skin of the lateral forearm from the elbow to the base of the thumb. Its loss accompanies musculocutaneous nerve injury and upper trunk plexus lesions (Erb palsy) and its sensory potential separates a C6 radiculopathy (normal potential) from an upper trunk plexopathy (reduced potential); it is compressed by the biceps aponeurosis in athletes and injured during venepuncture of the cephalic vein.

anatomy.location: Continues the musculocutaneous nerve after it has supplied the coracobrachialis, biceps and brachialis, emerging between the biceps and brachialis lateral to the biceps tendon just above the elbow, piercing the deep fascia and dividing into anterior and posterior branches that run down the lateral forearm with the cephalic vein to the wrist and the thenar eminence.

nerve-lateral-antebrachial-cutaneous.function: Purely sensory, it carries sensation from the lateral forearm through the musculocutaneous nerve, the lateral cord and the upper trunk to the C6 dorsal root ganglion (with a C5 contribution); the dermatome overlap with C6 is close, so its sensory potential is preserved in a C6 root lesion (proximal to the ganglion) and lost in an upper trunk or lateral cord lesion, the electrophysiological basis of localizing lateral arm numbness. It is entrapped where it pierces the fascia beside the biceps tendon, producing lateral forearm pain and numbness with elbow extension and pronation, and it is at risk in cephalic vein cannulation and elbow surgery.

nerve-lateral-femoral-cutaneous.name: Lateral femoral cutaneous nerve
nerve-lateral-femoral-cutaneous.summary: A purely sensory branch of the lumbar plexus (L2–L3) that crosses iliacus and passes under or through the inguinal ligament just medial to the anterior superior iliac spine to supply the skin of the anterolateral thigh. Its entrapment at the ligament by obesity, pregnancy, tight belts or prolonged hip flexion produces meralgia paresthetica: burning, tingling and numbness over the lateral thigh with no weakness and no reflex change.

anatomy.location: Lateral border of psoas, across iliacus deep to its fascia, under the lateral end of the inguinal ligament about 1 cm medial to the anterior superior iliac spine, then over sartorius into the thigh, dividing into anterior and posterior branches.

nerve-lateral-femoral-cutaneous.function: Sensation of the anterolateral thigh from the greater trochanter to the knee; no motor fibers.

nerve-long-thoracic.name: Long thoracic nerve
nerve-long-thoracic.summary: Arising directly from the C5, C6 and C7 roots before they form the trunks, the long thoracic nerve descends behind the plexus and over the outer surface of serratus anterior, which it supplies segmentally. Its long superficial course makes it vulnerable to stretch (carrying heavy loads, sports), to surgery in the axilla and to neuralgic amyotrophy; the resulting serratus palsy produces winging of the scapula when the arm is pushed forward. Because it leaves the roots proximal to the trunks, its involvement points to a root or very proximal lesion rather than a trunk or cord lesion.

nerve-medial-antebrachial-cutaneous.name: Medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve
synonyms: medial cutaneous nerve of the forearm
nerve-medial-antebrachial-cutaneous.summary: The medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve is a sensory branch of the medial cord of the brachial plexus (C8, T1) that runs down the medial arm with the basilic vein, pierces the deep fascia at the middle of the arm and divides into anterior and posterior branches that supply the skin of the medial forearm from the elbow to the wrist. It is the sensory territory that distinguishes a lower trunk or medial cord plexus lesion from an ulnar neuropathy: the ulnar nerve does not supply the forearm skin, so numbness of the medial forearm with a weak, numb hand means the lesion is in the plexus (Klumpke palsy, neurogenic thoracic outlet syndrome, Pancoast tumor), not at the elbow. Its sensory potential is the electrophysiological marker of that distinction.

anatomy.location: Arises from the medial cord in the axilla, descends medial to the brachial artery and then with the basilic vein, pierces the deep fascia with the vein above the elbow and divides into anterior and posterior branches over the medial epicondyle to supply the medial half of the forearm skin down to the wrist.

nerve-medial-antebrachial-cutaneous.function: Purely sensory, it carries touch, pain and temperature from the medial forearm through the medial cord and lower trunk to the C8 and T1 dorsal root ganglia; its territory is the key to separating lower plexus lesions from ulnar neuropathy, because the ulnar nerve's sensory supply stops at the wrist, and a normal medial antebrachial cutaneous sensory potential with an abnormal ulnar one places the lesion in the ulnar nerve, whereas both abnormal places it in the medial cord or lower trunk. It is injured by axillary surgery and by venepuncture and cannulation of the basilic vein, producing a painful neuroma, and it is harvested as a graft.

nerve-medial-brachial-cutaneous.name: Medial brachial cutaneous nerve
synonyms: medial cutaneous nerve of the arm
nerve-medial-brachial-cutaneous.summary: The medial brachial cutaneous nerve is the smallest branch of the medial cord (T1, with a T2 contribution through the intercostobrachial nerve) and supplies the skin of the medial arm and the axilla. It is clinically a marker of the T1 root and the lower plexus: numbness of the medial arm accompanies a Pancoast tumor, a lower trunk injury and neurogenic thoracic outlet syndrome, and the intercostobrachial nerve that joins it is cut in axillary dissection for breast cancer, leaving the numb inner arm that patients notice after surgery.

nerve-medial-brachial-cutaneous.function: Purely sensory, it carries sensation from the medial arm and the floor of the axilla through the medial cord and lower trunk to the T1 (and via the intercostobrachial nerve the T2) dorsal root ganglia, so its territory is the dermatomal marker of the lowest root of the plexus; loss of sensation here with a wasted hand and a Horner syndrome points to a Pancoast tumor at the apex of the lung invading the lower trunk and the sympathetic chain, and loss after axillary surgery reflects section of the intercostobrachial nerve, a benign but permanent numbness. Pain in its territory can be referred cardiac pain, since T1-T2 also receive the heart.

nerve-median.name: Median nerve
nerve-median.summary: Formed by lateral and medial roots from the lateral and medial cords (C6–T1), the median nerve runs down the arm with the brachial artery, passes through the cubital fossa medial to the biceps tendon, between the heads of pronator teres and under the flexor digitorum superficialis arch (giving the pure motor anterior interosseous nerve), and enters the hand through the carpal tunnel beneath the flexor retinaculum. It supplies most forearm flexors and pronators, the LOAF muscles of the hand (lateral two lumbricals, opponens, abductor pollicis brevis, flexor pollicis brevis) and sensation to the lateral three and a half digits. Carpal tunnel syndrome is the commonest entrapment neuropathy of all.

nerve-musculocutaneous.name: Musculocutaneous nerve
nerve-musculocutaneous.summary: The terminal branch of the lateral cord (C5–C7) that pierces coracobrachialis, runs between biceps and brachialis supplying all three, and emerges lateral to the biceps tendon as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm. It is rarely injured alone (heavy lifting, shoulder surgery, strenuous exercise), and its lesion produces weak elbow flexion and supination with an absent biceps reflex and numbness over the lateral forearm; brachioradialis (radial nerve) still allows some flexion.

nerve-obturator.name: Obturator nerve
nerve-obturator.summary: Formed from the anterior divisions of L2–L4 inside psoas, the obturator nerve runs along the pelvic side wall and leaves through the obturator canal to supply the adductor muscles of the thigh (adductor longus, brevis and magnus, gracilis, obturator externus) and a patch of skin on the medial thigh. nerve-phrenic.name: Phrenic nerve
synonyms: C3, C4, C5 keep the diaphragm alive
nerve-phrenic.summary: Formed mainly from C4 with contributions from C3 and C5 at the lateral border of the anterior scalene, the phrenic nerve descends on that muscle, enters the thorax between the subclavian artery and vein, and runs in front of the lung root over the pericardium to reach the diaphragm, which it supplies motor fibers and to which it also gives sensory fibers (plus the pericardium, mediastinal pleura and peritoneum under the diaphragm). Its interruption paralyzes a hemidiaphragm, which is tolerated at rest but produces orthopnea; bilateral loss, as in high cervical cord injury, Guillain–Barré syndrome or neuralgic amyotrophy, causes respiratory failure.

The course was built as a smoothed polyline whose waypoints were read off named Z-Anatomy objects (the C4 spinal ganglion, the anterior surface of scalenus anterior, the gap between the subclavian vein and artery, the brachiocephalic vein, the aortic arch on the left and the superior vena cava on the right, the pericardial surface of the heart and the diaphragm) and swept as a 1.5 mm tube; the waypoints are listed in pipeline/config/derived_nerves.yaml. It shows the route, not this specimen's nerve, and the accessory phrenic nerve is not modeled.

html.summary: Formed mainly from C4 with contributions from C3 and C5 at the lateral border of the anterior scalene, the phrenic nerve descends on that muscle, enters the thorax between the subclavian artery and vein, and runs in front of the lung root over the pericardium to reach the diaphragm, which it supplies motor fibers and to which it also gives sensory fibers (plus the pericardium, mediastinal pleura and peritoneum under the diaphragm). Its interruption paralyzes a hemidiaphragm, which is tolerated at rest but produces orthopnea; bilateral loss, as in high cervical cord injury, Guillain–Barré syndrome or neuralgic amyotrophy, causes respiratory failure.

nerve-posterior-antebrachial-cutaneous.name: Posterior antebrachial cutaneous nerve
synonyms: posterior cutaneous nerve of the forearm
nerve-posterior-antebrachial-cutaneous.summary: The posterior antebrachial cutaneous nerve is a sensory branch of the radial nerve given off in the spiral groove of the humerus, together with the inferior lateral brachial cutaneous nerve, supplying the skin of the posterior arm below the deltoid and the posterior forearm to the wrist. Its involvement marks the level of a radial nerve lesion: it is spared in posterior interosseous and superficial radial lesions at the elbow and forearm and lost in lesions at or above the spiral groove, such as the Saturday night palsy and humeral fracture, so posterior forearm numbness with wrist drop places the injury in the arm.

nerve-posterior-antebrachial-cutaneous.function: Purely sensory, it carries sensation from the posterior forearm and lower lateral arm through the radial nerve and the posterior cord to the C5-C8 dorsal root ganglia; because it leaves the radial nerve in the spiral groove, its territory is anesthetic in high radial lesions (axilla, spiral groove, humeral fracture) and spared in lesions below the elbow (posterior interosseous entrapment, superficial radial injury), a bedside way to place the lesion along the radial nerve. It is also the nerve whose territory hurts in lateral epicondylitis mimics and after elbow surgery.

nerve-posterior-femoral-cutaneous.name: Posterior femoral cutaneous nerve
synonyms: posterior cutaneous nerve of the thigh
nerve-posterior-femoral-cutaneous.summary: The posterior femoral cutaneous nerve arises from the sacral plexus (S1, S2, S3), leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen below the piriformis with the sciatic and inferior gluteal nerves and descends under the gluteus maximus and along the back of the thigh deep to the fascia, supplying the skin of the lower buttock, the perineum, the posterior thigh and the upper calf. It is the sensory nerve that separates a sciatic neuropathy from a sacral plexopathy or radiculopathy: numbness of the posterior thigh with a foot drop means the plexus or the roots, because the sciatic nerve itself supplies no thigh skin; it is injured with the sciatic nerve in hip surgery and injections and is compressed by prolonged sitting and by the hamstring origin.

nerve-posterior-femoral-cutaneous.function: Purely sensory, it carries sensation from the lower buttock, the perineum and posterior scrotum or labium, the posterior thigh and the upper posterior calf through the sacral plexus to the S1-S3 dorsal root ganglia; its territory is spared in sciatic neuropathy at the thigh, which is why posterior thigh numbness with sciatic-type weakness places the lesion at the sciatic notch, the plexus or the roots (piriformis region, pelvic tumor, sacral fracture, radiation). Its perineal branch explains perineal numbness in sacral plexopathy, and the inferior cluneal branches explain the buttock pain of ischial bursitis and of sitting on a hard seat, sometimes called wallet neuritis when the nerve is compressed against the ischial tuberosity.

nerve-pudendal.name: Pudendal nerve
nerve-pudendal.summary: The pudendal nerve carries the S2–S4 fibers that supply the perineum: motor to the external anal and urethral sphincters and the muscles of the pelvic floor and erection, sensory to the perineal skin, the external genitalia and the anal canal below the pectinate line, and the afferent limb of the reflexes that control continence and sexual function. It leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen, hooks around the sacrospinous ligament beside the ischial spine and re-enters through the lesser sciatic foramen into the pudendal canal on the lateral wall of the ischiorectal fossa. It is stretched in childbirth and prolonged cycling, blocked at the ischial spine for obstetric anesthesia, and entrapped in Alcock's canal to produce perineal pain that is worse sitting; its S2–S4 origin makes it the peripheral counterpart of the conus and cauda equina in sphincter localization.

The parasympathetic pelvic splanchnic nerves from the same segments, though separate, run alongside for erection and bladder emptying.

nerve-radial.name: Radial nerve
nerve-radial.summary: The largest branch of the posterior cord (C5–T1), the radial nerve supplies every extensor of the elbow, wrist and fingers. It spirals around the back of the humerus in the radial groove with the profunda brachii artery, where it is compressed against the bone during deep sleep (Saturday night palsy) or torn by humeral shaft fractures, pierces the lateral intermuscular septum, and divides in front of the lateral epicondyle into a superficial sensory branch (dorsal radial hand) and the posterior interosseous nerve, which passes through supinator to the finger extensors. Wrist drop with sparing of triceps is its signature.

nerve-sciatic.name: Sciatic nerve
nerve-sciatic.summary: The thickest nerve in the body, formed from L4–S3 in the sacral plexus, leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen below piriformis, runs down the posterior thigh between the ischial tuberosity and the greater trochanter deep to gluteus maximus, supplies the hamstrings and the ischial part of adductor magnus, and divides above the knee into the tibial and common peroneal nerves, which together supply everything below the knee. Its two divisions are already separate bundles within the trunk, and the lateral (peroneal) division is more vulnerable to stretch and compression, so sciatic lesions often look like peroneal palsies with subtle tibial involvement.

nerve-superficial-radial.name: Superficial branch of the radial nerve
nerve-superficial-radial.summary: The superficial branch of the radial nerve is the sensory continuation of the radial nerve after it divides at the elbow, running down the forearm beneath the brachioradialis, emerging between its tendon and the extensor carpi radialis longus in the distal forearm and crossing the anatomical snuffbox to supply the skin of the dorsolateral hand and the dorsum of the thumb, index and middle fingers to the distal joints. It is compressed by tight watch straps and handcuffs (Wartenberg syndrome or cheiralgia paresthetica), injured by wrist surgery, cannulation and de Quervain release, and its sensory potential is the standard radial sensory study that separates a radial nerve lesion from a C6-C7 radiculopathy.

anatomy.location: Leaves the radial nerve in front of the lateral epicondyle, descends under the brachioradialis lateral to the radial artery, pierces the deep fascia about eight centimeters above the wrist between the brachioradialis and extensor carpi radialis longus tendons, crosses the snuffbox superficially and divides into dorsal digital nerves for the thumb, index, middle and half of the ring finger over the dorsum of the hand.

nerve-superficial-radial.function: Purely sensory, it carries sensation from the radial dorsum of the hand and the dorsum of the lateral fingers through the radial nerve and the posterior cord to the C6 and C7 dorsal root ganglia; its territory is spared in the posterior interosseous syndrome (which separates from it at the elbow) and lost in higher radial lesions, and its conduction study is normal in a C6-C7 radiculopathy because the lesion is proximal to the ganglion. It is entrapped where it pierces the fascia between the brachioradialis and extensor carpi radialis longus, producing pain and paresthesias of the dorsal hand aggravated by pronation and by anything tight around the wrist.

html.summary: The superficial branch of the radial nerve is the sensory continuation of the radial nerve after it divides at the elbow, running down the forearm beneath the brachioradialis, emerging between its tendon and the extensor carpi radialis longus in the distal forearm and crossing the anatomical snuffbox to supply the skin of the dorsolateral hand and the dorsum of the thumb, index and middle fingers to the distal joints. It is compressed by tight watch straps and handcuffs (Wartenberg syndrome or cheiralgia paresthetica), injured by wrist surgery, cannulation and de Quervain release, and its sensory potential is the standard radial sensory study that separates a radial nerve lesion from a C6-C7 radiculopathy.
html.function: Purely sensory, it carries sensation from the radial dorsum of the hand and the dorsum of the lateral fingers through the radial nerve and the posterior cord to the C6 and C7 dorsal root ganglia; its territory is spared in the posterior interosseous syndrome (which separates from it at the elbow) and lost in higher radial lesions, and its conduction study is normal in a C6-C7 radiculopathy because the lesion is proximal to the ganglion. nerve-superior-gluteal.name: Superior gluteal nerve
nerve-superior-gluteal.summary: The superior gluteal nerve (L4, L5, S1) leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen above the piriformis, the only nerve to do so, and runs between the gluteus medius and minimus with the superior gluteal artery to supply those two muscles and the tensor fasciae latae, the abductors and medial rotators of the hip that hold the pelvis level in single-leg stance. Its loss produces the Trendelenburg sign and a waddling gait, and it is injured by hip replacement through a lateral approach, by intramuscular injections in the wrong quadrant and by L5 radiculopathy; abductor weakness in an L5 lesion is the sign that separates the root from a peroneal neuropathy, which spares the gluteus medius.

anatomy.location: From the sacral plexus in the pelvis, through the suprapiriform part of the greater sciatic foramen with the superior gluteal vessels, then laterally between the gluteus medius and minimus, supplying both, and forward to end in the tensor fasciae latae.

nerve-superior-gluteal.function: Motor to the gluteus medius, gluteus minimus and tensor fasciae latae, which abduct and medially rotate the thigh and, more importantly, stabilize the pelvis on the stance leg during walking; when they are weak the pelvis drops toward the swing side (the Trendelenburg sign) and the trunk lurches over the stance leg, producing a waddling gait when bilateral. The nerve carries L5 fibers predominantly, so abductor weakness is part of the L5 radiculopathy and lumbosacral plexopathy pictures and is absent in a common peroneal palsy at the fibular neck, the key bedside distinction in foot drop; it is also at risk in the lateral and anterolateral approaches to the hip, where the muscle split is limited to protect it, and in gluteal injections given too medially or too high.

nerve-suprascapular.name: Suprascapular nerve
nerve-suprascapular.summary: A branch of the upper trunk (C5–C6) that runs back through the suprascapular notch under the transverse scapular ligament to supply supraspinatus, then around the spinoglenoid notch to supply infraspinatus, with sensory fibers to the shoulder joint but no cutaneous branch. It is compressed at either notch (ganglion cysts, repetitive overhead activity in athletes) and injured in upper trunk lesions and neuralgic amyotrophy, producing a painless or aching shoulder with weak abduction initiation and external rotation and visible wasting of the spinati.

anatomy.location: From the upper trunk in the posterior triangle, laterally beneath the trapezius to the suprascapular notch, into the supraspinous fossa, then around the lateral border of the scapular spine (spinoglenoid notch) into the infraspinous fossa.

nerve-suprascapular.function: Motor supply to supraspinatus (initiation of abduction) and infraspinatus (external rotation); proprioceptive supply to the glenohumeral and acromioclavicular joints.

nerve-sural.name: Sural nerve
nerve-sural.summary: The sural nerve is a purely sensory nerve of the calf formed by the medial sural cutaneous branch of the tibial nerve joined by the peroneal communicating branch of the common peroneal nerve; it descends between the heads of the gastrocnemius, pierces the deep fascia in the mid-calf, runs beside the small saphenous vein behind the lateral malleolus and supplies the skin of the posterolateral leg, the lateral heel and the lateral border of the foot to the fifth toe. It matters clinically far beyond its small territory: its sensory action potential is the standard measure of a length-dependent polyneuropathy, its preservation in a foot drop points to a root rather than a nerve lesion, and it is the nerve most often biopsied for vasculitis and amyloid, leaving a patch of numbness on the lateral foot.

anatomy.location: Formed in the popliteal fossa or upper calf from tibial and common peroneal contributions (the level of union varies), descends superficially in the posterior calf lateral to the Achilles tendon, passes behind the lateral malleolus with the small saphenous vein, and ends as the lateral dorsal cutaneous nerve of the foot.

nerve-sural.function: Carries cutaneous sensation from the posterolateral calf, the lateral ankle and heel and the lateral border of the foot including the fifth toe, with S1 as its main root. Its accessibility and constant position make it the nerve of choice for sensory conduction studies and biopsy, and its composition of mixed large and small fibers allows histological assessment of both.

nerve-thoracodorsal.name: Thoracodorsal nerve
nerve-thoracodorsal.summary: The thoracodorsal nerve arises from the posterior cord of the brachial plexus (C6, C7, C8) between the subscapular nerves, descends along the posterior axillary wall with the thoracodorsal artery and enters the latissimus dorsi, which it supplies. It is at risk in axillary lymph node dissection and in posterior shoulder surgery, it is the nerve of the latissimus flap used in reconstruction, and its EMG places lesions in the posterior cord: latissimus weakness with radial and axillary signs means the posterior cord, whereas latissimus sparing points to the individual nerves.

anatomy.location: Leaves the posterior cord in the axilla between the upper and lower subscapular nerves, descends along the posterior axillary wall on the surface of the subscapularis and teres major with the thoracodorsal artery, and enters the deep surface of the latissimus dorsi near its tendon.

nerve-thoracodorsal.function: Motor to the latissimus dorsi, it adducts, extends and medially rotates the arm and pulls the body up in climbing and in transfers from a wheelchair, and it contributes to forced expiration and coughing; its loss weakens adduction against resistance (the patient cannot press the arm down against the examiner's hand) and is felt most by athletes and by paraplegics who depend on the latissimus for transfers. Its origin from the posterior cord makes it a cord marker in plexus lesions, and surgeons preserve it during axillary clearance or use it, with its artery, as the pedicle of the latissimus flap for breast and chest wall reconstruction and for restoring elbow flexion after brachial plexus injury.

nerve-tibial.name: Tibial nerve
nerve-tibial.summary: The larger terminal division of the sciatic nerve (L4–S3) runs straight through the popliteal fossa and down the back of the leg deep to soleus with the posterior tibial artery, supplying the plantar flexors and invertors (gastrocnemius, soleus, tibialis posterior, flexor digitorum longus, flexor hallucis longus), then passes behind the medial malleolus through the tarsal tunnel to divide into the medial and lateral plantar nerves for the sole. Sensation of the sole and heel and the ankle reflex belong to it. It is well protected and rarely injured proximally; distal entrapment in the tarsal tunnel causes burning sole pain.

nerve-ulnar.name: Ulnar nerve
nerve-ulnar.summary: The terminal branch of the medial cord (C8–T1) descends on the medial side of the arm, passes behind the medial epicondyle in the cubital tunnel (where it is palpable and vulnerable), enters the forearm between the heads of flexor carpi ulnaris, supplies that muscle and the ulnar half of flexor digitorum profundus, and crosses the wrist superficial to the flexor retinaculum through Guyon's canal to supply most of the small muscles of the hand (interossei, medial lumbricals, hypothenar muscles, adductor pollicis) and sensation to the little finger and half the ring finger. Its dorsal cutaneous branch arises above the wrist, so dorsal ulnar hand sensation separates elbow from wrist lesions.

anatomy.location: Medial arm on coracobrachialis, then behind the medial intermuscular septum, through the cubital tunnel behind the medial epicondyle, down the medial forearm under flexor carpi ulnaris with the ulnar artery, through Guyon's canal at the wrist lateral to the pisiform, into the hand as superficial (sensory) and deep (motor) branches.

html.summary: The terminal branch of the medial cord (C8–T1) descends on the medial side of the arm, passes behind the medial epicondyle in the cubital tunnel (where it is palpable and vulnerable), enters the forearm between the heads of flexor carpi ulnaris, supplies that muscle and the ulnar half of flexor digitorum profundus, and crosses the wrist superficial to the flexor retinaculum through Guyon's canal to supply most of the small muscles of the hand (interossei, medial lumbricals, hypothenar muscles, adductor pollicis) and sensation to the little finger and half the ring finger. Its dorsal cutaneous branch arises above the wrist, so dorsal ulnar hand sensation separates elbow from wrist lesions.
html.function: Finger abduction and adduction, thumb adduction, flexion of the ring and little fingers, power grip and fine finger control; sensation of the medial one and a half digits and the ulnar hand.
html.anatomy.location: Medial arm on coracobrachialis, then behind the medial intermuscular septum, through the cubital tunnel behind the medial epicondyle, down the medial forearm under flexor carpi ulnaris with the ulnar artery, through Guyon's canal at the wrist lateral to the pisiform, into the hand as superficial (sensory) and deep (motor) branches.
html.imaging.normalAppearance: Peripheral nerves of the limbs are outside the MNI brain volume; no atlas mesh is shown. Ultrasound and MR neurography image the nerve directly; electrodiagnosis localizes the lesion functionally. html.imaging.sequenceOfChoice: Nerve conduction studies across the elbow; ultrasound; MRI of the wrist for Guyon's canal

nerves-dorsal-cutaneous-foot.name: Dorsal cutaneous nerves of the foot
synonyms: medial dorsal cutaneous nerve of the foot
intermediate dorsal cutaneous nerve of the foot
nerves-dorsal-cutaneous-foot.summary: The medial and intermediate dorsal cutaneous nerves of the foot are the terminal branches of the superficial peroneal nerve, emerging through the deep fascia of the lower lateral leg and crossing the ankle to supply the skin of the dorsum of the foot and toes, except the first web space (deep peroneal), the lateral border of the foot (sural) and the medial border (saphenous). They are the sensory map of the superficial peroneal nerve and of the L5 dermatome on the dorsum of the foot, they are compressed where they pierce the fascia and at the ankle by tight boots, and they are injured in ankle arthroscopy and surgery, producing numbness and neuroma pain on the top of the foot.

anatomy.location: The superficial peroneal nerve pierces the deep fascia in the lower third of the lateral leg and divides into the medial dorsal cutaneous nerve, which crosses the ankle anterior to the lateral malleolus to the medial dorsum, the great toe and the second and third toes, and the intermediate dorsal cutaneous nerve, which runs more laterally to the lateral dorsum and the third to fifth toes; both lie subcutaneously over the extensor retinaculum.

nerves-dorsal-cutaneous-foot.function: Purely sensory, they carry sensation from the dorsum of the foot and toes through the superficial peroneal nerve to the L5 (medial) and S1 (lateral) dorsal root ganglia; their sparing of the first web space (deep peroneal), the lateral foot (sural) and the medial foot (saphenous) allows the examiner to assign dorsal foot numbness to the superficial peroneal nerve or the L5 root, and the superficial peroneal sensory potential separates the two (normal in a root lesion). They are entrapped where the superficial peroneal nerve pierces the fascia (with pain on plantar flexion and inversion) and compressed by boots at the ankle, and they are cut in anterolateral ankle portals and bunion surgery, leaving a numb dorsum or a painful neuroma.

nerves-pectoral.name: Medial and lateral pectoral nerves
nerves-pectoral.summary: The lateral pectoral nerve (C5-C7) from the lateral cord and the medial pectoral nerve (C8-T1) from the medial cord cross the axilla to supply the pectoralis major and minor, the lateral nerve the clavicular and upper sternal parts of the major and the medial nerve the lower sternal part and the minor; they are named for the cords they arise from, not for their positions. They are the motor markers of the cords in plexus lesions, they are injured in breast and axillary surgery and by the pectoralis minor in thoracic outlet syndromes, and the pectoral reflex and the palpable contraction of the muscle during adduction give a bedside test of the C5-T1 roots.

anatomy.location: The lateral pectoral nerve leaves the lateral cord, crosses the axillary artery and pierces the clavipectoral fascia to enter the deep surface of the pectoralis major; the medial pectoral nerve leaves the medial cord behind the axillary artery, passes through or around the pectoralis minor, supplying it, and ends in the lower pectoralis major; a loop between the two nerves crosses the artery.

nerves-pectoral.function: Motor to the pectoralis major (adduction, medial rotation and flexion of the arm, with the clavicular head flexing and the sternal head adducting) and the pectoralis minor (depression and protraction of the scapula), they let the arm be pressed against the chest and the body be pushed up from a chair; their two-cord origin makes the pectoralis major a map of the plexus, with clavicular-head weakness indicating the upper roots and lateral cord and sternal-head weakness the lower roots and medial cord. The pectoral reflex, elicited by tapping the tendon with the arm abducted, tests C5-T1 and is brisk in cervical myelopathy. The nerves are divided in radical mastectomy and can be used as donors for nerve transfer.

bestView.label: pectoral nerves crossing the axilla to the pectoralis major and minor

neuromuscular-junction.name: Neuromuscular junction
neuromuscular-junction.summary: The chemical synapse between a motor axon terminal and a skeletal muscle fiber. Acetylcholine released in quanta from the terminal crosses the cleft, binds nicotinic receptors on the folded post-synaptic membrane to produce an end-plate potential and a muscle action potential, and is hydrolysed by acetylcholinesterase. Disease of the junction produces fatigable weakness without sensory loss, wasting or reflex change: post-synaptic antibodies in myasthenia gravis, pre-synaptic calcium-channel antibodies in the Lambert–Eaton syndrome, and toxins (botulinum, organophosphates, neuromuscular blockers) at various steps.

anatomy.location: Motor end plates near the middle of each muscle fiber where the terminal branches of the motor axon end; one junction per fiber, many per motor unit.

subdivisions.name: Presynaptic terminal
subdivisions.note: voltage-gated calcium channels, acetylcholine vesicles; target of Lambert–Eaton antibodies and botulinum toxin

subdivisions.name: Synaptic cleft
subdivisions.note: acetylcholinesterase in the basal lamina; target of organophosphates and pyridostigmine

subdivisions.name: Postsynaptic membrane
subdivisions.note: junctional folds with nicotinic acetylcholine receptors and MuSK; target of myasthenia gravis antibodies and of non-depolarizing blockers

neuromuscular-junction.function: Reliable one-to-one transmission of the motor neuron action potential to the muscle fiber with a large safety factor, which disease erodes to produce fatigability.

bestView.label: cervical cord; the junction is in the muscles, not imaged

imaging.normalAppearance: Not imaged directly. The imaging task in junction disease is the thymus: CT of the chest for thymoma or hyperplasia in myasthenia gravis, and a search for small-cell lung cancer in the Lambert–Eaton syndrome.

pathology.finding: Anterior mediastinal soft-tissue mass; thymic hyperplasia in younger patients.

pathology.pathology: Small-cell lung cancer in Lambert–Eaton syndrome

nuclei-viscero-sensory-motor.name: Viscero-sensory-motor nuclei complex
synonyms: solitary, dorsal vagal and hypoglossal nuclear complex
nuclei-viscero-sensory-motor.summary: The viscero-sensory-motor complex is the block of gray matter in the dorsal medulla that holds the visceral afferent and efferent machinery of the vagus and glossopharyngeal nerves together with the hypoglossal nucleus. It is drawn as a single label because 7 T imaging cannot separate the nucleus of the solitary tract, the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus and the hypoglossal nucleus in a living brain, and because functionally they act as a unit: taste and visceral afferents arrive in the solitary nucleus, and the reflex responses leave through the adjacent parasympathetic and motor columns. This is the floor of the fourth ventricle at the level of the vagal trigone, and it is where blood pressure, heart rate, gastric secretion, swallowing, coughing and vomiting are put together.

anatomy.location: Dorsal medulla under the floor of the fourth ventricle and, more caudally, around the central canal, from the level of the striae medullares down to the obex and a little below it. The solitary tract and its nucleus lie laterally, the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus makes the vagal trigone medial to it, and the hypoglossal nucleus forms the hypoglossal trigone next to the midline; the area postrema sits at the obex on the ventricular surface outside the blood-brain barrier. Posterior spinal and medial branches of the vertebral and posterior inferior cerebellar arteries supply the complex.

subdivisions.name: Nucleus of the solitary tract
subdivisions.note: Visceral and gustatory afferent column, topographically ordered from taste rostrally to gut caudally

subdivisions.name: Dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus
subdivisions.note: Preganglionic parasympathetic column for heart, airway and gut

subdivisions.name: Hypoglossal nucleus
subdivisions.note: Motor column for the tongue, adjacent to the midline

efferents.to: Nucleus ambiguus and the pharyngeal and laryngeal muscles

nuclei-viscero-sensory-motor.function: Afferents from the vagus and glossopharyngeal nerves carrying taste, arterial baroreceptor and chemoreceptor signals, airway irritant information and gastrointestinal distension enter the solitary tract and end in a topographic order along the solitary nucleus, taste rostrally and cardiorespiratory and gastrointestinal input caudally. The hypoglossal nucleus, immediately medial, supplies the tongue and is recruited in swallowing, chewing and airway maintenance during sleep. The reflexes assembled here include the baroreflex, the chemoreflex, the cough and gag reflexes, the swallowing sequence and emesis, and the area postrema adds a chemosensitive trigger zone that samples the blood directly.

pitfalls: SEVEN-TESLA TEMPLATE: the outline shown here is the group probability map of the Brainstem Navigator thresholded at 0.35, not a boundary you can trace on a clinical scan. PUBLIC EDITION - LOCATION MARKER: the 7 T probabilistic outline of this nucleus may not be redistributed, so the openly shareable build of the atlas shows a landmark-anchored ellipsoid instead: an ellipsoid of about 86 mm3 per side, the volume published by Singh et al. (2019), centered in the dorsomedial medulla just deep to the floor of the fourth ventricle, at and below the obex, and clipped to the brainstem. It marks where the nucleus lies, not where its border runs -- do not read a shape, an edge or a neighbour relation off it, and note that its position is a textbook relation to open landmarks, not a measured centroid.

nucleus-accumbens.name: Nucleus accumbens
nucleus-accumbens.summary: The ventral striatum, where the head of the caudate and the putamen merge beneath the anterior limb of the internal capsule, next to the septal area. It receives dopamine from the ventral tegmental area (mesolimbic pathway) and input from the amygdala, hippocampus and prefrontal cortex, and projects to the ventral pallidum. It encodes reward prediction and motivation, is the substrate of addiction and of apathy, and is a target of deep brain stimulation for obsessive-compulsive disorder and depression.

nucleus-ambiguus.name: Nucleus ambiguus
nucleus-ambiguus.summary: A column of large motor neurons buried in the reticular formation of the lateral medulla, ventromedial to the spinal trigeminal nucleus and dorsal to the olive. It supplies the striated muscles of the pharynx, larynx and upper esophagus through the glossopharyngeal and vagus nerves and the cranial part of the accessory nerve, and its most rostral part gives the stylopharyngeus its motor supply. Because it sits in the lateral medullary wedge supplied by PICA, dysphagia and hoarseness are cardinal signs of the Wallenberg syndrome.

anatomy.location: Lateral tegmentum of the open medulla, deep to the surface, forming a longitudinal column from the level of the cochlear nuclei down to the pyramidal decussation; ventromedial to the spinal trigeminal complex and lateral to the hypoglossal nucleus.

nucleus-ambiguus.function: Lower motor neurons for swallowing, phonation and elevation of the palate; its neurons also drive the cardioinhibitory vagal outflow to the heart in the caudal part.

bestView.label: lateral medullary tegmentum dorsal to the olive
column of the nucleus in the lateral medulla

imaging.normalAppearance: Not visible on routine MRI; localized by its position in the lateral tegmentum behind the olive. Lateral medullary infarcts that involve it show diffusion restriction in this region.

Because it sits in the lateral medullary wedge supplied by PICA, dysphagia and hoarseness are cardinal signs of the Wallenberg syndrome.
html.function: Lower motor neurons for swallowing, phonation and elevation of the palate; its neurons also drive the cardioinhibitory vagal outflow to the heart in the caudal part.
html.anatomy.location: Lateral tegmentum of the open medulla, deep to the surface, forming a longitudinal column from the level of the cochlear nuclei down to the pyramidal decussation; ventromedial to the spinal trigeminal complex and lateral to the hypoglossal nucleus.
html.imaging.normalAppearance: Not visible on routine MRI; localized by its position in the lateral tegmentum behind the olive. Lateral medullary infarcts that involve it show diffusion restriction in this region.
html.imaging.sequenceOfChoice: DWI through the medulla; videofluoroscopic swallow study for aspiration risk

nucleus-basalis-meynert.name: Nucleus basalis of Meynert
nucleus-basalis-meynert.summary: The nucleus basalis of Meynert is the largest of the basal forebrain cholinergic groups, a loose cluster of big neurons in the substantia innominata beneath the globus pallidus and the anterior commissure, extending from the diagonal band back to the level of the optic tract, medial to the amygdala. It is the principal source of acetylcholine for the neocortex and the amygdala and it modulates attention, arousal and cortical plasticity. Its neurons carry tau and Lewy pathology early and their loss underlies the cholinergic deficit of Alzheimer disease, Parkinson disease dementia and dementia with Lewy bodies; the nucleus is a target of deep brain stimulation trials and its volume on MRI predicts cognitive decline.

anatomy.location: Substantia innominata of the ventral forebrain, below the anterior commissure and the ventral pallidum, above the anterior perforated substance and the optic tract, lateral to the hypothalamus and medial to the amygdala and the temporal stem.

nucleus-basalis-meynert.function: Nucleus basalis neurons project topographically through the medial and lateral cholinergic pathways to every neocortical area and to the amygdala, and release acetylcholine that increases cortical excitability and signal-to-noise, holds attention on relevant stimuli, and permits the cortical map changes of learning; they fire to novel, rewarding or salient events driven by the amygdala, the hypothalamus and the brainstem, and pause during slow-wave sleep. They also modulate cerebral blood flow through cholinergic innervation of cortical vessels. Their degeneration, with reduced cortical choline acetyltransferase, precedes and predicts the cognitive decline of Alzheimer and Lewy body disease and explains why cholinergic drugs help attention more than memory.

bestView.label: nucleus basalis in the substantia innominata under the pallidum
basal forebrain lateral to the hypothalamus above the optic tract

nucleus-cuneiform.name: Cuneiform nucleus
synonyms: mesencephalic locomotor region (with the pedunculopontine nucleus)
nucleus-cuneiform.summary: The cuneiform nucleus is a glutamatergic cell group in the dorsolateral tegmentum of the caudal midbrain, packed between the periaqueductal gray and the lateral lemniscus and sitting just above and behind the pedunculopontine nucleus. Together with that neighbor it forms the mesencephalic locomotor region, the small patch of midbrain whose stimulation makes an animal walk and whose firing rate sets how fast. Where the pedunculopontine nucleus is cholinergic and concerned with starting and permitting movement, the cuneiform nucleus is the speed and urgency control: it drives fast, goal-directed and escape locomotion through the medullary reticulospinal system, and it is coupled to the defensive circuitry of the periaqueductal gray. Interest in it is clinical as well as physiological, because freezing of gait and falls in Parkinson disease resist dopamine and the mesencephalic locomotor region has become a deep brain stimulation target for them.

anatomy.location: Caudal midbrain tegmentum at the level of the inferior colliculus, immediately lateral to the periaqueductal gray and dorsal to the pedunculopontine nucleus, with the lateral lemniscus and the brachium of the inferior colliculus on its lateral side and the decussation of the superior cerebellar peduncles below and in front. It extends caudally toward the isthmus, where it merges with the isthmic reticular formation, and rostrally it thins out beneath the inferior collicular plate. Its blood comes from perforators of the superior cerebellar and posterior cerebral arteries.

afferents.from: Substantia nigra pars reticulata and internal pallidum

efferents.to: Gigantocellular reticular formation of the pons and medulla
Pedunculopontine nucleus and substantia nigra pars compacta

nucleus-cuneiform.function: The cuneiform nucleus converts a decision to move into a locomotor command. Glutamatergic neurons project caudally to the gigantocellular and magnocellular reticular formation of the pons and medulla, which in turn drive the spinal pattern generators through the medial reticulospinal tract; the strength of that drive grades locomotor speed and gait pattern rather than simply switching walking on. Inputs arrive from the motor and premotor cortex, from the internal pallidum and the substantia nigra pars reticulata, whose tonic inhibition rises in parkinsonism, from the subthalamic nucleus, and from the lateral hypothalamus and the periaqueductal gray, which is why the same region drives escape running and the freezing that precedes it. The nucleus also contributes to postural set and to the autonomic adjustments that accompany effort, raising heart rate and ventilation before the first step is taken. Because its output is glutamatergic and reticulospinal rather than dopaminergic, its dysfunction produces axial motor failure that levodopa cannot correct, and stimulating it in animals restores locomotion after nigral lesions.

lesionEffects.mechanism: Loss of glutamatergic drive to the pontomedullary reticulospinal system

nucleus-gracilis-cuneatus.name: Gracile and cuneate nuclei
nucleus-gracilis-cuneatus.summary: The gracile and cuneate nuclei sit in the dorsal lower medulla beneath the gracile and cuneate tubercles and receive the ascending fibers of the posterior columns: the gracile nucleus from the leg and lower trunk (fasciculus gracilis), the cuneate nucleus from the arm and upper trunk (fasciculus cuneatus). Their axons cross as the internal arcuate fibers to form the medial lemniscus. The accessory cuneate nucleus, just lateral, sends unconscious proprioception from the arm to the cerebellum through the inferior cerebellar peduncle.

anatomy.location: Dorsal closed medulla just above the pyramidal decussation, medial (gracile) and lateral (cuneate) to each other under the tubercles that bulge into the caudal floor of the fourth ventricle region; the accessory cuneate nucleus lies lateral to the cuneate nucleus.

nucleus-laterodorsal-tegmental.name: Laterodorsal tegmental nucleus and central gray of the pons
nucleus-laterodorsal-tegmental.summary: The laterodorsal tegmental nucleus is a cholinergic cell group in the central gray of the upper pons, lying in the floor of the fourth ventricle just medial to the locus coeruleus. With the pedunculopontine nucleus it makes up the Ch5-Ch6 cholinergic system of the brainstem, the source of acetylcholine for the thalamus, and it is one of the two engines of the ascending arousal system that switch the thalamocortical loop from burst firing to the tonic mode of waking and REM sleep. Its neurons are REM-on: they fire fastest during REM sleep and during waking and fall silent in non-REM sleep. The label used here also contains the surrounding central gray of the rhombencephalon, because 7 T imaging cannot separate the nucleus from the periventricular gray it sits in.

anatomy.location: Central gray of the rostral pons in the floor of the fourth ventricle, medial and slightly dorsal to the locus coeruleus, lateral to the medial longitudinal fasciculus and above the level of the abducens nucleus, extending rostrally into the isthmus where it becomes continuous with the periaqueductal gray and with the pedunculopontine territory. The superior cerebellar peduncle bounds it laterally. Blood supply is from the superior cerebellar artery and dorsal perforators of the basilar artery, and its periventricular position makes it vulnerable in thiamine deficiency.

afferents.from: Nucleus of the solitary tract and periaqueductal gray

nucleus-laterodorsal-tegmental.function: Cholinergic neurons of the laterodorsal tegmental nucleus project densely to the thalamus, including the intralaminar and reticular nuclei and the specific relay nuclei, and to the lateral hypothalamus, the basal forebrain, the ventral tegmental area and the medial prefrontal cortex. Acetylcholine released on thalamic neurons depolarizes them out of the burst firing that produces sleep spindles and slow waves and into the single-spike mode required for cortical arousal, so this nucleus is a switch between sleep and waking rather than a carrier of specific information. Its projection to the ventral tegmental area gates dopamine burst firing and therefore reward signaling, giving cholinergic brainstem control over motivation and drug reinforcement. During REM sleep the same neurons drive the pontine reticular formation to generate rapid eye movements and the cortical activation of dreaming, while the noradrenergic and serotonergic systems are silent. Afferents come from the prefrontal cortex, the lateral hypothalamus including the orexin neurons, the periaqueductal gray and the nucleus of the solitary tract, tying arousal to appetite, threat and visceral state.
