nucleus-microcellular-tegmental-parabige.name: Microcellular tegmental and parabigeminal nuclei
nucleus-microcellular-tegmental-parabige.summary: The microcellular tegmental nucleus and the parabigeminal nucleus are two small, closely apposed cell groups at the lateral edge of the caudal midbrain tegmentum, drawn as one label because 7 T imaging cannot reliably separate them. The parabigeminal nucleus is the primate equivalent of the nucleus isthmi of lower vertebrates: a thin cholinergic shell lying against the lateral lemniscus that is reciprocally and topographically wired with the superior colliculus, and that sharpens which point in space the colliculus selects for the next orienting movement. The microcellular tegmental nucleus lies just medial to it and belongs to the isthmic reticular territory, contributing to arousal and to the premotor control of eye and head movements. Both are far too small to see clinically, but they matter for the physiology of covert attention and of collicular target selection.

anatomy.location: Lateral tegmentum of the caudal midbrain at and just below the level of the inferior colliculus, sandwiched between the lateral lemniscus laterally, the brachium of the inferior colliculus above and the cuneiform and pedunculopontine territory medially. The parabigeminal component hugs the outer surface of the lemniscus as a curved lamina; the microcellular tegmental component sits a little deeper and more medially, at the transition from midbrain to isthmus. Perforators from the superior cerebellar artery and the quadrigeminal branch of the posterior cerebral artery supply the region.

afferents.from: Frontal eye field and cortical eye fields
Lateral lemniscus territory and inferior colliculus

nucleus-microcellular-tegmental-parabige.function: The parabigeminal nucleus receives a dense topographic projection from the superficial layers of the superior colliculus and sends cholinergic fibers back to the same collicular point and, more weakly, to the opposite colliculus. That loop behaves as a winner-take-all circuit: it amplifies the collicular representation of the currently selected target and suppresses competing locations, so it is treated as a substrate of covert spatial attention and of stimulus salience. It also projects to the lateral geniculate nucleus and the pretectum, coupling attentional selection to the earliest stages of the visual pathway. The microcellular tegmental nucleus shares the connections of the surrounding isthmic reticular formation, projecting to the oculomotor and pontine gaze structures and receiving collicular and cortical eye-field input, so the pair sits at the junction of orienting, arousal and premotor gaze control. Their cholinergic output means that the same neuromodulator that supports cortical arousal is used locally to bias which part of the visual world is acted upon next.

nucleus-parabrachial-lateral.name: Lateral parabrachial nucleus

nucleus-parabrachial-lateral.function: The lateral parabrachial nucleus is the second-order station of the ascending interoceptive and nociceptive pathway. It receives the caudal, viscerosensory part of the nucleus of the solitary tract, lamina I of the spinal and trigeminal dorsal horns and the area postrema, and projects to the central nucleus of the amygdala, the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis, the paraventricular and lateral hypothalamus, the periaqueductal gray and the midline and ventromedial posterior thalamus. nucleus-parabrachial-medial.name: Medial parabrachial nucleus
nucleus-parabrachial-medial.summary: The medial parabrachial nucleus lies against the medial face of the superior cerebellar peduncle, just inside its lateral partner, and is the pontine taste and respiratory relay. In primates the gustatory information that reaches the rostral nucleus of the solitary tract is passed mainly straight to the thalamus, but the medial parabrachial nucleus remains part of the visceral afferent chain and carries taste, gastric and cardiorespiratory signals toward the hypothalamus and the amygdala. The Kölliker-Fuse nucleus lies at its ventrolateral corner and the mesencephalic trigeminal tract runs nearby. It is supplied by the superior cerebellar artery and long circumferential branches of the basilar artery.

nucleus-parabrachial-medial.function: The medial parabrachial nucleus receives the rostral, gustatory part of the nucleus of the solitary tract and the visceral afferents that report gastric distension, airway irritation and blood pressure, and projects to the ventral posteromedial thalamus, the lateral hypothalamus, the central amygdala and the insular cortex. Loss of this control with an intact medullary rhythm generator yields apneusis, while its ascending arm contributes to the sensation of dyspnea. The nucleus also receives descending input from the insula, the amygdala and the hypothalamus, which is how emotion changes the breathing pattern.

nucleus-parvicellular-reticular-alpha.name: Parvicellular reticular nucleus, alpha part
nucleus-parvicellular-reticular-alpha.summary: The parvicellular reticular nucleus is the small-celled lateral part of the medullary reticular formation, and its alpha subdivision lies at the rostral end of that column just behind the trigeminal complex. It is the premotor organizer of the cranial motor nuclei: it receives trigeminal, gustatory and cortical input and distributes it to the trigeminal motor, facial, ambiguus and hypoglossal nuclei, coordinating the muscle sequences of chewing, licking, swallowing, facial expression and airway protection. It is the lateral, sensory-driven counterpart of the giant-celled medial column that projects to the spinal cord, and it is the reason a lesion in the lateral medulla can disorganize swallowing even when each individual motor nucleus is intact.

It lies within the field supplied by the posterior inferior cerebellar artery and by lateral perforating branches of the vertebral artery, which is why it is damaged in the lateral medullary syndrome.

nucleus-parvicellular-reticular-alpha.function: Parvicellular reticular neurons receive the spinal and principal trigeminal nuclei, the nucleus of the solitary tract, the cerebral cortex through corticoreticular fibers and the cerebellum, and project short axons to the motor nuclei of the trigeminal, facial, glossopharyngeal, vagus and hypoglossal nerves. They therefore act as pattern generators and premotor interneurons for orofacial behavior: the rhythmic jaw movements of chewing, the sequenced pharyngeal contraction of swallowing, the coordinated closure and expulsion of coughing and vomiting, and the reflex responses of the face to trigeminal stimulation such as the corneal blink and the jaw jerk modulation. Because the same neurons carry cortical commands to the bulbar motor nuclei, they form part of the corticobulbar route that produces pseudobulbar palsy when interrupted bilaterally above the medulla. The alpha subdivision is the part most closely tied to the trigeminal system and to chewing. Its output is bilateral for most muscles, which is why unilateral lesions typically cause incoordination rather than paralysis.

nucleus-solitarius.name: Nucleus of the solitary tract
nucleus-solitarius.summary: The visceral sensory nucleus of the brainstem. It surrounds the solitary tract in the dorsolateral medulla and receives taste from the anterior tongue (via the facial nerve), the posterior tongue (glossopharyngeal) and the epiglottis (vagus) in its rostral part, and general visceral afferents from the carotid sinus and body, the aortic arch, the heart, lungs and gut in its caudal part. nucleus-subcoeruleus.name: Subcoeruleus nucleus
nucleus-subcoeruleus.summary: The subcoeruleus nucleus is a small group of glutamatergic and noradrenergic neurons lying just ventral and lateral to the locus coeruleus in the dorsal tegmentum of the upper pons. In humans it corresponds to the sublaterodorsal nucleus of the rat, and it is the generator of the muscle atonia of REM sleep: its glutamatergic neurons fire during REM and excite inhibitory neurons of the ventromedial medulla and the spinal cord, which hyperpolarize motor neurons so that dreams are not acted out. Loss of these neurons produces REM sleep behavior disorder, in which patients punch, kick and shout during dreaming, and that disorder is the earliest reliable clinical marker of Parkinson disease, dementia with Lewy bodies and multiple system atrophy, often preceding the movement disorder by a decade or more.

anatomy.location: Dorsolateral tegmentum of the rostral pons immediately below and lateral to the locus coeruleus, in the angle between the superior cerebellar peduncle laterally, the medial longitudinal fasciculus medially and the floor of the fourth ventricle above. It merges caudally with the pontine reticular formation and rostrally with the laterodorsal tegmental territory. It lies in the territory of short circumferential branches of the basilar artery and of the superior cerebellar artery, and it is close enough to the locus coeruleus that the two are nearly always affected together.

nucleus-subcoeruleus.function: During REM sleep the subcoeruleus is one of the few brainstem regions that becomes more active rather than less. Its glutamatergic neurons project to glycinergic and GABAergic premotor neurons in the ventromedial medulla and directly to the spinal ventral horn, and the resulting postsynaptic inhibition of alpha motor neurons produces the near-complete skeletal atonia that defines REM. The same population is held in check during waking by GABAergic neurons of the ventrolateral periaqueductal gray and adjacent tegmentum, and it is released when those neurons fall silent at REM onset; the switch is reciprocal, so damage on either side of it produces either REM without atonia or a failure to enter REM at all. Ascending fibers reach the thalamus and basal forebrain and contribute to cortical activation, and noradrenergic neurons intermingled with the glutamatergic ones share the projections of the locus coeruleus. In the synucleinopathies the subcoeruleus degenerates early, at Braak stage 2, before the substantia nigra.

(2022) -- placed ventrolateral to the locus coeruleus meta mask, which is the public edition's own locus coeruleus, and clipped to the brainstem. The meta mask is a sampling volume of interest and is deliberately larger than the locus coeruleus itself, so the two surfaces may touch or overlap; that overlap is an artefact of the anchor, not an anatomical claim. It marks where the nucleus lies, not where its border runs -- do not read a shape, an edge or a neighbour relation off it, and note that its position is a textbook relation to open landmarks, not a measured centroid.

html.summary: The subcoeruleus nucleus is a small group of glutamatergic and noradrenergic neurons lying just ventral and lateral to the locus coeruleus in the dorsal tegmentum of the upper pons. In humans it corresponds to the sublaterodorsal nucleus of the rat, and it is the generator of the muscle atonia of REM sleep: its glutamatergic neurons fire during REM and excite inhibitory neurons of the ventromedial medulla and the spinal cord, which hyperpolarize motor neurons so that dreams are not acted out. Loss of these neurons produces REM sleep behavior disorder, in which patients punch, kick and shout during dreaming, and that disorder is the earliest reliable clinical marker of Parkinson disease, dementia with Lewy bodies and multiple system atrophy, often preceding the movement disorder by a decade or more.
html.function: During REM sleep the subcoeruleus is one of the few brainstem regions that becomes more active rather than less. Its glutamatergic neurons project to glycinergic and GABAergic premotor neurons in the ventromedial medulla and directly to the spinal ventral horn, and the resulting postsynaptic inhibition of alpha motor neurons produces the near-complete skeletal atonia that defines REM. The same population is held in check during waking by GABAergic neurons of the ventrolateral periaqueductal gray and adjacent tegmentum, and it is released when those neurons fall silent at REM onset; the switch is reciprocal, so damage on either side of it produces either REM without atonia or a failure to enter REM at all. Ascending fibers reach the thalamus and basal forebrain and contribute to cortical activation, and noradrenergic neurons intermingled with the glutamatergic ones share the projections of the locus coeruleus. In the synucleinopathies the subcoeruleus degenerates early, at Braak stage 2, before the substantia nigra.
html.anatomy.location: Dorsolateral tegmentum of the rostral pons immediately below and lateral to the locus coeruleus, in the angle between the superior cerebellar peduncle laterally, the medial longitudinal fasciculus medially and the floor of the fourth ventricle above. It merges caudally with the pontine reticular formation and rostrally with the laterodorsal tegmental territory. It lies in the territory of short circumferential branches of the basilar artery and of the superior cerebellar artery, and it is close enough to the locus coeruleus that the two are nearly always affected together.
html.imaging.normalAppearance: Not resolvable at 3 T. Neuromelanin-sensitive sequences show the locus coeruleus as a bright dot in the dorsal pons; the subcoeruleus lies immediately ventrolateral to it and reduced signal in that region has been reported in REM sleep behavior disorder.

occipital-pole.name: Occipital pole
occipital-pole.summary: The occipital pole is the posterior tip of the hemisphere where the calcarine sulcus reaches the surface and the primary visual cortex spreads onto the lateral convexity, representing the central visual field (the macula) with a huge cortical magnification. It receives a dual blood supply from the calcarine branch of the posterior cerebral artery and from the terminal branches of the middle cerebral artery, which is why the macula is spared in many PCA infarcts and why the pole is selectively damaged in watershed injury and in hypotension. Bilateral polar lesions cause central scotomas and loss of reading, and the pole is the site of the visual auras of occipital epilepsy and of the release hallucinations of visual loss.

anatomy.location: Posterior extremity of the hemisphere, behind the parieto-occipital sulcus and the preoccipital notch, where the medial, lateral and inferior surfaces of the occipital lobe converge; the calcarine sulcus ends here and the macular representation extends onto the lateral surface.

occipital-pole.function: The posterior calcarine cortex at the pole receives the foveal projection, with the central few degrees occupying as much cortex as the whole peripheral field, and analyzes the fine detail, color and stereopsis needed for reading, face recognition and skilled hand work; it feeds the fusiform and lateral occipital areas that identify letters and objects. The vertical meridian is represented at the border with the opposite hemisphere through the splenium, and the pole contributes to the maintenance of fixation and to the smallest voluntary saccades. Its loss on one side produces a congruous contralateral paracentral scotoma or a hemianopia without macular sparing.

bestView.label: occipital pole with the macular representation
posterior tip of the hemisphere at the end of the calcarine sulcus

imaging.normalAppearance: Rounded posterior tip of the hemisphere on axial and sagittal images, where the calcarine sulcus reaches the surface; the poles are often asymmetric with one petalia projecting further back, a normal variant.

pathology.finding: Bilateral restricted diffusion of the occipital tips after hypotension or cardiac arrest with central scotomas and impaired reading despite preserved peripheral fields.
Calcarine infarct extending to the pole when the MCA collateral is poor, producing a complete hemianopia without macular sparing.
Central colored or flashing auras, ictal blindness or amaurosis, occipital spikes increased by eye closure.

lesionEffects.deficit: Contralateral paracentral scotoma or hemianopia without macular sparing
lesionEffects.mechanism: Loss of the foveal representation at the occipital pole

lesionEffects.deficit: Bilateral central scotomas and impaired reading
lesionEffects.mechanism: Bilateral polar damage in border-zone injury
Ictal activation of the macular cortex

examination: Central fields with a red target and the Amsler grid
Reading acuity in addition to distance acuity
Perimetry for paracentral and macular defects
pearls: The macula has two arteries; the occipital pole is spared by a PCA stroke and hit by a hypotensive one

oculomotor-nucleus.name: Oculomotor and Edinger–Westphal nuclei
oculomotor-nucleus.latin: Nucleus nervi oculomotorii; nucleus accessorius nervi oculomotorii
oculomotor-nucleus.summary: A cluster of subnuclei in the ventral periaqueductal gray of the rostral midbrain at the level of the superior colliculus. The somatic subnuclei supply the medial, superior and inferior recti, the inferior oblique and the levator palpebrae; the Edinger–Westphal nucleus supplies preganglionic parasympathetic fibers to the ciliary ganglion for pupil constriction and accommodation. Two anatomical quirks matter clinically: the superior rectus subnucleus projects to the opposite eye and the single central caudal nucleus supplies both levators, so a nuclear lesion causes bilateral ptosis and contralateral superior rectus weakness, unlike a nerve lesion.

anatomy.location: Ventral part of the periaqueductal gray on either side of the midline at the superior colliculus level, dorsal to the MLF; the fascicles run ventrally through the tegmentum, red nucleus and medial crus to exit in the interpeduncular fossa.

subdivisions.name: Somatic subnuclei
subdivisions.note: medial rectus, inferior rectus, inferior oblique (ipsilateral); superior rectus (contralateral); levator palpebrae (bilateral, central caudal nucleus)

subdivisions.name: Edinger–Westphal nucleus
subdivisions.note: preganglionic parasympathetic for the sphincter pupillae and ciliary muscle; also the efferent relay of the light and near reflexes

oculomotor-nucleus.function: Moves the eye in most directions, raises the lid, constricts the pupil and accommodates the lens; receives the MLF for conjugate gaze and pretectal input for the light reflex.

bestView.label: ventral periaqueductal gray at the superior colliculus level
oculomotor nerve emerging in the interpeduncular fossa

imaging.normalAppearance: The nuclear complex is not resolved; the nerve is visible on thin T2 leaving the interpeduncular fossa between the posterior cerebral and superior cerebellar arteries. Nuclear lesions appear as small paramedian dorsal midbrain spots.

optic-chiasm.name: Optic chiasm
optic-chiasm.summary: The X-shaped junction where the two optic nerves meet above the pituitary and exchange fibers: axons from the nasal retina of each eye (which see the temporal visual field) cross to the opposite optic tract, while temporal retinal fibers stay uncrossed. This partial decussation converts an eye-based map into a hemifield-based map. Because the crossing fibers occupy the middle of the chiasm, a pituitary tumor pushing up from below or a craniopharyngioma pressing down produces the bitemporal hemianopia that is the signature of chiasmal disease.

anatomy.location: Suprasellar cistern above the diaphragma sellae and pituitary, in front of the infundibulum and the floor of the third ventricle, below the anterior cerebral and anterior communicating arteries, and between the supraclinoid internal carotid arteries; usually centered over the sella but pre- or post-fixed in some people.

subdivisions.name: Crossing (nasal) fibers
subdivisions.note: central and inferior part; inferonasal fibers loop forward into the opposite nerve (Wilbrand's knee)

subdivisions.name: Uncrossed (temporal) fibers
subdivisions.note: lateral parts of the chiasm

subdivisions.name: Macular fibers
subdivisions.note: posterior and superior, crossing near the posterior chiasm

efferents.note: to the LGN, pretectum and superior colliculus

optic-chiasm.function: Redistribution of retinal fibers so that each optic tract carries the contralateral half of the visual field from both eyes; conveys pupillary afferents onward to the pretectum.

bestView.label: chiasm above the pituitary between the carotids
chiasm in the suprasellar cistern in front of the infundibulum
X-shaped chiasm with the optic nerves in front and tracts behind

imaging.normalAppearance: A flat band of white matter crossing the suprasellar cistern on coronal T1, about 3–4 mm thick; on sagittal images it lies just above the diaphragma. Elevation or thinning by a mass, T2 brightness (glioma, demyelination) and enhancement are the key findings.

pathology.finding: Suprasellar extension of a sellar mass stretching the chiasm upward; bitemporal hemianopia, superior quadrants first.
Cystic calcified suprasellar mass compressing the chiasm from above/behind; inferior quadrants may go first.
Fusiform T2-bright enlargement of the chiasm and nerves in a child with neurofibromatosis 1.
Swollen enhancing chiasm with bilateral visual loss.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: Coronal and sagittal T1 (pre/post contrast) and T2 through the sella; formal perimetry

lesionEffects.mechanism: Crossing nasal fibers in the middle of the chiasm

lesionEffects.deficit: Junctional scotoma: central loss in one eye with superotemporal loss in the other
lesionEffects.mechanism: Lesion at the junction of the optic nerve and chiasm (Wilbrand's knee)
Lateral compression of the uncrossed fibers, e.g. by calcified carotids
Long-standing compression

examination: Confrontation fields testing each eye separately with a red target for temporal desaturation
Acuity and color vision
Fundoscopy for band (bow-tie) atrophy of the discs
Endocrine symptoms
pearls: A field defect that respects the vertical midline in both eyes and is temporal on both sides is the chiasm

pedunculopontine-nucleus.name: Pedunculopontine nucleus
pedunculopontine-nucleus.summary: The pedunculopontine nucleus is a cluster of cholinergic and glutamatergic neurons in the caudal midbrain and rostral pontine tegmentum, lateral to the decussation of the superior cerebellar peduncles and beneath the inferior colliculus. It is the brainstem locomotor region: it initiates and paces gait and postural adjustments through the reticulospinal system and it is part of the ascending arousal system and of the REM sleep circuitry. It is reciprocally connected with the basal ganglia and degenerates in Parkinson disease and progressive supranuclear palsy, which is why freezing of gait and falls do not respond to dopamine; it has been a target of deep brain stimulation for these axial symptoms.

anatomy.location: Mesopontine tegmentum at the junction of the midbrain and pons, lateral to the superior cerebellar peduncle decussation, medial to the medial lemniscus, below the inferior colliculus and behind the substantia nigra, extending along the lateral edge of the periaqueductal gray.

afferents.from: Globus pallidus internus and substantia nigra pars reticulata

efferents.to: Pontomedullary reticular formation and spinal cord
Substantia nigra pars compacta and subthalamic nucleus

pedunculopontine-nucleus.function: Cholinergic pedunculopontine neurons project to the thalamus, the substantia nigra pars compacta and the subthalamic nucleus, supporting arousal and REM sleep and modulating dopamine release, while glutamatergic and GABAergic neurons project to the pontomedullary reticular formation and the spinal cord to trigger and sustain locomotion and to adjust posture; the nucleus receives the internal pallidum and the substantia nigra pars reticulata, whose excessive inhibition in parkinsonism suppresses it. It also relays motor cortex commands for gait initiation and turns and participates in the startle reflex. Loss of its cholinergic neurons correlates with freezing, falls and REM sleep behavior disorder.

bestView.label: pedunculopontine nucleus in the mesopontine tegmentum
tegmentum at the midbrain-pons junction below the inferior colliculus

imaging.normalAppearance: A small tegmental region lateral to the superior cerebellar peduncle decussation on axial images at the level of the inferior colliculus; identified by atlases and by tractography for stimulation planning.

pathology.pathology: Parkinson disease and progressive supranuclear palsy (axial symptoms)
pathology.finding: Mesopontine tegmental atrophy and reduced cholinergic markers on PET correlate with freezing of gait and falls; routine MRI is normal or shows midbrain atrophy in PSP.
Electrode in the mesopontine tegmentum lateral to the superior cerebellar peduncle for refractory freezing; results are variable.
Restricted diffusion in the tegmentum at the midbrain-pontine junction with gait failure, hypersomnolence and REM sleep disturbance.

lesionEffects.deficit: Freezing of gait and postural instability
lesionEffects.mechanism: Loss of the mesencephalic locomotor drive to the reticulospinal system

lesionEffects.deficit: REM sleep behavior disorder and reduced arousal
lesionEffects.mechanism: Loss of cholinergic REM-on and arousal neurons
Cholinergic and non-dopaminergic degeneration

examination: Gait initiation, turning and dual-task walking to elicit freezing
Pull test for postural instability
Sleep history for dream enactment
pearls: Dopamine does not fix freezing because the pedunculopontine nucleus is cholinergic

pitfalls: Freezing of gait in a levodopa-responsive patient who no longer responds is a pedunculopontine, not a dose, problem

periaqueductal-grey.name: Periaqueductal gray
periaqueductal-grey.summary: The sleeve of gray matter around the cerebral aqueduct throughout the midbrain. It is the brain's descending pain-control center: opioid-sensitive neurons here drive the raphe nuclei and locus coeruleus, which in turn suppress pain transmission in the dorsal horn. It also coordinates defensive behaviors, vocalization, micturition and autonomic responses to threat. It surrounds the oculomotor and trochlear nuclei and the MLF, and it is one of the classic sites of Wernicke encephalopathy.

anatomy.location: Concentric gray matter around the aqueduct from the posterior commissure down to the upper fourth ventricle, bordered ventrally by the oculomotor and trochlear nuclei and the MLF and dorsally by the tectum.

periaqueductal-grey.function: Endogenous analgesia (opioid and stimulation-produced), fight-or-flight and freezing responses, vocalization, and control of micturition through the pontine micturition center.

bestView.label: gray matter ring around the aqueduct
periaqueductal gray along the aqueduct

imaging.normalAppearance: Slightly brighter than the surrounding tegmentum on T2 as a ring around the aqueduct; symmetrical FLAIR hyperintensity here is abnormal.

pathology.finding: Symmetrical FLAIR hyperintensity of the periaqueductal gray, medial thalami, mammillary bodies and tectum; may enhance acutely.
pathology.timing: Changes can resolve within days of thiamine

pathology.finding: Small lesion around the aqueduct causing vertical gaze abnormalities, INO or pupil changes.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: Axial FLAIR and DWI through the midbrain; give thiamine before confirming

lesionEffects.deficit: Loss of descending pain inhibition, allodynia
lesionEffects.mechanism: Periaqueductal analgesia circuitry

lesionEffects.deficit: Ophthalmoplegia and gaze palsies in Wernicke encephalopathy
lesionEffects.mechanism: Adjacent oculomotor, trochlear and MLF structures

pia-mater.name: Pia mater
pia-mater.summary: The innermost meninx, a thin vascular membrane that clings to the brain and cord and follows every sulcus and fissure. It carries the blood vessels that enter the brain, forming the perivascular (Virchow–Robin) spaces around penetrating arteries, and it thickens on the cord as the denticulate ligaments and the filum terminale. With the arachnoid it forms the leptomeninges, the site of leptomeningeal metastasis and of the enhancement seen in meningitis. The glia limitans beneath it is the outer boundary of the brain proper.

anatomy.location: Directly on the surface of the brain and spinal cord, dipping into the sulci, ensheathing the vessels entering the brain, and forming the denticulate ligaments and filum terminale of the cord.

pia-mater.function: Vascular support of the brain surface, formation of perivascular spaces that drain interstitial fluid, mechanical anchoring of the cord, and part of the blood–brain interface.

arteries: pial branches of all cerebral arteries

bestView.label: perivascular spaces along the lenticulostriate arteries in the basal ganglia

pineal-gland.name: Pineal gland
pineal-gland.summary: A small midline endocrine gland attached to the posterior wall of the third ventricle by a stalk containing the habenular and posterior commissures, lying in the quadrigeminal cistern above the superior colliculi and below the splenium. It secretes melatonin in the dark under sympathetic control from the superior cervical ganglion, calcifies with age (a useful midline marker on CT), and is the site of germ cell and pineal parenchymal tumors that compress the dorsal midbrain and the aqueduct.

anatomy.location: Midline in the quadrigeminal cistern between the splenium of the corpus callosum above and the superior colliculi below, behind the third ventricle, attached by the pineal stalk whose laminae contain the habenular and posterior commissures; the internal cerebral veins pass above it to the vein of Galen.

pineal-gland.function: Melatonin synthesis and circadian and seasonal signaling; the calcified pineal is an anatomical midline landmark.

bestView.label: pineal gland below the splenium and above the tectum
midline calcified gland in the quadrigeminal cistern

Beta-hCG secretion by germ cell tumors

Papilledema
Pubertal staging in children
pearls: A teenage boy with headache and inability to look up has a pineal tumor until proven otherwise

html.summary: A small midline endocrine gland attached to the posterior wall of the third ventricle by a stalk containing the habenular and posterior commissures, lying in the quadrigeminal cistern above the superior colliculi and below the splenium. It secretes melatonin in the dark under sympathetic control from the superior cervical ganglion, calcifies with age (a useful midline marker on CT), and is the site of germ cell and pineal parenchymal tumors that compress the dorsal midbrain and the aqueduct.
html.function: Melatonin synthesis and circadian and seasonal signaling; the calcified pineal is an anatomical midline landmark.
html.anatomy.location: Midline in the quadrigeminal cistern between the splenium of the corpus callosum above and the superior colliculi below, behind the third ventricle, attached by the pineal stalk whose laminae contain the habenular and posterior commissures; the internal cerebral veins pass above it to the vein of Galen.
html.imaging.normalAppearance: Calcified in most adults on CT (a shift indicates mass effect); on MRI it is a small enhancing midline structure with frequent benign cysts under 1 cm. A pineal cyst with a thin wall and no nodularity is normal.
html.imaging.sequenceOfChoice: Sagittal T1+Gd; CT for calcification pattern; tumor markers (AFP, beta-hCG) in CSF and serum

pituitary-infundibulum.name: Pituitary gland and infundibulum
pituitary-infundibulum.summary: The pituitary sits in the sella turcica under the diaphragma sellae, connected to the hypothalamus by the infundibulum, and is flanked by the cavernous sinuses with their carotid arteries and cranial nerves III, IV, V1, V2 and VI, and overlain by the optic chiasm. The anterior lobe (adenohypophysis) makes growth hormone, prolactin, ACTH, TSH, LH and FSH under hypothalamic releasing hormones delivered by the portal veins; the posterior lobe (neurohypophysis) stores vasopressin and oxytocin made in the hypothalamus. Its tumors present with hormone excess, hypopituitarism, bitemporal hemianopia or, in apoplexy, sudden headache and ophthalmoplegia.

anatomy.location: Sella turcica of the sphenoid bone, roofed by the diaphragma sellae through which the stalk passes; the optic chiasm lies above and slightly in front, the cavernous sinuses lateral, the sphenoid sinus below.

subdivisions.name: Adenohypophysis (anterior lobe)
subdivisions.note: pars distalis, pars tuberalis, pars intermedia; hormone-producing cells fed by the hypophyseal portal system

subdivisions.name: Neurohypophysis (posterior lobe)
subdivisions.note: axon terminals of supraoptic and paraventricular neurons; T1-bright on MRI because of neurosecretory granules

subdivisions.name: Infundibulum (stalk)
subdivisions.note: portal vessels and hypothalamo-hypophyseal tract; normally 2–3 mm thick

relations.anterior: tuberculum sellae and anterior clinoid processes
relations.lateral: cavernous sinus with the internal carotid artery and cranial nerves III, IV, V1, V2, VI
relations.superior: diaphragma sellae, suprasellar cistern, optic chiasm

pituitary-infundibulum.function: Master endocrine gland: growth, lactation, adrenal and thyroid drive, gonadal function; water balance and uterine contraction through the posterior lobe.

bestView.label: pituitary in the sella between the cavernous sinuses, chiasm above
gland, stalk and the posterior pituitary bright spot

Focal hypoenhancing lesion under 10 mm on dynamic contrast T1, often with stalk deviation.
Hemorrhage or infarction within an adenoma: T1-bright or heterogeneous mass with sudden headache, visual loss and ophthalmoplegia.

Non-enhancing cyst between the anterior and posterior lobes, often T1-bright from proteinaceous content, with a characteristic intracystic nodule; usually incidental.

Destruction or compression of the anterior lobe
Stalk or posterior lobe disease (rare with adenomas, common with infiltration or surgery)

lesionEffects.deficit: Hormone excess: acromegaly, Cushing disease, galactorrhea

Eye movements and facial sensation for cavernous sinus involvement
Look for acromegalic or cushingoid features, galactorrhea
Postural blood pressure and hydration

planum-polare.name: Planum polare
planum-polare.summary: The planum polare is the smooth superior surface of the anterior temporal lobe in front of Heschl's gyrus, forming the floor of the anterior part of the lateral sulcus beneath the frontal operculum and facing the anterior insula. It is auditory association cortex of the anterior belt and parabelt (part of area 22) and it processes the temporal structure of sounds, melody and the prosody of voices, feeding the anterior stream of sound identification. It is a middle cerebral artery inferior division territory, is involved with the insula in operculo-insular seizures, and is part of the auditory cortex that is spared in cortical deafness only when both Heschl's gyri survive.

anatomy.location: Anterior part of the upper surface of the superior temporal gyrus, hidden within the lateral sulcus between the temporal pole in front, Heschl's gyrus behind, the insula medially and the frontal operculum above.

efferents.to: Temporal pole and anterior superior temporal gyrus

planum-polare.function: The planum polare contains the anterior auditory belt fields that respond to the pitch contour and rhythm of sounds, to melodies and to the emotional tone of the voice, particularly on the right, and it feeds the anterior stream of sound identification that runs to the temporal pole and the inferior frontal gyrus. It also receives visceral and gustatory information from the adjacent insula and participates in the integration of hearing with emotion through its amygdala connections. Seizures involving it produce auditory auras of distorted sound or music, and lesions produce amusia and impaired recognition of the emotional intonation of speech.

bestView.label: planum polare in the floor of the anterior Sylvian fissure
upper surface of the anterior temporal lobe facing the insula

imaging.normalAppearance: The flat upper surface of the anterior temporal lobe seen on coronal images through the anterior insula, beneath the Sylvian cistern; it slopes upward toward Heschl's gyrus posteriorly.

pathology.finding: Cortical restricted diffusion on the superior temporal surface and the adjacent insula with impaired recognition of prosody and music.
Auditory distortion, music or voices at onset with fear or a throat sensation; scalp EEG is often equivocal.
CSF-signal cyst in the anterior Sylvian fissure flattening the planum polare and displacing the temporal pole, usually incidental.

lesionEffects.deficit: Amusia and impaired recognition of emotional prosody (right)
lesionEffects.mechanism: Loss of the anterior belt cortex processing pitch contour and melody

lesionEffects.deficit: Impaired identification of voices and complex sounds
lesionEffects.mechanism: Disruption of the anterior auditory identification stream

lesionEffects.deficit: Auditory illusions and hallucinations during seizures
lesionEffects.mechanism: Ictal activation of anterior auditory association cortex

examination: Ask the patient to hum a familiar tune and to recognize melodies
Identify the emotion in sentences spoken with varied intonation
Seizure history of distorted sounds or music

planum-temporale.name: Planum temporale
planum-temporale.summary: The planum temporale is the flat triangular surface of the superior temporal gyrus behind Heschl's gyrus, forming the floor of the posterior lateral sulcus beneath the parietal operculum. It is larger on the left in most people, one of the earliest described anatomical asymmetries of the language brain, and it contains auditory association cortex that decodes the spectral and temporal structure of speech and locates sounds in space, forming the start of the dorsal auditory stream to Wernicke's area, the supramarginal gyrus and the frontal speech cortex. It is supplied by the inferior division of the middle cerebral artery, and lesions contribute to Wernicke and conduction aphasia, to impaired sound localization, and to the auditory hallucinations of schizophrenia, in which its asymmetry is reduced.

anatomy.location: Posterior part of the superior surface of the temporal lobe, behind the transverse temporal gyrus of Heschl and in front of the point where the lateral sulcus turns upward into the supramarginal gyrus; it faces the parietal operculum across the posterior Sylvian fissure.

efferents.to: Supramarginal gyrus and inferior frontal gyrus

planum-temporale.function: The planum temporale analyzes the rapidly changing spectral patterns of speech and other complex sounds and computes where a sound comes from and whether it is moving; in the left hemisphere it is the entry point of the dorsal stream that maps phonology onto articulation through the arcuate fasciculus, and it contains a sensorimotor interface used in repetition and in monitoring one's own voice. It is also engaged when reading silently, when listening to music, and in the perception of the timing of sounds. Its size asymmetry relates to language lateralization but is only loosely tied to handedness.

bestView.label: planum temporale behind Heschl's gyrus on the superior temporal surface
floor of the posterior Sylvian fissure beneath the parietal operculum

imaging.normalAppearance: Flat superior temporal surface behind the transverse temporal gyrus on axial images through the level of the thalamus and posterior insula; the left planum is longer and reaches further back in most brains.

pathology.pathology: Conduction or Wernicke aphasia from a posterior MCA branch infarct
pathology.finding: Restricted diffusion in the posterior superior temporal plane and the underlying arcuate fibers with impaired repetition and phonemic paraphasias.
Bilateral posterior superior temporal lesions, usually sequential strokes, with inability to interpret sounds despite normal audiometry.

lesionEffects.mechanism: Damage to the sensorimotor speech interface at the start of the dorsal stream

lesionEffects.deficit: Impaired sound localization in the contralateral hemispace
lesionEffects.mechanism: Loss of the spatial auditory processing of the posterior temporal plane

lesionEffects.deficit: Contribution to word deafness when bilateral
lesionEffects.mechanism: Loss of speech-sound decoding in both auditory association cortices

examination: Repetition of words and non-words and of long sentences
Localization of sounds made behind the patient on each side
Comprehension of speech in noise, which fails early with posterior temporal lesions
pearls: Repetition failure with fluent speech and good comprehension points to the posterior superior temporal plane and the arcuate fasciculus

plexus-brachial.name: Brachial plexus
plexus-brachial.summary: The ventral rami of C5–T1 reorganize in the neck and axilla into the brachial plexus so that fibers from each root are redistributed to several nerves: roots form trunks (upper C5–C6, middle C7, lower C8–T1) between the scalene muscles, trunks split into anterior and posterior divisions behind the clavicle, divisions regroup into cords named for their position around the axillary artery (lateral, posterior, medial), and cords give the terminal nerves. The sequence 'roots, trunks, divisions, cords, branches' is the key to localizing plexus injuries: upper trunk lesions (Erb) paralyze the shoulder and elbow flexors, lower trunk lesions (Klumpke) the hand, and cord lesions produce recognizable combinations that no single nerve or root explains.

anatomy.location: From the intervertebral foramina of C5–T1 through the interscalene triangle (roots and trunks), over the first rib behind the clavicle (divisions), and around the axillary artery in the axilla (cords) to the terminal branches at the lower border of pectoralis minor.

subdivisions.name: Roots (C5–T1)
subdivisions.note: dorsal scapular nerve (C5), long thoracic nerve (C5–C7), contributions to the phrenic nerve

subdivisions.name: Trunks
subdivisions.note: upper (C5–C6): suprascapular nerve and nerve to subclavius; middle (C7); lower (C8–T1)

subdivisions.name: Divisions
subdivisions.note: anterior divisions → flexors (lateral and medial cords); posterior divisions → extensors (posterior cord)

subdivisions.name: Lateral cord
subdivisions.note: musculocutaneous nerve, lateral root of the median nerve, lateral pectoral nerve

subdivisions.name: Posterior cord
subdivisions.note: axillary and radial nerves, subscapular and thoracodorsal nerves

subdivisions.name: Medial cord
subdivisions.note: ulnar nerve, medial root of the median nerve, medial pectoral, medial cutaneous nerves of arm and forearm

plexus-brachial.function: Motor and sensory supply of the entire upper limb and shoulder girdle, plus sympathetic fibers distributed with the nerves.

bestView.label: cervical cord: the plexus roots emerge at C5–T1 below the MNI volume

imaging.normalAppearance: Peripheral nerves of the limbs are outside the MNI brain volume; no atlas mesh is shown. Ultrasound and MR neurography image the nerve directly; electrodiagnosis localizes the lesion functionally. MR neurography of the plexus shows the trunks and cords as bright fascicular structures on STIR; thickening, enhancement or discontinuity indicate injury, inflammation or infiltration.

pathology.finding: Pseudomeningocele at an avulsed root on cervical MRI or CT myelography; thickened T2-bright trunks in stretch injury.
Enhancing mass infiltrating the lower plexus (Pancoast tumor, breast cancer, painful, Horner) versus diffuse thickening without mass after radiation (painless, myokymia on EMG).
Focal nerve constrictions or T2 hyperintensity in the upper trunk and its branches with denervation edema in shoulder muscles.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: MR neurography (STIR, T1+Gd); EMG/NCS to separate root, plexus and nerve

lesionEffects.mechanism: Upper trunk C5–C6: deltoid, biceps, supraspinatus, infraspinatus, brachioradialis

lesionEffects.deficit: Klumpke palsy: claw hand with intrinsic wasting, often with Horner syndrome
lesionEffects.mechanism: Lower trunk C8–T1, T1 sympathetic fibers

lesionEffects.deficit: Weak elbow flexion and forearm pronation with lateral forearm numbness
lesionEffects.mechanism: Lateral cord: musculocutaneous and lateral median fibers

lesionEffects.deficit: Weak wrist and finger extension plus deltoid weakness
lesionEffects.mechanism: Posterior cord: radial and axillary nerves

lesionEffects.deficit: Hand intrinsic and finger flexor weakness with medial arm numbness
lesionEffects.mechanism: Medial cord: ulnar and medial median fibers

plexus-lumbosacral.name: Lumbar and sacral plexuses
plexus-lumbosacral.summary: The ventral rami of L1–S4 form two linked plexuses in the posterior abdominal wall and pelvis. The lumbar plexus (L1–L4) lies within psoas major and gives the iliohypogastric, ilioinguinal, genitofemoral and lateral femoral cutaneous nerves, the obturator nerve (medial thigh) and the femoral nerve (anterior thigh). The lumbosacral trunk (L4–L5) joins the sacral plexus (S1–S4) on piriformis in the pelvis to give the sciatic nerve (posterior thigh and everything below the knee), the superior and inferior gluteal nerves and the pudendal nerve. Plexopathies here come from diabetes (painful proximal diabetic neuropathy), pelvic tumors, retroperitoneal hematoma and radiation, and are recognized by deficits that span more than one nerve and more than one root.

anatomy.location: Lumbar plexus within the substance of psoas major in front of the lumbar transverse processes; lumbosacral trunk crossing the pelvic brim; sacral plexus on the anterior surface of piriformis in the pelvis behind the internal iliac vessels.

subdivisions.name: Lumbar plexus L1–L4
subdivisions.note: iliohypogastric, ilioinguinal, genitofemoral, lateral femoral cutaneous (L2–L3), femoral (L2–L4, posterior divisions), obturator (L2–L4, anterior divisions)

subdivisions.name: Lumbosacral trunk L4–L5
subdivisions.note: joins the sacral plexus

subdivisions.name: Sacral plexus L4–S4
subdivisions.note: superior gluteal (L4–S1), inferior gluteal (L5–S2), sciatic (L4–S3), posterior femoral cutaneous, pudendal (S2–S4)

pontine-nuclei.name: Pontine nuclei and transverse pontine fibers
pontine-nuclei.summary: The basis pontis is packed with pontine nuclei, the relay through which the cerebral cortex talks to the cerebellum. Corticopontine fibers from the frontal, parietal, temporal and occipital lobes descend in the crus cerebri and end here; the pontine neurons send their axons across the midline as the transverse pontine fibers into the contralateral middle cerebellar peduncle. Scattered among them run the corticospinal and corticobulbar bundles, which is why basis pontis lesions combine hemiparesis with ataxia.

anatomy.location: Ventral pons (basis pontis) on both sides of the midline, between the corticospinal bundles, from the pontomedullary junction to the pontomesencephalic junction; the transverse fibers form the bulk of the ventral pontine surface.

afferents.via: corticopontine fibers in the crus cerebri

pontine-nuclei.function: Cortico-ponto-cerebellar relay: transmits motor plans and sensory context from the cortex to the cerebellum for coordination of skilled movement and, through the crossed projection, gives the cerebellum its contralateral cortical connection.

bestView.label: basis pontis in front of the tegmentum

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: DWI and T2 through the pons

Scattered among them run the corticospinal and corticobulbar bundles, which is why basis pontis lesions combine hemiparesis with ataxia.
html.function: Cortico-ponto-cerebellar relay: transmits motor plans and sensory context from the cortex to the cerebellum for coordination of skilled movement and, through the crossed projection, gives the cerebellum its contralateral cortical connection.
html.anatomy.location: Ventral pons (basis pontis) on both sides of the midline, between the corticospinal bundles, from the pontomedullary junction to the pontomesencephalic junction; the transverse fibers form the bulk of the ventral pontine surface.
html.imaging.normalAppearance: The basis pontis is homogeneous white matter with slightly grayer punctate nuclei on T1; the transverse fibers give the ventral pons a striated look on high-resolution axial images. Central pontine myelinolysis spares the peripheral rim and the corticospinal bundles.
html.imaging.sequenceOfChoice: DWI and T2 through the pons

posterior-commissure.name: Posterior commissure
posterior-commissure.summary: The posterior commissure is a bundle of crossing fibers in the roof of the aqueduct at the junction of the third ventricle and the midbrain, beneath the pineal gland and above the superior colliculi. It connects the pretectal nuclei of the two sides and the nuclei of the posterior commissure, and it carries the crossed fibers of the pupillary light reflex and of the vertical gaze system, so it explains why each pupil constricts when the other is illuminated and why pineal region tumors that press on it cause the light-near dissociation and upgaze palsy of the dorsal midbrain (Parinaud) syndrome. With the anterior commissure it defines the AC-PC line of stereotactic space.

anatomy.location: Midline bundle in the dorsal wall of the aqueduct at its entry from the third ventricle, below the pineal recess and the habenular commissure, above the periaqueductal gray and the rostral interstitial nucleus of the medial longitudinal fasciculus, at the level of the superior colliculi.

afferents.from: Interstitial nucleus of Cajal and nucleus of the posterior commissure
Rostral interstitial nucleus of the MLF

efferents.to: Contralateral oculomotor and trochlear nuclei (vertical gaze)

posterior-commissure.function: Pretectal olivary nucleus neurons that receive retinal input project through the posterior commissure to the contralateral Edinger-Westphal nucleus as well as the ipsilateral one, giving the consensual light reflex; the interstitial nucleus of Cajal and the nucleus of the posterior commissure send fibers across it to coordinate the two eyes in vertical gaze and to relay upgaze commands from the rostral interstitial nucleus to the oculomotor nuclei, and lid-eye coordination uses the same route. Damage disconnects the pretectum from the oculomotor complex and interrupts upgaze and lid retraction control, producing Collier's sign and convergence-retraction nystagmus.

bestView.label: posterior commissure in the roof of the aqueduct beneath the pineal
crossing fibers above the superior colliculi

imaging.normalAppearance: A tiny dark bundle at the junction of the third ventricle and the aqueduct on midline sagittal T1 images, below the pineal gland and above the superior colliculi; the AC-PC line is drawn to its center.

pathology.pathology: Pineal region tumor with dorsal midbrain syndrome
pathology.finding: Germinoma, pineoblastoma or pineocytoma compressing the posterior commissure and the tectum with hydrocephalus; upgaze palsy, light-near dissociation and convergence-retraction nystagmus.
Medial thalamic hematoma extending down to the posterior commissure region with forced downgaze and small pupils.
Stretching of the posterior commissure by the dilated third ventricle and aqueduct producing a sunset sign in children and upgaze palsy in adults.

lesionEffects.mechanism: Interruption of crossing vertical gaze fibers from the rostral interstitial nucleus
Disconnection of the pretectal nuclei from the Edinger-Westphal nuclei

lesionEffects.deficit: Lid retraction (Collier sign) and convergence-retraction nystagmus
lesionEffects.mechanism: Loss of the commissural lid and convergence control

examination: Upward saccades and pursuit; try an optokinetic drum moving downward to elicit convergence-retraction nystagmus
Pupillary light and near responses
Eyelid position at rest and on downgaze
pearls: Parinaud syndrome is the posterior commissure under pressure: think pineal tumor, hydrocephalus or a top-of-the-basilar embolus
Light-near dissociation from a dorsal midbrain lesion has big pupils; Argyll Robertson pupils are small
The AC-PC line ends here, so a pineal mass that displaces the commissure also corrupts stereotactic coordinates

pitfalls: Isolated upgaze limitation in the elderly is common and benign; the full dorsal midbrain syndrome needs the pupils and the nystagmus

posterior-spinal-arteries.name: Posterior spinal arteries
posterior-spinal-arteries.summary: Two small arteries, one on each side, that descend on the posterolateral surface of the cord near the entry of the dorsal roots. They arise from the vertebral or posterior inferior cerebellar arteries, form a plexiform chain reinforced by posterior radicular arteries, and supply the posterior third of the cord: the posterior columns and the tips of the dorsal horns. Because the paired vessels interconnect richly, isolated posterior spinal artery infarcts are rare.

anatomy.location: Originate from the intracranial vertebral artery or from PICA, descend along the posterolateral sulcus of the medulla and spinal cord medial to the dorsal roots, and receive posterior radicular branches at many levels.

posterior-spinal-arteries.function: Supply the posterior white columns (gracile and cuneate fasciculi) and the posterior gray horns, that is, proprioception, vibration and fine touch pathways for the whole cord below the level.

bestView.label: posterolateral medulla at the origin of the posterior spinal arteries
posterior surface of the medulla and cervical cord

imaging.normalAppearance: Rarely resolved on routine MRI; seen on high-resolution axial T2 as tiny dots on the posterolateral surface of the cord. The territory is the posterior third of the cord on axial images.

pathology.finding: T2 hyperintensity and restricted diffusion confined to the posterior columns over one or more segments, with preserved motor function and pain sensation.
pathology.pitfalls: The pattern overlaps with subacute combined degeneration and tabes; the acute onset and diffusion restriction distinguish infarction

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: Axial and sagittal T2 with DWI

lesionEffects.deficit: Loss of vibration and proprioception below the level with sensory ataxia
lesionEffects.mechanism: Posterior columns

lesionEffects.deficit: Loss of segmental deep tendon reflexes
lesionEffects.mechanism: Dorsal horn and afferent limb of the reflex at the infarcted level

examination: Vibration at the malleoli and joint position sense at the toes
Romberg test
Compare pin-prick (should be preserved) with vibration (lost)
pearls: Posterior column loss with preserved pain and power after a vascular event points to the posterior spinal arteries
The rich posterior anastomotic chain explains why posterior cord infarcts are far rarer than anterior ones

pprf.name: Paramedian pontine reticular formation
pprf.summary: A cluster of burst neurons in the pontine reticular formation adjacent to the abducens nucleus that generates horizontal saccades. It receives commands from the contralateral frontal eye field and the ipsilateral superior colliculus and fires the abducens nucleus on its own side, so the eyes jump toward the side of the active PPRF. A unilateral lesion abolishes voluntary and reflex saccades toward the lesion, but because the vestibular pathways bypass it, the oculocephalic reflex can still drive the eyes there.

anatomy.location: Ventral and lateral to the abducens nucleus in the paramedian tegmentum of the caudal pons, extending rostrally toward the trochlear level.

pprf.function: Saccade generation in the horizontal plane; integrates cortical, collicular and cerebellar commands and feeds the abducens nucleus.

bestView.label: paramedian caudal pontine tegmentum anterior to the abducens nucleus

imaging.normalAppearance: Not resolved on routine MRI; localized to the paramedian tegmentum of the caudal pons. Lesions here produce the same imaging as abducens nuclear lesions: small paramedian tegmental spots on FLAIR or DWI.

pathology.finding: Small restricted-diffusion lesion in the paramedian tegmentum with ipsilateral saccadic gaze palsy.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: Thin FLAIR/DWI

lesionEffects.deficit: Loss of horizontal saccades toward the side of the lesion, with the eyes deviated away
lesionEffects.mechanism: Burst neurons for ipsilateral gaze

lesionEffects.deficit: Preserved vestibulo-ocular reflex toward the lesion
lesionEffects.mechanism: Vestibular input reaches the abducens nucleus directly

lesionEffects.deficit: Wrong-way gaze deviation compared with a hemispheric lesion
lesionEffects.mechanism: Pontine lesion: eyes look away from the lesion and toward the hemiparesis

examination: Voluntary saccades and pursuit to each side
Oculocephalic (doll's eye) maneuver to separate PPRF from nuclear lesions
Note the direction of resting gaze deviation relative to the hemiparesis
pearls: Hemispheric lesion: eyes look toward the lesion, away from the weak limbs. Pontine lesion: eyes look away from the lesion, toward the weak limbs
A gaze palsy overcome by head turning is supranuclear (PPRF); one that is not is nuclear (abducens)

precuneus.name: Precuneus
precuneus.summary: The precuneus is the medial surface of the parietal lobe, a quadrilateral area behind the paracentral lobule and in front of the parieto-occipital sulcus, above the posterior cingulate gyrus and the splenium. It is a hub of the default mode network with the posterior cingulate, active in self-referential thought, episodic memory retrieval, mental imagery and the sense of first-person perspective, and it is one of the first regions to lose metabolism and to accumulate amyloid in Alzheimer disease. It is supplied by the anterior cerebral artery through the pericallosal and parieto-occipital branches, and it is compressed by parasagittal and falcine tumors; bilateral disconnection contributes to the loss of consciousness in generalized seizures and anesthesia.

anatomy.location: Medial parietal cortex between the marginal branch of the cingulate sulcus in front, the parieto-occipital sulcus behind and the subparietal sulcus below, continuous over the superior margin with the superior parietal lobule.

efferents.to: Frontal eye field and premotor cortex

precuneus.function: The precuneus retrieves autobiographical memories and imagines scenes from a first-person point of view, integrating egocentric space with the self; together with the posterior cingulate it is the most metabolically active region of the resting brain and deactivates during attention-demanding tasks. Its dorsal part guides visually directed reaching and shifts of spatial attention with the superior parietal lobule, and its ventral part connects with the hippocampus through the cingulum and the retrosplenial cortex. Loss of its function produces impaired navigation, disturbed self-awareness and, when bilateral with the posterior cingulate, the amnesia and disorientation of early Alzheimer disease.

bestView.label: precuneus on the medial parietal surface in front of the parieto-occipital sulcus
medial parietal cortex above the splenium

imaging.normalAppearance: Medial parietal cortex on midline sagittal images between the marginal ramus of the cingulate sulcus and the deep parieto-occipital sulcus; the subparietal sulcus separates it from the posterior cingulate below.

pathology.finding: Hypometabolism of the precuneus and posterior cingulate on FDG-PET and early amyloid deposition, preceding lateral parietal and temporal changes.
Dural-based enhancing mass indenting the medial parietal cortex with sensory seizures or contralateral leg symptoms.
Symmetric vasogenic edema of the parieto-occipital cortex including the precuneus, with headache, seizures and visual symptoms.
pathology.timing: Resolves within days to weeks with control of blood pressure

lesionEffects.deficit: Impaired episodic memory retrieval and mental imagery
lesionEffects.mechanism: Loss of the precuneus-posterior cingulate retrieval hub
Disconnection of the precuneus and retrosplenial cortex from the hippocampus

lesionEffects.deficit: Contralateral leg sensory symptoms and seizures
lesionEffects.mechanism: Involvement of the adjacent paracentral lobule by a medial parietal lesion

examination: Route finding and describing familiar routes
Autobiographical memory for specific events
Sensation and strength of the contralateral leg
pearls: The precuneus and posterior cingulate go dark on FDG-PET years before Alzheimer dementia is diagnosed
Medial parietal lesions disturb the sense of self and of place more than any sensory modality
A parasagittal mass can be silent until the leg is affected or a sensory seizure occurs

pitfalls: Precuneal atrophy is hard to judge visually; rely on FDG-PET or quantitative volumetry when early Alzheimer disease is the question

presubiculum.name: Presubiculum
presubiculum.summary: The presubiculum is the strip of cortex between the subiculum and the entorhinal cortex on the medial surface of the parahippocampal gyrus, together with the parasubiculum forming the transition from the three-layered hippocampus to the six-layered cortex. It contains head-direction cells that signal which way the animal faces, receives the anterior thalamus and the retrosplenial cortex, and projects to the medial entorhinal cortex, so it supplies the compass that the entorhinal grid and the hippocampal place cells need. It is a small target but part of the medial temporal region injured in Alzheimer disease, in limbic encephalitis and in mesial temporal epilepsy, and it contributes to the spatial disorientation of those conditions.

anatomy.location: Narrow cortical zone on the upper medial surface of the parahippocampal gyrus, medial to the subiculum and lateral to the entorhinal cortex, running along the hippocampal formation from head to tail beside the hippocampal sulcus.

presubiculum.function: Presubicular neurons receive the anterodorsal thalamic nucleus, whose head-direction signal derives from vestibular input via the mammillary bodies, together with the retrosplenial cortex and the subiculum, and they project this heading information to the medial entorhinal cortex and back to the anterior thalamus; the result is a stable compass that anchors the grid cells and place cells of the hippocampal map to the visual landmarks of the environment. The presubiculum also carries hippocampal output back to the retrosplenial cortex and receives a strong visual input from the parahippocampal cortex. Its damage produces loss of directional sense with preserved recognition of places.

bestView.label: presubiculum between the subiculum and the entorhinal cortex
medial parahippocampal transition cortex along the hippocampus

imaging.normalAppearance: Not separable from the subiculum and entorhinal cortex on clinical MRI; it occupies the medial lip of the parahippocampal gyrus beside the hippocampal sulcus on coronal images, identified by subfield atlases.

pathology.finding: Medial temporal atrophy involving the parahippocampal transition cortex with the entorhinal cortex; tau spreads through this zone from entorhinal to hippocampal fields.
Bilateral medial temporal FLAIR hyperintensity and swelling including the parahippocampal cortex, with amnesia and disorientation.
Mammillary body and medial thalamic signal change disrupts the anterior thalamic input to the presubiculum, with loss of directional sense as part of the amnesia.

lesionEffects.deficit: Loss of directional sense and heading
lesionEffects.mechanism: Loss of the presubicular head-direction network
Disconnection of the retrosplenial-presubicular-entorhinal navigation circuit
Part of the entorhinal-hippocampal memory system

examination: Ask the patient to point toward home or toward a landmark from the clinic
Route learning and description of familiar routes
Delayed recall
pearls: The head-direction cells of the presubiculum are the brain's compass; the vestibular system feeds them through the mammillary bodies and anterior thalamus
Directional sense and place recognition are separable: retrosplenial-presubicular lesions lose the former
This transition cortex is the road along which Alzheimer tau travels from the entorhinal cortex into the hippocampus

pitfalls: Presubicular structures appear only in subfield atlases; a report that names them is describing atlas labels, not visible anatomy

pretectal-area.name: Pretectal area
pretectal-area.summary: A group of small nuclei at the junction of the midbrain and diencephalon, just in front of the superior colliculus and beside the posterior commissure. They are the central relay of the pupillary light reflex: each receives retinal fibers from both eyes via the optic tract and brachium of the superior colliculus and projects to both Edinger–Westphal nuclei, partly through the posterior commissure. This bilateral wiring is why light in one eye constricts both pupils and why a pretectal lesion produces light-near dissociation rather than blindness.

anatomy.location: Rostral to the superior colliculus at the level of the posterior commissure, lateral to the aqueduct's upper end, between the tectum and the pulvinar.

pretectal-area.function: Afferent center of the pupillary light reflex; contributes to the accommodation reflex and to vertical gaze through the posterior commissure and interstitial nucleus of Cajal.

bestView.label: junction of the tectum and thalamus at the posterior commissure
rostral to the superior colliculus beneath the pineal

imaging.normalAppearance: Not resolved on routine MRI; the region is the dorsal midbrain–diencephalic junction just below the pineal and behind the third ventricle.

pathology.finding: Pineal tumor, tectal glioma, hydrocephalus or infarct compressing or involving the posterior commissure and pretectum.
Imaging usually normal; the lesion is in the pretectal light-reflex fibers (classically neurosyphilis).

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: Sagittal and axial T2 of the pineal region; serology for syphilis when pupils dissociate

lesionEffects.deficit: Light-near dissociation: pupils react to near but not to light
lesionEffects.mechanism: Interruption of the light reflex arc while the near reflex reaches Edinger–Westphal by a more ventral route

lesionEffects.deficit: Bilateral mid-dilated pupils with poor light reaction plus up-gaze palsy
lesionEffects.mechanism: Pretectum and posterior commissure (Parinaud)

lesionEffects.deficit: Relative afferent pupillary defect is NOT produced
lesionEffects.mechanism: Lesions here are usually bilateral; RAPD needs an asymmetric afferent lesion in front of the pretectum

examination: Pupil reaction to light then to a near target
Up-gaze and convergence-retraction nystagmus
Swinging flashlight test to exclude an afferent (optic nerve) cause
pearls: Light-near dissociation localizes to the pretectum or the ciliary ganglion; up-gaze palsy alongside it makes it the dorsal midbrain
Argyll Robertson pupils are small and irregular; Adie pupils are large and slow

putamen.name: Putamen
putamen.summary: The largest and most lateral basal ganglion, a convex shell of gray matter lateral to the globus pallidus (together forming the lentiform nucleus) and separated from the insula by the external capsule, claustrum and extreme capsule. With the caudate it forms the striatum, and its part of the striatum is the motor one: it receives the sensorimotor cortex and dopamine from the substantia nigra and projects to the pallidum through the direct and indirect pathways. It is the first target of Parkinson disease dopamine loss (posterior putamen), the site of the lenticulostriate hypertensive hemorrhage, and a common site of lacunar infarcts and of toxic and metabolic injury.

anatomy.location: Lateral part of the lentiform nucleus, lateral to the external medullary lamina and globus pallidus, medial to the external capsule, claustrum and insula, and lateral to the internal capsule; connected to the caudate head anteriorly across the anterior limb.

putamen.function: Motor input stage of the basal ganglia: selects and scales movements through the direct (facilitatory) and indirect (inhibitory) pathways under dopaminergic modulation; motor habit learning.

bestView.label: putamen lateral to the globus pallidus and internal capsule
lentiform nucleus with the putamen lateral

imaging.normalAppearance: Gray matter lateral to the darker (iron-rich) globus pallidus on axial T2; loses its normal outline early in MCA stroke (obscured lentiform nucleus sign). Bilateral symmetric putaminal signal change points to toxic, metabolic, mitochondrial or prion disease; a putaminal rim of T2 hyperintensity with atrophy suggests multiple system atrophy.

pathology.finding: Hyperdense hematoma centered on the putamen, extending medially into the capsule or into the ventricle.
Small restriction in the putamen or adjacent capsule.
Putaminal atrophy with a lateral T2-hyperintense rim and hypointensity of the posterior putamen.
Bilateral putaminal necrosis or T2 change.
Obscuration of the lentiform nucleus outline within hours.

lesionEffects.deficit: Contralateral hemiparesis with a large hemorrhage
lesionEffects.mechanism: Extension into the internal capsule
Loss of dopaminergic input to the posterior putamen
Striatal lesions disrupting the indirect pathway

lesionEffects.mechanism: Toxic injury (methanol, CO, Wilson)

examination: Rest tremor, rigidity with cogwheeling, bradykinesia with decrement on finger tapping
Observe posture and gait, arm swing
Look for dystonic posturing and chorea

pyramid.name: Medullary pyramid and pyramidal decussation
pyramid.summary: The pyramids are the two longitudinal ridges on the ventral medulla, one on each side of the anterior median fissure, each carrying about a million corticospinal axons from the ipsilateral motor cortex. At the lower end of the medulla most of these fibers cross in the pyramidal decussation to form the lateral corticospinal tract; the minority that stay uncrossed form the anterior corticospinal tract. Because the pyramid is fed by the anterior spinal artery and paramedian vertebral perforators, it is the motor component of the medial medullary syndrome.

anatomy.location: Ventral surface of the medulla from the pontomedullary junction to the cervicomedullary junction, lateral to the anterior median fissure and medial to the preolivary sulcus from which the hypoglossal rootlets emerge; the decussation lies at the level of the foramen magnum.

pyramid.function: Conducts the corticospinal tract, the main pathway for voluntary skilled movement of the contralateral limbs, and marks the point where that control crosses the midline.

html.summary: The pyramids are the two longitudinal ridges on the ventral medulla, one on each side of the anterior median fissure, each carrying about a million corticospinal axons from the ipsilateral motor cortex. At the lower end of the medulla most of these fibers cross in the pyramidal decussation to form the lateral corticospinal tract; the minority that stay uncrossed form the anterior corticospinal tract. Because the pyramid is fed by the anterior spinal artery and paramedian vertebral perforators, it is the motor component of the medial medullary syndrome.

raphe-dorsal.name: Dorsal raphe nucleus
raphe-dorsal.summary: The dorsal raphe nucleus is the largest serotonergic nucleus of the brain, a midline column in the ventral periaqueductal gray of the caudal midbrain and rostral pons, beneath the aqueduct and between the trochlear nuclei and the medial longitudinal fasciculi. Its neurons send serotonin to the cortex, striatum, thalamus, amygdala and hippocampus and regulate mood, anxiety, impulsivity, appetite, sleep and pain, forming the anatomical target of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors. It fires during waking and falls silent in REM sleep, it inhibits the trigeminovascular system in migraine, and it degenerates early in Parkinson disease, contributing to the depression and sleep disturbance that precede the motor signs.

anatomy.location: Ventral part of the periaqueductal gray in the midline of the caudal midbrain and upper pons, extending from the level of the oculomotor nucleus to the locus coeruleus, between the two medial longitudinal fasciculi and above the decussation of the superior cerebellar peduncles.

afferents.via: medial forebrain bundle and local fibers

efferents.to: Cerebral cortex, striatum, thalamus, amygdala and hippocampus
Substantia nigra and ventral tegmental area
Spinal trigeminal nucleus and dorsal horn

raphe-dorsal.function: Dorsal raphe serotonergic neurons project rostrally through the medial forebrain bundle to the whole forebrain, where serotonin acting through many receptor subtypes modulates cortical excitability, the emotional responses of the amygdala, the reward computations of the striatum and the stress reactivity of the hippocampus; they promote patience and behavioral inhibition, suppress feeding and pain, and their tonic activity is high in waking and absent in REM sleep, permitting the REM-on neurons of the pons to fire. The nucleus receives the prefrontal cortex, the lateral habenula, the hypothalamus and the locus coeruleus, and its neurons express autoreceptors whose desensitization underlies the delayed onset of antidepressant action. Descending projections modulate the trigeminal nucleus and dorsal horn.

bestView.label: dorsal raphe nucleus in the ventral periaqueductal gray

Loss of the wake-active serotonergic tone that gates REM sleep

raphe-linear-caudal-rostral.name: Caudal-rostral linear raphe nucleus complex
raphe-linear-caudal-rostral.summary: The caudal and rostral linear raphe nuclei form a slender midline column in the midbrain tegmentum, running from just behind the interpeduncular fossa up toward the posterior hypothalamus between the two red nuclei. They are the most rostral of the raphe nuclei and are unusual in being chemically mixed: serotonergic neurons of the B8 group are interleaved with dopaminergic neurons that belong to the same continuum as the ventral tegmental area, so the column contributes to both the serotonergic and the mesolimbic ascending systems. Its projections reach the ventral striatum, the amygdala, the septum and the interpeduncular nucleus, and it is of interest in reward, motivation and the sleep-wake control of REM. Like all the raphe nuclei it is invisible on clinical imaging and is known in living humans only from 7 T templates.

anatomy.location: Midline of the midbrain tegmentum between the medial longitudinal fasciculi and above the interpeduncular nucleus, extending from the level of the trochlear nucleus caudally to the posterior hypothalamic border rostrally, with the red nuclei on either side and the ventral tegmental area lying just ventrolateral. The caudal linear nucleus lies below and behind, the rostral linear nucleus above and in front, and the two are continuous. Thalamoperforating and posterior communicating perforators supply the column, which is why paramedian midbrain infarcts involve it together with the red nucleus and the oculomotor fascicles.

raphe-linear-caudal-rostral.function: The linear raphe complex sends serotonergic and dopaminergic fibers rostrally through the medial forebrain bundle to the nucleus accumbens, olfactory tubercle, amygdala, septum and prefrontal cortex, and it projects heavily to the interpeduncular nucleus, which links it to the habenular system that signals disappointment and aversive outcomes. Its dopaminergic neurons form part of the A10 group and are recruited by reward prediction and by novelty; its serotonergic neurons modulate the same targets with an opposing, patience-promoting influence, so the column is a place where two ascending modulatory systems are physically intermingled. Descending and local projections reach the dorsal raphe, the ventral tegmental area and the pontine reticular formation. Activity is highest in waking, falls in non-REM sleep and is lowest in REM, a pattern shared with the other serotonergic raphe nuclei and required for the orderly release of REM sleep. Because it is small and midline, both linear nuclei are usually damaged together or not at all.

imaging.normalAppearance: Not separable from the surrounding paramedian tegmentum on clinical MRI; the column occupies the midline strip between the red nuclei on axial images at the level of the oculomotor nucleus.

pathology.finding: Restricted diffusion in the midline tegmentum, often bilateral from a single artery of Percheron, with hypersomnolence, vertical gaze palsy and apathy.

lesionEffects.mechanism: Loss of mixed serotonergic and dopaminergic drive to the ventral striatum
Damage to the paramedian ascending arousal system
Loss of the wake-active serotonergic tone that gates REM sleep

PUBLIC EDITION - LOCATION MARKER: the 7 T probabilistic outline of this nucleus may not be redistributed, so the openly shareable build of the atlas shows a landmark-anchored ellipsoid instead: a 111 mm3 ellipsoid -- 110.7 mm3 for the whole midline complex in the volume table of Singh et al. (2021) -- centered on the midline of the midbrain tegmentum at the posterior border of the red nuclei, ventral to the periaqueductal grey, and clipped to the brainstem.
