raphe-magnus.name: Raphe magnus nucleus
raphe-magnus.summary: The raphe magnus nucleus is the serotonergic midline nucleus of the rostral medulla and the output stage of the descending pain control system. Together with the surrounding gigantocellular and paragigantocellular cells it forms the rostral ventromedial medulla, the relay through which the periaqueductal gray suppresses or facilitates transmission in the spinal and trigeminal dorsal horns. Opioid analgesia, stimulation-produced analgesia and the analgesia of stress all work through this link, and the same neurons can facilitate rather than inhibit nociception, which is why the system is implicated in the maintenance of chronic pain and in opioid-induced hyperalgesia. It is a midline structure, so it is nearly always affected on both sides at once.

anatomy.location: Midline of the rostral medulla in front of the fourth ventricle floor and behind the pyramids, at and just below the pontomedullary junction, between the two medial lemnisci and above the raphe obscurus and pallidus. The nucleus ambiguus and the ventrolateral medulla lie laterally, and the gigantocellular reticular nucleus surrounds it. Median perforating branches of the vertebral and basilar arteries supply it, which links it to medial medullary rather than lateral medullary infarction.

efferents.to: Spinal dorsal horn laminae I, II and V
efferents.via: raphespinal fibers in the dorsolateral funiculus

raphe-magnus.function: Serotonergic and enkephalinergic neurons of the raphe magnus project down the dorsolateral funiculus to laminae I, II and V of the spinal dorsal horn and to the spinal trigeminal nucleus, where they suppress the transmission of nociceptive signals from primary afferents to projection neurons. The pathway is driven by the periaqueductal gray, which itself is engaged by the hypothalamus, the amygdala and the anterior cingulate cortex, so attention, expectation and fear can change how much pain reaches consciousness; placebo analgesia and the relief produced by systemic opioids both require this descending arm. Two functional classes of neuron have been described, one that pauses just before a nocifensive reflex and facilitates pain and one that fires before it and inhibits, and a shift toward facilitation is thought to help maintain chronic and neuropathic pain states. The nucleus also modulates the trigeminovascular system in migraine and contributes serotonergic tone to motor neurons and to the respiratory network.

imaging.normalAppearance: Not visible on clinical MRI; the midline of the rostral medulla in front of the fourth ventricle is the landmark, and functional imaging studies localize descending pain modulation to this region.

pathology.finding: Structural imaging is normal; functional imaging shows altered engagement of the periaqueductal gray and rostral ventromedial medulla.

lesionEffects.deficit: Loss of descending pain inhibition with widespread hyperalgesia
lesionEffects.mechanism: Interruption of the serotonergic projection to the dorsal horn
Loss of the periaqueductal-ventromedial medullary relay
Loss of medullary serotonergic tone

examination: Ask whether pain is widespread and disproportionate to the injury
Test conditioned pain modulation: does a distant painful stimulus reduce local pain
Review opioid dose escalation with worsening pain, the signature of hyperalgesia
pearls: Pain is not simply received; the medulla decides how much of it gets through

raphe-median.name: Median raphe nucleus
raphe-median.summary: The median raphe nucleus is the serotonergic nucleus of the midline pontine tegmentum, below and behind the dorsal raphe, between the medial longitudinal fasciculi and the reticular formation, with the superior central nucleus of Bechterew. Its neurons project mainly to the hippocampus, the septum, the hypothalamus and the medial cortex, where serotonin regulates hippocampal theta rhythm, memory consolidation, anxiety and stress resilience, and it acts as a brake on the dorsal raphe and the amygdala. It is part of the pontine sleep circuitry and contributes to the serotonergic modulation of breathing and of the cardiovascular reflexes, and its damage in pontine strokes and in neurodegeneration adds anxiety, memory impairment and sleep disturbance to the classical signs.

anatomy.location: Midline of the rostral pontine tegmentum in the paramedian reticular formation, below the dorsal raphe and the aqueduct-fourth ventricle junction, above the pontine nuclei and the basis pontis, between the medial longitudinal fasciculi and lateral to the midline seam.

raphe-median.function: Median raphe serotonergic neurons reach the hippocampus and septal area through the medial forebrain bundle and the fornix and desynchronize hippocampal theta, tuning memory encoding and acting as a resilience system that damps the response to stress and fear; they inhibit the amygdala and the dorsal raphe, which are more anxiogenic, and project to the suprachiasmatic nucleus to modulate circadian entrainment. Together with the medullary raphe they modulate the respiratory chemoreflex and sympathetic tone, and their activity across the sleep-wake cycle mirrors the dorsal raphe. The nucleus receives the prefrontal cortex, the lateral habenula and the hypothalamus.

imaging.normalAppearance: The midline of the rostral pontine tegmentum on axial images, in front of the fourth ventricle and behind the basis pontis; not resolved as a discrete nucleus.

pathology.finding: Restricted diffusion in the paramedian pontine tegmentum with gaze palsy, internuclear ophthalmoplegia and often mood and sleep change.

pathology.pathology: Multiple system atrophy or Parkinson disease (functional)

examination: Anxiety and mood assessment in pontine lesions

raphe-nuclei.name: Raphe nuclei
raphe-nuclei.summary: The raphe nuclei are a chain of serotonergic cell groups in the midline of the brainstem from the caudal medulla to the rostral midbrain. The rostral group, the dorsal and median raphe nuclei of the midbrain and rostral pons, sends serotonin to the entire forebrain and regulates mood, sleep, appetite, aggression and the sensitivity to pain, and is the target of antidepressant and migraine drugs; the caudal group, the raphe magnus, obscurus and pallidus of the medulla, projects to the spinal cord to inhibit pain transmission in the dorsal horn and to facilitate motor neurons, breathing and thermoregulation. Migraine, depression, sudden infant death and the serotonin syndrome all involve raphe circuitry.

anatomy.location: Midline of the brainstem tegmentum from the medullary decussation to the midbrain periaqueductal gray: the nucleus raphe magnus at the level of the facial nucleus, the dorsal raphe in the ventral periaqueductal gray, the median raphe in the rostral pontine tegmentum, with smaller groups (obscurus, pallidus, pontis) between.

afferents.note: to the raphe magnus for analgesia

efferents.to: Cerebral cortex, hippocampus, striatum, thalamus, hypothalamus
efferents.via: medial forebrain bundle (dorsal and median raphe)

efferents.to: Spinal motor neurons and intermediolateral column

raphe-nuclei.function: Serotonin released from the rostral raphe into the cortex, hippocampus, striatum, thalamus and hypothalamus modulates mood and anxiety, promotes satiety, sets the sleep–wake cycle (the raphe fires during waking, slows in slow-wave sleep and stops in REM), constrains impulsive aggression and modulates cortical vasomotor tone in migraine. The nucleus raphe magnus, driven by the periaqueductal gray, sends serotonergic and enkephalinergic fibers down the dorsolateral funiculus to the dorsal horn, where they inhibit spinothalamic neurons, the basis of stimulation-produced and opioid analgesia. The caudal raphe also facilitates respiratory chemosensitivity, motor neuron excitability and heat production.

imaging.normalAppearance: The raphe is the midline seam of the tegmentum and is not visible as a distinct structure; the dorsal raphe lies beneath the aqueduct in the ventral periaqueductal gray and the raphe magnus in the midline of the caudal pons.

pathology.finding: Symmetric central pontine T2 hyperintensity sparing the periphery and the corticospinal tracts after rapid sodium correction, involving the raphe and crossing fibers.

raphe-obscurus.name: Raphe obscurus nucleus
raphe-obscurus.summary: The raphe obscurus is a serotonergic midline nucleus of the caudal medulla, lying between the hypoglossal nuclei and the inferior olives and extending down toward the cervical cord. Its neurons are central chemoreceptors: they are directly sensitive to carbon dioxide and to the resulting fall in pH, and they excite the respiratory rhythm generator and the motor neurons of the airway and the diaphragm, so the nucleus is part of the system that keeps ventilation matched to metabolism and that arouses a sleeping person when carbon dioxide rises. It also supplies serotonin to the motor neurons of the ventral horn and the cranial motor nuclei, where it sets their background excitability. Abnormalities of medullary serotonergic nuclei including this one have been reported in the sudden infant death syndrome.

raphe-pallidus.name: Raphe pallidus nucleus
raphe-pallidus.summary: The raphe pallidus is the most ventral of the midline serotonergic nuclei, a thin sheet lying just behind the pyramids in the rostral and middle medulla. It is the sympathetic premotor nucleus for thermoregulation: neurons here receive the hypothalamic command for heat production and relay it to the sympathetic preganglionic neurons of the thoracic cord that drive brown adipose tissue, cutaneous vasoconstriction, shivering and the tachycardia of a febrile response. The pathway from the preoptic hypothalamus through the raphe pallidus is the final common route by which fever, cold defense and psychological stress raise body temperature, which is why it is invoked in explanations of stress-induced hyperthermia and of the autonomic storms seen after brain injury.

anatomy.location: Midline of the medulla immediately dorsal to the pyramids and ventral to the raphe magnus, from the pontomedullary junction down to the middle of the medulla, spreading a little laterally over the pyramidal surface. Its blood supply is from median perforators of the vertebral and anterior spinal arteries, the same vessels that serve the pyramids, so a medial medullary infarct can include it.

efferents.to: Intermediolateral cell column of the thoracic cord

raphe-pallidus.function: Sympathetic premotor neurons of the raphe pallidus receive a disynaptic command from the median preoptic and dorsomedial hypothalamus that carries both the thermoregulatory set point and the prostaglandin-mediated signal of fever, and they project directly to the intermediolateral cell column of the thoracic spinal cord. Their firing raises sympathetic outflow to brown adipose tissue, producing non-shivering thermogenesis, constricts cutaneous vessels to conserve heat, recruits shivering through connections with somatic motor pathways and accelerates the heart. The same neurons are engaged by psychological stress, producing the rise in core temperature and heart rate that accompanies acute anxiety, and by inflammatory signals reaching the brain through prostaglandin E2. Serotonergic and glutamatergic subpopulations are intermingled, and the descending projection also modulates spinal nociception in parallel with the raphe magnus. Cooling the body, blocking prostaglandin synthesis or interrupting this pathway all reduce fever by acting at successive points along the same chain.

raphe-paramedian.name: Paramedian raphe nucleus
raphe-paramedian.summary: The paramedian raphe nucleus is a serotonergic group lying just off the midline of the pontine tegmentum, immediately lateral to the median raphe nucleus with which it is usually considered together as the B8 cell group. Its distinguishing feature is its output to the hippocampus and the septum: through the fornix and the cingulum it supplies the septohippocampal system with serotonin, and by doing so it desynchronizes the hippocampal theta rhythm. Where the median raphe suppresses theta, the paramedian group contributes to the same control, so this small nucleus is part of the machinery that decides whether the hippocampus is in an exploratory, theta-dominated state or a quiet one. It is also part of the ascending serotonergic system that regulates mood, anxiety and sleep.

anatomy.location: Paramedian pontine tegmentum immediately lateral to the midline raphe at the level of the rostral pons, between the median raphe nucleus medially and the pontine reticular nucleus laterally, ventral to the medial longitudinal fasciculus and dorsal to the pontine base. It extends from the isthmus down toward the level of the abducens nucleus. Paramedian perforating branches of the basilar artery supply it, so it is caught in the same paramedian pontine infarcts that produce pure motor hemiparesis from damage to the pontine base a few millimeters in front of it.

raphe-paramedian.function: The paramedian raphe sends serotonergic axons rostrally through the medial forebrain bundle to the medial septum, the hippocampus, the interpeduncular nucleus and the medial prefrontal cortex, and it receives the prefrontal cortex, the lateral habenula and the hypothalamus. Its hippocampal projection acts on the septohippocampal pacemaker: increased serotonergic tone suppresses the theta rhythm and shifts the hippocampus toward a desynchronized state, while a fall in tone allows theta to emerge during exploration and REM sleep. This gives the nucleus a role in the switching between encoding and consolidation states and, through the same targets, in anxiety and behavioral inhibition; drugs that raise synaptic serotonin change hippocampal rhythmicity through this route. Like the other serotonergic nuclei it is wake-active and REM-off, so its silence at REM onset helps permit the cholinergic activation of dreaming. Descending fibers reach the pontine and medullary reticular formation and modulate motor tone and pain transmission.

red-nucleus.name: Red nucleus
red-nucleus.summary: A large, iron-rich, ovoid nucleus in the midbrain tegmentum at the level of the superior colliculus, pink in fresh specimens and dark on T2-weighted MRI. It receives the crossed outflow of the cerebellar dentate and interposed nuclei through the superior cerebellar peduncle and input from the motor cortex, and it sends the rubrospinal tract (crossed, to flexor motor neurons) and the central tegmental tract (uncrossed, to the inferior olive). The oculomotor fascicles pass straight through it, which is why red nucleus lesions come packaged with a third nerve palsy as the Claude and Benedikt syndromes.

reticular-formation-isthmic.name: Isthmic reticular formation
reticular-formation-isthmic.summary: The isthmic reticular formation occupies the narrow waist between the midbrain and the pons, the isthmus rhombencephali, where the tegmentum is squeezed between the superior cerebellar peduncles as they turn medially to decussate. It is a transition zone rather than a nucleus with a sharp border: rostrally it becomes the mesencephalic reticular formation, caudally the oral pontine reticular nucleus, and embedded in it are the cholinergic pedunculopontine and laterodorsal tegmental cell groups. Functionally it is a critical link of the ascending arousal system, and its position explains why small lesions at the mesopontine junction produce coma out of proportion to their size. It also contributes premotor neurons to vertical gaze and to the startle response.

The trochlear nucleus and the anterior medullary velum lie at its dorsal margin. Blood supply is from the superior cerebellar artery and short circumferential branches of the upper basilar artery.

reticular-formation-isthmic.function: The isthmic reticular formation is a relay of the ascending arousal system. Its glutamatergic and cholinergic neurons project rostrally to the intralaminar and reticular nuclei of the thalamus, to the basal forebrain and to the hypothalamus, keeping the thalamocortical system in the desynchronized state that permits waking consciousness; this is the narrowest part of that pathway, and it is here that bilateral tegmental damage abolishes arousal while the cortex remains intact. Descending projections join the pontine reticular formation and the reticulospinal system, contributing to postural tone, to the acoustic startle reflex and to autonomic adjustment. Locally the isthmus houses premotor neurons for vertical and torsional eye movements that communicate with the trochlear and oculomotor nuclei and with the rostral interstitial nucleus of the medial longitudinal fasciculus. It receives the prefrontal and cingulate cortex, the hypothalamus, the periaqueductal gray, the superior colliculus and the spinoreticular fibers that carry nociceptive information, so pain and threat can raise arousal directly.

Descending projections join the pontine reticular formation and the reticulospinal system, contributing to postural tone, to the acoustic startle reflex and to autonomic adjustment. Locally the isthmus houses premotor neurons for vertical and torsional eye movements that communicate with the trochlear and oculomotor nuclei and with the rostral interstitial nucleus of the medial longitudinal fasciculus. It receives the prefrontal and cingulate cortex, the hypothalamus, the periaqueductal gray, the superior colliculus and the spinoreticular fibers that carry nociceptive information, so pain and threat can raise arousal directly.
html.anatomy.location: Tegmentum of the isthmus, between the caudal border of the inferior colliculus above and the rostral pons below, bounded laterally by the superior cerebellar peduncle and the lateral lemniscus, dorsally by the periaqueductal gray as it becomes the central gray of the pons, and ventrally by the decussation of the superior cerebellar peduncles and the medial lemniscus. The trochlear nucleus and the anterior medullary velum lie at its dorsal margin. Blood supply is from the superior cerebellar artery and short circumferential branches of the upper basilar artery.
html.imaging.normalAppearance: On sagittal T1 the isthmus is the narrowing between the midbrain and the bulging pons, behind the interpeduncular cistern and in front of the anterior medullary velum; the reticular formation itself is not distinguishable from surrounding tegmental gray at clinical field strength.

reticular-formation-medullary-inferior.name: Inferior medullary reticular formation
reticular-formation-medullary-inferior.summary: The inferior medullary reticular formation is the caudal half of the medullary reticular core, the field that lies between the inferior olive in front and the dorsal nuclei behind and that runs down to become continuous with the reticular gray of the cervical cord. Its medial, large-celled part gives rise to the lateral reticulospinal tract, which inhibits extensor tone and shapes posture and locomotion, while its lateral, small-celled part organizes the bulbar motor nuclei. It also contains the ventromedial region through which REM sleep atonia is imposed on spinal motor neurons, and it holds the caudal parts of the respiratory and cardiovascular networks, so lesions here mix disorders of posture, breathing and blood pressure. The 7 T atlas separates a medial and a lateral part, offered here as hidden subdivisions.

anatomy.location: Central tegmentum of the caudal medulla from about the level of the obex down to the cervicomedullary junction, between the inferior olivary nucleus and pyramid in front and the hypoglossal, vagal and gracile and cuneate nuclei behind, with the spinal trigeminal complex laterally and the midline raphe medially. It is continuous rostrally with the superior medullary reticular formation and caudally with the intermediate gray of the upper cervical cord. Median and lateral perforating branches of the vertebral artery and the posterior inferior cerebellar artery supply it.

subdivisions.name: Medial part (iMRtm)
subdivisions.note: Large-celled column giving rise to the lateral reticulospinal tract and to the REM atonia pathway

subdivisions.name: Lateral part (iMRtl)
subdivisions.note: Small-celled premotor field for the bulbar motor nuclei and the reflexes of the airway

afferents.from: Cerebellar fastigial nucleus and vestibular nuclei

reticular-formation-medullary-inferior.function: The medial column of large cells here gives rise to the lateral reticulospinal tract, which descends in the lateral funiculus and inhibits extensor motor neurons and gamma motor neurons; with the medial reticulospinal tract from the pons it forms the pair of systems whose imbalance explains decerebrate and decorticate posturing and much of the spasticity that follows a hemispheric lesion, since the corticoreticular fibers that drive it run in the internal capsule and corona radiata. The ventromedial part receives the pontine subcoeruleus and contains the glycinergic and GABAergic premotor neurons that produce REM sleep atonia and, when abnormally recruited in waking, cataplexy. Lateral small-celled neurons coordinate the pharyngeal, laryngeal and tongue muscles for swallowing, coughing and vomiting. Ascending collaterals contribute to arousal, and spinoreticular afferents carrying diffuse nociceptive information terminate throughout, giving this region a role in the affective response to pain and in the reflex cardiovascular and respiratory answer to injury.

reticular-formation-medullary-superior.name: Superior medullary reticular formation
reticular-formation-medullary-superior.summary: The superior medullary reticular formation is the rostral half of the medullary reticular core, occupying the tegmentum from the pontomedullary junction down to about the level of the obex. It contains the gigantocellular nucleus and, in its ventrolateral corner, the rostral ventrolateral medulla, the cluster of sympathetic premotor neurons that sets resting arterial pressure. This is where the baroreflex is completed, where the respiratory rhythm is generated in the pre-Bötzinger complex a little more laterally, and where the descending pain modulatory pathway from the periaqueductal gray is relayed to the spinal cord alongside the raphe magnus. Its ascending projections contribute to arousal and its descending ones to postural tone, so a lesion here can produce coma, hemodynamic collapse and abnormal breathing at once. The 7 T atlas separates a medial and a lateral part.

anatomy.location: Tegmentum of the rostral medulla from the pontomedullary junction to about the obex, dorsal to the inferior olivary nucleus and the pyramid, ventral to the vagal and hypoglossal nuclear column, lateral to the midline raphe and medial to the spinal trigeminal complex. The nucleus ambiguus and the rostral ventrolateral medulla lie in its ventrolateral part. It is supplied by median and lateral perforators of the vertebral artery, by the anterior spinal artery and by the posterior inferior cerebellar artery, so both medial and lateral medullary syndromes encroach on it.

subdivisions.name: Medial part (sMRtm)
subdivisions.note: Gigantocellular column giving rise to reticulospinal fibers and to ascending arousal collaterals

subdivisions.name: Lateral part (sMRtl)
subdivisions.note: Ventrolateral field holding the sympathetic premotor neurons and the ventral respiratory column

reticular-formation-medullary-superior.function: Sympathetic premotor neurons of the rostral ventrolateral medulla project directly to the intermediolateral cell column and maintain the tonic vasoconstrictor drive that produces resting blood pressure; they are inhibited through the caudal ventrolateral medulla by baroreceptor signals arriving in the nucleus of the solitary tract, which is the whole of the baroreflex arc. Neighboring neurons of the ventral respiratory column generate the inspiratory rhythm and pattern it with the pontine parabrachial nuclei. Gigantocellular neurons give rise to reticulospinal fibers that modulate axial and limb tone and relay corticoreticular commands for posture and locomotion, and the same territory relays descending analgesia from the periaqueductal gray to the dorsal horn. Ascending fibers reach the thalamus, hypothalamus and basal forebrain and contribute to the reticular activating system, while spinoreticular and trigeminoreticular afferents make pain and visceral distress raise arousal, blood pressure and ventilation together. This convergence is why the rostral medulla is the most autonomically dangerous few cubic centimeters in the nervous system.

imaging.normalAppearance: Homogeneous tegmental gray between the olive and the fourth ventricle floor on axial T2 of the upper medulla; the functional subregions are not separable at clinical field strength.

Interruption of the ascending reticular projection

reticular-formation-mesencephalic.name: Mesencephalic reticular formation
reticular-formation-mesencephalic.summary: The mesencephalic reticular formation is the diffuse core of the midbrain tegmentum, lying between the periaqueductal gray behind, the red nucleus and substantia nigra in front and the medial lemniscus laterally. It is the rostral end of the ascending reticular activating system, the point at which brainstem arousal signals hand over to the thalamus, the hypothalamus and the basal forebrain, and lesions here cause coma more reliably than lesions anywhere else in the brainstem. Embedded within it are the premotor structures for vertical gaze, the interstitial nucleus of Cajal and the rostral interstitial nucleus of the medial longitudinal fasciculus, so the same region controls upward and downward saccades, ocular torsion and head-eye coordination. The 7 T atlas divides it into anterior, dorsal and lateral parts, which the atlas offers as hidden subdivisions of this structure.

anatomy.location: Central tegmentum of the midbrain from the level of the superior colliculus to the isthmus, bounded dorsally by the periaqueductal gray, ventrally by the red nucleus and the substantia nigra, medially by the midline raphe and the medial longitudinal fasciculus and laterally by the medial lemniscus and the spinothalamic tract. The oculomotor and trochlear nuclei and their fascicles run through it, as do the superior cerebellar peduncle fibers on their way to the red nucleus and thalamus. Perfusion comes from paramedian midbrain perforators of the basilar tip and posterior cerebral arteries and from short circumferential branches.

subdivisions.name: Lateral part (mRtl)

reticular-formation-mesencephalic.function: This region is where arousal is generated and gaze is composed. Glutamatergic and cholinergic reticular neurons project to the intralaminar, midline and reticular nuclei of the thalamus and to the basal forebrain and posterior hypothalamus, and their tonic firing keeps the cortex desynchronized and responsive; the projection is bilateral, so unilateral damage rarely causes coma while bilateral paramedian damage does. Within the same territory the rostral interstitial nucleus of the medial longitudinal fasciculus generates vertical and torsional saccades and the interstitial nucleus of Cajal holds vertical gaze position and coordinates eye and head torsion through the posterior commissure, so lesions here produce upgaze or downgaze palsy, skew deviation and ocular tilt reactions. Descending fibers join the reticulospinal and tectospinal systems to orient the head, and reciprocal connections with the superior colliculus, the frontal eye field, the cerebellum and the periaqueductal gray tie orienting, arousal and defensive behavior together. Spinoreticular and trigeminoreticular afferents let pain wake the brain.

reticular-formation-pontine.name: Pontine reticular nucleus, oral and caudal parts
reticular-formation-pontine.summary: The oral and caudal pontine reticular nuclei form the large medial reticular column of the pons, the region traditionally called the paramedian pontine reticular formation. It does four things that matter at the bedside: it generates horizontal saccades and drives the abducens nucleus for conjugate gaze to its own side, it is the obligatory relay of the acoustic startle reflex, it supplies the medial reticulospinal tract that sets axial and antigravity tone, and it is the effector arm of the REM atonia circuit. Because it also carries the ascending arousal projection through the upper pons, destructive lesions here produce coma, ipsilateral gaze palsy and, when the ventral pons is spared, the locked-in state.

anatomy.location: Medial tegmentum of the pons on both sides of the midline raphe, from the isthmus to the pontomedullary junction. The oral part occupies the rostral half around and above the level of the trigeminal motor nucleus; the caudal part lies below it, next to the abducens nucleus and the genu of the facial nerve. The medial longitudinal fasciculus and the tectospinal tract run along its medial edge, the medial lemniscus lies ventrally and the transverse pontine fibers and corticospinal tract are in front. Paramedian perforating branches of the basilar artery supply it, so its lesions accompany basilar branch occlusion and pontine hemorrhage.

afferents.from: Frontal eye field and superior colliculus
Cerebellar fastigial nucleus and vestibular nuclei

efferents.via: excitatory burst neuron projection for horizontal saccades

reticular-formation-pontine.function: Excitatory burst neurons in the paramedian pontine reticular formation fire a high-frequency burst immediately before every ipsilateral horizontal saccade and drive the abducens nucleus, whose motor neurons move the ipsilateral lateral rectus while its interneurons cross in the medial longitudinal fasciculus to the contralateral medial rectus subnucleus; omnipause neurons in the midline raphe hold the bursters silent between saccades. A lesion therefore produces an ipsilateral conjugate gaze palsy that, unlike a frontal lesion, cannot be overcome by the oculocephalic maneuver. The caudal part contains giant reticular neurons that relay the acoustic startle response from the cochlear nuclei to the spinal cord within a few synapses and that give rise to the medial reticulospinal tract, which facilitates extensor and axial muscles; loss of this drive contributes to the decerebrate posture. During REM sleep the same region, driven by the subcoeruleus and the cholinergic tegmental nuclei, produces rapid eye movements and, through the ventromedial medulla, muscle atonia. Ascending collaterals contribute to the reticular activating system.

html.function: Excitatory burst neurons in the paramedian pontine reticular formation fire a high-frequency burst immediately before every ipsilateral horizontal saccade and drive the abducens nucleus, whose motor neurons move the ipsilateral lateral rectus while its interneurons cross in the medial longitudinal fasciculus to the contralateral medial rectus subnucleus; omnipause neurons in the midline raphe hold the bursters silent between saccades. A lesion therefore produces an ipsilateral conjugate gaze palsy that, unlike a frontal lesion, cannot be overcome by the oculocephalic maneuver. The caudal part contains giant reticular neurons that relay the acoustic startle response from the cochlear nuclei to the spinal cord within a few synapses and that give rise to the medial reticulospinal tract, which facilitates extensor and axial muscles; loss of this drive contributes to the decerebrate posture. During REM sleep the same region, driven by the subcoeruleus and the cholinergic tegmental nuclei, produces rapid eye movements and, through the ventromedial medulla, muscle atonia. Ascending collaterals contribute to the reticular activating system.
html.anatomy.location: Medial tegmentum of the pons on both sides of the midline raphe, from the isthmus to the pontomedullary junction. The oral part occupies the rostral half around and above the level of the trigeminal motor nucleus; the caudal part lies below it, next to the abducens nucleus and the genu of the facial nerve. The medial longitudinal fasciculus and the tectospinal tract run along its medial edge, the medial lemniscus lies ventrally and the transverse pontine fibers and corticospinal tract are in front. Paramedian perforating branches of the basilar artery supply it, so its lesions accompany basilar branch occlusion and pontine hemorrhage.
html.imaging.normalAppearance: The pontine tegmentum lies behind the transverse pontine fibers and in front of the fourth ventricle and is homogeneous on clinical T1 and T2; the reticular nuclei are defined by position rather than by signal.

reticular-formation.name: Reticular formation
reticular-formation.summary: A diffuse network of neurons and interlacing fibers occupying the core of the tegmentum from the medulla to the midbrain. It contains the vital centers for breathing, blood pressure and heart rate in the medulla, the pontine gaze and micturition centers, and the ascending reticular activating system that keeps the cortex awake through cholinergic, noradrenergic, serotonergic and histaminergic projections relayed by the thalamus and hypothalamus. Reticulospinal tracts from the pons and medulla set muscle tone and posture. Damage above the pons causes coma; damage in the medulla stops breathing.

anatomy.location: Central tegmentum throughout the brainstem, medial to the cranial nerve nuclei and lateral to the raphe, extending rostrally into the intralaminar thalamus and caudally into the spinal cord intermediate gray.

subdivisions.name: Median (raphe) column
subdivisions.note: serotonergic nuclei: mood, pain modulation, sleep

subdivisions.name: Medial (magnocellular) column
subdivisions.note: reticulospinal tracts and the ascending activating system; pontine and medullary reticular nuclei

subdivisions.name: Lateral (parvocellular) column
subdivisions.note: cranial nerve reflex integration, respiratory and cardiovascular centers, area postrema connections

reticular-formation.function: Arousal and consciousness, respiratory and cardiovascular control, coordination of brainstem reflexes (cough, gag, vomiting, swallowing), modulation of pain and of spinal motor tone.

bestView.label: central pontine tegmentum
tegmental core from medulla to midbrain

imaging.normalAppearance: No discrete boundary on MRI; it is the tegmental core behind the basis pontis and crura. Lesions that cause coma are those involving the paramedian tegmentum of the upper pons and midbrain on both sides.

pathology.pathology: Pontine or midbrain tegmental infarct or hemorrhage with coma
pathology.finding: Bilateral or midline tegmental lesion of the rostral pons/midbrain; small lesions here cause coma while much larger basis pontis lesions do not.
Tonsillar herniation or a posterior fossa mass compressing the medulla, with respiratory irregularity.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: DWI and T2 through the brainstem; examine for herniation

lesionEffects.mechanism: Ascending reticular activating system in the rostral pons and midbrain
Medullary respiratory centers
Reflex integration in the lateral reticular formation

lesionEffects.deficit: Changes in muscle tone and posture
lesionEffects.mechanism: Reticulospinal tracts

pearls: A small bilateral lesion in the upper pontine or midbrain tegmentum is enough for coma; the cortex must be widely damaged to do the same

rimlf.name: Rostral interstitial nucleus of the MLF (vertical gaze center)
rimlf.summary: The vertical counterpart of the PPRF. The riMLF lies in the rostral midbrain tegmentum near the junction with the thalamus, just above the oculomotor nucleus, and its burst neurons generate vertical and torsional saccades. It receives cortical and collicular commands and projects to the oculomotor and trochlear nuclei of both sides, the up-gaze fibers crossing in the posterior commissure. Nearby, the interstitial nucleus of Cajal integrates vertical gaze holding. Lesions of the riMLF or the posterior commissure produce the vertical gaze palsies of the dorsal midbrain syndrome and of top-of-the-basilar strokes.

anatomy.location: Rostral midbrain tegmentum at the mesodiencephalic junction, dorsomedial to the red nucleus and rostral to the oculomotor nuclei, near the posterior commissure and the interstitial nucleus of Cajal.

rimlf.function: Generates vertical (up and down) and torsional saccades and, with the interstitial nucleus of Cajal, holds vertical gaze position.

bestView.label: mesodiencephalic junction dorsomedial to the red nucleus
rostral midbrain tegmentum below the posterior commissure

imaging.normalAppearance: Not resolved; the lesions that cause vertical gaze palsy are paramedian rostral midbrain or bilateral thalamomesencephalic infarcts, best seen on DWI, or dorsal midbrain compression on sagittal T2.

pathology.finding: Bilateral paramedian thalamic and rostral midbrain restricted diffusion with vertical gaze palsy and somnolence.
Midbrain atrophy with the hummingbird sign on sagittal T1; vertical saccades slow long before the palsy is complete.
pathology.timing: Atrophy is visible by the time down-gaze is clearly impaired

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: DWI for infarcts; sagittal T1 for midbrain atrophy

Posterior commissure carrying crossed up-gaze fibers (Parinaud)
Vestibular pathways reach the nuclei directly: the palsy is supranuclear

Vertical oculocephalic reflex to show a supranuclear palsy
Look for lid retraction and convergence-retraction nystagmus
pearls: Down-gaze palsy points to the riMLF, up-gaze palsy to the posterior commissure
A supranuclear vertical gaze palsy (overcome by head movement) in a falling elderly patient suggests progressive supranuclear palsy

roots-c5-t1.name: Cervical roots C5–T1
roots-c5-t1.summary: The five roots of the brachial plexus each carry a recognizable package of muscle, reflex and dermatome that lets a cervical radiculopathy be assigned to a level at the bedside: C5 shoulder abduction and the lateral upper arm; C6 elbow flexion, wrist extension and the thumb; C7 elbow extension, wrist flexion and the middle finger; C8 finger flexion and the little finger; T1 finger abduction and the medial arm. Because cervical roots exit above their vertebra, the C6 root is compressed by the C5–C6 disc and the C7 root by the C6–C7 disc, the two commonest levels; C8 exits below C7.

anatomy.location: Ventral rami leaving the intervertebral foramina between C4–C5 (C5 root) and T1–T2 (T1 root), passing between the scalene muscles into the posterior triangle to form the trunks of the plexus.

subdivisions.name: C5
subdivisions.note: deltoid, supraspinatus, infraspinatus, biceps (with C6), rhomboids; biceps reflex; lateral upper arm

subdivisions.name: C6
subdivisions.note: biceps, brachioradialis, extensor carpi radialis, pronator teres; biceps and brachioradialis reflexes; thumb and lateral forearm

subdivisions.name: C7
subdivisions.note: triceps, wrist flexors, finger extensors, pronator teres, latissimus; triceps reflex; middle finger

subdivisions.name: C8
subdivisions.note: finger flexors, thumb flexors and extensors, hand intrinsics (with T1); finger flexor reflex; little finger and medial forearm

subdivisions.name: T1
subdivisions.note: hand intrinsics (interossei, abductor pollicis brevis); medial arm; sympathetic fibers to the eye

roots-c5-t1.function: Segmental motor, sensory and (T1) sympathetic supply to the upper limb, redistributed by the brachial plexus.

bestView.label: upper cervical cord above the C5–T1 segments

imaging.normalAppearance: Peripheral nerves of the limbs are outside the MNI brain volume; no atlas mesh is shown. pathology.finding: Posterolateral disc protrusion at C5–C6 or C6–C7 narrowing the foramen and contacting the exiting root.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: Cervical MRI; EMG including paraspinal muscles to confirm a root level

lesionEffects.deficit: Neck pain radiating to the thumb with weak biceps and brachioradialis and a reduced biceps reflex
lesionEffects.mechanism: C6 radiculopathy (C5–C6 disc)

lesionEffects.deficit: Pain to the middle finger with weak triceps and wrist flexion and a reduced triceps reflex
lesionEffects.mechanism: C7 radiculopathy (C6–C7 disc)

lesionEffects.deficit: Shoulder pain with weak deltaoid and external rotation
lesionEffects.mechanism: C5 radiculopathy

Key muscle for each root and the reflexes
Dermatomal sensation: thumb (C6), middle finger (C7), little finger (C8)
Check for myelopathy signs in the legs (cord compression at the same level)

roots-l2-s1.name: Lumbosacral roots L2–S1
roots-l2-s1.summary: The lumbosacral roots descend obliquely from the conus as the cauda equina before leaving through their foramina, so a posterolateral disc at one level compresses the root that has not yet exited (the L4–L5 disc compresses L5, the L5–S1 disc compresses S1) while a far-lateral disc catches the root above. Each root has a bedside signature: L2–L3 hip flexion and anterior thigh; L4 knee extension, foot inversion, the knee jerk and the medial leg; L5 dorsiflexion, great toe extension, hip abduction and the dorsum of the foot; S1 plantar flexion, hip extension, the ankle jerk and the lateral foot and sole. L5 and S1 radiculopathies account for most sciatica.

anatomy.location: Roots leaving the conus at T12–L1 and descending in the cauda equina to their foramina; the exiting root passes below the pedicle of the same-numbered vertebra, the traversing root of the next level crosses the disc.

subdivisions.name: L2–L3
subdivisions.note: iliopsoas, adductors, quadriceps (partly); anterior and medial thigh

subdivisions.name: L4
subdivisions.note: quadriceps, tibialis anterior (inversion component); knee reflex; medial leg to the medial malleolus

subdivisions.name: L5
subdivisions.note: extensor hallucis longus, tibialis anterior, peroneals, gluteus medius, hamstrings (partly); no reliable reflex (medial hamstring); dorsum of the foot, great toe, lateral leg

subdivisions.name: S1
subdivisions.note: gastrocnemius, soleus, gluteus maximus, hamstrings; ankle reflex; lateral foot, sole, posterior calf

subdivisions.name: S2–S4
subdivisions.note: pelvic floor, sphincters; perineum

roots-l2-s1.function: Segmental motor, sensory and autonomic supply to the lower limb and perineum.

bestView.label: cord (the lumbosacral roots lie in the lumbar canal, below the MNI volume)

imaging.normalAppearance: Peripheral nerves of the limbs are outside the MNI brain volume; no atlas mesh is shown. pathology.finding: Posterolateral L4–L5 or L5–S1 protrusion compressing the traversing L5 or S1 root in the lateral recess.

lesionEffects.deficit: Sciatica to the great toe, weak dorsiflexion and great toe extension, weak hip abduction (Trendelenburg), reflexes preserved
lesionEffects.mechanism: L5 radiculopathy (L4–L5 disc)

lesionEffects.deficit: Sciatica to the lateral foot, weak plantar flexion and absent ankle jerk

lesionEffects.mechanism: L3–L4 radiculopathy (femoral stretch test positive)

Knee and ankle reflexes

segment-vertebral-levels.name: Spinal segments versus vertebral levels
segment-vertebral-levels.summary: Because the vertebral column outgrows the cord, each cord segment lies higher than the vertebra of the same number, and the discrepancy increases caudally: cervical segments lie about one vertebra above their spine, upper thoracic two, lower thoracic three, and the whole lumbar and sacral cord lies opposite T10–L1. Clinicians need this in two directions: to convert the sensory level found at the bedside into the vertebral level to image, and to convert the vertebra injured on the scan into the segments and deficits expected. Roots leave through the foramen of the same number below the pedicle (cervical roots above their vertebra, C8 below C7), which decides which root a disc compresses.

anatomy.location: Cervical cord segments opposite C1–C7 vertebrae; T1–T6 segments opposite C7–T4; T7–T12 segments opposite T5–T9; L1–L5 opposite T10–T12; sacral segments opposite L1; conus at L1–L2.

subdivisions.note: segment = vertebra + 1 (C8 segment lies at C7)

subdivisions.name: Upper thoracic
subdivisions.note: segment = vertebra + 2

subdivisions.name: Lower thoracic
subdivisions.note: segment = vertebra + 3

subdivisions.name: Lumbar and sacral
subdivisions.note: L1–S5 segments compressed into the T10–L1 region

subdivisions.name: Root exit
subdivisions.note: cervical roots exit above the same-numbered vertebra (C1–C7), C8 below C7, thoracic and lumbar roots below the same-numbered vertebra

segment-vertebral-levels.function: A mapping rule rather than a structure: allows translation between clinical segmental findings and vertebral imaging levels.

bestView.label: cervicomedullary junction: C1 segment opposite the atlas

imaging.normalAppearance: On sagittal spine MRI count vertebrae from C2 (or from the sacrum) to name the level of a lesion; the cord segment involved is then inferred by the rule above. A thoracic sensory level at T10 means imaging the T7–T8 vertebrae, not T10 alone.

pathology.pathology: Disc herniation and the root affected
pathology.finding: A posterolateral C5–C6 disc compresses the C6 root; an L4–L5 disc compresses L5; a far-lateral disc compresses the root above.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: Sagittal T2 of the whole spine when the level is uncertain

septal-area.name: Septal area
septal-area.summary: The septal area is a small region of gray matter on the medial surface of the frontal lobe beneath the rostrum of the corpus callosum and in front of the anterior commissure and the lamina terminalis, continuous below with the septum pellucidum. It contains the medial and lateral septal nuclei and the nucleus of the diagonal band, which form the main cholinergic input to the hippocampus through the fornix and connect the limbic system to the hypothalamus and the reward circuitry of the accumbens. It is one of the sites where lesions produce memory disturbance and where stimulation produces pleasure, and it is damaged by anterior communicating artery aneurysm rupture and its surgery, which is why those patients are often amnestic and disinhibited.

anatomy.location: Medial surface of the frontal lobe below the rostrum of the corpus callosum, anterior to the anterior commissure, medial to the head of the caudate and the accumbens, above the orbital cortex; the septum pellucidum extends up from it between the lateral ventricles.

afferents.via: stria terminalis and ventral amygdalofugal pathway

septal-area.function: The medial septal nucleus and the vertical limb of the diagonal band send cholinergic and GABAergic fibers through the fornix to the hippocampus, where they pace the theta rhythm that underlies memory encoding and spatial navigation. The lateral septal nucleus receives the hippocampal output from the fornix and relays it to the hypothalamus and the brainstem, linking memory to emotional and autonomic responses, and it is part of the reward circuit that includes the accumbens, the ventral tegmental area and the medial forebrain bundle. The septal area also modulates aggression and social behavior through its projections to the hypothalamus and amygdala.

bestView.label: septal area beneath the rostrum, in front of the anterior commissure
septal nuclei medial to the caudate head and accumbens

imaging.normalAppearance: A thin strip of gray matter beneath the rostrum of the corpus callosum, continuous with the septum pellucidum above and the paraterminal gyrus below; it is not resolved as a discrete nucleus on clinical MRI but its position medial to the accumbens and below the frontal horns is constant.

pathology.finding: Basal forebrain and septal infarcts after vasospasm or surgical clipping, with restricted diffusion medial to the caudate heads and beneath the rostrum, bilateral in many.
Cavum septi pellucidi or a subependymoma of the septum bulging into the frontal horns; central neurocytoma attached to the septum with calcification.

lesionEffects.mechanism: Loss of septohippocampal cholinergic drive and of the fornix pathway after basal forebrain infarction
Loss of septal modulation of hypothalamic and amygdalar aggression circuits (septal rage in animals)
Interruption of the reward circuit through the accumbens and medial forebrain bundle

examination: Test recent memory and confabulation in every patient after anterior communicating aneurysm surgery
Ask the family about personality change and irritability
Look for coexisting frontal signs (grasp, utilization behavior) from the neighboring orbital cortex
pearls: Basal forebrain amnesia after anterior communicating aneurysm rupture is a septal and diagonal band lesion, not a hippocampal one

pitfalls: Septal lesions are rarely isolated; most 'septal' syndromes are basal forebrain infarcts that also involve the diagonal band and the accumbens

sinus-cavernous.name: Cavernous sinus
sinus-cavernous.summary: A plexus of venous channels within the dura on each side of the sella and sphenoid body, more important for what passes through it than for the blood it drains. The internal carotid artery and the abducens nerve run inside it; the oculomotor, trochlear, ophthalmic and maxillary nerves lie in its lateral wall. It receives the ophthalmic veins from the orbit and the sphenoparietal sinus and drains to the petrosal sinuses, and the two sides communicate around the pituitary. Its lesions, whether thrombosis from facial infection, a carotid-cavernous fistula, a pituitary tumor or a meningioma, all produce the cavernous sinus syndrome of ophthalmoplegia, facial numbness in V1/V2, proptosis and chemosis, with a Horner syndrome from the carotid sympathetic plexus.

anatomy.location: Lateral to the sella turcica and sphenoid body from the superior orbital fissure to the petrous apex, medial to the temporal lobe and uncus; roofed by dura carrying the anterior clinoid process and bounded medially by the pituitary and sphenoid sinus.

subdivisions.name: Contents (within the sinus)
subdivisions.note: internal carotid artery (cavernous segment) with its sympathetic plexus, abducens nerve

subdivisions.name: Lateral wall (from above down)
subdivisions.note: oculomotor nerve, trochlear nerve, ophthalmic nerve V1, maxillary nerve V2

subdivisions.name: Tributaries
subdivisions.note: superior and inferior ophthalmic veins, sphenoparietal sinus, superficial middle cerebral vein

subdivisions.name: Drainage
subdivisions.note: superior and inferior petrosal sinuses, intercavernous sinuses, emissary veins to the pterygoid plexus

sinus-cavernous.function: Venous drainage of the orbit and anterior cranial base; conduit for the internal carotid artery and the nerves of eye movement and facial sensation.

arteries: (venous structure) drains territories of the cerebral arteries

bestView.label: cavernous sinuses either side of the pituitary with the carotid flow voids inside
cavernous sinus lateral to the sella from the orbital fissure to the petrous apex

imaging.normalAppearance: On coronal T1+Gd the sinus enhances homogeneously around the dark carotid flow void, with a flat or concave lateral wall; a convex, bulging, asymmetric or non-enhancing sinus is abnormal. Cranial nerves III, IV, V1 and V2 are seen as dots in the lateral wall on high-resolution T2.

pathology.finding: Expanded sinus with filling defects on contrast, engorged superior ophthalmic vein, proptosis, usually from facial or sphenoid infection.
Enlarged sinus and superior ophthalmic vein with arterialized flow; DSA confirms.

pathology.pathology: Cavernous sinus meningioma or pituitary adenoma extension
pathology.finding: Enhancing tissue encasing the carotid with a convex lateral wall.
Enhancing inflammatory tissue in the sinus and orbital apex responding to steroids.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: Coronal T1+Gd and thin T2 through the sella; CT/MR venography; DSA for fistula

lesionEffects.deficit: Ophthalmoplegia of III, IV and VI, sometimes complete
lesionEffects.mechanism: Nerves in and beside the sinus

lesionEffects.deficit: Numbness of the forehead and cheek (V1, V2), sparing the jaw (V3)
lesionEffects.mechanism: Lateral wall nerves; V3 leaves through the foramen ovale below the sinus
Obstruction of the ophthalmic veins

lesionEffects.deficit: Horner syndrome with a sixth nerve palsy
lesionEffects.mechanism: Sympathetic plexus on the cavernous carotid next to the abducens nerve
Carotid-cavernous fistula

examination: Eye movements in all directions, ptosis, pupil
Corneal reflex and sensation in V1, V2 and V3
Proptosis, conjunctival injection, listen for an orbital bruit
Visual acuity and fundoscopy (venous congestion)
pearls: Multiple ocular motor palsies with V1/V2 numbness on one side is the cavernous sinus or superior orbital fissure; add optic nerve involvement and it is the orbital apex
Horner syndrome plus abducens palsy is almost pathognomonic of a cavernous sinus lesion

sinus-petrosal.name: Superior and inferior petrosal sinuses
sinus-petrosal.summary: Two channels draining the cavernous sinus backward: the superior petrosal sinus runs along the petrous ridge in the attached margin of the tentorium to the transverse sinus, and the inferior petrosal sinus runs in the groove between the petrous bone and the clivus to the jugular bulb. The superior sinus crosses the trigeminal root at Meckel's cave and the inferior sinus passes beside the abducens nerve in Dorello's canal and the glossopharyngeal and vagus nerves at the jugular foramen. The inferior petrosal sinus is catheterized to sample pituitary ACTH in Cushing disease.

anatomy.location: Superior petrosal sinus along the superior border of the petrous temporal bone from the cavernous sinus to the transverse sinus; inferior petrosal sinus along the petro-occipital fissure from the cavernous sinus to the jugular foramen.

sinus-petrosal.function: Drainage of the cavernous sinus and of the cerebellum, brainstem and inner ear (via the labyrinthine and petrosal veins) into the lateral sinuses and jugular bulb.

arteries: (venous structure) drains territories of the cerebral arteries

bestView.label: superior petrosal sinus along the petrous ridge
inferior petrosal sinus beside the clivus

imaging.normalAppearance: Thin channels seen on contrast-enhanced venography along the petrous ridge and the clivus; the inferior petrosal sinus is the route for petrosal sampling, and the petrosal veins are involved in dural fistulas of the tentorium.

pathology.finding: Abnormal arterialized flow in the petrosal veins and superior petrosal sinus with cortical venous reflux; risk of hemorrhage.
Inflammation of the petrous apex with abducens palsy and facial pain from involvement of Dorello's canal and Meckel's cave.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: CT/MR venography; DSA

lesionEffects.deficit: Abducens palsy with retro-orbital pain and otitis (Gradenigo)
lesionEffects.mechanism: Inflammation at the petrous apex where the nerve and inferior petrosal sinus run
Superior petrosal sinus at Meckel's cave
Dural fistula draining through the petrosal veins

Ear examination
Auscultate the mastoid for a bruit
pearls: Sixth nerve palsy plus facial pain plus ear discharge is the petrous apex

sinus-straight.name: Straight sinus and inferior sagittal sinus
sinus-straight.summary: The inferior sagittal sinus runs in the free edge of the falx above the corpus callosum and joins the great cerebral vein of Galen at the anterior edge of the tentorium to form the straight sinus, which runs backward along the junction of the falx and tentorium to the confluence. The straight sinus therefore drains the deep venous system (internal cerebral and basal veins) from the thalami, basal ganglia and deep white matter; its thrombosis produces bilateral thalamic edema, coma and a picture easily confused with an artery of Percheron infarct or a tumor.

anatomy.location: Inferior sagittal sinus in the lower free margin of the falx; straight sinus from the falcotentorial junction behind the splenium to the internal occipital protuberance, sloping downward and backward.

sinus-straight.function: Drainage of the deep cerebral veins (via the vein of Galen) and the medial hemisphere (inferior sagittal sinus) to the confluence of sinuses.

arteries: (venous structure) drains territories of the cerebral arteries

bestView.label: straight sinus along the falcotentorial junction behind the splenium
straight sinus running back to the confluence

imaging.normalAppearance: A straight dark channel from the splenium to the occipital protuberance on sagittal T1/T2 and venography; thrombosis shows as absent flow with T1-bright clot and bilateral thalamic swelling.

pathology.pathology: Deep venous thrombosis (straight sinus, vein of Galen, internal cerebral veins)
pathology.finding: Absent flow in the deep venous system with bilateral thalamic and basal ganglia edema and hemorrhage.
pathology.pitfalls: Bilateral thalamic swelling without diffusion restriction: check the venogram before diagnosing tumor or Percheron infarct

pathology.finding: Enhancing mass at the falcotentorial junction compressing the straight sinus.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: MR venography with T1 and SWI

lesionEffects.deficit: Coma or fluctuating consciousness with bilateral thalamic swelling
lesionEffects.mechanism: Deep venous congestion

lesionEffects.deficit: Memory and behavioral change after recovery
lesionEffects.mechanism: Thalamic injury
Impaired deep venous drainage

examination: Level of consciousness and vertical gaze
Memory and orientation
Fundoscopy
pearls: Bilateral thalamic edema in a young person: deep venous thrombosis first, then everything else

sinus-superior-sagittal.name: Superior sagittal sinus
sinus-superior-sagittal.summary: The largest dural venous sinus, running in the attached edge of the falx from the crista galli to the internal occipital protuberance, where it turns (usually to the right) into a transverse sinus at the confluence. It receives the superior cerebral (bridging) veins from the convexity, the lateral lacunae with their arachnoid granulations that return CSF to the blood, and emissary and diploic veins. Its thrombosis, the commonest cerebral venous thrombosis, causes headache, seizures, bilateral parasagittal hemorrhagic infarcts and raised intracranial pressure, and it is the sinus invaded by parasagittal meningiomas.

anatomy.location: Midline along the vault in the upper margin of the falx, triangular in section, enlarging posteriorly; lateral lacunae extend into the dura beside it in the parietal region.

sinus-superior-sagittal.function: Drainage of the superior and medial cerebral cortex and the diploë; absorption of CSF through the arachnoid granulations in its lacunae.

arteries: (venous structure) drains territories of the cerebral arteries

bestView.label: triangular sinus at the top of the falx
sinus along the vault from front to back

imaging.normalAppearance: A triangular dark flow void at the vertex on coronal T2 and a dense triangle enhancing on contrast CT (the empty delta sign is a filling defect in thrombosis); MR or CT venography shows it as a continuous channel. Absent flow, T1-bright thrombus and bilateral parasagittal edema are the thrombosis triad.

pathology.finding: Absent flow in the sinus on MR venography, dense clot on CT (cord sign) and empty delta on contrast CT, with bilateral parasagittal hemorrhagic venous infarcts.
pathology.timing: Thrombus is isointense on T1 in the first days, bright from day 5 to ~4 weeks

pathology.finding: Enhancing mass narrowing or occluding the sinus.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: CT venography or MR venography with T1/SWI for thrombus

lesionEffects.deficit: Headache, papilledema and raised intracranial pressure
lesionEffects.mechanism: Impaired venous outflow and CSF absorption
Parasagittal venous congestion and infarction
Extensive thrombosis with edema

examination: Fundoscopy for papilledema

Seizure history; risk factors: pregnancy, contraceptives, dehydration, infection, thrombophilia
pearls: Headache with bilateral or unusual hemorrhagic infarcts that do not fit an arterial territory is venous thrombosis until proven otherwise

sinus-transverse-sigmoid.name: Transverse and sigmoid sinuses
sinus-transverse-sigmoid.summary: From the confluence of sinuses each transverse sinus runs laterally in the attached margin of the tentorium along the occipital bone, receives the superior petrosal sinus and inferior cerebral and cerebellar veins, and then curves down as the sigmoid sinus in an S-shaped groove of the mastoid to leave the skull through the jugular foramen as the internal jugular vein. The right side is usually dominant. Their proximity to the mastoid air cells and middle ear made septic thrombosis a classic complication of otitis (lateral sinus thrombosis), and thrombosis or stenosis here is the venous lesion most closely linked with idiopathic intracranial hypertension.

anatomy.location: Transverse sinus in the posterior attached edge of the tentorium from the internal occipital protuberance to the petrous bone; sigmoid sinus in the sigmoid sulcus of the temporal bone behind the mastoid, ending at the jugular bulb.

sinus-transverse-sigmoid.function: Main outflow of the brain's venous blood from the confluence to the internal jugular veins; drainage of the inferior cerebral, cerebellar and petrosal veins.

arteries: (venous structure) drains territories of the cerebral arteries

bestView.label: transverse sinus along the occipital bone at the tentorial attachment
sigmoid sinus curving behind the mastoid to the jugular foramen
transverse sinus in the tentorial margin

imaging.normalAppearance: Broad flow voids along the occipital bone and behind the mastoids; asymmetry of calibre is normal (usually right dominant) and arachnoid granulations cause smooth filling defects. Thrombosis shows a dense sinus on CT, absent flow on venography and temporal or cerebellar venous infarcts; bilateral distal transverse sinus stenosis is typical of idiopathic intracranial hypertension.

pathology.finding: Absent flow with clot signal, often with mastoiditis or otitis (septic thrombosis), temporal lobe venous infarct or hemorrhage.
Bilateral smooth narrowing of the distal transverse sinuses with an empty sella and flattened globes.
Salt-and-pepper enhancing mass at the jugular foramen invading the sigmoid sinus.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: CT/MR venography; temporal bone CT for mastoid disease

lesionEffects.mechanism: Venous hypertension

lesionEffects.deficit: Temporal lobe venous infarction with aphasia or seizures
lesionEffects.mechanism: Vein of Labbé congestion

lesionEffects.deficit: Lower cranial nerve palsies with jugular foramen involvement
lesionEffects.mechanism: Adjacent IX, X, XI at the jugular foramen

lesionEffects.deficit: Otitis with fever and headache (septic lateral sinus thrombosis)
lesionEffects.mechanism: Spread from the mastoid

spinal-cord.name: Spinal cord
spinal-cord.summary: A cylinder of nervous tissue about 45 cm long in the adult, running from the foramen magnum to the conus medullaris at the L1–L2 disc, enclosed by the three meninges inside the vertebral canal. Its central H-shaped gray matter contains the motor neurons, sensory relay neurons and autonomic neurons of 31 segments; the surrounding white matter carries the long tracts in three funiculi. Two rules make cord lesions localizable: tracts have a fixed cross-sectional position (motor lateral, pain anterolateral, proprioception posterior), and the sensory level and reflex pattern mark the segment. Because the cord ends at L1–L2, lumbar puncture below L3 is safe and cauda equina lesions below the conus are lower motor neuron lesions.

anatomy.location: Vertebral canal from the cervicomedullary junction at the foramen magnum to the conus medullaris at the lower border of L1 (range T12–L3), with cervical and lumbosacral enlargements for the limbs, suspended by the denticulate ligaments and anchored below by the filum terminale; the cord segments lie progressively higher than the vertebrae of the same number.

subdivisions.name: Gray matter
subdivisions.note: anterior horn (motor), posterior horn (sensory), lateral horn T1–L2 (sympathetic) and S2–S4 (parasympathetic), central canal

subdivisions.name: White matter
subdivisions.note: posterior, lateral and anterior funiculi carrying the ascending and descending tracts

subdivisions.name: Segments
subdivisions.note: 8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral, 1 coccygeal, each with a pair of roots

subdivisions.name: Enlargements
subdivisions.note: cervical C5–T1 for the arm, lumbosacral L2–S3 for the leg

relations.anterior: vertebral bodies, posterior longitudinal ligament, discs
relations.lateral: pedicles and intervertebral foramina with the roots

spinal-cord.function: Conducts all sensory information from the body to the brain and all motor commands from the brain to the body, and contains the segmental reflex circuits (stretch, withdrawal), the central pattern generators for locomotion and the autonomic outflow for the trunk, limbs, bladder, bowel and sexual function.

bestView.label: cervicomedullary junction and upper cervical cord (the only part within the MNI volume)
cross-section of the upper cervical cord
cord descending through the foramen magnum

imaging.normalAppearance: The upper cervical cord is in the MNI volume; the rest needs a dedicated spine MRI. Sagittal T2 shows the cord as intermediate signal within bright CSF; axial T2 at 3 T shows the butterfly of gray matter. Cord signal change, swelling, atrophy, compression and the level of a lesion relative to the vertebrae are the key observations. Below the foramen magnum this atlas shows a curved reformat of the open PAM50 template (De Leener 2018), which images the brainstem and the whole cord at 0.5 mm but stores the cord straightened: its 475 mm of cord is resampled along the arc length of the atlas's own curved cord surface, so the brain MRI continues into a cord MRI in the same millimetre frame. It is a template average, so it shows the normal cord, the surrounding CSF and the vertebral levels but no individual variation, and its gray-matter butterfly is faint. The openly shareable edition may not redistribute PAM50, so below the foramen magnum it shows an average built here from openly licensed scans instead: ten spine-generic T2 volumes (0.8 mm isotropic, with manually labeled discs and nerve rootlets) for the cervical and upper thoracic cord, handing over to fourteen whole-spine sagittal T2 volumes of the Fudan lumbosacral dataset (0.6 mm in plane, 3.3 mm slices) for the rest of the cord, the conus and the lumbosacral sac. Each subject was straightened along its own cord, level-matched on its intervertebral discs and averaged, so vertebral levels are group means; spinal levels are measured on the rootlets only from C2 to T1 and follow the classical vertebral rule below that, which the readout marks.

pathology.pathology: Spinal cord compression (metastasis, disc, epidural abscess)
pathology.finding: Extradural mass displacing and flattening the cord with T2 signal change in the compressed segment; an emergency.
T2-bright intramedullary lesion: short (under 2 segments, peripheral) in MS, long (3 or more segments, central, swollen) in neuromyelitis optica and other longitudinally extensive myelitis.
Anterior two-thirds T2 hyperintensity with owl's eye anterior horns on axial images and restricted diffusion.
Central CSF-signal cavity within the cord, often with a Chiari malformation.
Inverted V T2 hyperintensity of the posterior columns over several cervical segments.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: Sagittal and axial T2 with T1 and contrast; DWI for infarct; CT for bone

lesionEffects.deficit: Weakness below the level with upper motor neuron signs, lower motor neuron signs at the level
lesionEffects.mechanism: Descending tracts interrupted and anterior horn cells destroyed at the segment
Ascending tracts interrupted; the level is one to two segments below the lesion for spinothalamic modalities
Descending autonomic pathways

lesionEffects.deficit: Spinal shock: flaccidity and areflexia after acute complete lesions
lesionEffects.mechanism: Transient loss of segmental excitability below the lesion

lesionEffects.deficit: Autonomic dysreflexia and orthostatic hypotension in lesions above T6
lesionEffects.mechanism: Loss of supraspinal control of the sympathetic outflow

examination: Sensory level to pin-prick and vibration, checked front and back
Power by myotome and the pattern of reflexes: absent at the level, brisk below
Plantar responses, clonus, tone
Anal tone, perianal sensation, bladder scan
Look for a Lhermitte sign, spinal tenderness and a girdle pain
pearls: Bilateral limb signs with a sensory level and sphincter disturbance and a normal face is the spinal cord
Spinal cord compression is the neurological emergency where hours matter: image the whole spine the same day
The sensory level on the trunk marks the lesion; the cord segment lies about one vertebra higher in the cervical region and two in the thoracic

pitfalls: A normal cervical MRI does not exclude a thoracic lesion; image the whole cord when the level is unclear
Early cord compression can present with pain alone

spinal-grey-anterior-horn.name: Anterior (ventral) horn
spinal-grey-anterior-horn.summary: The motor part of the spinal gray matter. It contains the alpha motor neurons that innervate skeletal muscle (the lower motor neurons), the gamma motor neurons for muscle spindles, and the interneurons, including Renshaw cells, that shape their output. Motor neurons are arranged somatotopically: medial groups supply axial muscles, lateral groups the limbs (present only in the enlargements), with flexors dorsal to extensors. Their death, as in poliomyelitis, spinal muscular atrophy and motor neuron disease, produces the lower motor neuron picture of weakness, wasting, fasciculations and lost reflexes.

anatomy.location: Anterior part of the gray matter on each side, largest in the cervical and lumbosacral enlargements where the lateral motor columns for the limbs are added to the medial columns for the trunk.

subdivisions.name: Medial motor column
subdivisions.note: axial and trunk muscles, all levels

subdivisions.name: Lateral motor column
subdivisions.note: limb muscles, C5–T1 and L2–S3; proximal muscles medial, distal muscles lateral

subdivisions.name: Phrenic nucleus
subdivisions.note: C3–C5, diaphragm

html.summary: The motor part of the spinal gray matter. It contains the alpha motor neurons that innervate skeletal muscle (the lower motor neurons), the gamma motor neurons for muscle spindles, and the interneurons, including Renshaw cells, that shape their output. Motor neurons are arranged somatotopically: medial groups supply axial muscles, lateral groups the limbs (present only in the enlargements), with flexors dorsal to extensors. Their death, as in poliomyelitis, spinal muscular atrophy and motor neuron disease, produces the lower motor neuron picture of weakness, wasting, fasciculations and lost reflexes.

spinal-grey-posterior-horn.name: Posterior (dorsal) horn
spinal-grey-posterior-horn.summary: The sensory part of the spinal gray matter, where dorsal root fibers end and are processed before ascending. Its laminae are functionally stacked: the marginal zone (lamina I) and substantia gelatinosa (lamina II) receive pain and temperature fibers and are the site of opioid and gate-control modulation, the nucleus proprius (laminae III–V) handles touch and gives rise to the spinothalamic tract, and Clarke's column (lamina VII, C8–L3) sends proprioception to the cerebellum. Central sensitization here underlies chronic pain, and its destruction by a syrinx produces the dissociated sensory loss of the central cord syndrome.

anatomy.location: Posterior part of the gray matter on each side, reaching toward the posterolateral sulcus where the dorsal rootlets enter; capped by the substantia gelatinosa and Lissauer's tract.

spinal-nerve-root-dermatome.name: Spinal nerve roots and dermatomes
spinal-nerve-root-dermatome.summary: Each segment of the cord gives a ventral (motor) and a dorsal (sensory) root that unite in the intervertebral foramen into a spinal nerve, which immediately divides into a dorsal ramus for the back and a ventral ramus for the limbs and trunk. The skin supplied by one dorsal root is its dermatome and the muscles supplied by one ventral root its myotome; because adjacent dermatomes overlap, a single root lesion produces pain and paresthesia in the dermatome but only patchy numbness, whereas the myotome pattern and the lost reflex localize the root. The key landmarks are C6 thumb, C7 middle finger, C8 little finger, T4 nipple, T10 umbilicus, L4 medial leg, L5 dorsum of the foot and great toe, S1 lateral foot and sole.

anatomy.location: Roots run from the cord to the foramina, increasingly obliquely downward; cervical roots emerge above their vertebra (C8 below C7), thoracic and lumbar roots below theirs; the dorsal root ganglion sits in the foramen.

subdivisions.name: Cervical roots C5–T1

spinal-segment-cervical.name: Cervical spinal cord (C1-C8)
spinal-segment-cervical.summary: The cervical cord runs from the decussation of the pyramids at the foramen magnum to the lower border of the seventh cervical vertebra, and it carries every long tract that serves the trunk and both pairs of limbs, which is why a single lesion here can be catastrophic. Its upper four segments are narrow and supply the neck, the diaphragm through the phrenic motor pool at C3, C4 and C5, and the trapezius and sternocleidomastoid through the spinal accessory nucleus that reaches down to C5 or C6. From C5 to T1 the cord swells into the cervical enlargement, whose large anterior horns hold the motor neurons of the arm and whose dorsal roots build the brachial plexus. A complete lesion above C4 abolishes spontaneous breathing; a complete lesion at C5 leaves a patient who can flex the elbow but cannot extend the wrist; at C6 wrist extension returns; at C7 the elbow extends and at C8 and T1 the small hand muscles are the last to go.

anatomy.location: From the level of the pyramidal decussation, where the medulla becomes the cord at the foramen magnum, down to the lower border of the C7 vertebral body, inside the widest part of the vertebral canal. The cord is oval in cross-section here, wider from side to side than from front to back, and reaches its greatest width in the cervical enlargement opposite the C5 and C6 vertebrae. The dentate ligaments anchor it to the dura on each side, and the vertebral arteries and the anterior spinal artery lie in front of it.

subdivisions.name: C1-C4 (high cervical)
subdivisions.note: Neck, diaphragm through the phrenic pool at C3-C5, and the spinal accessory nucleus; a complete lesion here is ventilator dependent.

subdivisions.name: C5-T1 (cervical enlargement)
subdivisions.note: Large anterior horns for the upper limb; the dorsal roots here form the brachial plexus and the segment gives the classical arm myotomes.

spinal-segment-cervical.function: The cervical cord supplies the neck, the diaphragm and the upper limbs and transmits everything below. Its anterior horns contain the motor pools for the neck, shoulder girdle, arm and hand, arranged so that proximal muscles lie medially and the intrinsic hand muscles most laterally, and the phrenic pool sits ventromedially at C3 to C5. Its posterior horns receive the dorsal roots that carry sensation from the back of the head, the neck and the whole upper limb. The lateral horn is absent above T1, so the sympathetic outflow to the head leaves through the T1 segment and travels back up the chain; a cervical cord lesion nonetheless interrupts the descending sympathetic pathway in the lateral funiculus and produces an ipsilateral Horner syndrome. The corticospinal, spinothalamic and dorsal column pathways are all fully assembled at this level, and their somatotopy, with sacral fibers lying most laterally in the corticospinal and spinothalamic tracts, explains why an expanding central lesion spares the sacral dermatomes until late.

arteries: ascending and deep cervical radicular arteries

bestView.label: cross-section of the upper cervical cord at the foramen magnum
cervicomedullary junction; the rest of the cervical cord lies below the MNI volume

imaging.normalAppearance: On sagittal T2 the cervical cord is a smooth band of intermediate signal within bright CSF, widening between C4 and C6; on axial T2 the gray matter is a faint butterfly inside the paler white matter. The cord occupies well under half the canal in a normal adult.

pathology.finding: Canal narrowing with cord flattening at one or more disc levels and a pancake of T2 hyperintensity in the central cord, often with gadolinium enhancement in severe compression.
Hyperextension injury in a stenotic canal with central cord edema and weakness that is worse in the hands than the legs, often with preserved sacral sensation.
Fracture or facet dislocation on CT with cord swelling and hemorrhage on MRI; the neurological level is set by the lowest segment with normal power and sensation.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: Sagittal and axial T2 of the whole cervical cord, with STIR for cord edema and CT for the bony injury.

lesionEffects.mechanism: Complete lesion above C4 removing the phrenic motor pool and all descending motor tracts

lesionEffects.deficit: Weak hands with relatively strong legs
lesionEffects.mechanism: Central cord injury damaging the medially placed arm fibers of the corticospinal tract first

lesionEffects.mechanism: Damage to the decussating spinothalamic fibers in the anterior white commissure, as in syringomyelia

Work down the key myotomes C5 elbow flexion, C6 wrist extension, C7 elbow extension, C8 finger flexion, T1 finger abduction
