spinal-segment-lumbar.name: Lumbar spinal cord (L1-L5)
spinal-segment-lumbar.summary: The five lumbar cord segments are packed into the vertebral canal opposite the T10, T11 and T12 vertebral bodies, far above the lumbar vertebrae they are named for, and together with the upper sacral segments they form the lumbosacral enlargement whose broad anterior horns supply the leg. The L1 and L2 segments carry the last of the sympathetic outflow and the cremasteric reflex, L2 to L4 supply the hip flexors, adductors and quadriceps and the knee jerk, and L4 and L5 supply ankle dorsiflexion, inversion and eversion. Their long roots have to travel far down the canal to reach their own foramina, so they run in the cauda equina beside the cord itself. A lesion confined to these segments, the epiconus syndrome, gives weak hips and knees with a preserved knee jerk pattern that shifts as the level rises, an absent ankle jerk, and less bladder involvement than a true conus lesion.

anatomy.location: In the vertebral canal opposite the T10, T11 and upper T12 vertebral bodies, immediately above the sacral segments and the conus medullaris. The cord is at its widest from side to side here, the lumbosacral enlargement, and it is surrounded by the descending roots of the cauda equina, which crowd the subarachnoid space so that a small mass at this level can compress both cord and roots at once. The great anterior radicular artery of Adamkiewicz usually enters between T9 and L2 and supplies this part of the cord.

subdivisions.name: L1-L2
subdivisions.note: Last of the sympathetic outflow, the cremasteric reflex and Clarke column, the origin of the posterior spinocerebellar tract.

subdivisions.name: L3-L5
subdivisions.note: Quadriceps, adductors and ankle dorsiflexors; the knee jerk is L3-L4 and the L5 myotome extends the great toe.

spinal-segment-lumbar.function: The lumbar cord provides the motor supply of the hip flexors, adductors, quadriceps and ankle dorsiflexors and receives sensation from the front of the thigh, the medial leg and the dorsum of the foot. Its anterior horns are large and somatotopically arranged, with the trunk muscles medial and the distal leg muscles lateral, and Clarke column at L1 and L2 is the origin of the posterior spinocerebellar tract carrying unconscious proprioception from the leg. The last preganglionic sympathetic neurons of the intermediolateral column lie at L1 and L2 and supply the pelvic vessels, and the L1 and L2 segments run the cremasteric reflex. Because these segments sit opposite the low thoracic vertebrae, a burst fracture of T12 damages lumbar cord and not lumbar roots, which is the commonest reason for the mismatch between the fracture level on a radiograph and the neurological level at the bedside.

spinal-segment-sacral.name: Sacral and coccygeal spinal cord (S1-S5, Co)
spinal-segment-sacral.summary: The sacral and coccygeal segments make up the conus medullaris, the tapering tip of the cord that lies opposite the T12 and L1 vertebrae and ends at the L1-L2 disc in most adults. They are the smallest segments but they carry the reflex machinery of the pelvic floor: the parasympathetic nucleus at S2, S3 and S4 that empties the bladder and rectum and produces erection, Onuf nucleus that holds the motor neurons of the external urethral and anal sphincters, and the afferents of the saddle area. A lesion confined to the conus therefore produces early, symmetric retention with overflow incontinence, saddle anesthesia, impotence and absent anal and bulbocavernosus reflexes, with little or no leg weakness, and it is separated from a cauda equina lesion by being symmetric, less painful and less likely to abolish the ankle jerks on one side only.

anatomy.location: In the vertebral canal opposite the T12 and L1 vertebral bodies, forming the conus medullaris, which tapers to the filum terminale at about the L1-L2 intervertebral disc in the adult and one or two levels lower in the newborn. The conus lies surrounded by the roots of the cauda equina, which fill the lumbar theca below it, and it is supplied by a fine anastomotic basket rather than by a single feeding artery.

subdivisions.name: S1-S2
subdivisions.note: Plantar flexors and small muscles of the foot, the ankle jerk and sensation of the sole and the back of the thigh.

subdivisions.name: S2-S4
subdivisions.note: Pelvic parasympathetic nucleus, Onuf nucleus for the external sphincters, and the saddle dermatomes.

subdivisions.name: S5 and coccygeal
subdivisions.note: The last dermatome, a small patch of skin over the coccyx, and the origin of the filum terminale.

spinal-segment-sacral.function: The sacral cord supplies the small muscles of the foot and the pelvic floor, receives sensation from the back of the thigh, the sole and the perineum, and runs the autonomic control of the bladder, bowel and genitals. Its parasympathetic preganglionic neurons at S2 to S4 leave in the pelvic splanchnic nerves to contract the detrusor and relax the internal sphincter, while the somatic motor neurons of Onuf nucleus hold the external sphincters closed; the balance between them is what continence is. The S1 segment supplies the gastrocnemius and soleus and the ankle jerk, S2 to S4 the anal and bulbocavernosus reflexes, and the coccygeal segment a small patch of skin over the coccyx. Because the sacral fibers of the spinothalamic tract lie most laterally, an intramedullary lesion higher up spares sacral sensation until late, the sacral sparing that separates an intrinsic cord lesion from an extrinsic compression.

arteries: lateral sacral and iliolumbar radicular arteries

bestView.label: cord cross-section; the conus lies at the thoracolumbar junction, below the MNI volume
rostral cord in the volume; the conus is at the L1-L2 disc far caudal to it

imaging.normalAppearance: On sagittal T2 the conus tapers smoothly from the lumbosacral enlargement and ends at or above the L1-L2 disc; the filum terminale continues as a thin midline strand among the cauda equina roots.

pathology.pathology: Tethered cord with a low conus

pitfalls: DERIVED MESH: the four cord blocks are cut from the Z-Anatomy cord surface, not segmented on an individual. Their boundaries are now measured rather than assumed: the PAM50 spinal template is reformatted along this cord's own centerline, and each block is cut at the PAM50 C8/T1, T12/L1 and L5/S1 spinal-level boundaries on a plane normal to the local centerline tangent. PAM50 is a template average of adult cords, so the levels are representative rather than personal; use the blocks for orientation, never to read a level off a patient's image.

PUBLIC EDITION - VERTEBRAL-LANDMARK CUT: the measured block boundaries are spinal-level boundaries of a template whose data may not be redistributed, so the openly shareable build of the atlas ships the older construction instead -- the same Z-Anatomy cord surface cut by horizontal planes at its own vertebral-body landmarks, using the classical cord-segment / vertebra rule (cervical opposite C1-C7, thoracic opposite T1-T9/T10, lumbar opposite T10-T12, sacral and coccygeal opposite T12-L1). Those boundaries are a textbook rule applied to one model, not a measurement, so this block marks roughly where the level sits and nothing more. (This is the S1-S5 and coccygeal block.) The public block now stops at the conus: its lower cut is the middle of the Z-Anatomy L1-L2 intervertebral disc, and the taper below that plane is a separate filum terminale surface rather than part of the sacral cord.

html.summary: The sacral and coccygeal segments make up the conus medullaris, the tapering tip of the cord that lies opposite the T12 and L1 vertebrae and ends at the L1-L2 disc in most adults. They are the smallest segments but they carry the reflex machinery of the pelvic floor: the parasympathetic nucleus at S2, S3 and S4 that empties the bladder and rectum and produces erection, Onuf nucleus that holds the motor neurons of the external urethral and anal sphincters, and the afferents of the saddle area. A lesion confined to the conus therefore produces early, symmetric retention with overflow incontinence, saddle anesthesia, impotence and absent anal and bulbocavernosus reflexes, with little or no leg weakness, and it is separated from a cauda equina lesion by being symmetric, less painful and less likely to abolish the ankle jerks on one side only.

The S1 segment supplies the gastrocnemius and soleus and the ankle jerk, S2 to S4 the anal and bulbocavernosus reflexes, and the coccygeal segment a small patch of skin over the coccyx. Because the sacral fibers of the spinothalamic tract lie most laterally, an intramedullary lesion higher up spares sacral sensation until late, the sacral sparing that separates an intrinsic cord lesion from an extrinsic compression.
html.anatomy.location: In the vertebral canal opposite the T12 and L1 vertebral bodies, forming the conus medullaris, which tapers to the filum terminale at about the L1-L2 intervertebral disc in the adult and one or two levels lower in the newborn. The conus lies surrounded by the roots of the cauda equina, which fill the lumbar theca below it, and it is supplied by a fine anastomotic basket rather than by a single feeding artery.

html.imaging.sequenceOfChoice: Sagittal and axial T2 of the thoracolumbar junction with contrast when a tumor or tethering is suspected.

spinal-segment-thoracic.name: Thoracic spinal cord (T1-T12)
spinal-segment-thoracic.summary: The thoracic cord is the long, slender middle third of the cord, the part with the smallest cross-section, the poorest blood supply and the narrowest bony canal, which together make it the segment where compression and infarction do the most damage for the least warning. It has no limb enlargement, so its anterior horns are small and supply only the intercostal and abdominal muscles, but its lateral horn runs the entire sympathetic outflow of the body from T1 to L2, and the T1 segment supplies the sympathetic fibers of the head. Because the thoracic dermatomes wrap the trunk in neat bands, a lesion here declares itself as a sensory level: the nipple line is T4, the xiphisternum T6 and the umbilicus T10. A complete thoracic lesion gives spastic paraplegia with a sensory level and a neurogenic bladder, with normal arms.

anatomy.location: From the lower border of the C7 vertebral body to about the T9 or T10 vertebral body, so that the twelve thoracic cord segments are compressed into nine or ten vertebral levels and each segment lies two to three vertebrae above the bone of the same number. The canal is at its narrowest and the cord at its thinnest between T4 and T9, and the cord is held in the middle of the canal by the dentate ligaments with the thoracic aorta and its intercostal arteries in front of the vertebral bodies.

subdivisions.name: T1-T6 (upper thoracic)
subdivisions.note: Sympathetic supply to the head, neck and heart, and the upper intercostal muscles; a lesion at or above T6 permits autonomic dysreflexia.

subdivisions.name: T7-T12 (lower thoracic)
subdivisions.note: Lower intercostal and abdominal muscles, the splanchnic sympathetic outflow, and the T10 dermatome at the umbilicus.

spinal-segment-thoracic.function: The thoracic cord carries the whole motor and sensory traffic of the lower limbs and pelvis through, innervates the intercostal and abdominal muscles for breathing, coughing and posture, and houses the intermediolateral cell column, the preganglionic sympathetic neurons that reach every blood vessel, sweat gland, viscus and the adrenal medulla. Its dermatomes are the most reliable segmental map in the body, which is why a sensory level found on the trunk is the single most useful sign in acute myelopathy. The upper thoracic segments also carry the sympathetic supply of the heart, and T5 to T9 supply the splanchnic nerves; a lesion above T6 removes descending control of that outflow and allows autonomic dysreflexia, in which a distended bladder or bowel drives a dangerous surge of blood pressure with a reflex bradycardia and flushing above the lesion.

bestView.label: cord cross-section; the thoracic cord itself lies below the MNI volume
cervicomedullary junction, the rostral end of the cord shown in the volume

imaging.normalAppearance: On sagittal T2 the thoracic cord is a uniform, slender band with no enlargement, narrowing further as it descends until it swells into the lumbar enlargement; the anterior median fissure and the posterior septum are not resolved at routine resolution.

pathology.finding: Epidural soft tissue from a vertebral body deposit indenting the thecal sac with cord signal change; the sensory level on examination is usually a few segments below the true lesion.

pathology.pathology: Spinal cord infarction in the anterior spinal artery territory
pathology.finding: Pencil-like or owl-eye T2 hyperintensity restricted to the anterior two-thirds of the cord with restricted diffusion, classically after aortic surgery or dissection.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: Whole-spine sagittal T2 with axial images through the level, and contrast when a tumor or myelitis is suspected.

lesionEffects.deficit: Spastic paraplegia with a sensory level on the trunk
lesionEffects.mechanism: Interruption of the corticospinal and spinothalamic tracts at one thoracic segment

spinal-trigeminal-nucleus-tract.name: Spinal trigeminal nucleus and tract
spinal-trigeminal-nucleus-tract.latin: Nucleus et tractus spinalis nervi trigemini
spinal-trigeminal-nucleus-tract.summary: Pain and temperature fibers from the face enter the pons in the trigeminal root, turn downward as the spinal trigeminal tract and descend through the medulla into the upper cervical cord, synapsing along the way in the spinal trigeminal nucleus that lies medial to the tract. Second-order axons cross to join the trigeminothalamic tract. This descending course explains the signature crossed sensory loss of lateral brainstem lesions: facial pain loss on the side of the lesion, body pain loss on the opposite side. The nucleus also receives pain fibers from the ear and pharynx carried by cranial nerves VII, IX and X.

anatomy.location: Lateral tegmentum of the medulla and caudal pons, just deep to the surface and medial to the inferior cerebellar peduncle, continuous below with the substantia gelatinosa of the upper cervical dorsal horn (C2–C3) and above with the principal sensory nucleus.

subdivisions.name: Pars oralis
subdivisions.note: rostral, near the principal nucleus; touch from the perioral region

subdivisions.name: Pars interpolaris
subdivisions.note: mid-medulla, dental pain

subdivisions.name: Pars caudalis
subdivisions.note: lower medulla to C3; the main relay for facial pain and temperature, laminated like the dorsal horn, with an onion-skin somatotopy (perioral rostral, peripheral face caudal)

spinal-trigeminal-nucleus-tract.function: Relays facial and oral pain, temperature and crude touch, plus pain from the external ear, tympanic membrane and pharynx; afferent limb of the corneal reflex.

spinal-white-columns.name: White columns of the spinal cord
spinal-white-columns.summary: The white matter of the cord is arranged in three funiculi on each side, each carrying a fixed set of tracts, which is what makes cord syndromes localizable in cross-section. The posterior funiculus (fasciculus gracilis and cuneatus) carries uncrossed fine touch, vibration and proprioception upward; the lateral funiculus carries the crossed lateral corticospinal tract (motor, the leg fibers lateral), the crossed spinothalamic tract (pain and temperature, sacral fibers lateral), the spinocerebellar tracts and the descending autonomic fibers; the anterior funiculus carries the anterior corticospinal, vestibulospinal and reticulospinal tracts. Lamination explains why an expanding central lesion spares sacral sensation and why extrinsic compression affects the legs first.

anatomy.location: Surrounding the gray matter: posterior funiculus between the posterior horns and the posterior median septum, lateral funiculus between the posterior and anterior horns, anterior funiculus between the anterior horn and the anterior median fissure; the anterior white commissure crosses in front of the central canal.

subdivisions.name: Posterior funiculus
subdivisions.note: fasciculus gracilis (medial, leg and lower trunk, all levels) and fasciculus cuneatus (lateral, arm and upper trunk, above T6)

subdivisions.name: Lateral funiculus
subdivisions.note: lateral corticospinal (arm medial, leg lateral), lateral spinothalamic (arm medial, sacral lateral), posterior and anterior spinocerebellar, rubrospinal, descending autonomic

subdivisions.name: Anterior funiculus
subdivisions.note: anterior corticospinal, vestibulospinal, reticulospinal, tectospinal, anterior spinothalamic, MLF

subdivisions.name: Anterior white commissure
subdivisions.note: crossing spinothalamic fibers, damaged first by a syrinx

spinal-white-columns.function: Conduction of all ascending sensory and descending motor and autonomic traffic between the segments and the brain.

bestView.label: posterior, lateral and anterior funiculi around the gray matter of the upper cervical cord

imaging.normalAppearance: White matter is slightly darker than gray on axial T2 at 3 T; tract-selective signal change is diagnostic: posterior columns in B12 deficiency and copper deficiency, lateral corticospinal tracts in ALS and hereditary spastic paraplegia, anterior two-thirds in infarction.

pathology.finding: Inverted V or dumbbell T2 hyperintensity of the posterior columns in the cervical and upper thoracic cord.

splanchnic-nerves.name: Splanchnic nerves
splanchnic-nerves.summary: The splanchnic nerves carry the sympathetic outflow from the thoracic and lumbar cord to the abdominal and pelvic viscera, bypassing the paravertebral chain to synapse in the prevertebral ganglia. The greater (T5–T9), lesser (T10–T11) and least (T12) splanchnic nerves pierce the diaphragm to reach the celiac, superior mesenteric and aorticorenal ganglia, and the lumbar splanchnic nerves (L1–L2) reach the inferior mesenteric and hypogastric plexuses. They also carry the visceral pain afferents from the gut, whose cell bodies lie in the thoracolumbar dorsal root ganglia, which is why visceral pain is referred to the dermatomes of those segments and why a celiac plexus block relieves pancreatic cancer pain. The pelvic splanchnic nerves, despite the name, are the parasympathetic outflow of S2–S4 and are described with the sacral parasympathetic system.

anatomy.location: Preganglionic sympathetic fibers leave the T5–L2 intermediolateral column through the white rami, pass through the sympathetic chain without synapsing, and form the greater, lesser and least thoracic splanchnic nerves on the vertebral bodies, which pierce the crura of the diaphragm, and the lumbar splanchnic nerves from the lumbar chain; they end in the prevertebral ganglia around the origins of the celiac, superior mesenteric and inferior mesenteric arteries and in the hypogastric plexus.

afferents.from: Visceral afferents from the abdominal viscera (pain, distension)
afferents.via: run with the sympathetic fibers to the T5–L2 dorsal root ganglia

efferents.to: Celiac, superior mesenteric, aorticorenal and inferior mesenteric ganglia; adrenal medulla
efferents.via: greater, lesser, least and lumbar splanchnic nerves

splanchnic-nerves.function: Postganglionic fibers from the prevertebral ganglia follow the arteries to the gut, liver, pancreas, spleen, kidneys and adrenal medulla, inhibiting peristalsis and secretion, constricting splanchnic vessels to redistribute blood in exercise and hemorrhage, and controlling the sphincters; the greater splanchnic nerve's preganglionic fibers synapse directly on adrenal medullary cells to release catecholamines. Afferent fibers running with them signal distension, ischemia and inflammation of the viscera and mediate referred pain, and the splanchnic bed is the largest reservoir controlled by sympathetic tone, so its loss in autonomic failure causes orthostatic hypotension and postprandial hypotension.

bestView.label: T5–L2 segments of the cord: intermediolateral column and the origin of the splanchnic outflow
thoracic cord: intermediolateral cell column at the lateral horn

imaging.normalAppearance: The nerves themselves are not seen on neuraxis imaging; their cord origin is the lateral horn of the thoracic and upper lumbar segments. On body CT the celiac ganglia lie beside the celiac trunk as small soft tissue nodules, the landmark for celiac plexus block.

pathology.finding: Soft tissue encasing the celiac trunk and superior mesenteric origin from pancreatic carcinoma, the anatomical basis of intractable epigastric and back pain.
Cord injury or transverse myelitis at or above T6 disconnecting the splanchnic outflow, with autonomic dysreflexia and neurogenic shock.

lesionEffects.mechanism: Loss of splanchnic vasoconstriction in autonomic failure or high cord lesions
Unopposed splanchnic sympathetic discharge below a cord lesion above T6 in response to bladder or bowel distension
Sympathetic overactivity or loss of coordinated control after cord injury or surgery
Convergence of splanchnic afferents on T5–L2 dorsal horn neurons shared with somatic dermatomes

examination: Lying and standing blood pressure, including after meals
Abdominal examination for distension in cord-injured patients with hypertension and headache
Map referred pain to dermatomes: epigastrium T5–T9, umbilicus T10, suprapubic T11–L1

A celiac plexus block interrupts both the sympathetic efferents and the pain afferents of the upper abdomen
Referred pain follows the splanchnic afferents to the thoracolumbar dorsal horn, not the vagus

pitfalls: The pelvic splanchnic nerves are parasympathetic (S2–S4), not sympathetic, despite the shared name

subarachnoid-space-cisterns.name: Subarachnoid space and basal cisterns
subarachnoid-space-cisterns.summary: The CSF-filled space between the arachnoid and the pia covers the whole brain and spinal cord and widens into cisterns wherever the arachnoid bridges a hollow: the cisterna magna behind the medulla, the pontine and interpeduncular cisterns in front of the brainstem, the suprasellar (chiasmatic) cistern around the optic chiasm and circle of Willis, the ambient and quadrigeminal cisterns around the midbrain, and the Sylvian cisterns. Cranial nerves and the major arteries run through these cisterns, blood collects in them after aneurysm rupture, and their effacement is the imaging sign of herniation.

subdivisions.note: between the cerebellum and medulla, receiving CSF from the foramen of Magendie

subdivisions.name: Pontine and interpeduncular cisterns
subdivisions.note: basilar artery, CN VI, III, and the basilar tip

subdivisions.name: Suprasellar (chiasmatic) cistern
subdivisions.note: optic chiasm, infundibulum, circle of Willis

subdivisions.name: Ambient and quadrigeminal cisterns
subdivisions.note: around the midbrain: PCA, SCA, CN IV, vein of Galen

subdivisions.name: Sylvian cisterns

prepontine and ambient cisterns around the brainstem

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: Non-contrast CT for blood and herniation; FLAIR and T1+Gd for meningeal disease

subiculum.name: Subiculum
subiculum.summary: The subiculum is the transitional cortex between CA1 of the hippocampus and the entorhinal cortex of the parahippocampal gyrus, forming the floor of the hippocampal formation on the medial temporal surface. It is the main output station of the hippocampus: it receives CA1 and the entorhinal cortex and projects through the fornix to the mammillary bodies, the anterior thalamus, the septal area and the accumbens, and back to the entorhinal cortex, so the Papez circuit and the hippocampal control of the stress axis both pass through it. It is affected early in Alzheimer disease and is the site of the earliest tau spread from the entorhinal cortex.

anatomy.location: Cortical band on the inferomedial surface of the hippocampal formation between CA1 laterally and the presubiculum and entorhinal cortex medially, on the upper surface of the parahippocampal gyrus, extending from the hippocampal head to the tail.

subiculum.function: Subicular pyramidal cells integrate the output of CA1 with direct entorhinal input and encode place, head direction and the salience of context; through the fornix they carry the hippocampal memory signal to the mammillary bodies and the anterior thalamic nuclei, completing the Papez circuit, and to the accumbens, where memory and motivation meet. They also send inhibitory control to the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis via the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis, so hippocampal damage raises cortisol. Bursting subicular neurons are a major generator of epileptiform discharges in sclerotic hippocampi, and they are the earliest hippocampal cells to develop Alzheimer tangles after the entorhinal cortex.

bestView.label: subiculum between CA1 and the entorhinal cortex on the parahippocampal surface
subiculum along the medial hippocampal formation

imaging.normalAppearance: The inferomedial gray band of the hippocampal formation on coronal T2 images, where the hippocampus flattens onto the parahippocampal gyrus; it continues medially into the entorhinal cortex without a visible border on routine MRI.

pathology.finding: Early subicular and CA1 atrophy on subfield volumetry, with widening of the hippocampal sulcus and temporal horn.
Hippocampal atrophy in which the subiculum is relatively preserved but hyperexcitable, sustaining seizures.
Punctate delayed diffusion lesions in the lateral hippocampus at the CA1-subiculum border.
pathology.timing: Seen at 24-72 hours after the episode

lesionEffects.mechanism: Loss of the hippocampal output to the diencephalon and cortex
Loss of subicular place and head-direction signals
Loss of hippocampal inhibition of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis

examination: Delayed recall and recognition
Route finding and orientation
Consider cortisol dysregulation in patients with bilateral hippocampal disease and mood change
pearls: The subiculum is the hippocampus's exit: the fornix is mostly subicular axons
The Papez circuit begins here, not in CA1
In sclerotic hippocampi the surviving subiculum keeps the seizures going

pitfalls: Subfield names on MRI reports depend on the atlas used; treat subicular volumes as research measures

substantia-nigra-pars-compacta.name: Substantia nigra, pars compacta
substantia-nigra-pars-compacta.summary: The pars compacta is the dorsal, densely cellular part of the substantia nigra, a band of large neuromelanin-pigmented dopamine neurons in the midbrain tegmentum between the crus cerebri and the red nucleus. Its axons form the nigrostriatal pathway to the caudate and putamen, where dopamine sets the gain of the direct and indirect basal ganglia pathways, enabling movement to be initiated, scaled and learned. Loss of most of its neurons, with Lewy bodies in the survivors, is Parkinson disease, and the neuromelanin and iron changes of the nucleus are now visible on MRI; it is also the site of the dopaminergic lesion of MPTP toxicity and of the neurodegeneration in progressive supranuclear palsy and multiple system atrophy.

anatomy.location: Dorsal part of the substantia nigra across the whole midbrain, lying on the crus cerebri ventrally and beneath the pars reticulata's dorsal border, medial to the medial lemniscus, lateral to the ventral tegmental area and the interpeduncular fossa, from the level of the subthalamus down to the pons.

substantia-nigra-pars-compacta.function: Dopaminergic pars compacta neurons fire tonically to provide the background dopamine that D1 and D2 receptors in the striatum need for the direct pathway to facilitate and the indirect pathway to suppress movement, and they burst to reward prediction errors, teaching the striatum which actions are worth repeating; their ventral tier neurons, which project to the putamen, are the most vulnerable in Parkinson disease. The neurons receive the striatum, the pallidum, the subthalamic nucleus, the pedunculopontine nucleus and the prefrontal cortex, and they also send dopamine to the pallidum, the subthalamic nucleus and the thalamus. With about 60 percent of the neurons lost and 80 percent of striatal dopamine gone, bradykinesia and rigidity appear.

bestView.label: pars compacta between the crus cerebri and the red nucleus
substantia nigra in the midbrain tegmentum

imaging.normalAppearance: On neuromelanin-sensitive T1 images the pars compacta is a bright band dorsal to the crus cerebri; on susceptibility-weighted images its dorsolateral part shows the swallow-tail sign of nigrosome-1, which is lost in Parkinson disease.

pathology.finding: Loss of the dorsolateral nigral hyperintensity (swallow-tail sign) on SWI and reduced neuromelanin signal; dopamine transporter SPECT shows reduced putaminal uptake, worse contralateral to the affected side.
Restricted diffusion of the ventral midbrain tegmentum with contralateral hemiparkinsonism and oculomotor signs.
Midbrain atrophy with the hummingbird sign and reduced midbrain area; nigral neuromelanin loss also present.

lesionEffects.deficit: Contralateral bradykinesia, rigidity and rest tremor
lesionEffects.mechanism: Loss of striatal dopamine from the ipsilateral nigrostriatal pathway
Advanced bilateral nigral loss with non-dopaminergic degeneration
Loss of dopaminergic reward prediction signals

examination: Finger tapping, rapid alternating movements and arm swing for bradykinesia; cogwheel rigidity with activation
Rest tremor at 4-6 Hz and its asymmetry
Response to a levodopa challenge when the diagnosis is in doubt
pearls: Parkinson disease begins as a one-sided disease because the two nigrae die at different rates
The swallow tail on SWI disappears when nigrosome-1 dies
Dopamine replacement treats the striatal deficit; it cannot stop the nigral loss

pitfalls: Symmetric parkinsonism with early falls or autonomic failure is not Parkinson disease; the nigra is involved in all the parkinsonian syndromes, and the pattern of spread decides

substantia-nigra-pars-reticulata.name: Substantia nigra, pars reticulata
substantia-nigra-pars-reticulata.summary: The pars reticulata is the ventral, cell-sparse part of the substantia nigra that lies on the crus cerebri and is a dispersed continuation of the internal segment of the globus pallidus. Its GABAergic neurons are an output nucleus of the basal ganglia: they tonically inhibit the superior colliculus, the ventral anterior and mediodorsal thalamus and the pedunculopontine nucleus, and they pause to release saccades, orofacial movements and cognitive actions. It is central to the control of eye movements and to the propagation of seizures, it is disinhibited in parkinsonism and overinhibited in chorea, and it is the reason a nigral lesion affects gaze and axial movement as well as the limbs.

anatomy.location: Ventral substantia nigra spread along the dorsal surface of the crus cerebri from the medial edge near the interpeduncular fossa to the lateral edge of the peduncle, beneath the pars compacta and continuous rostrally with the internal pallidum through the cerebral peduncle.

substantia-nigra-pars-reticulata.function: Pars reticulata neurons fire tonically at high rates and hold the superior colliculus, the ventral anterior and mediodorsal thalamus and the brainstem locomotor region under inhibition; striatal direct-pathway neurons inhibit them to release a movement, and subthalamic input excites them to stop one, so they are the final common path of the oculomotor, orofacial and prefrontal basal ganglia loops much as the internal pallidum is for the limbs. Their projection to the superior colliculus gates saccades and their dendrites receive dopamine from the pars compacta, which sets their excitability. Reduced GABAergic output from the nigra to the colliculus underlies the seizure-suppressing effect of nigral inhibition in animal models.

bestView.label: pars reticulata on the dorsal surface of the crus cerebri
ventral substantia nigra above the cerebral peduncle

imaging.normalAppearance: On T2 and susceptibility-weighted images the pars reticulata is the dark, iron-rich band immediately dorsal to the crus cerebri, distinct from the brighter pars compacta behind it; its iron increases in Parkinson disease.

pathology.finding: Increased susceptibility signal in the pars reticulata and loss of the compacta's swallow-tail sign; quantitative susceptibility mapping tracks progression.
Marked hypointensity of the substantia nigra and globus pallidus on T2, with the eye-of-the-tiger sign in PKAN.
Restricted diffusion of the crus and ventral tegmentum with contralateral hemiparesis and parkinsonism, and gaze abnormalities from reticulata involvement.

lesionEffects.deficit: Impaired saccade initiation and slowed eye movements
lesionEffects.mechanism: Loss of reticulata control of the superior colliculus

lesionEffects.deficit: Contribution to parkinsonian akinesia (over-inhibition) or chorea (under-inhibition)
lesionEffects.mechanism: Altered tonic inhibition of the thalamus and brainstem
Loss of nigral gating of the collicular seizure-propagation pathway

examination: Saccade latency and velocity, especially antisaccades
Bradykinesia and axial rigidity
Seizure history in patients with nigral pathology
pearls: The pars reticulata is the pallidum of the eyes and the face

Nigral output silences the superior colliculus; a saccade is a moment of nigral silence

subdivisions.name: Pars compacta

substantia-nigra.function: Dopaminergic modulation of striatal activity enabling movement initiation and reward learning (pars compacta); tonic inhibition of thalamus and superior colliculus controlling movement and saccades (pars reticulata).

pigmented band between crus and tegmentum

Midbrain atrophy (hummingbird sign) with nigral involvement.

subthalamic-nucleus.name: Subthalamic nucleus
subthalamic-nucleus.summary: A small lens-shaped nucleus below the thalamus, above the substantia nigra and medial to the internal capsule as it becomes the crus. It is the only glutamatergic (excitatory) nucleus of the basal ganglia: it receives inhibitory input from the external pallidum in the indirect pathway and direct cortical input (the hyperdirect pathway), and drives the internal pallidum and nigral pars reticulata. Its destruction, classically by a lacunar infarct from posterior perforators, releases wild flinging movements of the opposite limbs (hemiballismus); its stimulation is the most widely used deep brain stimulation target for Parkinson disease.

anatomy.location: Ventral to the thalamus and zona incerta, dorsomedial to the internal capsule and crus cerebri, rostral and dorsolateral to the substantia nigra, at the mesodiencephalic junction; about 12 mm lateral to the midline and 4 mm below the AC–PC line.

subthalamic-nucleus.function: Excitatory driver of the basal ganglia output nuclei; braking and stopping of movement, selection among competing motor programs, and (through limbic and associative subregions) impulse control and mood.

bestView.label: subthalamic nucleus dorsomedial to the internal capsule at the mesodiencephalic junction
STN above the substantia nigra, below the thalamus

imaging.normalAppearance: A small hypointense (iron) oval on T2 and SWI dorsolateral to the red nucleus and above the nigra, best seen on coronal or axial 3 T images; it is the target on stereotactic planning MRI. The MASSP mesh in this atlas outlines it.

pathology.finding: Small restricted-diffusion lesion in the subthalamic region from a posterior perforator.

lesionEffects.mechanism: Suppression of the overactive nucleus in Parkinson disease

superior-cerebellar-peduncle.name: Superior cerebellar peduncle
superior-cerebellar-peduncle.summary: The main outflow of the cerebellum. Axons of the dentate and interposed nuclei ascend in the superior peduncle along the lateral wall of the upper fourth ventricle, cross completely in the caudal midbrain (decussation of the superior cerebellar peduncles), and end in the contralateral red nucleus and the ventral lateral thalamus, which relays to the motor cortex. This double crossing (cerebellum → contralateral thalamus/cortex → contralateral corticospinal tract → back to the original side) is why cerebellar signs are ipsilateral to the lesion. A smaller afferent component, the anterior spinocerebellar tract, enters through this peduncle.

anatomy.location: Dorsolateral upper pons forming the lateral boundary of the rostral fourth ventricle, running upward and medially into the tegmentum of the caudal midbrain where the two sides decussate ventral to the aqueduct at the level of the inferior colliculus.

superior-cerebellar-peduncle.function: Carries the dentatorubrothalamic and interposito-rubral outflow that shapes cortical motor commands and drives the rubrospinal tract; receives the anterior spinocerebellar tract.

bestView.label: dorsolateral upper pons beside the fourth ventricle
decussation in the caudal midbrain tegmentum
peduncle climbing from the dentate nucleus to the midbrain

imaging.normalAppearance: The peduncles are the two white-matter walls of the upper fourth ventricle on axial T2; the decussation is a subtle central band in the caudal midbrain tegmentum. The HCP dentatorubrothalamic tract mesh in this atlas shows the full course to the thalamus.

pathology.pathology: Midbrain tegmental infarct at the decussation
pathology.finding: Small restricted-diffusion lesion in the central caudal midbrain tegmentum; bilateral ataxia because both crossing bundles are hit.

lesionEffects.mechanism: Lesion below the decussation

html.summary: The main outflow of the cerebellum. Axons of the dentate and interposed nuclei ascend in the superior peduncle along the lateral wall of the upper fourth ventricle, cross completely in the caudal midbrain (decussation of the superior cerebellar peduncles), and end in the contralateral red nucleus and the ventral lateral thalamus, which relays to the motor cortex. This double crossing (cerebellum → contralateral thalamus/cortex → contralateral corticospinal tract → back to the original side) is why cerebellar signs are ipsilateral to the lesion. A smaller afferent component, the anterior spinocerebellar tract, enters through this peduncle.
html.function: Carries the dentatorubrothalamic and interposito-rubral outflow that shapes cortical motor commands and drives the rubrospinal tract; receives the anterior spinocerebellar tract.
html.anatomy.location: Dorsolateral upper pons forming the lateral boundary of the rostral fourth ventricle, running upward and medially into the tegmentum of the caudal midbrain where the two sides decussate ventral to the aqueduct at the level of the inferior colliculus.

html.imaging.sequenceOfChoice: FLAIR and DWI through the upper pons and midbrain

superior-colliculus.name: Superior colliculus
superior-colliculus.summary: The upper pair of bumps on the tectum, a layered structure that maps the visual field and directs the eyes and head toward things of interest. Its superficial layers receive direct retinal and visual cortical input; its deep layers integrate auditory and somatosensory maps and send tectospinal, tectobulbar and tecto-reticular fibers that drive saccades and orienting movements. It lies next to the pretectal area and the posterior commissure, so tumors or hydrocephalus pressing on the dorsal midbrain combine up-gaze palsy with pupillary light-near dissociation.

anatomy.location: Dorsal midbrain forming the rostral half of the tectum, behind the aqueduct and periaqueductal gray, below the pineal gland and the posterior commissure; the brachium of the superior colliculus links it to the lateral geniculate body.

subdivisions.name: Superficial layers
subdivisions.note: retinotopic visual map from the retina and striate cortex

subdivisions.name: Intermediate and deep layers
subdivisions.note: multisensory motor map; saccade and head-turn commands to the PPRF, riMLF and spinal cord

superior-colliculus.function: Visual grasp reflex: orients eyes and head to novel stimuli; contributes to saccade generation and to blinking and avoidance responses to visual threat.

bestView.label: rostral tectal plate behind the aqueduct
superior colliculus above the inferior colliculus, under the pineal

imaging.normalAppearance: The colliculi form the posterior surface of the midbrain on sagittal T1 as two stacked bumps; the superior colliculus is the upper one, just below the pineal. Flattening of the tectum by hydrocephalus is best seen on sagittal images.

pathology.finding: Bulbous T2-bright enlargement of the tectal plate compressing the aqueduct with hydrocephalus; often non-enhancing and indolent.

pathology.pathology: Pineal region tumor with dorsal midbrain compression
pathology.finding: Mass in the pineal region flattening the superior colliculi and posterior commissure; Parinaud syndrome.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: Sagittal T2/T1 of the tectum and pineal region; look for aqueductal obstruction

lesionEffects.mechanism: Compression of the posterior commissure and adjacent pretectum (dorsal midbrain syndrome)

lesionEffects.deficit: Impaired visual orienting and saccades to the opposite side
lesionEffects.mechanism: Loss of the collicular motor map
Neighboring pretectal nuclei

Pupil reactions to light and near
Test saccades to sudden peripheral targets
pearls: Up-gaze palsy in a young person with headache: think pineal tumor or hydrocephalus pressing on the tectum

superior-olivary-complex.name: Superior olivary complex and lateral lemniscus
superior-olivary-complex.summary: The first binaural station of the auditory pathway. Axons from the cochlear nuclei cross in the trapezoid body of the caudal pons and converge on the superior olivary complex of both sides, whose neurons compare timing (medial superior olive) and intensity (lateral superior olive) between the two ears to localize sound. Output ascends in the lateral lemniscus to the inferior colliculus. The complex also gives rise to the olivocochlear bundle that tunes the outer hair cells and to the efferent limb of the stapedius reflex through the facial nucleus.

anatomy.location: Ventral tegmentum of the caudal pons, dorsal to the trapezoid body and lateral to the medial lemniscus, just ventromedial to the facial motor nucleus; the lateral lemniscus climbs along the lateral surface of the pontine tegmentum to the inferior colliculus.

superior-olivary-complex.function: Sound localization by interaural time and level differences, the acoustic stapedius reflex, and efferent control of the cochlea.

bestView.label: ventral caudal pontine tegmentum behind the trapezoid body
lateral lemniscus on the lateral upper pons

imaging.normalAppearance: Not resolved on routine MRI; localized to the ventral tegmentum of the caudal pons. Pontine lesions here rarely cause deafness because the pathway is already bilateral.

pathology.pathology: Pontine tegmental lesion with hyperacusis or poor localization
pathology.finding: Tegmental infarct or plaque in the caudal pons; hearing is preserved but sound localization and the stapedius reflex are impaired.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: FLAIR/DWI; audiometry with stapedius reflex testing

lesionEffects.mechanism: Binaural comparison neurons
Efferent limb of the stapedius reflex
Ascending lateral lemniscus fibers

examination: Hearing thresholds are normal; test localization of a sound source with eyes closed
Stapedius reflex on tympanometry
Facial movement and corneal reflex for neighboring structures
pearls: Unilateral deafness never comes from the pons or above
Brainstem auditory evoked potentials map lesions of this pathway wave by wave

pitfalls: PUBLIC EDITION - LOCATION MARKER: the 7 T probabilistic outline of this nucleus may not be redistributed, so the openly shareable build of the atlas shows a landmark-anchored ellipsoid instead: an ellipsoid of about 18 mm3 per side, the 16 mm3 right and 20 mm3 left volumes published by Garcia-Gomar et al. (2019), centered in the ventrolateral pontine tegmentum at the level of the trapezoid body, lateral to the medial lemniscus, and clipped to the brainstem. It marks where the nucleus lies, not where its border runs -- do not read a shape, an edge or a neighbour relation off it, and note that its position is a textbook relation to open landmarks, not a measured centroid.

sympathetic-trunk.name: Sympathetic trunk and ganglia
sympathetic-trunk.summary: A chain of ganglia running along each side of the vertebral column from the skull base to the coccyx, receiving preganglionic fibers from the T1–L2 segments through white rami communicantes and distributing postganglionic fibers to every spinal nerve through gray rami, to the head along the carotid arteries and to the viscera through cardiac, pulmonary and splanchnic nerves. Its three cervical ganglia (superior, middle and stellate) carry the entire sympathetic supply of the head and neck, so lesions of the chain in the neck or chest apex (Pancoast tumor, carotid dissection, surgery) cause Horner syndrome.

anatomy.location: Paravertebral gutter on each side from C1 to the coccyx: cervical ganglia in front of the transverse processes behind the carotid sheath, thoracic ganglia on the heads of the ribs, lumbar ganglia on the vertebral bodies, sacral ganglia medial to the anterior sacral foramina, joining at the ganglion impar.

subdivisions.name: Superior cervical ganglion
subdivisions.note: C1–C4 level; postganglionic fibers to the head (pupil, lid, face sweating) via the internal carotid plexus

subdivisions.name: Middle cervical and stellate (cervicothoracic) ganglia
subdivisions.note: C6–T1; upper limb, heart

subdivisions.name: Thoracic ganglia
subdivisions.note: cardiac and pulmonary nerves; greater, lesser and least splanchnic nerves to the abdomen

subdivisions.name: Lumbar and sacral ganglia
subdivisions.note: lower limb and pelvic viscera

sympathetic-trunk.function: Distribution of sympathetic outflow: vasoconstriction, sweating, piloerection, pupil dilation, cardiac acceleration, bronchodilation and inhibition of gut motility; adrenal medullary stimulation.

bestView.label: upper cervical region; the chain lies in the paravertebral gutter outside the brain volume

imaging.normalAppearance: Not seen as a discrete structure on routine imaging; the stellate ganglion region at the lung apex and the cervical chain behind the carotid sheath are evaluated on chest CT or neck MRI when a Horner syndrome is being explained.

pathology.finding: Apical lung mass invading the stellate ganglion and lower brachial plexus: Horner syndrome with C8–T1 pain and hand weakness.
Mural hematoma of the internal carotid with a partial Horner syndrome from the sympathetic plexus on the artery.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: Chest CT for the apex; neck MRI/MRA for the carotid

lesionEffects.mechanism: Preganglionic (second-order) fibers in the chain or stellate ganglion, or postganglionic fibers along the carotid
Loss of vasoconstrictor and sudomotor supply

lesionEffects.deficit: Loss of the adrenal and cardiac response to stress
lesionEffects.mechanism: Extensive sympathetic failure

examination: Pupil asymmetry in light and dark, ptosis, facial sweating
Skin temperature and sweat pattern of the limbs
Pharmacological pupil testing (apraclonidine, hydroxyamphetamine) to grade the lesion
pearls: Horner syndrome with anhidrosis of the whole face is preganglionic (chain); without anhidrosis it is postganglionic (carotid)

temporal-pole.name: Temporal pole
temporal-pole.summary: The temporal pole is the anterior tip of the temporal lobe, tucked into the middle cranial fossa behind the greater wing of the sphenoid and lateral to the cavernous sinus. It is paralimbic cortex (Brodmann area 38) linking the anterior temporal semantic hub to the amygdala and orbitofrontal cortex through the uncinate fasciculus, and it gives faces, voices and objects their personal and emotional meaning. It is contused in head injury when the brain strikes the sphenoid ridge, it is the epicenter of semantic dementia, it is resected in anterior temporal lobectomy for epilepsy, and it is one of the sites where herpes encephalitis begins.

anatomy.location: Rounded anterior end of the temporal lobe in the middle cranial fossa, in front of the anterior end of the superior, middle and inferior temporal gyri and lateral to the uncus, its medial surface facing the tentorial edge and the cavernous sinus.

afferents.from: Inferior and superior temporal association cortex

temporal-pole.function: The anterior temporal lobe binds the multimodal features of a concept, its appearance, sound, name and associations, into a single representation and links it with emotional value from the amygdala and orbitofrontal cortex; the right pole is critical for recognizing familiar people and the left for naming them and for the meaning of words. It also participates in social cognition and in the autonomic and emotional coloring of memories. Seizures arising here give the rising epigastric aura, fear, deja vu and olfactory hallucinations of medial temporal epilepsy, and bilateral loss produces the placid, hyperoral, visually agnosic Kluver-Bucy state.

bestView.label: temporal pole in the middle cranial fossa lateral to the cavernous sinus
anterior temporal tip behind the sphenoid wing

imaging.normalAppearance: Anterior tip of the temporal lobe on coronal images through the sella, with the middle cranial fossa floor below and the sphenoid wing in front; the polar cortex is thick and its gyri are short and variable.

pathology.finding: Hemorrhagic contusion of the anterior temporal tip after head injury, often with an orbitofrontal contusion on the same or opposite side.
Severe asymmetric anterior temporal atrophy, usually left, with a knife-edge temporal pole and preserved posterior cortex.
Asymmetric T2/FLAIR signal and restricted diffusion in the medial and anterior temporal lobe extending to the insula and orbital cortex, sparing the putamen.
pathology.timing: Changes are present within days; CT is often normal early

lesionEffects.deficit: Loss of word meaning and of knowledge about objects (left)
lesionEffects.mechanism: Degeneration of the anterior temporal semantic hub of the dominant hemisphere

lesionEffects.deficit: Inability to recognize familiar faces and people (right)
lesionEffects.mechanism: Loss of the person-identity node in the right anterior temporal lobe

lesionEffects.deficit: Emotional blunting and Kluver-Bucy features when bilateral
lesionEffects.mechanism: Disconnection of the temporal sensory hierarchy from the amygdala and orbitofrontal cortex

examination: Single-word comprehension and naming of low-frequency objects; ask what a word means
Famous face recognition and identification
Seizure history for auras of fear, deja vu, smell and epigastric rising
pearls: Semantic dementia is an anterior temporal disease: fluent speech empty of nouns and loss of the meaning of words
The temporal pole is injured with the orbitofrontal cortex in the same fall; look at both
Herpes encephalitis attacks the anterior temporal lobe and insula but spares the putamen, a distinction from MCA infarct

tentorium-cerebelli.name: Tentorium cerebelli and incisura
tentorium-cerebelli.summary: A tent-shaped dural fold that roofs the posterior cranial fossa, separating the cerebellum from the occipital lobes and dividing the cranial cavity into supratentorial and infratentorial compartments. Its free anterior edge forms the tentorial incisura (notch) through which the midbrain passes, accompanied by the oculomotor nerves, the posterior cerebral and superior cerebellar arteries and the basal veins. This notch is the site of the herniation syndromes: the uncus herniates down through it and the cerebellar vermis herniates up through it. The transverse sinuses run in its attached margin and the straight sinus along its junction with the falx.

anatomy.location: Attached posteriorly to the transverse sulci of the occipital bone, laterally to the petrous ridges and anteriorly to the clinoid processes; the falx cerebri is attached to its upper surface in the midline; the free edge surrounds the midbrain.

tentorium-cerebelli.function: Support of the occipital lobes, compartmentalization of pressure between the supratentorial and infratentorial spaces, and housing of the transverse and straight sinuses.

arteries: tentorial branches of the internal carotid (meningohypophyseal trunk)

bestView.label: tentorium separating occipital lobe from cerebellum
tentorium from the straight sinus to the occipital bone; the incisura in front

imaging.normalAppearance: A dense line sloping from the vertex of the posterior fossa to the petrous ridges on coronal images; on axial CT its edge appears as a V or Y shape and blood along it (tentorial subdural) is common after trauma. The perimesencephalic cisterns at the incisura should be open; their effacement means transtentorial herniation.

pathology.finding: Medial temporal lobe displaced through the incisura with effaced ambient cistern, midbrain compression and a dilated ipsilateral pupil.
Superior vermis pushed through the incisura by a posterior fossa mass, flattening the quadrigeminal cistern.
Dural-based enhancing mass on either surface of the tentorium.
Dense blood along the tentorium after trauma.

lesionEffects.mechanism: Uncus compressing the oculomotor nerve at the incisura

lesionEffects.deficit: Contralateral hemiparesis, or ipsilateral via Kernohan notch

PCA compressed against the tentorial edge
Trochlear nerve running along the free edge

Visual fields after recovery from herniation
Eye movements
pearls: The tentorial notch is where supratentorial pressure meets the brainstem; the blown pupil is its alarm

territory-aca-major.name: ACA major territory
territory-aca-major.summary: The anterior cerebral artery major territory is the medial surface of the frontal and parietal lobes from the frontal pole to the parieto-occipital sulcus, the superior margin of the hemisphere for a centimeter or two onto the convexity, the corpus callosum except the splenium, and, through the recurrent artery of Heubner, the caudate head and the anterior limb of the internal capsule. This level-2 map merges the cortical and deep ACA domains. Infarction is uncommon because the anterior communicating artery provides a collateral, and it produces contralateral leg weakness, abulia, urinary incontinence and, with the callosum, disconnection signs; bilateral infarction from a single azygos trunk or after anterior communicating aneurysm surgery produces akinetic mutism.

anatomy.location: Medial frontal and parietal cortex (superior frontal gyrus, paracentral lobule, cingulate gyrus, precuneus, medial orbital cortex), the superior convexity margin, the genu, body and part of the splenium of the corpus callosum, the septal area and, via Heubner's artery, the caudate head and anterior limb, bordered laterally by the MCA territory and posteriorly by the PCA territory at the parieto-occipital sulcus.

afferents.from: Anterior cerebral artery A1-A5 segments, recurrent artery of Heubner

efferents.to: Superior sagittal sinus via superior cerebral veins

territory-aca-major.function: The territory contains the leg and foot areas of the motor and sensory cortex in the paracentral lobule, the supplementary motor area and anterior cingulate that initiate movement and speech, the medial prefrontal cortex of motivation and social behavior, the micturition center of the medial frontal lobe and the callosal fibers that join the hemispheres; its deep part carries the frontal-striatal loops through the caudate head. Infarction therefore produces leg-predominant weakness, apraxia of gait, abulia, incontinence and, on the left, transcortical motor aphasia; the parasagittal border zone with the MCA is the site of watershed infarcts that produce bilateral proximal weakness (man-in-a-barrel).

bestView.label: ACA territory on the medial hemisphere
ACA domain over the superior margin and the corpus callosum

imaging.normalAppearance: On the overlay the ACA domain covers the medial surface and the superior rim of the convexity and the corpus callosum; the boundary with the MCA territory runs along the superior frontal sulcus region on the convexity.

pathology.finding: Restricted diffusion of the medial frontal cortex and the paracentral lobule, sometimes the caudate head, with contralateral leg weakness and abulia.

pathology.pathology: Bilateral ACA infarct (azygos ACA or vasospasm after AComm aneurysm)
pathology.finding: Symmetric medial frontal infarcts with akinetic mutism, paraparesis and incontinence.
Midline shift with the cingulate gyrus under the falx and a secondary ACA infarct on the side of the mass.

lesionEffects.deficit: Contralateral leg-predominant weakness and sensory loss
lesionEffects.mechanism: Paracentral lobule infarction
Medial frontal and anterior cingulate infarction
Medial frontal micturition and gait control areas

lesionEffects.deficit: Callosal disconnection: left-hand apraxia and agraphia
lesionEffects.mechanism: Infarction of the genu and body of the corpus callosum

examination: Leg strength and gait initiation
Spontaneous speech and initiative
Bladder control and grasp reflexes
pearls: Leg weaker than arm means ACA; face and arm weaker than leg means MCA
The anterior communicating artery is the collateral that makes ACA strokes rare
Akinetic mutism after aneurysm surgery is bilateral ACA territory ischemia

territory-aca.name: ACA territory
territory-aca.summary: The cortex and white matter perfused by the anterior cerebral artery: the medial surface of the frontal and parietal lobes from the frontal pole back to the parieto-occipital sulcus, a thin strip over the superior convexity, the anterior corpus callosum and, through the recurrent artery of Heubner and medial lenticulostriates, the head of the caudate and the anterior limb of the internal capsule. Clinically it is the territory of the leg, of initiative and of bladder control.

territory-aica.name: AICA territory
territory-aica.summary: The lateral caudal pons, the middle cerebellar peduncle, the inner ear and the anterior inferior cerebellum perfused by the anterior inferior cerebellar artery. Infarction combines lateral pontine signs with deafness and vertigo, and because the labyrinthine artery is an end artery the cochlea is often the first casualty. The territory is small and variable: when AICA is hypoplastic, PICA takes over the cerebellar part, and when PICA is hypoplastic, AICA extends downward, so the border with the PICA territory is the least predictable in the posterior fossa.

territory-anterior-choroidal-thalamoperf.name: Anterior choroidal and thalamoperforating territory
territory-anterior-choroidal-thalamoperf.summary: This combined territory groups the deep region supplied by the anterior choroidal artery from the internal carotid with the anterior thalamoperforating (tuberothalamic) domain of the posterior communicating artery: the lower posterior limb of the internal capsule, the medial pallidum, the optic tract and lateral geniculate body, the cerebral peduncle, the hippocampal head, the uncus and the anterior thalamus. It is the territory of the anterior choroidal syndrome (hemiparesis, hemisensory loss and hemianopia without cortical signs) and of the tuberothalamic infarct (amnesia, apathy and facial paresis for emotional movement), two of the most instructive deep strokes because a single small vessel produces three long-tract signs or a frontal-limbic syndrome.

territory-anterior-choroidal-thalamoperf.function: The anterior choroidal artery runs from the carotid along the optic tract to the choroidal fissure, giving perforators to the posterior limb (corticospinal, thalamocortical and optic radiation fibers), the pallidum, the optic tract and geniculate, the medial temporal lobe and the peduncle; the tuberothalamic artery from the posterior communicating supplies the anterior thalamic nuclei and the ventral anterior nucleus that carry the Papez memory circuit and the frontal-thalamic loops. Occlusion of the former produces the triad of hemiparesis, hemianesthesia and hemianopia; of the latter, amnesia, abulia and a facial paresis of emotional expression, with hypophonia and, on the left, thalamic aphasia.

territory-basilar-paramedian.name: Basilar paramedian (pontine) territory
territory-basilar-paramedian.summary: The medial pons and, by extension, the medial medulla and midbrain perfused by the paramedian perforators of the basilar and vertebral arteries. It contains the corticospinal tract, the medial lemniscus, the abducens and facial nuclei, the MLF and the hypoglossal and oculomotor nuclear regions, so infarcts here produce the classic crossed brainstem syndromes and, when bilateral, the locked-in state.

territory-basilar.name: Basilar (pontine) territory
territory-basilar.summary: The basilar territory is the pons and the ventral midbrain supplied by the paramedian, short circumferential and long circumferential branches of the basilar artery. This level-1 domain covers the whole pons, so it includes the paramedian pontine lacunes of small vessel disease (pure motor hemiparesis, ataxic hemiparesis, dysarthria-clumsy hand), the lateral pontine syndromes of the circumferential branches (Millard-Gubler, Foville and the AICA syndrome), and the bilateral ventral pontine infarction of basilar occlusion that produces the locked-in state. The paramedian branches are end-arteries with no collateral, which is why the pons is the commonest brainstem site of lacunes and of hypertensive hemorrhage.

anatomy.location: The entire pons (basis and tegmentum) and the ventral and paramedian midbrain, from the pontomedullary junction to the interpeduncular fossa, including the middle cerebellar peduncle's proximal part; paramedian branches supply the medial basis and tegmentum, short circumferential branches the lateral basis, and long circumferential branches (AICA, SCA) the lateral tegmentum and peduncles; bounded below by the vertebral and PICA territories of the medulla and above by the PCA thalamic and midbrain domains.

afferents.from: Paramedian, short circumferential and long circumferential branches of the basilar artery

efferents.to: Anterior pontomesencephalic vein and petrosal veins

territory-basilar.function: The territory contains the corticospinal and corticopontine fibers of the basis pontis, the pontine nuclei, the medial lemniscus and MLF, the abducens and facial nuclei and the pontine gaze center, the trigeminal nuclei, the vestibular and cochlear nuclei, the locus coeruleus and the pontine reticular formation that sustains consciousness and breathing, so ischemia produces the crossed pontine syndromes (ipsilateral VI or VII palsy with contralateral hemiparesis), internuclear ophthalmoplegia and gaze palsy, and, when bilateral, coma or the locked-in state. Thrombosis of the basilar trunk, embolism to its top and hypertensive lipohyalinosis of its perforators are the three mechanisms.

territory-inferior-cerebellar.name: Inferior cerebellar (PICA/AICA) territory
territory-inferior-cerebellar.summary: The inferior cerebellar territory combines the domains of the posterior inferior and anterior inferior cerebellar arteries: the inferior and posterior cerebellar surface, the tonsils, the inferior vermis with the nodulus, the flocculus, and the lateral medulla and lateral caudal pons. It is the territory of the lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome and the lateral pontine (AICA) syndrome, of the isolated vertigo of medial PICA infarction that mimics vestibular neuritis, and of the large PICA infarct that swells against the fourth ventricle and herniates the tonsils. Its arteries arise from the vertebral (PICA) and basilar (AICA) trunks and are occluded by vertebral dissection, atherosclerosis and embolism.

anatomy.location: Posterior and inferior cerebellar surface (Crus II, lobules VII-X, the tonsils and inferior vermis) from PICA, the anterior inferior surface with the flocculus and the middle cerebellar peduncle region from AICA, the lateral medulla (PICA and vertebral perforators) and the lateral caudal pontine tegmentum and inner ear (AICA and labyrinthine artery); bounded above by the SCA territory and medially by the medullary and pontine paramedian territories.

efferents.to: Inferior cerebellar veins to the transverse and sigmoid sinuses

territory-inferior-cerebellar.function: The territory holds the vestibulocerebellum and the vestibular nuclei, the lateral medullary tegmentum with the spinal trigeminal tract, the spinothalamic tract, the nucleus ambiguus and the descending sympathetic fibers, the lateral pontine tegmentum with the facial and cochlear nuclei, and the inner ear, so ischemia produces vertigo, nystagmus and truncal ataxia, the crossed sensory loss and bulbar palsy of Wallenberg syndrome, or the facial palsy and deafness of the AICA syndrome; the PICA domain of the inferior cerebellum swells dangerously because the posterior fossa has no room. Collaterals between PICA, AICA and SCA over the surface vary and determine the infarct's size.

territory-lateral-lenticulostriate.name: Lateral lenticulostriate territory
territory-lateral-lenticulostriate.summary: The lateral lenticulostriate territory is the deep region supplied by the lateral striate arteries that rise from the M1 segment through the anterior perforated substance: the posterior putamen, the lateral globus pallidus, the body of the caudate and the upper part of the capsule's posterior limb and the corona radiata. It is the most important small-vessel territory of the hemisphere: it is the site of the pure motor lacune and of the striatocapsular infarct after MCA embolism, the site of the hypertensive putaminal hemorrhage that is the commonest intracerebral bleed, and it has no collateral supply, so it is the irreversible core of every MCA occlusion.

anatomy.location: Posterior two-thirds of the putamen, the lateral part of the globus pallidus, the body of the caudate, the upper two-thirds of the capsule's posterior limb together with the adjacent corona radiata, between the medial lenticulostriate territory in front, the anterior choroidal territory below and behind in the lower posterior limb, and the insular and cortical MCA territories laterally.

territory-lateral-lenticulostriate.function: The territory contains the corticospinal and corticobulbar fibers and the thalamocortical sensory fibers of the posterior limb, the motor striatum and the lateral pallidum, so its infarction produces the classic capsular syndrome of contralateral face-arm-leg hemiparesis with or without sensory loss, dysarthria and, from the striatum, later dystonia or chorea; a striatocapsular infarct from transient M1 occlusion adds cortical signs (aphasia, neglect) from the hypoperfused convexity. html.summary: The lateral lenticulostriate territory is the deep region supplied by the lateral striate arteries that rise from the M1 segment through the anterior perforated substance: the posterior putamen, the lateral globus pallidus, the body of the caudate and the upper part of the capsule's posterior limb and the corona radiata. It is the most important small-vessel territory of the hemisphere: it is the site of the pure motor lacune and of the striatocapsular infarct after MCA embolism, the site of the hypertensive putaminal hemorrhage that is the commonest intracerebral bleed, and it has no collateral supply, so it is the irreversible core of every MCA occlusion.

territory-mca-frontal.name: MCA territory, frontal
territory-mca-frontal.summary: The frontal MCA territory is the lateral frontal lobe supplied by the superior division of the middle cerebral artery: the inferior and middle frontal gyri, the precentral gyrus for the face and arm, the frontal operculum and the frontal eye field. It is the territory of the classical superior division stroke: contralateral face-arm weakness, gaze deviation toward the lesion and, on the left, Broca aphasia, with relative sparing of the leg, the visual fields and comprehension. Its border with the ACA territory along the superior frontal sulcus is a watershed, and its deep boundary is the corona radiata supplied by the medullary arteries and the lenticulostriates.

anatomy.location: Lateral frontal convexity from the frontal pole back to the central sulcus, including the middle and inferior frontal gyri, the lateral part of the superior frontal gyrus, the precentral gyrus below the leg area and the frontal operculum, extending into the underlying white matter to the corona radiata; bounded above by the ACA territory and behind by the parietal MCA territory.

territory-mca-frontal.function: The territory contains the motor cortex of the face, tongue and arm, the premotor and frontal eye field areas, the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and, on the left, the Broca region, so its infarction produces a brachiofacial hemiparesis, ipsiversive gaze deviation, executive dysfunction and non-fluent aphasia; it is supplied by the orbitofrontal, prefrontal, precentral and central branches of the superior division, and collaterals from the ACA over the convexity limit the infarct in slow occlusions. Its deep white matter is a common site of internal border-zone infarcts when the carotid is stenosed.

territory-mca-insular.name: MCA territory, insular
territory-mca-insular.summary: The insular MCA territory is the insula, the claustrum and the extreme and external capsules, supplied by short perforating branches of the M2 segments as they course over the insular surface. It is the first cortex to lose its gray-white distinction in an M1 occlusion (the insular ribbon sign) because it is the most distal territory of the perforators with no leptomeningeal collateral, and it is infarcted in almost every MCA stem stroke. Insular infarction adds autonomic instability, cardiac arrhythmia and altered taste and pain perception to the hemispheric signs, and its right-sided involvement carries the highest risk of sudden cardiac death after stroke.

anatomy.location: The insular cortex within the Sylvian fissure (anterior and posterior lobules), the claustrum, the extreme and external capsules, and the medial surface of the opercula facing the insula; bounded laterally by the opercular parts of the frontal, parietal and temporal territories and medially by the lenticulostriate territory of the putamen.

afferents.from: Short insular perforators from the M2 segments

efferents.to: Deep middle cerebral vein to the basal vein of Rosenthal

territory-mca-insular.function: The insula is the visceral and interoceptive cortex: it contains the primary gustatory cortex, the vestibular cortex, the cortical representation of pain and of visceral sensation, and the autonomic control areas that set heart rate and blood pressure, with the right anterior insula driving sympathetic and the left parasympathetic tone; it is also part of the language system on the left (articulation) and of the salience network on both sides. Its infarction produces cardiac arrhythmias, blood pressure lability, troponin rise and altered taste, contributes to apraxia of speech and impaired swallowing, and, when it is the only region infarcted, suggests a lenticulostriate or M2 perforator occlusion.

territory-mca-major.name: MCA major territory
territory-mca-major.summary: The middle cerebral artery major territory is the largest arterial domain of the hemisphere, the lateral convexity from the frontal pole to the occipital pole together with the insula, the temporal lobe convexity and, through the lenticulostriate arteries, the striatum and the internal capsule. This level-2 territory map merges the frontal, parietal, temporal, occipital and insular MCA subterritories with the lenticulostriate domains, and it is the region infarcted by an M1 occlusion: the malignant MCA infarct that swells to threaten herniation and the stroke that carries the whole textbook of hemispheric signs, contralateral face-arm-leg hemiplegia, hemianesthesia, hemianopia, gaze deviation and aphasia or neglect.

anatomy.location: Lateral surface of the frontal, parietal and temporal lobes, the lateral occipital lobe, the insula and opercula, the claustrum and the extreme capsule, and the deep structures supplied by the lenticulostriates (putamen, caudate body, lateral pallidum, upper internal capsule), bounded by the ACA territory along the superior margin, the PCA territory on the inferomedial temporal and occipital surface, and the anterior choroidal territory in the posterior limb.

afferents.from: Middle cerebral artery M1-M4 segments and lenticulostriate arteries

efferents.to: Superficial and deep middle cerebral veins

territory-mca-major.function: It contains the primary motor and sensory cortex for the face and arm, the frontal eye field, the language areas of the dominant hemisphere and the attention network of the non-dominant one, the auditory cortex, the insula and the striatum, so that occlusion of the stem produces the most extensive single-artery syndrome in neurology. Perfusion depends on the circle of Willis and on leptomeningeal collaterals from the ACA and PCA, which define the penumbra that thrombectomy tries to save; the deep lenticulostriate territory has no collaterals and infarcts first. Complete territory infarction swells over three days and can herniate, especially in young patients with no room for edema.

territory-mca-occipital.name: MCA territory, occipital
territory-mca-occipital.summary: The occipital MCA territory is the small lateral occipital domain supplied by the temporo-occipital and angular branches of the middle cerebral artery: the lateral occipital gyri and the occipital pole convexity, where the MCA shares the macular cortex with the posterior cerebral artery. It explains macular sparing after PCA occlusion and it is the cortex most exposed to border-zone ischemia between the MCA and PCA; its infarction contributes to the visual perceptual deficits of posterior MCA strokes and the bilateral posterior watershed syndrome of hypotension with Balint features. Its boundary with the PCA territory is variable, and the lateral occipital cortex may be PCA-supplied in some individuals.

anatomy.location: Lateral surface of the occipital lobe (superior and inferior lateral occipital gyri) and the lateral part of the occipital pole, with the underlying white matter continuous with the stratum sagittale; bounded medially and inferiorly by the PCA territory at the lateral occipital sulcus region and in front by the parietal and temporal MCA territories.

efferents.to: Vein of Labbe and superficial occipital veins to the transverse sinus

territory-mca-occipital.function: The territory contains dorsal and ventral extrastriate visual areas (motion, shape and part of the lateral occipital complex) and, at the pole, part of the macular primary visual cortex, so its infarction impairs motion perception, visual attention and shape recognition in the contralateral field and, combined with the parietal territory, produces the optic ataxia and simultanagnosia of the parieto-occipital watershed; its dual supply is the anatomical basis of macular sparing in PCA strokes and of the occipital pole infarct of hypotension. The temporo-occipital artery reaches it from the inferior division and the angular artery from above.

territory-mca-parietal.name: MCA territory, parietal
synonyms: posterior parietal and angular artery territory
territory-mca-parietal.summary: The parietal MCA territory is the lateral parietal lobe supplied by the anterior and posterior parietal and angular branches of the middle cerebral artery: the postcentral gyrus below the leg area, the supramarginal and angular gyri and the lateral superior parietal lobule. It is the domain of cortical sensory loss, of neglect and anosognosia on the right, of Gerstmann syndrome and conduction aphasia on the left, and of the optic radiation fibers that give an inferior quadrantanopia. Its posterior edge with the PCA territory is the parieto-occipital watershed, the classic site of border-zone infarction in hypotension and carotid disease.

anatomy.location: Lateral parietal convexity behind the central sulcus, including the postcentral gyrus (except the medial leg area), the supramarginal and angular gyri and the lateral superior parietal lobule, with the underlying white matter of the parietal corona radiata and part of the stratum sagittale; bounded above by the ACA territory, behind by the PCA territory and below by the temporal MCA territory at the Sylvian fissure.

afferents.from: Anterior and posterior parietal and angular arteries of the MCA

efferents.to: Superior anastomotic vein of Trolard and the superior sagittal sinus

territory-mca-parietal.function: The territory holds the primary somatosensory cortex for the face and arm, the secondary somatosensory cortex, the inferior parietal association cortex of language, praxis, calculation and attention, and the superior parietal cortex of spatial and visuomotor function, so its infarction produces cortical sensory loss and astereognosis, ideomotor apraxia, neglect or Gerstmann syndrome, and a field defect from the parietal fibers of the optic radiation. It is supplied by the posterior parietal and angular arteries, which arise from either division of the MCA, and its convexity has leptomeningeal collaterals from the PCA and ACA that make it both the site of and the protection against watershed ischemia.

territory-mca-temporal.name: MCA territory, temporal
territory-mca-temporal.summary: The temporal MCA territory is the lateral temporal lobe supplied by the inferior division of the middle cerebral artery: the superior, middle and part of the inferior temporal gyri, the temporal pole, Heschl's gyrus and the planum temporale, with the underlying temporal stem and Meyer's loop of the optic radiation. It is the territory of Wernicke aphasia on the left and of auditory neglect and aprosodia on the right, both with a superior quadrantanopia and no weakness, the pattern of the inferior division stroke that is often mistaken for confusion or psychiatric illness. Its inferior edge with the PCA territory on the inferior temporal gyrus is a watershed.

anatomy.location: Lateral temporal convexity from the temporal pole to the temporo-occipital junction, including the superior and middle temporal gyri, the upper inferior temporal gyrus, the transverse temporal gyri and the planum temporale, and the underlying white matter including the temporal stem and Meyer's loop; bounded above by the Sylvian fissure and the parietal territory, below by the PCA territory and medially by the anterior choroidal territory.

territory-mca.name: MCA territory
territory-mca.summary: The largest cortical territory: almost the entire lateral convexity of the hemisphere, the insula and the underlying white matter, plus the deep territory of the lenticulostriate arteries. It holds the face, hand and arm areas of the motor and sensory cortices, both language areas in the dominant hemisphere, the frontal eye field, the auditory cortex and the parietal association cortex, so an MCA stroke is the prototype of the 'cortical' syndrome.

territory-mca.function: Motor and sensory control of the contralateral face, hand and arm; language (dominant); spatial attention and body schema (non-dominant); saccadic gaze control; hearing; the optic radiation passing through the parietotemporal white matter.
