territory-medial-lenticulostriate.name: Medial lenticulostriate territory
territory-medial-lenticulostriate.summary: The medial lenticulostriate territory is the deep region supplied by the medial striate arteries that arise from the proximal M1 and the A1 segment, including the recurrent artery of Heubner: the head of the caudate, the anterior limb of the internal capsule and the anterior part of the putamen and pallidum. It is a perforator territory without collaterals, infarcted by small vessel disease, by proximal MCA or ACA embolism and by vasospasm after anterior communicating aneurysm rupture, and its strokes produce frontal-subcortical signs, abulia, confusion, executive dysfunction, with mild face-arm weakness and dysarthria rather than the dense hemiplegia of the lateral lenticulostriate territory.

anatomy.location: Head of the caudate nucleus, the anterior limb and genu of the internal capsule, the anterior third of the putamen and the anterior globus pallidus, and the adjacent anterior perforated substance, between the medial ACA territory of the septal region and the lateral lenticulostriate territory of the posterior putamen and posterior limb.

afferents.from: Medial lenticulostriate arteries from M1 and the recurrent artery of Heubner from A1-A2

efferents.to: Thalamostriate and septal veins to the internal cerebral vein

territory-medial-lenticulostriate.function: The territory contains the anterior thalamic radiation and the frontopontine and corticostriatal fibers of the anterior limb, the caudate head of the prefrontal basal ganglia loops and the anterior putamen, so ischemia produces the picture of a frontal lobe lesion without cortical involvement: abulia, inattention, executive dysfunction, disinhibition or agitation and, on the left, transcortical motor aphasia, with mild contralateral weakness of the face and arm from the genu. The recurrent artery of Heubner is the single largest vessel of the territory and is at risk during anterior communicating aneurysm surgery; the other medial striate arteries arise from the M1 segment and are occluded by the same emboli that block the MCA.

territory-pca-major.name: PCA major territory
territory-pca-major.summary: The posterior cerebral artery major territory is the occipital lobe, the inferomedial temporal lobe (parahippocampal and fusiform gyri, hippocampus), the splenium and, through the thalamoperforating, thalamogeniculate and posterior choroidal arteries, most of the thalamus and part of the midbrain. This level-2 map merges the occipital and temporal PCA cortical domains with the thalamic and midbrain perforator territories, and it is the territory infarcted in a P1 or P2 occlusion, most often embolic from the heart or the vertebrobasilar system. Its signature is a contralateral homonymous hemianopia, with memory loss, alexia, visual agnosia and thalamic sensory loss according to the extent, and bilateral infarction produces cortical blindness.

anatomy.location: Medial and inferior occipital lobe (calcarine cortex, cuneus, lingual gyrus), the occipital pole, the inferomedial temporal lobe (parahippocampal, fusiform and inferior temporal gyri, hippocampus), the splenium, and the deep territory of the thalamus (except the tuberothalamic part when the PComm supplies it), the subthalamus and the medial midbrain; bounded by the MCA territory laterally and the ACA territory at the parieto-occipital sulcus.

afferents.from: Posterior cerebral artery P1-P4 segments and perforators

efferents.to: Basal vein of Rosenthal and the great cerebral vein, transverse sinus

territory-pca-major.function: The territory contains the primary and association visual cortex, the ventral visual stream of object and face recognition, the medial temporal memory system, the splenial fibers that join the two visual cortices and the thalamic relays of sensation, arousal and memory, so its infarction produces visual, memory and sensory syndromes rather than weakness, unless the midbrain peduncle is involved. Leptomeningeal collaterals from the MCA spare the occipital pole (macular sparing) in many cases; the perforator territories have none. Embolic occlusion of the basilar tip involves both PCAs and the thalami at once.

territory-pca-occipital.name: PCA territory, occipital
territory-pca-occipital.summary: The occipital PCA territory is the medial and inferior occipital lobe supplied by the calcarine and parieto-occipital arteries, the terminal branches of the posterior cerebral artery: the calcarine cortex, the cuneus, the lingual gyrus, the occipital fusiform gyrus and the medial occipital pole. It is the territory of the homonymous hemianopia, congruous and often macular-sparing, and of the visual agnosias, achromatopsia and alexia that follow ventral occipital infarction; bilateral infarction produces cortical blindness. It is supplied through a single P2-P3 trunk that embolism from the vertebrobasilar system or the heart blocks, and its cortex is exposed to the posterior watershed on its lateral edge.

anatomy.location: Medial occipital surface (cuneus, calcarine cortex, lingual gyrus) and the inferior occipital surface (occipital fusiform gyrus), the medial part of the occipital pole and the parieto-occipital sulcus region, with the underlying white matter of the optic radiation's posterior part and the forceps major; bounded laterally by the MCA occipital territory and in front by the temporal PCA territory and the ACA territory at the precuneus.

efferents.to: Internal occipital veins to the great cerebral vein and the transverse sinus

territory-pca-occipital.function: The territory contains the primary visual cortex and the ventral extrastriate areas of color, form and reading, so its infarction produces a contralateral hemianopia or quadrantanopia (depending on which calcarine bank is involved), hemiachromatopsia, and, in the dominant hemisphere with the splenium, alexia without agraphia; the occipital pole receives collateral MCA supply and survives in many occlusions, and leptomeningeal anastomoses with the MCA along the lateral occipital surface determine the size of the infarct. It is also the region affected in posterior reversible encephalopathy, migraine aura and occipital epilepsy, all of which mimic transient ischemia.

territory-pca-temporal.name: PCA territory, temporal
synonyms: anterior and posterior temporal artery territory
territory-pca-temporal.summary: The temporal PCA territory is the inferomedial temporal lobe supplied by the anterior and posterior temporal branches of the posterior cerebral artery's P2 segment: the parahippocampal, fusiform and inferior temporal gyri, the hippocampus (with the anterior choroidal artery) and the temporal pole's inferior surface. It is the territory of the memory and recognition syndromes of PCA stroke: amnesia, prosopagnosia and visual agnosia, and it contributes the upper quadrant defect through Meyer's loop. It borders the MCA temporal territory along the inferior temporal gyrus, a watershed, and it is the cortex compressed against the tentorium and infarcted by PCA compression during uncal herniation.

anatomy.location: Inferomedial temporal lobe from the temporal pole to the occipito-temporal junction, including the parahippocampal gyrus, the hippocampus, the fusiform gyrus and the inferior temporal gyrus, resting on the tentorium and the middle cranial fossa floor; bounded laterally by the MCA temporal territory, medially by the anterior choroidal territory of the hippocampal head and posteriorly by the occipital PCA territory.

territory-pca-temporal.function: The territory contains the medial temporal memory system (hippocampus, entorhinal and parahippocampal cortex) and the ventral visual recognition cortex (fusiform face and word areas, inferior temporal object areas), so its infarction produces amnesia, which is severe and permanent when bilateral, prosopagnosia and landmark agnosia on the right, and associative agnosia and alexia on the left, together with the upper quadrant defect from the temporal optic radiation. The P2 segment runs in the ambient cistern beside the uncus and is compressed in uncal herniation, producing a secondary PCA infarct of this territory.

It is the anatomical substrate of the Wallenberg syndrome and of the inferior cerebellar infarct that swells against the fourth ventricle.

territory-posterior-choroidal-thalamoper.name: Posterior choroidal and thalamoperforating territory
territory-posterior-choroidal-thalamoper.summary: This combined deep territory groups the paramedian (posterior thalamoperforating) domain of the P1 segment with the thalamogeniculate and posterior choroidal domains of the P2 segment: the medial and paramedian thalamus, the intralaminar nuclei, the ventrolateral and ventral posterior nuclei, the pulvinar and geniculate bodies, the posterior thalamus and the medial midbrain. It is the territory of the paramedian thalamic infarct with its somnolence, vertical gaze palsy and amnesia, bilateral when a single artery of Percheron supplies both sides, and of the thalamogeniculate pure sensory stroke that becomes the Dejerine-Roussy pain syndrome; it is also where hypertensive thalamic hemorrhage occurs.

anatomy.location: The medial, paramedian, ventral, posterior and lateral thalamus except the anterior tuberothalamic domain, the subthalamus, the medial midbrain and the posterior choroid plexus, between the anterior choroidal-tuberothalamic territory in front, the PCA cortical territories behind and the basilar territory below in the midbrain.

afferents.from: Posterior thalamoperforating (paramedian) arteries from P1, thalamogeniculate and posterior choroidal arteries from P2

efferents.to: Internal cerebral veins and the great cerebral vein

territory-posterior-choroidal-thalamoper.function: The paramedian arteries from P1 supply the intralaminar and mediodorsal nuclei that sustain arousal and memory and the medial midbrain with the rostral interstitial nucleus of the MLF for vertical gaze; the thalamogeniculate arteries from P2 supply the ventral posterior sensory relay and the ventrolateral motor relay; the posterior choroidal arteries supply the pulvinar, the geniculate bodies and the posterior thalamus. Infarction produces, respectively, hypersomnolence with vertical gaze palsy and amnesia, hemisensory loss with delayed central pain and ataxia, and visual field and attention deficits; the paramedian vessels have no collateral and are occluded by basilar tip embolism, so a top-of-the-basilar stroke involves this territory on both sides.

bestView.label: paramedian, thalamogeniculate and posterior choroidal territory of the thalamus
deep PCA domain of the thalamus and medial midbrain

imaging.normalAppearance: On the overlay this domain covers most of the thalamus behind the anterior nuclei and the medial midbrain; on imaging a paramedian infarct is a symmetric medial thalamic diffusion lesion and a thalamogeniculate infarct a small posterolateral one.

pathology.finding: Bilateral symmetric paramedian thalamic restricted diffusion with or without a V-shaped midbrain lesion, presenting with coma or hypersomnolence, vertical gaze palsy and amnesia.
Small posterolateral thalamic diffusion lesion with contralateral hemisensory loss; central pain develops in a third.
Hyperdense thalamic hematoma with hemisensory loss, hemiparesis and, when medial, drowsiness and downward gaze deviation with small pupils.

lesionEffects.deficit: Hypersomnolence, vertical gaze palsy and amnesia
lesionEffects.mechanism: Paramedian thalamic and medial midbrain infarction

lesionEffects.deficit: Contralateral hemisensory loss and delayed thalamic pain
lesionEffects.mechanism: Thalamogeniculate infarction of the ventral posterior nuclei
Posterior choroidal infarction of the geniculate and pulvinar

Sensation on the face, arm and leg
Visual fields and delayed recall

territory-sca.name: SCA territory
territory-sca.summary: The superior cerebellum, dentate nucleus, superior cerebellar peduncle and dorsolateral rostral pons perfused by the superior cerebellar artery. It is the cerebellar territory that produces the purest limb ataxia, because the dentate nucleus and its outflow through the superior peduncle sit inside it, and the one whose infarcts most often come from cardiac emboli lodging at the basilar tip.

anatomy.location: Cerebellar hemisphere and vermis above the horizontal fissure (anterior lobe and the upper part of the posterior lobe), the dentate nucleus and the other deep nuclei, the superior cerebellar peduncle as it climbs toward the midbrain, and the dorsolateral tegmentum of the upper pons where the spinothalamic tract and descending sympathetic fibers run.

territory-sca.function: Coordination of the ipsilateral limbs through the dentate nucleus and the dentatorubrothalamic outflow in the superior peduncle; relay of pain and temperature (spinothalamic tract) and sympathetic outflow to the head in the rostral pontine tegmentum.

bloodSupply.note: Territory boundaries in this atlas come from a probabilistic stroke-lesion atlas (Liu et al. 2023) and shift between individuals with the anatomy of the circle of Willis.

bestView.label: superior cerebellar hemisphere under the tentorium
territory above the horizontal fissure

imaging.normalAppearance: The upper cerebellum on axial slices just below the tentorium; the boundary with the PICA territory runs along the horizontal fissure.

pathology.finding: Wedge of restricted diffusion in the superior cerebellum reaching the tentorial surface, with variable rostral pontine involvement.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: DWI; CTA

lesionEffects.deficit: Ipsilateral limb ataxia and intention tremor
lesionEffects.mechanism: Dentate nucleus and superior peduncle
Spinothalamic tract in the rostral pons
Sympathetic fibers in the tegmentum

territory-superior-cerebellar.name: Superior cerebellar artery territory
territory-superior-cerebellar.summary: The superior cerebellar artery territory is the superior surface of the cerebellum, the anterior lobe and upper posterior lobe with the superior vermis, together with the dentate nucleus, the superior cerebellar peduncle and the dorsolateral upper pons and lower midbrain. It is the territory of the SCA syndrome: ipsilateral limb ataxia and dysarthria, contralateral loss of pain and temperature from the lateral tegmentum, and, in large infarcts, cerebellar swelling with upward transtentorial herniation. It borders the AICA and PICA territories on the cerebellar surface in a variable watershed, and its cortical branches receive collaterals from those arteries, so its infarcts are often smaller than the full domain.

anatomy.location: Superior surface of both cerebellar hemispheres and the superior vermis (lobules I-VI, upper Crus I), the deep white matter with the dentate nucleus, the superior cerebellar peduncle and the dorsolateral tegmentum of the rostral pons and caudal midbrain; bounded below by the AICA and PICA territories at the horizontal fissure region and medially by the basilar territory of the pons.

afferents.from: Superior cerebellar artery (medial and lateral branches)

efferents.to: Superior cerebellar veins to the great cerebral vein and the straight sinus

territory-superior-cerebellar.function: The territory contains the anterior lobe's sensorimotor cortex for the limbs and trunk, the cerebellar outflow through the dentate nucleus and superior peduncle, the spinothalamic tract and the lateral lemniscus in the upper pontine tegmentum, the superior cerebellar peduncle's decussation and the trochlear nucleus region, so its infarction produces ipsilateral ataxia and intention tremor, dysarthria, contralateral spinothalamic sensory loss, and sometimes a contralateral trochlear palsy or Horner syndrome; its infarcts are usually embolic and often accompany PCA infarcts from the basilar tip. Swelling of a large SCA infarct compresses the midbrain and the aqueduct from above.

bestView.label: superior cerebellar artery territory on the upper cerebellum
SCA domain of the superior vermis and anterior lobe

imaging.normalAppearance: On the overlay the SCA domain covers the superior cerebellar surface beneath the tentorium and the upper pontine tegmentum; on imaging an SCA infarct is a wedge of the superior cerebellum reaching the tentorial surface.

pathology.finding: Hyperdense superior cerebellar hematoma with acute ataxia, vomiting and headache.

lesionEffects.mechanism: Anterior lobe, dentate and superior peduncle infarction
Paravermian and dentate outflow infarction

lesionEffects.deficit: Contralateral loss of pain and temperature
lesionEffects.mechanism: Spinothalamic tract in the lateral upper pontine tegmentum
Swelling of the superior cerebellum against the midbrain

Pin-prick on the side opposite the ataxia

territory-vertebrobasilar-major.name: Vertebrobasilar major territory
territory-vertebrobasilar-major.summary: The vertebrobasilar major territory is the whole posterior fossa supply of the vertebral and basilar arteries and their branches: the medulla, the pons, the midbrain, the cerebellum and, at the top, the thalamic and occipital territories of the posterior cerebral arteries when they are included. This level-2 map merges the basilar (pontine), superior cerebellar and inferior cerebellar (PICA and AICA) domains, and it is the territory of the posterior circulation stroke, whose warning symptoms (vertigo, diplopia, dysarthria, ataxia, crossed signs) are missed more often than those of the anterior circulation. Basilar occlusion infarcts the pons and midbrain and is fatal or leaves the patient locked in unless the artery is opened.

anatomy.location: Medulla, pons and midbrain (paramedian and lateral territories), the cerebellum (superior surface from the SCA, anterior inferior from AICA, posterior inferior from PICA), the inner ear (labyrinthine artery) and, via the PCAs, the thalamus and occipital lobes; bounded above by the tentorium and the PCA-MCA border and below by the spinal territory of the anterior spinal artery.

afferents.from: Vertebral and basilar arteries and their branches

efferents.to: Petrosal, transverse and sigmoid sinuses via posterior fossa veins

territory-vertebrobasilar-major.function: It supplies the cranial nerve nuclei, the ascending and descending long tracts, the reticular activating system, the respiratory and cardiovascular centers, the cerebellar circuits and the vestibular system, so ischemia produces combinations of cranial nerve, cerebellar, long-tract and consciousness disturbance that name the level. The two vertebral arteries and the circle of Willis provide collaterals, and paramedian perforators from the basilar have none, which is why pontine lacunes are common; occlusion of the basilar trunk is a thrombotic disease of the elderly and a dissection of the young.

bestView.label: vertebrobasilar territory of the brainstem and cerebellum
posterior circulation domain of the pons and cerebellum

imaging.normalAppearance: On the overlay the vertebrobasilar domain covers the brainstem and cerebellum; on imaging the basilar artery is a flow void in front of the pons and a hyperdense basilar on CT is the sign of its thrombosis.

pathology.finding: Absent basilar opacification with hyperdense basilar sign on plain CT; DWI shows paramedian pontine and midbrain infarcts, often with cerebellar and occipital lesions.
pathology.timing: Thrombectomy improves outcome up to 24 hours in selected patients

pathology.finding: Tapered stenosis or intramural hematoma of the V2-V3 segments in a young patient with neck pain and a PICA-territory infarct.
Restricted diffusion in paramedian pontine, lateral medullary or cerebellar territories; early DWI can be negative in small brainstem lesions.

lesionEffects.deficit: Crossed brainstem syndromes: cranial nerve palsy with contralateral long-tract signs
lesionEffects.mechanism: Ischemia of one brainstem level
Cerebellar and vestibular ischemia
Basilar trunk occlusion infarcting the pons

lesionEffects.deficit: Cortical blindness and amnesia at the top
lesionEffects.mechanism: Bilateral PCA involvement

Neck pain history and vascular imaging of the vertebral arteries

territory-watershed.name: Watershed (borderzone) territories
territory-watershed.summary: Borderzones between adjacent arterial territories are the last parts of the brain to be perfused and the first to fail when perfusion pressure drops. The cortical (external) watersheds lie between the ACA and MCA and between the MCA and PCA on the convexity; the internal (subcortical) watershed lies in the corona radiata and centrum semiovale between the deep lenticulostriate perforators and the superficial MCA branches. Watershed infarcts point to hypotension or a proximal stenosis rather than embolism.

anatomy.location: Anterior cortical watershed: a strip along the superior frontal sulcus from the frontal pole to the vertex; posterior cortical watershed: the parieto-occipital region where MCA, ACA and PCA meet; internal watershed: the deep white matter of the corona radiata and centrum semiovale lateral to the lateral ventricles.

territory-watershed.function: Not a functional unit; these zones contain the motor and sensory cortex for the proximal arm and shoulder (anterior watershed), the parietal visual association cortex (posterior watershed) and the descending motor fibers in the corona radiata (internal watershed).

bloodSupply.note: Territory boundaries in this atlas come from a probabilistic stroke-lesion atlas (Liu et al. 2023) and shift between individuals with the anatomy of the circle of Willis.

pathology.finding: Wedge-shaped diffusion restriction between the ACA and MCA or MCA and PCA territories, often bilateral after global hypotension or unilateral distal to a tight carotid stenosis.

thalamus-anterior-nuclei.name: Anterior thalamic nuclei
thalamus-anterior-nuclei.summary: The anterior nuclear group forms the tubercle at the front of the thalamus and is a station on the Papez circuit of memory: it receives the mammillothalamic tract from the mammillary bodies (and direct fibers from the hippocampal formation via the fornix) and projects to the cingulate gyrus. Lesions of the nuclei or of the mammillothalamic tract, as in tuberothalamic and paramedian infarcts, produce amnesia, and the nucleus is a target for deep brain stimulation in epilepsy.

anatomy.location: Anterosuperior pole of the thalamus, bulging into the floor of the lateral ventricle behind the foramen of Monro, enclosed by the anterior limb of the internal medullary lamina.

efferents.via: anterior limb of the internal capsule

thalamus-anterior-nuclei.function: Relay of hippocampal–mammillary memory information to the cingulate cortex; contributes to spatial memory and to the propagation of seizures through the limbic circuit.

bestView.label: anterior thalamic tubercle behind the foramen of Monro

imaging.normalAppearance: The anterior tubercle is identifiable on axial T1 as the anterior tip of the thalamus; individual nuclei are not resolved. The mammillothalamic tract is visible on 7 T and on the Neudorfer atlas mesh in this atlas.

pathology.finding: Anterior thalamic restriction from the polar artery (a PComm branch) with amnesia, apathy and language change on the left.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: DWI; coronal T1 for mammillary bodies

lesionEffects.mechanism: Interruption of the Papez circuit at the anterior nucleus or mammillothalamic tract
Anterior thalamic connections to the cingulate and frontal cortex
Bilateral anterior thalamic lesions

Orientation and confabulation
Verbal fluency

thalamus-lateral-posterior-ventral-poste.name: Lateral posterior / ventral posterior group
thalamus-lateral-posterior-ventral-poste.summary: This thalamic group combines the lateral posterior nucleus of the dorsal tier with the adjacent ventral posterior nuclei, the somatosensory relay of the thalamus, as segmented by the MIAL thalamic atlas. The ventral posterolateral nucleus receives the medial lemniscus and spinothalamic tract from the body and the ventral posteromedial nucleus receives trigeminal and taste input from the face, both projecting to the postcentral gyrus; the lateral posterior nucleus is an associative nucleus linked with the superior parietal lobule for spatial attention and visually guided action. Infarction of this region by the thalamogeniculate arteries produces the pure sensory stroke and, later, the thalamic pain of the Dejerine-Roussy syndrome.

anatomy.location: Posterolateral thalamus behind the ventrolateral nucleus and in front of the pulvinar, lateral to the internal medullary lamina and the centromedian nucleus, above the medial geniculate body, with the lateral posterior nucleus dorsal and the ventral posterior nuclei ventral within the group.

afferents.from: Trigeminal sensory nuclei and nucleus solitarius

efferents.to: Superior parietal lobule (from the lateral posterior nucleus)

thalamus-lateral-posterior-ventral-poste.function: The ventral posterolateral nucleus relays touch, vibration, proprioception, pain and temperature from the contralateral body to the primary somatosensory cortex with a precise somatotopy (leg lateral, arm medial), and the ventral posteromedial nucleus does the same for the face and relays taste to the insular-opercular cortex; both are gated by the reticular nucleus and by corticothalamic feedback. The lateral posterior nucleus receives the superior colliculus and the parietal cortex and participates in directing attention and reaching in space. Damage produces contralateral hemianesthesia of all modalities, with a characteristic delayed central pain syndrome as the surviving spinothalamic input is reorganized.

thalamus-mediodorsal.name: Mediodorsal nucleus
thalamus-mediodorsal.summary: The largest medial nucleus, reciprocally connected with the prefrontal cortex and receiving input from the amygdala, olfactory cortex, basal ganglia and hypothalamus. It supports executive function, emotional tone, working memory and, with the anterior nuclei, declarative memory. Bilateral damage (paramedian thalamic infarction, thiamine deficiency, prion disease) produces a syndrome of amnesia, apathy and altered arousal; its paramedian perforators come from the P1 segment, sometimes as a single artery of Percheron.

anatomy.location: Medial thalamus between the internal medullary lamina and the midline nuclei of the third ventricular wall, behind the anterior nuclei and above the hypothalamus.

thalamus-mediodorsal.function: Prefrontal relay for executive function, emotional regulation, working memory and attention; contributes to the limbic memory circuit and to olfactory processing.

thalamus-pulvinar-medial-centrolateral.name: Medial pulvinar / centrolateral group
thalamus-pulvinar-medial-centrolateral.summary: This MIAL atlas group gathers the medial pulvinar with the intralaminar nuclei of the posterior internal medullary lamina, the centrolateral, centromedian and parafascicular nuclei, which lie between the mediodorsal nucleus and the ventral tier. The medial pulvinar is an associative nucleus linked with the temporal, parietal and prefrontal cortex and the amygdala, supporting attention and the integration of visual and limbic information, whereas the intralaminar nuclei are the thalamic part of the ascending arousal system and the main thalamic input to the striatum. Paramedian thalamic infarcts that involve this region cause hypersomnolence, apathy and memory loss, and bilateral lesions produce coma or akinetic mutism.

anatomy.location: Posteromedial thalamus: the medial pulvinar behind the mediodorsal nucleus above the posterior commissure, and the intralaminar nuclei within the internal medullary lamina between the mediodorsal nucleus medially and the ventral and lateral nuclei laterally, the centromedian nucleus lying just in front of the pulvinar.

thalamus-pulvinar-medial-centrolateral.function: The intralaminar nuclei receive the reticular activating system, the spinothalamic tract and the pallidum and project diffusely to the cortex and massively to the striatum, sustaining arousal, driving cortical readiness and providing the striatum with salience signals; the centromedian-parafascicular complex is part of the basal ganglia loop and a target of stimulation for epilepsy and Tourette syndrome. The medial pulvinar connects the temporal and parietal association cortex, the frontal eye field and the amygdala, and directs attention and filters distracting information. The paramedian arteries from the P1 segment supply the whole group, sometimes from a single artery of Percheron on both sides.

thalamus-pulvinar.name: Pulvinar
thalamus-pulvinar.summary: The large posterior cushion of the thalamus overhanging the midbrain and the geniculate bodies. It is the association nucleus for vision and attention, reciprocally connected with the parietal, temporal and occipital association cortices and the superior colliculus. Left pulvinar lesions contribute to thalamic aphasia and right ones to neglect; bilateral pulvinar hyperintensity on diffusion imaging is the signature of variant Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease, and it is the thalamic target of Fabry disease and some metabolic disorders.

anatomy.location: Posterior pole of the thalamus above the superior colliculus and behind the ventral posterior nuclei, medial to the lateral geniculate body and bordering the atrium of the lateral ventricle.

efferents.to: parietal, temporal and occipital association cortex

thalamus-va-vl.name: Ventral anterior and ventral lateral nuclei (VA/VL)
thalamus-va-vl.latin: Nucleus ventralis anterior; nucleus ventralis lateralis
thalamus-va-vl.summary: The motor thalamus. The ventral anterior nucleus receives the inhibitory outflow of the basal ganglia (globus pallidus interna and substantia nigra reticulata) and projects to the premotor and prefrontal cortex; the ventral lateral nucleus receives the crossed cerebellar outflow from the dentate and interposed nuclei (and pallidal input to its anterior part) and projects to the primary motor and premotor cortex. Both loops pass through here, so a VL lesion can abolish a contralateral tremor, which is why the VL (VIM) nucleus is the target for thalamotomy and deep brain stimulation in tremor.

anatomy.location: Anterior part of the ventral tier of the lateral thalamus, in front of the VPL/VPM, lateral to the mediodorsal nucleus and medial to the internal capsule; VA is anterior, VL behind it.

thalamus-va-vl.function: Relay of basal ganglia and cerebellar output to the motor cortices; integration of movement selection (VA, pallidal) and movement timing and coordination (VL, cerebellar).

thalamus-ventral-anterior.name: Ventral anterior nucleus
thalamus-ventral-anterior.summary: The ventral anterior nucleus is the most rostral of the ventral tier of thalamic nuclei, lying behind the anterior nuclear group and in front of the ventrolateral nucleus, bounded laterally by the internal capsule and medially by the internal medullary lamina. It is the thalamic relay of the basal ganglia to the premotor and prefrontal cortex: it receives the inhibitory output of the internal pallidum and the substantia nigra pars reticulata and projects to the supplementary motor area, the premotor cortex and the prefrontal cortex, so it is the node through which the basal ganglia select and initiate actions. It is affected in tuberothalamic infarcts and in the thalamic degeneration of some dementias, and it is a target of pallidothalamic surgery.

anatomy.location: Anterior part of the ventral thalamus lateral to the internal medullary lamina, behind the anterior nuclei, in front of the ventrolateral nucleus, above the zona incerta and the fields of Forel through which its pallidal input arrives.

afferents.via: thalamic fasciculus (ansa lenticularis and lenticular fasciculus)

efferents.to: Supplementary motor area and premotor cortex
Prefrontal cortex and frontal eye field

thalamus-ventral-anterior.function: Pallidal and nigral fibers reach the ventral anterior nucleus through the thalamic fasciculus and inhibit it tonically; when the basal ganglia release a movement or a thought by pausing this inhibition, the nucleus drives the supplementary motor area and premotor cortex to initiate the action and the prefrontal cortex to shift cognitive set. Its magnocellular part carries the nigral output to the prefrontal and frontal eye fields, participating in saccade initiation and executive function. Reduced pallidothalamic release in parkinsonism starves it and slows initiation; excess release in chorea and ballismus overdrives it. It is the thalamic station of the motor and prefrontal loops of the basal ganglia.

thalamus-ventral-posterior-ventrolateral.name: Ventral posterior / ventrolateral group (VPL/VPM)
thalamus-ventral-posterior-ventrolateral.summary: This MIAL thalamic atlas group covers the ventral posterolateral and ventral posteromedial nuclei together with the posterior part of the ventrolateral nucleus, the somatosensory and cerebellar relay region at the ventral posterolateral corner of the thalamus, supplied by the thalamogeniculate arteries. It transmits touch, proprioception, pain and temperature from the contralateral body and face to the postcentral gyrus and cerebellar timing signals to the motor cortex, so its infarction produces the classic thalamic sensory stroke with ataxia (the sensory-ataxic and hypesthetic-ataxic hemiparesis lacunes) and its stimulation is used for tremor. Thalamic hemorrhage most often begins here.

anatomy.location: Ventral posterior part of the thalamus lateral to the internal medullary lamina and the centromedian nucleus, behind the anterior ventrolateral nucleus and in front of the pulvinar, against the posterior limb of the internal capsule laterally and above the medial geniculate body and the subthalamus.

thalamus-ventral-posterior-ventrolateral.function: Lemniscal, spinothalamic and trigeminothalamic axons terminate in a somatotopic map and their thalamocortical neurons relay to the somatosensory cortex under the control of the reticular nucleus and the cortex itself, so that sensory transmission is gated by attention and sleep; the adjacent cerebellar-receiving territory relays dentate and interposed output to the motor cortex. Because these functions are packed together in a few millimeters, a single small infarct here produces contralateral sensory loss with ataxia and, when the internal capsule is involved, weakness. Partial lesions that spare the spinothalamic input to the medial thalamus set up the central pain syndrome.

thalamus-ventrolateral.name: Ventrolateral nucleus
thalamus-ventrolateral.summary: The ventrolateral nucleus lies in the ventral tier of the thalamus behind the ventral anterior nucleus and in front of the ventral posterior nuclei, lateral to the internal medullary lamina. It is the motor thalamus: its posterior part receives the dentatorubrothalamic tract from the contralateral cerebellum and projects to the primary motor cortex, while its anterior part receives the internal pallidum and projects to the premotor and supplementary motor cortex. thalamus.name: Thalamus
thalamus.summary: Two egg-shaped masses of gray matter forming the walls of the third ventricle and the floor of the lateral ventricles, the thalamus is the gateway to the cortex: every sensory modality except smell, the outflow of the cerebellum and basal ganglia, and the limbic circuits are relayed here before reaching their cortical targets, and the cortex projects back to every nucleus. Its nuclei are grouped by the internal medullary lamina into anterior, medial and lateral tiers plus intralaminar, midline and reticular nuclei. Clinically the lateral group is the somatosensory relay (pure sensory stroke, thalamic pain), the anterior and medial groups serve memory and attention (amnesia, apathy, coma with bilateral lesions), and the posterior pulvinar and geniculate bodies serve vision and hearing.

tract-acoustic-radiation.name: Acoustic radiation
tract-acoustic-radiation.summary: The acoustic radiation is the short bundle from the medial geniculate body to the primary auditory cortex on Heschl's gyrus, running through the sublenticular part of the internal capsule beneath the lentiform nucleus. Because each cochlea is represented in both medial geniculate bodies after the extensive crossing in the brainstem, a unilateral lesion of the radiation does not cause deafness but impairs sound localization and the recognition of speech in noise from the contralateral side, and bilateral lesions cause cortical deafness. The reconstruction shows the bundle passing laterally under the putamen to the superior temporal plane; it is crossed by MCA perforators and by the fibers of the internal capsule and is damaged in lenticulostriate and MCA infarcts.

anatomy.location: From the medial geniculate body, laterally and forward through the sublenticular limb of the internal capsule beneath the putamen and the globus pallidus, above the temporal stem, to the transverse temporal gyrus of Heschl in the floor of the Sylvian fissure, a short thick bundle a few centimeters long.

tract-acoustic-radiation.function: It conveys the tonotopically ordered auditory signal, already binaural after processing in the superior olive, lateral lemniscus and inferior colliculus, to the core auditory cortex, where frequency, intensity and timing are mapped; corticofugal fibers run back in it to the geniculate and colliculus. Because of the bilateral representation, unilateral damage produces subtle deficits (impaired localization, extinction of contralateral sounds on dichotic testing, poorer speech-in-noise perception), and only bilateral interruption, usually from sequential strokes, produces cortical deafness or auditory agnosia. The bundle is one of the last to myelinate and is affected in periventricular injury of prematurity.

tract-arcuate-fasciculus.name: Arcuate fasciculus
synonyms: long segment of the superior longitudinal fasciculus
tract-arcuate-fasciculus.summary: The arcuate fasciculus is the curved bundle that arches around the posterior end of the Sylvian fissure to connect the posterior superior and middle temporal gyri with the inferior frontal gyrus and the ventral premotor cortex, the dorsal language pathway of the dominant hemisphere. It carries the phonological form of words from the temporal to the frontal speech areas, so its interruption produces conduction aphasia, fluent speech with good comprehension but failed repetition and phonemic paraphasias. It is larger on the left in most people, it is the bundle awake mapping protects during perisylvian surgery, and in the right hemisphere it serves prosody, visuospatial processing and tone in music.

anatomy.location: From the posterior superior and middle temporal gyri and the planum temporale, upward and forward through the white matter of the supramarginal gyrus, arching over the posterior insula deep to the parietal and frontal opercula, to end in the pars opercularis, the ventral precentral gyrus and the middle frontal gyrus; it forms the deep, long segment of the superior longitudinal fasciculus system.

tract-arcuate-fasciculus.function: The bundle links the auditory word-form and phonological processing of the posterior temporal cortex with the articulatory planning of the frontal operculum, making repetition, reading aloud, verbal working memory rehearsal and the learning of new words possible; its temporo-parietal and fronto-parietal indirect segments through the supramarginal gyrus add a sensorimotor interface for speech. Damage anywhere along it produces phonemic paraphasias that the patient notices and tries to correct, disproportionate repetition failure and difficulty with unfamiliar words, the core of conduction aphasia, and partial lesions during surgery produce transient phonological errors. On the right it contributes to the melody and emotional tone of speech and to spatial attention.

tract-cingulum-frontoparietal.name: Cingulum, fronto-parietal
tract-cingulum-frontoparietal.summary: The dorsal part of the cingulum bundle runs in the white matter of the cingulate gyrus above the corpus callosum, from the subgenual and anterior cingulate cortex back to the posterior cingulate and the precuneus, collecting and distributing fibers along its length. It is the backbone of the medial default mode and limbic networks, connecting the anterior thalamic radiation and the medial prefrontal cortex with the posterior cingulate, retrosplenial cortex and parietal cortex, and it carries the fibers that cingulotomy divides for pain and obsessive-compulsive disorder. Its integrity is reduced in Alzheimer disease, mild cognitive impairment and depression, and its interruption by anterior cerebral artery infarcts, butterfly gliomas and callosal surgery produces attention, memory and motivational deficits.

anatomy.location: Within the cingulate gyrus from the subcallosal region forward of the genu, over the body of the corpus callosum in the depth of the cingulate gyrus, to the splenium, where it continues as the parahippocampal cingulum; it receives and gives off fibers to the medial frontal, cingulate, precuneal and parietal cortex along the way.

tract-cingulum-frontoparietal.function: The dorsal cingulum links the anterior cingulate and medial prefrontal cortex with the posterior cingulate, precuneus and retrosplenial cortex, carrying the executive, motivational and attentional signals of the medial frontal lobe to the posterior memory and self-referential regions and returning memory retrieval signals forward; it also carries the anterior thalamic projection to the cingulate cortex and the cingulate's input to the motor and prefrontal cortex. Interruption reduces attention and executive function, disturbs the affective component of pain (the target of cingulotomy), and disconnects memory retrieval from the frontal strategy, and its degeneration parallels the posterior cingulate hypometabolism of early Alzheimer disease.

tract-cingulum-parahippocampal.name: Cingulum, parahippocampal
tract-cingulum-parahippocampal.summary: The parahippocampal cingulum is the ventral continuation of the cingulum bundle below the splenium, running through the isthmus into the white matter of the parahippocampal gyrus toward the entorhinal cortex and the temporal pole. It closes the Papez circuit by carrying the anterior thalamic and posterior cingulate output to the entorhinal cortex, and it links the retrosplenial navigation cortex with the parahippocampal place area, so it serves both memory and spatial orientation. It is the medial temporal white matter that atrophies with the hippocampus in Alzheimer disease and mesial temporal sclerosis, and it is interrupted by PCA infarcts, temporal lobectomy and posterior medial temporal tumors, producing amnesia and topographical disorientation.

anatomy.location: From the retrosplenial cortex behind and below the splenium, through the isthmus of the cingulate gyrus, downward and forward in the white matter of the parahippocampal gyrus medial to the collateral sulcus and lateral to the hippocampus, to the entorhinal cortex, the perirhinal cortex and the temporal pole.

afferents.from: Retrosplenial and posterior cingulate cortex, anterior thalamus

efferents.to: Entorhinal and perirhinal cortex, temporal pole

tract-cingulum-parahippocampal.function: It conveys the posterior cingulate and retrosplenial cortex's spatial and self-referential signals and the anterior thalamic memory signal to the entorhinal cortex, the gateway of the hippocampus, and returns hippocampal-entorhinal output to the posterior cingulate, forming the loop through which episodes are encoded with their spatial context and retrieved; the retrosplenial-parahippocampal link converts the allocentric map into the egocentric view used for navigation. tract-corticobulbar.name: Corticobulbar tract
tract-corticobulbar.summary: The corticobulbar tract carries the motor command from the face, tongue and larynx areas of the precentral gyrus and the premotor cortex to the motor nuclei of the cranial nerves in the brainstem, running with the corticospinal tract through the genu and posterior limb of the internal capsule and the medial crus cerebri before leaving it at each level to reach the trigeminal, facial, ambiguus and hypoglossal nuclei. Because most nuclei receive both hemispheres, a unilateral lesion produces only lower facial weakness and mild tongue and palatal deviation, whereas bilateral lesions produce the pseudobulbar palsy of spastic dysarthria, dysphagia and emotional lability. The reconstruction shows the bundle from the lateral motor cortex to the pons and medulla.

anatomy.location: From the ventral precentral gyrus and frontal operculum through the corona radiata into the genu of the internal capsule, then the medial part of the middle of the crus cerebri, descending in the basis pontis and pyramid and sending crossed and uncrossed fibers to the trigeminal motor nucleus, the facial nucleus, the nucleus ambiguus and the hypoglossal nucleus, largely through interneurons of the reticular formation.

afferents.from: Ventral precentral gyrus and frontal operculum

efferents.to: Trigeminal motor, facial, ambiguus and hypoglossal nuclei

tract-corticobulbar.function: It provides voluntary control of chewing, facial expression, phonation, swallowing and tongue movement, with bilateral supply to most nuclei except the lower facial subnucleus and part of the hypoglossal nucleus, which receive mainly crossed fibers; it also carries the corticoreticular fibers that inhibit the brainstem reflex centers for laughing and crying, so bilateral loss releases pathological emotional expression. Unilateral damage gives contralateral lower facial weakness and transient dysarthria; bilateral damage from repeated strokes, motor neuron disease or bilateral opercular lesions gives a slow, strained voice, a brisk jaw jerk and a tongue that cannot move but does not waste.

tract-corticopontine-frontal.name: Frontopontine tract
tract-corticopontine-frontal.summary: The frontopontine tract carries fibers from the prefrontal, premotor and supplementary motor cortex to the pontine nuclei of the same side, traveling through the anterior limb of the internal capsule and the medial fifth of the crus cerebri to end in the basis pontis, from which the pontocerebellar fibers cross into the contralateral cerebellar hemisphere. It is the largest of the corticopontine projections and the frontal lobe's route to the cerebellum, carrying the intended motor plan and the cognitive signals that the posterior cerebellum processes. Its interruption contributes to the ataxia of capsular and midbrain lesions on the side opposite the cerebellar signs (ataxic hemiparesis) and to the cognitive changes of frontal-cerebellar disconnection.

anatomy.location: From the prefrontal, premotor and supplementary motor cortex through the corona radiata and the anterior limb of the internal capsule, descending in the medial part of the crus cerebri (medial to the corticospinal fibers) and ending in the ipsilateral pontine nuclei of the basis pontis at all levels.

afferents.from: Prefrontal, premotor and supplementary motor cortex

tract-corticopontine-frontal.function: The tract sends the frontal cortex's motor plans and cognitive commands to the pontine nuclei, whose axons cross in the middle cerebellar peduncle to the contralateral cerebellar cortex, particularly the posterior lobe and Crus I-II, which return a corrected signal through the dentate nucleus and the thalamus; it is the input limb of the cerebrocerebellar loop that lets the cerebellum predict and time both movement and thought. Because the pathway crosses at the pons and the cerebellar outflow crosses again at the superior cerebellar peduncle, a frontopontine lesion produces ataxia on the side of the hemiparesis, the mechanism of the ataxic hemiparesis of capsular and pontine lacunes.

bestView.label: frontopontine fibers from the frontal lobe to the basis pontis

imaging.normalAppearance: Tractography shows a bundle from the frontal lobe through the anterior limb and the medial crus into the pons, lying medial to the corticospinal tract in the peduncle; not separable on conventional MRI.

pathology.finding: Small infarct of the posterior limb, corona radiata or basis pontis interrupting corticopontine and corticospinal fibers together, with weakness and ataxia in the same limbs.

tract-corticopontine-occipital.name: Occipitopontine tract
tract-corticopontine-occipital.summary: The occipitopontine tract, with the temporopontine fibers (the bundle of Turck), carries fibers from the occipital and posterior temporal visual cortex to the pontine nuclei through the retrolenticular internal capsule and the lateral edge of the crus cerebri. It brings the cerebellum the visual motion and target signals needed for smooth pursuit, the visual guidance of locomotion and the visual calibration of the vestibulo-ocular reflex, ending in the dorsolateral pontine nuclei that project to the flocculus, the paraflocculus and the vermis. Its interruption impairs smooth pursuit toward the side of the lesion and the visual control of balance, and it is part of the crossed cerebellar diaschisis that follows occipital and temporal strokes.

anatomy.location: From the extrastriate occipital cortex, the temporo-occipital motion area and the posterior temporal cortex through the stratum sagittale and the retrolenticular internal capsule, descending along the lateral border of the crus cerebri to the dorsolateral pontine nuclei and the nucleus reticularis tegmenti pontis.

afferents.from: Extrastriate occipital cortex and the temporo-occipital motion area

efferents.to: Dorsolateral pontine nuclei and nucleus reticularis tegmenti pontis

tract-corticopontine-occipital.function: Visual motion signals from the temporo-occipital motion complex and the visual cortex reach the dorsolateral pontine nuclei through this tract, and the pontine neurons relay them across the middle cerebellar peduncle to the flocculus, the ventral paraflocculus and the oculomotor vermis, which generate the pursuit command and adapt the vestibulo-ocular reflex to visual error; the tract also carries the optic flow information that the cerebellum uses to control walking and posture. Lesions of the pathway produce ipsiversive pursuit deficits (pursuit toward the side of the lesion is impaired, because the cerebellar pursuit signal crosses twice), impaired optokinetic responses and difficulty using vision for balance.

tract-corticopontine-parietal.name: Parietopontine tract
tract-corticopontine-parietal.summary: The parietopontine tract carries fibers from the somatosensory and posterior parietal cortex to the ipsilateral pontine nuclei, descending through the posterior limb and retrolenticular part of the internal capsule and the lateral part of the crus cerebri, lateral to the corticospinal fibers. Together with the temporopontine and occipitopontine fibers it gives the cerebellum the sensory context of movement, the position of the limbs and of visual targets in space, which the cerebellum uses to guide reaching and to update its predictions. Its lesions contribute to the ataxia and dysmetria of parietal and capsular strokes and it is one of the pathways involved in the optic ataxia of parietal damage.

anatomy.location: From the postcentral gyrus, the superior and inferior parietal lobules and the parietal operculum through the corona radiata and the posterior part of the posterior limb and retrolenticular capsule, descending in the lateral fifth of the crus cerebri to the pontine nuclei, especially their dorsolateral part.

afferents.from: Postcentral gyrus and posterior parietal cortex

tract-corticopontine-parietal.function: The tract conveys tactile, proprioceptive and visuospatial information, already processed in the parietal cortex, to the pontine nuclei and thence, after crossing in the middle cerebellar peduncle, to the contralateral cerebellar hemisphere, chiefly the intermediate zone and the posterior lobe; this lets the cerebellum compare the intended movement with the sensed state of the limb and the target and correct it, and it underlies the cerebellar contribution to reaching and to eye-hand coordination. Interruption produces dysmetria and impaired visually guided reaching on the side opposite the lesion, together with the parietal sensory deficits, and it participates in the crossed cerebellar diaschisis that follows parietal strokes.

tract-corticospinal.name: Corticospinal tract
tract-corticospinal.summary: The corticospinal tract is the great descending motor pathway from the precentral gyrus, premotor and supplementary motor cortex and the postcentral gyrus to the spinal cord, reconstructed here from diffusion tractography as the bundle that runs through the corona radiata, the posterior limb of the internal capsule, the middle of the crus cerebri, the basis pontis and the medullary pyramid. Most of its fibers cross in the pyramidal decussation to form the lateral corticospinal tract, so a lesion above the decussation weakens the opposite side and one below it the same side. It is the substrate of the upper motor neuron syndrome and of capsular, pontine and medullary strokes, and its integrity on tractography predicts recovery of hand function after stroke.

anatomy.location: From the motor cortex through the corona radiata, converging into the posterior limb of the internal capsule (face anterior, leg posterior), the middle three-fifths of the crus cerebri, the scattered bundles of the basis pontis and the pyramid of the medulla, where 85-90 percent cross to the contralateral lateral column and the rest descend uncrossed in the anterior column.

afferents.via: origin (sensory fibers to the dorsal horn)

efferents.to: Dorsal horn and dorsal column nuclei

tract-corticospinal.function: It carries the voluntary motor command, especially for fractionated finger movements and for the face and tongue through its corticobulbar companions; its monosynaptic connections to spinal motor neurons are what make skilled hand movement possible, and its collaterals to the dorsal horn and the brainstem set the gain of reflexes. Its loss produces weakness with the upper motor neuron pattern of extensor-flexor imbalance, spasticity from loss of accompanying corticoreticular fibers, hyperreflexia and the extensor plantar response. The tractography reconstruction follows the bundle from cortex to the caudal medulla and shows its somatotopy in the capsule and the peduncle.

tract-corticostriatal-anterior.name: Corticostriatal tract, anterior
tract-corticostriatal-anterior.summary: The anterior corticostriatal bundle groups the fibers from the prefrontal and orbitofrontal cortex to the head of the caudate and the anterior putamen and the ventral striatum, the cortical input of the associative and limbic loops of the basal ganglia. These projections carry the goals, rules and reward expectations that the striatum uses to select behavior, and their targets are the parts of the striatum most affected in obsessive-compulsive disorder, addiction and Huntington disease. The bundle runs through the anterior corona radiata and the external and anterior internal capsule to the striatum, and its interruption or dysfunction produces apathy, disinhibition and impaired habit and reward learning rather than motor signs.

tract-corticostriatal-anterior.function: Prefrontal corticostriatal axons synapse on the striatal medium spiny neurons of the direct and indirect pathways in the associative (caudate) and limbic (ventral) striatum, where dopamine from the ventral tegmental area and the medial substantia nigra gates their effect; through the pallidum and the mediodorsal and ventral anterior thalamus the loop returns to the same prefrontal areas, allowing the cortex to learn which actions and strategies are rewarded and to switch between them. Dysfunction of the loop underlies compulsions, apathy and impulse disorders, and its striatal targets degenerate first in Huntington disease.

tract-corticostriatal-posterior.name: Corticostriatal tract, posterior
tract-corticostriatal-posterior.summary: The posterior corticostriatal bundle carries fibers from the parietal, temporal and occipital association cortex to the body and tail of the caudate and the posterior putamen, the cortical input of the visual and associative loops of the basal ganglia. These projections bring the striatum the visuospatial, auditory and object information it needs for attention, eye movement selection and the learning of stimulus-response habits, and their targets include the tail of the caudate that curves into the temporal lobe beside the amygdala. The bundle is less familiar than its frontal counterpart but explains the neglect, visual attention deficits and altered saccade selection that accompany posterior striatal and parietal lesions.

The tail of the caudate receives the inferior temporal cortex and holds long-term object values. Interruption impairs visual habit learning, produces subtle neglect and reduces the efficiency of visual search, and the caudate tail is affected in Huntington disease and in temporal lobe pathology.

tract-corticostriatal-superior.name: Corticostriatal tract, superior
tract-corticostriatal-superior.summary: The superior corticostriatal bundle contains the fibers from the motor, premotor and somatosensory cortex to the putamen and the body of the caudate, the cortical input of the motor loop of the basal ganglia. It descends through the corona radiata to the dorsolateral striatum, where the somatotopic representation of the body in the putamen is built from these terminals, and it is the pathway through which the cortex tells the basal ganglia what movement is planned so that the direct and indirect pathways can release it and suppress its competitors. Its degeneration and its abnormal dopaminergic modulation underlie the motor signs of Parkinson disease and Huntington disease, and it is interrupted in striatocapsular infarcts.

anatomy.location: From the precentral and postcentral gyri, the premotor cortex and the supplementary motor area through the corona radiata, entering the putamen and the body of the caudate from above and laterally through the internal and external capsules with a somatotopic order (leg dorsal, face ventral).

tract-corticostriatal-superior.function: Sensorimotor corticostriatal axons excite the medium spiny neurons of the putamen, whose direct-pathway cells then inhibit the internal pallidum to release the movement while indirect-pathway cells increase pallidal output to stop competing movements; dopamine from the substantia nigra strengthens or weakens these corticostriatal synapses according to outcome, making the loop the site of motor habit learning. Copies of the same corticofugal axons continue to the brainstem and spinal cord. Loss of dopamine leaves the corticostriatal input unable to drive the direct pathway, producing bradykinesia; loss of the indirect-pathway striatal neurons in Huntington disease leaves it unopposed, producing chorea; and striatal infarcts produce dystonia and hemichorea.

tract-dentatorubrothalamic.name: Dentatorubrothalamic tract
tract-dentatorubrothalamic.summary: The dentatorubrothalamic tract is the main outflow of the cerebellum, from the dentate nucleus through the superior cerebellar peduncle, crossing in the decussation of the peduncles in the caudal midbrain, passing through and around the contralateral red nucleus, and ending in the ventrolateral thalamus, from which the motor cortex is reached. It is the pathway through which the cerebellum times and coordinates voluntary movement, and it is the reason cerebellar signs are ipsilateral: it crosses once here and the corticospinal tract crosses back. Its interruption produces contralateral (after the decussation) or ipsilateral (before it) ataxia and tremor, its lesion in the midbrain gives the Holmes rubral tremor, and it is the bundle that tremor surgery targets in the thalamus and the posterior subthalamic area.

anatomy.location: From the dentate nucleus in the cerebellar white matter, forward and upward in the superior cerebellar peduncle along the roof of the fourth ventricle, decussating in the tegmentum at the level of the inferior colliculus, ascending through and around the red nucleus and the prerubral field, through the zona incerta and field H of Forel, to the ventral intermediate and ventrolateral nuclei of the thalamus.

tract-dentatorubrothalamic.function: The tract carries the dentate nucleus's prediction-corrected motor signal, derived from the cerebellar hemisphere's comparison of intended and actual movement, to the motor and premotor cortex through the ventrolateral thalamus, giving movements their timing, smoothness and end-point accuracy; collaterals to the red nucleus feed the rubrospinal and the rubro-olivary loop for motor learning, and its rhythmic activity is what drives cerebellar and Holmes tremor. Because it crosses in the midbrain, a lesion of the peduncle or the dentate produces ipsilateral ataxia, a lesion above the decussation contralateral ataxia; combined damage to the tract and the nigrostriatal fibers in the midbrain produces the slow, coarse rest-postural-intention tremor of Holmes.

tract-frontal-aslant.name: Frontal aslant tract
tract-frontal-aslant.summary: The frontal aslant tract is an oblique bundle within the frontal lobe that connects the supplementary motor area and the pre-supplementary motor area on the medial surface with the pars opercularis of the inferior frontal gyrus on the lateral surface, running downward and laterally through the white matter of the superior and middle frontal gyri. It is the pathway of speech initiation and of the control of action: on the left it links the medial frontal drive to speak with the lateral articulatory area, and its lesions produce reduced spontaneous speech, stuttering and mutism; on both sides it participates in stopping actions and in the executive control of movement. It is damaged in medial frontal surgery, in ACA-MCA watershed infarcts and in the non-fluent variant of primary progressive aphasia.

anatomy.location: From the supplementary and pre-supplementary motor area and the anterior cingulate cortex, obliquely downward and laterally through the white matter deep to the superior and middle frontal gyri, to the pars opercularis and the ventral premotor cortex, lateral to the cingulum and medial to the SLF.

afferents.from: Supplementary and pre-supplementary motor area, anterior cingulate

efferents.to: Pars opercularis and ventral premotor cortex

tract-frontal-aslant.function: The tract carries the medial frontal signals that initiate and sequence speech and other self-generated actions to the lateral frontal cortex that executes them, so that the supplementary motor area can start an utterance and the inferior frontal gyrus can shape it; it also carries inhibitory control signals from the pre-supplementary motor area that stop or switch actions, and it supports verbal fluency and the planning of word sequences. Disconnection produces a transcortical motor pattern of speech with preserved repetition but reduced initiation and fluency, stuttering-like dysfluency, and, after surgery, a transient mutism that recovers as the lateral cortex reorganizes; in progressive non-fluent aphasia the tract degenerates with the inferior frontal gyrus.

tract-inferior-fronto-occipital-fascicul.name: Inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus
tract-inferior-fronto-occipital-fascicul.summary: The inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus is the longest association bundle of the hemisphere, running from the occipital and posterior temporal cortex forward through the temporal stem and the extreme capsule, beneath the insula, to the inferior frontal gyrus, the orbitofrontal cortex and the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex. It is the ventral semantic pathway that carries visual and lexical meaning directly to the frontal lobe, bypassing the temporal pole, and it is the bundle whose stimulation during awake surgery produces semantic paraphasias; it also carries visual information to the frontal eye field and the prefrontal cortex for attention and reading. It is spared in most strokes because it lies deep, but it is infiltrated by insular and temporal gliomas and damaged in the temporal stem.

anatomy.location: From the extrastriate occipital cortex and the posterior temporal and parietal cortex, converging into the stratum sagittale and the temporal stem, passing through the ventral extreme and external capsule beneath the insula (the narrow part of the bundle), and fanning out in the frontal lobe to the inferior frontal gyrus, the orbitofrontal cortex and the middle frontal gyrus.

afferents.from: Extrastriate occipital and posterior temporal-parietal cortex

efferents.to: Inferior frontal gyrus, orbitofrontal and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex

tract-inferior-fronto-occipital-fascicul.function: The bundle links visual object and word forms and the temporal semantic cortex with the frontal areas that select meaning, plan speech and direct attention, forming, with the uncinate and inferior longitudinal fasciculi, the ventral stream of language; stimulation of it interrupts naming with semantic errors (saying cat for dog), which is why it is the boundary that limits insular and temporal resection in the dominant hemisphere. It also participates in reading, in visual attention and in the transfer of emotional visual information to the orbitofrontal cortex. Damage produces semantic paraphasias, impaired comprehension of complex material and, on the right, visuospatial and social-perceptual deficits; its ventral route is the reason semantic function survives many perisylvian strokes.

tract-inferior-longitudinal-fasciculus.name: Inferior longitudinal fasciculus
tract-inferior-longitudinal-fasciculus.summary: The inferior longitudinal fasciculus runs along the length of the temporal lobe beneath the lateral ventricle, connecting the occipital visual areas with the anterior temporal lobe, the amygdala and the temporal pole. It is the ventral visual stream in white matter: it carries the identity of objects, faces and written words forward from the occipito-temporal cortex to the anterior temporal semantic and emotional systems, so its lesions produce visual agnosia, prosopagnosia, pure alexia and visual amnesia, and its right-sided damage produces landmark agnosia. It runs beneath the optic radiation in the stratum sagittale and is injured in PCA infarcts, temporal lobe surgery and herpes encephalitis, and it degenerates in semantic dementia.

anatomy.location: From the lingual, fusiform and lateral occipital cortex forward in the inferolateral temporal white matter beneath the temporal horn and lateral to the hippocampus, medial to the inferior and middle temporal gyri, to the anterior fusiform and inferior temporal cortex, the temporal pole and the amygdala; it lies below and lateral to the optic radiation and the IFOF in the stratum sagittale.

tract-inferior-longitudinal-fasciculus.function: It carries the output of the occipito-temporal object, face and word-form areas to the anterior temporal cortex, where these percepts acquire meaning and personal significance, and to the amygdala, where they acquire emotional value; it also carries feedback from memory and emotion back to the visual areas, biasing perception, and it takes part in reading through the visual word form area. Disconnection leaves perception intact but severs it from recognition: the patient sees the face, copies the word or describes the object but cannot recognize or read it, and cannot learn new visual material. Right-sided lesions produce prosopagnosia and topographical agnosia, left-sided ones pure alexia and associative agnosia, and bilateral ones a profound visual agnosia.

tract-middle-longitudinal-fasciculus.name: Middle longitudinal fasciculus
tract-middle-longitudinal-fasciculus.summary: The middle longitudinal fasciculus runs along the superior temporal gyrus beneath its cortex, from the temporal pole and the anterior superior temporal gyrus backward to the angular gyrus and the superior parietal lobule, lying medial to the arcuate fasciculus and lateral to the inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus. It links the auditory and language cortex of the superior temporal gyrus with the multimodal parietal cortex, supporting the integration of language with spatial and attentional processing, and it is thought to carry sentence-level and auditory-spatial information; its lesions contribute to comprehension deficits, to auditory neglect and to the temporo-parietal disconnection seen after posterior MCA infarcts and temporal gliomas.

tract-optic-radiation.name: Optic radiation
tract-optic-radiation.summary: The optic radiation carries visual information from the lateral geniculate nucleus to the calcarine cortex, sweeping around the lateral ventricle in the temporal and parietal white matter: the lower-field fibers run directly back through the parietal lobe, while the upper-field fibers loop forward over the temporal horn as Meyer's loop before turning back. The reconstruction shows the whole geniculocalcarine tract from the geniculate body to the occipital pole. Lesions produce homonymous field defects whose shape names the location, a pie-in-the-sky superior quadrantanopia for the temporal loop and an inferior quadrantanopia for the parietal fibers, and the loop is the reason temporal lobectomy risks a field defect.

anatomy.location: From the lateral geniculate nucleus through the retrolenticular part of the internal capsule, fanning out as Meyer's loop over the temporal horn (upper field, inferior fibers) and as the direct bundle through the parietal white matter lateral to the atrium (lower field, superior fibers), converging on the calcarine cortex above and below the sulcus, with macular fibers in the middle.

tract-optic-radiation.function: It relays the retinotopically ordered output of the geniculate to the primary visual cortex, keeping the upper and lower fields separate so that partial lesions produce quadrantic defects; fibers from the two eyes are mixed, so radiation lesions produce congruous homonymous defects, and the macular fibers travel centrally to the occipital pole. The sapphire-blue tractography bundle is used to plan temporal lobe surgery, because Meyer's loop reaches within a centimeter or two of the temporal pole, and the radiation is injured in MCA and PCA infarcts, in periventricular leukomalacia and in temporal and parietal tumors, adding a field defect that patients rarely notice until they are tested.

tract-reticulospinal.name: Reticulospinal tract
tract-reticulospinal.summary: The reticulospinal tract descends from the pontine and medullary reticular formation to the spinal cord, bilaterally with an ipsilateral predominance, in the anterior and lateral funiculi, reconstructed here from its brainstem origin down to the cervicomedullary junction. It is the main non-pyramidal motor pathway for posture, locomotion and axial and proximal movement: the pontine (medial) component facilitates extensor tone and the medullary (lateral) component inhibits it and gates reflexes, and both carry the cortex's commands for gross movement, the startle response and the autonomic outflow to the intermediolateral column. It is what keeps a patient with a corticospinal lesion able to stand and walk, and its imbalance after such lesions produces spasticity; its loss below the lesion in a complete cord injury produces flaccidity and autonomic failure.

anatomy.location: From the pontine reticular formation (nucleus reticularis pontis oralis and caudalis) mainly ipsilaterally in the anterior funiculus (medial reticulospinal tract) and from the medullary gigantocellular reticular formation bilaterally in the lateral funiculus (lateral reticulospinal tract), descending the whole length of the cord to the ventromedial gray of the ventral horn and the intermediolateral column.

efferents.to: Ventral horn interneurons and axial motor neurons

tract-reticulospinal.function: The pontine reticulospinal fibers excite axial and proximal extensor motor neurons and set the postural tone that supports the body against gravity, and the medullary fibers inhibit them and dampen stretch reflexes; the cortex controls both through corticoreticular fibers that run with the corticospinal tract, so a capsular lesion removes cortical drive to the inhibitory medullary system and leaves the pontine facilitatory system unopposed, producing spasticity. The tract also carries the locomotor commands from the mesencephalic locomotor region and the pedunculopontine nucleus that generate stepping, the startle reflex, and descending sympathetic and respiratory control. It underlies the recovery of gross movement and gait after stroke and the abnormal postures of decerebrate rigidity.

tract-superior-longitudinal-fasciculus-i.name: Superior longitudinal fasciculus I
tract-superior-longitudinal-fasciculus-i.summary: The dorsal branch of the superior longitudinal fasciculus runs in the white matter of the superior frontal and superior parietal gyri, above the cingulum and medial to the corona radiata, connecting the superior parietal lobule and the precuneus with the supplementary motor area, the dorsal premotor cortex and the superior frontal gyrus. It is the wiring of the dorsal attention and reaching network: it carries the spatial location of targets and the state of the limbs from the parietal cortex to the premotor areas that plan reaching, and it contributes to the voluntary orienting of attention. Lesions produce optic ataxia and impaired reaching and contribute to neglect, and it is involved in parasagittal lesions and in the border zone between the anterior and middle cerebral arteries.

anatomy.location: From the superior parietal lobule and the precuneus forward in the dorsomedial white matter beneath the superior frontal gyrus and above the cingulate sulcus, lateral to the cingulum, to the supplementary motor area, the dorsal premotor cortex and the superior frontal gyrus.

efferents.to: Supplementary motor area, dorsal premotor cortex and superior frontal gyrus

tract-superior-longitudinal-fasciculus-i.function: It links the parietal representation of visual space and limb position with the frontal areas that plan arm movements and gaze shifts, so that a reach is aimed and updated; it also carries the top-down signals of the dorsal attention network from the frontal eye field and premotor cortex to the parietal cortex, directing attention voluntarily to a location. The right SLF I contributes more to spatial attention and the left to bimanual coordination and sequencing. Interruption produces optic ataxia (misreaching in the peripheral field), difficulty in bimanual tasks and, with the other SLF branches, neglect; it is one of the bundles injured in the parieto-frontal watershed and in ACA-MCA border-zone infarcts.

tract-superior-longitudinal-fasciculus-i.name: Superior longitudinal fasciculus II
tract-superior-longitudinal-fasciculus-i.summary: The middle branch of the superior longitudinal fasciculus is the main lateral association bundle of the hemisphere, running in the white matter of the middle frontal gyrus and the inferior parietal lobule, lateral to the corona radiata and above the insula, connecting the angular gyrus and the posterior inferior parietal cortex with the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and the frontal eye field. It is the fronto-parietal wiring of spatial attention and working memory, larger on the right, and its damage is the strongest white-matter predictor of persistent neglect after right-hemisphere stroke; on the left it contributes to the phonological loop and to the indirect language pathways.

anatomy.location: From the angular gyrus and the posterior part of the inferior parietal lobule forward through the white matter lateral to the corona radiata and above the arcuate fasciculus, beneath the middle frontal gyrus, to the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, the frontal eye field and the posterior middle frontal gyrus.

afferents.from: Angular gyrus and posterior inferior parietal lobule

efferents.to: Dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and frontal eye field

tract-superior-longitudinal-fasciculus-i.function: It carries the parietal salience and spatial maps to the frontal eye field and the prefrontal cortex and returns the top-down attentional commands, so that attention can be shifted voluntarily and maintained on the contralateral hemispace; its right-hemisphere dominance underlies the right hemisphere's control of attention to both sides, which is why right lesions produce left neglect and left lesions rarely produce right neglect. It also carries working memory information between the parietal and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex. Interruption produces neglect and extinction, impaired visual search and reduced spatial working memory, and disconnection of the SLF II is as important as cortical damage in the persistence of neglect.

tract-superior-longitudinal-fasciculus-i.function: The SLF III carries the sensorimotor representations of speech (the felt and heard consequences of articulation) from the supramarginal gyrus to the frontal operculum, forming the anterior indirect segment of the language loop that supports articulation and repetition, and it carries the inferior parietal representations of hand and tool actions to the ventral premotor cortex for imitation, gesture and the understanding of others' actions. On the right it takes part in spatial attention with the SLF II and in the perception of one's own body. Interruption produces phonemic errors and apraxia of speech on the left, ideomotor apraxia on either side (more on the left) and, on the right, contributes to neglect and to the sense of limb ownership.
