tract-thalamic-radiation-anterior.name: Anterior thalamic radiation
tract-thalamic-radiation-anterior.summary: The anterior thalamic radiation is the bundle of fibers between the anterior and mediodorsal thalamic nuclei and the prefrontal cortex, running through the anterior limb of the internal capsule between the caudate head and the lentiform nucleus. It carries the limbic and executive traffic of the frontal lobe: the anterior nuclei's contribution to the Papez memory circuit, the mediodorsal nucleus's link with the dorsolateral and orbitofrontal cortex, and the corticothalamic feedback that shapes attention and working memory. Lesions of the anterior limb produce apathy, executive dysfunction and memory impairment without weakness, and the radiation is the target of the anterior capsulotomy used for obsessive-compulsive disorder and of anterior thalamic stimulation for epilepsy.

anatomy.location: From the anterior and mediodorsal thalamic nuclei forward through the anterior limb of the internal capsule, between the head of the caudate medially and the lentiform nucleus laterally, fanning into the corona radiata to the prefrontal cortex, the anterior cingulate and the orbitofrontal cortex; it runs with the frontopontine fibers.

efferents.to: Prefrontal, orbitofrontal and anterior cingulate cortex

tract-thalamic-radiation-anterior.function: It is the two-way channel between the thalamus and the prefrontal cortex: the anterior nuclei relay mammillary and hippocampal memory signals to the cingulate and prefrontal cortex, the mediodorsal nucleus relays amygdalar, olfactory and pallidal signals to the orbitofrontal and dorsolateral cortex and mediates working memory and reward-guided decisions, and prefrontal corticothalamic fibers return through it to tune thalamic gating. Interruption disconnects the frontal lobe from the limbic thalamus, producing abulia, poor planning, disinhibition and a diencephalic-type amnesia, the picture of anterior capsular, caudate and anterior thalamic strokes and of the anterior limb lesions seen in schizophrenia research.

bestView.label: anterior thalamic radiation in the anterior limb of the internal capsule

tract-thalamic-radiation-posterior.name: Posterior thalamic radiation
tract-thalamic-radiation-posterior.summary: The posterior thalamic radiation connects the pulvinar and the lateral posterior nucleus with the parietal and occipital association cortex, running through the retrolenticular part of the internal capsule lateral to the atrium of the lateral ventricle, alongside and mixed with the optic radiation. It carries the thalamic contribution to visual attention, spatial perception and the integration of vision with somatosensation, and lesions of this region combine field defects from the optic radiation with neglect, visuospatial disorganization and, on the left, alexia and agraphia. The stratum sagittale that contains it is the corridor for the posterior cerebral and middle cerebral artery watershed and a common site of periventricular leukomalacia and of glioma spread.

anatomy.location: From the pulvinar and lateral posterior nucleus backward and laterally through the retrolenticular internal capsule into the stratum sagittale lateral to the atrium and the occipital horn, fanning to the posterior parietal cortex, the angular gyrus, the lateral occipital cortex and the posterior temporal cortex.

efferents.to: Posterior parietal, angular and lateral occipital cortex

tract-thalamic-radiation-posterior.function: The pulvinar receives the superior colliculus, the visual cortex and the parietal cortex and uses this bundle to coordinate attention across the visual field, to bind the features of an attended object and to suppress distracters; the lateral posterior nucleus contributes to the spatial and reaching functions of the superior parietal lobule; and corticothalamic fibers return through it from the parietal and occipital cortex. Because it shares the stratum sagittale with the optic radiation, its lesions add attentional and perceptual deficits to a hemianopia, and disconnection of the pulvinar from the parietal cortex on the right is one of the mechanisms of neglect. It is also the route by which the thalamus reaches the visual word form and angular gyrus regions on the left.

bestView.label: posterior thalamic radiation from the pulvinar to the parieto-occipital cortex
retrolenticular fibers lateral to the atrium

imaging.normalAppearance: Tractography shows a posterior bundle from the pulvinar through the retrolenticular capsule into the parieto-occipital white matter, overlapping the optic radiation; on T2 the stratum sagittale lateral to the atrium contains both.

pathology.finding: Restricted diffusion in the parieto-occipital white matter lateral to the atrium with hemianopia, neglect or visuospatial impairment.

tract-thalamic-radiation-superior.name: Superior thalamic radiation
tract-thalamic-radiation-superior.summary: The superior thalamic radiation carries the fibers between the ventral tier of the thalamus and the sensorimotor cortex through the capsule's posterior limb and the corona radiata: the ventral posterior nuclei's somatosensory projection to the postcentral gyrus and the ventrolateral and ventral anterior nuclei's motor projection to the precentral gyrus and premotor cortex. It is the thalamocortical half of the sensorimotor system, running beside the descending corticospinal fibers, so posterior limb lesions produce sensory and motor deficits together, and thalamocortical disconnection in the corona radiata produces cortical-type sensory loss with an intact thalamus.

anatomy.location: From the ventral anterior, ventrolateral and ventral posterior nuclei laterally through the capsule's posterior limb, interdigitating with the corticospinal tract, and upward through the corona radiata to the precentral and postcentral gyri and the paracentral lobule, with the leg fibers posterior and the face fibers anterior in the capsule.

afferents.from: Ventral posterior, ventrolateral and ventral anterior nuclei

efferents.to: Postcentral and precentral gyri, premotor cortex
Ventral thalamic nuclei and reticular nucleus

tract-thalamic-radiation-superior.function: It delivers touch, proprioception, pain and temperature from the ventral posterior nuclei to the somatosensory cortex and the cerebellar and pallidal motor signals from the ventrolateral and ventral anterior nuclei to the motor and premotor cortex, and it returns corticothalamic fibers that regulate thalamic gating and generate sleep spindles and the alpha rhythm through the reticular nucleus. Its interruption produces contralateral hemianesthesia of cortical type (impaired localization, two-point discrimination and graphesthesia with relative preservation of pain) and contributes to ataxia and bradykinesia from loss of the motor thalamic input. It is damaged in lenticulostriate and anterior choroidal infarcts and in periventricular hemorrhage.

tract-uncinate-fasciculus.name: Uncinate fasciculus
tract-uncinate-fasciculus.summary: The uncinate fasciculus is the hook-shaped bundle that curves around the stem of the Sylvian fissure through the limen insulae, connecting the anterior temporal lobe, the temporal pole and the amygdala with the orbitofrontal and ventral prefrontal cortex. It is the pathway that lets emotion, memory and social meaning from the temporal lobe reach the decision-making cortex of the frontal lobe, and it carries proper names and person knowledge from the temporal pole to the inferior frontal gyrus. It is the last bundle to mature, in the third decade, it is damaged in temporal lobe epilepsy and its surgery, in frontotemporal dementia and in head injury, and its disconnection contributes to memory for names, emotional regulation and social conduct.

anatomy.location: From the temporal pole, the anterior superior, middle and inferior temporal gyri, the uncus and the amygdala, curving upward and forward through the limen insulae and the ventral extreme capsule (medial to the IFOF), then fanning into the gyrus rectus, the orbital gyri and the inferior frontal gyrus.

afferents.from: Temporal pole, anterior temporal gyri, uncus and amygdala

efferents.to: Orbitofrontal cortex, gyrus rectus and inferior frontal gyrus

tract-uncinate-fasciculus.function: It transmits the emotional value and the identity of stimuli from the amygdala and the temporal pole to the orbitofrontal cortex, which uses them to guide choices and social behavior, and returns frontal regulation to the amygdala; on the left it carries proper-name retrieval and the semantic-frontal connection for naming people, and it contributes to episodic memory encoding by linking the temporal memory system with the frontal strategic system. Bilateral damage or degeneration produces impaired social and emotional judgement, disinhibition and poor name retrieval, the picture of behavioral variant frontotemporal dementia, and its left-sided lesion after temporal lobectomy impairs naming of famous people and memory.

imaging.normalAppearance: Tractography shows a hook-shaped bundle from the anterior temporal lobe around the Sylvian stem into the orbitofrontal cortex; on coronal T2 the limen insulae, where it passes, is the narrow white-matter bridge between the temporal and frontal lobes.

trigeminal-nuclei.name: Trigeminal sensory and motor nuclei
trigeminal-nuclei.summary: The trigeminal nerve has the longest nuclear column in the brainstem. The principal (chief) sensory nucleus in the rostral pons receives discriminative touch from the face; the spinal nucleus below it receives pain and temperature; the mesencephalic nucleus above it is the only place where primary sensory cell bodies sit inside the central nervous system, serving jaw proprioception; and the motor nucleus, medial to the principal nucleus, drives the muscles of mastication. Together they let a single pontine lesion produce facial numbness with a weak jaw deviating toward the lesion.

anatomy.location: Principal sensory and motor nuclei: lateral tegmentum of the mid-pons at the level of the trigeminal root entry. Mesencephalic nucleus: a slender column along the lateral edge of the periaqueductal gray up to the superior colliculus. Spinal nucleus: descending through the medulla to C2–C3.

subdivisions.note: fine touch and pressure from the face; projects in the trigeminal lemniscus, mostly crossed, to VPM

subdivisions.name: Motor nucleus
subdivisions.note: masseter, temporalis, pterygoids, mylohyoid, anterior digastric, tensor tympani, tensor veli palatini; bilateral corticobulbar input

subdivisions.name: Mesencephalic nucleus
subdivisions.note: proprioception from jaw muscles and periodontal ligament; afferent limb of the jaw jerk

subdivisions.name: Spinal nucleus
subdivisions.note: pain, temperature and crude touch (see the spinal trigeminal entry)

trigeminal-nuclei.function: All facial somatic sensation, the sensory side of the corneal, blink and jaw-jerk reflexes, and motor control of chewing.

trochlear-nucleus.name: Trochlear nucleus
trochlear-nucleus.summary: A small motor nucleus in the ventral periaqueductal gray at the level of the inferior colliculus, just below the oculomotor complex. Its axons do something no other cranial nerve does: they run dorsally around the aqueduct, cross in the superior medullary velum and exit from the dorsal surface of the brainstem below the inferior colliculi. The nerve therefore supplies the contralateral superior oblique, and a nuclear or fascicular lesion causes a palsy on the opposite side while a lesion of the emerged nerve causes an ipsilateral palsy.

anatomy.location: Ventral periaqueductal gray at the inferior colliculus level, dorsal to the MLF, in line with the oculomotor nucleus above it.

trochlear-nucleus.function: Motor supply to the superior oblique muscle, which depresses the adducted eye and intorts the abducted eye; keeps the eyes level during head tilt.

Its axons do something no other cranial nerve does: they run dorsally around the aqueduct, cross in the superior medullary velum and exit from the dorsal surface of the brainstem below the inferior colliculi. The nerve therefore supplies the contralateral superior oblique, and a nuclear or fascicular lesion causes a palsy on the opposite side while a lesion of the emerged nerve causes an ipsilateral palsy.

uncus.name: Uncus
uncus.summary: The uncus is the hook-shaped anteromedial end of the parahippocampal gyrus, where the gyrus turns back on itself over the hippocampal head, lying in the medial temporal lobe against the tentorial edge, lateral to the cerebral peduncle and the oculomotor nerve. It contains the primary olfactory (piriform) cortex, the cortical nuclei of the amygdala and the anterior entorhinal cortex, so it is the cortex of smell and of the olfactory and gustatory auras of temporal seizures. Its clinical fame comes from uncal herniation: when a supratentorial mass pushes the uncus through the tentorial incisura it compresses the third nerve and the midbrain, producing the dilated pupil, hemiplegia and coma that neurosurgeons act on within minutes.

anatomy.location: Medial tip of the temporal lobe, anterior and medial to the hippocampal head, bounded medially by the free edge of the tentorium and the crural and ambient cisterns, with the oculomotor nerve, the posterior cerebral artery and the cerebral peduncle just medial to it.

Because it sits at the entrance to the hippocampus, seizures spreading through it produce olfactory hallucinations of burning or rotting smells (uncinate fits), lip smacking and chewing automatisms and an epigastric aura. vein-basal.name: Basal vein (of Rosenthal)
vein-basal.summary: The basal vein of Rosenthal is the paired deep vein of the base of the brain. It forms under the anterior perforated substance where the deep middle cerebral vein from the insula meets the anterior cerebral and striate veins, then curves backward around the cerebral peduncle through the crural and ambient cisterns, climbs over the lateral surface of the midbrain beside the posterior cerebral artery and the trochlear nerve, and ends in the great cerebral vein of Galen behind the pineal gland. Its course makes it the venous equivalent of an arterial circle at the skull base, linking the sylvian, deep and posterior fossa drainage; for the surgeon it is the vein that must be preserved when working in the ambient cistern, and for the radiologist it is the channel whose congestion explains temporal and midbrain edema in deep venous thrombosis.

anatomy.location: From the anterior perforated substance below the anterior commissure (about x = 13, y = 2, z = -16 in MNI coordinates) backward and medially through the crural cistern between the uncus and the cerebral peduncle, then through the ambient cistern lateral to the midbrain and medial to the parahippocampal gyrus, and finally over the pulvinar into the quadrigeminal cistern, where it joins the internal cerebral vein and its fellow to form the great cerebral vein. It runs with the posterior cerebral artery, above the trochlear nerve and below the optic tract.

vein-basal.function: The basal vein drains the medial temporal lobe including the hippocampus and the amygdala, the insula and the deep sylvian region through the deep middle cerebral vein, the anterior perforated substance and the striatum through the inferior striate veins, the hypothalamus, the midbrain and the choroid plexus of the temporal horn. Because it is assembled from three embryological segments (striate, peduncular and mesencephalic), it is one of the most variable veins in the skull: any of the three may be absent, and the vein may drain forward into the cavernous or sphenoparietal sinus, laterally into the superior petrosal sinus or backward into the transverse sinus rather than into the vein of Galen. That variability matters clinically, because a basal vein that empties into the vein of Galen makes the deep system the only outlet for the medial temporal lobe, whereas one that drains anteriorly gives it an escape route. In the ambient cistern the vein also forms the posterior half of the anastomotic venous ring around the midbrain that connects the two sides.

vein-great-cerebral.name: Great cerebral vein and deep venous system
vein-great-cerebral.latin: Vena magna cerebri (Galeni); venae cerebri internae
vein-great-cerebral.summary: The deep structures drain through a system of veins that converge on the great cerebral vein of Galen beneath the splenium. The internal cerebral veins form at the foramen of Monro from the thalamostriate and septal veins, run back in the roof of the third ventricle (velum interpositum) and unite as the vein of Galen, which is joined by the basal veins of Rosenthal (draining the insula, medial temporal lobe and midbrain) and empties into the straight sinus. Thrombosis of this system produces bilateral thalamic infarction, and vein of Galen malformations in infants cause heart failure and hydrocephalus.

vein-internal-cerebral.name: Internal cerebral vein
vein-internal-cerebral.summary: The internal cerebral vein is the paired collector of the deep white matter, the basal ganglia and the thalamus. It begins behind the foramen of Monro at the venous angle, where the anterior septal vein meets the thalamostriate vein, and runs backward for three to four centimeters as a straight paramedian channel in the roof of the third ventricle, inside the two layers of tela choroidea that form the velum interpositum. Under the splenium of the corpus callosum the two internal cerebral veins converge and join the two basal veins of Rosenthal to make the great cerebral vein of Galen. Because it lies within a millimeter or two of the midline and drains structures on both sides through the choroidal and subependymal veins, occlusion of one internal cerebral vein rarely stays unilateral: the classic result is bilateral thalamic swelling with a deep coma out of proportion to the size of the lesion.

anatomy.location: In the roof of the third ventricle, paired and paramedian, between about 2 and 6 mm from the midline, running from the foramen of Monro (roughly y = 0, z = +10 in MNI coordinates) posteriorly to the quadrigeminal cistern under the splenium (roughly y = -38). The vein lies in the velum interpositum between the fornix above and the roof of the third ventricle and the internal medullary lamina of the thalamus below; the medial posterior choroidal artery accompanies it, and the choroid plexus of the third ventricle hangs beneath it.

vein-internal-cerebral.function: The internal cerebral vein carries the deep venous return of the hemisphere: the anterior septal vein from the septum pellucidum and the anterior corpus callosum, the thalamostriate vein from the caudothalamic groove draining the caudate nucleus, the internal capsule and the deep periventricular white matter, the superior choroidal vein from the choroid plexus of the lateral ventricle, the direct lateral vein and the posterior thalamic (internal occipital) tributaries. Its territory is therefore the paraventricular white matter, the caudate, the internal capsule and most of the thalamus. Unlike the cortical veins, which have many surface anastomoses, the deep system is close to an end-drainage arrangement, so obstruction raises pressure quickly in a region with no collateral outlet. Flow is slow and pressure is low in health, which is why the vein is only faintly seen without contrast and why a thrombus in it produces venous congestion rather than immediate infarction: edema first, then petechial hemorrhage as the capillary bed fails.

veins-deep-cerebral.name: Deep cerebral veins
veins-deep-cerebral.summary: The deep cerebral veins drain the white matter, basal ganglia, thalamus and ventricular walls into the great cerebral vein of Galen and so into the straight sinus. On each side the septal vein from the frontal horn and the thalamostriate vein from the groove between caudate and thalamus join behind the foramen of Monro to form the internal cerebral vein, which runs back in the roof of the third ventricle beside its partner; the basal vein of Rosenthal collects the insula, the anterior perforated substance and the medial temporal lobe and curves around the midbrain to join them. Thrombosis of this system swells both thalami and produces coma, and the veins are the landmarks of transcallosal and pineal region surgery and of the venous phase of angiography, where the venous angle marks the foramen of Monro.

Look at the thalami on CT in any obtunded patient with a prothrombotic state
pearls: Bilateral thalamic swelling in a young patient is deep venous thrombosis until proven otherwise; the artery of Percheron is the arterial mimic
A developmental venous anomaly drains normal brain; never resect it, but look for the cavernoma that often accompanies it

pitfalls: Slow flow in the internal cerebral veins can look like thrombosis on time-of-flight MRV; confirm with contrast-enhanced venography

html.summary: The deep cerebral veins drain the white matter, basal ganglia, thalamus and ventricular walls into the great cerebral vein of Galen and so into the straight sinus. On each side the septal vein from the frontal horn and the thalamostriate vein from the groove between caudate and thalamus join behind the foramen of Monro to form the internal cerebral vein, which runs back in the roof of the third ventricle beside its partner; the basal vein of Rosenthal collects the insula, the anterior perforated substance and the medial temporal lobe and curves around the midbrain to join them. Thrombosis of this system swells both thalami and produces coma, and the veins are the landmarks of transcallosal and pineal region surgery and of the venous phase of angiography, where the venous angle marks the foramen of Monro.
html.function: The deep veins have no valves and drain a large volume of the central white matter, the striatum and the thalamus through the subependymal and medullary veins into the internal cerebral veins, and the deep temporal lobe and diencephalon through the basal veins; the system is separate from the superficial cortical veins but connects with them through anastomotic medullary veins, which enlarge when either route is blocked. Their orientation and displacement on angiography and MR venography reveal masses of the deep structures.
html.anatomy.location: Internal cerebral veins in the velum interpositum in the roof of the third ventricle, from the foramen of Monro to the pineal region, joined by the basal veins beneath the splenium to form the great cerebral vein, which enters the straight sinus at the junction of the falx and tentorium.
html.imaging.normalAppearance: Paired flow voids in the roof of the third ventricle on T2, enhancing on post-contrast T1 and bright on MR venography; the great vein curves up beneath the splenium into the straight sinus. The thalamostriate veins run in the caudothalamic groove and are seen on susceptibility imaging as they enter the venous angle.

veins-superficial-cerebral.name: Superficial cerebral (bridging) veins
veins-superficial-cerebral.summary: The cortex drains through superficial veins that run in the subarachnoid space and cross the subdural space as bridging veins to enter the dural sinuses: the superior cerebral veins into the superior sagittal sinus, the superficial middle cerebral vein along the Sylvian fissure into the cavernous or sphenoparietal sinus, and the two large anastomotic veins, Trolard (to the superior sagittal sinus) and Labbé (to the transverse sinus). The bridging veins tear with acceleration of the brain relative to the skull, producing subdural hematoma, especially in atrophic elderly and anticoagulated patients; cortical vein thrombosis causes focal seizures and lobar hemorrhage.

anatomy.location: Over the convexity in the sulci and on the gyri beneath the arachnoid, converging on the sinuses; the bridging segments cross the subdural space near the vertex, the vein of Labbé runs over the posterior temporal lobe to the transverse sinus.

veins-superficial-cerebral.function: Venous drainage of the cerebral cortex and subcortical white matter into the dural sinuses; the anastomotic veins provide alternative routes when a sinus is occluded.

arteries: (venous structure) drains territories of the cerebral arteries

bestView.label: bridging veins entering the superior sagittal sinus at the vertex
vein of Labbé crossing the posterior temporal lobe to the transverse sinus

imaging.normalAppearance: Cortical veins are dark on T2 and SWI and enhance on contrast images; a thrombosed cortical vein is a dense cord on CT, bright on T1 and blooming on SWI, with adjacent edema or hemorrhage. Subdural hematoma is the imaging footprint of torn bridging veins.

pathology.finding: Tubular SWI hypointensity and T1 hyperintensity of a cortical vein with adjacent edema, hemorrhage or infarct; seizures and focal deficits.
Crescentic collection from bridging vein rupture.
Temporal lobe venous hemorrhagic infarct with transverse sinus thrombosis.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: SWI and T1 with venography; CT for hematoma

lesionEffects.deficit: Subdural hematoma with headache, confusion, hemiparesis
lesionEffects.mechanism: Bridging vein rupture
Cortical vein thrombosis

lesionEffects.deficit: Aphasia with a temporal venous infarct
lesionEffects.mechanism: Vein of Labbé occlusion on the dominant side

examination: Level of consciousness and lateralizing signs
Seizure history
Anticoagulant use and fall history
pearls: Atrophy stretches the bridging veins: minor trauma in the elderly is enough for a subdural

veins-venat-atlas.name: Cerebral veins and sinuses (VENAT atlas iso-surface)
veins-venat-atlas.summary: This mesh is the intracranial venous tree extracted from a population atlas of the cerebral veins built from 7 T quantitative susceptibility maps: the iso-surface of the average venous partial-volume map, thresholded inside the brain, so that it shows the channels that are present in almost everyone. It contains the superior sagittal sinus along the attached margin of the falx, the transverse and sigmoid sinuses, the torcular, the straight sinus in the tentorium, the great cerebral vein, the paired internal cerebral veins in the roof of the third ventricle, the basal veins around the midbrain and the larger cortical and medullary veins. It is the venous counterpart of the arterial iso-surface in this atlas: it sits exactly on the template MRI, so the veins can be read against the slices without any registration error, and it shows what a normal venogram should contain.

anatomy.location: The whole intracranial venous compartment inside the template brain mask, from the vertex where the superior sagittal sinus begins to the torcular and the transverse and sigmoid sinuses at the skull base, including the deep veins in the roof of the third ventricle and the ambient cisterns.

afferents.from: Cortical, medullary and deep cerebral veins

veins-venat-atlas.function: Read as an anatomical reference, the surface answers the questions a venogram raises: where a sinus should run, how the deep veins relate to the ventricles and the corpus callosum, and which cortical veins reach which sinus. Because it is an average of many people, its channels are smoother and slightly wider than any individual's, the small cortical veins that vary from person to person fall below the threshold and are missing, and normal variants such as a hypoplastic left transverse sinus are averaged away. That is exactly what makes it useful as a template: a vessel that is present here is present in almost everyone, so its absence on a patient's venogram is worth explaining, while a vessel missing here may still be normal in an individual. The venous tree also explains the two rules that separate venous from arterial disease: venous lesions cross arterial territory boundaries, and they are usually edematous before they are hemorrhagic.

arteries: Cerebral arteries feed the capillary bed drained by these veins
bloodSupply.venous: The whole intracranial venous outflow, ending at the jugular bulbs and the vertebral venous plexus

bestView.label: midline sinuses, deep veins and the straight sinus
transverse sinuses and the torcular
superior sagittal sinus and the deep venous system

imaging.normalAppearance: On MR and CT venography the normal venous tree looks like this surface: a continuous superior sagittal sinus, two transverse sinuses that are commonly asymmetric, a straight sinus running from the vein of Galen to the torcular, and two thin internal cerebral veins under the corpus callosum. Susceptibility-weighted imaging adds the medullary and cortical veins that are too variable to survive averaging.

pathology.finding: A filling defect or absent flow in a sinus that the atlas shows should be continuous, with the empty delta sign after contrast and, on unenhanced CT, a hyperdense cord along the expected course.
pathology.pitfalls: Flow gaps, arachnoid granulations and a hypoplastic transverse sinus all mimic thrombosis on time-of-flight venography; confirm with contrast-enhanced or susceptibility imaging

pathology.finding: Edema and petechial hemorrhage that do not respect arterial territory borders, in the drainage field of the occluded channel rather than in a cortical wedge.
Arterialized flow in a sinus or a cortical vein with retrograde cortical venous drainage, which is the feature that predicts hemorrhage.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: Contrast-enhanced MR venography, with susceptibility-weighted imaging for the small veins

lesionEffects.mechanism: This is an imaging-derived reference, not a structure with a lesion syndrome

lesionEffects.deficit: Shows where an absent channel should have been
lesionEffects.mechanism: The averaged tree marks the expected course of every constant sinus and deep vein

examination: Compare a patient's venogram with the atlas surface before calling a sinus absent
Follow each sinus from the vertex to the jugular bulb rather than looking at one slice
pearls: A vessel present in the average atlas is present in nearly everybody: its absence needs an explanation
The atlas is thicker than a real vein; use it for course, not for caliber
The deep veins and the straight sinus are the constant part of the map; the cortical veins are the variable part

pitfalls: Averaging removes normal variants; a channel absent here can still be normal in one person
The threshold that keeps the sinuses clean also removes the smallest cortical veins

ventral-diencephalon.name: Ventral diencephalon
ventral-diencephalon.summary: The ventral diencephalon is the FreeSurfer segmentation label that groups the structures below the thalamus that are hard to separate on T1-weighted images: the hypothalamus, the mammillary bodies, the subthalamic nucleus, the zona incerta and fields of Forel, the substantia nigra and red nucleus at the diencephalic-midbrain junction, the optic tract, the ventral tegmental area and the geniculate region. It is used in this atlas as the container mesh for the hypothalamic and subthalamic nuclei that the higher-resolution atlases subdivide, and its volume is a crude but reproducible measure of the diencephalon in dementia and in hypothalamic disease.

anatomy.location: The tissue between the thalamus above and the interpeduncular cistern and cerebral peduncles below, from the optic chiasm and lamina terminalis in front to the posterior commissure and the midbrain behind, lateral to the third ventricle and medial to the internal capsule and the optic tract.

ventral-diencephalon.function: The label spans the hypothalamus (autonomic, endocrine, circadian and behavioral control), the subthalamus (motor control through the subthalamic nucleus and the pallidothalamic pathways), the mammillary bodies (memory), the optic tract (vision), the substantia nigra and ventral tegmental area (dopamine) and the red nucleus (cerebellar outflow); functionally it is the crossroads through which the limbic forebrain, the basal ganglia, the cerebellum and the brainstem exchange fibers with the thalamus and the cortex. Its individual components are described in their own entries; the container is useful for volumetric follow-up and as a landmark region for the thalamoperforating and anterior choroidal artery territories.

bestView.label: ventral diencephalon below the thalamus and beside the third ventricle
hypothalamus and subthalamus in front of the midbrain

imaging.normalAppearance: Gray matter beneath the thalamus and around the lower third ventricle on coronal images, extending from the chiasm to the midbrain; the FreeSurfer label includes the optic tract and the upper substantia nigra, so it is not a pure gray-matter structure.

pathology.finding: Restricted diffusion in the subthalamic-hypothalamic region with contralateral hemiballismus, hemiparesis or amnesia depending on the artery.
Mass in the ventral diencephalon with endocrine, sleep and behavioral disturbance; enhancement pattern distinguishes glioma, germinoma and hamartoma.
Symmetric FLAIR hyperintensity of the medial thalami, mammillary bodies and periventricular hypothalamus.

lesionEffects.mechanism: Hypothalamic component
Subthalamic and zona incerta component
Mammillary body and mammillothalamic component

examination: Endocrine screen, temperature and sleep history
Movement examination for ballismus, tremor and parkinsonism
Memory testing
pearls: The ventral diencephalon label is a segmentation convenience; when a lesion is here, ask which of its residents is hit
Its volume shrinks in Alzheimer disease and in hypothalamic disorders and is a reproducible measure
It is the region where the anterior choroidal, thalamoperforating and posterior communicating arteries meet

pitfalls: Automated volumes of the ventral diencephalon include the optic tract and part of the midbrain; interpret changes with the anatomy in mind

ventral-tegmental-area.name: Ventral tegmental area
ventral-tegmental-area.summary: The ventral tegmental area is the group of dopamine neurons in the ventromedial midbrain tegmentum medial to the substantia nigra, above the interpeduncular nucleus and lateral to the midline, the source of the mesolimbic and mesocortical dopamine systems. Its axons run in the medial forebrain bundle to the nucleus accumbens, the amygdala, the hippocampus and the prefrontal cortex and signal reward prediction, motivation and salience; it is the substrate of addiction, of the reinforcing effects of every drug of abuse, of anhedonia and of the positive symptoms treated by dopamine antagonists. It is relatively spared in Parkinson disease but contributes to apathy and to the dopamine dysregulation syndrome, and it is damaged in Wernicke encephalopathy and paramedian midbrain infarcts.

anatomy.location: Ventromedial midbrain tegmentum on each side of the midline, medial to the substantia nigra pars compacta and the medial lemniscus, dorsal to the interpeduncular nucleus and the fossa, ventral to the red nucleus and the oculomotor nerve fibers, extending from the mammillary bodies to the rostral pons.

afferents.via: descending medial forebrain bundle and cholinergic fibers

afferents.from: Lateral habenula (via the rostromedial tegmental nucleus)

efferents.via: mesolimbic pathway in the medial forebrain bundle

ventral-tegmental-area.function: Dopamine neurons of the ventral tegmental area burst when a reward is better than predicted and pause when it is worse, teaching the accumbens and the prefrontal cortex which cues and actions lead to reward; tonic activity sets motivation and effort. Mesocortical dopamine tunes prefrontal working memory in an inverted-U relation, and mesolimbic dopamine drives approach behavior and the incentive value of cues, which drugs of abuse hijack by raising accumbens dopamine directly or through the ventral tegmental area. GABAergic and glutamatergic neurons within the area modulate the dopamine cells and project to the same targets, and the area receives the prefrontal cortex, the lateral hypothalamus (orexin), the pedunculopontine and laterodorsal tegmental nuclei, the lateral habenula and the raphe.

bestView.label: ventral tegmental area medial to the substantia nigra
ventromedial midbrain tegmentum above the interpeduncular fossa

imaging.normalAppearance: The paramedian ventral midbrain tegmentum between the red nuclei and the interpeduncular fossa on axial images; on neuromelanin-sensitive images it is continuous with the medial pars compacta.

pathology.finding: Restricted diffusion of the ventromedial midbrain with third nerve palsy, contralateral ataxia or hemiparesis and apathy or hypersomnia.
FLAIR hyperintensity of the periaqueductal gray and the medial midbrain tegmentum including the ventral tegmental area, with the mammillary bodies.
Increased striatal dopamine release to drugs and cues and elevated presynaptic dopamine synthesis in psychosis on PET; structural MRI normal.

lesionEffects.deficit: Apathy, anhedonia and loss of motivation
lesionEffects.mechanism: Loss of mesolimbic dopamine reward signaling
Loss of mesocortical dopamine to the prefrontal cortex

lesionEffects.deficit: Contribution to hypersomnia after midbrain lesions
lesionEffects.mechanism: Loss of the arousal-promoting dopaminergic component of the ascending systems

examination: Apathy and reward responsiveness history
Working memory and attention testing
Substance use history, because this system is the target of every addictive drug
pearls: The ventral tegmental area is where wanting is made; every drug of abuse raises its dopamine in the accumbens
Antipsychotics treat delusions by blocking the receptors that mesolimbic dopamine drives, and cause parkinsonism by blocking the nigrostriatal ones
Thiamine deficiency injures this region along with the mammillary bodies; apathy is part of Wernicke encephalopathy

pitfalls: Apathy after a midbrain or thalamic stroke is often labeled depression; it lacks the sadness and reflects dopaminergic disconnection

ventricle-fourth.name: Fourth ventricle
ventricle-fourth.summary: A tent-shaped cavity between the pons and medulla in front and the cerebellum behind. Its diamond-shaped floor, the rhomboid fossa, is a clinical map of cranial nerve nuclei: the facial colliculus and hypoglossal and vagal trigones bulge into it, and the area postrema (vomiting trigger zone) lies at its caudal tip. CSF leaves it through the median foramen of Magendie and the two lateral foramina of Luschka into the subarachnoid space. Tumors in it (ependymoma, medulloblastoma) and cerebellar swelling around it cause acute hydrocephalus.

anatomy.location: Between the dorsal pons and upper medulla (floor) and the cerebellum (roof), continuous above with the aqueduct and below with the central canal; lateral recesses extend around the inferior cerebellar peduncles to open at the cerebellopontine angles.

subdivisions.name: Floor (rhomboid fossa)
subdivisions.note: medial eminence, facial colliculus, hypoglossal and vagal trigones, vestibular area, area postrema

subdivisions.name: Roof
subdivisions.note: superior medullary velum and superior cerebellar peduncles above, inferior medullary velum and tela choroidea with choroid plexus below

subdivisions.name: Lateral recesses and foramina of Luschka
subdivisions.note: openings at the cerebellopontine angles

subdivisions.name: Foramen of Magendie
subdivisions.note: median opening into the cisterna magna

ventricle-fourth.function: Passage of CSF from the aqueduct into the subarachnoid space; its floor houses the pontine and medullary cranial nerve nuclei; the area postrema senses blood-borne toxins and triggers vomiting.

bestView.label: fourth ventricle between the pons and cerebellum
tent-shaped ventricle with its fastigium under the vermis
lateral recesses extending toward the cerebellopontine angles

imaging.normalAppearance: A CSF-filled triangle behind the pons on axial images and a tent with its apex (fastigium) pointing into the vermis on sagittal images. Compression or effacement by cerebellar swelling is an emergency sign; a mass inside it in a child is usually ependymoma or medulloblastoma.

pathology.finding: Medulloblastoma (arising from the vermis, restricted diffusion) or ependymoma (plastic tumor squeezing through the foramina of Luschka and Magendie) with obstructive hydrocephalus.

pathology.pathology: Effaced fourth ventricle from cerebellar infarct or hemorrhage
pathology.finding: Loss of the fourth ventricular lumen with dilatation of the third and lateral ventricles; needs urgent neurosurgical evaluation.
Cystic dilatation of the fourth ventricle with vermian hypoplasia and an enlarged posterior fossa.

lesionEffects.deficit: Acute hydrocephalus with headache, vomiting and decreased consciousness
lesionEffects.mechanism: Obstruction of the ventricle by tumor or surrounding swelling
Area postrema at the caudal tip

lesionEffects.deficit: Cranial nerve VI, VII, X and XII signs

Eye movements, facial movement, palate and tongue
Gait and truncal ataxia

ventricle-lateral-inferior-horn.name: Lateral ventricle, inferior (temporal) horn
ventricle-lateral-inferior-horn.summary: The inferior horn of the lateral ventricle curves forward and downward from the atrium into the medial temporal lobe, ending behind the amygdala, with the hippocampus bulging into its floor and the tail of the caudate and the stria terminalis in its roof. It is the ventricular space that dilates first in obstructive hydrocephalus and in the trapped-ventricle syndrome, that widens with hippocampal atrophy in Alzheimer disease and mesial temporal sclerosis, and whose choroid plexus and fissure are the site of choroidal fissure cysts; its relation to the hippocampus makes it the approach corridor for temporal lobe surgery, and its dilatation on the opposite side is a sign of uncal herniation.

anatomy.location: Temporal horn of the lateral ventricle within the medial temporal lobe, running from the collateral trigone forward and inferiorly to a blind end just behind the amygdala; floor formed by the hippocampus and the collateral eminence, roof by the tapetum of the corpus callosum, the caudate tail and the stria terminalis, medial wall by the choroid fissure and the fimbria.

afferents.from: Choroid plexus of the atrium and inferior horn

efferents.to: Atrium and body of the lateral ventricle toward the foramen of Monro

ventricle-lateral-inferior-horn.function: The inferior horn is part of the CSF pathway from the choroid plexus of the lateral ventricle to the foramen of Monro, though its own plexus (continuous with that of the atrium through the choroidal fissure) contributes to CSF production; its size reflects the volume of the surrounding medial temporal structures and the pressure in the ventricular system. It is bounded by the structures of memory, so its enlargement is a marker of hippocampal loss, and it lies next to the optic radiation in its lateral wall, which is why temporal horn surgery risks a superior quadrantanopia. Its anterior tip is the landmark for the amygdala on coronal images.

bestView.label: temporal horn above the hippocampus
inferior horn curving into the medial temporal lobe

imaging.normalAppearance: A thin CSF-signal slit above the hippocampus on coronal images, often barely visible in young adults; the choroid plexus within it enhances normally. Its anterior tip lies just behind the amygdala.

pathology.finding: Rounding and dilatation of the temporal horns is the earliest and most sensitive sign of raised ventricular pressure, preceding frontal horn enlargement.

pathology.pathology: Mesial temporal sclerosis and Alzheimer disease
pathology.finding: Asymmetric or bilateral widening of the temporal horn with hippocampal atrophy; rated with the medial temporal atrophy scale.
Isolated dilatation of one temporal horn from obstruction at the atrium by tumor, hemorrhage or adhesions, causing mass effect and herniation.
Small CSF-signal cyst in the choroidal fissure medial to the temporal horn, a normal variant that must not be called a tumor or a dilated horn.

lesionEffects.deficit: Sign of raised intracranial pressure or hydrocephalus
lesionEffects.mechanism: Dilatation of the temporal horns with obstruction of CSF flow
Ex vacuo widening as the medial temporal lobe shrinks

lesionEffects.deficit: Superior quadrantanopia after surgery or with lateral-wall lesions
lesionEffects.mechanism: Injury to the optic radiation in the lateral wall of the horn

examination: Measure temporal horn width on every CT read for hydrocephalus
Grade medial temporal atrophy on coronal T1 in cognitive complaints
Visual fields after temporal lobe surgery
pearls: Round temporal horns on CT mean hydrocephalus; slit-like ones mean it has been treated or never was
The temporal horn widens as the hippocampus shrinks; the two are measured together
A trapped temporal horn is a surgical emergency that looks like a cyst

pitfalls: Asymmetry of the temporal horns is common in normal brains; it is the combination with hippocampal signal or size change that matters

html.summary: The inferior horn of the lateral ventricle curves forward and downward from the atrium into the medial temporal lobe, ending behind the amygdala, with the hippocampus bulging into its floor and the tail of the caudate and the stria terminalis in its roof. It is the ventricular space that dilates first in obstructive hydrocephalus and in the trapped-ventricle syndrome, that widens with hippocampal atrophy in Alzheimer disease and mesial temporal sclerosis, and whose choroid plexus and fissure are the site of choroidal fissure cysts; its relation to the hippocampus makes it the approach corridor for temporal lobe surgery, and its dilatation on the opposite side is a sign of uncal herniation.
html.function: The inferior horn is part of the CSF pathway from the choroid plexus of the lateral ventricle to the foramen of Monro, though its own plexus (continuous with that of the atrium through the choroidal fissure) contributes to CSF production; its size reflects the volume of the surrounding medial temporal structures and the pressure in the ventricular system. It is bounded by the structures of memory, so its enlargement is a marker of hippocampal loss, and it lies next to the optic radiation in its lateral wall, which is why temporal horn surgery risks a superior quadrantanopia. Its anterior tip is the landmark for the amygdala on coronal images.
html.anatomy.location: Temporal horn of the lateral ventricle within the medial temporal lobe, running from the collateral trigone forward and inferiorly to a blind end just behind the amygdala; floor formed by the hippocampus and the collateral eminence, roof by the tapetum of the corpus callosum, the caudate tail and the stria terminalis, medial wall by the choroid fissure and the fimbria.
html.imaging.normalAppearance: A thin CSF-signal slit above the hippocampus on coronal images, often barely visible in young adults; the choroid plexus within it enhances normally. Its anterior tip lies just behind the amygdala.

ventricle-lateral.name: Lateral ventricles
ventricle-lateral.summary: Each cerebral hemisphere contains a C-shaped lateral ventricle that follows the curve of the caudate nucleus and hippocampus: a frontal horn in front of the foramen of Monro, a body beneath the corpus callosum, a trigone (atrium) where the posterior and inferior horns diverge, an occipital horn and a temporal (inferior) horn ending near the amygdala. Choroid plexus in the body, atrium and temporal horn produces most of the CSF. The ventricles are the first structures to change shape with hydrocephalus, atrophy or a mass, so their size and symmetry are read on every scan.

anatomy.location: Frontal horn between the genu of the corpus callosum and the caudate head, lateral to the septum pellucidum; body under the callosal body with the thalamus in its floor; atrium at the splenium; occipital horn indenting the calcar avis; temporal horn in the medial temporal lobe above the hippocampus.

subdivisions.name: Frontal (anterior) horn
subdivisions.note: in front of the foramen of Monro; caudate head lateral, septum medial; no choroid plexus

subdivisions.name: Body
subdivisions.note: roof corpus callosum, floor thalamus and caudate body, medial wall fornix

subdivisions.name: Atrium (trigone)
subdivisions.note: junction of body, occipital and temporal horns; large glomus of choroid plexus

subdivisions.name: Occipital (posterior) horn
subdivisions.note: variable in size, often asymmetrical; calcar avis on the medial wall

subdivisions.name: Temporal (inferior) horn
subdivisions.note: roof tail of caudate and stria terminalis, floor hippocampus; first to enlarge in obstructive hydrocephalus

ventricle-lateral.function: Contain and circulate CSF produced by the choroid plexus toward the third ventricle through the interventricular foramina; buffer the brain against pressure changes.

bestView.label: bodies and frontal horns at the level of the foramen of Monro
frontal horns with the caudate heads lateral
temporal horns above the hippocampi

pathology.finding: Dilated lateral and third ventricles with rounded frontal horns, dilated temporal horns and periventricular hypodensity (transependymal edema) out of proportion to sulcal size; the fourth ventricle is normal if the aqueduct is blocked.

Hyperdense blood layering in the occipital horns and filling the ventricles, from an intracerebral hemorrhage rupturing through or from germinal matrix bleeding in preterm infants.
Enlarged ventricles proportional to enlarged sulci, no temporal horn dilatation or transependymal edema.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: Non-contrast CT for acute ventricular size; MRI T2/FLAIR for the cause

lesionEffects.deficit: Headache, vomiting, papilledema, sixth nerve palsy
lesionEffects.mechanism: Raised pressure from obstructed CSF outflow

lesionEffects.deficit: Gait apraxia, urinary incontinence, cognitive slowing
lesionEffects.mechanism: Chronic ventricular enlargement stretching periventricular fibers (normal pressure hydrocephalus)
Dilated third ventricle and suprapineal recess pressing on the tectum

examination: Fundoscopy for papilledema
Gait: short steps, wide base, feet stuck to the floor (magnetic gait)
Bedside cognition and continence history
In infants: head circumference and fontanelle
pearls: Temporal horns visible on a CT of an adult mean hydrocephalus until proven otherwise
Big ventricles with big sulci is atrophy; big ventricles with small sulci is hydrocephalus

pitfalls: Asymmetric occipital horns are a common normal variant
Cavum septum pellucidum and cavum vergae are normal CSF spaces between the leaves of the septum, not a cyst

ventricle-third.name: Third ventricle
ventricle-third.summary: A narrow midline slit between the two thalami and hypothalami, connected to the lateral ventricles in front through the interventricular foramina of Monro and to the fourth ventricle behind through the cerebral aqueduct. Its walls are the thalamus above and the hypothalamus below, its floor descends to the optic chiasm, infundibulum and mammillary bodies, and its roof carries choroid plexus. Masses of the pituitary, hypothalamus, pineal region or a colloid cyst at the foramen of Monro obstruct it, and its dilatation in hydrocephalus presses on the hypothalamus and chiasm.

anatomy.location: Midline diencephalon, bounded laterally by the thalami (often joined across it by the interthalamic adhesion) and hypothalami, anteriorly by the lamina terminalis and anterior commissure, posteriorly by the pineal recess and posterior commissure, and inferiorly by the optic and infundibular recesses.

subdivisions.name: Anterior wall
subdivisions.note: lamina terminalis, anterior commissure, columns of the fornix

subdivisions.name: Floor
subdivisions.note: optic chiasm, infundibulum, tuber cinereum, mammillary bodies, tegmentum of the midbrain

subdivisions.name: Roof
subdivisions.note: ependyma with choroid plexus beneath the fornix

subdivisions.name: Posterior wall
subdivisions.note: pineal recess, habenular and posterior commissures, opening of the aqueduct

ventricle-third.function: CSF conduit between the lateral and fourth ventricles; its wall structures (hypothalamus, thalamus) and floor recesses are important landmarks for pituitary and pineal region disease.

bestView.label: slit-like midline ventricle between the thalami
recesses of the floor and the aqueduct behind
third ventricle at the level of the foramen of Monro

imaging.normalAppearance: A thin midline CSF slit on axial and coronal images, wider in the elderly; on sagittal T2 the optic and infundibular recesses point down toward the sella. A ballooned third ventricle with a bowed floor indicates obstructive hydrocephalus.

pathology.pathology: Colloid cyst of the foramen of Monro
pathology.finding: Round T1-bright, T2-variable cyst at the anterior roof of the third ventricle obstructing both foramina; can cause sudden death from acute hydrocephalus.
Suprasellar cystic and calcified mass elevating the floor of the third ventricle.
Rounded third ventricle with downward bowing of the floor and dilated recesses; the target for endoscopic third ventriculostomy.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: Sagittal T2 (CISS) for the floor and aqueduct; CT for calcification

lesionEffects.deficit: Intermittent severe headache with drop attacks
lesionEffects.mechanism: Ball-valve obstruction of the foramina of Monro by a colloid cyst
Mass in the floor pressing on the chiasm and hypothalamus
Hypothalamic wall involvement
Fornix and mammillary body damage from surgery or tumor

examination: Visual fields and acuity
Fundoscopy
Endocrine history: thirst, weight, menses, libido
Memory testing
pearls: A young adult with positional thunderclap headaches and a round lesion at the foramen of Monro has a colloid cyst and needs neurosurgical review

vestibular-nuclei.name: Vestibular nuclei
synonyms: superior, lateral (Deiters), medial and inferior vestibular nuclei
vestibular-nuclei.summary: Four nuclei beneath the lateral part of the fourth ventricular floor at the pontomedullary junction receive the vestibular nerve and cerebellar input and distribute it to the eye movement nuclei (through the MLF), the spinal cord (vestibulospinal tracts), the cerebellum and the thalamus. They generate the vestibulo-ocular reflex that keeps vision stable during head movement and the postural reflexes that keep us upright. Their involvement is why vertigo, nystagmus and vomiting open the lateral medullary and AICA syndromes.

anatomy.location: Lateral floor of the fourth ventricle (vestibular area) from the upper medulla into the lower pons, medial to the inferior cerebellar peduncle and lateral to the solitary and dorsal vagal nuclei.

subdivisions.name: Superior nucleus
subdivisions.note: vestibulo-ocular reflex via the MLF

subdivisions.name: Lateral (Deiters) nucleus
subdivisions.note: lateral vestibulospinal tract; extensor tone against gravity

subdivisions.name: Medial nucleus
subdivisions.note: medial vestibulospinal tract and MLF; head–eye coordination

subdivisions.name: Inferior nucleus
subdivisions.note: integration with the cerebellum and spinal input

vestibular-nuclei.function: Sense of head position and motion; vestibulo-ocular and vestibulospinal reflexes; input to the cerebellum and to conscious vestibular perception in the thalamus and cortex.

bestView.label: lateral floor of the fourth ventricle at the pontomedullary junction
vestibular area under the lateral recess

imaging.normalAppearance: Not resolved on routine MRI; the region is the lateral ventricular floor near the lateral recess. In a patient with acute vertigo, a normal DWI in the first 48 hours does not exclude a small infarct here.

pathology.finding: Dorsolateral medullary or lateral pontine restricted diffusion in a patient with acute vestibular syndrome; HINTS examination is more sensitive than early DWI.
pathology.pitfalls: Up to a fifth of small posterior fossa infarcts are DWI-negative in the first two days

pathology.finding: Small FLAIR lesion in the dorsolateral pontomedullary junction with vertigo and nystagmus.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: DWI (repeat after 48 h if negative and central signs are present); HINTS bedside battery

lesionEffects.mechanism: Asymmetric vestibular tone

lesionEffects.deficit: Nystagmus that changes direction with gaze, or vertical or torsional nystagmus
lesionEffects.mechanism: Central vestibular nuclei rather than the labyrinth
Vestibulospinal imbalance

lesionEffects.deficit: Skew deviation and ocular tilt reaction
lesionEffects.mechanism: Central otolithic pathways

Gait and Romberg
Hearing (preserved in medullary lesions, lost in AICA lesions)
pearls: A normal head impulse with direction-changing nystagmus and skew deviation means the vertigo is central

zona-incerta.name: Zona incerta
zona-incerta.summary: The zona incerta is a thin sheet of gray matter in the subthalamus between the thalamus above and the subthalamic nucleus and cerebral peduncle below, separated from them by the lenticular and thalamic fasciculi (fields H1 and H2 of Forel). It is a neglected hub that receives cortex, basal ganglia, brainstem and spinal input and sends inhibitory projections to the thalamus, the superior colliculus, the brainstem and the spinal cord, gating sensory transmission, arousal, feeding and posture. Clinically it matters because deep brain stimulation electrodes for tremor and Parkinson disease pass through or end in it, and stimulation of its caudal part relieves tremor at least as well as the ventral intermediate nucleus; hemorrhage or infarction here produces contralateral hemiballismus-like movements or ataxia.

anatomy.location: Subthalamic region between the thalamic fasciculus (H1) above and the lenticular fasciculus (H2) below, extending from the posterior hypothalamus in front to the pretectum and the midbrain reticular formation behind, lateral to the red nucleus and medial to the internal capsule, above the subthalamic nucleus.

afferents.from: Brainstem reticular formation and spinal cord

efferents.to: Superior colliculus and brainstem premotor nuclei

zona-incerta.function: Zona incerta neurons are mostly GABAergic and inhibit the higher-order thalamic nuclei, so that attention and cortical state control which sensory signals reach the cortex; they also drive the superior colliculus and brainstem premotor centers for orienting and posture, modulate pain in the spinal dorsal horn, and influence feeding and drinking through hypothalamic connections. Its rostral part participates in the sleep-wake and arousal networks, and its caudal part, traversed by cerebellothalamic fibers, is the target of tremor surgery. Because the pallidothalamic fibers of the ansa lenticularis and lenticular fasciculus wrap around it, lesions here mimic pallidal or subthalamic damage.

bestView.label: zona incerta between the thalamus and the subthalamic nucleus
subthalamic region lateral to the red nucleus

imaging.normalAppearance: A thin gray band on coronal T2 images beneath the thalamus and above the subthalamic nucleus, separated by the dark fiber bundles of Forel's fields; visible on high-resolution or susceptibility-weighted images used for stimulation planning.

pathology.pathology: Deep brain stimulation for tremor (caudal zona incerta target)
pathology.finding: Electrode tip in the posterior subthalamic area on postoperative CT fused to preoperative MRI; the target lies posteromedial to the subthalamic nucleus.
Small hyperdense hemorrhage in the subthalamic region with contralateral hemiballismus or hemichorea.
Restricted diffusion in the subthalamic and paramedian thalamic region with contralateral ataxia, tremor and sensory change.

lesionEffects.mechanism: Involvement of the subthalamic nucleus and the pallidothalamic fibers passing beside the zona incerta
Interruption of cerebellothalamic fibers traversing its caudal part
Loss of incertal inhibition of higher-order thalamic nuclei

examination: Observe for ballistic or choreic movements of the contralateral limbs
Finger-nose testing for a cerebellar-outflow tremor
Sensory testing for a thalamic component
pearls: The zona incerta is the uncertain zone between thalamus and subthalamus: electrodes aimed at either end up here
Caudal zona incerta stimulation stops tremor by silencing the cerebellothalamic fibers that pass through it
Hemiballismus after a small subthalamic stroke usually resolves within weeks

pitfalls: Ballismus after a stroke is often called a seizure; it is a subthalamic release phenomenon and responds to dopamine blockers

cn-01-olfactory.name: Olfactory nerve (CN I)
cn-01-olfactory.summary: Smell is carried by about twenty bundles of unmyelinated axons from the olfactory receptor neurons in the roof of the nasal cavity through the cribriform plate to the olfactory bulb, which relays through the olfactory tract directly to the primary olfactory (piriform) cortex of the uncus and to the amygdala and entorhinal cortex, bypassing the thalamus. It is the only sensory system that reaches the cortex without a thalamic relay and the only one with continuously regenerating receptor neurons. Its bundles shear on the cribriform plate in head injury, its bulb and tract are compressed by subfrontal meningiomas, and loss of smell is an early feature of Parkinson and Alzheimer disease and of viral infection.

anatomy.location: Receptor neurons in the olfactory epithelium of the superior nasal cavity; axons through the cribriform plate of the ethmoid; olfactory bulb and tract on the orbital surface of the frontal lobe in the olfactory sulcus, dividing at the anterior perforated substance into medial and lateral olfactory striae; lateral stria to the uncus.

cn-01-olfactory.function: Sense of smell and much of flavour; olfactory-limbic connections for memory and emotion; warning of smoke, gas and spoiled food.

bestView.label: olfactory bulbs beneath the frontal lobes above the cribriform plate
olfactory tracts in the olfactory sulci on the orbital surface

imaging.normalAppearance: Thin coronal T2 through the anterior cranial fossa shows the olfactory bulbs as small ovoid structures beneath the gyri recti, above the cribriform plate; they are absent in Kallmann syndrome and atrophic after trauma or viral infection. Subfrontal masses and cribriform plate fractures are seen on coronal CT and MRI.

pathology.finding: Dural-based enhancing subfrontal mass compressing the olfactory tracts and orbitofrontal cortex, with anosmia and personality change.
Contusion of the orbitofrontal cortex and gliosis or atrophy of the bulbs after cribriform plate injury.
Absent or hypoplastic olfactory bulbs and sulci with hypogonadotropic hypogonadism.
Dumbbell mass across the cribriform plate from the nasal vault into the anterior cranial fossa.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: Coronal thin T2 and T1+Gd of the anterior skull base; CT for the cribriform plate

lesionEffects.mechanism: Shearing of the filaments, compression of the bulb or tract
Regeneration after injury or seizures of the uncus

lesionEffects.deficit: Personality change and optic atrophy with anosmia (Foster Kennedy)
lesionEffects.mechanism: Subfrontal mass compressing the olfactory tract and optic nerve with contralateral papilledema

examination: Test each nostril separately with a non-irritant odour (coffee, vanilla); ammonia stimulates the trigeminal nerve and is not a smell test
Ask about flavour of food, smoke detection and safety
Examine the nose for obstruction
pearls: Anosmia after a fall onto the back of the head means the frontal lobes hit the front of the skull: check for orbitofrontal contusion

pitfalls: Most anosmia is nasal (rhinitis, polyps) or post-viral, not neurological

nuclei.component: SVA (primary olfactory cortex, no brainstem nucleus)

ganglia.name: (none; receptor neurons are the first-order cells)

cn-02-optic.name: Optic nerve (CN II)
cn-02-optic.summary: The optic nerve is not a peripheral nerve but a tract of the central nervous system: the axons of the retinal ganglion cells, myelinated by oligodendrocytes and wrapped in all three meninges with a subarachnoid space, so it swells with raised intracranial pressure (papilledema) and is attacked by multiple sclerosis (optic neuritis). It runs from the optic disc through the orbit and the optic canal to the chiasm, where nasal fibers cross, and continues as the optic tract to the lateral geniculate body, the pretectum and the superior colliculus. Its lesions cause monocular visual loss with a relative afferent pupillary defect, and lesions from the chiasm backward cause binocular field defects.

anatomy.location: Optic disc → intraorbital segment (25 mm, S-shaped to allow eye movement, surrounded by the extraocular muscle cone) → intracanalicular segment (in the optic canal with the ophthalmic artery) → intracranial segment (10 mm, above the cavernous sinus and below the ACA) → chiasm in the suprasellar cistern → optic tract around the cerebral peduncle.

cn-02-optic.function: Transmission of visual information (acuity, color, fields) from the retina to the lateral geniculate body and visual cortex, and of the afferent limb of the pupillary light reflex to the pretectum.

bestView.label: intraorbital optic nerves converging on the optic canals
chiasm above the pituitary
optic tracts around the cerebral peduncles to the lateral geniculate bodies

imaging.normalAppearance: The nerve is a cord of intermediate signal within a CSF-filled sheath on coronal fat-saturated T2 (the sheath widens in raised pressure); the chiasm is a flat band above the sella. Optic neuritis shows T2 hyperintensity and enhancement of a segment; meningioma of the sheath enhances around a normal nerve (tram-track).

pathology.finding: Swollen, T2-bright, enhancing segment of the nerve on fat-saturated coronal images; long segments and chiasmal involvement suggest neuromyelitis optica, perineural enhancement suggests MOG antibody disease.
pathology.timing: Enhancement lasts about 30 days

pathology.finding: Distended optic nerve sheaths, flattened posterior globes, protrusion of the disc into the vitreous, empty sella.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: Coronal fat-saturated T2 and T1+Gd of the orbits and chiasm; CT for the canal

html.summary: The optic nerve is not a peripheral nerve but a tract of the central nervous system: the axons of the retinal ganglion cells, myelinated by oligodendrocytes and wrapped in all three meninges with a subarachnoid space, so it swells with raised intracranial pressure (papilledema) and is attacked by multiple sclerosis (optic neuritis). It runs from the optic disc through the orbit and the optic canal to the chiasm, where nasal fibers cross, and continues as the optic tract to the lateral geniculate body, the pretectum and the superior colliculus. Its lesions cause monocular visual loss with a relative afferent pupillary defect, and lesions from the chiasm backward cause binocular field defects.
html.function: Transmission of visual information (acuity, color, fields) from the retina to the lateral geniculate body and visual cortex, and of the afferent limb of the pupillary light reflex to the pretectum.
html.anatomy.location: Optic disc → intraorbital segment (25 mm, S-shaped to allow eye movement, surrounded by the extraocular muscle cone) → intracanalicular segment (in the optic canal with the ophthalmic artery) → intracranial segment (10 mm, above the cavernous sinus and below the ACA) → chiasm in the suprasellar cistern → optic tract around the cerebral peduncle.
html.imaging.normalAppearance: The nerve is a cord of intermediate signal within a CSF-filled sheath on coronal fat-saturated T2 (the sheath widens in raised pressure); the chiasm is a flat band above the sella. Optic neuritis shows T2 hyperintensity and enhancement of a segment; meningioma of the sheath enhances around a normal nerve (tram-track).
html.imaging.sequenceOfChoice: Coronal fat-saturated T2 and T1+Gd of the orbits and chiasm; CT for the canal

cn-03-oculomotor.name: Oculomotor nerve (CN III)
cn-03-oculomotor.summary: The oculomotor nerve carries motor fibers from the oculomotor nucleus to four of the six extraocular muscles (medial, superior and inferior recti, inferior oblique) and the levator palpebrae, and parasympathetic fibers from the Edinger–Westphal nucleus to the ciliary ganglion for the pupil and lens. It leaves the midbrain into the interpeduncular fossa between the posterior cerebral and superior cerebellar arteries, runs beside the posterior communicating artery and the uncus, enters the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus and passes through the superior orbital fissure. Because the pupillary fibers lie on its surface, compression (aneurysm, herniation) involves the pupil early while microvascular ischemia of the core spares it, the single most important distinction in third nerve palsies.

cn-03-oculomotor.function: Elevation, depression and adduction of the eye, elevation of the upper lid, pupillary constriction and accommodation.

cranial.nuclearVsPeripheral: Nuclear lesions differ from nerve lesions in two ways set by the wiring of the complex: the levator is supplied by a single midline caudal nucleus, so nuclear lesions cause bilateral ptosis, and each superior rectus subnucleus supplies the opposite eye, so a nuclear lesion weakens elevation of the contralateral eye. Fascicular lesions in the midbrain add contralateral signs from the red nucleus, superior cerebellar peduncle or crus.
cranial.supranuclear: Conjugate gaze commands reach the nucleus through the MLF (horizontal, from the contralateral abducens nucleus) and the riMLF and posterior commissure (vertical). A supranuclear gaze palsy spares the vestibulo-ocular reflex and never causes ptosis, pupil change or diplopia, which separates it from a nuclear or nerve lesion.

cn-04-trochlear.name: Trochlear nerve (CN IV)
cn-04-trochlear.summary: The thinnest cranial nerve and the only one to emerge from the back of the brainstem and to cross before leaving: from the nucleus in the caudal midbrain the fibers curve dorsally around the aqueduct, decussate in the superior medullary velum and exit below the inferior colliculus to supply the contralateral superior oblique. Its long subarachnoid course around the midbrain and along the free edge of the tentorium makes it the nerve most often damaged by closed head injury. Palsy produces vertical diplopia worse looking down and in (reading, stairs) with a compensatory head tilt away from the affected eye.

anatomy.location: Nucleus in the periaqueductal gray at the inferior colliculus → fibers dorsally around the aqueduct, crossing in the superior medullary velum → exit on the dorsal midbrain below the inferior colliculus → around the cerebral peduncle in the ambient cistern beneath the free edge of the tentorium → lateral wall of the cavernous sinus below III → superior orbital fissure outside the annulus → superior oblique.

cn-04-trochlear.function: Depression of the adducted eye, intorsion of the abducted eye; keeps the eyes level during head tilt.

cn-05-trigeminal.name: Trigeminal nerve (CN V)
cn-05-trigeminal.summary: The largest cranial nerve carries all somatic sensation from the face, scalp, cornea, oral and nasal cavities, teeth and dura, and motor supply to the muscles of mastication. Its sensory root leaves the lateral pons, crosses the prepontine cistern to the trigeminal ganglion in Meckel's cave, and splits into the ophthalmic (V1, superior orbital fissure), maxillary (V2, foramen rotundum) and mandibular (V3, foramen ovale) divisions; the smaller motor root passes beneath the ganglion into V3. Its brainstem nuclei span from the midbrain to the upper cervical cord, which is why facial sensory loss can point to lesions at almost any brainstem level and why a lateral medullary infarct numbs the face.

anatomy.location: Root entry zone on the lateral mid-pons at the junction with the middle cerebellar peduncle → prepontine cistern over the petrous apex (compressed here by the SCA in trigeminal neuralgia) → Meckel's cave with the ganglion → V1 in the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus to the superior orbital fissure, V2 through the foramen rotundum to the pterygopalatine fossa and infraorbital canal, V3 through the foramen ovale to the infratemporal fossa.

cn-05-trigeminal.function: Sensation of the face, cornea, mouth, teeth, anterior two-thirds of the tongue (touch), nasal cavity and supratentorial dura; mastication; proprioception of the jaw; tensor tympani and tensor veli palatini.

cn-06-abducens.name: Abducens nerve (CN VI)
cn-06-abducens.summary: A purely motor nerve from the abducens nucleus in the caudal pons to the lateral rectus. It leaves the pontomedullary junction, climbs the clivus in the prepontine cistern, pierces the dura and bends sharply over the petrous apex through Dorello's canal under the petroclinoid ligament, runs inside the cavernous sinus beside the carotid artery and enters the orbit through the superior orbital fissure within the annulus. Its long intracranial course, its tethering at the petrous apex and its position next to the carotid make it the nerve most often affected by raised intracranial pressure (a false localizing sign), by skull base disease and by cavernous sinus lesions; the result is horizontal diplopia worse at distance and on gaze to the affected side.

cn-06-abducens.function: Abduction of the eye; through the nucleus, conjugate horizontal gaze.

cn-07-facial.name: Facial nerve (CN VII)
cn-07-facial.summary: The facial nerve is really two nerves travelling together: the motor root to the muscles of facial expression, stapedius, stylohyoid and posterior digastric, and the nervus intermedius carrying taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, parasympathetic fibers to the lacrimal, nasal, submandibular and sublingual glands, and a little skin sensation from the ear. After looping over the abducens nucleus it leaves the pontomedullary junction, crosses the cerebellopontine angle with the eighth nerve into the internal acoustic meatus, and follows a long tortuous canal through the temporal bone (labyrinthine, tympanic and mastoid segments) to the stylomastoid foramen and the parotid gland. Its lesion produces the peripheral facial palsy that involves the forehead, whereas a corticobulbar lesion spares it; the accompanying loss of taste, tearing or stapedius reflex tells you how far up the canal the lesion sits.

anatomy.location: Motor nucleus in the caudal pontine tegmentum → internal genu around the abducens nucleus → exit at the lateral pontomedullary junction (cerebellopontine angle) with the nervus intermedius and VIII → internal acoustic meatus (anterosuperior quadrant) → labyrinthine segment to the geniculate ganglion (greater petrosal nerve leaves) → tympanic segment along the medial wall of the middle ear (nerve to stapedius leaves) → mastoid segment (chorda tympani leaves) → stylomastoid foramen → through the parotid gland dividing into temporal, zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular and cervical branches.

cn-07-facial.function: Facial expression and eye closure, stapedius reflex, taste from the anterior tongue and palate, lacrimation and salivation (except parotid), sensation of part of the external ear.

The HCP1065 mesh in this atlas shows the cisternal segment.

cranial.nuclearVsPeripheral: Nuclear and fascicular lesions in the pons produce the same complete hemifacial weakness as nerve lesions but come with neighbors: an ipsilateral abducens palsy or gaze palsy (facial colliculus), contralateral hemiparesis (Millard–Gubler), and usually no taste or lacrimal change because those fibers join the nerve only at the cerebellopontine angle.
cranial.supranuclear: The upper facial subnucleus receives corticobulbar input from both hemispheres and the lower subnucleus mainly from the contralateral hemisphere, so a stroke spares the forehead. Emotional smiling uses a separate limbic pathway, which explains the patient whose voluntary smile is weak but who smiles symmetrically at a joke (or vice versa).

cn-08-vestibulocochlear.name: Vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII)
cn-08-vestibulocochlear.summary: Two nerves in one sheath: the cochlear nerve carrying hearing from the spiral ganglion of the cochlea to the cochlear nuclei, and the vestibular nerve carrying head motion and position from the semicircular canals and otolith organs (vestibular ganglion of Scarpa) to the vestibular nuclei and cerebellum. Both run from the inner ear through the internal acoustic meatus with the facial nerve and across the cerebellopontine angle to the pontomedullary junction. The nerve is the site of the vestibular schwannoma, the commonest cerebellopontine angle tumor, and of vestibular neuritis; its lesions cause unilateral sensorineural deafness, tinnitus and vertigo, and the pattern of nystagmus and the head impulse test separate these peripheral lesions from central vestibular disease.

anatomy.location: Spiral ganglion in the modiolus of the cochlea and vestibular ganglion in the fundus of the internal acoustic meatus → cochlear nerve (anteroinferior) and superior and inferior vestibular nerves (posterior) in the meatus with VII (anterosuperior) → cerebellopontine angle cistern → entry at the lateral pontomedullary junction into the cochlear and vestibular nuclei at the lateral recess of the fourth ventricle.

cn-08-vestibulocochlear.function: Hearing (frequency, intensity, timing) and the vestibular senses of angular acceleration (semicircular canals) and linear acceleration and gravity (utricle and saccule), driving the vestibulo-ocular and vestibulospinal reflexes and spatial orientation.

cn-09-glossopharyngeal.name: Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX)
cn-09-glossopharyngeal.summary: A mixed nerve of the medulla with five components: taste and general sensation from the posterior third of the tongue, the pharynx, tonsils and middle ear; visceral afferents from the carotid sinus and carotid body; parasympathetic secretomotor fibers to the parotid gland through the otic ganglion; and motor supply to the stylopharyngeus. It leaves the medulla as rootlets behind the olive with the vagus and accessory nerves, passes through the jugular foramen with them, and descends between the internal jugular vein and carotid to the tongue and pharynx. It is the afferent limb of the gag reflex and of the carotid sinus reflex, and it is rarely injured alone; skull base lesions involve it with X and XI in the jugular foramen syndrome.

anatomy.location: Rootlets from the posterolateral sulcus of the upper medulla behind the olive → cerebellomedullary cistern with X and XI → anterior part of the jugular foramen (with the inferior petrosal sinus) → between the internal jugular vein and internal carotid artery, curving forward over stylopharyngeus to the base of the tongue and the pharyngeal wall.

cn-09-glossopharyngeal.function: Taste and sensation of the posterior tongue and oropharynx, sensation of the middle ear, carotid baroreceptor and chemoreceptor afferents, parotid secretion, elevation of the pharynx (stylopharyngeus), afferent limb of the gag reflex.

html.summary: A mixed nerve of the medulla with five components: taste and general sensation from the posterior third of the tongue, the pharynx, tonsils and middle ear; visceral afferents from the carotid sinus and carotid body; parasympathetic secretomotor fibers to the parotid gland through the otic ganglion; and motor supply to the stylopharyngeus.
