cn-10-vagus.name: Vagus nerve (CN X)
cn-10-vagus.summary: The wanderer: the longest cranial nerve, leaving the medulla behind the olive, passing through the jugular foramen and descending in the carotid sheath through the neck into the thorax and abdomen. It carries motor fibers from nucleus ambiguus to the palate, pharynx and larynx (including the recurrent laryngeal nerve to all intrinsic laryngeal muscles except cricothyroid), parasympathetic fibers from the dorsal motor nucleus to the heart, lungs and gut as far as the splenic flexure, visceral afferents from the same organs to the solitary nucleus, taste from the epiglottis, and a little skin sensation from the ear. Its lesions cause dysphagia, nasal speech, hoarseness and loss of the gag and cough reflexes; the palate rises to the intact side and the vocal cord lies paralyzed.

anatomy.location: Rootlets from the posterolateral sulcus of the medulla below IX → cerebellomedullary cistern → jugular foramen (pars vascularis, with XI) → superior and inferior ganglia → carotid sheath between the internal jugular vein and the carotid artery → thoracic inlet (the right recurrent laryngeal nerve loops under the subclavian artery, the left under the aortic arch) → esophageal plexus → anterior and posterior vagal trunks through the esophageal hiatus.

cn-10-vagus.function: Swallowing, phonation and palatal elevation; cough and gag reflexes; cardiac slowing, bronchoconstriction, gastric secretion and gut motility; visceral sensation from the thorax and abdomen including the baroreceptor input of the aortic arch; taste from the epiglottis.

cn-11-accessory.name: Accessory nerve (CN XI)
cn-11-accessory.summary: The spinal accessory nerve arises from a column of motor neurons in the upper five cervical segments, climbs through the foramen magnum to join briefly with the cranial root (which really belongs to the vagus and is distributed with it), leaves through the jugular foramen and descends across the posterior triangle of the neck to supply sternocleidomastoid and trapezius. Its superficial course in the posterior triangle makes it the cranial nerve most often injured by surgery (lymph node biopsy, neck dissection), producing a dropped shoulder, weak shrug and difficulty abducting the arm above the horizontal with lateral winging of the scapula.

cn-11-accessory.function: Head turning to the opposite side and head flexion (sternocleidomastoid); shoulder elevation, scapular retraction and upward rotation for arm abduction above 90 degrees (trapezius).

cn-12-hypoglossal.name: Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII)
cn-12-hypoglossal.summary: A purely motor nerve to the tongue. From the hypoglossal nucleus beneath the floor of the fourth ventricle the fibers pass ventrally between the medial lemniscus and the inferior olive and emerge as rootlets in the preolivary sulcus, leave the skull through the hypoglossal canal and curve down and forward between the carotid and jugular vessels to enter the tongue, supplying all its intrinsic muscles and the genioglossus, hyoglossus and styloglossus (the palatoglossus belongs to the vagus). A lower motor neuron lesion wastes half the tongue and deviates it toward the weak side; because its intramedullary fibers run through the medial medulla it is part of the medial medullary syndrome, and skull base tumors, carotid dissection and neck surgery injure it peripherally.

anatomy.location: Nucleus in the dorsal paramedian medulla beneath the hypoglossal trigone → fibers ventrally through the medulla lateral to the medial lemniscus → rootlets in the preolivary sulcus between the pyramid and olive → hypoglossal canal in the occipital condyle → descends between the internal carotid artery and internal jugular vein, crosses the carotid bifurcation and the loop of the lingual artery, and enters the tongue above the hyoid.

cn-12-hypoglossal.function: Movement of the tongue for speech, chewing and swallowing: protrusion (genioglossus), retraction (styloglossus), depression (hyoglossus) and shape changes (intrinsic muscles).

A lower motor neuron lesion wastes half the tongue and deviates it toward the weak side; because its intramedullary fibers run through the medial medulla it is part of the medial medullary syndrome, and skull base tumors, carotid dissection and neck surgery injure it peripherally.
html.function: Movement of the tongue for speech, chewing and swallowing: protrusion (genioglossus), retraction (styloglossus), depression (hyoglossus) and shape changes (intrinsic muscles).
html.anatomy.location: Nucleus in the dorsal paramedian medulla beneath the hypoglossal trigone → fibers ventrally through the medulla lateral to the medial lemniscus → rootlets in the preolivary sulcus between the pyramid and olive → hypoglossal canal in the occipital condyle → descends between the internal carotid artery and internal jugular vein, crosses the carotid bifurcation and the loop of the lingual artery, and enters the tongue above the hyoid.
html.imaging.normalAppearance: The rootlets are seen leaving the preolivary sulcus on thin T2; the hypoglossal canal is assessed on skull base CT and contrast MRI. Denervation of half the tongue appears as fatty, atrophic hemitongue on T1 and CT, a sign that may reveal the lesion before the patient notices.
html.imaging.sequenceOfChoice: Skull base MRI with contrast and CT; carotid imaging; DWI
html.cranial.nuclearVsPeripheral: Nuclear lesions are medial medullary and are accompanied by contralateral hemiparesis and lemniscal loss; the nucleus is also a favorite of motor neuron disease, where bilateral wasting and fasciculations are the rule. Peripheral lesions are isolated or come with the other lower cranial nerves at the skull base.
html.cranial.supranuclear: The genioglossus receives mainly contralateral corticobulbar input, so a hemispheric stroke deviates the tongue toward the hemiparetic side (away from the lesion), without wasting; bilateral lesions make the tongue small, stiff and slow (pseudobulbar).

pathway-anterior-corticospinal.name: Anterior corticospinal tract
pathway-anterior-corticospinal.summary: The 10–15% of pyramidal fibers that do not cross in the medulla continue down the anterior funiculus beside the anterior median fissure as the anterior (ventral) corticospinal tract. Most of them cross at their segment of termination through the anterior white commissure to reach motor neurons of the trunk and proximal limb muscles, and some end bilaterally, so axial muscles have bilateral cortical control. This is why trunk and neck strength are relatively preserved in hemiplegia and why bilateral corticospinal lesions are needed to paralyze the trunk.

pathway-anterior-spinocerebellar.name: Anterior spinocerebellar tract
pathway-anterior-spinocerebellar.modality: proprioceptive and interneuronal feedback from the lower limb
pathway-anterior-spinocerebellar.summary: Neurons at the base of the dorsal horn and in the intermediate gray of the lumbosacral cord send axons that mostly cross in the anterior white commissure, ascend in the anterolateral funiculus in front of the posterior spinocerebellar tract, pass through the medulla and pons, and enter the cerebellum through the superior cerebellar peduncle, where most cross back so that each side of the cerebellum still receives information from its own side of the body. It carries less pure proprioception and more information about the activity of spinal interneurons, telling the cerebellum what the spinal circuits are doing with the descending commands.

pathway-anterior-spinothalamic.name: Anterior spinothalamic tract
pathway-anterior-spinothalamic.summary: Fibers carrying light touch and pressure that do not require fine localization end in the dorsal horn, cross in the anterior white commissure and ascend in the anterior funiculus as the anterior spinothalamic tract, merging with the lateral spinothalamic tract in the brainstem as the spinal lemniscus. Because crude touch travels both here and in the posterior columns, touch is rarely lost completely by a single cord lesion, which is why pain and temperature (single route) and vibration and position (single route) are the discriminating modalities in cord examination.

pathway-auditory.name: Auditory pathway
pathway-auditory.summary: Hair cells of the organ of Corti excite spiral ganglion neurons whose axons form the cochlear nerve to the dorsal and ventral cochlear nuclei. From there the pathway becomes bilateral almost immediately: fibers cross in the trapezoid body to the contralateral superior olivary complex and lateral lemniscus, others ascend ipsilaterally, and further crossings occur at the inferior colliculus. All fibers relay in the inferior colliculus, then the medial geniculate body, and reach Heschl's gyrus through the acoustic radiation. The extensive crossing means a unilateral central lesion never causes deafness; unilateral deafness is always the cochlea, nerve or cochlear nuclei.

pathway-basal-ganglia-loops.name: Basal ganglia direct and indirect loops
pathway-basal-ganglia-loops.summary: The basal ganglia form loops from the cortex through the striatum, pallidum and thalamus back to the cortex. In the direct pathway, cortical excitation of striatal neurons inhibits the internal pallidum and substantia nigra reticulata, releasing the thalamus and facilitating movement; in the indirect pathway, striatal neurons inhibit the external pallidum, which disinhibits the subthalamic nucleus, whose excitation of the internal pallidum suppresses the thalamus and movement. Dopamine from the substantia nigra compacta excites the direct (D1) and inhibits the indirect (D2) pathway, so its loss tips the balance toward inhibition (parkinsonism), while loss of striatal indirect neurons (Huntington) or of the subthalamic nucleus (hemiballismus) tips it toward excess movement.

pathway-cerebellar-circuits.name: Cerebellar afferent and efferent circuits
pathway-cerebellar-circuits.summary: Information enters the cerebellum as mossy fibers (from the pontine nuclei carrying cortical plans, the spinal cord carrying proprioception, and the vestibular nuclei) and climbing fibers (from the contralateral inferior olive), both exciting the Purkinje cells through the granule cell layer; Purkinje cells inhibit the deep nuclei, which provide the only output. The lateral hemisphere talks to the dentate nucleus, the superior cerebellar peduncle, the contralateral red nucleus and the ventral lateral thalamus, and so to the motor cortex; the vermis talks to the fastigial nucleus and the vestibular and reticular nuclei. Because the outflow crosses in the midbrain and the corticospinal tract crosses again in the medulla, the cerebellum controls the same side of the body, and the pontine input crosses once, so it works with the opposite cortex.

pathway-corticobulbar.name: Corticobulbar tract
pathway-corticobulbar.modality: voluntary control of the face, tongue, jaw, palate, pharynx and larynx
pathway-corticobulbar.summary: Corticobulbar fibers arise from the face and mouth areas of the motor cortex, descend with the corticospinal tract through the genu of the internal capsule and the medial crus, and peel off in the brainstem to the motor nuclei of V, VII, IX, X, XI and XII. pathway-dcml.name: Dorsal column–medial lemniscus pathway
pathway-dcml.summary: Large myelinated fibers from mechanoreceptors and proprioceptors enter through the dorsal root and ascend uncrossed in the posterior columns (fasciculus gracilis for the leg and lower trunk, fasciculus cuneatus for the arm) to the gracile and cuneate nuclei in the lower medulla. Second-order axons cross as the internal arcuate fibers (sensory decussation) to form the medial lemniscus, which ascends through the brainstem to the ventral posterolateral nucleus of the thalamus, whose neurons project through the posterior limb of the internal capsule to the postcentral gyrus. The pathway crosses in the medulla, so cord lesions give ipsilateral loss and brainstem lesions contralateral loss, and its separation from the spinothalamic tract in the cord explains dissociated sensory loss.

pathway-gustatory.name: Gustatory pathway
pathway-gustatory.summary: Taste buds on the anterior two-thirds of the tongue signal through the chorda tympani of the facial nerve, those on the posterior third through the glossopharyngeal nerve, and those on the epiglottis and pharynx through the vagus; all these fibers, with cell bodies in the geniculate, petrosal and nodose ganglia, end in the rostral part of the nucleus of the solitary tract. Second-order axons ascend mainly uncrossed in the central tegmental tract to the ventral posteromedial thalamus and then to the gustatory cortex in the frontal operculum and anterior insula, with connections to the orbitofrontal cortex where taste and smell combine into flavour. Loss of taste therefore localizes to the peripheral nerves far more often than to the brain.

pathway-horizontal-gaze.name: Horizontal gaze pathway
pathway-horizontal-gaze.summary: Looking to the left requires the left lateral rectus and the right medial rectus to contract together. The command starts in the right frontal eye field (for voluntary saccades) or the parieto-occipital cortex (for pursuit), descends to the left paramedian pontine reticular formation, which fires the left abducens nucleus; that nucleus contains both the motor neurons for the left lateral rectus and the interneurons whose axons cross and ascend in the right MLF to the right medial rectus subnucleus of the oculomotor nucleus. Lesions of the frontal eye field, the PPRF, the abducens nucleus and the MLF each produce a characteristic and localizable pattern.

pathway-lateral-corticospinal.name: Lateral corticospinal tract
pathway-lateral-corticospinal.modality: voluntary skilled movement of the limbs
pathway-lateral-corticospinal.summary: The main voluntary motor pathway. Pyramidal neurons of the motor and premotor cortex send axons through the corona radiata, the posterior limb of the internal capsule, the middle of the crus cerebri and the basis pontis to the medullary pyramid, where about 85–90% cross in the pyramidal decussation to descend in the lateral funiculus of the cord as the lateral corticospinal tract, ending on interneurons and, for the hand, directly on motor neurons of the anterior horn. pathway-lateral-spinothalamic.name: Lateral spinothalamic tract
pathway-lateral-spinothalamic.summary: Small myelinated and unmyelinated pain and temperature fibers end in the dorsal horn (laminae I, II and V) within a segment or two of their entry; second-order neurons cross in the anterior white commissure over one to two segments and ascend in the anterolateral funiculus as the spinothalamic tract, joined in the brainstem by spinoreticular and spinomesencephalic fibers, to the ventral posterolateral thalamus and then the somatosensory cortex and insula. The early crossing is the key: cord lesions cause contralateral loss beginning one or two segments below the lesion, and a central cord lesion catches the crossing fibers of both sides for a band of dissociated loss.

pathway-oculosympathetic.name: Oculosympathetic pathway
pathway-oculosympathetic.modality: pupillary dilation, lid elevation, facial sweating
pathway-oculosympathetic.summary: The sympathetic supply to the eye is a three-neuron chain that travels a remarkable distance: from the hypothalamus down the brainstem tegmentum and lateral cervical cord to the ciliospinal center at C8–T2; out through the T1 root over the lung apex and up the cervical chain to the superior cervical ganglion; and finally along the internal carotid artery through the cavernous sinus and the ophthalmic division to the dilator pupillae and Müller's muscle, with the sweat fibers leaving on the external carotid. pathway-olfactory.name: Olfactory pathway
pathway-olfactory.summary: Olfactory receptor neurons in the nasal epithelium send unmyelinated axons through the cribriform plate to synapse in the glomeruli of the olfactory bulb on mitral and tufted cells, whose axons form the olfactory tract. At the anterior perforated substance the tract divides: the lateral stria ends in the primary olfactory cortex of the uncus (piriform cortex), the amygdala and the entorhinal cortex, and the medial stria in the septal area and, through the anterior commissure, the opposite bulb. Smell is the only sense that reaches the cortex without a thalamic relay and one of the few that is largely ipsilateral, and its cortical stations in the medial temporal lobe explain olfactory auras in temporal lobe epilepsy.

pathway-papez-limbic.name: Papez circuit and limbic connections
pathway-papez-limbic.summary: The classical memory circuit runs from the hippocampus through the fornix to the mammillary bodies, from there by the mammillothalamic tract to the anterior thalamic nuclei, on to the cingulate gyrus, and back through the cingulum bundle and entorhinal cortex to the hippocampus. Every station is a site of clinical amnesia: the hippocampus in Alzheimer disease, anoxia and herpes encephalitis, the fornix in surgery, the mammillary bodies in thiamine deficiency, the anterior and mediodorsal thalamus in stroke, and the cingulate in tumors. The amygdala, orbitofrontal cortex and mediodorsal thalamus form a parallel limbic loop for emotion and social behavior.

pathway-posterior-spinocerebellar.name: Posterior spinocerebellar tract
pathway-posterior-spinocerebellar.modality: unconscious proprioception from the leg and lower trunk
pathway-posterior-spinocerebellar.summary: Proprioceptive fibers from muscle spindles, tendon organs and joints of the leg and trunk end in Clarke's column (nucleus dorsalis, C8–L3); its neurons send uncrossed axons up the lateral funiculus as the posterior spinocerebellar tract into the inferior cerebellar peduncle to the vermis and paravermis. pathway-pupillary-light-reflex.name: Pupillary light reflex pathway
pathway-pupillary-light-reflex.summary: Light in either eye constricts both pupils because the pathway is bilateral at two points. Retinal ganglion cell axons leave the optic tract before the lateral geniculate body and reach the pretectal nuclei of both sides (via the brachium of the superior colliculus and the posterior commissure); each pretectal nucleus projects to both Edinger–Westphal nuclei; each Edinger–Westphal nucleus sends preganglionic fibers in the oculomotor nerve to the ciliary ganglion, whose postganglionic fibers reach the sphincter pupillae through the short ciliary nerves. Asymmetric afferent lesions produce the relative afferent pupillary defect, efferent lesions a fixed dilated pupil, and pretectal lesions light-near dissociation.

pathway-reticulospinal.name: Reticulospinal tracts
pathway-reticulospinal.modality: posture, locomotion, tone and autonomic modulation
pathway-reticulospinal.summary: The pontine and medullary reticular formation send two tracts to the cord: the pontine (medial) reticulospinal tract, uncrossed in the anterior funiculus, which facilitates extensors and axial muscles, and the medullary (lateral) reticulospinal tract, partly crossed in the lateral funiculus, which inhibits extensor tone and modulates reflexes and pain transmission. pathway-rubrospinal.name: Rubrospinal tract
pathway-rubrospinal.modality: flexor facilitation of the upper limb
pathway-rubrospinal.summary: Neurons of the magnocellular red nucleus send axons that cross immediately in the ventral tegmental decussation of the midbrain and descend in the lateral funiculus of the cord just in front of the lateral corticospinal tract, ending on interneurons that excite flexor and inhibit extensor motor neurons, mainly of the arm. Small in humans, it matters clinically in two ways: it is one reason cerebellar and red nucleus lesions affect limb movement, and its preserved flexor drive to the arms after lesions above the red nucleus produces decorticate posturing, while lesions below the red nucleus remove it and leave extensor (decerebrate) posturing.

pathway-tectospinal.name: Tectospinal tract
pathway-tectospinal.modality: reflex turning of the head toward stimuli
pathway-tectospinal.summary: Neurons of the deep layers of the superior colliculus send axons that cross in the dorsal tegmental decussation just below the periaqueductal gray, descend near the MLF through the brainstem and end in the cervical cord, where they drive neck motor neurons to turn the head toward a visual, auditory or somatosensory stimulus. It is the spinal component of the orienting response and works with the tectobulbar fibers that move the eyes toward the same target, so that gaze and head turn arrive together and the fovea lands on whatever attracted attention.

decussation.note: Crosses beneath the periaqueductal gray at the level of the colliculi.

pathway-tectospinal.termination: Motor neurons and interneurons of the upper cervical cord for neck muscles.

lesionEffectsByLevel.effects: Impaired reflex orienting of the head and eyes to the contralateral side; rarely isolated

pearls: This tract is why a sudden sound makes you turn your head before you know why

pathway-trigeminothalamic.name: Trigeminal sensory pathways
pathway-trigeminothalamic.modality: touch, pain, temperature and proprioception of the face
pathway-trigeminothalamic.summary: Facial sensation uses the same logic as body sensation but with the trigeminal nuclei standing in for the dorsal horn and dorsal column nuclei. Touch fibers end in the principal sensory nucleus in the pons; pain and temperature fibers descend in the spinal trigeminal tract to the spinal nucleus in the medulla and upper cervical cord; jaw proprioception has its cell bodies in the mesencephalic nucleus. Second-order axons cross to form the trigeminal lemniscus (ventral trigeminothalamic tract), which ascends beside the medial lemniscus to the ventral posteromedial thalamus and then to the face area of the postcentral gyrus. The long descending tract is why facial pain loss is ipsilateral in lateral medullary lesions and why it is the face, not the body, that gives the crossed pattern.

origin.note: Cell bodies of all modalities except jaw proprioception in the trigeminal ganglion; jaw spindle afferents in the mesencephalic nucleus.

neuronChain.synapse: principal sensory nucleus (touch) or spinal trigeminal nucleus (pain, temperature)

decussation.level: Pons and medulla, at the level of each nucleus

waypoints.note: pain and temperature descend to the spinal nucleus (pars caudalis)

lower part of the postcentral gyrus

pathway-trigeminothalamic.termination: Ventral posteromedial nucleus of the thalamus and the face region of the primary somatosensory cortex.

pathway-vertical-gaze.name: Vertical gaze pathway
pathway-vertical-gaze.summary: Vertical saccades are generated by the rostral interstitial nucleus of the MLF in the rostral midbrain, which drives the oculomotor and trochlear nuclei of both sides; up-gaze commands cross through the posterior commissure, which is why dorsal midbrain compression abolishes up-gaze first. Because the vestibular route bypasses the riMLF, a supranuclear vertical gaze palsy (progressive supranuclear palsy, Parinaud) can be overcome by the oculocephalic reflex.

pathway-vestibular-vor.name: Vestibular pathways and vestibulo-ocular reflex
pathway-vestibular-vor.modality: balance, spatial orientation and gaze stabilization
pathway-vestibular-vor.summary: Hair cells of the semicircular canals and otolith organs excite the vestibular ganglion neurons whose axons form the vestibular nerve to the four vestibular nuclei and directly to the flocculonodular lobe. The nuclei send excitatory and inhibitory projections through the MLF to the abducens, trochlear and oculomotor nuclei, producing the vestibulo-ocular reflex that moves the eyes opposite to head rotation with a latency of a few milliseconds, descend as the vestibulospinal tracts for posture, and ascend through the thalamus to the vestibular cortex in the posterior insula and temporoparietal junction. Because the two labyrinths are balanced, a unilateral loss creates a bias interpreted as rotation (vertigo) with nystagmus beating away from the lesion.

origin.note: Hair cells of the three semicircular canal cristae and the utricular and saccular maculae; bipolar neurons of Scarpa's ganglion.

neuronChain.synapse: vestibular nuclei (superior, lateral, medial, inferior) and cerebellar flocculonodular lobe
ocular motor nuclei via the MLF; spinal cord via the vestibulospinal tracts; thalamus (VPL/VPI) for perception; cerebellum

decussation.level: MLF at the level of the vestibular nuclei

ascending to the ocular motor nuclei

pathway-vestibulospinal.name: Vestibulospinal tracts
pathway-vestibulospinal.summary: Two tracts carry vestibular information to the cord. The lateral vestibulospinal tract from the lateral (Deiters) nucleus descends uncrossed the whole length of the cord in the anterior funiculus and excites extensor (antigravity) motor neurons, driven by the otoliths and by the cerebellar vermis and fastigial nucleus; the medial vestibulospinal tract from the medial nucleus descends in the MLF to the cervical cord, bilaterally, to coordinate head and neck position with eye movements. Together with the reticulospinal tracts they make up the medial (ventromedial) descending system for posture, and their unopposed extensor drive is what produces decerebrate rigidity.

origin.note: Lateral vestibular nucleus (lateral tract) and medial vestibular nucleus (medial tract), receiving the vestibular nerve and cerebellar input.

neuronChain.synapse: spinal interneurons and directly on extensor motor neurons

waypoints.note: lateral and medial nuclei at the pontomedullary junction
lateral tract in the ventrolateral medulla; medial tract in the MLF
anterior funiculus; the medial tract ends in the cervical cord, the lateral runs to the sacral cord

pathway-vestibulospinal.termination: Extensor motor neurons of the trunk and limbs (lateral tract) and neck motor neurons (medial tract, bilateral).

lesionEffectsByLevel.level: Brainstem transection between the vestibular nuclei and the red nucleus
lesionEffectsByLevel.effects: Decerebrate rigidity: unopposed extensor drive

pathway-visual.name: Visual pathway
pathway-visual.summary: Light falling on the retina is converted by photoreceptors, bipolar cells and ganglion cells into action potentials that leave the eye in the optic nerve. At the chiasm the fibers from the nasal retina (temporal field) cross so that each optic tract carries the opposite hemifield from both eyes to the lateral geniculate body. Geniculate neurons project as the optic radiation: fibers for the upper field loop forward into the temporal lobe (Meyer's loop) and fibers for the lower field pass through the parietal lobe, all ending in the calcarine cortex with the macula at the pole. The pathway is the most precisely localizable in neurology: the shape of the field defect, its congruity, macular sparing and the pupils together give the level.

origin.note: Retinal ganglion cells (third-order neurons of the retina) form the optic nerve; the pathway is CNS from the retina onward.

neuronChain.synapse: lateral geniculate nucleus (also pretectum, superior colliculus, suprachiasmatic nucleus)
layer IV of the striate cortex via the optic radiation

decussation.note: Nasal retinal fibers (about 53%) cross; temporal fibers remain uncrossed.

waypoints.note: optic nerve from the disc through the optic canal
optic tract around the cerebral peduncle carrying the contralateral hemifield

Meyer's loop through the temporal lobe (upper field)

pathway-visual.termination: Primary visual cortex lining the calcarine sulcus, with onward projection to extrastriate areas (V2–V5), the ventral stream (temporal) and the dorsal stream (parietal).
pathway-visual.somatotopy: Retinotopic throughout: upper retina (lower field) stays superior in the tract, radiation (parietal) and cortex (cuneus); lower retina (upper field) runs inferiorly (Meyer's loop, lingual gyrus); macula central in the nerve, posterior in the chiasm, occupying the occipital pole.

syn-aca-infarct.name: Anterior cerebral artery infarction
syn-aca-infarct.presentation: A patient develops sudden weakness that is much worse in the leg than the arm, with the face almost spared, together with sensory loss over the same leg. They may be abulic and slow to respond, incontinent of urine, and show a grasp reflex in the affected hand. With a large or bilateral infarct there is akinetic mutism. Speech is preserved apart from a transient transcortical motor aphasia when the dominant hemisphere is involved.

deficits.distribution: leg more than arm, face spared
deficits.sign: Upper motor neuron weakness of the leg with extensor plantar
Cortical sensory loss of the leg
Abulia, apathy, perseveration, grasp reflex
Urinary incontinence from loss of the paracentral micturition area

syn-aca-infarct.reasoning: The anterior cerebral artery runs in the interhemispheric fissure and supplies the medial surface of the frontal and parietal lobes, which is where the leg and foot are represented in the motor and sensory homunculus of the paracentral lobule. The corticospinal fibers from this area cross in the medullary pyramidal decussation, so the weakness is contralateral to the infarct, and it follows the homunculus rather than the whole hemibody: the leg is weakest, the shoulder may be weak, and the face and hand, which sit on the lateral convexity in middle cerebral territory, are spared. The medial frontal lobe includes the supplementary motor area and the anterior cingulate gyrus, whose loss gives abulia and, bilaterally, akinetic mutism; the paracentral lobule holds the cortical bladder control area, explaining the incontinence. Recurrent artery of Heubner involvement adds face and arm weakness from the anterior limb of the internal capsule and caudate head, a pattern that can mislead toward the middle cerebral artery.

imagingFindings.finding: Restricted diffusion in the medial frontal and parietal cortex and the paracentral lobule along the interhemispheric fissure, sometimes extending to the caudate head.
Cut-off of the A2 segment; a vasospasm after anterior communicating aneurysm rupture is a common cause of bilateral infarcts.

imagingHint.label: paracentral lobule in the ACA territory

commonCauses: Vasospasm after anterior communicating artery aneurysm rupture
Anterior cerebral artery dissection or atherosclerosis

syn-accessory-palsy.name: Spinal accessory nerve palsy
syn-accessory-palsy.presentation: Weeks after a lymph node biopsy in the posterior triangle of the neck, a patient complains of a dull ache in the shoulder, difficulty lifting the arm above the head and a shoulder that hangs lower than the other. The upper trapezius is wasted, the scapula sits low and rotated with lateral winging that increases on abducting the arm, and shrugging is weak; turning the head against resistance is normal because the sternocleidomastoid branch left the nerve higher up.

deficits.sign: Shoulder droop, weak shrug, weak abduction above 90°, lateral scapular winging on abduction
Weak head turning to the opposite side and flexion; spared in posterior triangle lesions
Aching from traction on the unsupported shoulder girdle and stretched ligaments

syn-accessory-palsy.reasoning: The spinal root of the accessory nerve arises from the upper five cervical segments, ascends through the foramen magnum, leaves the skull through the jugular foramen and descends in the neck, first supplying the sternocleidomastoid and then crossing the posterior triangle superficially, beneath only skin and platysma, to reach the trapezius. That exposed course is where surgeons find and injure it during lymph node biopsy, neck dissection or carotid surgery. The nerve is the uncrossed motor supply of the ipsilateral trapezius and sternocleidomastoid, so the deficit is on the side of the injury: without the trapezius the shoulder is not held up and the scapula cannot be rotated upward to allow full abduction, so the arm cannot be raised above the horizontal, and the scapula drifts downward and laterally with its lateral border winging when the arm is abducted, a pattern that differs from the medial winging on forward pushing of a long thoracic nerve palsy. Whether the sternocleidomastoid is spared tells the level: it is weak with lesions at the jugular foramen or upper neck, spared with the common posterior triangle lesions. Cortical control of the sternocleidomastoid is ipsilateral and of the trapezius contralateral, a curiosity that explains the head deviation of hemispheric seizures.

imagingFindings.finding: Denervation of the trapezius with a preserved sternocleidomastoid in posterior triangle lesions, or of both muscles in jugular foramen lesions; normal serratus anterior.

syn-adie-tonic-pupil.name: Adie tonic pupil
syn-adie-tonic-pupil.presentation: A young woman notices in the mirror that one pupil is larger than the other. In bright light the difference is obvious and the large pupil barely constricts; when she reads, that pupil slowly narrows and then stays small for a long time after she looks up again. Vision is normal apart from difficulty focusing at near. Her ankle reflexes are absent. There is no ptosis, no diplopia and no headache.

deficits.sign: Dilated pupil with absent or segmental (vermiform) light reaction and slow tonic constriction to near with slow redilation
Blurred near vision from tonic accommodation and ciliary muscle paresis
Absent deep tendon reflexes in Holmes–Adie syndrome

syn-adie-tonic-pupil.reasoning: The ciliary ganglion in the orbit contains the postganglionic parasympathetic neurons for the sphincter pupillae and the ciliary muscle, and receives its preganglionic input from the Edinger–Westphal nucleus through the oculomotor nerve. Damage to the ganglion or the short ciliary nerves, usually a benign idiopathic denervation and occasionally viral or traumatic, removes the final pathway to the iris sphincter and ciliary muscle of that eye, so the pupil dilates, fails to react to light and accommodation is lost; the deficit is ipsilateral because the ganglion serves only its own eye. Over the following weeks the surviving fibers sprout. About thirty times more ganglion cells serve the ciliary muscle than the sphincter, so the regenerating fibers that reach the iris are mostly accommodative ones, and the sphincter comes to be driven by the near effort rather than by light: light-near dissociation with a slow, tonic near response and slow redilation, because the misdirected fibers fire tonically. The denervated sphincter also develops receptor supersensitivity, so dilute pilocarpine that does not affect the normal pupil constricts the tonic pupil, the diagnostic test. Segments of the iris still innervated produce the worm-like segmental contractions seen at the slit lamp. html.presentation: A young woman notices in the mirror that one pupil is larger than the other. syn-aica-lateral-pontine.name: Lateral pontine syndrome (AICA infarct)
syn-aica-lateral-pontine.presentation: A patient develops sudden vertigo and vomiting with deafness in one ear, a complete facial palsy on the same side, and clumsiness of the arm and leg on that side. Pain sensation is lost on that side of the face and on the opposite side of the body, and there may be a Horner syndrome. Weakness is absent. syn-aica-lateral-pontine.reasoning: The anterior inferior cerebellar artery supplies the lateral caudal pons, the middle cerebellar peduncle, the anterior inferior cerebellum and, through the labyrinthine artery, the inner ear. These are all ipsilateral, so the facial palsy, deafness, vertigo and ataxia are on the side of the lesion. The corticospinal fibers in the basis pontis and the medial lemniscus lie in the paramedian territory of the basilar perforators and are spared, hence no weakness or proprioceptive loss. imagingFindings.finding: Restricted diffusion in the lateral caudal pons, middle cerebellar peduncle and anterior inferior cerebellum (flocculus region).

imagingHint.label: lateral caudal pons and middle cerebellar peduncle

commonCauses: Basilar artery atherosclerosis occluding the AICA origin

syn-alexia-without-agraphia.name: Alexia without agraphia
syn-alexia-without-agraphia.presentation: A patient writes a sentence at the examiner's request and then, a minute later, cannot read what they have written, although they can spell words aloud, understand spoken language and copy letters slowly stroke by stroke. They have a right homonymous hemianopia and often cannot name colors. The combination follows a left posterior cerebral artery infarct that included the splenium of the corpus callosum.

deficits.sign: Pure alexia: cannot read words, may read letter by letter; writing and spelling intact
Right homonymous hemianopia
Color anomia; sometimes object agnosia

syn-alexia-without-agraphia.reasoning: Reading requires that visual word forms reach the language areas of the left hemisphere. After a left occipital infarct the left visual cortex is gone, so the right visual field is blind (the fibers from each retina's nasal half cross in the chiasm, so the left calcarine cortex sees the right hemifield). Words can still be seen in the left visual field by the right occipital lobe, but for them to be read the information must cross to the left angular gyrus through the splenium of the corpus callosum. When the same infarct, supplied by the posterior cerebral artery, also destroys the splenium, the intact right visual cortex is disconnected from the language hemisphere: the patient sees the word but cannot read it. Writing, which arises in the left angular gyrus and frontal cortex without needing visual input, is preserved, as is spelling aloud and recognizing words spelled to them. Color anomia has the same disconnection basis, since color perception in the right occipital lobe cannot reach the left naming areas. The syndrome is a disconnection, not a cortical language deficit, and the crossing structure involved is the callosum rather than any brainstem decussation.

imagingFindings.pathology: Left PCA infarct with splenial extension
imagingFindings.finding: Restricted diffusion in the left calcarine cortex and lingual gyrus extending into the splenium of the corpus callosum.
Enhancing mass of the splenium and left occipital lobe (glioma, lymphoma) producing progressive alexia.

imagingHint.label: left calcarine cortex and splenium

mimics.name: Alexia with agraphia
mimics.howToDistinguish: Writing also impaired; lesion in the left angular gyrus

mimics.name: Hemianopic dyslexia
mimics.howToDistinguish: Reads slowly because of the field defect but can read when text is placed in the intact field

mimics.name: Aphasic alexia
mimics.howToDistinguish: Reading loss is part of a broader aphasia

management: Acute stroke treatment
Reading rehabilitation: letter-by-letter and tactile letter-tracing strategies
Field defect counseling and driving restriction

syn-als-pattern.name: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis: mixed upper and lower motor neuron pattern
syn-als-pattern.presentation: A patient in their sixties develops weakness and wasting of one hand with twitching visible under the skin of the arms, and over months the weakness spreads to the other limbs and to the tongue, so that speech becomes slurred and swallowing difficult. Reflexes are brisk in wasted limbs, the jaw jerk is exaggerated and the plantars are extensor, yet there is no sensory loss, no sphincter disturbance and eye movements remain normal to the end.

deficits.sign: Lower motor neuron signs: wasting, fasciculation, cramps, weakness
Upper motor neuron signs: hyperreflexia in wasted limbs, spasticity, Hoffmann, Babinski, brisk jaw jerk
Mixed bulbar and pseudobulbar palsy: wasted fasciculating tongue with a brisk jaw jerk, dysarthria, dysphagia, emotional lability
No sensory loss; sphincters and eye movements spared
Respiratory failure from diaphragm weakness; orthopnea

syn-als-pattern.reasoning: Motor neuron disease destroys both the upper motor neurons, the pyramidal cells of the motor cortex whose axons form the corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts, and the lower motor neurons in the anterior horns of the cord and the motor nuclei of the brainstem, while sparing everything else. Loss of the lower motor neurons denervates muscle, producing wasting, weakness and the spontaneous discharges of dying motor units seen as fasciculations; loss of the upper motor neurons removes the descending inhibition of the surviving spinal reflex arcs, producing hyperreflexia and extensor plantars. The unique combination of a brisk reflex in a wasted, fasciculating muscle can only occur when both neurons of the motor pathway degenerate together. The corticospinal tracts cross in the medulla and the disease is bilateral, so the upper motor neuron signs are widespread without a lateralizing pattern, though the disease begins focally and spreads to contiguous regions. The sensory pathways, the oculomotor nuclei and the sacral Onuf nucleus that supplies the sphincters are spared for reasons that are not fully understood, and their preservation is part of the diagnostic criteria: any sensory level, sphincter loss or ophthalmoplegia should prompt a search for another diagnosis, above all compressive cervical myelopathy, which produces a similar arm-and-leg pattern. Diagnosis requires upper and lower motor neuron signs in several body regions with EMG evidence of denervation in clinically unaffected muscles.

imagingFindings.finding: Often normal; bilateral corticospinal tract T2/FLAIR hyperintensity from the corona radiata to the pons and a hypointense precentral gyrus rim on SWI in some. Cervical MRI is done to exclude myelopathy.

commonCauses: Progressive muscular atrophy (lower motor neuron only) or primary lateral sclerosis (upper only) variants

mimics.howToDistinguish: Sensory signs, neck pain, compression on MRI; no bulbar signs

mimics.name: Multifocal motor neuropathy with conduction block
mimics.howToDistinguish: Pure lower motor neuron, asymmetric, distal, treatable; conduction block on NCS

mimics.name: Kennedy disease (spinobulbar muscular atrophy)
mimics.howToDistinguish: X-linked, slow, gynecomastia, perioral fasciculations, mild sensory neuropathy

mimics.name: Inclusion body myositis
mimics.howToDistinguish: Finger flexor and quadriceps weakness; CK raised; biopsy

Multidisciplinary care: respiratory monitoring with early non-invasive ventilation, gastrostomy before weight loss, communication aids

syn-anosmia.name: Anosmia and olfactory localization
eponyms: Foster Kennedy syndrome (with a subfrontal mass)
syn-anosmia.presentation: A patient who fell and struck the back of the head can no longer smell coffee or gas and finds food tasteless. Another, with a slowly changing personality, has lost the sense of smell in one nostril without noticing, and has a swollen optic disc on the other side. Testing each nostril separately with familiar non-irritant odors reveals the loss; ammonia, which is felt through the trigeminal nerve, is still detected and unmasks a functional complaint.

deficits.sign: Anosmia or hyposmia to non-irritant odors with preserved perception of irritants (trigeminal)
Unilateral anosmia from a bulb or tract lesion, usually unnoticed by the patient
Complaint of loss of taste from loss of flavor; sweet, salt, sour and bitter preserved
Personality change and apathy with a subfrontal tumor; Foster Kennedy syndrome with ipsilateral optic atrophy and contralateral papilledema

syn-anosmia.reasoning: Olfactory receptor neurons in the roof of the nasal cavity send unmyelinated axons in bundles through the cribriform plate to the olfactory bulb, which lies on the plate under the frontal lobe; the bulb's output runs back in the olfactory tract to the piriform cortex of the uncus and the amygdala, mostly on the same side, with a smaller crossed component through the anterior commissure. Because the pathway is largely uncrossed and each nostril is served by its own bulb, unilateral anosmia localizes to the nasal cavity, cribriform plate, bulb or tract of that side, and a unilateral loss is the earliest sign of an olfactory groove meningioma, which then compresses the optic nerve on the same side and raises intracranial pressure, producing the classic combination of ipsilateral optic atrophy and contralateral papilledema. Bilateral loss most often reflects disease of the nasal mucosa or a shearing injury of the olfactory filaments against the cribriform plate when the brain moves on impact, especially with occipital blows. Cortical lesions rarely abolish smell because the projection is bilateral at the level of the piriform cortex, but irritative lesions of the uncus produce olfactory hallucinations. Flavor depends on retronasal smell, so anosmic patients complain of tasteless food although the gustatory pathway is intact. Loss of smell is also an early sign of Parkinson and Alzheimer disease, in which the olfactory bulb is among the first structures affected.

imagingFindings.finding: Contusion of the gyrus recti and orbital frontal cortex, hemosiderin on SWI, and atrophy of the olfactory bulbs on coronal thin-section T2.
Enhancing subfrontal extra-axial mass on the cribriform plate displacing the frontal lobes and optic nerves, with hyperostosis on CT.
Mucosal thickening, polyps or obstruction of the olfactory cleft on sinus CT.
Small or absent bulbs in Kallmann syndrome (congenital) and reduced volume in post-viral and neurodegenerative anosmia.

imagingHint.label: olfactory bulbs on the cribriform plate beneath the frontal lobes

mimics.name: Ageusia
mimics.howToDistinguish: True taste loss is rare; test the four tastes on the tongue

mimics.name: Functional anosmia
mimics.howToDistinguish: Claims not to detect ammonia, which is a trigeminal stimulus

mimics.name: Nasal obstruction
mimics.howToDistinguish: Conductive loss that fluctuates and responds to decongestants

syn-anterior-choroidal-infarct.name: Anterior choroidal artery infarction
syn-anterior-choroidal-infarct.presentation: A patient presents with a hemiparesis affecting face, arm and leg, hemisensory loss and a homonymous hemianopia, yet is alert with intact language and no neglect. The triad of motor, sensory and visual loss without cortical signs is the classic anterior choroidal syndrome. Some patients show only a pure motor or sensorimotor lacunar picture; others have a peculiar sectoral field defect sparing a horizontal wedge.

deficits.sign: Hemiparesis from the posterior limb of the internal capsule
Hemihypesthesia from the thalamocortical fibers in the posterior capsule
Homonymous hemianopia, sometimes with sparing of a horizontal sector

syn-anterior-choroidal-infarct.reasoning: The anterior choroidal artery arises from the internal carotid just beyond the posterior communicating origin and runs backward beneath the optic tract to enter the temporal horn, supplying on the way the posterior limb of the internal capsule, the retrolenticular fibers, the optic tract, part of the lateral geniculate body and the medial temporal lobe. All three long pathways pass through this small territory: the corticospinal tract, whose fibers cross in the pyramidal decussation, the thalamocortical sensory radiation carrying the crossed spinothalamic and lemniscal input, and the optic tract and lateral geniculate body carrying the contralateral hemifield. A single small infarct therefore reproduces the deficit of a whole hemisphere lesion but without aphasia, neglect or field loss from cortical damage, because the cortex is intact. The lateral geniculate has a dual supply, anterior choroidal and lateral posterior choroidal, which explains the unusual sectoranopias: loss of the anterior choroidal portion spares the horizontal wedge fed by the other vessel.

imagingFindings.finding: Restricted diffusion in the posterior limb of the internal capsule extending down to the medial temporal lobe and lateral geniculate body, elongated in the anteroposterior direction.
The artery is usually too small to show an occlusion; the parent carotid may show atheroma or dissection.

imagingHint.label: posterior limb of the internal capsule

commonCauses: Surgical clipping or coiling of nearby aneurysms

mimics.howToDistinguish: No visual field defect

mimics.name: MCA stem infarct
mimics.howToDistinguish: Cortical signs (aphasia, neglect) and gaze deviation present

mimics.name: PCA infarct
mimics.howToDistinguish: Hemianopia with little or no weakness

syn-anterior-cord.name: Anterior cord syndrome (anterior spinal artery)
syn-anterior-cord.presentation: During or after aortic surgery, or with sudden back pain in a patient with a dissecting aorta, both legs become paralyzed within minutes to hours. Pain and temperature sensation are lost below the level on both sides and the bladder does not empty, but the patient can still feel the position of the toes and a tuning fork on the ankle. Initially the legs are flaccid and areflexic; spasticity emerges over weeks.

deficits.sign: Paraplegia or quadriplegia: flaccid at first (spinal shock), then spastic; segmental lower motor neuron signs at the level
Loss of pain and temperature with a sensory level
Vibration and position sense intact (posterior columns spared)
Retention then reflex incontinence; autonomic dysfunction
Sudden severe back pain at onset in ischemic cases

syn-anterior-cord.reasoning: A single anterior spinal artery, fed by the vertebral arteries above and by a few radicular arteries below, of which the artery of Adamkiewicz in the lower thoracic region is the largest, supplies the anterior two-thirds of the cord: the anterior horns, the lateral and anterior white columns with the corticospinal and spinothalamic tracts, and the intermediolateral columns. The posterior columns are fed by the paired posterior spinal arteries with their rich pial anastomosis. Occlusion of the anterior artery or of its dominant feeder therefore infarcts everything except the posterior columns, bilaterally, because the vessel is midline. The corticospinal tracts, having crossed in the medulla, serve the same-side limbs, and the spinothalamic tracts, having crossed in the cord, serve the opposite side, but since both sides of the cord are infarcted the weakness and the pain-temperature loss are simply bilateral below the lesion, with a level. The preserved vibration and proprioception, carried in the intact posterior columns, are the diagnostic dissociation. Spinal shock with flaccidity and areflexia precedes the emergence of spasticity as the isolated cord segments recover excitability.

Coexisting bone marrow signal change in the adjacent vertebral body supports a vascular cause.

syn-anton.name: Anton syndrome (cortical blindness with denial)
syn-anton.presentation: A patient who has suffered bilateral occipital infarcts, often after a basilar embolus or a cardiac arrest, walks into furniture and describes objects that are not there, yet insists that they can see, blaming the light or their glasses. The pupils react normally to light, the fundi are normal, and there is no blink to threat. The confabulated descriptions are the clue that the patient is unaware of the blindness.

deficits.sign: Cortical blindness: no perception of light, normal pupils, absent blink to threat, preserved optokinetic response absent

syn-anton.reasoning: Both calcarine cortices receive the crossed visual input from the contralateral hemifields, so bilateral destruction abolishes all conscious vision while the retina, optic nerves, chiasm, tracts and pretectal pupillary pathway remain intact; the pupils react because the pupillary light fibers leave the optic tract for the pretectum before reaching the geniculate and cortex. Both occipital lobes are supplied by the posterior cerebral arteries, which arise together from the basilar tip, so an embolus there or a period of profound hypotension affects both at once. The denial is thought to arise when the visual association cortex and its connections to the parietal and frontal monitoring systems are involved along with the primary cortex, so that the absence of visual input is not registered and the patient fills the gap with plausible confabulated scenes, much as a patient with neglect denies the left side. Preserved blink to threat or a startle to a bright light argues for some surviving cortex and a better prognosis.

syn-aphasia-broca.name: Broca (expressive, non-fluent) aphasia
syn-aphasia-broca.presentation: Speech is effortful, slow and reduced to a few content words with the grammar stripped out ('go... hospital... wife'), and repeating a sentence is as hard as producing one. Comprehension of conversation is good, though complex grammatical sentences ('the lion was killed by the tiger; which animal died?') may defeat the patient. Writing is as impaired as speech. There is usually right facial and arm weakness, and the patient is frustrated and aware of the problem.

syn-aphasia-broca.reasoning: Broca's area occupies the pars opercularis and triangularis of the inferior frontal gyrus of the dominant hemisphere, in front of the face area of the motor cortex, and is supplied by the superior division of the middle cerebral artery. Comprehension survives because the posterior temporal cortex is in inferior division territory. Language is lateralized to the left hemisphere in almost all right-handers and most left-handers, and the network is entirely uncrossed at the cortical level, so the aphasia itself has no side; the accompanying weakness is contralateral because the corticobulbar and corticospinal fibers from the neighboring motor cortex cross in the brainstem, and the face and arm are affected because they sit next to Broca's area on the lateral convexity. syn-aphasia-conduction-global.name: Conduction and global aphasia
syn-aphasia-conduction-global.presentation: In conduction aphasia the patient speaks fluently with frequent phonemic slips that they notice and try to correct, understands well, but cannot repeat even short phrases, which is the giveaway. In global aphasia, after a large left middle cerebral artery infarct, speech is reduced to a few stereotyped syllables, comprehension is nearly absent, repetition is impossible, and there is a dense right hemiplegia with hemianopia.

A lesion of the supramarginal gyrus or the underlying white matter disconnects the two intact language areas: comprehension and fluent production survive, but the transfer fails, so repetition collapses and the patient produces phonemic errors that their intact monitoring detects. syn-aphasia-wernicke.name: Wernicke (receptive, fluent) aphasia
syn-aphasia-wernicke.presentation: The patient speaks in long, well-articulated but empty sentences peppered with wrong words and invented words, does not follow commands, cannot repeat, and seems unaware that anything is wrong, sometimes becoming angry when not understood. Strength is normal. A right superior quadrantanopia may be found if the examiner thinks to test the fields. The initial diagnosis is frequently confusion or psychosis.

Right superior quadrantanopia from Meyer's loop

syn-aphasia-wernicke.reasoning: Wernicke's area, the posterior part of the superior temporal gyrus of the dominant hemisphere behind Heschl's gyrus, holds the sound representations of words that both comprehension and word selection depend on. When it is destroyed, the incoming speech signal cannot be decoded, and the outgoing speech, produced by an intact Broca's area, is fluent but unmonitored and full of phonemic and semantic errors. Repetition fails because the input side of the arcuate loop is gone. Like all cortical language disorders the aphasia is uncrossed and simply reflects left hemisphere dominance; only the field defect obeys crossing logic. The anosognosia is intrinsic to the loss of self-monitoring and, together with the absence of weakness, explains why these patients are so often sent to psychiatry.

syn-argyll-robertson.name: Argyll Robertson pupils
syn-argyll-robertson.presentation: Both pupils are small and irregular and do not constrict to even the brightest light, but they constrict promptly when the patient looks at a near target and redilate slowly afterward. Vision is normal and there is no ptosis. The patient may have absent ankle reflexes, lightning pains and a sensory ataxia from tabes dorsalis; the finding was classically a sign of late neurosyphilis and today prompts serological testing.

deficits.sign: Small, irregular pupils that fail to react to light but constrict to near (light-near dissociation)

syn-argyll-robertson.reasoning: The light reflex and the near reflex share the same final pathway from the Edinger–Westphal nucleus through the oculomotor nerve and the ciliary ganglion to the sphincter pupillae, but they reach the nucleus by different routes: the light reflex arrives from the pretectal nuclei, which lie dorsally beneath the posterior commissure and receive bilateral retinal input, whereas the near response is driven from the cortex by fibers descending more ventrally in the midbrain tegmentum. A lesion of the periaqueductal region that damages the pretectal nuclei or their bilateral connections to the Edinger–Westphal nuclei abolishes the light reaction of both pupils while leaving the near reaction intact: light-near dissociation. The pupils are small because the same periaqueductal process is thought to interrupt the supranuclear inhibitory fibers that normally hold the Edinger–Westphal neurons in check, and irregular because of chronic iris damage. Both pupils are involved because the pretectal connections are bilateral and the lesion is midline; there is no ipsilateral or contralateral pattern. Vision is normal because the retinogeniculate fibers to the lateral geniculate leave the tract before the pretectum. The same dissociation with large rather than small pupils occurs in the dorsal midbrain syndrome from a pineal tumor and in the Adie tonic pupil from ciliary ganglion damage with aberrant regeneration, so pupil size and reactivity speed separate the three.

syn-axillary-neuropathy.name: Axillary nerve palsy
syn-axillary-neuropathy.presentation: After an anterior shoulder dislocation or a fracture of the surgical neck of the humerus, a patient cannot lift the arm sideways once the first few degrees are achieved by the supraspinatus, the rounded contour of the shoulder flattens as the deltoid wastes, and there is a patch of numbness over the outer upper arm. External rotation may be mildly weak from teres minor involvement. Sleeping with the arm over a chair back or crutch pressure can produce the same picture.

deficits.distribution: 'regimental badge' area over the lateral deltoid
deficits.sign: Sensory loss over the upper lateral arm (upper lateral cutaneous nerve of the arm)

syn-axillary-neuropathy.reasoning: The axillary nerve is a terminal branch of the posterior cord carrying C5 and C6 fibers; it leaves the axilla backward through the quadrangular space beneath the shoulder joint capsule, curls around the surgical neck of the humerus with the posterior circumflex humeral vessels and supplies the deltoid and teres minor and a patch of skin over the deltoid. Its intimate relation to the inferior joint capsule and the surgical neck is why an anterior dislocation of the humeral head or a fracture at the surgical neck stretches or tears it, and why it is at risk during shoulder surgery and from crutches pressing into the axilla. It is an uncrossed peripheral nerve, so the deficit is on the side of the injury: the deltoid, the main abductor and flexor of the shoulder, is paralyzed, but the supraspinatus, supplied by the suprascapular nerve, still initiates abduction, so the first few degrees are possible and the patient compensates by hitching the shoulder. The sensory territory is small and constant, over the deltoid, and its loss confirms the nerve rather than a root: a C5 radiculopathy would weaken the supraspinatus, the biceps and the rhomboids as well and produce a broader sensory loss with neck pain. Most closed injuries are neurapraxic and recover within months, and the deltoid is examined after every shoulder dislocation and before its reduction.

syn-balint.name: Balint syndrome
syn-balint.presentation: The patient can read individual letters but not a word, describes one object in a picture while missing the scene, cannot reach accurately for a cup that they see, and cannot shift their gaze voluntarily to a new target even though their eyes move freely at random. Acuity and fields may be normal or show lower quadrant defects. The syndrome typically follows bilateral hypotensive watershed infarcts or posterior cortical atrophy.

syn-balint.reasoning: The dorsal visual stream runs from the occipital lobe up into the superior parietal lobule of each hemisphere and computes where objects are in space, guiding the eyes and hands toward them. Each hemisphere handles the contralateral field, but bilateral damage is needed for the full syndrome, because one intact parietal lobe can crudely cover both sides. The bilateral parieto-occipital cortex lies in the posterior watershed zone between middle and posterior cerebral territories, so the usual cause is a global drop in perfusion. Ventral stream areas in the occipitotemporal cortex are spared, which is why single objects and letters are still recognized: the failure is in binding several objects into a scene (simultanagnosia), in using visual information to program saccades (ocular apraxia, distinct from the motor palsy of a brainstem gaze center lesion) and in using it to program reaching (optic ataxia, distinct from cerebellar ataxia because reaching to a sound or to the patient's own body is accurate). Nothing crosses at this level; the syndrome is bilateral cortical, and the contralateral field defects, when present, come from the adjacent optic radiations.

syn-basilar-occlusion.name: Basilar artery occlusion
syn-basilar-occlusion.presentation: The story begins hours or days earlier with vertigo, double vision, slurred speech or transient weakness switching sides, then the patient becomes quadriparetic and drowsy or comatose. Examination reveals bilateral extensor plantars, pinpoint reactive pupils, absent horizontal eye movements, facial weakness and often ocular bobbing. Some patients remain fully aware but can move nothing except their eyes vertically: the locked-in state.

syn-basilar-occlusion.reasoning: The basilar artery is a single midline vessel formed by the two vertebral arteries, so its occlusion removes the supply of both sides of the pons at once through the paramedian and short circumferential branches. The corticospinal tracts descend through the basis pontis as scattered bundles before they cross in the medulla, so bilateral pontine infarction paralyzes all four limbs, and the corticobulbar fibers to the facial, ambiguus and hypoglossal nuclei are lost with them, paralyzing the face and bulbar muscles. The abducens nuclei, paramedian pontine reticular formation and both MLFs occupy the dorsal pontine tegmentum, so horizontal gaze fails bilaterally, while the vertical gaze center in the midbrain is spared, which is why a locked-in patient can still look up and down. The descending sympathetic fibers run through the pontine tegmentum bilaterally, giving small pupils that still react because the parasympathetic pathway in the midbrain is intact. Whether the patient is comatose or locked in depends on whether the tegmental reticular formation infarcts along with the base.

syn-benedikt.presentation: The patient has a third nerve palsy on one side and, on the other, a coarse tremor that is present at rest, worsens with posture and becomes wild on reaching, together with ataxia, choreoathetoid movements and sometimes mild weakness. This combination of an oculomotor palsy with contralateral involuntary movements marks a lesion of the midbrain tegmentum that includes the red nucleus.

deficits.sign: Third nerve palsy
Holmes (rubral) tremor: rest, postural and intention components; ataxia
Choreoathetosis or hemiballismus-like movements from the nigra and subthalamic connections
Mild hemiparesis if the lesion reaches the crus

syn-benedikt.reasoning: The red nucleus sits in the midbrain tegmentum at the level of the superior colliculus, receiving the crossed dentatothalamic fibers from the opposite cerebellum and sending the rubrospinal tract, which crosses immediately, to the contralateral cord. A lesion here interrupts cerebellar outflow after its decussation and damages the red nucleus and the neighboring substantia nigra, so the resulting tremor and ataxia are contralateral, following the same double-crossing logic as the Claude syndrome: cerebellar information that crossed once in the superior cerebellar peduncle would have been re-crossed by the corticospinal tract to serve the opposite limbs. The characteristic Holmes tremor, slow and present at rest as well as on action, is attributed to the combined loss of cerebellothalamic and nigrostriatal input, and it typically appears weeks after the acute lesion. Ventral extension into the crus adds contralateral weakness, blending the syndrome with Weber.

imagingHint.label: red nucleus and oculomotor fascicle

syn-bppv.name: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo
syn-bppv.presentation: The patient wakes, rolls over in bed and the room spins violently for twenty seconds, then settles; the same thing happens when looking up to a shelf or bending to tie shoes. There is no hearing loss and no vertigo when still. The Dix–Hallpike test with the affected ear down reproduces the vertigo after a few seconds' latency, with a torsional upbeating nystagmus that fatigues and reverses on sitting up.

deficits.sign: Brief positional vertigo with latency, torsional-upbeat nystagmus on Dix–Hallpike, fatigability
Normal hearing; no tinnitus
Mild unsteadiness between attacks; no ataxia

syn-bppv.reasoning: Otoconia dislodged from the utricular macula fall into the posterior semicircular canal, the most dependent canal, where they float in the endolymph. When the head moves into the plane of that canal the debris sinks, dragging the endolymph and deflecting the cupula, which the brain interprets as sustained rotation in the plane of the canal; the deflection stops once the particles settle, hence the latency of a few seconds while the debris starts to move and the short duration. The posterior canal projects through the vestibular nerve and nuclei to the ipsilateral superior oblique and the contralateral inferior rectus, so the nystagmus is torsional toward the affected (lower) ear and upbeating, an exact fingerprint of the canal involved, and reverses when the patient sits up and the debris moves back. Repeating the maneuver disperses the debris, so the response fatigues, and the cerebellum suppresses it with repetition. The horizontal canal variant gives a horizontal geotropic or apogeotropic nystagmus on rolling in bed. The peripheral origin is confirmed by the latency, the brevity, the fatigability and the absence of any other neurological sign; positional nystagmus that is purely vertical, persistent, without latency or unfatigable points instead to the cerebellar nodulus or the fourth ventricle region, and requires imaging.

imagingFindings.finding: Diagnosis is clinical by Dix–Hallpike or supine roll test; imaging is normal and unnecessary in typical cases.

imagingHint.label: vestibular nerve entering the internal acoustic meatus

syn-brown-sequard.name: Brown-Séquard syndrome (hemicord)
syn-brown-sequard.presentation: After a stab wound to the back, or with a lateral disc or tumor pressing on one side of the cord, a patient has weakness of the leg on one side with brisk reflexes and an upgoing toe, cannot feel a tuning fork or joint movement in that same leg, yet reports that pin-prick and cold are lost in the other leg, starting a couple of segments below the injury. At the level of the lesion itself there is a narrow band of complete sensory loss and flaccid weakness on the injured side.

deficits.sign: Spastic weakness with hyperreflexia and extensor plantar (lateral corticospinal tract)
Loss of vibration and position sense (posterior column)

deficits.distribution: from 1–2 segments below the lesion downward
deficits.sign: Loss of pain and temperature (spinothalamic tract)

deficits.distribution: at the level of the lesion
deficits.sign: Segmental lower motor neuron weakness and a band of anesthesia from anterior horn and root damage

syn-brown-sequard.reasoning: The three long tracts of the cord cross at different places, and a lesion of one half of the cord separates them. The lateral corticospinal tract has already crossed in the medulla, so it carries the motor command for the same side of the body, and cutting it produces ipsilateral upper motor neuron weakness below the lesion. The posterior columns carry uncrossed proprioceptive and vibration fibers, which cross only in the medulla after relaying in the gracile and cuneate nuclei, so their interruption gives ipsilateral loss of those modalities. The spinothalamic tract, by contrast, is formed by second-order fibers that crossed in the anterior white commissure within one or two segments of their entry, so it carries pain and temperature from the opposite side, and its section gives contralateral loss beginning a segment or two below the lesion, where the fibers entering at the lesion level have not yet crossed. Fibers crossing at the level of the lesion are caught on both sides, and the damaged dorsal root and anterior horn add an ipsilateral segmental band of complete sensory loss and flaccid weakness that marks the level exactly. Light touch survives on both sides because it travels by both routes. The dissociation, with weakness and proprioceptive loss on one side and pain loss on the other, is unique to the cord and cannot be produced by any brain lesion.

imagingFindings.finding: Hemicord signal change and hemorrhage at the level of the wound on T2 and gradient echo; CT for bone and metal fragments.
Lateral disc herniation, meningioma or schwannoma indenting one side of the cord with cord signal change.

imagingHint.label: one half of the cervical cord

commonCauses: Lateral cervical disc herniation or spondylosis

mimics.howToDistinguish: Facial sensory loss and cranial nerve signs; no limb weakness

mimics.name: Peripheral nerve or plexus injury

syn-bulbar-vs-pseudobulbar.name: Bulbar versus pseudobulbar palsy
syn-bulbar-vs-pseudobulbar.presentation: Two patients cannot swallow or speak clearly. The first has a flaccid, wasted, fasciculating tongue, a nasal voice, an absent gag and an absent jaw jerk: bulbar palsy, the lower motor neurons of the medulla have died. The second has a small, spastic tongue that cannot be protruded, strangled slow speech, an exaggerated gag and jaw jerk, and laughs or cries without feeling either: pseudobulbar palsy, the corticobulbar tracts have been cut on both sides.

deficits.sign: Bulbar: flaccid dysarthria, nasal regurgitation, wasted fasciculating tongue, absent gag and jaw jerk
Pseudobulbar: spastic dysarthria, dysphagia, small spastic tongue, brisk gag and jaw jerk
Pseudobulbar affect: involuntary laughing and crying
Mixed upper and lower motor neuron limb signs when the cause is motor neuron disease

syn-bulbar-vs-pseudobulbar.reasoning: The muscles of the tongue, palate, pharynx and larynx are driven by lower motor neurons in the hypoglossal nucleus and nucleus ambiguus of the medulla (the 'bulb'), and those neurons in turn receive corticobulbar input from both hemispheres, crossed and uncrossed. Destruction of the medullary nuclei or their nerves gives a lower motor neuron picture of flaccid weakness with wasting, fasciculation and loss of the reflexes whose efferent limb they form; the bilateral cortical input is irrelevant once the final pathway is gone. Because the corticobulbar projection is bilateral, a lesion of the tract on one side causes little more than transient dysarthria; a pseudobulbar palsy requires both corticobulbar tracts to be interrupted, typically by successive lacunar strokes in the two internal capsules or the pons, by bilateral demyelination, or by the upper motor neuron degeneration of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. The muscles are then weak but spastic, the jaw jerk and gag are exaggerated because the brainstem reflex arcs are released from cortical inhibition, and the loss of cortical control over the brainstem circuits that generate laughing and crying produces the emotional incontinence. In motor neuron disease both mechanisms coexist, giving a wasted fasciculating tongue with a brisk jaw jerk, a combination that is diagnostic.

imagingFindings.finding: Multiple old lacunar infarcts in both internal capsules, corona radiata or basis pontis with confluent white matter disease.
Symmetric corticospinal tract T2 hyperintensity and precentral hypointensity on SWI; tongue atrophy; medulla otherwise normal.
Infarct, syrinx, tumor or demyelination involving the nucleus ambiguus and hypoglossal nucleus.

imagingHint.label: medullary motor nuclei

commonCauses: Brainstem tumor, syringobulbia, Guillain–Barré, myasthenia, polio (bulbar)

mimics.name: Myasthenia gravis
mimics.howToDistinguish: Fatigable bulbar weakness without wasting or reflex change; ptosis; antibody positive

mimics.name: Oculopharyngeal muscular dystrophy or myopathy
mimics.howToDistinguish: Ptosis and dysphagia with a family history; no fasciculation, normal reflexes

mimics.name: Kennedy disease
mimics.howToDistinguish: Slowly progressive lower motor neuron bulbar and limb weakness in men with gynecomastia

syn-callosal-disconnection.name: Callosal disconnection syndrome
syn-callosal-disconnection.presentation: After surgical division of the corpus callosum for epilepsy, or an infarct or tumor of its body, a right-handed patient can name objects placed in the right hand but not in the left, cannot write with the left hand or copy a drawing with the right, and the left hand may button what the right hand unbuttons. Reading in the left visual field is impossible. In daily life the deficits are subtle and are found only when each hemisphere is tested alone.

deficits.sign: Left-hand tactile anomia and left-hand agraphia; left ideomotor apraxia to verbal command
Right-hand constructional apraxia (right hemisphere skills unavailable to the left hand's controller)
Left hemialexia: words in the left field cannot be read
Intermanual conflict, alien hand phenomena and diagonistic dyspraxia after anterior callosal lesions

syn-callosal-disconnection.reasoning: Sensation and motor control are crossed: the left hand reports to the right hemisphere and the left visual field projects to the right occipital cortex, whereas language lives in the left hemisphere. In an intact brain the corpus callosum transfers information between the hemispheres in milliseconds, so what the right hemisphere feels or sees can be named. When the callosum is divided, the right hemisphere still perceives the object in the left hand and can select it by touch from a tray, but the name cannot reach the left hemisphere's speech areas; the left hand cannot write because the right hemisphere has no access to the left hemisphere's language, and it cannot carry out a verbal command because the praxis programs of the left parietal lobe cannot cross to the right motor cortex. The right hand, controlled by the left hemisphere, loses the visuospatial skill of the right parietal lobe, hence its constructional apraxia. Words in the left visual field reach only the right occipital lobe and cannot cross the splenium to the left angular gyrus, a left hemialexia that is the mirror of alexia without agraphia. Anterior callosal lesions disconnect the supplementary motor areas and produce conflict between the hands. Each hemisphere is intact, so ordinary behavior, which uses both eyes and both hands, is nearly normal, and the syndrome reveals itself only when input is lateralized.

imagingFindings.finding: Restricted diffusion in the body or splenium of the corpus callosum, from anterior or posterior cerebral artery pericallosal branch occlusion.
Surgical division of the anterior two-thirds or the whole callosum on sagittal T1.
'Butterfly' glioblastoma crossing the callosum, or the callososeptal lesions of multiple sclerosis; Marchiafava–Bignami necrosis in alcoholism.

imagingHint.label: body and splenium of the corpus callosum

commonCauses: Glioblastoma or lymphoma of the callosum

mimics.name: Left parietal apraxia
mimics.howToDistinguish: Bilateral apraxia; naming intact in both hands

mimics.name: Left hemineglect
mimics.howToDistinguish: Left field and hand ignored rather than unnamed; awareness deficit

mimics.name: Corticobasal degeneration
mimics.howToDistinguish: Progressive asymmetric rigidity, dystonia and alien limb with cortical sensory loss

management: Test each hand and each visual field separately when a callosal lesion is suspected
Treat the underlying lesion; callosotomy deficits are mild and adapt
Occupational therapy strategies using bimanual and verbal cues
