syn-carpal-tunnel.name: Carpal tunnel syndrome
syn-carpal-tunnel.presentation: A middle-aged woman wakes at night with numb, painful hands that she shakes to relieve, and drops small objects during the day. Tingling involves the thumb, index and middle fingers and the radial half of the ring finger but spares the little finger and the palm; the thenar eminence is wasted in advanced cases and thumb abduction is weak. Tapping the wrist (Tinel) or holding it flexed (Phalen) reproduces the tingling.

deficits.distribution: palmar thumb, index, middle and radial ring finger
deficits.sign: Nocturnal paresthesias and later sensory loss in the median digital distribution, sparing the thenar palm
Thenar wasting and weak thumb abduction and opposition; long flexors spared
Aching pain radiating proximally

syn-carpal-tunnel.reasoning: The median nerve enters the hand beneath the flexor retinaculum in the carpal tunnel together with the nine flexor tendons, and any increase in the contents or decrease in the space of the tunnel compresses it: tenosynovitis, fluid retention in pregnancy, hypothyroidism, acromegaly, amyloid, diabetes and repetitive wrist flexion. Compression damages the large myelinated fibers first, producing paresthesias that are worst at night when the wrist flexes during sleep and venous congestion rises. The palmar cutaneous branch leaves the nerve above the tunnel and passes over the retinaculum, so sensation over the thenar eminence is spared, a point that separates carpal tunnel syndrome from a proximal median lesion or a C6–C7 radiculopathy. The motor branch to the thenar muscles arises within or just beyond the tunnel, so the abductor pollicis brevis and opponens waste while the flexor pollicis longus and the pronator, supplied in the forearm, are normal; the first two lumbricals are also affected but are hard to test. The lesion is peripheral and ipsilateral, and though it is often bilateral, one hand usually dominates. Nerve conduction shows slowing across the wrist with normal forearm conduction, which confirms the site. Sensory symptoms that include the little finger, the forearm, or weakness of the finger flexors point elsewhere.

imagingFindings.finding: Prolonged median distal sensory and motor latencies across the wrist with normal ulnar values; denervation of the abductor pollicis brevis in severe cases.
Enlarged cross-sectional area of the median nerve proximal to the tunnel (above about 10 mm²) with flattening beneath the retinaculum.
Ganglion, tenosynovitis, amyloid or anomalous muscle within the carpal tunnel in atypical cases.

imagingHint.label: median nerve at the wrist (virtual)

commonCauses: Pregnancy, hypothyroidism, diabetes, acromegaly, rheumatoid arthritis

mimics.name: C6–C7 radiculopathy
mimics.howToDistinguish: Neck pain, sensory loss including the forearm and thenar palm, reflex change, normal distal latencies

mimics.name: Pronator syndrome (proximal median)
mimics.howToDistinguish: Thenar palm numb, forearm pain, flexor pollicis longus weak

mimics.name: Polyneuropathy
mimics.howToDistinguish: Bilateral, symmetric, feet involved, sural response abnormal

mimics.howToDistinguish: Medial forearm sensory loss and interosseous weakness

Corticosteroid injection into the tunnel for temporary relief

syn-cavernous-sinus-thrombosis.name: Septic cavernous sinus thrombosis
syn-cavernous-sinus-thrombosis.presentation: A patient with a boil on the upper lip or a sinus infection develops high fever, severe headache and a red, swollen, protruding eye with drooping lid; within a day the eye cannot move, the forehead is numb, the retinal veins are engorged and the other eye starts to swell as the infection crosses the midline. Untreated, meningitis, carotid narrowing with stroke and death follow within days; treated early with antibiotics and anticoagulation most survive.

deficits.sign: Painful proptosis, chemosis, lid edema and retinal venous engorgement from ophthalmic vein obstruction; spreads to the other eye within days

deficits.distribution: VI first, then III and IV
deficits.sign: Ophthalmoplegia beginning with abduction failure
Forehead and cheek numbness, reduced corneal reflex
Fever, rigors, drowsiness from sepsis and meningitis
Hemiparesis from carotid arteritis and narrowing within the sinus

syn-cavernous-sinus-thrombosis.reasoning: The facial veins have no valves and drain into the cavernous sinus through the ophthalmic veins and the pterygoid plexus, so an infection of the central face, the orbit, the sphenoid or ethmoid sinuses, the teeth or the ear can propagate thrombophlebitis backward into the sinus. Within the sinus the thrombus obstructs the ophthalmic veins, congesting the orbit and retina on that side, and the inflammation involves the nerves in its walls, uncrossed nerves serving the ipsilateral eye and face: the abducens nerve, floating free beside the carotid, fails first, then the oculomotor and trochlear nerves in the lateral wall, and the ophthalmic and maxillary divisions of the trigeminal nerve, while the sympathetic plexus on the carotid may add a Horner. The two cavernous sinuses communicate through the intercavernous sinuses around the pituitary, so the thrombosis spreads across within days and the picture becomes bilateral, which is the clue that separates it from an orbital cellulitis or a tumor. The carotid artery runs through the sinus and can be narrowed by the surrounding inflammation, producing cerebral infarction, and the infection reaches the meninges and the pituitary. Staphylococcus aureus is the usual organizm, and the diagnosis is confirmed by venography showing the filling defect and the dilated superior ophthalmic vein, though it should be treated on clinical suspicion.

imagingFindings.finding: Filling defect with expansion and convex bulging of the lateral walls of the cavernous sinus, dilated thrombosed superior ophthalmic vein, proptosis and orbital fat stranding; enhancement of the sinus walls and dura.
Sphenoid or ethmoid sinusitis, facial cellulitis, dental or orbital abscess on contrast CT of the sinuses and orbits.

imagingHint.label: cavernous sinus beside the sella

commonCauses: Facial furuncle or cellulitis in the 'danger triangle'
Otitis and mastoiditis (via the petrosal sinuses)
Invasive fungal sinusitis in diabetics and the immunosuppressed

mimics.howToDistinguish: Unilateral, cranial nerves spared initially, no contralateral spread

mimics.name: Cavernous sinus tumor or Tolosa–Hunt

html.presentation: A patient with a boil on the upper lip or a sinus infection develops high fever, severe headache and a red, swollen, protruding eye with drooping lid; within a day the eye cannot move, the forehead is numb, the retinal veins are engorged and the other eye starts to swell as the infection crosses the midline. syn-cavernous-sinus.name: Cavernous sinus syndrome
syn-cavernous-sinus.presentation: The patient has a painful, swollen, red eye with a drooping lid that is fixed in all directions, numbness of the forehead and cheek on the same side, and sometimes a small pupil. A diabetic with a fever and a black eschar in the nose is a surgical emergency; a patient with a pituitary tumor develops the same signs slowly; a young person after a head injury may have a pulsating, bruit-bearing eye from a fistula.

syn-central-cord-syringomyelia.name: Central cord syndrome and syringomyelia
syn-central-cord-syringomyelia.presentation: A young adult notices painless burns and cuts on the fingers, then weakness and wasting of the hands. Examination shows loss of pain and temperature over the shoulders, arms and upper chest in a cape distribution while light touch, vibration and position sense are normal in the same area; the arm reflexes are absent, the hand muscles are wasted, and later the legs become spastic. In an elderly person a hyperextension neck injury produces the acute version, with weakness of the arms far worse than the legs.

deficits.distribution: cape distribution over shoulders and arms (cervical syrinx)
deficits.sign: Dissociated loss of pain and temperature with preserved touch and proprioception

syn-central-cord-syringomyelia.reasoning: The center of the cord, around the central canal, is where the second-order pain and temperature fibers from both sides cross in the anterior white commissure before ascending in the spinothalamic tracts. A cavity that expands from the central canal (a syrinx) or a hemorrhagic contusion of the central gray in hyperextension injury destroys these crossing fibers over the segments involved, so pain and temperature are lost bilaterally in exactly those dermatomes, while the posterior columns, which carry vibration and proprioception uncrossed at the periphery of the cord, and the spinothalamic fibers from the lower body, which crossed below the lesion and are already ascending in the lateral funiculus, are spared: a suspended, dissociated sensory loss. In the cervical cord this produces the cape or shawl distribution. As the cavity widens it reaches the anterior horns, producing wasting and areflexia of the hands and arms at the level, and then the medial part of the lateral funiculus, where the arm fibers of the corticospinal tract lie closest to the center, so spasticity appears in the legs and weakness in the arms exceeds that in the legs; the sacral fibers of the spinothalamic tract lie outermost and are spared until late (sacral sparing). syn-central-transtentorial-herniation.name: Central (downward) transtentorial herniation
syn-central-transtentorial-herniation.presentation: A patient with diffuse brain swelling or a midline mass becomes progressively less responsive without a dilating pupil. First they are drowsy with small reactive pupils, sighs and yawns, and their arms flex when a painful stimulus is applied; then they breathe in a crescendo-decrescendo rhythm, the pupils become mid-sized and fixed, the eyes stop moving with the head, and the limbs extend; finally breathing becomes rapid then irregular, the pupils dilate, and the limbs are flaccid.

deficits.sign: Progressive decline from drowsiness to coma as the reticular activating system is compressed level by level
Small reactive (diencephalic stage), then mid-position fixed (midbrain), then dilated (terminal)
Decorticate (flexor) posturing at the diencephalic stage, decerebrate (extensor) posturing at the midbrain-pontine stage, flaccidity at the medullary stage
Loss of oculocephalic and caloric responses as the pons is involved
Cheyne–Stokes then central hyperventilation, ataxic breathing and apnea

syn-central-transtentorial-herniation.reasoning: A diffuse increase in the volume of both hemispheres, or a midline mass, pushes the diencephalon and the upper brainstem downward through the tentorial notch, and the signs appear in rostrocaudal order as each level is compressed and its perforating arteries are stretched. At the diencephalic stage the thalamus and hypothalamus are compressed, consciousness fades, the pupils are small because the descending sympathetic pathway from the hypothalamus is interrupted while the midbrain parasympathetic outflow is intact, and the limbs adopt the decorticate posture, with the arms flexed by the rubrospinal and other brainstem flexor pathways that are still connected below the red nucleus while cortical control is lost. At the midbrain stage the third nerve nuclei and the pretectal light reflex pathways fail, so the pupils become mid-sized and fixed, the vertical gaze pathways are lost, and because the red nucleus and its rubrospinal tract are now disconnected, only the pontine vestibulospinal and reticulospinal extensor drives reach the cord, producing decerebrate extension. At the pontine stage the horizontal gaze centers and the vestibulo-ocular arcs are destroyed, so the eyes no longer move with head turning or caloric stimulation, breathing becomes rapid and regular, and at the medullary stage the respiratory centers fail and the limbs are flaccid. The Duret hemorrhages produced by shearing of the basilar perforators during descent make the pontine stage irreversible. Because the herniation is midline and symmetric, there is no lateralizing pupil and no ipsilateral or contralateral pattern to read, which is the clinical difference from uncal herniation.

imagingFindings.finding: Effacement of the suprasellar, perimesencephalic and quadrigeminal cisterns, downward displacement of the pineal calcification, obliteration of the basal cisterns, compressed ventricles.

syn-central-vs-peripheral-vertigo.name: Central versus peripheral vertigo
syn-central-vs-peripheral-vertigo.presentation: A patient arrives with acute vertigo, vomiting and nystagmus. The question is whether the labyrinth or the brainstem is at fault, and three bedside tests answer it better than an early scan: the head impulse test, the direction of nystagmus on gaze to each side, and the cover test for skew deviation. A peripheral lesion gives an abnormal head impulse, unidirectional nystagmus and no skew; any one of a normal head impulse, direction-changing nystagmus or skew deviation means the lesion is central.

deficits.sign: Abnormal head impulse toward the lesion, unidirectional horizontal-torsional nystagmus suppressed by fixation, hearing may be affected
Normal head impulse, gaze-evoked direction-changing or vertical nystagmus not suppressed by fixation, skew deviation
Central: cannot stand unaided; peripheral: veers but stands
Diplopia, dysarthria, dysphagia, facial numbness, Horner or limb ataxia

syn-central-vs-peripheral-vertigo.reasoning: The vestibulo-ocular reflex is a three-neuron arc from the semicircular canals through the vestibular nuclei to the ocular motor nuclei, and its speed and gain depend on the peripheral input. When one labyrinth or nerve fails, the reflex cannot follow a rapid head turn toward that side and the patient makes a corrective saccade, so a positive head impulse test proves the periphery is at fault; central lesions leave the reflex intact, so a normal head impulse in a patient with continuous vertigo means the imbalance arises in the vestibular nuclei, the cerebellar flocculus or their connections, and the commonest such lesion is a posterior circulation stroke. The direction of peripheral nystagmus is fixed by the side of the dead labyrinth and stays the same in all gaze positions, whereas cerebellar and brainstem lesions impair gaze-holding so the fast phase reverses when the patient looks the other way, and fixation, which uses cerebellar pathways, suppresses only peripheral nystagmus. Vertical (downbeat, upbeat) or purely torsional nystagmus arises from the vertical canal pathways in the MLF and cerebellum and is always central. Skew deviation, a vertical misalignment of the eyes with head tilt, results from an imbalance of the otolith pathways after they have crossed in the brainstem and is a central sign. The crossed sensory loss, Horner, dysphagia or limb ataxia of a lateral medullary or cerebellar infarct confirm the localization. Hearing loss, in contrast, favors a peripheral cause, because the cochlear and vestibular labyrinths share the labyrinthine artery and the eighth nerve, with the important exception of AICA territory infarction.

imagingFindings.finding: Restricted diffusion in the lateral medulla, inferior cerebellum or peduncles; early DWI misses up to a fifth of small brainstem infarcts, so repeat if the examination is central.
imagingFindings.pitfalls: CT is nearly useless for acute posterior fossa ischemia

syn-cerebellar-hemispheric.name: Cerebellar hemisphere syndrome
syn-cerebellar-hemispheric.presentation: The patient's arm and leg on one side are clumsy: the finger overshoots the target and wobbles as it approaches, rapid alternating movements are irregular, the heel slides off the shin, and the outstretched arm rebounds when released. Speech is slurred and scanning, the eyes show nystagmus that is coarser on looking toward the affected side, and the gait veers toward that side. Strength and sensation are normal and reflexes are pendular.

deficits.sign: Dysmetria, intention tremor, dysdiadochokinesia, rebound, hypotonia
Scanning, slurred dysarthria
Gaze-evoked nystagmus, coarser toward the lesion; saccadic dysmetria
Veering and falling toward the side of the lesion

syn-cerebellar-hemispheric.reasoning: Each cerebellar hemisphere coordinates the limbs of its own side, a consequence of double crossing: its output through the dentate nucleus and superior cerebellar peduncle decussates in the midbrain to reach the contralateral thalamus and motor cortex, and the motor cortex then acts on the body through the corticospinal tract, which crosses back in the medulla. Signs of a hemispheric lesion are therefore ipsilateral, and any 'crossed' cerebellar sign means the lesion has moved above the decussation into the midbrain, thalamus or cortex. The lateral hemisphere and dentate plan and time skilled multi-joint movements, so their loss produces dysmetria, intention tremor and the decomposition of movement, while hypotonia and pendular reflexes reflect the loss of cerebellar facilitation of the motor cortex and gamma motor neurons. The cerebellum does not initiate movement or carry sensation, so power, reflex grading and sensation are normal and the deficit is one of accuracy. Nystagmus and the slow saccades reflect involvement of the flocculus and vermis or the outflow to the ocular motor nuclei. Acute unilateral causes are vascular; chronic unilateral causes are tumors, abscess and demyelination.

imagingFindings.finding: Restricted diffusion in the PICA, AICA or SCA territory of the hemisphere; watch for swelling.

syn-cerebellar-vermian-midline.name: Midline (vermian) cerebellar syndrome
syn-cerebellar-vermian-midline.presentation: The patient cannot stand or walk without a wide base and falls in any direction, yet when lying in bed the finger-nose and heel-shin tests are almost normal. A child with a midline tumor presents with morning headache, vomiting and a stumbling gait; an alcoholic with anterior vermian degeneration presents with a gait ataxia that has developed over years while the arms remain coordinated. Head titubation and truncal sway when sitting are common.

syn-cerebellar-vermian-midline.reasoning: The vermis and the flocculonodular lobe receive spinocerebellar and vestibular input that is uncrossed and bilateral, and send their output through the fastigial nuclei to the vestibular and reticular nuclei of both sides, which drive the vestibulospinal and reticulospinal tracts that keep the trunk upright. A midline lesion therefore produces a symmetric disorder of balance and gait without lateralization, and because the lateral hemispheres and dentate nuclei that coordinate the limbs are spared, the limbs test surprisingly well when the trunk is supported: this dissociation between severe truncal ataxia and mild limb ataxia is the signature of a vermian lesion. There is no ipsilateral or contralateral rule to apply, because the affected structures are midline and project bilaterally. The nodulus and flocculus calibrate the vestibulo-ocular reflex and hold gaze, so their involvement produces positional nystagmus and vertigo that mimic a peripheral vestibular disorder, and the vermis lies over the fourth ventricle, so midline tumors in children obstruct CSF flow early. The anterior vermis degenerates selectively in chronic alcohol exposure, producing a leg-and-gait syndrome with spared arms.

syn-cerebellopontine-angle.name: Cerebellopontine angle syndrome
syn-cerebellopontine-angle.presentation: Hearing in one ear has been fading for two years with tinnitus, and the patient now notices imbalance rather than spinning vertigo. Later the cheek becomes numb and the corneal reflex on that side is lost; eventually there is facial weakness, ataxia of the arm and leg on the same side, and, with large tumors, headache and papilledema. The sequence eighth, fifth, seventh nerves and then cerebellum tells the story of a slowly growing mass at the angle.

deficits.sign: Progressive sensorineural hearing loss with poor speech discrimination and tinnitus
Imbalance more than vertigo; canal paresis on caloric testing
Facial numbness with a depressed corneal reflex
Late lower motor neuron facial weakness (the nerve is surprisingly resistant)
Ataxia from compression of the cerebellar hemisphere and middle peduncle
Headache, papilledema, hydrocephalus with large tumors

syn-cerebellopontine-angle.reasoning: The cerebellopontine angle is the wedge of cistern between the pons, the middle cerebellar peduncle and the petrous bone, containing the seventh and eighth nerves on their way to the internal acoustic meatus, with the trigeminal root above and the ninth, tenth and eleventh nerves below. All of these are uncrossed peripheral nerves, so every sign is on the side of the mass. A vestibular schwannoma starts in the meatus on the superior vestibular nerve and compresses the cochlear nerve first, so the earliest symptom is unilateral retrocochlear hearing loss in which speech discrimination is worse than the pure-tone threshold predicts, and because the vestibular loss is gradual the brain compensates and the patient feels unsteady rather than vertiginous. As the tumor grows into the angle it stretches the trigeminal root, dulling the corneal reflex and facial sensation, then flattens the facial nerve, which tolerates stretching remarkably well, and finally indents the cerebellar hemisphere and peduncle, producing ipsilateral ataxia (cerebellar signs are ipsilateral because of the double crossing of cerebellar output and corticospinal fibers). Very large tumors displace the brainstem and obstruct the fourth ventricle. Bilateral tumors define neurofibromatosis type 2.

imagingFindings.finding: Avidly enhancing mass centered on the internal acoustic meatus with an 'ice-cream cone' extension into the angle, widening the porus acusticus; small intracanalicular tumors need thin post-contrast or CISS images.

Lobulated non-enhancing mass insinuating around nerves, bright on DWI (distinguishes it from an arachnoid cyst).

imagingHint.label: cerebellopontine angle at the internal acoustic meatus

mimics.name: Presbycusis

mimics.name: Bell palsy
mimics.howToDistinguish: Sudden, complete facial palsy without deafness

management: Any asymmetric sensorineural hearing loss: MRI of the internal acoustic meatus with contrast
Options: observation with serial MRI, stereotactic radiosurgery, or microsurgical resection depending on size, hearing and age

syn-cerebral-venous-sinus-thrombosis.name: Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis
syn-cerebral-venous-sinus-thrombosis.presentation: A woman in the postpartum period, or on the combined contraceptive pill, develops a headache that builds over days and is worse lying flat, then has a focal seizure and weakness of one leg, and the fundi show swollen discs. CT shows a hemorrhagic lesion that does not fit an arterial territory, near the vertex; CT venography shows a filling defect in the superior sagittal sinus. Deep venous thrombosis produces bilateral thalamic swelling and coma; cavernous sinus thrombosis a painful ophthalmoplegia with proptosis.

deficits.sign: Subacute progressive headache, worse lying down, with papilledema (raised pressure)

syn-cerebral-venous-sinus-thrombosis.reasoning: The dural venous sinuses drain the cerebral veins to the internal jugular veins: the superior sagittal sinus collects the superficial veins from the convexities, the great cerebral vein and straight sinus drain the deep structures, and the transverse and sigmoid sinuses carry both to the jugular bulb. Thrombosis of a sinus obstructs venous outflow from the region it drains without interrupting arterial inflow, so blood continues to arrive but cannot leave; capillary pressure rises, fluid leaks into the tissue, and the swollen, congested cortex is prone to seizures and to hemorrhage into the edematous tissue. These venous infarcts do not respect arterial territories, are often bilateral or parasagittal when the superior sagittal sinus is involved, since the veins of both leg areas drain into it, and can be hemorrhagic from the start. Because the superior sagittal sinus drains both hemispheres, deficits are often bilateral, and when unilateral they are contralateral to the congested cortex, since the corticospinal fibers cross in the medulla. The clinical clue is a headache that has progressed over days in a patient with a prothrombotic state, and the diagnosis is made by imaging the veins, not the arteries.

imagingFindings.finding: Absent flow in the superior sagittal, transverse or sigmoid sinus on MR or CT venography; the 'empty delta' sign on contrast CT; a hyperdense sinus or cortical vein (cord sign) on plain CT.

T1-bright subacute clot within the sinus and a blooming cortical vein on SWI.

imagingHint.label: superior sagittal sinus at the vertex

commonCauses: Local infection (otitis, mastoiditis, sinusitis) for lateral and cavernous sinuses
Head injury, lumbar puncture, dural puncture

mimics.name: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension
mimics.howToDistinguish: Normal venography; no seizures or focal deficits

mimics.name: Arterial stroke
mimics.howToDistinguish: Abrupt onset, territorial infarct on DWI, no venous filling defect

mimics.name: Meningitis or encephalitis
mimics.howToDistinguish: Fever, CSF pleocytosis; may coexist

syn-cervical-spondylotic-myelopathy.name: Cervical spondylotic myelopathy
syn-cervical-spondylotic-myelopathy.presentation: An older patient reports that their hands have become clumsy, buttons are difficult and writing has deteriorated, while their family notices a stiff, unsteady gait. Examination shows wasting of the intrinsic hand muscles with absent or inverted reflexes at one cervical level, brisk reflexes below it with clonus, extensor plantars, a positive Hoffmann sign and reduced vibration sense in the feet; neck movement may be limited and painful.

deficits.sign: Lower motor neuron weakness and wasting of the hands with reduced reflexes at the compressed segments
Spastic paraparesis with hyperreflexia, clonus, Hoffmann sign and extensor plantars
Reduced vibration and position sense, sensory ataxia, Lhermitte sign
Spastic, broad-based gait; frequent falls
Urgency and frequency late

syn-cervical-spondylotic-myelopathy.reasoning: Degenerative disc bulging, osteophytes, facet hypertrophy and a thickened ligamentum flavum narrow the cervical canal, most often at C5–C6 and C6–C7, so that the cord is squeezed with every extension of the neck and its venous drainage and pial arteries are compromised. The compression damages the cord at the level of the stenosis and the long tracts passing through it. At the level, the anterior horn cells and the exiting roots are injured, producing lower motor neuron signs confined to those myotomes, typically wasting of the hand and forearm with loss of the corresponding reflex; the inverted supinator reflex, in which tapping the brachioradialis tendon produces finger flexion instead, shows a C5–C6 segmental lesion with hyperactive segments below. Below the level, the lateral corticospinal tracts, which crossed in the medulla and so serve the same side, are damaged bilaterally by the midline compression, giving spasticity and hyperreflexia in the legs, and the posterior columns, uncrossed until the medulla, give bilateral loss of vibration and proprioception. The spinothalamic tracts lie anterolaterally and are affected less. The combination of segmental lower motor neuron signs in the arms and upper motor neuron signs in the legs mimics motor neuron disease, but the sensory signs, the sphincter symptoms and the neck pain point to a compressive lesion.

imagingFindings.finding: Multilevel canal stenosis with cord flattening and intramedullary T2 hyperintensity at the most compressed level; T1 hypointensity implies irreversible change.

imagingFindings.pathology: Ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament
imagingFindings.finding: Calcified ligament behind the vertebral bodies narrowing the canal, common in East Asian patients.
Cord compression worsens in extension on flexion-extension imaging.

imagingHint.label: cervical cord at C5–C7

commonCauses: Ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament

mimics.name: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
mimics.howToDistinguish: No sensory signs, bulbar involvement, fasciculations widespread; EMG shows denervation in unaffected regions

mimics.name: Multiple sclerosis
mimics.howToDistinguish: Relapsing course, brain lesions, optic neuritis

mimics.name: Subacute combined degeneration
mimics.howToDistinguish: Low B12, no compression on MRI

mimics.name: Carpal tunnel and ulnar neuropathy
mimics.howToDistinguish: Hand symptoms in a nerve distribution without leg signs

management: MRI of the cervical spine; surgical decompression for progressive myelopathy or cord signal change
Avoid neck hyperextension and contact sports
Nerve conduction studies to exclude a coexisting peripheral entrapment

syn-chiari-tonsillar-ectopia.name: Chiari I malformation and tonsillar ectopia
syn-chiari-tonsillar-ectopia.presentation: A young adult has occipital headaches that are triggered by coughing, straining or laughing and last seconds to minutes. Over time they notice that their hands are numb to heat and they have burned themselves without pain, a cape-like loss from an associated syrinx. Examination may show downbeat nystagmus, a lower cranial nerve palsy, limb ataxia or spastic legs. Many cases are incidental findings on MRI.

deficits.sign: Cough-induced occipital headache (Valsalva-related)

deficits.distribution: cape distribution over arms and shoulders
deficits.sign: Dissociated loss from an associated cervical syrinx
Downbeat nystagmus from cervicomedullary compression
Dysphagia, hoarseness, sleep apnea from medullary compression

syn-chiari-tonsillar-ectopia.reasoning: In Chiari I malformation the cerebellar tonsils lie more than about five millimeters below the foramen magnum, crowding the cervicomedullary junction and obstructing the normal to-and-fro movement of CSF between the cranial and spinal compartments with each heartbeat and each Valsalva maneuver. The transient pressure difference across the foramen during coughing displaces the tonsils further and stretches the dura and lower cranial nerve roots, producing the characteristic short occipital headaches. The obstruction also drives CSF into the central canal of the cervical cord, producing syringomyelia in a substantial fraction of patients; the expanding cavity first destroys the fibers of the spinothalamic tract crossing in the anterior white commissure, which gives the bilateral dissociated loss of pain and temperature in the arms and shoulders with preserved touch and proprioception, before spreading to the anterior horns and lateral columns. Compression of the medulla and the lower cerebellum accounts for downbeat nystagmus, lower cranial nerve palsies and ataxia; because the compressed structures are midline, most signs are bilateral and there is no lateralizing rule. The malformation is often silent, and an incidental ectopia without a syrinx or symptoms needs only observation.

imagingFindings.finding: Peg-shaped cerebellar tonsils extending more than 5 mm below the basion–opisthion line on a sagittal T1 image, with crowding of the foramen magnum and effacement of the cisterna magna.

imagingHint.label: cerebellar tonsils at the foramen magnum

commonCauses: Raised intracranial pressure from a mass (acquired, an emergency)

mimics.howToDistinguish: Normal MRI

mimics.name: Tonsillar herniation from a mass
mimics.howToDistinguish: Acute, with drowsiness and a supratentorial or posterior fossa lesion

mimics.name: Intracranial hypotension
mimics.howToDistinguish: Orthostatic headache with dural enhancement and slumping of the brainstem

Posterior fossa decompression for symptomatic patients or a progressive syrinx
Do not perform a lumbar puncture when the tonsils are low without considering the risk of further descent

syn-chiasmal-bitemporal.name: Chiasmal syndrome (bitemporal hemianopia)
syn-chiasmal-bitemporal.presentation: The patient keeps bumping into door frames and has stopped driving because cars appear from nowhere on either side, yet reads normally. Field testing shows loss of the temporal half of the field in each eye, respecting the vertical meridian, worse in the upper quadrants. There may be amenorrhea, galactorrhea, acromegalic features or the fatigue of hypopituitarism, and a large adenoma is found on MRI. Sudden headache and visual loss with ophthalmoplegia mean pituitary apoplexy.

deficits.sign: Bitemporal hemianopia respecting the vertical midline, upper quadrants first with lesions from below
Acuity preserved unless the nerves are involved; junctional scotoma with anterior lesions
Hyperprolactinemia, acromegaly, Cushing features or hypopituitarism
Ocular motor palsies with lateral extension or apoplexy

syn-chiasmal-bitemporal.reasoning: At the optic chiasm the fibers from the nasal half of each retina, which see the temporal half of the visual field, cross to the opposite optic tract, while the temporal retinal fibers, which see the nasal field, stay on the same side. A lesion of the middle of the chiasm interrupts only the crossing fibers, so each eye loses its temporal field and nothing else: the bitemporal hemianopia is the one field defect that is neither monocular nor homonymous, and it identifies the chiasm with certainty. The chiasm sits about a centimeter above the pituitary fossa, so a pituitary adenoma growing upward through the diaphragma sellae presses on its lower surface first, where the fibers from the inferior nasal retina cross, which serve the upper temporal fields; the defect therefore begins in the superior quadrants and descends. A craniopharyngioma pressing from above does the reverse. The lower nasal fibers make a forward loop (Wilbrand's knee) into the opposite optic nerve, so a lesion at the junction of one nerve and the chiasm causes a central scotoma in that eye with an upper temporal defect in the other, the junctional scotoma. Patients often have normal acuity and pass reading tests, because the intact nasal fields overlap in the center, but the two hemifields no longer overlap for depth perception, so they misjudge distances and cannot fuse images beyond the fixation point.

imagingFindings.finding: Sellar mass with suprasellar extension elevating and flattening the chiasm; 'snowman' shape at the diaphragma; compare its signal with the normal gland.

imagingHint.label: optic chiasm above the pituitary fossa

commonCauses: Internal carotid or anterior communicating aneurysm

mimics.name: Bilateral optic neuropathy
mimics.howToDistinguish: Defects do not respect the vertical meridian; acuity and color reduced

mimics.name: Tilted discs or nasal retinal disease
mimics.howToDistinguish: Temporal defects that cross the vertical meridian; fundus abnormal

mimics.name: Bilateral homonymous defects
mimics.howToDistinguish: Respect the vertical meridian but are homonymous, not bitemporal

syn-claude.name: Claude syndrome (dorsal midbrain tegmentum)
syn-claude.presentation: A patient develops a third nerve palsy on one side and, on the opposite side, an ataxic arm and leg with dysmetria and an intention tremor, without weakness. The combination of an ipsilateral oculomotor palsy and contralateral cerebellar signs places the lesion in the midbrain tegmentum, where the third nerve fascicles cross the superior cerebellar peduncle decussation and the red nucleus.

deficits.sign: Third nerve palsy, often with pupil involvement
Limb ataxia, dysmetria and intention tremor
No significant weakness (crus cerebri spared)

syn-claude.reasoning: The dentate nucleus sends its output through the superior cerebellar peduncle, which decussates in the caudal midbrain and then ends in or passes through the red nucleus of the opposite side on its way to the thalamus. A lesion of the paramedian midbrain tegmentum at the level of the red nucleus therefore interrupts cerebellar outflow that has already crossed, and since that outflow, after relaying in the thalamus and motor cortex, would have crossed again through the corticospinal tract to reach the limbs on the side of the original cerebellar hemisphere, the ataxia appears on the side opposite the midbrain lesion. The oculomotor fascicles run through the same region on their way from the nucleus to the interpeduncular fossa and are lost on the side of the lesion, since the nerve is the final ipsilateral motor pathway. The crus cerebri lies ventral to the lesion and is spared, so there is no hemiplegia, which separates Claude from Weber; involvement of the red nucleus itself with rubral tremor and some weakness makes it Benedikt. The supplying vessels are the paramedian perforators from the top of the basilar and the proximal posterior cerebral artery.

imagingFindings.finding: Small area of restricted diffusion in the paramedian midbrain tegmentum at the level of the red nucleus.

mimics.howToDistinguish: Ataxia would be ipsilateral to the cerebellar lesion

syn-cn3-palsy.name: Oculomotor nerve palsy: pupil-involving versus pupil-sparing
syn-cn3-palsy.presentation: A patient presents with a drooping eyelid; when it is lifted, the eye is turned down and out and cannot look up, down or in, and the patient sees double. In one version the pupil on that side is large and does not react to light and the patient has a severe headache: this is an aneurysm until proven otherwise. In the other version, in a diabetic or hypertensive patient with periorbital ache, the pupil is normal and the palsy resolves in weeks.

deficits.distribution: medial, superior, inferior rectus and inferior oblique
deficits.sign: Eye down and out with loss of adduction, elevation and depression; diplopia
Complete ptosis
Fixed dilated pupil (compressive) or spared pupil (ischemic)

syn-cn3-palsy.reasoning: The oculomotor nerve is the final, uncrossed motor pathway to four extraocular muscles, the levator and the pupillary sphincter, so all signs are on the side of the nerve. The parasympathetic pupillary fibers travel on the surface of the nerve, superomedially, immediately beneath the posterior communicating artery as the nerve passes forward from the interpeduncular fossa toward the cavernous sinus; an enlarging aneurysm at the junction of the internal carotid and posterior communicating arteries, an expanding uncus during herniation, or a tumor presses on these outer fibers first, so the pupil dilates early and sometimes before the muscles are affected. The vasa nervorum that fail in diabetes and hypertension supply the core of the nerve, where the somatic motor fibers run, while the surface pupillary fibers are nourished by the surrounding CSF and pial vessels and survive, hence a complete external palsy with a normal pupil. The rule is not absolute: partial or early compression can spare the pupil for a time, and ischemia occasionally involves it slightly, so a pupil-sparing but incomplete palsy, or a spared pupil that later dilates, still requires imaging of the posterior communicating artery. html.presentation: A patient presents with a drooping eyelid; when it is lifted, the eye is turned down and out and cannot look up, down or in, and the patient sees double. In one version the pupil on that side is large and does not react to light and the patient has a severe headache: this is an aneurysm until proven otherwise. syn-cn4-palsy.name: Trochlear nerve palsy
syn-cn4-palsy.presentation: After a minor head injury, or with no history at all, a patient complains of vertical double vision that is worst reading or going down stairs, and tilts the head away from the affected eye to fuse the images. The affected eye sits slightly higher, the hypertropia increases when they look toward the nose and when the head is tilted toward the affected shoulder. Old photographs may show that the head tilt has been present for years.

deficits.sign: Hypertropia worse on contralateral gaze and ipsilateral head tilt (three-step test); excyclotorsion
Compensatory head tilt away from the affected eye, chin down
Vertical diplopia worst in downgaze and reading

syn-cn4-palsy.reasoning: The trochlear nucleus lies in the caudal midbrain at the level of the inferior colliculus, and its axons run dorsally, cross in the superior medullary velum and exit from the dorsal surface of the brainstem, the only cranial nerve to do either; the nerve then supplies the contralateral superior oblique after its long course around the midbrain and through the cavernous sinus. A nuclear or fascicular lesion in the midbrain therefore paralyzes the superior oblique of the opposite eye, whereas a lesion of the nerve after it has crossed, which is the usual situation, paralyzes the eye on the same side. The superior oblique depresses the adducted eye and intorts it, so its loss leaves the eye slightly elevated and extorted, with the diplopia greatest in downgaze and adduction, and the patient tilts the head toward the opposite shoulder to intort the eye by using the intact muscles; tilting toward the affected side calls on the paralyzed muscle and increases the deviation, the basis of the Bielschowsky head tilt test. The thin nerve is vulnerable to shearing at the tentorial edge in closed head injury, and bilateral palsies after trauma are common because both nerves cross in the same small velum. Decompensation of a congenital palsy, recognized by a large vertical fusional range and a lifelong head tilt, is the other common presentation.

imagingFindings.finding: Imaging is usually normal; look at the dorsal midbrain and the tentorial edge for contusion or hemorrhage.
Lesion at the level of the inferior colliculus producing a contralateral palsy, sometimes with a Horner on the side of the lesion.

imagingHint.label: dorsal midbrain at the inferior colliculus where the nerves cross

commonCauses: Congenital palsy decompensating in adult life
Microvascular ischemia in diabetes and hypertension

mimics.name: Skew deviation
mimics.howToDistinguish: Vertical misalignment with intorsion of the higher eye and central signs; head tilt test negative or reversed

mimics.name: Ocular myasthenia
mimics.howToDistinguish: Variable and fatigable

mimics.name: Thyroid eye disease (inferior rectus restriction)
mimics.howToDistinguish: Hypotropia of the affected eye, restricted elevation, proptosis

management: Three-step test to confirm; check old photographs for a long-standing head tilt
Observe microvascular and traumatic palsies for spontaneous recovery over months; prisms meanwhile
Strabismus surgery for persistent decompensated palsies

syn-cn6-palsy.name: Abducens nerve palsy and its false-localizing value
syn-cn6-palsy.presentation: A patient develops horizontal double vision that is worse when looking to one side and at distance, and turns the head toward that side to avoid it. The affected eye cannot abduct past the midline, or does so incompletely, while all other movements are normal. In one patient the cause is a diabetic microvascular lesion that recovers; in another, headache and papilledema reveal raised intracranial pressure from a tumor nowhere near the pons.

deficits.sign: Abduction deficit with esotropia greatest on gaze to the affected side and at distance
Head turned toward the affected side
Headache, papilledema, sometimes bilateral palsies

syn-cn6-palsy.reasoning: The abducens nerve leaves the pontomedullary junction and runs the longest intracranial course of any cranial nerve, ascending the clivus in the subarachnoid space, bending sharply over the petrous apex beneath the petroclinoid ligament to enter Dorello's canal, and running through the body of the cavernous sinus to the lateral rectus. It is uncrossed, so an abduction deficit is on the side of the nerve. That long vertical course and the sharp bend at the petrous ridge make it the nerve most vulnerable to any process that shifts the brainstem downward or raises intracranial pressure, so a sixth nerve palsy, especially if bilateral, is a classic false-localizing sign that must not be taken to mean pontine disease. A nuclear lesion is recognized because the nucleus also contains the interneurons for the contralateral medial rectus, so nuclear damage causes a conjugate gaze palsy rather than an isolated abduction deficit, usually with an ipsilateral facial palsy from the overlying facial genu. In the cavernous sinus the nerve lies medially beside the carotid artery with the oculosympathetic fibers briefly attached, so a sixth nerve palsy with an ipsilateral Horner syndrome points to the sinus; at the petrous apex it is accompanied by facial pain and deafness in Gradenigo syndrome.

imagingFindings.finding: Papilledema correlates: distended optic nerve sheaths, flattened posterior globes, partially empty sella; mass, venous thrombosis or IIH as the cause.
Enhancing chordoma, meningioma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma or cavernous sinus mass along the nerve's course.
Demyelination or infarct at the facial colliculus giving a gaze palsy rather than an isolated palsy.

imagingHint.label: abducens nerve rising from the pontomedullary junction along the clivus

commonCauses: Raised intracranial pressure of any cause
Clival tumor, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, cavernous sinus disease

mimics.name: Thyroid eye disease (medial rectus restriction)
mimics.howToDistinguish: Abduction limited by a tight medial rectus; forced duction positive; proptosis

mimics.name: Ocular myasthenia
mimics.howToDistinguish: Variable, fatigable, normal pupils

mimics.name: Duane syndrome
mimics.howToDistinguish: Congenital; globe retraction and narrowing of the fissure on adduction

mimics.name: Convergence spasm
mimics.howToDistinguish: Miosis on attempted lateral gaze; functional

syn-complete-transection-spinal-shock.name: Complete cord transection and spinal shock
syn-complete-transection-spinal-shock.presentation: After a fall or a road accident the patient cannot move or feel anything below the level of the injury. For the first days to weeks the legs are flaccid, all reflexes below the level are absent, the bladder is distended and painless, the bowel is silent and, in cervical injuries, the blood pressure is low with a slow pulse and the skin warm. Then the reflexes return and become exaggerated, the legs stiffen and flex in spasms, and the bladder empties reflexly and unpredictably.

deficits.sign: Complete paralysis: flaccid in spinal shock, then spastic with clonus and flexor spasms
Complete sensory loss with a sharp level; a band of hyperesthesia just above
Areflexia in spinal shock; later hyperreflexia, extensor plantars, mass reflex
Retention with overflow, then reflex (spastic) bladder in lesions above the conus
Neurogenic shock (hypotension, bradycardia) acutely; autonomic dysreflexia later

syn-complete-transection-spinal-shock.reasoning: Complete transection interrupts every ascending and descending tract at one level, so all sensation from below, whichever side it crossed on, and all motor commands to below, whichever side they came from, are lost bilaterally with a sharp sensory level that marks the segment. The level of the sensory loss on the trunk gives the segment, and the last working muscle group gives the motor level; a cervical lesion produces quadriplegia, a thoracic lesion paraplegia. Spinal shock is the temporary loss of all reflex activity in the isolated cord below the lesion, attributed to the sudden withdrawal of the tonic facilitation that descending reticulospinal and vestibulospinal pathways normally supply to spinal motor neurons and interneurons; without it the stretch reflex arcs, though anatomically intact, are silent, the bladder wall is atonic and, when the lesion lies above the sympathetic outflow at T1–T6, the loss of descending sympathetic drive causes vasodilatation and unopposed vagal bradycardia. Over days to weeks the isolated segments regain and then exceed their excitability through receptor upregulation and sprouting, producing spasticity, hyperreflexia, the mass reflex in which a small stimulus triggers flexor spasms, sweating and bladder emptying, and autonomic dysreflexia, in which a distended bladder or bowel below a high lesion provokes uncontrolled sympathetic discharge and severe hypertension because the cord's sympathetic neurons have no descending brake. Priapism and the bulbocavernosus reflex return early and their recovery marks the end of spinal shock.

imagingFindings.finding: Cord discontinuity or extensive T2 hyperintensity with hemorrhage (T2* dark) at the fracture level; hematoma length predicts outcome.
Burst fracture, facet dislocation or translation narrowing the canal; CT of the whole spine for other levels.
Epidural abscess, metastasis or transverse myelitis producing the same complete syndrome over hours to days.

imagingHint.label: cervicothoracic cord

mimics.name: Incomplete cord syndromes
mimics.howToDistinguish: Some function preserved below the level, sacral sparing

mimics.name: Guillain–Barré syndrome
mimics.howToDistinguish: No sensory level, ascending, cranial nerves involved, CSF protein raised

mimics.name: Functional paralysis
mimics.howToDistinguish: Inconsistent findings, normal reflexes and imaging

management: Immobilize, maintain mean arterial pressure and oxygenation, and obtain CT and MRI urgently; early surgical decompression and stabilization
Catheterize the bladder, prevent pressure sores and thromboembolism, protect the airway in cervical lesions
Recognize and treat autonomic dysreflexia (sit the patient up, empty the bladder or bowel)

syn-conus-vs-cauda-equina.name: Conus medullaris versus cauda equina syndrome
syn-conus-vs-cauda-equina.presentation: A patient with a large central lumbar disc prolapse has severe back and leg pain, numbness of the buttocks and perineum, weakness of both legs and cannot pass urine. In cauda equina syndrome the pain is severe and asymmetric, the weakness is flaccid and asymmetric with absent ankle reflexes, and the bladder is affected late; in a conus lesion the onset is sudden, saddle anesthesia and sphincter loss are early and symmetric, pain is mild, and the knee reflexes may be brisk. Both are emergencies.

deficits.sign: Saddle anesthesia: symmetric and early in conus lesions, asymmetric and later in cauda equina
Painless retention with overflow, fecal incontinence, impotence; early in conus, late in cauda equina
Conus: mild symmetric weakness, brisk knees possible; cauda: marked asymmetric flaccid weakness with areflexia
Severe radicular pain in cauda equina; mild or absent in conus
Absent anal and bulbocavernosus reflexes in both

syn-conus-vs-cauda-equina.reasoning: The spinal cord ends at the conus medullaris opposite L1–L2, and below that the lumbar and sacral roots hang as the cauda equina in the lumbar cistern. The conus contains the sacral segments S2–S5: the parasympathetic neurons for the bladder and rectum, the motor neurons for the sphincters and the sensory relay for the perineum, all packed into a centimeter or two of cord, so a lesion of the conus is symmetric and hits the sacral functions first and hardest, giving early saddle anesthesia and sphincter failure with little leg weakness, while the lumbar roots that have already left the cord above may be spared; if the lesion extends upward into the lumbar segments or spares the sacral roots that pass beside it, upper motor neuron signs such as brisk knee jerks can coexist. The cauda equina, by contrast, is a bundle of peripheral nerve roots, so its compression produces a lower motor neuron and radicular picture: severe pain in the distribution of the compressed roots, asymmetric flaccid weakness and areflexia, dermatomal sensory loss that becomes a saddle distribution as the lower sacral roots at the center of the bundle are engulfed, and sphincter loss that appears later because the sacral roots are the smallest and most central. Neither has a crossed component: both are bilateral because the structures involved lie in the midline of the canal. The distinction matters less than the recognition, since both require MRI within hours and decompression before the sphincters are permanently lost.

imagingFindings.finding: Large central disc extrusion, tumor or abscess filling the lumbar canal and compressing the roots; sagittal and axial T2 of the lumbar spine.
Intramedullary tumor (ependymoma), infarct, demyelination or metastasis at T12–L1 with signal change in the conus; contrast needed.
Bladder ultrasound showing retention above 200 mL supports the diagnosis and monitors recovery.

imagingHint.label: conus medullaris at T12–L1

commonCauses: Spinal stenosis, trauma, epidural abscess or hematoma
Metastasis or primary tumor (cauda: schwannoma, myxopapillary ependymoma; conus: ependymoma, metastasis)

mimics.name: Bilateral lumbosacral radiculopathy without sacral involvement
mimics.howToDistinguish: No saddle anesthesia or sphincter change

mimics.name: Lumbosacral plexopathy
mimics.howToDistinguish: Unilateral, sphincters spared

mimics.name: Cervical or thoracic myelopathy
mimics.howToDistinguish: Sensory level higher, spasticity dominant

management: Rectal examination, perineal sensation and a bladder scan in every patient with back pain and sphincter symptoms; emergency MRI of the whole spine
Surgical decompression as soon as possible, ideally within 24–48 hours of sphincter involvement
Catheterization and bowel management; MRI of the whole neuraxis for intramedullary lesions

syn-cubital-tunnel.name: Ulnar neuropathy at the elbow
syn-cubital-tunnel.presentation: A patient who leans on the elbow at a desk, or who had an elbow fracture years ago, has numbness of the little finger and the ulnar half of the ring finger on both the palmar and dorsal surfaces, weakness of finger spreading, and a hand that is wasted between the thumb and index finger. The ring and little fingers curl into a claw; when pinching a sheet of paper the thumb flexes at its tip (Froment sign). Tapping behind the medial epicondyle sends tingling into the little finger.

deficits.distribution: little finger, ulnar half of the ring finger, dorsal and palmar ulnar hand
deficits.sign: Sensory loss in the ulnar territory including the dorsum of the hand; forearm spared

deficits.distribution: interossei, hypothenar, adductor pollicis, medial lumbricals, flexor digitorum profundus to the ring and little fingers
deficits.sign: Weak finger abduction and adduction, wasting of the first dorsal interosseous, Froment sign, ulnar claw of the ring and little fingers, Wartenberg sign
Aching at the elbow with Tinel sign in the ulnar groove

syn-cubital-tunnel.reasoning: The ulnar nerve passes behind the medial epicondyle in the ulnar groove and then beneath the aponeurosis between the two heads of the flexor carpi ulnaris (the cubital tunnel), where it is superficial, tethered and stretched by elbow flexion and compressed by leaning; a previous fracture, arthritis or a shallow groove that lets the nerve dislocate adds to the injury. All the ulnar-innervated muscles lie distal to the elbow, so an elbow lesion weakens the flexor carpi ulnaris and the ulnar half of the flexor digitorum profundus as well as the hand intrinsics, whereas a lesion at the wrist (Guyon's canal) spares the forearm muscles and, depending on the site, the sensory branches. The dorsal cutaneous branch leaves the nerve several centimeters above the wrist, so dorsal ulnar hand sensation is lost with an elbow lesion but spared with a wrist lesion, and the medial forearm, supplied by the medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve from the plexus, is spared with any ulnar lesion, which distinguishes it from a C8 root or lower trunk lesion. The claw posture is produced by paralysis of the medial two lumbricals and interossei, which normally flex the knuckles and extend the fingers, and it is paradoxically less severe in high lesions because the paralyzed profundus no longer flexes the fingertips (the ulnar paradox). Froment sign reflects substitution of the median flexor pollicis longus for the paralyzed adductor pollicis. The lesion is peripheral and ipsilateral; conduction slowing or block across the elbow confirms the site.

imagingFindings.finding: Slowing of ulnar motor conduction or conduction block across the elbow segment with normal forearm and wrist conduction; denervation in the first dorsal interosseous and flexor carpi ulnaris; dorsal ulnar cutaneous response reduced.
Swollen hypoechoic ulnar nerve in the groove or beneath the cubital tunnel aponeurosis, with subluxation on flexion in some.
Old fracture, arthritis, ganglion or accessory anconeus compressing the nerve.

commonCauses: Leaning on the elbow, prolonged flexion (habitual, occupational, perioperative)

syn-dejerine-medial-medullary.name: Medial medullary syndrome (Dejerine)
syn-dejerine-medial-medullary.presentation: A patient develops weakness of one arm and leg with the face spared, loses vibration and position sense on the same weak side, and on protruding the tongue it deviates to the other side, the side opposite the weakness. Pain and temperature sensation are normal. This contralateral limb weakness with ipsilateral tongue palsy is one of the classic crossed brainstem syndromes.

deficits.sign: Hemiparesis with upper motor neuron signs (pyramid)
Loss of vibration and position sense (medial lemniscus)
Lower motor neuron tongue weakness: deviation toward the lesion, later atrophy and fasciculation
Pain and temperature intact (spinothalamic tract lies laterally)

syn-dejerine-medial-medullary.reasoning: The paramedian medulla is fed by the anterior spinal artery and paramedian vertebral branches and contains three structures in a vertical row: the pyramid ventrally, the medial lemniscus behind it, and the hypoglossal nucleus and nerve dorsally. The pyramid carries corticospinal fibers that have not yet crossed, because the pyramidal decussation lies just below, so the weakness is contralateral and spares the face, whose corticobulbar fibers have already left the tract above this level. The medial lemniscus, formed by the internal arcuate fibers that crossed at the sensory decussation, carries contralateral vibration and proprioception, so those modalities are lost on the same side as the weakness. The hypoglossal nucleus and its emerging root are ipsilateral structures, so the tongue is paralyzed on the side of the lesion and pushes toward it when protruded, because the intact genioglossus pushes across. The spinothalamic tract lies far laterally, out of the anterior spinal territory, which is why pain and temperature are preserved and why the picture is the mirror image of the lateral medullary syndrome.

imagingFindings.finding: Restricted diffusion in the paramedian ventral medulla, sometimes bilateral, adjacent to the anterior median fissure.
Vertebral artery stenosis, occlusion or dissection on the side of the tongue palsy.

imagingHint.label: paramedian medulla: pyramid, medial lemniscus, hypoglossal nucleus

html.reasoning: The paramedian medulla is fed by the anterior spinal artery and paramedian vertebral branches and contains three structures in a vertical row: the pyramid ventrally, the medial lemniscus behind it, and the hypoglossal nucleus and nerve dorsally. The pyramid carries corticospinal fibers that have not yet crossed, because the pyramidal decussation lies just below, so the weakness is contralateral and spares the face, whose corticobulbar fibers have already left the tract above this level. The medial lemniscus, formed by the internal arcuate fibers that crossed at the sensory decussation, carries contralateral vibration and proprioception, so those modalities are lost on the same side as the weakness. syn-epidural-hematoma.name: Epidural (extradural) hematoma
syn-epidural-hematoma.presentation: A young man is knocked out briefly in a fall, wakes and talks normally, then over the next few hours develops a worsening headache, vomits, becomes drowsy and is found with a dilated pupil on the side of the injury and weakness of the opposite limbs. The skull X-ray or CT shows a fracture of the temporal bone crossing the groove of the middle meningeal artery, and beneath it a lens-shaped clot pressing the brain inward.

deficits.sign: Initial concussion, lucid interval, then progressive deterioration to coma as the clot expands
Dilated fixed pupil from uncal herniation
Hemiparesis from compression of the hemisphere and the cerebral peduncle
Severe headache and vomiting

syn-epidural-hematoma.reasoning: The dura mater is the periosteum of the inner table of the skull, and the middle meningeal artery runs in a groove on the inner surface of the thin squamous temporal bone between the bone and the dura. A blow to the temple fractures the bone across the groove and tears the artery, and arterial blood at systemic pressure strips the dura from the skull, accumulating in the potential space between them. Because the dura is firmly attached at the sutures, the clot cannot spread across them and instead grows inward as a biconvex lens, in contrast to the crescentic subdural hematoma that spreads freely over the hemisphere beneath the dura. Because the underlying brain is often uninjured, prompt evacuation produces full recovery, which makes recognition of the lucid interval critical.

syn-erb-duchenne.name: Upper brachial plexus palsy (Erb–Duchenne)
syn-erb-duchenne.presentation: After a difficult delivery with shoulder dystocia, or a motorcycle crash in which the shoulder was forced down while the head went the other way, the arm hangs limp at the side, rotated inward with the elbow straight and the forearm pronated, the wrist and fingers flexed: the 'waiter's tip'. The hand grips normally. Sensation is reduced over the outer shoulder and the lateral forearm, and the biceps and brachioradialis reflexes are absent.

deficits.distribution: shoulder abductors and external rotators, elbow flexors, supinator
deficits.sign: Weak deltoid, supraspinatus, infraspinatus, biceps, brachialis, brachioradialis; arm adducted, internally rotated, extended and pronated

syn-erb-duchenne.reasoning: Forcing the head and shoulder apart stretches the upper part of the brachial plexus, the C5 and C6 roots and the upper trunk they form, while the lower roots are protected by their more horizontal course. The lesion is peripheral and uncrossed, so everything is ipsilateral. syn-facial-palsy-peripheral-vs-central.name: Facial palsy: peripheral (Bell) versus central
syn-facial-palsy-peripheral-vs-central.presentation: A patient wakes with one side of the face drooping. If the forehead is smooth and the eye will not close, taste is odd and sounds are loud in that ear, the whole nerve has failed from its nucleus onward: Bell palsy. If the forehead wrinkles symmetrically and the eye closes while the mouth droops, and the arm on the same side is weak, the lesion is in the opposite hemisphere: a stroke. The forehead decides.

deficits.sign: Lower motor neuron facial palsy: cannot wrinkle the forehead, close the eye or smile; Bell phenomenon
Upper motor neuron facial weakness with preserved forehead and emotional smile
Loss of taste on the anterior tongue, hyperacusis, reduced tearing depending on the level in the canal
Associated hemiparesis or dysarthria when central

syn-facial-palsy-peripheral-vs-central.reasoning: The facial motor nucleus in the caudal pons has two functional halves. The part supplying the upper face receives corticobulbar input from both hemispheres, whereas the part supplying the lower face receives input mainly from the contralateral motor cortex, crossing at the level of the nucleus. A lesion of the corticobulbar fibers on one side, in the cortex, corona radiata, internal capsule or crus, therefore leaves the forehead moving, because the other hemisphere still drives it, and weakens the contralateral lower face; the accompanying arm weakness is on the same side as the facial weakness, since the corticospinal fibers cross further down in the medulla. A lesion of the nucleus or the nerve itself, in the pons, cerebellopontine angle, facial canal or parotid, removes the final common pathway to all the ipsilateral facial muscles, including the frontalis, and the paralysis is complete and on the side of the lesion. Emotional smiling uses a separate limbic route to the nucleus and often survives a central lesion, a further clue. The level of a peripheral lesion within the temporal bone is read from the branches: loss of tearing places it at or proximal to the geniculate ganglion, hyperacusis proximal to the stapedius branch, loss of taste proximal to the chorda tympani, and none of these means a lesion at or beyond the stylomastoid foramen. Bell palsy is a presumed viral inflammation of the nerve within the narrow labyrinthine segment of the canal.

imagingFindings.finding: Enhancement of the labyrinthine segment and geniculate ganglion of the facial nerve; imaging is reserved for atypical or non-recovering cases.

syn-femoral-neuropathy.name: Femoral neuropathy
syn-femoral-neuropathy.presentation: After a long operation in the lithotomy position, or with a retroperitoneal hematoma in an anticoagulated patient, a patient cannot straighten the knee and the leg buckles on stairs. The quadriceps is weak and later wasted, the knee jerk is absent, and sensation is reduced over the front of the thigh and the inner side of the leg down to the ankle. Hip adduction is normal, which separates the lesion from the L3–L4 roots or the lumbar plexus.

syn-femoral-neuropathy.reasoning: The femoral nerve forms in the psoas from the L2–L4 roots, emerges at its lateral border, runs in the groove between the psoas and iliacus beneath the iliac fascia, and passes under the inguinal ligament to divide into branches for the quadriceps and sartorius and the saphenous nerve for the medial leg. Within the pelvis it is vulnerable to compression by a hematoma in the iliacus muscle in anticoagulated or hemophiliac patients, to stretching by prolonged hip flexion and abduction in the lithotomy position, to retractors in pelvic surgery and to diabetic ischemia. A lesion here paralyzes the quadriceps and, if proximal, the iliopsoas, abolishes the knee reflex whose arc runs through the nerve, and produces sensory loss over the anterior thigh and along the saphenous territory on the medial leg. The obturator nerve arises from the same roots but leaves the plexus separately through the obturator foramen, so hip adduction is preserved in a femoral neuropathy and lost in a lumbar plexus or L3–L4 root lesion, and the L4 root is further distinguished by its contribution to the tibialis anterior. Diabetic lumbosacral radiculoplexus neuropathy (diabetic amyotrophy) produces a painful, asymmetric picture that begins in femoral territory but spreads beyond it, with weight loss.

syn-foville.name: Foville syndrome (dorsal caudal pontine)
syn-foville.presentation: The patient cannot look toward one side with either eye, has a complete facial palsy on that same side, and a hemiparesis on the opposite side. Unlike a sixth nerve palsy, both eyes fail to move toward the lesion, and the gaze palsy cannot be overcome by turning the head. There may be a contralateral hemisensory loss.

deficits.sign: Gaze palsy toward the lesion (abducens nucleus or PPRF), not overcome by the oculocephalic reflex when nuclear
Peripheral-type facial palsy
Hemiparesis from the corticospinal tract
Hemisensory loss from the medial lemniscus

syn-foville.reasoning: The dorsal caudal pons contains the abducens nucleus and the paramedian pontine reticular formation, which together generate conjugate horizontal gaze toward the same side: the abducens nucleus contains the motor neurons for the ipsilateral lateral rectus and the interneurons that cross into the contralateral MLF to drive the opposite medial rectus. Destroying it therefore paralyzes gaze toward the lesion in both eyes, and because the nucleus is the final common pathway, vestibular input cannot overcome the palsy, unlike a lesion of the PPRF or the frontal eye field. The facial nerve fibers loop around the abducens nucleus (the facial colliculus) and are caught with it, so the ipsilateral face is completely paralyzed. The corticospinal fibers in the basis pontis, still uncrossed above the pyramidal decussation, are involved when the lesion extends ventrally, producing contralateral hemiparesis. The syndrome is thus Millard–Gubler with a gaze palsy in place of, or in addition to, the sixth nerve palsy, and the gaze palsy is what proves that the lesion is dorsal and involves the nucleus rather than the fascicle.

syn-gerstmann.name: Gerstmann syndrome
syn-gerstmann.presentation: A right-handed patient is found unable to do simple arithmetic, to write a sentence, to name or point to individual fingers, and to tell left from right, either on themselves or on the examiner, while speaking fluently and understanding well. There may be a mild alexia and constructional difficulty. The combination points to the dominant angular gyrus.

syn-gerstmann.reasoning: The angular gyrus of the dominant hemisphere is a hub where visual, somatosensory and language information converge, at the junction of the parietal, temporal and occipital lobes. It maps the body schema onto language, which is why identifying fingers, telling left from right, manipulating numbers and writing, all of which require translating between spatial and verbal representations, fail together. Each of these functions depends on the intact, uncrossed cortical association network of one hemisphere, so the syndrome is a consequence of a left-sided lesion in right-handed people and has no contralateral or crossed component apart from any accompanying field defect, which is contralateral because the optic radiation on its way to the calcarine cortex carries the opposite hemifield. The supplying vessel is the angular branch of the inferior division of the middle cerebral artery; larger infarcts add Wernicke aphasia or alexia, and the pure tetrad is rare enough that its localizing value is debated, but its presence should always send the examiner to the left parietal lobe.

syn-guillain-barre.name: Guillain–Barré syndrome
syn-guillain-barre.presentation: Two weeks after a diarrheal illness a young adult develops tingling in the feet and hands and, over the following days, weakness that begins in the legs and climbs to the arms and face, so that within a week they cannot walk and both sides of the face are weak. The reflexes have disappeared, sensation is only mildly reduced, and the pulse and blood pressure swing unpredictably. Breathing becomes shallow, and the vital capacity is measured every few hours.

deficits.distribution: legs then arms, proximal and distal, ascending
deficits.sign: Rapidly progressive symmetric flaccid weakness reaching a nadir within 4 weeks
Areflexia or hyporeflexia
Paresthesias with mild objective loss; back and limb pain from root inflammation
Bilateral facial weakness in half, dysphagia, ophthalmoplegia in the Miller Fisher variant

Respiratory failure requiring ventilation in a quarter

syn-guillain-barre.reasoning: An infection, most often Campylobacter jejuni, provokes antibodies that cross-react with gangliosides on peripheral nerve myelin or axons, and within weeks the immune attack strips myelin from the spinal roots and peripheral nerves, or in the axonal forms destroys the axons at the nodes of Ranvier. Because the roots are inflamed where they leave the cord and the process is diffuse, weakness is symmetric, involves proximal as well as distal muscles and is not length-dependent, distinguishing it from the toxic and metabolic neuropathies; it ascends because the longest fibers and the most heavily myelinated motor fibers fail first, but it is not a lesion at any level of the cord, so there is no sensory level, no sphincter loss at the outset and no upper motor neuron sign. The reflex arcs run through the demyelinated roots, so all reflexes are lost early, even in muscles that are still strong, which is the sign that most reliably points away from a spinal cord or muscle disease. Cranial nerves are involved because their roots are similarly attacked, the facial nerve most often, and the autonomic fibers in the vagus and sympathetic chain because they are peripheral nerves too. Everything is bilateral and peripheral; there is no crossing to reason about. syn-hearing-loss.name: Conductive versus sensorineural hearing loss
syn-hearing-loss.presentation: A patient cannot hear well in one ear. A tuning fork placed on the forehead is heard louder in the affected ear if the problem is in the ear canal, drum or ossicles, and louder in the good ear if the cochlea or nerve is at fault; placed on the mastoid and then held beside the ear, it is heard longer through the bone than the air in conductive loss and longer through the air in sensorineural loss. Unilateral sensorineural loss needs an MRI; conductive loss needs an otoscope.

deficits.sign: Weber lateralizes to the affected ear, Rinne negative (bone > air); low-frequency loss on audiometry
Weber lateralizes to the good ear, Rinne positive (air > bone); high-frequency or all-frequency loss with reduced discrimination in nerve lesions
Vertigo or imbalance accompanies labyrinthine and nerve lesions but not middle ear disease
Bilateral central lesions cause cortical deafness or word deafness; unilateral central lesions never cause deafness

syn-hearing-loss.reasoning: Sound reaches the cochlea by two routes: through the ear canal, drum and ossicles (air conduction) or directly through the skull bones (bone conduction). A conductive lesion blocks the air route and leaves bone conduction intact, so the affected ear hears the forehead fork better than the good ear, which is distracted by ambient noise entering through its open air route, and hears the mastoid fork longer than the fork beside the canal. A sensorineural lesion of the cochlea or the cochlear nerve reduces both routes equally, so the fork on the forehead is heard better by the healthy cochlea and the normal air-over-bone advantage persists. Above the cochlear nuclei the auditory pathway crosses partially at several levels, in the trapezoid body, the lateral lemniscus and the inferior colliculus, so each auditory cortex receives input from both ears and a unilateral brainstem, thalamic or cortical lesion causes at most subtle localization or discrimination deficits, never deafness in one ear: unilateral hearing loss is always peripheral, in the ear or the eighth nerve. Nerve (retrocochlear) lesions are distinguished from cochlear ones by speech discrimination far worse than the pure-tone loss predicts, absent acoustic reflexes and prolonged interpeak latencies on brainstem auditory evoked potentials, and require MRI for a schwannoma. Sudden sensorineural loss is an emergency treated with steroids; a conductive loss with a normal drum in a young adult suggests otosclerosis.

mimics.howToDistinguish: Inconsistent audiometry; normal otoacoustic emissions and evoked potentials

syn-hemiballismus.name: Hemiballismus
syn-hemiballismus.presentation: An elderly hypertensive or poorly controlled diabetic patient suddenly begins to fling one arm and leg in wide, violent, uncontrollable movements that continue while awake, exhaust the patient and may injure the limb. The movements involve the proximal joints, look like throwing, and stop in sleep. Strength, sensation and cognition are normal. Over weeks the flinging usually subsides into a milder chorea and then resolves.

deficits.sign: Large-amplitude flinging (ballistic) movements of one side of the body
No weakness, spasticity or reflex change
Facial and lingual involvement with grimacing in some

syn-hemiballismus.reasoning: The subthalamic nucleus is the only excitatory nucleus in the basal ganglia loop: it receives inhibition from the external pallidum and drives the internal pallidum and substantia nigra reticulata, which in turn inhibit the motor thalamus. Its output is the brake in the indirect pathway that suppresses unwanted movement. A small infarct or hemorrhage that destroys the nucleus on one side removes that excitatory drive, so the internal pallidum falls silent, the ventral lateral thalamus is released from inhibition and fires excessively on the motor and premotor cortex, which discharges the flinging, involuntary movements. The basal ganglia loops of each hemisphere serve the contralateral body through the corticospinal tract, which crosses in the medulla, so a right subthalamic lesion produces left hemiballismus. The movements are not weakness, because the corticospinal system is intact, and they cease in sleep because cortical drive falls. The subthalamic nucleus is supplied by perforators from the posterior communicating and posterior cerebral arteries and is a typical site for hypertensive lacunes and small hemorrhages; nonketotic hyperglycemia produces the same syndrome from striatal dysfunction, with a characteristic T1-bright putamen on MRI. Lesions of the striatum, the pallidum or the thalamus can also cause hemichorea-hemiballismus, and dopamine-blocking drugs help by reducing the thalamocortical overactivity. Spontaneous recovery is the rule as the remaining circuit adapts.

imagingFindings.finding: Small area of restricted diffusion or hemorrhage in the contralateral subthalamic nucleus, below the thalamus and above the substantia nigra on coronal images.

Striatal or pallidal infarct, tumor or demyelination on the side opposite the movements.

imagingHint.label: subthalamic nucleus beneath the thalamus

commonCauses: Lacunar infarct of the subthalamic nucleus

mimics.name: Focal motor seizure
mimics.howToDistinguish: Rhythmic, brief, with impaired awareness or spread; EEG

mimics.name: Hemichorea from Huntington or Sydenham chorea
mimics.howToDistinguish: Bilateral over time, family history or streptococcal illness, smaller amplitude

mimics.name: Tardive dyskinesia
