syn-hemineglect.name: Hemispatial neglect
syn-hemineglect.presentation: After a right hemisphere stroke, the patient ignores the left side of space: they eat from the right half of the plate, shave the right side of the face, bisect lines far to the right, and when asked to draw a clock crowd all the numbers on the right. They may deny that the left arm belongs to them, insist they are not weak, and, when touched on both sides, feel only the right. The head and eyes are turned to the right.

deficits.sign: Visual, tactile and motor neglect with extinction on double simultaneous stimulation
Anosognosia and asomatognosia; constructional apraxia; dressing apraxia
Gaze and head deviation toward the lesion
Left hemiparesis when the infarct extends anteriorly

syn-hemineglect.reasoning: The right inferior parietal lobule and the adjacent temporoparietal junction direct spatial attention to both halves of space, whereas the left parietal lobe attends mainly to the right; a right lesion therefore leaves nothing to attend to the left, while a left lesion is compensated by the right hemisphere and causes only mild, transient right neglect. This asymmetry, not any decussation, is why neglect is overwhelmingly a right hemisphere sign affecting the contralateral left side. Neglect is not a sensory loss: the visual pathways and somatosensory cortex may be intact, and the deficit is in awareness and orienting, which is why stimuli are perceived when presented alone but extinguished when a competing stimulus is presented on the right. Right frontal and thalamic lesions produce milder versions through the same network. The gaze deviation reflects the unopposed drive of the intact left frontal eye field, which pushes the eyes to the right, and the anosognosia and denial of the left arm belong to the same failure to represent the left side of the body and its state.

imagingFindings.finding: Restricted diffusion in the right supramarginal and angular gyri or the temporoparietal junction, often part of a larger MCA infarct.
Any right parietal mass lesion produces neglect; look for midline shift.

imagingHint.label: right inferior parietal lobule

commonCauses: Right MCA infarct (stem or inferior division)
Tumor of the right parietal lobe

mimics.name: Left homonymous hemianopia
mimics.howToDistinguish: Hemianopic patients turn to compensate and are aware; neglect patients do not search and deny

mimics.name: Left hemisensory loss
mimics.howToDistinguish: Sensation is present when tested alone; extinction only with bilateral stimulation

mimics.name: Global inattention or delirium
mimics.howToDistinguish: No lateralized pattern

management: Acute stroke treatment
Neglect rehabilitation: prism adaptation, visual scanning training, approaching from the neglected side

syn-homonymous-hemianopia.name: Homonymous hemianopia and its variants
syn-homonymous-hemianopia.presentation: The patient does not see things on one side, reads only half a line, and has been bumping into objects on that side. Confrontation shows loss of the same half of the visual field in both eyes. Whether the defect is a quadrant or a hemifield, whether the two eyes' defects match exactly, whether the macular region is spared and whether a pupil defect is present together tell the examiner where along the retrochiasmal pathway the lesion lies.

deficits.sign: Homonymous hemianopia; congruity increases as the lesion moves posteriorly
Superior quadrantanopia from Meyer's loop in the temporal lobe
Inferior quadrantanopia from the parietal radiation
Relative afferent pupillary defect only with optic tract lesions

syn-homonymous-hemianopia.reasoning: Behind the chiasm every structure carries the opposite half of the visual world from both eyes, because the crossed nasal fibers of one eye have joined the uncrossed temporal fibers of the other: a lesion of the optic tract, lateral geniculate body, optic radiation or occipital cortex therefore produces a homonymous defect in the contralateral field. Where along that pathway the lesion sits is read from four features. Congruity: in the tract the fibers from the two eyes are not yet aligned, so the defect differs between the eyes, whereas in the calcarine cortex corresponding points are precisely superimposed and the defects are identical. Pupils: the light reflex afferents leave the tract before the geniculate, so only a tract lesion produces a contralateral relative afferent pupillary defect. Shape: the radiation splits after the geniculate, the upper field fibers looping forward through the temporal lobe (Meyer's loop) and the lower field fibers passing through the parietal lobe, so temporal lesions give superior quadrant ('pie in the sky') and parietal lesions inferior quadrant defects, and geniculate lesions give sector defects from its dual blood supply. Macular sparing: the occipital pole receives collateral supply from the middle cerebral artery, so posterior cerebral infarcts often spare the central few degrees. Bilateral occipital lesions produce cortical blindness with normal pupils, and lesions of the occipital tip alone produce a homonymous central scotoma.

imagingFindings.finding: Restricted diffusion in the calcarine cortex, the commonest cause of an isolated congruous hemianopia with macular sparing.
Infarct, hemorrhage, tumor or resection cavity in the optic radiation; quadrantic defect matches the lobe.
Tumor, aneurysm or demyelination around the tract lateral to the hypothalamus; later 'bow-tie' atrophy of the contralateral disc.

imagingHint.label: optic radiation through the temporal and parietal lobes

commonCauses: Middle cerebral artery infarct involving the radiation

mimics.howToDistinguish: Patient does not search the neglected side but sees a stimulus presented alone; extinction on double stimulation

mimics.name: Bitemporal hemianopia

mimics.name: Functional visual loss
mimics.howToDistinguish: Fields tubular or spiraling, inconsistent

syn-horizontal-gaze-palsy-pontine.name: Pontine horizontal gaze palsy
syn-horizontal-gaze-palsy-pontine.presentation: After a pontine stroke the patient cannot look toward the side of the lesion with either eye, and at rest the eyes drift toward the opposite side, away from the lesion and toward any hemiparesis. This is the reverse of the hemispheric pattern, where the eyes look toward the lesion and away from the weak limbs. Distinguishing the two is a bedside way to tell a pontine from a hemispheric stroke.

deficits.sign: Gaze palsy toward the lesion; eyes deviated away from the lesion
Hemiparesis when the basis pontis is involved; the eyes look toward the weak side
Oculocephalic reflex overcomes a PPRF lesion but not an abducens nuclear lesion

syn-horizontal-gaze-palsy-pontine.reasoning: The frontal eye field of each hemisphere sends its saccade command across the midline to the paramedian pontine reticular formation of the opposite side, which fires the adjacent abducens nucleus to move both eyes toward that side. A right hemispheric lesion therefore removes the drive to the left PPRF: the patient cannot look left, and the unopposed left hemisphere pushes the eyes to the right, toward the lesion; with the crossed corticospinal fibers also damaged, the weak limbs are on the left, so the eyes look away from the hemiparesis. A left pontine lesion of the PPRF or abducens nucleus removes leftward gaze at its final stage: the eyes cannot look left, toward the lesion, and drift right, away from it; the uncrossed corticospinal fibers in the left basis pontis produce a right hemiparesis, so now the eyes look toward the weak limbs. The vestibulo-ocular reflex reaches the abducens nucleus directly from the vestibular nuclei, bypassing the PPRF, so a PPRF lesion (supranuclear) can be overcome by head turning and caloric stimulation whereas an abducens nuclear lesion cannot, and a nuclear lesion adds an ipsilateral facial palsy from the facial colliculus.

imagingFindings.finding: Restricted diffusion in the dorsal paramedian caudal pons; may extend ventrally into the corticospinal fibers.

imagingHint.label: PPRF and abducens nucleus

mimics.name: Sixth nerve palsy

mimics.name: Seizure with gaze deviation
mimics.howToDistinguish: Eyes deviate away from an irritative focus and jerk; transient

syn-horner.name: Horner syndrome
syn-horner.presentation: One pupil is smaller than the other and the difference is greater in a dim room, the eyelid on that side droops a millimeter or two and the lower lid sits slightly higher, giving the eye a sunken look. The affected side of the face may not sweat. Depending on the cause there may be neck pain, hoarseness, weakness of the hand, or a brainstem syndrome; in a child a lighter iris on the affected side implies a congenital lesion.

deficits.sign: Miosis with dilation lag; anisocoria greatest in darkness
Mild ptosis (Müller's muscle) and 'upside-down ptosis' of the lower lid; apparent enophthalmos
Anhidrosis of the face with central and preganglionic lesions; spared with postganglionic lesions

syn-horner.reasoning: The sympathetic pathway to the eye is entirely uncrossed, a three-neuron chain from the hypothalamus through the lateral brainstem and cervical cord to the ciliospinal center at C8–T2, then out through the T1 root over the lung apex and up the cervical chain to the superior cervical ganglion, and finally along the internal carotid artery through the cavernous sinus to the dilator pupillae and the smooth muscle of the lids. A lesion anywhere along this route produces the same ipsilateral triad, so the syndrome itself localizes only to the pathway, and the company it keeps localizes the lesion: first-order lesions (lateral medullary infarct, cervical cord) come with brainstem or cord signs and anhidrosis of the whole half of the body; second-order lesions (apical lung tumor, neck trauma, thyroid or carotid surgery) come with hand weakness, arm pain or a neck scar and facial anhidrosis; third-order lesions (carotid dissection, cavernous sinus disease, cluster headache) spare sweating, because the sudomotor fibers to the face leave the chain with the external carotid artery. The pupil is small because the dilator is paralyzed while the parasympathetic sphincter, reaching the eye by the third nerve, is intact, which is why the anisocoria widens in the dark and both pupils react normally to light.

imagingFindings.finding: Crescentic intramural hematoma around a narrowed lumen on fat-saturated T1; string sign or tapered occlusion on angiography.

mimics.name: Third nerve palsy with ptosis
mimics.howToDistinguish: The pupil is large, not small, and ptosis is marked

mimics.name: Adie tonic pupil
mimics.howToDistinguish: The larger pupil is abnormal; poor light reaction, tonic near response

syn-huntington-chorea.name: Huntington disease and chorea
syn-huntington-chorea.presentation: A person in their forties whose parent died in a psychiatric hospital becomes irritable and depressed, then clumsy and fidgety; over a few years the fidgeting becomes continuous flowing, dance-like movements of the limbs, trunk and face, with an unsteady lurching gait, darting eyes that cannot hold fixation, and a slow decline in judgment and memory. syn-huntington-chorea.reasoning: An expanded CAG repeat in the huntingtin gene produces a protein that kills the medium spiny neurons of the striatum, beginning with those of the indirect pathway, which express D2 receptors and enkephalin and project to the external pallidum. Each striatum serves the contralateral body through the crossed corticospinal projection, and the degeneration is bilateral and symmetric, so the chorea is generalized. syn-hydrocephalus.name: Hydrocephalus: obstructive versus communicating
syn-hydrocephalus.presentation: A child with a large head and a bulging fontanelle whose eyes are forced downward, or an adult with a morning headache that wakes them, vomiting, blurred vision from swollen optic discs and double vision from a sixth nerve palsy, has hydrocephalus. If the CT shows dilated lateral and third ventricles with a normal fourth, the block is in the aqueduct; if all four ventricles are dilated, the block is outside them, at the basal cisterns or the arachnoid granulations, after meningitis or subarachnoid hemorrhage.

deficits.sign: Headache worse in the morning and on lying, vomiting, drowsiness; coma with acute obstruction
Papilledema with enlarged blind spots and transient visual obscurations; late optic atrophy
Sixth nerve palsies from raised pressure; sunset eyes and Parinaud signs from third ventricular dilatation pressing on the tectum
Spastic, magnetic gait from stretching of the leg fibers around the dilated frontal horns
Urgency and incontinence from stretched periventricular frontal fibers

syn-hydrocephalus.reasoning: Cerebrospinal fluid is secreted by the choroid plexus of the lateral, third and fourth ventricles, flows through the foramina of Monro, the third ventricle, the aqueduct and the fourth ventricle, leaves through the foramina of Luschka and Magendie into the subarachnoid space and is absorbed into the venous sinuses through the arachnoid granulations. Obstruction anywhere along the route dilates the ventricles upstream of the block, and the pattern of dilatation locates it: a block at one foramen of Monro traps one lateral ventricle; a block in the aqueduct, the narrowest part, dilates both lateral ventricles and the third but leaves the fourth normal; a block at the fourth ventricular outlets dilates all four; and failure of absorption at the granulations or obstruction of the basal cisterns by blood, pus or carcinomatosis, called communicating hydrocephalus because the ventricles still communicate with the subarachnoid space, dilates all four together with the cisterns. The distinction matters because a lumbar puncture is dangerous in obstructive hydrocephalus, where the lumbar sac is not in communication with the ventricles and drainage can precipitate herniation, but is diagnostic and sometimes therapeutic in communicating hydrocephalus. The signs are those of raised intracranial pressure, bilateral and without an ipsilateral or contralateral pattern: papilledema from transmission of pressure along the optic nerve sheaths, sixth nerve palsies from stretching of the long abducens nerves, and, when the third ventricle balloons back over the tectum, the up-gaze palsy of the dorsal midbrain syndrome. The leg fibers of the corticospinal tract sweep around the frontal horns on their way to the internal capsule and are stretched first, giving the characteristic gait and bladder disturbance.

imagingFindings.finding: Dilated lateral and third ventricles with a normal fourth ventricle (aqueduct stenosis or tectal tumor) or all four dilated with an outlet block; rounded frontal horns, periventricular low density from transependymal CSF flow, effaced sulci.
All four ventricles dilated with prominent basal cisterns; look for the cause: leptomeningeal enhancement, subarachnoid blood, previous meningitis.
Sagittal T2 and CISS show aqueduct stenosis, a tectal glioma, a colloid cyst at the foramen of Monro or a fourth ventricular tumor; absent aqueductal flow void.

imagingHint.label: lateral and third ventricles

commonCauses: Posterior fossa tumor or Chiari malformation
Colloid cyst of the third ventricle

mimics.name: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension
mimics.howToDistinguish: Small or normal ventricles with papilledema

mimics.name: Cerebral atrophy (hydrocephalus ex vacuo)
mimics.howToDistinguish: Ventricles and sulci enlarged in proportion, no pressure signs

mimics.name: Normal pressure hydrocephalus
mimics.howToDistinguish: Chronic triad in the elderly with normal opening pressure

management: Urgent CT in any patient with headache, vomiting and papilledema; do not perform a lumbar puncture in obstructive hydrocephalus

Treat the underlying tumor or cyst

syn-hypoglossal-palsy.name: Hypoglossal nerve palsy
syn-hypoglossal-palsy.presentation: On protrusion the tongue deviates toward one side, and that half of the tongue is wasted and ripples with fasciculations. The patient has mild slurring of lingual consonants and difficulty moving food around the mouth. In a young patient with neck pain and a Horner syndrome the cause is a carotid dissection pressing on the nerve; in an older patient a skull base tumor; bilateral involvement with a brisk jaw jerk means motor neuron disease.

deficits.sign: Tongue deviates toward the lesion on protrusion; atrophy and fasciculation (lower motor neuron)
Mild lingual dysarthria and difficulty manipulating food
Horner syndrome when the carotid sheath is involved

syn-hypoglossal-palsy.reasoning: The hypoglossal nucleus in the medulla and its nerve supply the intrinsic and extrinsic muscles of the ipsilateral half of the tongue. Protrusion is performed by the two genioglossus muscles pushing the tongue forward and toward the opposite side, so when one is paralyzed the intact muscle pushes the tongue toward the weak side: the tongue points to the lesion in a lower motor neuron palsy. Wasting and fasciculation confirm that the lesion is nuclear or infranuclear. The nucleus receives corticobulbar input mainly from the contralateral hemisphere, so a capsular stroke produces deviation away from the lesion without atrophy and with associated face and arm weakness on the same side as the tongue deviation. The nerve leaves through the hypoglossal canal and descends in the neck between the internal carotid artery and the internal jugular vein before turning forward over the carotid bifurcation, which is why carotid dissection, carotid endarterectomy and tumors of the carotid space are the commonest peripheral causes and why a Horner syndrome from the sympathetic plexus often accompanies them. A nuclear lesion in the medial medulla adds contralateral hemiparesis and proprioceptive loss (Dejerine). Bilateral lower motor neuron tongue weakness with upper motor neuron limb signs is the hallmark of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.

imagingFindings.finding: Crescentic intramural hematoma in the upper cervical internal carotid artery on fat-saturated T1, with luminal narrowing.
Enhancing lesion of the hypoglossal canal or clivus (chordoma, metastasis, meningioma, glomus); CT shows canal widening or erosion.
Fatty atrophy and T2 hyperintensity of one half of the tongue on axial images, a useful sign of a chronic lesion.

imagingHint.label: hypoglossal nucleus and nerve in the medulla; canal at the skull base

mimics.name: Upper motor neuron tongue weakness
mimics.howToDistinguish: Deviates away from a hemispheric lesion, no atrophy or fasciculation, associated hemiparesis

mimics.name: Facial palsy
mimics.howToDistinguish: Apparent tongue deviation from the asymmetric mouth; check with the lips held symmetric

mimics.name: Pseudobulbar palsy
mimics.howToDistinguish: Spastic, slow tongue without wasting; brisk jaw jerk

management: MRI of the medulla, skull base and neck with MRA of the carotid
Speech therapy; most dissection-related palsies recover
Look for fasciculations and limb signs to exclude motor neuron disease

syn-hypothalamic-syndromes.name: Hypothalamic syndromes
syn-hypothalamic-syndromes.presentation: A child with a suprasellar tumor stops growing, drinks and passes enormous volumes of dilute urine, sleeps at odd hours and becomes either wasted or obese with an insatiable appetite. An adult with a lesion of the same region has a body temperature that swings without infection, faints on standing, has lost the ability to feel thirst and has become emotionally flat or explosively angry. Visual field loss from the neighboring chiasm and the endocrine failure of the pituitary are frequent companions.

deficits.sign: Diabetes insipidus (supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei); adipsia or hypernatremia with anterior lesions; SIADH with irritative lesions
Hyperthermia with anterior (preoptic) lesions, hypothermia or poikilothermia with posterior lesions
Hyperphagia and obesity with ventromedial lesions; anorexia and emaciation (diencephalic syndrome of infancy) with lateral lesions
Hypersomnia with posterior lesions, insomnia with anterior lesions; disrupted circadian rhythm (suprachiasmatic nucleus)
Hypopituitarism, growth failure, precocious or delayed puberty, hyperprolactinemia from stalk compression
Rage, apathy, emotional lability; amnesia with mammillary body involvement

syn-hypothalamic-syndromes.reasoning: The hypothalamus is a few grams of tissue in the walls and floor of the third ventricle that regulates the internal environment through three routes: the pituitary, by releasing hormones into the portal vessels and by sending vasopressin and oxytocin down the stalk to the posterior lobe; the autonomic nervous system, through descending fibers to the brainstem and spinal preganglionic neurons; and behavior, through the limbic system. Its nuclei are arranged so that the anterior region houses the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei that make vasopressin, the preoptic heat-loss center and the sleep-promoting neurons, while the posterior region contains the heat-conserving and arousal (orexin) neurons and the mammillary bodies of the memory circuit, and the medial tuberal region holds the ventromedial satiety and arcuate feeding nuclei beside the lateral feeding area. A lesion can therefore be localized by its combination of effects: anterior lesions cause hyperthermia, insomnia and diabetes insipidus, posterior lesions hypothermia, hypersomnia and amnesia, ventromedial lesions hyperphagia and rage, lateral lesions anorexia. Because the paired nuclei sit on either side of the narrow third ventricle and each projects bilaterally, most syndromes require bilateral or midline lesions and show no lateralization, with no ipsilateral or contralateral rule to apply, and the neighboring chiasm and pituitary stalk are almost always involved by the same mass, adding the bitemporal field defect and hypopituitarism. Craniopharyngiomas, hypothalamic gliomas, germinomas, sarcoidosis, Langerhans cell histiocytosis and surgery of the region are the usual causes.

imagingFindings.finding: Craniopharyngioma (cystic, calcified), optic-hypothalamic glioma (T2-bright infiltrating mass), germinoma (enhancing, often with a pineal twin) or hamartoma of the tuber cinereum in the floor of the third ventricle; thickened enhancing stalk in histiocytosis, sarcoidosis and hypophysitis.

imagingFindings.pathology: Loss of the posterior pituitary bright spot
imagingFindings.finding: Absent T1 hyperintensity of the neurohypophysis in central diabetes insipidus.

imagingFindings.pathology: Wernicke encephalopathy and other symmetric lesions
imagingFindings.finding: Symmetric FLAIR change around the third ventricle and in the mammillary bodies.

imagingHint.label: hypothalamus in the walls of the third ventricle

commonCauses: Sarcoidosis, Langerhans cell histiocytosis, lymphocytic hypophysitis
Surgery or radiotherapy of the region, subarachnoid hemorrhage, trauma

mimics.name: Primary endocrine disease
mimics.howToDistinguish: Single hormone axis, no thirst, temperature or sleep disturbance

mimics.name: Psychogenic polydipsia
mimics.howToDistinguish: Water deprivation concentrates the urine; no lesion

mimics.name: Pituitary adenoma
mimics.howToDistinguish: Sellar origin, hypopituitarism and chiasmal compression without hypothalamic dysregulation until very large

management: MRI of the sella and hypothalamus with contrast; full pituitary hormone profile, paired serum and urine osmolality; tumor markers and CSF cytology for germ cell tumors
Replace deficient hormones, especially cortisol before thyroxine; desmopressin for diabetes insipidus with careful fluid balance in adipsic patients
Treat the lesion (surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy) with an awareness that hypothalamic damage from treatment causes obesity and sleep disturbance

syn-idiopathic-intracranial-hypertension.name: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension
syn-idiopathic-intracranial-hypertension.presentation: An overweight young woman has daily headaches that are worse on waking and on bending, a whooshing pulsatile noise in the ears, brief episodes of visual dimming on standing and horizontal double vision. Both optic discs are swollen, the blind spots are enlarged and one eye cannot fully abduct, but the rest of the examination is normal, the MRI shows no mass and small ventricles, and the lumbar puncture opening pressure is thirty-five centimeters of CSF with normal fluid.

deficits.sign: Daily headache worse on waking, lying and straining; pulsatile tinnitus
Papilledema with transient visual obscurations, enlarged blind spots, progressive constriction of the fields and, untreated, permanent visual loss
Unilateral or bilateral sixth nerve palsies (false localizing)
Alert, normal cognition; no focal deficit

syn-idiopathic-intracranial-hypertension.reasoning: The intracranial pressure rises without a mass, hydrocephalus or infection, most often in obese women of childbearing age, through mechanisms that are still debated but include impaired CSF absorption, raised venous pressure in the dural sinuses and, in many, stenosis of the transverse sinuses that may be cause or consequence. The raised pressure is transmitted throughout the subarachnoid space and along the optic nerve sheaths, where it obstructs axoplasmic flow in the optic nerve heads and produces papilledema; the swollen nerve fibers enlarge the blind spot and, if the pressure persists, die, constricting the field from the periphery and eventually destroying central vision, which makes the condition a threat to sight rather than to life. The abducens nerves, with their long course up the clivus and over the petrous apex, are stretched by the pressure and fail on one or both sides, giving diplopia that has nothing to do with the pons; a false-localizing sixth nerve palsy is the rule. Pulsatile tinnitus arises from turbulent venous flow through the compressed transverse sinuses, and the headache from stretching of the pain-sensitive dura. There is no focal lesion and no crossed or lateralized deficit apart from the sixth nerve palsy; the ventricles are small because the pressure is uniform, which separates the condition from hydrocephalus. The diagnosis requires papilledema, a normal neurological examination apart from sixth nerve palsy, normal imaging including venography to exclude sinus thrombosis, and a raised opening pressure with normal CSF composition.

imagingFindings.finding: Partially empty sella, flattening of the posterior globes, distension and tortuosity of the optic nerve sheaths, protrusion of the optic nerve heads, slit-like ventricles.
Bilateral narrowing of the distal transverse sinuses; also excludes venous sinus thrombosis, the essential mimic.
Opening pressure above 25 cm CSF in the lateral decubitus position with normal protein, glucose and cells.

imagingHint.label: optic nerve sheaths and posterior globes

commonCauses: Idiopathic, associated with obesity and recent weight gain
Drugs: tetracyclines, retinoids, growth hormone, steroid withdrawal
Secondary: venous sinus thrombosis, sleep apnea, anemia, endocrine disease (these are excluded by definition)

mimics.howToDistinguish: Identical presentation; MRV shows the thrombus; seizures and focal signs may occur

mimics.name: Hydrocephalus
mimics.howToDistinguish: Dilated ventricles

mimics.name: Malignant hypertension
mimics.howToDistinguish: Very high blood pressure with retinal hemorrhages and exudates

mimics.name: Pseudopapilledema (drusen)
mimics.howToDistinguish: Normal pressure; drusen on ultrasound or autofluorescence

Weight loss and acetazolamide; stop causative drugs

syn-ino.name: Internuclear ophthalmoplegia
syn-ino.presentation: A young woman notices double vision on looking to one side. When she looks to the right, the left eye stays in the midline or adducts slowly while the right eye abducts fully and shows jerky nystagmus; when she looks left, both eyes move normally. Asked to look at a pencil brought toward her nose, both eyes converge, proving that the medial rectus itself works. In an older patient with the same finding, a small pontine stroke is the likely cause.

deficits.distribution: adduction of the eye on the side of the lesion
deficits.sign: Adduction failure or slowing on contralateral gaze with preserved convergence
Dissociated nystagmus of the abducting eye
Skew deviation and vertical gaze-evoked nystagmus when bilateral

syn-ino.reasoning: Conjugate horizontal gaze depends on the abducens nucleus of one side driving the lateral rectus of its own eye and, through interneurons whose axons cross immediately and ascend in the contralateral MLF, the medial rectus subnucleus of the opposite oculomotor nucleus. A lesion of the MLF on one side cuts the ascending interneuron axons after they have crossed, so the medial rectus on the side of the lesion no longer receives the gaze command: on gaze away from the lesion the ipsilateral eye fails to adduct, and the syndrome is named for the side of the eye that does not adduct, which is the side of the MLF lesion. The abducting eye shows nystagmus, attributed to adaptive increased innervation sent to both yoked muscles. The medial rectus and its motor neurons are intact, so convergence, which uses a separate midbrain pathway, is preserved; this separates INO from a partial third nerve palsy. Bilateral INO in a young adult is almost diagnostic of multiple sclerosis because the MLFs lie side by side in the periventricular tegmentum; unilateral INO in the elderly is usually a paramedian pontine perforator infarct.

imagingFindings.finding: Small T2/FLAIR-bright lesion in the dorsal paramedian pons or midbrain along the MLF, often with other periventricular lesions; thin sagittal sections help.
Punctate restricted diffusion in the paramedian tegmentum in an older patient.

imagingHint.label: medial longitudinal fasciculus in the dorsal paramedian pons

mimics.name: Medial rectus (partial third nerve) palsy
mimics.howToDistinguish: Convergence also fails; ptosis or pupil signs may coexist

mimics.name: Myasthenia gravis
mimics.howToDistinguish: Pseudo-INO that fatigues and reverses with ice or edrophonium; ptosis common

mimics.name: One-and-a-half syndrome
mimics.howToDistinguish: Adds an ipsilateral conjugate gaze palsy

management: MRI of the brain with attention to the brainstem; evaluate for multiple sclerosis in the young
Stroke workup and secondary prevention in the elderly
Diplopia is usually mild and improves; prisms if persistent

syn-jugular-foramen-vernet.name: Jugular foramen syndrome (Vernet)
syn-jugular-foramen-vernet.presentation: The patient has become hoarse, chokes on liquids and has lost the ability to shrug one shoulder; the examiner finds that the palate lifts only on one side with the uvula pulled toward the healthy side, the gag is absent on the affected side, the sternocleidomastoid and upper trapezius are wasted, and taste and sensation are gone from the back of the tongue. Pulsatile tinnitus and a red mass behind the eardrum point to a glomus tumor.

deficits.sign: Palatal droop, uvula deviates to the intact side, dysphagia, hoarseness with vocal cord paralysis, absent gag
Loss of taste and sensation on the posterior third of the tongue and pharynx
Weak head turning to the opposite side and shoulder shrug; shoulder droop
Pulsatile tinnitus and conductive hearing loss with glomus jugulare tumors

syn-jugular-foramen-vernet.reasoning: The glossopharyngeal, vagus and accessory nerves leave the skull together through the jugular foramen alongside the jugular bulb, so a lesion at the foramen paralyzes all three on the same side; these are uncrossed lower motor neuron and sensory pathways, and every sign is ipsilateral. The vagus supplies the palate, pharynx and larynx through the pharyngeal plexus and the laryngeal nerves, so the palate on the affected side fails to lift and the uvula is drawn toward the intact side by the working muscles, the vocal cord lies in the paramedian position and the pharynx does not clear, hence hoarseness and aspiration. The glossopharyngeal nerve carries sensation and taste from the posterior tongue and is the afferent limb of the gag, which is therefore absent when the affected side is stimulated. The spinal accessory nerve, which has climbed through the foramen magnum to leave with them, supplies the sternocleidomastoid that turns the head to the opposite side and the trapezius that shrugs the shoulder. If the hypoglossal nerve, which exits through the neighboring hypoglossal canal, is added, the syndrome becomes Collet–Sicard, and involvement of the sympathetic chain below the skull base adds a Horner (Villaret): the combination maps the lesion's extent along the skull base. A nuclear lesion in the medulla would add crossed long-tract signs and spare the accessory nerve's spinal root.

imagingFindings.finding: Avidly enhancing mass expanding the jugular foramen with a 'salt and pepper' appearance from flow voids; permeative bone destruction on CT.

imagingFindings.pathology: Schwannoma or meningioma of the foramen
imagingFindings.finding: Smooth enlargement of the foramen with an enhancing mass; meningiomas show a dural tail and sclerosis.

imagingFindings.pathology: Skull base metastasis or nasopharyngeal carcinoma
imagingFindings.finding: Destructive lesion of the jugular foramen and petrous bone.

imagingHint.label: jugular foramen at the skull base

commonCauses: Schwannoma of IX, X or XI
Skull base metastasis or nasopharyngeal carcinoma
Jugular vein thrombosis or internal carotid dissection

mimics.name: Medullary infarct (Wallenberg)
mimics.howToDistinguish: Crossed sensory loss, Horner and ataxia; spinal accessory spared

mimics.name: Vagal palsy alone
mimics.howToDistinguish: Palatal and laryngeal signs without tongue sensory loss or shoulder weakness

mimics.name: Myasthenia gravis
mimics.howToDistinguish: Bilateral fatigable bulbar weakness

management: Contrast MRI of the skull base with CT for bone; catheter angiography if a glomus tumor is suspected
Swallow assessment; laryngoscopy for cord position
Surgery or radiotherapy according to tumor type

syn-klumpke.name: Lower brachial plexus palsy (Klumpke)
syn-klumpke.presentation: A patient who grabbed a branch while falling, or a baby delivered with the arm pulled upward, has a claw hand: the fingers cannot be spread or brought together, the small hand muscles are wasted, and grip is weak, while the shoulder and elbow work. Sensation is absent along the inner forearm and the little finger. A drooping lid and small pupil on the same side mean the T1 root has been torn from the cord.

deficits.distribution: intrinsic hand muscles, long finger flexors
deficits.sign: Claw hand with weak grip; wasting of the thenar, hypothenar and interossei; wrist flexion weak

deficits.distribution: medial forearm, medial hand and little finger (C8–T1)
deficits.sign: Sensory loss along the ulnar border of the forearm and hand
Horner syndrome when the T1 root is avulsed
Proximal muscles preserved

syn-klumpke.reasoning: Traction on the abducted arm stretches the lower roots of the plexus, C8 and T1, and the lower trunk they form. These fibers pass through the medial cord into the ulnar nerve for the interossei, the hypothenar muscles and the medial long finger flexors, and into the median nerve for the thenar muscles and the lateral finger flexors, so all the intrinsic muscles and the finger flexors fail together: the unopposed extensors and the loss of lumbrical action produce the claw posture, and grip is lost. The shoulder and elbow muscles, supplied from C5–C7 through the upper and middle trunks, are unaffected. The C8 and T1 dermatomes cover the medial forearm and the ulnar side of the hand, so sensory loss lies there; involvement of the medial forearm distinguishes a lower plexus lesion from an ulnar neuropathy, whose sensory territory stops at the wrist. The preganglionic sympathetic fibers for the eye leave the cord in the T1 root and pass through the stellate ganglion, so avulsion of the root also produces a Horner syndrome on the same side, a sign that the injury is at the cord and cannot be repaired. All signs are ipsilateral since the plexus is a peripheral structure. Chronic compression of the lower trunk by a cervical rib or fibrous band produces the same pattern slowly as neurogenic thoracic outlet syndrome, and infiltration by an apical lung tumor produces it with pain and a Horner.

imagingFindings.finding: T2 hyperintensity of the C8–T1 roots and lower trunk on MR neurography; pseudomeningocele at T1 with avulsion.
Apical mass invading the lower trunk and stellate ganglion in adults with painful progressive lower plexopathy.
Denervation in C8–T1 muscles of both ulnar and median territories; medial antebrachial cutaneous sensory response absent in postganglionic lesions, preserved in avulsion.

imagingHint.label: lower trunk of the brachial plexus over the first rib

commonCauses: Traction injury with the arm abducted
Obstetric injury (rare, usually with the whole plexus)
Cervical rib and neurogenic thoracic outlet syndrome

mimics.name: Ulnar neuropathy at the elbow
mimics.howToDistinguish: Sensory loss spares the medial forearm; median-innervated thenar muscles are normal

mimics.name: C8 radiculopathy
mimics.howToDistinguish: Neck pain, paraspinal denervation, no Horner

mimics.name: Combined median and ulnar neuropathy
mimics.howToDistinguish: Sensory loss follows nerve territories, sparing the forearm

management: Look for a Horner and image the lung apex in adult lower plexopathy
EMG to define the level; surgical exploration if no recovery
Hand therapy and splinting for the claw deformity

syn-kluver-bucy.name: Klüver–Bucy syndrome
syn-kluver-bucy.presentation: After recovering from herpes simplex encephalitis, or with a frontotemporal dementia or bilateral temporal injury, a patient becomes strangely placid, examines every object by putting it in the mouth, eats indiscriminately including inedible things, makes inappropriate sexual advances, cannot recognize familiar people or objects by sight, and is compulsively drawn to touch and inspect whatever comes into view. Memory is often severely impaired as well.

deficits.sign: Placidity, loss of fear and aggression, blunted emotional response
Hyperorality, dietary changes and hyperphagia; hypersexuality
Visual agnosia (psychic blindness) and hypermetamorphosis (compulsive attention to visual stimuli)
Amnesia when the hippocampi are involved

syn-kluver-bucy.reasoning: The amygdala attaches emotional and motivational value to what is perceived: it receives highly processed visual, auditory and gustatory information from the temporal cortex and returns outputs to the hypothalamus and brainstem that generate fear, aggression, feeding and sexual responses. When both amygdalae and the surrounding anterior temporal cortex are destroyed, objects are seen but stripped of their meaning and their emotional tag, so the patient shows no fear of things that should frighten, no disgust at things that should be avoided and no restraint in eating or sexual behavior, and returns to exploring the world by mouth and hand like an infant because visual recognition no longer suffices. The inferotemporal visual association cortex, adjacent to the amygdala, accounts for the visual agnosia, and the hippocampi, further back, for the amnesia. The syndrome requires bilateral lesions because each amygdala is connected with both hemispheres' association cortex and one is enough to sustain emotional evaluation; unilateral temporal lesions produce only subtle changes, and there is no ipsilateral or contralateral pattern. Herpes simplex encephalitis targets the medial temporal lobes bilaterally, which is why it is the commonest cause in adults; frontotemporal dementia, bilateral temporal trauma, hypoxia, Pick disease and bilateral temporal lobectomy are the others. The full syndrome as described in monkeys is rare in humans; partial forms with placidity and hyperorality are more common.

imagingFindings.finding: Bilateral, asymmetric T2/FLAIR hyperintensity and restricted diffusion in the medial temporal lobes, insula and cingulate, with hemorrhage and later cystic encephalomalacia of both anterior temporal lobes.
Bilateral anterior temporal atrophy, often asymmetric, with hypometabolism on FDG-PET.
Bilateral temporal contusions after trauma or hypoxic-ischemic injury of the hippocampi and amygdalae.

imagingHint.label: both amygdalae and unci

commonCauses: Frontotemporal dementia (semantic variant) and Pick disease
Bilateral temporal lobe trauma, hypoxia or surgery

mimics.name: Frontal lobe disinhibition
mimics.howToDistinguish: Disinhibition with intact recognition and without hyperorality or visual agnosia; orbitofrontal lesion

mimics.name: Prosopagnosia
mimics.howToDistinguish: Isolated failure to recognize faces from bilateral fusiform lesions, emotion intact

mimics.name: Delirium
mimics.howToDistinguish: Fluctuating attention with a metabolic cause

management: Treat the underlying cause (acyclovir for herpes encephalitis)
Behavioral management, supervision of eating and safety; selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors or carbamazepine may reduce hyperorality and hypersexuality
Support for caregivers; the syndrome partially improves after encephalitis

syn-lacunar-ataxic-hemiparesis.name: Ataxic hemiparesis
syn-lacunar-ataxic-hemiparesis.presentation: The patient has a mild hemiparesis, usually worse in the leg, but the striking feature is an incoordination on the same side that is out of proportion to the weakness: the heel-shin test is clumsy, the arm overshoots, and gait is unsteady toward the weak side. Sensation and speech are normal. The combination of pyramidal and cerebellar signs on one side of the body points to a small deep lesion.

deficits.sign: Mild upper motor neuron hemiparesis
Limb ataxia disproportionate to the weakness
Unsteady gait veering toward the weak side

syn-lacunar-ataxic-hemiparesis.reasoning: A single perforator infarct in the posterior limb of the internal capsule, the corona radiata or the basis pontis interrupts two systems that run side by side there: the corticospinal tract and the corticopontocerebellar connections. The corticospinal fibers have not yet crossed, so the weakness is contralateral. The cerebellar signs are on the same side as the weakness because the cerebellar loop crosses twice: corticopontine fibers cross in the pons to the opposite cerebellar hemisphere, and the dentatothalamic output crosses back in the midbrain to the original hemisphere and its motor cortex. Cutting the loop at the capsule or pons on one side therefore produces ataxia of the contralateral limbs, the same limbs weakened by the corticospinal lesion. The lesion is small, so there is no sensory loss or cortical sign. The pontine site is the commoner; leg-predominant weakness is characteristic because the leg fibers lie posteriorly in the capsule and dorsolaterally in the pons.

imagingFindings.finding: Small (under 15 mm) focus of restricted diffusion in the posterior limb of the internal capsule, corona radiata or basis pontis; CT is often normal in the first day.
Small CSF-intensity cavity with a FLAIR-bright rim, often multiple, with diffuse white matter hyperintensity of small vessel disease.

syn-lacunar-dysarthria-clumsy-hand.name: Dysarthria–clumsy hand syndrome
syn-lacunar-dysarthria-clumsy-hand.presentation: Speech becomes slurred and the patient complains that one hand has become clumsy: writing deteriorates and fine tasks are fumbled, although strength is nearly normal. Examination shows facial weakness of the lower face, tongue deviation, mild hand weakness with hyperreflexia and clumsiness, and sometimes an extensor plantar. Sensation is intact.

deficits.sign: Dysarthria with lower facial weakness and tongue deviation
Clumsiness and mild weakness of the hand with hyperreflexia
Impaired fine finger movements and dysmetria

syn-lacunar-dysarthria-clumsy-hand.reasoning: This is a small-vessel infarct in the paramedian basis pontis or the genu of the internal capsule, where the corticobulbar fibers to the facial and hypoglossal nuclei run beside the corticospinal fibers for the hand. The corticobulbar fibers cross at the level of the nuclei in the pons and medulla, and the corticospinal fibers cross in the pyramidal decussation, so both the facial weakness and the hand signs are contralateral to the lesion. Involvement of the corticopontocerebellar pathway, which crosses twice like all cerebellar loops, adds the clumsiness on the same side as the weakness. The lesion is too small to reach the sensory pathways in the pontine tegmentum or the posterior capsule, and the cortex is intact, so there is no sensory loss, aphasia or field defect. It is really a fragment of the pure motor syndrome in which the face and hand fibers, which lie most anteriorly in the capsule and most medially in the crus and pons, are picked out by an even smaller infarct.

syn-lacunar-pure-motor.name: Pure motor lacunar stroke
syn-lacunar-pure-motor.presentation: A hypertensive patient wakes with weakness of the face, arm and leg on one side, all roughly equally affected, and nothing else: sensation, vision, speech content and awareness are normal, though speech may be slurred by the facial weakness. There is no headache and the patient is fully alert. The weakness may stutter over hours before settling.

deficits.sign: Hemiparesis with hyperreflexia and extensor plantar
Dysarthria from corticobulbar involvement
Sensation preserved: the hallmark of a pure motor lacune

syn-lacunar-pure-motor.reasoning: The corticospinal and corticobulbar fibers for face, arm and leg are packed into a few square millimeters in the posterior limb and genu of the internal capsule and again in the basis pontis, so a single small perforator infarct removes all of them together, producing a hemiparesis that is proportional across the body rather than following the cortical homunculus. The fibers have not yet crossed at either site, so the paralysis is contralateral, as after a cortical lesion. What distinguishes the lacune is what is missing: the thalamocortical sensory fibers lie a few millimeters posterior in the capsule and in the tegmentum of the pons, the optic radiation is far lateral and the cortex is intact, so there is no sensory loss, no field defect and no aphasia or neglect. A capsular lacune and a pontine lacune are clinically identical; imaging decides. Because the lenticulostriate and paramedian pontine perforators are end arteries damaged by hypertension, the infarct is small and recovery is often good.

syn-lacunar-pure-sensory.name: Pure sensory lacunar stroke
syn-lacunar-pure-sensory.presentation: The patient describes numbness or tingling that came on over minutes and involves the face, arm, trunk and leg of one side, sometimes splitting the midline exactly. Strength, coordination, vision and speech are unaffected. The examiner may find surprisingly little objective loss compared with the complaint, or a clear reduction of all modalities on that side.

deficits.sign: Hemihypesthesia to touch, pin and vibration, often splitting the midline
Paresthesias and reduced pin-prick
No weakness; reflexes symmetric

syn-lacunar-pure-sensory.reasoning: The ventral posterior nuclei of the thalamus receive every ascending somatic sensory pathway after it has crossed: the medial lemniscus, which crossed in the medulla, the spinothalamic tract, which crossed in the spinal cord, and the trigeminal lemniscus from the face. A lacune in the thalamogeniculate perforator territory therefore removes all modalities from the whole contralateral half of the body including the face, a combination that a spinal lesion cannot produce and a brainstem lesion produces only with crossed facial involvement. The corticospinal tract lies in the adjacent internal capsule and is spared, so there is no weakness; an infarct big enough to reach it becomes a sensorimotor stroke. A small cortical infarct of the postcentral gyrus can cause a similar restricted hemisensory deficit, but it usually spares some modality and rarely splits the trunk at the midline. Some patients later develop central post-stroke pain, when the syndrome is renamed Dejerine–Roussy.

imagingFindings.finding: Small (under 15 mm) focus of restricted diffusion in the ventral posterolateral thalamus; CT is often normal in the first day.
Small CSF-intensity cavity with a FLAIR-bright rim, often multiple, with diffuse white matter hyperintensity of small vessel disease.

syn-lacunar-sensorimotor.name: Sensorimotor lacunar stroke
syn-lacunar-sensorimotor.presentation: Weakness and numbness of the face, arm and leg on one side develop together in an alert patient who speaks and sees normally. The pattern resembles a large hemispheric stroke but the patient has none of the cortical features and CT is normal or shows only a small deep lesion. It is the commonest of the lacunar syndromes to be over-investigated for a cortical cause.

deficits.sign: Hemiparesis with upper motor neuron signs
Hemihypesthesia to all modalities
No aphasia, neglect or field defect

syn-lacunar-sensorimotor.reasoning: The lesion sits at the boundary between the posterior limb of the internal capsule and the lateral thalamus, which is where the descending corticospinal tract and the ascending thalamocortical sensory radiation lie within a few millimeters of one another. It is supplied either by a lateral lenticulostriate branch of the middle cerebral artery or by a thalamogeniculate branch of the posterior cerebral artery, and an infarct slightly larger than the usual lacune spans both. The corticospinal tract has not yet crossed, and the sensory pathways have already crossed below, so both deficits appear on the contralateral side, together. What proves the lesion is deep rather than cortical is the absence of all cortical functions: the language areas, the parietal spatial cortex and the optic radiation are untouched, and the patient is alert with normal gaze. The differential from a small cortical infarct rests on this absence plus imaging, since a pure hemiparesis with hemianesthesia can also follow a striatocapsular infarct or an anterior choroidal artery infarct, the latter usually adding a field defect.

imagingFindings.finding: Small (under 15 mm) focus of restricted diffusion in the posterior limb of the internal capsule and adjacent thalamus; CT is often normal in the first day.
Small CSF-intensity cavity with a FLAIR-bright rim, often multiple, with diffuse white matter hyperintensity of small vessel disease.

mimics.howToDistinguish: Cortical signs (aphasia, neglect, field loss, gaze deviation) exclude a lacune

mimics.name: Small hemorrhage
mimics.howToDistinguish: Hyperdense on CT; same sites

mimics.name: Anterior choroidal artery infarct
mimics.howToDistinguish: Adds a homonymous hemianopia

management: Antiplatelet therapy, statin and blood pressure control
Thrombolysis when presenting within the window and disabling
Early mobilization; prognosis for recovery is good

html.presentation: Weakness and numbness of the face, arm and leg on one side develop together in an alert patient who speaks and sees normally. The pattern resembles a large hemispheric stroke but the patient has none of the cortical features and CT is normal or shows only a small deep lesion. It is the commonest of the lacunar syndromes to be over-investigated for a cortical cause.
html.reasoning: The lesion sits at the boundary between the posterior limb of the internal capsule and the lateral thalamus, which is where the descending corticospinal tract and the ascending thalamocortical sensory radiation lie within a few millimeters of one another. It is supplied either by a lateral lenticulostriate branch of the middle cerebral artery or by a thalamogeniculate branch of the posterior cerebral artery, and an infarct slightly larger than the usual lacune spans both. The corticospinal tract has not yet crossed, and the sensory pathways have already crossed below, so both deficits appear on the contralateral side, together. What proves the lesion is deep rather than cortical is the absence of all cortical functions: the language areas, the parietal spatial cortex and the optic radiation are untouched, and the patient is alert with normal gaze. The differential from a small cortical infarct rests on this absence plus imaging, since a pure hemiparesis with hemianesthesia can also follow a striatocapsular infarct or an anterior choroidal artery infarct, the latter usually adding a field defect.

syn-lambert-eaton.name: Lambert–Eaton myasthenic syndrome
syn-lambert-eaton.presentation: A long-term smoker develops weakness of the thighs and hips that makes rising from a chair and climbing stairs difficult, with aching muscles, a dry mouth and impotence. The weakness is worst after rest and improves briefly after a few seconds of effort; the reflexes are absent at first but appear after the patient contracts the muscle for ten seconds. Ptosis and diplopia are mild or absent, and swallowing is usually preserved. A small cell lung cancer is found in half the patients, sometimes years later.

deficits.sign: Proximal weakness that facilitates briefly with exercise
Absent or reduced reflexes that return after brief maximal contraction (post-exercise facilitation)
Dry mouth, constipation, erectile dysfunction, orthostatic hypotension, reduced sweating
Mild ptosis or diplopia; bulbar and respiratory involvement uncommon

syn-lambert-eaton.reasoning: Antibodies against the P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channels of the presynaptic motor nerve terminal reduce the calcium entry that triggers acetylcholine release, so each nerve impulse releases too few quanta and the endplate potential often fails to reach threshold. The muscle fibers and their receptors are normal, so the defect is presynaptic, the reverse of myasthenia gravis: because repetitive stimulation at high frequency or a brief voluntary contraction lets calcium accumulate in the terminal, transmission improves for a few seconds, which is why strength and reflexes facilitate with exercise and why the compound muscle action potential increments by more than 100% on rapid repetitive stimulation, whereas in myasthenia it decrements. The same calcium channels operate at the terminals of autonomic cholinergic neurons, so the parasympathetic and sudomotor failure that gives the dry mouth, constipation and erectile dysfunction is part of the disease and helps separate it from myasthenia. The antibodies arise in about half of patients as an immune response to a small cell lung carcinoma, which expresses the same channels, and the neurological syndrome typically precedes the tumor's detection; the remainder are autoimmune without cancer, often with other autoimmune disease. Everything is bilateral and symmetric, a disorder of transmission rather than of any anatomical pathway, so there is no crossing or lateralization to consider.

imagingFindings.finding: Small resting compound muscle action potentials, decrement at low-frequency stimulation, and an increment of over 100% after 10 seconds of maximal exercise or 50 Hz stimulation; increased jitter on single-fiber EMG.
Hilar or mediastinal mass on chest CT; FDG-PET if CT is negative, repeated over two years, since the tumor may lag the syndrome.
Serology alongside electrodiagnosis: P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channel antibodies in 85–90%; SOX1 antibodies favor a paraneoplastic cause.

imagingHint.label: the defect is at neuromuscular junctions throughout the body; the lumbosacral roots stand in for the proximal legs

commonCauses: Autoimmune non-paraneoplastic (often with thyroid disease or type 1 diabetes)

mimics.name: Myasthenia gravis
mimics.howToDistinguish: Ocular and bulbar predominance, fatigability without facilitation, normal reflexes and autonomic function, decrement without increment

mimics.name: Inflammatory myopathy
mimics.howToDistinguish: Proximal weakness with raised CK and myopathic EMG; reflexes preserved

mimics.name: Guillain–Barré or CIDP
mimics.howToDistinguish: Sensory symptoms, demyelinating conduction changes

mimics.name: Botulism
mimics.howToDistinguish: Acute, descending, with ophthalmoplegia and dilated pupils; also presynaptic

Amifampridine (3,4-diaminopyridine) improves strength; pyridostigmine adds little; immunosuppression or IVIG for severe cases
Treat the tumor: this often improves the neurological syndrome

syn-length-dependent-polyneuropathy.name: Length-dependent sensorimotor polyneuropathy
syn-length-dependent-polyneuropathy.presentation: A patient with long-standing diabetes describes numbness and burning of both feet that began in the toes and has crept up to the ankles over a year or two, with unsteadiness in the dark. The ankle reflexes are absent, vibration sense is lost at the toes and reduced at the ankles, pin-prick is dulled in a stocking distribution, and when the numbness reaches the knees the fingertips begin to tingle. Toe extension is mildly weak and the feet are dry and hairless.

deficits.sign: Symmetric distal loss of all modalities beginning in the toes; large-fiber loss gives vibration and proprioceptive loss with sensory ataxia, small-fiber loss gives burning pain and reduced pin-prick
Absent ankle reflexes with preserved knee reflexes until late

deficits.distribution: intrinsic foot muscles, toe and ankle dorsiflexors
deficits.sign: Mild distal weakness and wasting late in the course
Dry skin, hair loss, orthostatic hypotension, gastroparesis, erectile dysfunction in small-fiber and autonomic involvement

syn-length-dependent-polyneuropathy.reasoning: In a metabolic, toxic or hereditary neuropathy the axon is affected along its whole length, and the longest axons fail first because the distal part of a long axon is farthest from the cell body that maintains it. The longest axons in the body run from the dorsal root ganglia and anterior horns of the lumbosacral cord to the toes, so symptoms begin in the toes of both feet simultaneously and ascend, and when the sensory loss has reached mid-calf the axons of comparable length to the fingertips begin to fail, giving the glove that follows the stocking; the anterior trunk may develop a patch of loss when the intercostal axons reach the threshold length. The process is symmetric because both legs' axons are equally long, and there is no crossed pattern, since the lesion lies entirely in the peripheral nervous system in the ipsilateral nerves. Sensory fibers suffer before motor fibers in most axonal neuropathies, and the ankle reflex, whose afferent limb is the longest sensory arc, disappears first. Large-fiber loss removes vibration and proprioception and causes sensory ataxia and a positive Romberg; small-fiber loss produces burning pain, loss of pin-prick and temperature discrimination and autonomic failure, and may occur alone with normal conduction studies. Asymmetry, proximal onset, marked weakness, a rapid course or cranial nerve involvement argue against a length-dependent process and point to a demyelinating, vasculitic or infiltrative neuropathy.

imagingFindings.finding: Reduced sural and superficial peroneal sensory amplitudes, then reduced peroneal and tibial motor amplitudes with relatively preserved conduction velocities; distal denervation. Small-fiber neuropathy has normal studies.
Reduced intraepidermal nerve fiber density at the distal leg compared with the thigh.
Slowed conduction velocities, prolonged distal latencies and conduction block point to CIDP or hereditary demyelination instead.

imagingHint.label: lumbosacral roots and dorsal root ganglia

commonCauses: Alcohol and nutritional deficiency (B12, thiamine, B6 excess)

mimics.name: Lumbar spinal stenosis
mimics.howToDistinguish: Symptoms with walking relieved by sitting, asymmetric, root pattern

mimics.name: Bilateral tarsal tunnel
mimics.howToDistinguish: Soles only, dorsum spared

mimics.name: Myelopathy
mimics.howToDistinguish: Brisk reflexes and extensor plantars with a sensory level

mimics.name: Sensory neuronopathy (ganglionopathy)

management: Screen: glucose tolerance, B12, serum protein electrophoresis, renal and thyroid function; nerve conduction studies to confirm the axonal length-dependent pattern
Treat the cause and control pain with gabapentinoids, duloxetine or tricyclics

syn-locked-in.name: Locked-in syndrome
syn-locked-in.presentation: A patient lies motionless and mute after a brainstem stroke and is assumed to be comatose, until a nurse notices that they blink on request and can look up and down. They cannot move any limb, cannot speak or swallow, and cannot look to either side, but they hear, see, feel and understand everything. Ask for eye movements before concluding that a patient with bilateral pontine signs is unconscious.

deficits.sign: Quadriplegia with bilateral extensor plantars
Anarthria and aphagia; the face is paralyzed bilaterally
Loss of horizontal gaze with preserved vertical movement and blinking
Full awareness; EEG normal; sleep-wake cycles intact

syn-locked-in.reasoning: A lesion of the ventral pons destroys the corticospinal and corticobulbar fibers of both sides as they pass through the basis pontis on their way to the pyramidal decussation in the medulla, so every voluntary movement below the midbrain is lost bilaterally: limbs, face, tongue, palate and larynx. The horizontal gaze machinery, the abducens nuclei and the paramedian pontine reticular formation, sits in the caudal pontine tegmentum and is usually caught as well, whereas the vertical gaze center in the rostral midbrain, the oculomotor nuclei and the levator palpebrae are supplied from above the occlusion and survive, leaving vertical gaze and blinking as the only channels of output. The reticular activating system in the pontine and midbrain tegmentum is spared in the classic ventral lesion, so consciousness, sensation via the intact lemniscal and spinothalamic pathways in the tegmentum, and hearing are all preserved. The dissociation between an intact mind and a paralyzed body is the syndrome; when the tegmentum is also infarcted the patient is comatose instead.

imagingFindings.finding: Bilateral restricted diffusion in the basis pontis with relative sparing of the tegmentum; basilar occlusion on angiography.
Central pontine T2 hyperintensity (osmotic demyelination) or hematoma producing the same syndrome.

imagingHint.label: ventral pons

commonCauses: Trauma or tumor of the ventral pons

mimics.name: Coma
mimics.howToDistinguish: Locked-in patients blink and look vertically on command; EEG shows a normal awake rhythm

mimics.name: Severe Guillain–Barré syndrome
mimics.howToDistinguish: Peripheral, areflexic, ophthalmoplegia complete including vertical movements, normal brain MRI

mimics.name: Akinetic mutism
mimics.howToDistinguish: Patient can move but does not; lesion is frontal or thalamic

management: Establish yes/no communication with eye movements or blinks immediately and inform the team
Airway, nutrition and pressure care as for quadriplegia
Consider thrombectomy when presenting within the window with a basilar occlusion

syn-lumbar-stenosis.name: Lumbar spinal stenosis (neurogenic claudication)
syn-lumbar-stenosis.presentation: An older patient reports that walking brings on aching, heaviness and tingling in the buttocks and legs that force them to stop after a few hundred meters, and that the symptoms fade over minutes when they sit or lean forward on a shopping trolley; walking uphill and cycling are easier than walking downhill. At rest the examination is nearly normal, with mild reflex loss at most, and the pedal pulses are present. The distance walked before symptoms shrinks over years.

deficits.distribution: buttocks, thighs and calves, often asymmetric
deficits.sign: Neurogenic claudication: pain and paresthesias on standing and walking, relieved by sitting and lumbar flexion
Weakness or heaviness after walking; mild fixed weakness (foot drop) in advanced cases
Reduced or absent ankle reflexes, sometimes after exercise only
Urgency or retention with severe central stenosis

syn-lumbar-stenosis.reasoning: Degenerative narrowing of the lumbar canal by disc bulging, facet joint hypertrophy and a thickened ligamentum flavum, usually at L4–L5 and L3–L4, compresses the cauda equina and its blood supply. The canal is narrowest in extension, when the ligamentum flavum buckles inward and the disc bulges, and widest in flexion, so standing and walking, which extend the spine, provoke the symptoms and sitting, bending forward and cycling relieve them, the opposite of the vascular claudication that depends only on muscle work and is relieved by standing still. The roots of the cauda equina are peripheral nerve roots, so the deficit when it appears is lower motor neuron and radicular, with areflexia and dermatomal or multiradicular sensory symptoms, bilateral because the stenosis is central but often asymmetric, and there is no crossing to reason about because the lesion is below the cord. The intermittent nature of the symptoms is attributed to venous congestion and ischemia of the compressed roots during standing, which resolve on flexion, so the resting examination is often normal and a walk down the corridor before re-examination is the most useful bedside test. Lateral recess and foraminal stenosis produce a single-root picture instead, and severe central stenosis can progress to a cauda equina syndrome.

imagingFindings.finding: Trefoil canal with obliteration of the CSF around the cauda equina, ligamentum flavum hypertrophy and facet arthropathy at one or more levels on axial T2; redundant, tortuous roots above the stenosis.
Forward slip of L4 on L5 with facet arthropathy narrowing the canal; upright or flexion-extension views show instability.
Often normal at rest; multiradicular chronic denervation in advanced cases, useful to exclude polyneuropathy.

imagingHint.label: lumbar canal at L3–L5

commonCauses: Degenerative spondylosis with facet and ligamentum flavum hypertrophy

mimics.name: Vascular claudication
mimics.howToDistinguish: Calf pain with a fixed walking distance, relieved by standing still, absent pulses; ABI reduced

mimics.name: Hip osteoarthritis
mimics.howToDistinguish: Groin pain with hip rotation, limited range

mimics.name: Peripheral neuropathy
mimics.howToDistinguish: Constant distal sensory loss unrelated to posture

mimics.name: Cervical or thoracic myelopathy
mimics.howToDistinguish: Spastic gait with upper motor neuron signs

management: MRI of the lumbar spine correlated with the symptoms; walking test before re-examination
Physiotherapy in flexion, analgesia, epidural steroid injection for temporary relief
Decompressive laminectomy, with fusion when there is spondylolisthesis, for disabling claudication

syn-lumbosacral-plexopathy.name: Lumbosacral plexopathy
syn-lumbosacral-plexopathy.presentation: A diabetic patient in their sixties develops severe pain in one thigh followed over weeks by weakness and wasting of the quadriceps and hip muscles, with loss of the knee jerk and marked weight loss; the other leg may follow. In a patient with pelvic cancer or after pelvic radiotherapy, a similar painful or painless leg weakness involves both femoral and sciatic territories, a distribution too wide for one nerve and too patchy for the cord.

deficits.distribution: hip flexors, quadriceps, adductors (lumbar plexus) and/or gluteal, hamstring and leg muscles (sacral plexus)
deficits.sign: Weakness and wasting spanning several nerve and root territories
Severe pain at onset (diabetic, neoplastic); painless in radiation plexopathy
Reduced knee reflex (lumbar) or ankle reflex (sacral)

deficits.distribution: anterior thigh and medial leg, or posterior thigh, lateral leg and foot
deficits.sign: Multiradicular sensory loss without a level; perineum spared
Leg edema and sympathetic changes with pelvic tumor; sphincters spared

syn-lumbosacral-plexopathy.reasoning: The lumbar plexus forms within the psoas from the L1–L4 roots and gives the femoral, obturator and lateral femoral cutaneous nerves; the sacral plexus forms on the piriformis from L4–S3 and gives the sciatic, gluteal and pudendal nerves. A lesion of the plexus, lying between the roots and the individual nerves, produces a deficit that is broader than any one nerve and does not follow one root: a lumbar plexopathy weakens hip flexion, knee extension and adduction together (femoral plus obturator territory), which a femoral neuropathy cannot do, and a sacral plexopathy weakens the glutei and the sciatic muscles together, which a sciatic lesion cannot do. The lesion is peripheral and ipsilateral, though the diabetic form often spreads to the other side after a delay. The perineum and sphincters are spared because the sacral roots to the pudendal nerve leave the plexus separately and the conus is intact, and there is no sensory level, which separates plexopathy from a conus or cauda equina lesion; sensory nerve action potentials are reduced because the lesion is distal to the dorsal root ganglia, which separates it from a radiculopathy, in which they are preserved, and paraspinal muscles are spared. Diabetic radiculoplexus neuropathy is an inflammatory microvasculitis of the roots and plexus; malignant plexopathy is infiltration from cervical, prostatic, colorectal or lymphomatous tumor, painful and progressive; radiation plexopathy appears years after treatment, is painless and shows myokymia on EMG; and a psoas hematoma or abscess compresses the lumbar plexus acutely.

imagingFindings.finding: Enhancing tumor along the pelvic sidewall or in the psoas encasing the plexus; psoas hematoma or abscess displacing it; thickened enhancing plexus in diabetic and inflammatory forms on MR neurography.
Diffuse thickening and T2 change of the plexus within the radiation field without a discrete mass; myokymia on EMG.
Denervation across several nerve territories of one limb sparing the paraspinal muscles, with reduced sensory responses (postganglionic); myokymic discharges in radiation plexopathy.
No root compression matching the deficit; excludes cauda equina lesion.

imagingHint.label: lumbosacral plexus in the psoas and on the pelvic sidewall (virtual)

commonCauses: Pelvic malignancy (cervix, prostate, colorectal, lymphoma, sarcoma)
Retroperitoneal or psoas hematoma (anticoagulation) or abscess
Pelvic fracture or surgery, obstetric compression

mimics.name: Lumbosacral polyradiculopathy
mimics.howToDistinguish: Paraspinal denervation, preserved sensory responses, root compression or leptomeningeal enhancement on MRI

mimics.name: Femoral or sciatic mononeuropathy
mimics.howToDistinguish: Deficit confined to one nerve

mimics.name: Cauda equina or conus lesion
mimics.howToDistinguish: Bilateral, saddle anesthesia, sphincter loss

mimics.name: Hip disease
mimics.howToDistinguish: Pain on joint movement without neurological deficit

management: MRI of the pelvis and lumbar spine with contrast; EMG to define the distribution and exclude radiculopathy; screen for diabetes and malignancy
Diabetic amyotrophy: glycemic control, pain management, physiotherapy; immunotherapy is debated; recovery over 1–2 years
Treat tumor or hematoma; radiation plexopathy is managed supportively

syn-mca-inferior-division.name: Middle cerebral artery inferior division infarction
syn-mca-inferior-division.presentation: The patient is brought in speaking fluently but nonsensically, unaware that anything is wrong, and is sometimes mistaken for being confused or psychotic. Examination shows a superior quadrantanopia or hemianopia and, in the dominant hemisphere, poor comprehension and repetition with paraphasic speech; in the non-dominant hemisphere there is neglect, constructional apraxia and flat prosody. Weakness is absent or minimal, which makes the stroke easy to miss.

deficits.sign: Fluent (Wernicke) aphasia with impaired comprehension and repetition
Field defect from the temporal optic radiation (Meyer's loop)
Hemispatial neglect, anosognosia, aprosodia
Gerstmann features (acalculia, agraphia, finger agnosia, right-left confusion)

syn-mca-inferior-division.reasoning: The inferior division supplies the temporal lobe and the inferior parietal lobule: the superior temporal gyrus with Wernicke's area, the angular and supramarginal gyri, and the deep temporal white matter through which Meyer's loop of the optic radiation runs. The motor and somatosensory cortices belong to the superior division, so strength and primary sensation are preserved. The optic radiation carries the contralateral visual field: fibers for the upper field pass through the temporal lobe, so the defect is a contralateral superior quadrantanopia, becoming a full hemianopia when the parietal fibers are also involved. Language comprehension depends on the dominant posterior superior temporal gyrus, hence fluent aphasia with poor comprehension. The corresponding non-dominant parietal cortex builds the map of contralateral space, so its loss gives neglect of the left side and lack of awareness of the deficit. Because the corticospinal tract is untouched there is no crossed weakness to draw attention to the stroke, and the agitation of a Wernicke aphasic is often misread as a psychiatric emergency.

imagingFindings.finding: Restricted diffusion in the posterior superior temporal gyrus and inferior parietal lobule with preserved frontal cortex and deep nuclei.
Encephalomalacia of the posterior Sylvian region with ex-vacuo dilatation of the temporal horn.

imagingHint.label: posterior superior temporal gyrus

mimics.name: Acute psychosis or delirium
mimics.howToDistinguish: Field defect, paraphasias and neglect point to a focal lesion; DWI positive

mimics.name: Herpes encephalitis
mimics.howToDistinguish: Fever, seizures, temporal T2 change crossing vascular boundaries

mimics.name: Transcortical sensory aphasia
mimics.howToDistinguish: Repetition preserved; watershed location

management: Acute stroke treatment as for any MCA occlusion
Formal language and neglect assessment; neglect predicts poor rehabilitation outcome
Driving restriction because of the field defect

syn-mca-stem-infarct.name: Middle cerebral artery stem (M1) infarction
syn-mca-stem-infarct.presentation: The patient collapses with dense weakness of the face, arm and leg on one side, loss of sensation on the same side, a homonymous hemianopia and the eyes deviated toward the side of the lesion. If the dominant hemisphere is affected they are globally aphasic; if the non-dominant hemisphere, they neglect the left side and deny the deficit. Over the next two or three days the swelling brain may cause drowsiness and herniation, the malignant middle cerebral artery syndrome.

syn-mca-superior-division.name: Middle cerebral artery superior division infarction
syn-mca-superior-division.presentation: Weakness and numbness of the face and arm develop suddenly, with the leg relatively spared, and the eyes are turned toward the side of the infarct for the first day or two. In the dominant hemisphere the patient understands but cannot produce fluent speech: output is effortful and telegraphic, repetition is poor and there is often apraxia of the non-paralyzed hand. Non-fluent (Broca) aphasia with preserved comprehension

mimics.name: Inferior division infarct

mimics.howToDistinguish: Seizures, headache and a hemorrhagic cortical lesion on imaging

syn-meniere.name: Ménière disease
syn-meniere.presentation: A middle-aged patient describes attacks of spinning vertigo lasting from twenty minutes to several hours, preceded by a feeling of fullness in one ear, a roaring tinnitus and muffled hearing, with vomiting and unsteadiness during the attack. Between attacks hearing in that ear gradually declines, first for low tones and then across frequencies. Over years the vertigo burns out as the labyrinth is destroyed, leaving a deaf ear and occasional drop attacks.

deficits.sign: Episodic vertigo of 20 minutes to 12 hours with peripheral-type nystagmus during attacks
Fluctuating then progressive low-frequency sensorineural hearing loss with aural fullness and tinnitus
Tumarkin otolithic crises: sudden falls without loss of consciousness in late disease

syn-meniere.reasoning: The membranous labyrinth is filled with endolymph, produced by the stria vascularis and absorbed in the endolymphatic sac. In Ménière disease absorption fails and endolymph accumulates, distending the cochlear duct and the saccule (endolymphatic hydrops). The distended membranes stretch the hair cells, and periodic ruptures or leaks mix potassium-rich endolymph with perilymph, depolarizing and temporarily paralyzing the hair cells and their nerve fibers; the sudden loss of one labyrinth's output creates an acute imbalance between the two sides, perceived as rotation with nystagmus initially toward and then away from the affected ear as the labyrinth first fires excessively and then fails. Because the cochlea and vestibular labyrinth share the same fluid, hearing and balance are affected together, and the low-frequency apex of the cochlea, where the duct is most distensible, suffers first, producing the characteristic low-tone loss and fullness. Each attack leaves a little permanent hair cell damage, so hearing declines stepwise and the vestibular function is eventually lost, at which point the vertigo stops. The disorder is peripheral and unilateral in most patients, with no central or crossed signs, and the length of the attacks separates it from the seconds of BPPV and the days of neuritis. About a third of patients eventually develop disease in the other ear.

imagingFindings.finding: Delayed post-gadolinium 3D-FLAIR of the inner ear shows an enlarged non-enhancing endolymphatic space in the cochlea and vestibule; otherwise the MRI is normal.

imagingHint.label: inner ear and vestibulocochlear nerve

mimics.name: Vestibular migraine
mimics.howToDistinguish: Attacks with headache or photophobia; hearing preserved

mimics.name: Vestibular schwannoma
mimics.howToDistinguish: Progressive, non-fluctuating loss with poor discrimination; MRI

mimics.name: BPPV
mimics.howToDistinguish: Seconds-long positional attacks; hearing normal

mimics.name: Transient ischemic attack of the labyrinth
mimics.howToDistinguish: Vasculopath, brief, with other posterior circulation symptoms

management: Audiometry and MRI to exclude a retrocochlear cause
Salt restriction and a diuretic; vestibular suppressants during attacks
Intratympanic steroids or gentamicin, or endolymphatic sac surgery, for intractable vertigo
