syn-meralgia-paresthetica.name: Meralgia paresthetica
syn-meralgia-paresthetica.presentation: An overweight patient, or one who has recently lost weight or wears a heavy belt, complains of burning, tingling and numbness over an oval patch on the outer thigh, worse on standing and walking and relieved by sitting. There is no weakness, the knee reflex is normal and the sensory loss is sharply confined to the anterolateral thigh above the knee. Pressure just inside the anterior superior iliac spine reproduces the discomfort.

deficits.sign: Burning paresthesias, allodynia and later numbness in an oval area on the lateral thigh
No weakness; knee reflex normal
Pain worse with standing, hip extension and tight clothing

syn-meralgia-paresthetica.reasoning: The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve is a purely sensory branch of the lumbar plexus from the L2 and L3 roots that crosses the iliacus and leaves the pelvis by passing under, through or over the lateral end of the inguinal ligament just medial to the anterior superior iliac spine, where it turns sharply from a horizontal to a vertical course. At that angle it is compressed by a tight belt, a protuberant abdomen, pregnancy, prolonged hip extension or scar, and it can be injured during pelvic surgery or iliac crest bone harvest. Because the nerve carries no motor fibers and no reflex arc, the syndrome is purely sensory, which is its most useful feature: any weakness of the quadriceps or loss of the knee jerk means the femoral nerve or the L2–L4 roots are involved instead. The territory is the anterolateral thigh from the greater trochanter to the knee, which overlaps the L2–L3 dermatomes, but a root lesion would produce back pain, would extend medially and would involve the iliopsoas or quadriceps. The lesion is peripheral and ipsilateral, though it is bilateral in about a fifth of patients with obesity or diabetes. Sensory conduction of the nerve is technically difficult, so the diagnosis is clinical, confirmed if necessary by relief after a local anesthetic block at the inguinal ligament.

imagingFindings.finding: Enlarged, hypoechoic lateral femoral cutaneous nerve at the inguinal ligament; ultrasound also guides the diagnostic block.
Mass along the nerve's course over the iliacus when the onset is progressive or bilateral without a mechanical cause.

imagingHint.label: lateral femoral cutaneous nerve at the anterior superior iliac spine (virtual)

commonCauses: Obesity, pregnancy, tight belts and clothing
Prolonged hip extension or lying prone
Pelvic surgery, iliac crest harvest, hernia repair

mimics.name: L2–L3 radiculopathy

mimics.name: Femoral neuropathy
mimics.howToDistinguish: Quadriceps weakness and absent knee jerk

mimics.name: Trochanteric bursitis
mimics.howToDistinguish: Tenderness over the trochanter with normal sensation

syn-millard-gubler.name: Millard–Gubler syndrome (ventral pontine)
syn-millard-gubler.presentation: A patient has a complete facial palsy on one side, including the forehead, and a hemiparesis of the arm and leg on the opposite side. Often the eye on the side of the facial palsy cannot abduct, adding horizontal diplopia. Sensation may be preserved or reduced on the weak side. The crossed facial and limb weakness locates the lesion to the ventral pons.

deficits.sign: Lower motor neuron facial palsy from the facial nerve fascicle
Hemiparesis from the corticospinal fibers in the basis pontis
Abducens palsy when the sixth nerve fascicle is included
Hemisensory loss if the lesion extends to the medial lemniscus

syn-millard-gubler.reasoning: The facial nerve fascicle leaves the facial motor nucleus in the caudal pontine tegmentum, loops around the abducens nucleus and then runs ventrolaterally through the basis pontis to emerge at the pontomedullary junction; on its way it passes right through the field of corticospinal bundles descending in the basis pontis. A lesion of the ventrocaudal pons therefore hits the uncrossed corticospinal fibers, which will cross in the medulla and so paralyze the contralateral limbs, together with the facial nerve fibers, which are already the final lower motor neuron for the ipsilateral face and so paralyze the whole ipsilateral face including the forehead. The abducens fascicle runs a similar ventral course from its nucleus and is frequently caught, adding ipsilateral abduction failure. This 'alternating' pattern, cranial nerve on one side and limbs on the other, is the signature of a brainstem lesion, and the specific nerve names the level: facial and abducens for the caudal pons, oculomotor for the midbrain, hypoglossal for the medulla. The forehead involvement separates the pontine facial palsy from the forehead-sparing central weakness of a capsular lesion, where the face and limbs are weak on the same side.

imagingFindings.finding: Restricted diffusion in the ventrolateral caudal pons on the side of the facial palsy.
Hematoma or a 'popcorn' cavernoma with a hemosiderin rim in the ventral pons.
Expansile glioma of the pons in a child.

imagingHint.label: ventrolateral caudal pons

mimics.name: Bell palsy with an unrelated capsular stroke
mimics.howToDistinguish: Two lesions; the hemiparesis is on the same side as the facial palsy in a capsular lesion

mimics.name: Foville syndrome
mimics.howToDistinguish: Adds a conjugate gaze palsy from the abducens nucleus or PPRF (dorsal pons)

mimics.name: Cerebellopontine angle mass
mimics.howToDistinguish: Facial and eighth nerve signs without contralateral limb weakness

management: Acute stroke treatment when vascular
Eye protection for the paralyzed lid
Investigate for cavernoma or demyelination in young patients

syn-mononeuritis-multiplex.name: Mononeuritis multiplex
syn-mononeuritis-multiplex.presentation: A patient with a systemic illness, weight loss, fever, rash or a known connective tissue disease develops a painful foot drop, then weeks later numbness and weakness in the ulnar territory of the opposite hand, then a wrist drop. Each episode is a sudden, painful lesion of one named nerve, and the accumulation of several such lesions in a random, asymmetric pattern is the signature of nerve infarction from vasculitis, which needs urgent immunosuppression.

deficits.distribution: individual named nerves, asymmetric and stepwise (peroneal, ulnar, radial, median, tibial)
deficits.sign: Acute painful weakness in one nerve's distribution, accumulating over weeks to months
Sensory loss following named nerves rather than a stocking pattern
Deep aching and burning pain at the onset of each lesion
Fever, weight loss, purpura, arthralgia, renal or pulmonary involvement

syn-mononeuritis-multiplex.reasoning: Each peripheral nerve is supplied by small vasa nervorum, and when these vessels are inflamed and occluded by vasculitis, whether polyarteritis nodosa, ANCA-associated vasculitis, rheumatoid or cryoglobulinemic vasculitis or a non-systemic vasculitic neuropathy, the nerve infarcts at the watershed between its nutrient arteries, in the mid-thigh for the sciatic and peroneal fibers and the mid-arm for the ulnar and radial nerves. Because infarcts occur one nerve at a time and at random, the deficits are asymmetric, follow the anatomy of named nerves rather than roots or a stocking-glove length-dependent pattern, and accumulate stepwise; the lesions are peripheral and each is ipsilateral to its own nerve, with no crossing to reason about, and the process is 'multiplex' because both sides are eventually involved. Pain is prominent because ischemia inflames the nerve and its sheath. With time the many overlapping nerve infarcts merge into a confluent asymmetric polyneuropathy that can be mistaken for a length-dependent one, so the history of stepwise nerve-by-nerve onset is decisive. Nerve conduction shows axonal loss in the affected nerves with preserved conduction in their neighbors, and biopsy of an affected nerve with its accompanying muscle shows the vasculitis. Diabetes, leprosy, sarcoidosis, HIV, hepatitis B and C, lymphoma and hereditary neuropathy with liability to pressure palsies produce multiple mononeuropathies by other mechanisms.

imagingFindings.finding: Asymmetric axonal loss confined to individual nerves (reduced sensory and motor amplitudes) with normal neighboring nerves; later confluent asymmetric axonal polyneuropathy. Pseudo-conduction block early after an infarct.

Imaging is normal; biopsy of the sural or superficial peroneal nerve with peroneus brevis shows transmural inflammation and fibrinoid necrosis of epineurial vessels with axonal loss. MR neurography may show focal nerve enlargement and enhancement.
Microaneurysms of the renal and mesenteric arteries in polyarteritis nodosa; pulmonary nodules or sinus disease in ANCA vasculitis.

imagingHint.label: lumbosacral roots: the lesions themselves are in named peripheral nerves

commonCauses: ANCA-associated vasculitis (granulomatosis with polyangiitis, eosinophilic granulomatosis, microscopic polyangiitis)

mimics.howToDistinguish: Symmetric, distal, gradual, painless onset

mimics.name: Multiple entrapment neuropathies
mimics.howToDistinguish: Common sites (carpal tunnel, elbow, fibular head), painless, conduction slowing at the site

mimics.name: Multifocal motor neuropathy
mimics.howToDistinguish: Pure motor, conduction block, no pain

syn-multiple-sclerosis-pattern.name: Multiple sclerosis: the pattern of lesions in space and time
syn-multiple-sclerosis-pattern.presentation: A woman in her twenties had an episode of painful blurred vision in one eye three years ago that recovered; last year her legs became numb and stiff for a month; now she has double vision on looking to one side and a band of tingling around her chest, all worse after a hot bath. Examination shows a pale optic disc, an internuclear ophthalmoplegia, brisk reflexes with an extensor plantar, and reduced vibration sense at the ankles. Episodes separated in time and lesions separated in space, in a young adult, define the disease.

deficits.sign: Optic neuritis: subacute monocular visual loss with pain on eye movement and an afferent pupillary defect; later optic atrophy
Internuclear ophthalmoplegia, often bilateral
Partial myelitis: numbness, band-like tightness, Lhermitte sign, useless hand from posterior column lesions
Spastic paraparesis with hyperreflexia and extensor plantars; fatigue and Uhthoff phenomenon
Ataxia, intention tremor, scanning speech
Urgency, frequency, incomplete emptying
Cognitive slowing, depression, fatigue

syn-multiple-sclerosis-pattern.reasoning: Multiple sclerosis is an immune attack on central myelin that produces focal plaques of demyelination wherever oligodendrocyte myelin lies, with a predilection for the periventricular white matter around the small veins, the corpus callosum, the optic nerves, the brainstem tegmentum around the fourth ventricle and aqueduct, the cerebellar peduncles and the dorsolateral spinal cord. Each plaque blocks or slows conduction in the fibers passing through it, and the symptoms of an attack are those of the pathway interrupted: a plaque in the optic nerve, a central nervous system tract, causes monocular visual loss with an afferent pupillary defect; a plaque in the MLF disconnects the abducens interneurons from the contralateral medial rectus after they have crossed, producing an internuclear ophthalmoplegia, bilateral when the paramedian plaque spans both bundles; a dorsolateral cord plaque interrupts the uncrossed posterior column and the crossed lateral corticospinal tract on one side, giving ipsilateral proprioceptive loss and spasticity below it, often without a complete level; and cerebellar peduncle plaques give ipsilateral ataxia. Because plaques are scattered and each attack strikes a different site, the deficits accumulate in a distribution that no single lesion could produce, the dissemination in space, and because inflammation subsides and conduction partially recovers through remyelination and sodium channel redistribution, attacks remit, the dissemination in time, until progressive axonal loss produces steadily worsening disability. Heat blocks marginal conduction in demyelinated fibers, explaining the worsening in hot baths and the transient Uhthoff phenomenon. MRI now demonstrates dissemination in space and time in a single scan, and CSF oligoclonal bands show the intrathecal immune response. Neuromyelitis optica, with its long cord lesions and severe optic neuritis, and MOG antibody disease are the diseases most easily confused with it and require different treatment.

imagingFindings.finding: Ovoid T2/FLAIR-bright lesions perpendicular to the ventricles (Dawson fingers), in the corpus callosum, juxtacortical, infratentorial (pons, cerebellar peduncles) and spinal cord (short, eccentric, dorsolateral); central vein sign on SWI; hypointense 'black holes' on T1 for axonal loss.
Gadolinium enhancement, often ring or open-ring, in lesions of the last few weeks; simultaneous enhancing and non-enhancing lesions demonstrate dissemination in time.
Oligoclonal bands present in CSF but not serum in over 90% of established cases; mild lymphocytic pleocytosis.
Short-segment enhancement of the optic nerve; delayed visual evoked potentials afterward.

imagingHint.label: periventricular white matter and callosum where plaques cluster

commonCauses: Multiple sclerosis (relapsing-remitting, secondary progressive, primary progressive)

mimics.howToDistinguish: Bilateral optic neuritis with disc swelling, ADEM-like attacks, good recovery; MOG antibodies

html.presentation: A woman in her twenties had an episode of painful blurred vision in one eye three years ago that recovered; last year her legs became numb and stiff for a month; now she has double vision on looking to one side and a band of tingling around her chest, all worse after a hot bath. Examination shows a pale optic disc, an internuclear ophthalmoplegia, brisk reflexes with an extensor plantar, and reduced vibration sense at the ankles. Episodes separated in time and lesions separated in space, in a young adult, define the disease.
html.reasoning: Multiple sclerosis is an immune attack on central myelin that produces focal plaques of demyelination wherever oligodendrocyte myelin lies, with a predilection for the periventricular white matter around the small veins, the corpus callosum, the optic nerves, the brainstem tegmentum around the fourth ventricle and aqueduct, the cerebellar peduncles and the dorsolateral spinal cord. Each plaque blocks or slows conduction in the fibers passing through it, and the symptoms of an attack are those of the pathway interrupted: a plaque in the optic nerve, a central nervous system tract, causes monocular visual loss with an afferent pupillary defect; a plaque in the MLF disconnects the abducens interneurons from the contralateral medial rectus after they have crossed, producing an internuclear ophthalmoplegia, bilateral when the paramedian plaque spans both bundles; a dorsolateral cord plaque interrupts the uncrossed posterior column and the crossed lateral corticospinal tract on one side, giving ipsilateral proprioceptive loss and spasticity below it, often without a complete level; and cerebellar peduncle plaques give ipsilateral ataxia. Because plaques are scattered and each attack strikes a different site, the deficits accumulate in a distribution that no single lesion could produce, the dissemination in space, and because inflammation subsides and conduction partially recovers through remyelination and sodium channel redistribution, attacks remit, the dissemination in time, until progressive axonal loss produces steadily worsening disability. Heat blocks marginal conduction in demyelinated fibers, explaining the worsening in hot baths and the transient Uhthoff phenomenon. MRI now demonstrates dissemination in space and time in a single scan, and CSF oligoclonal bands show the intrathecal immune response. Neuromyelitis optica, with its long cord lesions and severe optic neuritis, and MOG antibody disease are the diseases most easily confused with it and require different treatment.

syn-myasthenia-gravis.name: Myasthenia gravis
syn-myasthenia-gravis.presentation: A woman in her twenties, or a man in his sixties, notices that by evening her eyelids droop and she sees double, that chewing tires halfway through a meal and her voice fades to a nasal whisper on the telephone, and that she cannot hold her arms up to dry her hair. In the morning everything is better. Examination shows fatigable ptosis on sustained upgaze, variable ophthalmoplegia that fits no single nerve, weakness of eye closure and neck flexion, normal reflexes, normal sensation and normal pupils.

deficits.sign: Fatigable ptosis and diplopia not conforming to a nerve pattern; pupils spared
Fatigable chewing, nasal dysarthria, dysphagia, myasthenic snarl
Fatigable proximal weakness worse with activity and in the evening
Myasthenic crisis: respiratory failure, often precipitated by infection or drugs
Normal reflexes, sensation and coordination

syn-myasthenia-gravis.reasoning: Antibodies against the acetylcholine receptor, or in a minority against muscle-specific kinase, reduce the number of functioning receptors at the postsynaptic membrane of the neuromuscular junction. Each nerve impulse still releases acetylcholine, but with fewer receptors the endplate potential is closer to the firing threshold, and because the amount of acetylcholine released falls during a train of impulses, successive endplate potentials drop below threshold and muscle fibers fail one by one: weakness that increases with use and recovers with rest, the defining feature. Muscles with a high firing rate and a low safety factor, the extraocular muscles and the levator, fail first, so ptosis and diplopia are the commonest presentation, and the pattern of eye movement weakness varies from hour to hour and fits no nerve or nuclear lesion; the pupil, a smooth muscle supplied by autonomic fibers, is never involved, which distinguishes ocular myasthenia from a third nerve palsy. The disease is a disorder of transmission, not of the nerve or the muscle, so there is no sensory loss, the reflexes are preserved, muscle bulk is normal until late and the nerve conduction velocities are normal, while repetitive stimulation at low frequency shows the decrement of failing junctions and single-fiber EMG shows jitter. Everything is bilateral though often asymmetric, and no crossing logic applies. The thymus is abnormal in most patients, hyperplastic in the young and a thymoma in about a tenth, and its removal helps. Bulbar and respiratory weakness can progress within hours to a crisis, and many drugs, including aminoglycosides, magnesium and beta-blockers, unmask or worsen the disease.

imagingFindings.finding: Anterior mediastinal mass (thymoma) or an enlarged thymus on contrast CT of the chest, required in every new diagnosis.
Decrement of more than 10% on 3 Hz repetitive nerve stimulation in a weak muscle; increased jitter and blocking on single-fiber EMG (most sensitive).

imagingHint.label: extraocular muscles and levator (the first muscles to fatigue)

mimics.name: Lambert–Eaton myasthenic syndrome
mimics.howToDistinguish: Proximal leg weakness that improves briefly with exercise, areflexia, dry mouth; increment on high-frequency stimulation; small cell lung cancer

mimics.name: Ocular motor nerve palsies
mimics.howToDistinguish: Fixed pattern, pupil may be involved, no fatigability

mimics.name: Botulism
mimics.howToDistinguish: Descending, fixed dilated pupils, autonomic failure

mimics.name: Oculopharyngeal or mitochondrial myopathy
mimics.howToDistinguish: Slowly progressive, non-fluctuating ptosis, no antibodies

mimics.name: Thyroid eye disease
mimics.howToDistinguish: Restrictive, with proptosis and lid retraction

management: Confirm with antibodies and electrodiagnosis; CT of the chest for thymoma; check thyroid function
Pyridostigmine for symptoms; corticosteroids and steroid-sparing immunosuppression for generalized disease; thymectomy for thymoma and for young antibody-positive patients
Crisis: measure vital capacity, intubate early, give intravenous immunoglobulin or plasma exchange; review the drug list for junction-blocking agents

syn-myopathy-pattern.name: Myopathy: the muscle disease pattern
syn-myopathy-pattern.presentation: A patient cannot rise from a low chair without using the arms, climbs stairs one at a time and cannot lift the arms to wash their hair, yet buttons, writing and walking on the flat are normal. The weakness is symmetric and proximal, the muscles are not wasted early and may be tender, the reflexes are preserved until the muscles are very weak, sensation is normal and there are no fasciculations. Dark urine, a rash over the knuckles and eyelids, or a family history each point to a cause.

deficits.distribution: proximal limb girdles, neck flexors, symmetric
deficits.sign: Symmetric proximal weakness: Gowers sign, difficulty rising and lifting the arms; distal strength preserved
Reflexes preserved in proportion to strength; lost only late
Normal sensation; no fasciculations
Myalgia, tenderness, cramps or contractures; myoglobinuria in necrotizing forms
Dysphagia, facial weakness, ptosis or respiratory failure in specific diseases

syn-myopathy-pattern.reasoning: In a myopathy the disease is in the muscle fiber itself, whether inflammatory, dystrophic, metabolic, toxic or endocrine, and the nerve supply is intact. Because the largest, most metabolically active muscles of the limb girdles and trunk are affected first and most, the weakness is proximal and symmetric, in contrast to the distal, length-dependent weakness of neuropathy and the asymmetric, regional weakness of anterior horn cell disease; sensation is normal because the sensory nerves and roots are untouched, and fasciculations are absent because the motor neuron is healthy. The reflex arc is intact, so reflexes persist until the muscle is too weak to generate a visible contraction, unlike the early areflexia of neuropathy. Nothing crosses and nothing lateralizes; the pattern is bilateral and symmetric, and any marked asymmetry (facioscapulohumeral dystrophy, inclusion body myositis with its finger flexor and quadriceps predilection) is itself a clue to the specific disease. Damaged fibers leak creatine kinase, which is raised in inflammatory, dystrophic and necrotizing myopathies but normal in steroid and many endocrine myopathies, and EMG shows small, short, polyphasic motor units that recruit early, the electrical signature of fibers dropping out of intact motor units, the opposite of the large units of reinnervation. The specific diagnosis rests on the tempo, the distribution, the skin and systemic features, the enzyme level, imaging of muscle edema or fatty replacement, and biopsy or genetic testing.

imagingFindings.finding: Small, short-duration, polyphasic motor unit potentials with early recruitment; fibrillations in inflammatory and necrotizing myopathies; normal nerve conduction.
STIR hyperintensity of inflamed muscles guiding biopsy in myositis; selective fatty infiltration patterns on T1 in dystrophies and inclusion body myositis.
Serum CK measured alongside electrodiagnosis: markedly raised in polymyositis, necrotizing myopathy and dystrophinopathies; normal in steroid myopathy and mild in inclusion body myositis.

imagingHint.label: the disease is in the muscles; the lumbosacral segments stand in for the limb girdles

commonCauses: Inflammatory: dermatomyositis, polymyositis, immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy, inclusion body myositis
Endocrine and toxic: hypothyroidism, Cushing syndrome or steroids, statins, alcohol, colchicine
Muscular dystrophies (Duchenne, Becker, limb-girdle, facioscapulohumeral, myotonic)
Metabolic: glycogen and lipid storage, mitochondrial disease, periodic paralysis

mimics.name: Myasthenia gravis
mimics.howToDistinguish: Fatigable ocular and bulbar weakness, normal CK, antibodies

mimics.name: Motor neuron disease
mimics.howToDistinguish: Fasciculations, wasting, upper motor neuron signs, asymmetric

mimics.name: Proximal neuropathy (CIDP, diabetic amyotrophy)
mimics.howToDistinguish: Areflexia, sensory loss, demyelinating conduction

mimics.name: Polymyalgia rheumatica
mimics.howToDistinguish: Pain and stiffness with normal strength and CK, raised ESR

syn-neurogenic-thoracic-outlet.name: Neurogenic thoracic outlet syndrome
syn-neurogenic-thoracic-outlet.presentation: A young adult with a long neck notices slowly progressive wasting of the thumb side of the hand, aching in the inner forearm and tingling of the little and ring fingers, worse with the arm raised. Examination shows the Gilliatt–Sumner hand: marked wasting of the abductor pollicis brevis with milder involvement of the hypothenar and interosseous muscles, and sensory loss along the medial forearm. A neck X-ray shows a cervical rib or an elongated C7 transverse process.

deficits.distribution: thenar (abductor pollicis brevis) more than hypothenar and interossei
deficits.sign: Wasting and weakness of the intrinsic hand muscles, thenar worst

deficits.distribution: medial forearm and ulnar hand (T1 > C8)
deficits.sign: Sensory loss and paresthesias along the medial forearm and little finger
Aching pain worse with arm elevation and carrying

syn-neurogenic-thoracic-outlet.reasoning: The lower trunk of the brachial plexus crosses the first rib behind the scalenus anterior, and in a minority of people a cervical rib or a fibrous band from an elongated C7 transverse process to the first rib lifts and angulates the trunk, stretching the T1 fibers most because they lie lowest and are draped most tightly over the band. The T1 root contributes most of the fibers for the abductor pollicis brevis, so the thenar wasting exceeds that of the hypothenar and interossei, which have a larger C8 contribution, a distribution that no single nerve lesion produces: it is more thenar than an ulnar neuropathy and involves the interossei and the medial forearm unlike a carpal tunnel syndrome. Sensory loss follows the T1 dermatome along the medial forearm and the C8 dermatome on the ulnar hand, and the medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve conduction is reduced, which is the most sensitive electrodiagnostic finding. All signs are ipsilateral to the band. True neurogenic thoracic outlet syndrome is rare; the far commoner 'disputed' form consists of arm pain and paresthesias without objective deficit, and vascular forms compress the subclavian vessels rather than the plexus, so an objective neurological deficit with the characteristic hand is the requirement for the diagnosis and for surgery.

imagingFindings.finding: Cervical rib or elongated C7 transverse process; a fibrous band is not seen but inferred. MR neurography may show the angulated lower trunk.

Reduced medial antebrachial cutaneous sensory response and reduced median motor amplitude with preserved median sensory response; denervation in the abductor pollicis brevis and first dorsal interosseous.
Subclavian artery stenosis or aneurysm with arm elevation, or venous thrombosis (Paget–Schroetter).

imagingHint.label: lower trunk over the first rib

commonCauses: Cervical rib with a fibrous band
Elongated C7 transverse process with a band

mimics.howToDistinguish: Thenar spared, forearm sensation spared, slowing across the elbow

mimics.name: Carpal tunnel syndrome
mimics.howToDistinguish: Sensory loss on the palmar thumb and index, no interosseous or forearm involvement

mimics.name: C8–T1 radiculopathy
mimics.howToDistinguish: Neck pain, paraspinal denervation

mimics.name: Motor neuron disease
mimics.howToDistinguish: No sensory loss, fasciculations, spreads beyond one limb

management: Confirm electrodiagnostically before surgery; X-ray and CT of the thoracic outlet
Resection of the cervical rib and band, or first rib, for objective neurogenic deficit
Physiotherapy and posture correction for disputed forms

syn-normal-pressure-hydrocephalus.name: Normal pressure hydrocephalus
syn-normal-pressure-hydrocephalus.presentation: An elderly patient shuffles into clinic with feet that seem glued to the floor, turning in several small steps, and the family report months of forgetfulness, slowness and, more recently, urinary urgency and wetting. There is no tremor and the arms swing normally. CT shows ventricles that are far larger than the sulci would predict, and after fifty milliliters of CSF is removed the gait improves for a few days.

deficits.sign: Magnetic, wide-based, shuffling gait with difficulty initiating steps and turning; upper body relatively spared
Slowing, apathy, poor attention and executive function; memory impaired secondarily
Urgency progressing to incontinence, often with indifference

syn-normal-pressure-hydrocephalus.reasoning: In normal pressure hydrocephalus CSF absorption through the arachnoid granulations is chronically impaired, often after old hemorrhage, infection or for no discoverable reason in the elderly, and the ventricles slowly enlarge while the intracranial pressure measured at a single lumbar puncture remains within the normal range, though prolonged monitoring shows intermittent pressure waves. The enlarged frontal horns stretch the periventricular white matter, and the fibers that run closest to the ventricular wall on their way from the medial frontal cortex to the internal capsule are those for the legs and for bladder control, together with the frontal-subcortical circuits that connect the prefrontal cortex to the basal ganglia and thalamus. Stretching and ischemia of these fibers explain the triad: a gait disorder that resembles parkinsonism in the legs but spares the arms, urinary urgency from loss of the frontal inhibition of the bladder reflex, and a subcortical dementia of slowing and apathy rather than the amnesia of Alzheimer disease. The process is bilateral and symmetric with no lateralizing or crossed signs. The distinction from atrophy rests on the disproportion between ventricular size and sulcal width, with crowding of the sulci at the vertex and widening of the Sylvian fissures, and from Alzheimer disease and vascular parkinsonism on the temporary improvement in gait after a large-volume lumbar puncture or a period of lumbar drainage, which also predicts the response to shunting. The gait responds best and earliest; established dementia responds least.

imagingFindings.finding: Ventriculomegaly out of proportion to sulcal atrophy (Evans index above 0.3), tight high-convexity sulci with widened Sylvian fissures (DESH), callosal angle under 90°, periventricular T2 change and an accentuated aqueductal flow void.
Normal opening pressure; objective gait improvement after removal of 30–50 mL of CSF or after 3 days of lumbar drainage predicts shunt response.
Hemosiderin from old subarachnoid hemorrhage, meningeal thickening from previous infection.

imagingHint.label: frontal horns and periventricular white matter

mimics.name: Alzheimer disease
mimics.howToDistinguish: Memory loss precedes gait change; hippocampal atrophy; no tap response

mimics.name: Vascular parkinsonism
mimics.howToDistinguish: Stepwise course with extensive white matter disease and lacunes

mimics.name: Parkinson disease
mimics.howToDistinguish: Rest tremor, asymmetric rigidity, reduced arm swing, levodopa response

mimics.name: Cervical myelopathy
mimics.howToDistinguish: Spasticity, sensory signs, compression on MRI

Ventriculoperitoneal shunt with an adjustable valve for responders; the gait improves most

syn-one-and-a-half.name: One-and-a-half syndrome
syn-one-and-a-half.presentation: The patient's eyes are fixed in the horizontal plane except for one movement: the eye opposite the lesion can still abduct, and it does so with nystagmus. Looking toward the side of the lesion is impossible with either eye, and looking away, the eye on the side of the lesion cannot adduct. Vertical movements and convergence are preserved. Often there is also a facial palsy on the side of the lesion.

deficits.sign: Horizontal gaze palsy toward the lesion (the 'one')
Internuclear ophthalmoplegia (the 'half')
Only surviving horizontal movement: abduction of the contralateral eye with nystagmus
Facial palsy when the facial colliculus is involved (eight-and-a-half syndrome)

syn-one-and-a-half.reasoning: A single lesion of the dorsal paramedian pons can destroy both the abducens nucleus or paramedian pontine reticular formation on one side and the adjacent MLF on the same side. Loss of the abducens nucleus paralyzes gaze toward the lesion in both eyes, because the nucleus contains the lateral rectus motor neurons for its own eye and the interneurons that cross to the opposite medial rectus; this is the 'one', a complete conjugate gaze palsy to the side of the lesion. The MLF on the side of the lesion carries the already-crossed interneuron axons from the opposite abducens nucleus up to the ipsilateral medial rectus subnucleus, so gaze away from the lesion fails in the ipsilateral eye; this is the 'half', an internuclear ophthalmoplegia. What survives is abduction of the contralateral eye, driven by the intact contralateral abducens nucleus, and it shows the dissociated nystagmus of any INO. Vertical gaze and convergence use midbrain pathways and are spared. The facial nerve loops over the abducens nucleus, so its involvement adds an ipsilateral peripheral facial palsy. The two lesion sites are within a few millimeters, which is why one small infarct or plaque produces the combination.

imagingFindings.finding: Small restricted diffusion focus in the paramedian dorsal pontine tegmentum at the level of the abducens nucleus.
FLAIR lesion at the floor of the fourth ventricle in the caudal pons with other demyelinating lesions.

imagingHint.label: abducens nucleus and adjacent MLF

syn-optic-neuritis.name: Optic neuritis
syn-optic-neuritis.presentation: A young woman notices that vision in one eye has become blurred and dim over two or three days, colors look washed out, and the eye aches when she moves it. Acuity is reduced, there is a central scotoma, the pupil on that side responds less briskly to light than the other (a relative afferent pupillary defect), and the disc is normal in two-thirds of cases or mildly swollen in the rest. Vision recovers over weeks, but the episode may be the first sign of multiple sclerosis.

deficits.sign: Reduced acuity and color vision with a central or cecocentral scotoma
Relative afferent pupillary defect
Pain on eye movement from traction on the inflamed nerve sheath at the orbital apex
Persisting desaturation of red and Uhthoff phenomenon (blurring with heat or exercise)

syn-optic-neuritis.reasoning: Each optic nerve carries the axons of all the ganglion cells of one retina, so a lesion in front of the chiasm produces a monocular deficit, and because the light reflex afferents travel in the same nerve, the pupil of the affected eye constricts less when light swings onto it (the pathway is uncrossed up to the chiasm, so the deficit is strictly ipsilateral), while both pupils stay equal in size because the efferent pathways are intact and bilateral: the relative afferent pupillary defect is the objective sign of a unilateral prechiasmal lesion. Inflammation and demyelination of the nerve, usually behind the disc (retrobulbar), block conduction in the papillomacular bundle first, which is why central vision and color suffer most. The nerve is a tract of the central nervous system with oligodendrocyte myelin and is attacked by the same process that produces multiple sclerosis elsewhere; the risk of MS after a first episode depends largely on whether the brain MRI already shows demyelinating lesions. The recovered nerve conducts slowly, which shows as a delayed visual evoked potential and as Uhthoff's phenomenon when a rise in temperature blocks marginal conduction. Bilateral, severe, poorly recovering or recurrent optic neuritis, especially with a long lesion on MRI, raises neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder or MOG antibody disease instead, where the treatment and prognosis differ.

imagingFindings.finding: T2 hyperintensity and gadolinium enhancement of a short segment of the intraorbital optic nerve on fat-suppressed coronal images.
Periventricular, juxtacortical, infratentorial or spinal cord demyelinating lesions on brain and cord MRI that determine the risk and diagnosis.

imagingHint.label: intraorbital optic nerve

commonCauses: Multiple sclerosis or clinically isolated syndrome

syn-parinaud-dorsal-midbrain.name: Parinaud (dorsal midbrain) syndrome
syn-parinaud-dorsal-midbrain.presentation: A young patient complains of double vision and blurred vision on looking up, and headache. Examination shows that neither eye can look up, the lids are retracted so the eyes look startled, the pupils are large and react to a near target but not to light, and when the patient tries to look up the eyes jerk inward and retract into the orbit. Downward gaze may follow. Papilledema is common because the aqueduct is compressed.

deficits.sign: Supranuclear up-gaze palsy, often overcome by the oculocephalic reflex early on
Light-near dissociation: mid-dilated pupils reacting to near but not to light
Lid retraction (Collier sign) and convergence-retraction nystagmus on attempted up-gaze
Headache and papilledema from obstructive hydrocephalus

syn-parinaud-dorsal-midbrain.reasoning: The pretectal area and posterior commissure lie just in front of the superior colliculi, beneath the pineal gland and above the aqueduct. Up-gaze commands from the rostral interstitial nucleus of the MLF cross through the posterior commissure to reach the oculomotor subnuclei of both sides, so compression of this small region abolishes up-gaze bilaterally while leaving the oculomotor nuclei, and therefore individual eye movements and the near response, intact. The pretectal nuclei that receive the light reflex afferents from both optic tracts are damaged, so the light reflex fails in both eyes, whereas the near reflex, which reaches the Edinger–Westphal nuclei from the cortex by a more ventral route, survives: light-near dissociation. Lid retraction and convergence-retraction nystagmus result from disinhibition of the levator and from co-contraction of all the extraocular muscles when the pretectum misfires. The aqueduct runs directly beneath, so a pineal tumor or a dilated third ventricle produces both the eye signs and hydrocephalus. Because the whole structure is midline and receives bilateral input, there is no ipsilateral or contralateral pattern; the syndrome is symmetric.

imagingFindings.finding: Enhancing mass in the pineal region compressing the tectum with dilatation of the lateral and third ventricles.
Dilated third and lateral ventricles with a normal fourth ventricle (aqueduct stenosis) and a distended suprapineal recess pressing on the tectum.
Restricted diffusion in the pretectum after a top-of-the-basilar embolus.

imagingHint.label: pretectum beneath the pineal, above the aqueduct

commonCauses: Pineal tumor (germinoma, pineoblastoma) in the young
Top of the basilar infarct or midbrain hemorrhage in the elderly

mimics.name: Progressive supranuclear palsy
mimics.howToDistinguish: Down-gaze affected first, slow progression, no hydrocephalus, older patient

mimics.name: Thyroid eye disease
mimics.howToDistinguish: Up-gaze restriction from a tight inferior rectus, forced duction abnormal, normal pupils

mimics.name: Bilateral third nerve nuclear lesion
mimics.howToDistinguish: Ptosis and other muscles involved

management: Urgent MRI and neurosurgical assessment; CSF diversion for hydrocephalus
Tumor markers (AFP, beta-hCG) in serum and CSF for germ cell tumors
Prisms or occlusion for diplopia

syn-parkinsonism.name: Parkinsonism
syn-parkinsonism.presentation: A patient in their sixties has noticed that one hand shakes at rest, stops shaking when they reach for a cup, and that handwriting has become small and cramped; a spouse says the face has lost its expression and the voice its volume. Examination finds a resting tremor at four to six cycles per second, cogwheel rigidity that appears when the other arm is moved, slow and decrementing finger tapping, a stooped posture with a shuffling gait and reduced arm swing on the affected side, and a tendency to fall backward when pulled.

deficits.sign: Bradykinesia: slow, small, decrementing repetitive movements; hypomimia, micrographia, hypophonia
Rigidity (lead-pipe, with cogwheeling when tremor coexists)
Rest tremor at 4–6 Hz, pill-rolling, suppressed by movement
Shuffling festinating gait, stooped posture, freezing, postural instability with retropulsion
Constipation, orthostatic hypotension, urinary urgency, anosmia and REM sleep behavior disorder, often preceding motor signs

syn-parkinsonism.reasoning: The dopaminergic neurons of the substantia nigra pars compacta project to the striatum, where dopamine facilitates the direct pathway through D1 receptors and inhibits the indirect pathway through D2 receptors, tilting the balance of the basal ganglia loops toward the release of movement. When more than half of these neurons have died, the direct pathway weakens and the indirect pathway is disinhibited, the subthalamic nucleus and internal pallidum become overactive, and the ventral lateral and ventral anterior thalamus are held under excessive inhibition, so the motor cortex receives too little thalamic drive: movements become small, slow and infrequent (bradykinesia), and the postural and locomotor programs of the brainstem are under-recruited, giving the stooped posture, shuffling gait and loss of postural reflexes. The abnormal synchronous oscillations of the pallidothalamic circuit that appear when dopamine is lost are relayed to the cortex as the rest tremor, which is suppressed when voluntary movement resets the circuit, and the rigidity reflects enhanced long-latency stretch reflexes. Each hemisphere's loop controls the contralateral body through the crossed corticospinal projection, so the asymmetric neuronal loss of Parkinson disease produces signs that begin on one side, opposite the more affected nigra, and remain asymmetric. The corticospinal tract itself is intact, so strength and reflexes are normal and the plantars are flexor. Lewy body pathology starts in the olfactory bulb, dorsal vagal nucleus and locus coeruleus years before it reaches the nigra, which explains the premotor anosmia, constipation and REM sleep behavior disorder. Symmetric onset, early falls, early dementia, ophthalmoplegia, marked autonomic failure or a poor levodopa response point to the atypical parkinsonian syndromes, and drugs that block dopamine receptors produce a symmetric reversible form.

imagingFindings.finding: Usually normal; loss of the dorsolateral nigral hyperintensity ('swallow tail') on high-resolution SWI, and neuromelanin loss on specialized sequences. MRI is done to exclude structural mimics.
Reduced striatal uptake, asymmetric and worse in the putamen, in Parkinson disease and the atypical degenerations; normal in essential tremor and drug-induced parkinsonism.

Midbrain atrophy ('hummingbird' sign) in progressive supranuclear palsy; putaminal rim and pontine 'hot cross bun' in multiple system atrophy; asymmetric cortical atrophy in corticobasal degeneration.
Extensive white matter disease and basal ganglia lacunes with lower-body predominant signs.

imagingHint.label: substantia nigra in the midbrain

commonCauses: Multiple system atrophy, progressive supranuclear palsy, corticobasal degeneration, dementia with Lewy bodies
Normal pressure hydrocephalus, Wilson disease (young), carbon monoxide or manganese toxicity

mimics.name: Essential tremor
mimics.howToDistinguish: Action and postural tremor, no bradykinesia or rigidity, often familial and alcohol-responsive

mimics.name: Normal pressure hydrocephalus
mimics.howToDistinguish: Gait and bladder first, ventriculomegaly, tap response

mimics.name: Depression or hypothyroidism
mimics.howToDistinguish: Slowing without rigidity or tremor

mimics.name: Dystonic tremor
mimics.howToDistinguish: Irregular, position-dependent, with dystonic posturing

management: Clinical diagnosis: bradykinesia plus tremor or rigidity, asymmetric, with a clear levodopa response; review drugs
Levodopa is the most effective therapy; dopamine agonists and MAO-B inhibitors in younger patients; physiotherapy and exercise throughout
Deep brain stimulation of the subthalamic nucleus or internal pallidum for motor fluctuations and dyskinesias

syn-parsonage-turner.name: Neuralgic amyotrophy (Parsonage–Turner syndrome)
syn-parsonage-turner.presentation: A young adult wakes with excruciating pain in one shoulder that lasts for days to two weeks and is unrelieved by position or ordinary analgesics; as the pain subsides, weakness and rapid wasting appear in the shoulder girdle, most often the serratus anterior, supraspinatus, infraspinatus and deltoid, with winging of the scapula. Sensory loss is minor, often a patch over the deltoid. The pattern of weakness fits several nerves and roots at once. Recovery takes months to years.

deficits.sign: Severe neuropathic pain for days to weeks preceding the weakness

deficits.distribution: shoulder girdle: serratus anterior, spinati, deltoid, biceps, in patchy combinations
deficits.sign: Weakness and rapid wasting appearing as the pain fades; scapular winging
Mild sensory loss out of proportion to the motor deficit
Orthopnea from phrenic involvement; pinch weakness from anterior interosseous involvement

syn-parsonage-turner.reasoning: Neuralgic amyotrophy is an inflammatory, presumably immune-mediated attack on the brachial plexus and its branches, often following an infection, vaccination, surgery or childbirth, and in a hereditary form linked to SEPT9 mutations. The inflammation strikes individual nerves and fascicles rather than the plexus as a whole, which is why the deficits are patchy and fit several different nerves at once: the long thoracic nerve to the serratus anterior, the suprascapular nerve to the spinati, the axillary nerve to the deltoid, the anterior interosseous nerve to the long flexors of the thumb and index, and the phrenic nerve, in any combination, without matching any single root or trunk. The lesions are peripheral and uncrossed, so everything is ipsilateral, though a fifth of patients have bilateral, asymmetric involvement. Motor fascicles are affected far more than sensory ones, explaining the striking wasting with little sensory loss, and the pain reflects the acute inflammation of the nerve trunks. Nerve imaging shows focal constrictions and swelling of the affected nerves, sometimes with an hourglass appearance, which supports the diagnosis and separates it from a cervical radiculopathy, in which the pain and weakness follow a single root and paraspinal muscles are denervated, and from a rotator cuff injury, which has no neurogenic wasting.

imagingFindings.finding: Denervation in muscles of several different nerves and roots of one limb without paraspinal involvement; reduced sensory responses in the affected nerves (postganglionic).

T2 hyperintensity and enlargement of the affected plexus elements or individual nerves on MR neurography, with denervation edema of the shoulder girdle muscles on STIR; hourglass constrictions on high-resolution ultrasound.
No compressive root lesion matching the deficit.

imagingHint.label: brachial plexus and its shoulder girdle branches

mimics.name: Cervical radiculopathy
mimics.howToDistinguish: Pain and weakness confined to one root, paraspinal denervation, compression on MRI

mimics.name: Rotator cuff tear
mimics.howToDistinguish: Weakness limited by pain without wasting or denervation

mimics.name: Traumatic plexopathy
mimics.howToDistinguish: History of stretch injury; deficits follow trunks or cords

mimics.name: Multifocal motor neuropathy
mimics.howToDistinguish: Painless, slowly progressive, conduction block

management: Strong analgesia in the painful phase; corticosteroids in the first two weeks may shorten it
Physiotherapy to maintain range and prevent frozen shoulder; EMG at 3–4 weeks to define the extent
Reassurance about slow recovery over 1–3 years; nerve exploration only for persistent hourglass constrictions

syn-pca-infarct.name: Posterior cerebral artery infarction
syn-pca-infarct.presentation: The patient notices that half the world has disappeared, often bumping into things on one side, sometimes with a headache. Examination shows a congruous homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing and intact pupils; strength is normal. Dominant-side infarcts may add alexia without agraphia and color anomia, and medial temporal involvement produces a transient amnesia. If the proximal artery is occluded, thalamic infarction adds hemisensory loss and, later, thalamic pain.

deficits.sign: Hemianopia with macular sparing
Alexia without agraphia, color anomia, visual agnosia
Transient anterograde amnesia
Thalamic hemisensory loss

syn-pca-infarct.reasoning: The posterior cerebral artery arises from the top of the basilar artery, curves around the midbrain and supplies the occipital lobe, the inferomedial temporal lobe, and through its proximal perforators the thalamus and midbrain. The calcarine cortex receives the contralateral visual hemifield: nasal retinal fibers cross in the chiasm, so each occipital lobe sees the opposite half of space from both eyes. The macular representation at the occipital pole often survives because it receives collateral flow from the middle cerebral artery, giving macular sparing, and the pupillary light fibers leave the optic tract before the geniculate, so the pupils react normally. Corticospinal fibers lie in middle cerebral territory, hence no weakness. In the dominant hemisphere, a lesion of the left occipital lobe plus the splenium of the corpus callosum disconnects the intact right visual cortex from the left angular gyrus, so the patient can write but cannot read what has been written. The hippocampus lies in the temporal branch territory and explains the amnesia, while proximal P1 occlusion involves the thalamoperforating branches and produces the sensory and midbrain signs.

imagingFindings.finding: Restricted diffusion in the calcarine cortex, lingual gyrus and cuneus, often extending to the medial temporal lobe and splenium; thalamus involved in proximal occlusions.
Absent flow in the P2 segment; check the basilar tip for a proximal embolus.

imagingHint.label: calcarine cortex

mimics.howToDistinguish: Hyperdense blood on CT, headache prominent

mimics.name: Migraine with aura
mimics.howToDistinguish: Positive scintillations that march and resolve within an hour

mimics.name: Posterior reversible encephalopathy
mimics.howToDistinguish: Bilateral, vasogenic edema, hypertension or immunosuppression

management: Acute stroke pathway
Field testing and reading assessment; driving restriction
Anticoagulation when cardioembolic

syn-peroneal-palsy-foot-drop.name: Common peroneal neuropathy (foot drop)
syn-peroneal-palsy-foot-drop.presentation: A thin patient who has lost weight, or who has been crossing the legs or lying with the leg against a bed rail, trips over the toes of one foot and lifts the knee high to clear it. The foot cannot be dorsiflexed or everted and the toes cannot be extended, but inversion and plantar flexion are strong, the ankle reflex is normal, and sensation is lost over the dorsum of the foot and the lateral lower leg. Tapping the nerve at the fibular neck tingles into the foot.

deficits.distribution: tibialis anterior, extensor hallucis and digitorum longus, peroneus longus and brevis
deficits.sign: Foot drop with weak eversion; steppage gait
Inversion and plantar flexion spared, ankle reflex normal

deficits.distribution: dorsum of the foot and lateral leg
deficits.sign: Sensory loss in the superficial and deep peroneal distribution

syn-peroneal-palsy-foot-drop.reasoning: The common peroneal nerve leaves the sciatic nerve above the knee, winds around the neck of the fibula just beneath the skin and passes through the fibrous tunnel of the peroneus longus origin to divide into the superficial branch, which everts the foot and supplies the lateral leg and most of the dorsum, and the deep branch, which dorsiflexes the ankle and toes and supplies the first web space. At the fibular neck the nerve lies on bone with no muscle cover, so it is compressed by crossing the legs, squatting, a tight cast, a bed rail during coma or surgery, or a ganglion, and rapid weight loss removes the fat that protected it. The result is weakness of dorsiflexion, toe extension and eversion with sensory loss on the dorsum and lateral leg. The muscles that separate it from the other causes of foot drop are those that share the same roots but travel by other nerves: the tibialis posterior (L5, tibial nerve), which inverts the foot, and the gluteus medius (L5, superior gluteal nerve), which abducts the hip, are weak in an L5 radiculopathy and normal in a peroneal palsy, and the plantar flexors and ankle reflex (S1, tibial nerve) are weak or absent in a sciatic lesion. The lesion is peripheral and ipsilateral. Conduction studies show slowing or block across the fibular head, and a preserved superficial peroneal sensory response with a foot drop points instead to a root lesion, where the dorsal root ganglion is spared.

imagingFindings.finding: Conduction block or focal slowing of the peroneal nerve across the fibular head with denervation of the tibialis anterior and peroneus longus but not the tibialis posterior or short head of biceps; superficial peroneal sensory response reduced.
Swollen nerve at the fibular neck or an intraneural ganglion arising from the tibiofibular joint.
Fracture, knee dislocation or hematoma with nerve involvement; denervation edema in the anterior compartment.

imagingHint.label: common peroneal nerve at the fibular neck (virtual)

commonCauses: Habitual leg crossing, squatting, weight loss
Fibular neck fracture or knee dislocation
Vasculitis, diabetes, hereditary neuropathy with pressure palsies (recurrent)

mimics.name: L5 radiculopathy
mimics.howToDistinguish: Back pain, weak inversion and hip abduction, sensory loss extending to the big toe and lateral thigh, paraspinal denervation

mimics.name: Sciatic neuropathy
mimics.howToDistinguish: Weak plantar flexion, absent ankle jerk, sole numb

mimics.name: Anterior horn or motor neuron disease
mimics.howToDistinguish: No sensory loss, fasciculation, spreads

mimics.name: Upper motor neuron foot drop
mimics.howToDistinguish: Spasticity, brisk reflexes, extensor plantar

management: Remove the compression and protect the fibular head; ankle-foot orthosis
Nerve conduction studies to localize and to establish conduction block (good prognosis) versus axonal loss
Surgical decompression for a ganglion or a persistent lesion

syn-physiologic-anisocoria.name: Physiologic anisocoria and the approach to unequal pupils
syn-physiologic-anisocoria.presentation: A patient, or a nurse, notices that one pupil is larger than the other. The size difference is under a millimeter, is the same in bright and dim light, both pupils react briskly, the lids are level and old photographs show the same asymmetry: this is physiologic anisocoria, present in a fifth of healthy people. If instead the difference is greater in the dark the small pupil is at fault (Horner), and if greater in the light the large pupil is at fault (third nerve, Adie, pharmacologic).

deficits.sign: Anisocoria under 1 mm, equal in light and dark, brisk reactions, normal lids and motility; benign
Anisocoria greater in the dark with dilation lag and mild ptosis: Horner syndrome

Anisocoria greater in the light with poor light reaction: third nerve palsy (with ptosis and ophthalmoplegia), Adie tonic pupil (slow near response) or pharmacologic mydriasis (no response to pilocarpine)

syn-physiologic-anisocoria.reasoning: Pupil size is the balance between the sphincter, driven by the parasympathetic fibers from the Edinger–Westphal nucleus through the third nerve and ciliary ganglion, and the dilator, driven by the three-neuron sympathetic chain, and both systems serve each eye separately and without crossing, so an efferent lesion produces an asymmetry between the two pupils, whereas an afferent lesion never does, because each retina drives both Edinger–Westphal nuclei equally. Which pupil is abnormal is found by changing the light: in darkness the dilator is working, so a paralyzed dilator leaves its pupil behind and the anisocoria grows, revealing a Horner syndrome on the side of the smaller pupil; in bright light the sphincter is working, so a paralyzed sphincter leaves its pupil large and the anisocoria grows, revealing a parasympathetic lesion on the side of the larger pupil. Physiologic anisocoria arises from a slight asymmetry of central inhibition of the Edinger–Westphal nuclei and therefore stays constant across lighting conditions, with normal reactions and no ptosis. The pharmacologic tests follow the same logic: apraclonidine reverses Horner anisocoria by stimulating the supersensitive dilator, dilute pilocarpine constricts the supersensitive Adie sphincter, and full-strength pilocarpine fails to constrict a pharmacologically blocked pupil but constricts a third nerve palsy pupil. Old photographs are the cheapest test of all.

imagingFindings.finding: No imaging needed; if obtained for other reasons the study is normal.
Imaging follows the pattern: neck and skull base for Horner (carotid dissection), CTA for a pupil-involving third nerve palsy (posterior communicating aneurysm).

imagingHint.label: both eyes: the pupils are compared, not imaged

commonCauses: Pharmacologic (scopolamine patch, nebulized ipratropium, plant alkaloids)
Iris trauma or synechiae, acute angle closure

mimics.howToDistinguish: Anisocoria greater in the dark, ptosis, dilation lag

mimics.name: Third nerve palsy
mimics.howToDistinguish: Anisocoria greater in the light with ptosis and ophthalmoplegia

mimics.name: Pharmacologic mydriasis
mimics.howToDistinguish: Very large pupil unresponsive to 1% pilocarpine; history of exposure

syn-pica-cerebellar-infarct.name: PICA cerebellar infarction with mass effect
syn-pica-cerebellar-infarct.presentation: A patient develops vertigo, vomiting, headache and an unsteady gait, veering to one side, with nystagmus and dysmetria of the limbs on that side, and is initially labeled as having labyrinthitis. Within one to three days they become drowsy, with a sixth nerve palsy and then a rising blood pressure and irregular breathing, as the swollen inferior cerebellum compresses the medulla and obstructs the fourth ventricle.

deficits.sign: Limb ataxia, gait ataxia with lateropulsion, gaze-evoked nystagmus
Vertigo and vomiting from the nodulus and flocculus
Drowsiness progressing to coma with obstructive hydrocephalus
False-localizing sixth nerve palsy and facial weakness from brainstem compression

syn-pica-cerebellar-infarct.reasoning: The posterior inferior cerebellar artery supplies the inferior surface of the cerebellar hemisphere, the tonsil and the inferior vermis in addition to the lateral medulla, and an embolus or thrombus lodging beyond the medullary branches produces a purely cerebellar infarct. Cerebellar signs are ipsilateral to the lesion because the hemisphere's output crosses in the midbrain and is crossed back by the corticospinal tract to reach its own side of the body, and the inferior vermis and flocculonodular lobe give the vertigo, nystagmus and truncal imbalance. The danger of the syndrome lies not in the deficit but in the anatomy of the posterior fossa: the inferior cerebellum lies against the medulla and fourth ventricle, and as the infarct swells over the following days it pushes the tonsils into the foramen magnum and the brainstem forward, obstructing CSF outflow. The resulting hydrocephalus and medullary compression cause a stepwise decline in consciousness, cranial nerve palsies and finally cardiorespiratory arrest, which decompression can prevent. The initial similarity to vestibular neuritis, which never causes limb ataxia or a positive HINTS pattern of central type, is the diagnostic trap.

imagingFindings.finding: Restricted diffusion in the inferior cerebellar hemisphere and tonsil, sometimes with the lateral medulla.

imagingHint.label: inferior cerebellar hemisphere and tonsil

mimics.name: Vestibular neuritis
mimics.howToDistinguish: Normal limb coordination, positive head impulse test, unidirectional nystagmus

mimics.name: Cerebellar hemorrhage
mimics.howToDistinguish: Hyperdense on CT from the outset

mimics.name: Lateral medullary syndrome
mimics.howToDistinguish: Bulbar signs and crossed sensory loss without significant hemispheric swelling

management: Admit to a monitored bed; repeat CT at any decline in consciousness
Suboccipital decompressive craniectomy and external ventricular drainage for deterioration from mass effect
Antithrombotic therapy and vertebral artery imaging

syn-pituitary-mass.name: Pituitary mass lesion
syn-pituitary-mass.presentation: A patient presents with a hormone syndrome, with visual loss, or with an incidental finding on a scan. A young woman has amenorrhea and galactorrhea from prolactin; a middle-aged man notices his rings and shoes no longer fit; another patient is tired, cold and has lost body hair as the normal gland is crushed. When the tumor reaches the chiasm the temporal fields go, and when it invades the cavernous sinus the eye movements fail. A sudden headache with visual collapse and ophthalmoplegia means the tumor has bled.

deficits.sign: Hypersecretion (prolactin, growth hormone, ACTH) or hypopituitarism from compression of the normal gland
Bitemporal hemianopia from chiasmal compression, superior quadrants first
Ocular motor palsies from lateral extension into the cavernous sinus
Headache from dural stretching; thunderclap headache with apoplexy
Diabetes insipidus and hypothalamic dysfunction with suprasellar extension (mostly craniopharyngioma)

syn-pituitary-mass.reasoning: The pituitary gland sits in the sella turcica, roofed by the diaphragma sellae, with the optic chiasm about a centimeter above the diaphragm, the cavernous sinuses and their carotid arteries and ocular motor nerves on either side, the sphenoid sinus below and the hypothalamus above through the stalk. A tumor of the anterior gland grows within this box, and its clinical expression is determined by what it secretes and by which neighbor it reaches. Hormonal effects come first: prolactin-secreting adenomas cause amenorrhea, galactorrhea and, in men, hypogonadism; growth hormone causes acromegaly; ACTH causes Cushing disease; and a large non-functioning tumor compresses the normal gland, so that the trophic hormones fail in a characteristic order, gonadotropins and growth hormone first, then thyroid and finally adrenal. Growth upward pushes the diaphragma and reaches the chiasm from below, compressing the crossing fibers from the inferior nasal retinae that carry the superior temporal fields, so the bitemporal hemianopia starts in the upper quadrants; because the chiasm is midline and both sets of crossing fibers are involved, the field loss is bilateral. Lateral growth invades the cavernous sinus and involves the uncrossed nerves in its wall, producing ipsilateral ophthalmoplegia. Hemorrhage or infarction of a tumor, pituitary apoplexy, expands the mass within hours, causing sudden headache, visual loss, ophthalmoplegia and acute adrenal insufficiency, which is life-threatening. Stalk compression by any mass raises prolactin modestly by removing dopaminergic inhibition, so a mildly raised prolactin does not prove a prolactinoma.

imagingFindings.finding: Sellar mass enhancing less than the normal gland on dynamic post-contrast T1, expanding the sella, elevating the chiasm and displacing the stalk; microadenomas under 10 mm, macroadenomas above.
Tumor encasing more than two-thirds of the cavernous carotid (Knosp grade) on coronal images.
Hemorrhage or infarction within an adenoma with fluid levels, T1 shortening and sudden enlargement; hyperdense on CT.
Cystic, calcified suprasellar mass in a child or older adult, often with hydrocephalus.

imagingHint.label: pituitary gland in the sella beneath the chiasm

mimics.name: Chiasmal glioma or meningioma
mimics.howToDistinguish: Arises above the sella; normal gland seen separately

mimics.name: Internal carotid aneurysm
mimics.howToDistinguish: Flow void on MRI, pulsatile; never biopsy

mimics.name: Physiological enlargement
mimics.howToDistinguish: Pregnancy, adolescence, primary hypothyroidism; homogeneous gland without a discrete lesion

management: Full pituitary hormone profile, formal perimetry and MRI of the sella

syn-poliomyelitis.name: Poliomyelitis and anterior horn cell disease
syn-poliomyelitis.presentation: A child, unvaccinated or in an outbreak, has a febrile illness with headache and neck stiffness and then, over a day or two, develops weakness that is patchy and asymmetric, worse in the legs, with pain and fasciculation in the affected muscles. The weak limbs are flaccid and areflexic but sensation is normal and the bladder recovers quickly. Decades later some survivors develop new weakness and fatigue in the same muscles, the post-polio syndrome. Enterovirus and West Nile virus now produce the same picture.

deficits.distribution: limbs, asymmetric and patchy, proximal and legs more than arms
deficits.sign: Acute flaccid paralysis with wasting and fasciculation; no sensory loss
Areflexia in the paralyzed muscles
Bulbar palsy with dysphagia and respiratory failure in the bulbar form
Normal sensation, the key feature separating it from Guillain–Barré and myelitis

syn-poliomyelitis.reasoning: Poliovirus, an enterovirus that enters through the gut, spreads to the central nervous system and infects the large motor neurons of the anterior horn and the motor nuclei of the brainstem selectively, destroying them and producing a purely lower motor neuron paralysis. The anterior horn cell is the final common pathway to muscle, so its death causes flaccid weakness with loss of the stretch reflex, whose efferent limb it forms, and denervation with wasting and fasciculation, while the sensory pathways, the dorsal horn and the long tracts are spared, so sensation is normal. Because the virus attacks scattered groups of motor neurons at different segments, the paralysis is asymmetric and patchy rather than following a level, unlike myelitis, and each side is affected independently, so there is no crossed or lateralized rule; the lumbar enlargement is affected most, and the bulbar nuclei in a minority, where involvement of the nucleus ambiguus and the respiratory centers is life-threatening. The preceding meningitic phase reflects the viral meningitis that accompanies the neuronal invasion. Surviving motor neurons sprout to re-innervate orphaned fibers, forming giant motor units; their later exhaustion after decades of overuse is the post-polio syndrome. Other enteroviruses (EV-D68, EV-A71), West Nile virus and spinal muscular atrophy produce the same anterior horn pattern by infection or degeneration.

imagingFindings.finding: T2 hyperintensity of the anterior horns (gray matter) over several segments, often asymmetric, without white matter change; brainstem nuclei may enhance in the bulbar form.
Lymphocytic pleocytosis with mildly raised protein; virus isolated from stool or throat, PCR of CSF for enteroviruses and West Nile virus.
Acute denervation in a patchy multisegmental distribution with normal sensory conduction; later giant motor units from reinnervation.

imagingHint.label: anterior horns of the lumbar enlargement

commonCauses: Non-polio enteroviruses (EV-D68, EV-A71) causing acute flaccid myelitis

mimics.name: Guillain–Barré syndrome
mimics.howToDistinguish: Symmetric, ascending, with sensory symptoms and raised CSF protein without cells; no fever at onset

mimics.name: Transverse myelitis
mimics.howToDistinguish: Sensory level, sphincter involvement, upper motor neuron signs later

mimics.name: Botulism
mimics.howToDistinguish: Descending paralysis with ophthalmoplegia and dilated pupils

mimics.name: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
mimics.howToDistinguish: Chronic, with upper motor neuron signs

management: Isolate the patient, notify public health, collect stool and CSF for virus identification; supportive care with respiratory monitoring
Physiotherapy and orthoses; avoid overexertion of weak muscles
Vaccination of contacts; recognize post-polio syndrome and manage fatigue and new weakness conservatively

syn-pontine-hemorrhage.name: Pontine hemorrhage
syn-pontine-hemorrhage.presentation: A hypertensive patient collapses and within minutes is deeply comatose with pinpoint pupils that still react to a bright light under magnification, quadriplegia with bilateral extensor plantars, absent horizontal eye movements even with head turning and caloric stimulation, ocular bobbing, a high fever and irregular breathing. Small hemorrhages confined to the tegmentum or the base produce instead a survivable lateral pontine or pure motor picture.

deficits.sign: Abrupt coma within minutes
Pinpoint but reactive pupils from bilateral interruption of the descending sympathetic fibers with intact parasympathetic outflow
Quadriplegia with bilateral extensor plantars; decerebrate posturing
Absent horizontal eye movements not overcome by oculocephalic or caloric stimulation; ocular bobbing
Hyperthermia and abnormal respiratory patterns

syn-pontine-hemorrhage.reasoning: The paramedian perforating branches of the basilar artery are small end arteries that develop lipohyalinosis and microaneurysms under chronic hypertension, and their rupture floods the center of the pons, usually at the junction of the base and tegmentum, from where the hematoma spreads across the midline and often into the fourth ventricle. Because the pons is compact, a single hematoma destroys bilateral structures at once. The corticospinal fibers of both sides, uncrossed at this level, are cut, so all four limbs are paralyzed; the pontine reticular formation that maintains arousal is destroyed, so coma is immediate; both abducens nuclei, both paramedian pontine reticular formations and both MLFs are involved, so no horizontal eye movement can be produced by any pathway, whereas vertical movements generated in the spared midbrain persist and, released, produce the bobbing. The descending sympathetic fibers pass through the tegmentum bilaterally and are interrupted while the midbrain parasympathetic outflow is intact, hence pinpoint pupils that react, a combination that separates a pontine lesion from opioid poisoning only by the accompanying signs. Hyperthermia reflects the loss of descending control over the hypothalamic set point. A hematoma confined to one side of the tegmentum produces instead an ipsilateral gaze palsy, facial palsy and contralateral sensory loss, and a small basal hematoma a pure motor hemiparesis, both with a far better outlook.

imagingFindings.finding: Hyperdense hematoma in the center of the pons, often extending into the fourth ventricle, with hydrocephalus; large hematomas over 5 mL or extending across the midline carry a poor prognosis.
'Popcorn' lesion with a hemosiderin rim, or flow voids, in younger patients without hypertension.

imagingHint.label: central pons at the basis–tegmentum junction

commonCauses: Hypertensive rupture of paramedian basilar perforators
Hemorrhagic transformation of a pontine infarct

mimics.name: Opioid overdose
mimics.howToDistinguish: Pinpoint pupils with coma but preserved eye movements and normal tone; responds to naloxone

mimics.name: Basilar artery occlusion
mimics.howToDistinguish: Similar deficits but evolution over hours with prodromal symptoms; no blood on CT

mimics.name: Central pontine myelinolysis
mimics.howToDistinguish: Subacute after sodium correction; T2 change without hemorrhage

management: Airway protection and blood pressure control; reverse anticoagulation
Ventricular drainage for hydrocephalus; surgical evacuation is rarely beneficial
Prognosis depends on hematoma volume and level of consciousness at presentation; discuss goals of care early

syn-posterior-cord-subacute-combined.name: Posterior cord syndrome and subacute combined degeneration
eponyms: subacute combined degeneration of the cord
syn-posterior-cord-subacute-combined.presentation: A patient who has had a gastrectomy, is a vegan, or takes metformin or uses nitrous oxide complains of tingling feet and unsteadiness in the dark. Examination shows loss of vibration and joint position sense in the feet with a positive Romberg test, brisk knee reflexes with absent ankle reflexes and extensor plantars, and a stamping gait; the electric shock down the spine on neck flexion (Lhermitte) may be present. Untreated, spastic paraparesis and dementia follow.

deficits.sign: Loss of vibration and position sense with sensory ataxia and positive Romberg (posterior columns)
Spastic weakness with extensor plantars (lateral corticospinal tracts)
Mixed picture: brisk knees with absent ankles when a peripheral neuropathy coexists
Pain and temperature relatively spared
Memory loss, irritability, dementia in vitamin B12 deficiency

syn-posterior-cord-subacute-combined.reasoning: The posterior columns carry uncrossed proprioceptive and vibration fibers from the ipsilateral leg (fasciculus gracilis, medially) and arm (fasciculus cuneatus, laterally) to the medulla, where they cross; bilateral damage in the cord therefore produces bilateral loss of those modalities below the lesion without any crossed pattern, and the loss of position sense removes the feedback that keeps the patient upright when vision is removed, hence the Romberg sign and the worsening in the dark. Vitamin B12 is needed for the methylation reactions that maintain myelin, and its deficiency produces a vacuolar demyelination that begins in the large, heavily myelinated fibers of the posterior columns at the cervical and upper thoracic levels and then involves the lateral corticospinal tracts, hence 'combined': proprioceptive loss plus spastic weakness, with the spinothalamic tracts largely spared. Because the same deficiency causes a peripheral neuropathy, the ankle reflexes may be lost while the knees are brisk, and because the cerebral white matter and optic nerves are also affected, cognitive change and visual loss can accompany the myelopathy. Nitrous oxide inactivates B12 and produces the same syndrome acutely. Copper deficiency, HIV vacuolar myelopathy and tabes dorsalis attack the same columns, and posterior spinal artery infarction is a rare vascular cause.

imagingFindings.finding: Symmetric T2 hyperintensity of the posterior columns over the cervical and upper thoracic cord, an 'inverted V' on axial images, without enhancement; may resolve with treatment.
Posterior column atrophy and signal change in late syphilis; CSF VDRL positive.
Acute restricted diffusion confined to the posterior columns after vertebral dissection or surgery.

imagingHint.label: posterior columns of the cervical cord

commonCauses: Vitamin B12 deficiency (pernicious anemia, gastrectomy, veganism, metformin, nitrous oxide abuse)

mimics.howToDistinguish: Distal loss of all modalities with areflexia and no upper motor neuron signs

mimics.name: Cervical spondylotic myelopathy
mimics.howToDistinguish: Neck pain, radicular arm symptoms, compressive cord lesion on MRI

mimics.name: Multiple sclerosis
mimics.howToDistinguish: Relapsing course, asymmetric lesions, brain MRI

syn-radial-neuropathy.name: Radial neuropathy (Saturday night palsy)
syn-radial-neuropathy.presentation: A patient wakes after falling asleep drunk with an arm draped over a chair and finds the wrist and fingers hanging limp: the wrist cannot be extended, the fingers cannot be straightened at the knuckles, and the thumb cannot be extended or abducted in the plane of the hand. Grip feels weak because the wrist cannot be stabilized, but with the wrist held up by the examiner the grip is strong. The triceps is spared and there is a small patch of numbness on the back of the hand between the thumb and index finger.

deficits.distribution: wrist and finger extensors, brachioradialis, supinator, thumb extensors and abductor
deficits.sign: Wrist drop and finger drop; weak brachioradialis; triceps spared in spiral groove lesions

deficits.distribution: dorsum of the first web space
deficits.sign: Small area of sensory loss on the dorsolateral hand; often minimal
Reduced brachioradialis reflex; triceps reflex normal
Apparent grip and interosseous weakness that corrects when the wrist is passively extended (false ulnar weakness)

syn-radial-neuropathy.reasoning: The radial nerve winds around the back of the humerus in the spiral groove, where it lies directly on bone and is compressed by the edge of a chair or by a fracture. The branches to the triceps leave above the groove, so a groove lesion spares elbow extension and the triceps reflex, whereas an axillary lesion (crutch palsy) paralyzes the triceps too and involves the posterior cutaneous nerve of the arm. Below the groove the nerve supplies the brachioradialis, the wrist extensors and, through the posterior interosseous branch, the finger and thumb extensors, so all of these fail together: the wrist drops, the fingers cannot extend at the metacarpophalangeal joints (the interphalangeal joints still extend through the lumbricals and interossei) and the thumb cannot extend. Because the finger flexors and the intrinsic muscles work best with the wrist extended, the patient's grip and finger spreading appear weak until the examiner supports the wrist, a trap that mimics a combined median and ulnar lesion. The superficial radial sensory branch supplies only the dorsum of the radial hand, so sensory loss is small, and the deep branch (posterior interosseous nerve) is purely motor, so an entrapment at the supinator produces finger drop with preserved wrist extension (radial deviation from the intact extensor carpi radialis) and no sensory loss at all. The nerve is peripheral and the deficit ipsilateral.

imagingFindings.finding: Conduction block or slowing of the radial nerve across the spiral groove with denervation in the extensor muscles but not the triceps; superficial radial sensory response reduced.
Midshaft humeral fracture with the nerve in the fracture line; ultrasound can show nerve continuity.

imagingHint.label: radial nerve in the spiral groove (virtual)

commonCauses: Compression in the spiral groove during deep sleep or intoxication

mimics.name: Cortical hand (small motor cortex infarct)

mimics.howToDistinguish: Bilateral wrist drop, abdominal pain, anemia

management: Wrist splint in extension to preserve function while awaiting recovery; most compressive palsies recover within 2–4 months
