syn-radiculopathy-cervical.presentation: Neck pain shoots down the arm in a band, worse when the head is turned and tilted toward that side, with tingling in specific fingers: the thumb for C6, the middle finger for C7, the little finger for C8. The corresponding reflex is lost, biceps and brachioradialis for C6, triceps for C7, and one muscle group is weak, deltoid and biceps for C5, wrist extensors for C6, triceps and finger extensors for C7, finger flexors and intrinsics for C8. Relief on placing the hand on the head is characteristic.

deficits.distribution: neck to arm in a dermatomal band
deficits.sign: Radicular pain and paresthesias worsened by neck extension and rotation (Spurling sign), relieved by shoulder abduction

deficits.distribution: dermatome (C5 lateral shoulder, C6 thumb, C7 middle finger, C8 little finger)
deficits.sign: Dermatomal sensory loss, often incomplete because of overlap
Weakness in the root's muscles across more than one nerve territory (C5 deltoid/biceps, C6 biceps/wrist extensors, C7 triceps/wrist flexors, C8 finger flexors/intrinsics)

syn-radiculopathy-cervical.reasoning: Each cervical spinal nerve leaves the canal through the intervertebral foramen above the vertebra of the same number (C6 exits between C5 and C6), so a C5–C6 disc herniation or foraminal osteophyte compresses the C6 root, and a C6–C7 lesion the C7 root, the two commonest. The root contains the dorsal root ganglion's central processes for one dermatome and the motor axons for one myotome, and because the myotome of a root is distributed among several peripheral nerves, root weakness crosses nerve territories, whereas nerve weakness crosses root territories: C7 weakness involves the triceps (radial nerve) and the wrist flexors (median nerve), which no single nerve lesion could produce. The reflex arc runs through the root, so the reflex of that segment is lost while others remain, which localizes the level more reliably than sensory testing, since adjacent dermatomes overlap. imagingFindings.finding: Posterolateral disc protrusion or uncovertebral osteophyte narrowing the foramen and contacting the exiting root on axial T2; sagittal images through the foramina.

imagingHint.label: cervical roots leaving the foramina

mimics.name: Carpal tunnel syndrome (vs C6–C7)
mimics.howToDistinguish: Sensory loss confined to the median territory, thenar weakness only, night symptoms, no neck pain

mimics.name: Ulnar neuropathy (vs C8)
mimics.howToDistinguish: Sensory loss in the little finger but sparing the medial forearm; no finger flexor weakness of the index

mimics.name: Brachial neuritis (Parsonage–Turner)
mimics.howToDistinguish: Severe pain first, then multi-root weakness with no compressive lesion

mimics.name: Rotator cuff or shoulder disease
mimics.howToDistinguish: Pain with shoulder movement, no neurological deficit

Foraminotomy or anterior discectomy for persistent deficit or intractable pain

syn-radiculopathy-lumbosacral.name: Lumbosacral radiculopathy (L4, L5, S1)
syn-radiculopathy-lumbosacral.presentation: A patient bends to lift something and feels pain in the back that shoots down the back of the leg into the foot, worse on coughing, sitting and bending, with tingling in the big toe or the little toe. Raising the straight leg reproduces the pain at thirty degrees. The findings give the root: weak dorsiflexion of the ankle and toes with numbness of the dorsum of the foot for L5, absent ankle reflex with weak plantar flexion and numbness of the lateral foot for S1, weak quadriceps with a reduced knee jerk and numbness of the medial leg for L4.

deficits.distribution: back to leg in a dermatomal band (sciatica)
deficits.sign: Radicular pain worse on sitting, bending and Valsalva; positive straight leg raise (L5, S1) or femoral stretch test (L4)

deficits.distribution: dermatome (L4 medial leg, L5 dorsum of the foot and big toe, S1 lateral foot and sole)
deficits.sign: Dermatomal sensory loss
L4 quadriceps; L5 extensor hallucis longus, tibialis anterior, hip abductors; S1 plantar flexors and gluteus maximus
Reduced knee jerk (L4) or ankle jerk (S1); L5 has no reliable reflex

The compressed root is inflamed and mechanically sensitive, so stretching it by raising the straight leg, which tenses the sciatic nerve and the L5 and S1 roots, reproduces the pain, and raising the opposite leg (crossed straight leg raise) is a specific though less sensitive sign; the L4 root is stretched instead by extending the hip with the knee flexed. The reflex arcs run through the roots, so the ankle reflex is lost with S1 and the knee reflex with L4. A large central disc herniation can compress the whole cauda equina and must be excluded by asking about perineal numbness and bladder function.

imagingFindings.finding: Posterolateral extrusion at L4–L5 or L5–S1 displacing the traversing root in the lateral recess on axial T2; far lateral discs compress the exiting root in the foramen.

imagingHint.label: lumbosacral roots below the conus

mimics.name: Common peroneal neuropathy (vs L5)
mimics.howToDistinguish: Foot drop with sparing of inversion and hip abduction; sensory loss over the dorsum only; conduction block at the fibular head

mimics.name: Hip or sacroiliac disease
mimics.howToDistinguish: Pain with joint movement, no neurological deficit

mimics.name: Lumbosacral plexopathy
mimics.howToDistinguish: Multiple roots' territories, often painful, with weight loss or diabetes

mimics.name: Cauda equina syndrome
mimics.howToDistinguish: Bilateral, saddle anesthesia, sphincter involvement: emergency

syn-ramsay-hunt.name: Ramsay Hunt syndrome (herpes zoster oticus)
syn-ramsay-hunt.presentation: A patient develops severe pain in and around one ear, followed within days by a complete facial palsy on that side and a crop of vesicles in the ear canal, on the eardrum or on the soft palate. Taste is lost on the front of the tongue and sounds are painfully loud. Many also have vertigo, tinnitus and hearing loss because the eighth nerve is inflamed alongside. Recovery is slower and less complete than in Bell palsy, and the pain may persist as postherpetic neuralgia.

deficits.sign: Lower motor neuron facial palsy, usually severe, with hyperacusis and loss of taste
Severe otalgia preceding the rash; postherpetic neuralgia after

deficits.distribution: external auditory canal, concha, tympanic membrane
deficits.sign: Vesicular eruption in the sensory territory of the facial nerve (and palate)
Vertigo, nystagmus, sensorineural hearing loss and tinnitus

syn-ramsay-hunt.reasoning: Varicella zoster virus that has lain dormant in the geniculate ganglion since childhood chickenpox reactivates and inflames the ganglion and the facial nerve within the narrow bony facial canal, where swelling compresses the nerve and blocks conduction. The facial nerve is the uncrossed lower motor neuron supply of the ipsilateral face, so the palsy is complete on that side including the forehead, and because the inflammation is at or proximal to the geniculate ganglion, the branches that leave distal to it are all affected: the greater petrosal nerve (reduced tearing), the nerve to the stapedius (hyperacusis) and the chorda tympani (loss of taste on the anterior two-thirds of the tongue). The geniculate ganglion also holds the cell bodies of the small cutaneous sensory territory of the facial nerve, the concha, the external auditory canal and the tympanic membrane, and of the taste and general sensory fibers to the palate, so the vesicles appear in exactly these places, which are the diagnostic clue. The vestibulocochlear nerve shares the internal acoustic meatus and is often involved by the spreading inflammation, adding vertigo and deafness, and less often the fifth, ninth and tenth nerves are affected. The virus damages axons more than the presumed viral inflammation of Bell palsy, hence the worse prognosis.

imagingFindings.pathology: Facial nerve and geniculate ganglion inflammation
imagingFindings.finding: Enhancement of the facial nerve in the labyrinthine segment and geniculate ganglion, often extending to the eighth nerve and the membranous labyrinth, on post-contrast T1 of the temporal bone.
Mild lymphocytic pleocytosis with VZV DNA on PCR when the diagnosis is uncertain or the brainstem is involved.

imagingHint.label: facial nerve at the geniculate ganglion in the temporal bone

commonCauses: Reactivation of varicella zoster virus in the geniculate ganglion

mimics.name: Bell palsy
mimics.howToDistinguish: No vesicles, less pain, no eighth nerve involvement; zoster sine herpete can mimic it and is diagnosed by PCR or serology

mimics.name: Otitis externa or media with facial palsy
mimics.howToDistinguish: Purulent discharge, drum changes, no vesicles

mimics.name: Lyme facial palsy
mimics.howToDistinguish: Tick exposure, erythema migrans, often bilateral

management: Look in the ear and at the palate of every patient with a facial palsy and ear pain
Antiviral (valacyclovir) plus prednisolone within 72 hours; eye protection
Audiology and vestibular assessment; analgesia for neuralgia

syn-rapd.name: Relative afferent pupillary defect
syn-rapd.presentation: Both pupils are the same size and both constrict when a light is shone in either eye, but when the light is swung quickly from the good eye to the bad eye, the bad eye's pupil dilates instead of staying small, and when swung back to the good eye both constrict again. This paradoxical dilation is the relative afferent pupillary defect, the most reliable objective sign of a unilateral or asymmetric optic nerve lesion, present even when acuity is normal.

deficits.sign: Paradoxical dilation of the affected pupil on the swinging flashlight test; no anisocoria
Usually reduced acuity, color desaturation or a field defect in the same eye
With an optic tract lesion, the RAPD is in the eye with the temporal field loss, contralateral to the lesion

syn-rapd.reasoning: The light reflex has a bilateral afferent input and a bilateral efferent output: light in one eye drives both pretectal nuclei through the crossed and uncrossed fibers of the chiasm, and each pretectal nucleus drives both Edinger–Westphal nuclei, so the direct and consensual responses are normally equal and the two pupils are always the same size. A lesion of one optic nerve reduces the signal from that eye but not the response of either pupil to the other eye, so the pupils remain equal, and the only way to expose the deficit is to compare the two afferent inputs directly by alternating the light between the eyes: when the light moves to the damaged eye the total drive to the pupils falls and both pupils dilate, which the examiner sees in the illuminated eye. This is why an RAPD never causes anisocoria, why it is graded by comparison rather than measured in absolute terms, and why it cannot be detected when both nerves are equally affected. Because the crossing nasal fibers outnumber the uncrossed temporal fibers, a lesion of one optic tract, which contains the crossed fibers of the contralateral eye and the uncrossed fibers of the ipsilateral eye, reduces the input from the contralateral eye more and produces a small RAPD in the eye opposite the lesion, together with a homonymous hemianopia. Lesions beyond the geniculate spare the pupil, so a hemianopia with an RAPD is a tract lesion. Dense cataract, corneal opacity or media disease do not produce an RAPD, since the light scattered through them still reaches the retina.

imagingFindings.finding: Enhancing segment of the optic nerve on fat-suppressed orbital images.
Meningioma, glioma or orbital mass along the nerve; canal narrowing on CT.
Lesion of the tract lateral to the hypothalamus with a contralateral hemianopia.

imagingHint.label: optic nerve from the globe to the chiasm

commonCauses: Large retinal detachment or central retinal artery or vein occlusion

mimics.name: Hippus
mimics.howToDistinguish: Rhythmic oscillation of both pupils unrelated to the side of illumination

mimics.name: Anisocoria of any cause
mimics.howToDistinguish: An efferent problem; the RAPD test compares constriction, not size

mimics.name: Dense media opacity
mimics.howToDistinguish: Does not produce an RAPD

syn-raymond.name: Raymond syndrome (ventral pontine abducens)
syn-raymond.presentation: A patient has an isolated inability to abduct one eye with horizontal diplopia, and a hemiparesis of the arm and leg on the opposite side, without facial weakness. The crossed pattern of a sixth nerve palsy and contralateral hemiplegia places the lesion in the ventral caudal pons where the abducens fascicle crosses the corticospinal bundles, medial to the site of the Millard–Gubler lesion.

deficits.sign: Abducens palsy: abduction deficit with esotropia
Hemiparesis with upper motor neuron signs
No facial palsy (distinguishes it from Millard–Gubler)

syn-raymond.reasoning: The abducens nerve fascicle leaves its nucleus in the dorsal pontine tegmentum and runs ventrally and slightly caudally through the paramedian basis pontis to emerge at the pontomedullary sulcus; on its way it passes between the corticospinal bundles descending in the basis pontis. A small paramedian ventral lesion cuts the fascicle, which is the final uncrossed motor pathway to the ipsilateral lateral rectus, together with the corticospinal fibers, which have not yet crossed and will decussate in the medulla to serve the contralateral limbs, producing the classical alternating pattern. The facial nerve fascicle emerges more laterally, so a strictly paramedian lesion spares the face, whereas a slightly more lateral lesion adds the facial palsy of the Millard–Gubler syndrome; a lesion extending dorsally to the abducens nucleus converts the palsy into a conjugate gaze palsy (Foville). The corticobulbar fibers to the lower face travel with the corticospinal tract, so a mild contralateral central facial weakness may occur, but a complete ipsilateral peripheral facial palsy is absent by definition. The syndrome is rare in pure form and is usually a paramedian pontine infarct from basilar perforator disease.

imagingFindings.finding: Small restricted diffusion focus in the paramedian caudal basis pontis on the side of the abducens palsy.
Hemorrhagic lesion in the ventral caudal pons on SWI.

imagingHint.label: paramedian caudal basis pontis

mimics.name: Millard–Gubler syndrome
mimics.howToDistinguish: Adds an ipsilateral peripheral facial palsy

mimics.name: Foville syndrome
mimics.howToDistinguish: Conjugate gaze palsy instead of a single sixth nerve palsy

mimics.name: Sixth nerve palsy with a coincidental capsular stroke
mimics.howToDistinguish: Two lesions; hemiparesis would include the face

management: Acute stroke pathway
Occlusion for diplopia; abducens palsies from small infarcts usually recover
MRI with contrast in younger patients to exclude demyelination or cavernoma

syn-sca-infarct.name: Superior cerebellar artery infarction
syn-sca-infarct.presentation: The patient presents with a sudden inability to walk, vomiting, dysarthria and a clumsy arm on one side. There may be a Horner syndrome on the same side and loss of pain sensation on the opposite side of the body, without facial involvement. Over the next two days drowsiness can develop as the swollen superior cerebellum compresses the brainstem and fourth ventricle.

deficits.sign: Limb and gait ataxia with dysarthria (superior cerebellar hemisphere and dentate)
Loss of body pain and temperature from the spinothalamic tract in the rostral lateral pons
Horner syndrome
Drowsiness and later coma from brainstem compression and hydrocephalus

syn-sca-infarct.reasoning: The superior cerebellar artery arises from the basilar just below its bifurcation, curves around the rostral pons beneath the tentorium and supplies the superior surface of the cerebellum, the dentate nucleus, the superior cerebellar peduncle and the lateral rostral pontine tegmentum. Cerebellar signs are ipsilateral because cerebellar hemisphere output crosses in the superior cerebellar peduncle decussation and is crossed back by the corticospinal tract, so each hemisphere governs its own side of the body. The lateral rostral pons carries the spinothalamic tract, which crossed in the cord and now carries body pain and temperature from the opposite side, and the uncrossed descending sympathetic fibers; the spinal trigeminal tract has already ended below this level, which is why the face is spared, unlike in the lateral medullary and AICA syndromes. The facial and abducens nuclei lie caudal to the territory, so there is no facial palsy or deafness. The superior cerebellum abuts the tentorium and the midbrain, so swelling produces upward herniation and aqueduct obstruction, the main threat to life.

imagingFindings.finding: Restricted diffusion in the superior cerebellar hemisphere and vermis, often in a wedge extending to the dentate.

imagingHint.label: superior cerebellar hemisphere

commonCauses: Cardioembolism (the SCA is the cerebellar artery most often embolized)

mimics.name: Lateral medullary syndrome
mimics.howToDistinguish: Facial sensory loss and bulbar palsy present; no dysarthria of cerebellar type

mimics.name: AICA infarct
mimics.howToDistinguish: Deafness and facial palsy

mimics.name: Cerebellar hemorrhage
mimics.howToDistinguish: Hyperdense on CT, headache and rapid deterioration

management: Stroke treatment and neurosurgical monitoring for swelling; suboccipital decompression or ventriculostomy if deteriorating
Anticoagulation for a cardiac source after the swelling phase

syn-sciatic-neuropathy.name: Sciatic neuropathy
syn-sciatic-neuropathy.presentation: After a hip replacement, a posterior hip dislocation or an injection into the buttock, a patient has a flail foot that neither dorsiflexes nor plantar flexes, weak knee flexion, and numbness of the whole foot and the lateral leg, sparing the inner side of the leg. The ankle reflex is absent and the knee reflex is normal. The peroneal division is usually worse than the tibial, so the picture can mimic a foot drop from the fibular head until the plantar flexors are examined.

deficits.distribution: hamstrings, all muscles below the knee
deficits.sign: Weak knee flexion; foot drop with weak eversion, inversion and plantar flexion (peroneal division usually more affected than tibial)

deficits.distribution: lateral leg, dorsum and sole of the foot
deficits.sign: Sensory loss in the peroneal and tibial territories; medial leg (saphenous) spared
Absent ankle jerk with preserved knee jerk
Deep pain in the buttock radiating down the leg

syn-sciatic-neuropathy.reasoning: The sciatic nerve carries the L4–S3 fibers of the sacral plexus out of the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen beneath the piriformis, runs down the posterior thigh supplying the hamstrings, and divides above the knee into the tibial and common peroneal nerves. Its two divisions are separate bundles from the outset, and the peroneal division, with fewer and larger fascicles and less connective tissue, tethered at the fibular head, is the more vulnerable to stretch, so a sciatic lesion at the hip frequently presents as a predominant foot drop that can be mistaken for a common peroneal palsy; the distinction rests on finding weakness of the tibial-innervated plantar flexors and invertors and the hamstrings, an absent ankle reflex and sensory loss on the sole. syn-subarachnoid-hemorrhage.name: Aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage and vasospasm
syn-subarachnoid-hemorrhage.presentation: A patient describes the worst headache of their life, reaching maximum intensity within seconds, with vomiting, neck stiffness and photophobia; some collapse and lose consciousness briefly. A third nerve palsy with a dilated pupil points to a posterior communicating aneurysm. If the patient survives the first days, a new focal deficit or confusion between days four and fourteen means vasospasm, and drowsiness with dilated ventricles means hydrocephalus.

Transient loss of consciousness at ictus; drowsiness from raised pressure or hydrocephalus
Pupil-involving third nerve palsy with posterior communicating aneurysms
Delayed ischemic deficits from vasospasm in the territory of the spasmed artery, days 4–14
Subhyaloid (Terson) hemorrhages on fundoscopy

syn-subarachnoid-hemorrhage.reasoning: Saccular aneurysms form at the branch points of the circle of Willis, where the muscular layer of the arterial wall is deficient: the anterior communicating, posterior communicating and middle cerebral bifurcation are the commonest sites. The arteries lie in the subarachnoid space bathed in CSF, so rupture floods the basal cisterns with arterial blood in seconds; the sudden rise in intracranial pressure explains the abrupt headache and the transient loss of consciousness, and blood irritating the meninges produces the neck stiffness that appears over the following hours. Because the hemorrhage lies outside the brain, there is often no focal deficit at first, unless the jet of blood or the expanding aneurysm has injured a neighbor: a posterior communicating aneurysm sits directly on the oculomotor nerve, and its enlargement or rupture compresses the superficial pupillary fibers first, giving a painful pupil-involving third nerve palsy that is a warning sign before rupture. Blood in the cisterns has two delayed consequences. It blocks the arachnoid granulations and the basal cisterns, producing communicating hydrocephalus, and its breakdown products cause the cerebral arteries to constrict from about the fourth day, most severely where the clot is thickest, so that delayed infarcts appear in the territory of the spasmed vessel and produce the focal deficits, contralateral weakness or aphasia, of that territory. Rebleeding, most likely in the first day, is the other early killer and the reason aneurysms are secured urgently.

imagingHint.label: basal cisterns around the circle of Willis

mimics.name: Migraine or thunderclap headache of other cause

mimics.name: Meningitis

syn-subdural-hematoma.name: Subdural hematoma
syn-subdural-hematoma.presentation: An elderly man on warfarin, or an alcoholic with atrophy, becomes confused, unsteady and drowsy over days to weeks, sometimes without remembering any injury; the family notice a fluctuating level of alertness, a headache and a slight weakness of one side. CT shows a crescent of blood over one hemisphere, dark if old and layered if it has rebled. In a young patient after a violent injury, the same crescent appears within hours, is bright white, and comes with a contused, swollen brain and a poor outlook.

deficits.sign: Fluctuating confusion and drowsiness (chronic); coma from the outset (acute with brain injury)
Hemiparesis from hemispheric compression; may be ipsilateral through Kernohan notch
Headache, worse over weeks in chronic hematomas
Unsteadiness and falls in the elderly, mimicking dementia or normal pressure hydrocephalus
Dilated pupil with uncal herniation in large collections

syn-subdural-hematoma.reasoning: The bridging veins run from the surface of the hemisphere through the subdural space and the dura to empty into the superior sagittal sinus, and they are torn when the brain moves relative to the skull: violently in acceleration-deceleration injury, or with trivial force in the elderly and in alcoholics, in whom cerebral atrophy has lengthened and stretched the veins across a widened subdural space. Venous blood at low pressure spreads freely between the dura and the arachnoid, which are not attached to each other, and so the hematoma forms a thin crescent over the whole convexity, crossing sutures but stopping at the falx and tentorium, the opposite of the epidural clot. In the acute form the same force that tears the veins contuses and swells the brain, and the mass effect and the brain injury combine to produce early coma and a high mortality. In the chronic form the small initial bleed is walled off by a vascular membrane that repeatedly rebleeds and secretes fluid, so the collection grows over weeks in a brain that has room to accommodate it, and the signs are those of a slowly increasing unilateral mass: fluctuating drowsiness, headache and a mild contralateral hemiparesis, since the compressed motor cortex and its corticospinal fibers serve the opposite side after crossing in the medulla, with the same risk of a false-localizing ipsilateral weakness from the Kernohan notch when the shift is large. Bilateral chronic hematomas cancel each other's shift and present as dementia or gait disorder, and anticoagulants and antiplatelet drugs are the commonest precipitants.

imagingFindings.finding: Hyperdense crescentic collection over the convexity crossing sutures, often with underlying contusions and marked midline shift.
Hypodense or isodense crescent with mass effect; isodense collections are missed unless the sulcal effacement and shift are noticed; mixed density and fluid levels with rebleeding.

imagingHint.label: subdural space over the convexity beneath the bridging veins

commonCauses: Head injury, often trivial in the elderly

mimics.name: Epidural hematoma
mimics.howToDistinguish: Biconvex, does not cross sutures, arterial, lucid interval

mimics.name: Dementia or normal pressure hydrocephalus
mimics.howToDistinguish: No crescent on CT; slower course

mimics.name: Stroke
mimics.howToDistinguish: Abrupt onset; DWI or hemorrhage within the brain

management: CT for any elderly or anticoagulated patient with confusion, headache or falls; reverse anticoagulation

syn-subfalcine-herniation.name: Subfalcine (cingulate) herniation
syn-subfalcine-herniation.presentation: A patient with a large frontal or parietal mass has a headache and is drowsy, and the CT shows the septum pellucidum and the anterior ventricles pushed far across the midline beneath the falx. If the displaced hemisphere pinches its anterior cerebral artery against the rigid falx, weakness of the opposite leg develops on top of whatever deficit the mass has already produced. The far lateral ventricle dilates because its foramen of Monro is kinked.

deficits.sign: Headache and depressed consciousness from the mass and raised pressure
Leg weakness from compression of the anterior cerebral artery against the falx (ACA infarct)
Trapped contralateral lateral ventricle from obstruction of the foramen of Monro
Abulia, incontinence, gait apraxia with bilateral medial frontal ischemia

syn-subfalcine-herniation.reasoning: The falx cerebri hangs in the interhemispheric fissure from the vault to the corpus callosum, and its free lower edge lies just above the cingulate gyrus and the pericallosal branches of the anterior cerebral arteries. A mass in one hemisphere displaces the hemisphere toward the other side, and the cingulate gyrus, the most medial structure, is pushed under the free edge of the falx, taking the anterior cerebral artery with it. The herniation itself is usually silent, being the commonest and least dangerous of the herniations, and it is recognized on imaging by the midline shift of the septum pellucidum and the asymmetric ventricles; the third ventricle and the foramen of Monro are distorted so that the ventricle on the opposite side cannot drain and dilates, adding to the pressure. When the shift is large the anterior cerebral artery is compressed against the falx, infarcting the medial frontal and parietal cortex where the leg is represented; the corticospinal fibers from that cortex cross in the medulla, so the leg weakness is contralateral to the herniating hemisphere and the artery, in addition to whatever deficit the mass itself has produced. Both anterior cerebral arteries can be involved because they lie side by side, giving bilateral leg weakness, abulia and incontinence. Progressive shift precedes transtentorial herniation, so the degree of midline shift on CT is a marker of danger.

imagingFindings.finding: Displacement of the septum pellucidum, third ventricle and anterior falx-adjacent structures across the midline, measured as midline shift in millimeters; dilated contralateral ventricle.
Restricted diffusion in the medial frontal and parietal cortex on the side of the compressed artery, sometimes bilateral.

imagingHint.label: cingulate gyrus beneath the free edge of the falx

mimics.name: Primary ACA infarct
mimics.howToDistinguish: Leg weakness without a mass or midline shift

mimics.name: Hydrocephalus
mimics.howToDistinguish: Ventricles dilated symmetrically without shift

management: Treat the mass and the raised pressure; midline shift above about 5 mm with clinical decline prompts surgical decompression
Serial CT to monitor shift and the trapped ventricle
Prevent secondary ACA infarction by early relief of the shift

syn-superior-orbital-fissure.name: Superior orbital fissure and orbital apex syndromes
syn-superior-orbital-fissure.presentation: After a facial fracture, or with a tumor or inflammation at the back of the orbit, a patient has a fixed, drooping eye that cannot move in any direction, a dilated pupil, numbness of the forehead and upper eyelid and loss of the corneal reflex, with a bulging, congested eye. If vision in that eye is also lost with an afferent pupillary defect, the lesion has extended medially to the optic canal: the orbital apex syndrome.

deficits.sign: Complete external ophthalmoplegia with ptosis
Dilated, fixed pupil (parasympathetic fibers in III) and loss of accommodation
Anesthesia in the ophthalmic division with an absent corneal reflex
Proptosis and chemosis from superior ophthalmic vein obstruction
Visual loss with a relative afferent pupillary defect when the optic canal is involved

syn-superior-orbital-fissure.reasoning: The superior orbital fissure is the gap between the greater and lesser wings of the sphenoid through which the oculomotor, trochlear and abducens nerves, the three branches of the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve (lacrimal, frontal and nasociliary) and the superior ophthalmic vein pass between the cavernous sinus and the orbit. All of these are uncrossed structures serving the ipsilateral eye, so a lesion at the fissure paralyzes all the ocular muscles and the levator, dilates the pupil because the parasympathetic fibers travel in the third nerve, and removes sensation from the forehead, upper lid, cornea and bridge of the nose, with venous congestion from obstruction of the ophthalmic vein. The optic nerve and the ophthalmic artery enter the orbit separately through the optic canal, medial to the fissure, so vision is spared in a pure fissure syndrome; a process that extends to involve the canal, as at the orbital apex where the fissure and canal converge, adds an optic neuropathy with visual loss and an afferent pupillary defect. The distinction from the cavernous sinus syndrome, which involves the same nerves a centimeter further back, rests on the maxillary division (V2) and the sympathetic plexus, which run through the sinus but not the fissure, so a Horner or cheek numbness points to the sinus.

imagingFindings.finding: Fracture line through the superior orbital fissure or optic canal with bone fragments and orbital hematoma on thin-section CT of the orbit.

Enhancing mass or inflammation at the apex (meningioma, lymphoma, metastasis, invasive fungal sinusitis, IgG4 disease, Tolosa–Hunt) extending through the fissure, with optic nerve involvement; fat-suppressed post-contrast coronal images.

imagingHint.label: orbital apex and superior orbital fissure

mimics.name: Cavernous sinus syndrome
mimics.howToDistinguish: Adds V2 sensory loss and a Horner syndrome; involves the carotid

mimics.name: Orbital cellulitis
mimics.howToDistinguish: Fever, painful proptosis, cranial nerves initially spared

mimics.name: Ocular myasthenia
mimics.howToDistinguish: Painless, variable, no sensory loss or proptosis

Optic canal decompression or high-dose steroids when vision is threatened; antifungal therapy and debridement for mucormycosis
Corneal protection for the anesthetic, non-blinking eye

syn-tarsal-tunnel.name: Tarsal tunnel syndrome
syn-tarsal-tunnel.presentation: A patient describes burning pain and tingling in the sole of the foot and the toes, worse after prolonged standing or walking and sometimes at night, with relief on resting or removing shoes. Sensation may be reduced on the sole while the dorsum of the foot and the heel are normal, and in long-standing cases the small muscles of the foot are wasted and the toes clawed. Tapping behind the medial malleolus reproduces the tingling.

deficits.distribution: sole of the foot and toes (medial and lateral plantar nerves)
deficits.sign: Burning paresthesias and sensory loss of the sole, sparing the dorsum; heel sometimes spared
Pain worse with standing and walking, Tinel sign at the flexor retinaculum
Weakness and wasting of the abductor hallucis and toe flexors with clawing in chronic cases; calf muscles and ankle reflex normal

syn-tarsal-tunnel.reasoning: Behind the medial malleolus the tibial nerve passes beneath the flexor retinaculum in the tarsal tunnel, with the tendons of the tibialis posterior, flexor digitorum longus and flexor hallucis longus and the posterior tibial vessels, and there divides into the medial and lateral plantar nerves for the sole and the intrinsic muscles and the calcaneal branch for the heel. Compression within the tunnel by tenosynovitis, a ganglion, varicosities, a bony spur after an ankle fracture, hindfoot valgus or a tight retinaculum produces the plantar sensory symptoms and, later, intrinsic muscle weakness. The muscles of the calf and the ankle reflex are supplied by the tibial nerve above the tunnel and are unaffected, which separates the syndrome from a proximal tibial or sciatic lesion, and the dorsum of the foot is supplied by the peroneal nerves and is spared, which separates it from a polyneuropathy that would involve the whole foot symmetrically on both sides. The calcaneal branch often leaves the nerve above the retinaculum, so heel sensation may be preserved. An S1 radiculopathy affects the sole too but adds calf weakness, an absent ankle reflex and back pain. The deficit is peripheral and ipsilateral. Electrodiagnosis is technically demanding, and the diagnosis rests on the clinical pattern, a positive Tinel sign, imaging of the tunnel and the response to a local anesthetic block.

Talocalcaneal coalition, exostosis or malunited fracture narrowing the tunnel.

syn-thalamic-dejerine-roussy.name: Thalamic syndrome (Dejerine–Roussy)
syn-thalamic-dejerine-roussy.presentation: A patient recovers from a small posterior stroke that took away sensation on one side of the body, only to develop, weeks or months later, a spontaneous burning pain over the same side that is made worse by light touch, cold or emotion. Examination shows reduced sensation to all modalities on that side, sometimes with a mild hemiparesis, choreoathetosis or a 'thalamic hand' with the fingers flexed at the knuckles and extended at the joints.

deficits.sign: Loss or reduction of all modalities including vibration and position sense

Transient hemiparesis when the adjacent internal capsule is involved
Ataxia and choreoathetosis from the ventral lateral nucleus and dentatothalamic fibers

syn-thalamic-dejerine-roussy.reasoning: The ventral posterolateral and ventral posteromedial nuclei of the thalamus are the final relay for both the medial lemniscus and the spinothalamic tract, both of which have already crossed in the brainstem or spinal cord, and for the crossed trigeminal lemniscus from the face. An infarct here therefore removes every somatic sensory modality from the contralateral face and body at once, which no single cord or brainstem lesion can do, because in those places the pain and proprioceptive pathways travel separately. The supply comes from the thalamogeniculate branches of the posterior cerebral artery, and lesions large enough to catch the adjacent posterior limb of the internal capsule add weakness. The delayed pain is attributed to loss of inhibitory thalamic and cortical processing of surviving spinothalamic input, so that residual input is perceived as intolerable. Involvement of the ventral lateral nucleus interrupts the cerebellar outflow after its decussation in the midbrain, which is why the ataxia and involuntary movements appear on the same side as the sensory loss.

imagingFindings.finding: Restricted diffusion in the lateral thalamus (VPL/VPM) in the thalamogeniculate territory, often small.

imagingHint.label: ventral posterolateral thalamus

commonCauses: Lacunar infarct of the thalamogeniculate artery

mimics.name: Parietal cortical lesion
mimics.howToDistinguish: Discriminative loss with preserved primary modalities; no burning pain

mimics.name: Lateral medullary syndrome
mimics.howToDistinguish: Crossed facial and body sensory loss, dissociated modalities

management: Neuropathic pain treatment (amitriptyline, gabapentinoids, lamotrigine) without expectation of complete relief
Explain the delayed onset so the patient does not fear a new stroke
Vascular risk factor control

html.presentation: A patient recovers from a small posterior stroke that took away sensation on one side of the body, only to develop, weeks or months later, a spontaneous burning pain over the same side that is made worse by light touch, cold or emotion. Examination shows reduced sensation to all modalities on that side, sometimes with a mild hemiparesis, choreoathetosis or a 'thalamic hand' with the fingers flexed at the knuckles and extended at the joints.
html.reasoning: The ventral posterolateral and ventral posteromedial nuclei of the thalamus are the final relay for both the medial lemniscus and the spinothalamic tract, both of which have already crossed in the brainstem or spinal cord, and for the crossed trigeminal lemniscus from the face. An infarct here therefore removes every somatic sensory modality from the contralateral face and body at once, which no single cord or brainstem lesion can do, because in those places the pain and proprioceptive pathways travel separately. The supply comes from the thalamogeniculate branches of the posterior cerebral artery, and lesions large enough to catch the adjacent posterior limb of the internal capsule add weakness. The delayed pain is attributed to loss of inhibitory thalamic and cortical processing of surviving spinothalamic input, so that residual input is perceived as intolerable. Involvement of the ventral lateral nucleus interrupts the cerebellar outflow after its decussation in the midbrain, which is why the ataxia and involuntary movements appear on the same side as the sensory loss.

syn-tonsillar-herniation.name: Tonsillar herniation (coning)
syn-tonsillar-herniation.presentation: A patient with a posterior fossa mass, or a patient with raised intracranial pressure who has just had a lumbar puncture, develops a stiff neck, holds the head tilted, vomits, and then abruptly becomes apneic with a slow pulse and a rising blood pressure. The pupils may be small and then dilate; the arms extend. Unless the pressure is relieved within minutes, breathing stops permanently while the heart continues.

deficits.sign: Apnea and ataxic breathing from medullary compression
Cushing response: hypertension, bradycardia and irregular respiration
Abrupt loss of consciousness
Neck stiffness, head tilt and occipital pain from dural stretching and tonsillar impaction
Dysphagia, bilateral sixth nerve palsies and downbeat nystagmus before the crisis

syn-tonsillar-herniation.reasoning: The foramen magnum is the only exit from the rigid skull, and the cerebellar tonsils lie directly above it beside the medulla. When the pressure in the posterior fossa rises, from a cerebellar hematoma, infarct or tumor, or when the pressure difference across the foramen is suddenly increased by withdrawing CSF from the lumbar sac in a patient with a supratentorial mass, the tonsils are forced down through the foramen, plugging it and compressing the medulla against the bony rim. The medulla contains the respiratory rhythm generators and the cardiovascular centers, so the first consequences are irregular breathing, the Cushing response of hypertension with reflex bradycardia as the medulla tries to maintain its own perfusion, and then apnea; the heart, which has its own rhythm, keeps beating after breathing stops, which is why the classical death from coning is respiratory. The obstruction of the foramen also blocks CSF outflow from the fourth ventricle and worsens the hydrocephalus that produced it. The structures crushed are midline and the compression is symmetric, so there is no lateralizing sign and no ipsilateral or contralateral rule to apply, and the warning signs are those of medullary and lower pontine irritation: neck stiffness and head tilt, vomiting, hiccups, downbeat nystagmus and bilateral abducens palsies. Chronic tonsillar descent in Chiari malformation is a different, slow process, but it explains why a lumbar puncture can precipitate acute coning even when the supratentorial pressure is modest.

imagingFindings.finding: Tonsils below the foramen magnum with obliteration of the cisterna magna and crowding of the foramen; posterior fossa mass with a compressed fourth ventricle and hydrocephalus.
Peg-shaped tonsils below the basion–opisthion line on sagittal T1 with an effaced cisterna magna and medullary compression.
Hyperdense cerebellar hematoma or hypodense swollen infarct with fourth ventricular effacement, the commonest acute causes.

imagingHint.label: cerebellar tonsils at the foramen magnum

commonCauses: Cerebellar hemorrhage or infarct with swelling
Lumbar puncture in the presence of raised intracranial pressure
Diffuse cerebral edema as the end stage of central herniation

mimics.name: Chiari I malformation
mimics.howToDistinguish: Chronic, cough headache, no acute deterioration

mimics.name: Vasovagal syncope during lumbar puncture
mimics.howToDistinguish: Brief, with recovery and no neurological signs

mimics.name: Brainstem stroke
mimics.howToDistinguish: Focal signs, cranial nerve pattern, no mass

management: Never perform a lumbar puncture in a patient with signs of raised intracranial pressure or a posterior fossa mass without imaging first
Emergency ventriculostomy and suboccipital decompression for posterior fossa masses with tonsillar descent
Intubate and ventilate, osmotherapy, head up

syn-top-of-basilar.name: Top of the basilar syndrome
syn-top-of-basilar.presentation: A patient suddenly becomes drowsy or briefly unresponsive and, on waking, has vertical gaze palsy, pupils that are small or unequal and react poorly, sometimes skew deviation, and visual field loss that can amount to cortical blindness. Some report vivid formed hallucinations or confabulate cheerfully. Limb weakness is often surprisingly mild for such a dramatic picture, because the embolus lodged at the basilar bifurcation and spared the pons.

deficits.sign: Somnolence or coma from the paramedian midbrain and thalamic reticular projections
Vertical gaze palsy, convergence-retraction nystagmus, skew deviation
Small, unequal or poorly reactive pupils from pretectal and third nerve nuclear involvement
Hemianopia or cortical blindness from bilateral PCA infarcts
Amnesia, confusion, peduncular hallucinosis

syn-top-of-basilar.reasoning: An embolus arriving up the basilar artery stops at its bifurcation, where it obstructs the thalamoperforating and mesencephalic perforators and one or both posterior cerebral arteries. The paramedian midbrain contains the rostral interstitial nucleus of the MLF and the posterior commissure, which generate and cross the vertical gaze commands, the oculomotor nuclei with their Edinger–Westphal components, and the ascending reticular activating system, so vertical gaze, pupils and arousal are all affected bilaterally. The thalamoperforators supply the medial thalamus, adding amnesia and confusion, and the posterior cerebral arteries carry the crossed visual pathways to both occipital lobes, so bilateral occlusion causes cortical blindness with preserved pupils when the pretectum is spared. The corticospinal tracts pass through the crus and pons below the level of the embolus and cross far below in the medulla, so the classic case has little weakness. When the clot extends back into the basilar trunk the syndrome merges with a basilar occlusion and the outcome becomes far worse.

imagingFindings.finding: Filling defect at the basilar bifurcation with absent flow in one or both P1 segments and the thalamoperforators.
Restricted diffusion in the paramedian midbrain, medial thalami and occipital lobes, frequently bilateral.
Dense basilar artery on non-contrast CT; check when a patient presents with unexplained coma.

imagingHint.label: paramedian midbrain and medial thalami

mimics.name: Metabolic coma
mimics.howToDistinguish: No vertical gaze palsy or pupillary asymmetry; symmetric brainstem reflexes

mimics.name: Non-convulsive status epilepticus
mimics.howToDistinguish: EEG; fluctuating awareness without the ocular signs

mimics.name: Artery of Percheron infarct
mimics.howToDistinguish: Bilateral medial thalamic infarcts without occipital involvement

management: Emergency thrombectomy for basilar occlusion
Airway protection when drowsy
Look for a cardiac source of embolism

syn-transverse-myelitis.name: Transverse myelitis
syn-transverse-myelitis.presentation: Over hours to a few days a previously well adult develops back pain, numbness rising from the feet to a level on the trunk, weakness of both legs and difficulty passing urine. Examination shows a sensory level to pin-prick, bilateral leg weakness that is flaccid at first and later spastic, and urinary retention. MRI shows a swollen, T2-bright segment of the cord; the length of the lesion and the findings in the brain and optic nerves decide between multiple sclerosis, neuromyelitis optica and a post-infectious or systemic cause.

deficits.sign: Paraparesis or quadriparesis, flaccid then spastic with extensor plantars
Loss of all modalities with a defined level, often with a band of pain or dysesthesia at the level
Urinary retention then urgency; constipation
Back pain and Lhermitte sign
Autonomic dysreflexia and sweating changes with cervical or upper thoracic lesions

syn-transverse-myelitis.reasoning: Inflammation of one or a few segments of the cord, whether from a demyelinating attack, a post-infectious immune reaction or a systemic disease, damages the gray matter and all the white matter tracts crossing that level on both sides, so the picture is that of a partial or complete cord transection: the corticospinal tracts, which crossed in the medulla and serve the same-side limbs, are interrupted bilaterally, the posterior columns, uncrossed until the medulla, and the spinothalamic tracts, crossed within the cord, are all affected, giving bilateral loss of every modality below a level that corresponds to the inflamed segment, and the autonomic pathways to the bladder and bowel fail. The dorsal root entry zone at the lesion accounts for the band of pain, and involvement of the anterior horns at the level for any segmental flaccid weakness. Which disease is present is inferred from the shape of the lesion: multiple sclerosis produces short, eccentric, partial lesions of less than two segments, often dorsolateral and asymmetric, giving a partial myelitis; neuromyelitis optica produces longitudinally extensive, centrally located lesions spanning three or more segments with severe bilateral deficits; and acute disseminated encephalomyelitis, infections and connective tissue diseases produce variable patterns with brain or systemic clues. Spinal shock accounts for the initial flaccidity and areflexia. The main differential is a compressive or vascular lesion, which imaging separates within hours.

imagingFindings.finding: Intramedullary T2 hyperintensity with cord swelling and patchy enhancement over one to several segments; no extrinsic compression. Longitudinally extensive (three or more segments) lesions favor neuromyelitis optica or MOG antibody disease; short, eccentric lesions favor multiple sclerosis.
Periventricular and juxtacortical lesions (MS), optic nerve enhancement or diencephalic and area postrema lesions (NMOSD).
Lymphocytic pleocytosis and raised protein; oligoclonal bands in MS, usually absent in NMOSD.

imagingHint.label: thoracic cord segment

commonCauses: Systemic lupus, Sjögren syndrome, sarcoidosis, Behçet disease
Viral myelitis (enterovirus, herpes viruses, HIV), Lyme, syphilis

mimics.name: Compressive myelopathy (disc, tumor, abscess, hematoma)
mimics.howToDistinguish: Extrinsic lesion on MRI; treatment is surgical

mimics.name: Spinal cord infarct
mimics.howToDistinguish: Onset within minutes, anterior cord pattern, restricted diffusion, aortic disease

mimics.name: Guillain–Barré syndrome
mimics.howToDistinguish: No sensory level, areflexia, cranial nerves, CSF protein high without cells

mimics.name: Dural arteriovenous fistula
mimics.howToDistinguish: Stepwise progressive myelopathy with flow voids on the cord surface

management: Urgent MRI of the whole spine with contrast and of the brain; lumbar puncture, aquaporin-4 and MOG antibodies, infectious and systemic serology
High-dose intravenous methylprednisolone; plasma exchange for poor responders; disease-modifying therapy according to the diagnosis
Bladder management, thromboprophylaxis and rehabilitation

syn-trigeminal-neuralgia.name: Trigeminal neuralgia
syn-trigeminal-neuralgia.presentation: An older patient describes electric shocks in the cheek and jaw that last a second or two, come in volleys, and are set off by chewing, brushing the teeth, a breath of cold air or a light touch to a particular spot on the face. Between attacks there is no pain and the examination is normal. In a young woman with bilateral or persistent pain, sensory loss or other cranial nerve signs, multiple sclerosis or a tumor must be sought.

deficits.distribution: V2 and/or V3 divisions, rarely V1
deficits.sign: Paroxysmal lancinating pain with trigger zones; no pain between attacks
Normal sensation and corneal reflex in classic cases; any deficit suggests a structural cause
Facial spasm with the pain (tic douloureux)

syn-trigeminal-neuralgia.reasoning: In most patients the trigeminal root is compressed and indented at its entry into the pons by a loop of the superior cerebellar artery, occasionally a vein, which demyelinates the large touch fibers at the root entry zone where central myelin gives way to peripheral myelin. The demyelinated fibers become hyperexcitable and generate ectopic bursts, and cross-talk between light-touch fibers and neighboring pain fibers means that a trivial touch stimulus is felt as an explosion of pain, which explains the trigger zones and the sparing of sensation between attacks. The nerve is the uncrossed sensory supply of the ipsilateral face, so the pain is strictly unilateral and confined to one or two divisions, most often the maxillary and mandibular. Because the second-order neurons for facial pain lie in the spinal trigeminal nucleus in the medulla, a demyelinating plaque along the root fibers as they enter the pons or descend in the spinal tract can produce the same pain, which is why multiple sclerosis is the commonest cause in the young and is the explanation for bilateral cases. A cerebellopontine angle tumor compresses the root from outside and adds sensory loss, a depressed corneal reflex or other cranial nerve signs.

imagingFindings.finding: Superior cerebellar artery loop contacting and distorting the trigeminal root at the pontine entry zone on thin-section heavily T2-weighted images (CISS/FIESTA) with MRA.
FLAIR-bright plaque in the pontine trigeminal root entry zone or along the spinal tract.
Meningioma, epidermoid or schwannoma compressing the nerve; epidermoids restrict diffusion.

imagingHint.label: trigeminal root entry zone at the lateral pons

commonCauses: Neurovascular compression by the superior cerebellar artery
Herpes zoster (postherpetic, continuous rather than paroxysmal)

mimics.name: Dental pain
mimics.howToDistinguish: Continuous, localized to a tooth, tender to percussion

mimics.name: Cluster headache
mimics.howToDistinguish: Orbital pain lasting 15–180 minutes with autonomic features

mimics.name: Glossopharyngeal neuralgia
mimics.howToDistinguish: Pain in the throat and ear triggered by swallowing

mimics.name: Postherpetic neuralgia
mimics.howToDistinguish: Constant burning with allodynia after a rash, usually V1

management: Carbamazepine or oxcarbazepine is first-line and its response supports the diagnosis
MRI with thin brainstem sequences in every patient to exclude MS and tumor and to show vascular contact
Microvascular decompression or ablative procedures (radiofrequency, gamma knife) for drug-resistant cases

syn-uncal-herniation.name: Uncal (lateral transtentorial) herniation
syn-uncal-herniation.presentation: A patient with a growing temporal hematoma becomes drowsy, and the pupil on the side of the lesion enlarges and stops reacting to light while the eye drifts down and out. Then the opposite arm and leg weaken and the plantar becomes extensor. If nothing is done the patient becomes unresponsive, the other pupil dilates, the posture becomes extensor and breathing becomes irregular. Occasionally the weakness appears on the same side as the mass, because the opposite peduncle has been crushed against the tentorial edge.

deficits.sign: Early dilated, sluggish pupil from third nerve compression; later fixed and dilated, then bilateral
Progressive drowsiness to coma as the midbrain is displaced and compressed
Hemiparesis with extensor plantar from compression of the ipsilateral cerebral peduncle
Kernohan notch: hemiparesis on the side of the mass from compression of the contralateral peduncle against the tentorium
Occipital infarct from compression of the posterior cerebral artery against the tentorial edge

syn-uncal-herniation.reasoning: The tentorium cerebelli separates the temporal lobes from the posterior fossa, leaving the tentorial notch through which the midbrain passes with the oculomotor nerves and the posterior cerebral arteries running beside it. An expanding lateral supratentorial mass pushes the medial temporal lobe, the uncus and parahippocampal gyrus, over the free edge of the tentorium into the notch. The first structure crushed is the oculomotor nerve, which runs forward from the midbrain beneath the uncus; its superficial pupilloconstrictor fibers fail before the motor fibers, so an enlarging, sluggish pupil on the side of the mass is the earliest sign, followed by ptosis and a down-and-out eye. The herniating uncus then presses on the cerebral peduncle, which carries the corticospinal fibers before their crossing in the medulla, so weakness appears on the opposite side; when the midbrain is instead displaced against the opposite tentorial edge, the contralateral peduncle is notched and the weakness appears on the same side as the mass, the false-localizing Kernohan sign, which is why the pupil, not the weakness, is trusted to indicate the side of the lesion. Compression and distortion of the midbrain reticular formation cause the decline in consciousness, and downward displacement stretches the paramedian perforating arteries, producing the Duret hemorrhages of the brainstem that make the late stages irreversible. The posterior cerebral artery is compressed against the tentorium, adding an occipital infarct in survivors.

imagingFindings.finding: Medial temporal lobe displaced into the suprasellar cistern, effacement of the ipsilateral ambient and suprasellar cisterns, midline shift, dilated contralateral temporal horn, midbrain rotation and widened contralateral ambient cistern.
Linear or flame-shaped hemorrhages in the midline of the midbrain and pons on SWI or CT after downward displacement.
Occipital restricted diffusion on the side of the herniation.

imagingHint.label: uncus at the tentorial notch beside the midbrain

commonCauses: Tumor or abscess of the temporal lobe

mimics.name: Primary third nerve palsy from an aneurysm
mimics.howToDistinguish: Alert patient, no hemiparesis or altered consciousness

mimics.name: Metabolic coma
mimics.howToDistinguish: Pupils small and reactive, no lateralizing signs

mimics.name: Pontine hemorrhage
mimics.howToDistinguish: Pinpoint reactive pupils, quadriplegia, abrupt coma

management: A dilating pupil in a patient with a mass is a surgical emergency: hyperventilate briefly, give mannitol or hypertonic saline, and evacuate the mass
Head elevation, sedation, avoid hypotension and hypoxia
Intracranial pressure monitoring and decompressive craniectomy when the mass cannot be removed

syn-vagal-palsy.name: Vagus nerve palsy
syn-vagal-palsy.presentation: A patient becomes hoarse with a breathy voice and a weak cough, and regurgitates fluid through the nose when drinking. On saying 'ah' the palate rises only on one side and the uvula swings toward the good side; laryngoscopy shows one vocal cord lying still in the paramedian position. A palsy of the recurrent laryngeal branch alone spares the palate and pharynx and points to the chest or thyroid.

deficits.sign: Palatal weakness with nasal speech and regurgitation; uvula deviates to the intact side
Hoarseness, breathy voice, weak cough; paramedian cord paralysis
Dysphagia and pooling on the affected side; reduced gag
Tachycardia and gastric atony are rare with unilateral lesions

syn-vagal-palsy.reasoning: The vagus carries the motor fibers from the nucleus ambiguus to the palate, pharynx and larynx of its own side, sensation from the pharynx, larynx and external ear, and the parasympathetic outflow from the dorsal motor nucleus to the thoracic and abdominal viscera. It is an uncrossed peripheral nerve, so a palsy is ipsilateral: the levator veli palatini fails on that side and the intact side pulls the uvula across, the pharyngeal constrictors do not clear the bolus and the vocal cord is paralyzed. Where the lesion lies is read from which branches are affected. A lesion at the skull base, in the jugular foramen, or high in the neck involves the pharyngeal branch, the superior laryngeal nerve and the recurrent laryngeal nerve together, so palate, pharynx and larynx are all weak, usually with the neighboring ninth and eleventh nerves. A lesion in the chest or the lower neck, at the aortic arch on the left or the subclavian artery on the right where the recurrent laryngeal nerves loop, or in the thyroid, catches only the recurrent nerve, paralyzing the cord while the palate lifts normally; the left nerve's longer course under the aortic arch makes left-sided cord palsy from mediastinal tumors the commonest pattern. A nuclear lesion in the medulla adds the crossed signs of the lateral medullary syndrome. Bilateral cord palsies cause stridor and are an airway emergency.

imagingFindings.pathology: Skull base or carotid space lesion
imagingFindings.finding: Enhancing mass at the jugular foramen or along the carotid sheath; look for denervation atrophy of the pharyngeal constrictors and cord.
Left hilar or aortopulmonary window mass, or thyroid mass, in a patient with isolated cord palsy.
Dorsolateral medullary restricted diffusion including the nucleus ambiguus.

imagingHint.label: vagus at the jugular foramen

commonCauses: Thyroid surgery, mediastinal and lung tumors (recurrent laryngeal)

mimics.name: Myasthenia gravis
mimics.howToDistinguish: Bilateral, fatigable, with ptosis

mimics.name: Laryngeal disease
mimics.howToDistinguish: Cords move; hoarseness from a mass or inflammation on laryngoscopy

mimics.name: Functional dysphonia
mimics.howToDistinguish: Normal cord movement on coughing

management: Laryngoscopy to document the cord and swallow assessment
Imaging from the medulla to the mediastinum for an isolated recurrent laryngeal palsy
Cord medialization procedures for persistent aspiration or dysphonia

syn-vestibular-neuritis.name: Vestibular neuritis
syn-vestibular-neuritis.presentation: Over a few hours a previously well adult develops continuous, severe rotatory vertigo with vomiting, and lies still because every head movement makes it worse. There is no hearing loss, no headache and no other neurological complaint. The eyes show a horizontal-torsional nystagmus beating away from one ear that increases on looking in the direction of the fast phase and is suppressed by fixation, and rapid head turning toward that ear produces a catch-up saccade. Symptoms settle over days to weeks.

deficits.sign: Acute prolonged vertigo with unidirectional horizontal-torsional nystagmus beating away from the lesion
Positive head impulse test toward the affected ear
Veering and falling toward the affected side; able to stand unaided
Normal hearing (labyrinthitis if hearing is lost)

syn-vestibular-neuritis.reasoning: The two labyrinths send a balanced tonic discharge to the vestibular nuclei, and the brain reads any asymmetry between them as rotation. The nystagmus follows Alexander's law, growing when gaze is directed toward the fast phase, is suppressed by visual fixation because the cerebellum can override a peripheral imbalance, and stays unidirectional whatever the direction of gaze: these three features separate a peripheral from a central lesion, along with the head impulse test, in which turning the head toward the dead labyrinth fails to generate the reflex eye movement and the patient makes a visible catch-up saccade. Recovery depends on cerebellar compensation, which requires movement, so vestibular suppressants are stopped early.

imagingFindings.finding: Usually normal; occasionally enhancement of the vestibular nerve in the internal acoustic meatus. Imaging is done to exclude stroke when the examination is not clearly peripheral.

imagingHint.label: vestibular nerve in the internal acoustic meatus

commonCauses: Presumed viral (herpes simplex reactivation) inflammation of the vestibular nerve

mimics.name: Cerebellar or lateral medullary stroke
mimics.howToDistinguish: Normal head impulse, direction-changing or vertical nystagmus, skew deviation, inability to stand; HINTS 'central' pattern

mimics.name: Labyrinthitis
mimics.howToDistinguish: Same vertigo with acute hearing loss

mimics.name: Vestibular migraine
mimics.howToDistinguish: Recurrent, shorter, with migraine features

mimics.name: Ménière disease

management: Apply the HINTS examination; a central pattern or any other neurological sign requires urgent MRI
Short course of antiemetics and vestibular suppressants, then early mobilization and vestibular rehabilitation
Corticosteroids within 3 days may hasten recovery

syn-wallenberg-lateral-medullary.name: Lateral medullary syndrome (Wallenberg)
syn-wallenberg-lateral-medullary.presentation: Sudden vertigo, vomiting and violent hiccups are followed by hoarseness and difficulty swallowing. The patient falls toward one side and has a drooping eyelid and small pupil on that side, with loss of pain and temperature sensation on that side of the face and on the opposite side of the body. Strength is normal, which surprises everyone. Neck pain in a young patient means vertebral dissection.

deficits.sign: Loss of facial pain and temperature (spinal trigeminal tract and nucleus)
Loss of body pain and temperature (spinothalamic tract)
Dysphagia, hoarseness, absent gag, palate droops on the side of the lesion with the uvula pulled to the intact side (nucleus ambiguus)
Vertigo, nystagmus, nausea, lateropulsion toward the lesion
Limb ataxia from the inferior cerebellar peduncle
Horner syndrome from the descending sympathetic fibers
Hiccups from the respiratory centers; sometimes central hypoventilation

syn-wallenberg-lateral-medullary.reasoning: The lateral medulla is supplied by the vertebral artery and its posterior inferior cerebellar branch, and a wedge-shaped infarct here cuts a characteristic set of structures. The spinothalamic tract has already crossed in the spinal cord, so body pain and temperature loss is contralateral, while the descending spinal trigeminal tract carries uncrossed facial pain fibers from the same side to the spinal nucleus, so facial loss is ipsilateral: this crossed sensory pattern is the fingerprint of a lateral brainstem lesion. The nucleus ambiguus, vestibular nuclei and inferior cerebellar peduncle are all ipsilateral structures, giving same-side bulbar palsy, vertigo and ataxia, and the descending sympathetic fibers from the hypothalamus run uncrossed through the lateral tegmentum, giving an ipsilateral Horner syndrome. The pyramid and the medial lemniscus lie medially, in the anterior spinal artery territory, and escape, so there is no weakness and vibration and position sense are preserved. This dissociation, with dramatic bulbar, cerebellar and pain-temperature signs but normal strength, is what distinguishes the syndrome from the medial medullary syndrome and from a pontine stroke, where the facial and abducens nuclei would be involved.

imagingFindings.finding: Restricted diffusion in the dorsolateral medulla, often small and missed on early CT; thin-section DWI needed.
imagingFindings.pitfalls: Early DWI can be negative in the brainstem; repeat at 24–48 h if the clinical picture is clear

imagingFindings.finding: Tapered stenosis or intramural hematoma of the V3–V4 vertebral segment on fat-saturated T1 and MRA.
Absent PICA or vertebral artery filling; cerebellar hemisphere infarct may coexist and swell.

imagingHint.label: dorsolateral medulla at the level of the olive

commonCauses: Vertebral artery dissection (younger patients, neck pain)

mimics.name: Vestibular neuritis
mimics.howToDistinguish: No dysphagia, Horner or crossed sensory loss; head impulse test positive

mimics.name: Medial medullary syndrome
mimics.howToDistinguish: Contralateral weakness and proprioceptive loss with tongue palsy; no facial sensory loss

mimics.name: Lateral pontine (AICA) infarct
mimics.howToDistinguish: Adds facial palsy and deafness; vertigo similar

management: Swallow assessment before any oral intake; aspiration is the main early danger
Antithrombotic therapy; anticoagulation or antiplatelet for dissection
Monitor breathing overnight in the first days (central hypoventilation)
Vestibular rehabilitation

Look at the pupils in dim light for Horner
Say 'ah' and watch the palate; test the gag
Finger-nose and heel-shin on the side of the lesion
Head impulse test and observe nystagmus direction

syn-watershed-infarct.name: Watershed (borderzone) infarction
syn-watershed-infarct.presentation: After an episode of hypotension, cardiac arrest or a tight carotid stenosis, a patient develops weakness that involves the proximal arm and thigh more than the hand and foot, a 'man in a barrel' pattern when bilateral. Dominant-hemisphere involvement produces transcortical aphasia in which repetition is strikingly preserved while spontaneous speech or comprehension fails; posterior lesions cause cortical visual problems such as Balint syndrome.

deficits.distribution: proximal arm and leg (shoulder and hip)
deficits.sign: Proximal weakness sparing the hand and foot
Transcortical motor or sensory aphasia with preserved repetition
Cortical visual dysfunction, Balint features when bilateral
Apathy and slowed cognition with bilateral deep white matter infarcts

syn-watershed-infarct.reasoning: The borderzones are the strips of cortex and white matter at the far ends of two adjacent arterial territories, where perfusion pressure is lowest: the anterior borderzone between the anterior and middle cerebral arteries along the superior frontal convexity, the posterior borderzone between the middle and posterior cerebral arteries in the parieto-occipital region, and the internal borderzone in the corona radiata between the deep perforators and the cortical branches. When systemic pressure falls or a carotid stenosis limits inflow, these strips infarct first. The anterior borderzone sits on the motor homunculus between the leg area (medial) and the face and hand area (lateral), which is the shoulder and hip representation, so the weakness is proximal; corticospinal fibers cross in the medulla, so it is contralateral. The perisylvian language cortex has the richest supply and survives, while the surrounding cortex that feeds it dies, producing the transcortical aphasias with intact repetition. Bilateral posterior borderzone infarcts disconnect the dorsal visual stream and produce simultanagnosia, optic ataxia and ocular apraxia.

imagingFindings.finding: Wedge-shaped restricted diffusion along the ACA–MCA and MCA–PCA boundaries, often bilateral after global hypotension.
A chain of small deep white matter infarcts in the corona radiata ('rosary' or 'string of pearls') on the side of a carotid stenosis.
High-grade stenosis or occlusion of the ipsilateral internal carotid artery.

imagingHint.label: anterior borderzone on the superior frontal convexity

commonCauses: High-grade carotid stenosis with a hypotensive episode

mimics.name: Embolic multi-territory infarcts
mimics.howToDistinguish: Random cortical distribution, not confined to boundaries

mimics.name: Hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy
mimics.howToDistinguish: Diffuse cortical and deep gray involvement after arrest, rather than strips

mimics.name: Spinal cord lesion
mimics.howToDistinguish: Bilateral proximal weakness can mimic, but a sensory level and reflex changes distinguish

management: Restore perfusion pressure; avoid aggressive blood pressure lowering
Evaluate and treat carotid stenosis (endarterectomy or stenting)
Cardiac and hemodynamic assessment

syn-weber.name: Weber syndrome (ventral midbrain)
syn-weber.presentation: A patient develops a drooping eyelid and a fixed dilated pupil with the eye turned down and out on one side, together with weakness of the face, arm and leg on the opposite side. The pattern of a third nerve palsy with crossed hemiplegia is the classic ventral midbrain syndrome and is most often caused by a small infarct in the territory of the posterior cerebral artery perforators.

deficits.sign: Complete third nerve palsy with ptosis, mydriasis and the eye down and out
Hemiplegia including the lower face (corticobulbar fibers in the crus)
Corticobulbar weakness

syn-weber.reasoning: The oculomotor nerve fascicles leave their nucleus in the periaqueductal gray and pass ventrally through the red nucleus and the medial part of the crus cerebri to emerge in the interpeduncular fossa. The middle three-fifths of the crus carry the corticospinal and corticobulbar fibers, which have not yet crossed; the corticobulbar fibers will cross at the level of the facial and hypoglossal nuclei and the corticospinal fibers at the pyramidal decussation. A ventral midbrain lesion therefore paralyzes the contralateral face, arm and leg together, in contrast to the medullary syndromes where the face is spared, while the oculomotor fibers, already the final lower motor neurons for the ipsilateral eye muscles and the parasympathetic supply to the pupil, are lost on the side of the lesion. The result is the alternating pattern of a cranial nerve palsy on one side and long tract signs on the other, and the identity of the nerve fixes the level at the midbrain. The pupil is involved because the parasympathetic fibers travel within the fascicle, unlike the ischemic peripheral third nerve palsy of diabetes, where they are usually spared.

imagingFindings.finding: Restricted diffusion in the medial crus cerebri and adjacent tegmentum on the side of the third nerve palsy.
Supratentorial mass with medial temporal lobe displacement and a compressed midbrain; false localizing when the opposite peduncle is pressed against the tentorium (Kernohan).

imagingHint.label: medial crus cerebri and oculomotor fascicle

commonCauses: Posterior cerebral artery or basilar perforator infarct
Midbrain tumor or aneurysm of the posterior cerebral artery

mimics.name: Peripheral third nerve palsy with a separate capsular stroke
mimics.howToDistinguish: Two lesions; the hemiparesis would be on the same side as the ptosis only by coincidence

mimics.name: Benedikt syndrome
mimics.howToDistinguish: Contralateral tremor and ataxia (red nucleus) rather than hemiplegia

mimics.name: Claude syndrome
mimics.howToDistinguish: Contralateral ataxia without weakness

management: Acute stroke management
Exclude an aneurysm or herniation urgently when the pupil is involved
Eye patching for diplopia while the palsy recovers

syn-wernicke-korsakoff.name: Wernicke encephalopathy and Korsakoff syndrome
syn-wernicke-korsakoff.presentation: A malnourished alcoholic, or a patient after bariatric surgery or with hyperemesis, is brought in confused and unsteady, and is found to have nystagmus and an inability to abduct either eye. Given glucose without thiamine, the confusion deepens. After treatment the ophthalmoplegia clears within hours and the gait improves over weeks, but the patient is left unable to form new memories, reciting invented explanations for the gaps and unconcerned by them: Korsakoff psychosis.

deficits.sign: Acute confusion, inattention and apathy (Wernicke); dense anterograde amnesia with confabulation and preserved intelligence (Korsakoff)
Nystagmus, bilateral sixth nerve palsies, conjugate gaze palsies, rarely complete ophthalmoplegia
Wide-based ataxic gait from the anterior vermis and vestibular nuclei; limbs relatively spared
Hypothermia, hypotension, tachycardia
Stupor and coma if untreated

syn-wernicke-korsakoff.reasoning: Thiamine is a cofactor for the enzymes of glucose metabolism, and the periventricular structures around the third and fourth ventricles and the aqueduct have the highest thiamine turnover; when the vitamin runs out, especially when a glucose load suddenly increases demand, these regions suffer a symmetric, bilateral, non-inflammatory injury with petechial hemorrhage. The affected structures explain each sign: the abducens and vestibular nuclei and the periaqueductal gray beneath the fourth ventricle and aqueduct account for the nystagmus and the bilateral sixth nerve and gaze palsies; the anterior vermis and the vestibular nuclei for the gait ataxia; the hypothalamus around the third ventricle for the hypothermia and autonomic instability; and the medial thalamus and reticular formation for the confusion and stupor. Because the process is symmetric and midline, there are no crossed or lateralized signs, and the triad is often incomplete, so the diagnosis must be considered in any confused malnourished patient. The mammillary bodies and the mediodorsal and anterior thalamic nuclei are stations of the Papez circuit through which the hippocampus consolidates new memories via the fornix and mammillothalamic tract, and their destruction, which is not reversed by treatment, leaves the isolated anterograde amnesia of Korsakoff syndrome: the patient cannot lay down new memories although remote memory, attention and reasoning survive, and fills the gaps with confabulation. Early thiamine reverses the eye signs within hours and prevents the amnesia; delay makes it permanent.

imagingFindings.finding: Symmetric FLAIR and T2 hyperintensity of the medial thalami, mammillary bodies, periaqueductal gray, tectum and around the third ventricle, sometimes enhancing; restricted diffusion acutely.
imagingFindings.pitfalls: Normal MRI does not exclude the diagnosis; treat on suspicion

imagingFindings.finding: Atrophy of the mammillary bodies and medial thalami on coronal T1 in the chronic stage.
Atrophy of the anterior superior vermis.

imagingHint.label: mammillary bodies and medial thalami around the third ventricle

commonCauses: Bariatric surgery, prolonged vomiting (hyperemesis gravidarum), starvation
Parenteral nutrition or glucose without thiamine

mimics.name: Alcohol withdrawal delirium
mimics.howToDistinguish: Tremor, agitation, hallucinations, autonomic overactivity without ophthalmoplegia; may coexist

mimics.name: Hepatic encephalopathy
mimics.howToDistinguish: Asterixis, raised ammonia, no eye signs

mimics.name: Top of the basilar stroke
mimics.howToDistinguish: Abrupt onset, vertical gaze palsy, pupillary signs, DWI positive

mimics.name: Miller Fisher syndrome
mimics.howToDistinguish: Ophthalmoplegia with ataxia and areflexia after infection, no confusion

management: Give high-dose parenteral thiamine immediately, before any glucose, to any patient at risk with confusion, ataxia or eye signs; do not wait for imaging or levels
Correct magnesium, which is required for thiamine to work; treat withdrawal
Continue thiamine and nutritional rehabilitation; Korsakoff amnesia recovers only partly

g-absence-seizure.definition: A brief generalized seizure of childhood with a blank stare, eyelid flutter and immediate recovery, produced by 3 Hz spike-and-wave discharges in thalamocortical circuits and provoked by hyperventilation; some drugs for focal epilepsy make it worse.

html.definition: A brief generalized seizure of childhood with a blank stare, eyelid flutter and immediate recovery, produced by 3 Hz spike-and-wave discharges in thalamocortical circuits and provoked by hyperventilation; some drugs for focal epilepsy make it worse.

g-abulia.definition: Loss of initiative, spontaneous speech and movement with preserved ability to respond when prompted, from bilateral medial frontal, anterior cingulate, caudate or anterior thalamic lesions; its extreme form is akinetic mutism.

html.definition: Loss of initiative, spontaneous speech and movement with preserved ability to respond when prompted, from bilateral medial frontal, anterior cingulate, caudate or anterior thalamic lesions; its extreme form is akinetic mutism.

g-achromatopsia-cerebral.definition: Loss of color perception with normal cones, from damage to the ventral occipito-temporal cortex (V4 region); unilateral lesions produce hemiachromatopsia in the contralateral field, which is missed unless colors are tested in each hemifield.

html.definition: Loss of color perception with normal cones, from damage to the ventral occipito-temporal cortex (V4 region); unilateral lesions produce hemiachromatopsia in the contralateral field, which is missed unless colors are tested in each hemifield.

g-agnosia.definition: Failure to recognize objects, faces or sounds despite intact primary perception, from lesions of the association cortex: visual agnosia (occipitotemporal), prosopagnosia (fusiform), astereognosis (parietal).

html.definition: Failure to recognize objects, faces or sounds despite intact primary perception, from lesions of the association cortex: visual agnosia (occipitotemporal), prosopagnosia (fusiform), astereognosis (parietal).

g-akinetic-mutism.definition: A state of wakefulness with open eyes and visual tracking but no spontaneous movement or speech, after bilateral anterior cingulate and medial frontal damage or bilateral paramedian thalamic lesions; distinguished from coma by the alert appearance and from the locked-in state by the absence of communicative eye movements.

html.definition: A state of wakefulness with open eyes and visual tracking but no spontaneous movement or speech, after bilateral anterior cingulate and medial frontal damage or bilateral paramedian thalamic lesions; distinguished from coma by the alert appearance and from the locked-in state by the absence of communicative eye movements.

g-akinetopsia.definition: Loss of the perception of visual motion, so that moving objects appear as a sequence of still frames, after bilateral damage to the temporo-occipital motion area (MT/V5). Acuity, color and form vision remain intact.
