html.definition: Loss of the perception of visual motion, so that moving objects appear as a sequence of still frames, after bilateral damage to the temporo-occipital motion area (MT/V5). Acuity, color and form vision remain intact.

g-alexia-without-agraphia.definition: Loss of reading with preserved writing after a left occipital infarct that also cuts the splenium, so that visual information from the intact right visual cortex cannot reach the left language cortex. The patient can write a sentence and cannot read it back.

html.definition: Loss of reading with preserved writing after a left occipital infarct that also cuts the splenium, so that visual information from the intact right visual cortex cannot reach the left language cortex. The patient can write a sentence and cannot read it back.

g-alpha-rhythm.definition: The 8-13 Hz posterior EEG rhythm of relaxed wakefulness with the eyes closed that attenuates on eye opening; its slowing or loss indicates encephalopathy.

html.definition: The 8-13 Hz posterior EEG rhythm of relaxed wakefulness with the eyes closed that attenuates on eye opening; its slowing or loss indicates encephalopathy.

g-amyloid-angiopathy.definition: Deposition of amyloid-beta in the walls of cortical and leptomeningeal arteries in the elderly, producing lobar hemorrhages, cortical microbleeds and superficial siderosis on susceptibility imaging, and transient focal neurological episodes; a contraindication to anticoagulation when severe.

html.definition: Deposition of amyloid-beta in the walls of cortical and leptomeningeal arteries in the elderly, producing lobar hemorrhages, cortical microbleeds and superficial siderosis on susceptibility imaging, and transient focal neurological episodes; a contraindication to anticoagulation when severe.

g-amyloid-plaque.definition: Extracellular deposit of amyloid-beta in the neocortex, accumulating years before symptoms in Alzheimer disease; detected by amyloid PET and by low CSF amyloid-beta 42.

html.definition: Extracellular deposit of amyloid-beta in the neocortex, accumulating years before symptoms in Alzheimer disease; detected by amyloid PET and by low CSF amyloid-beta 42.

g-anisocoria.definition: Unequal pupils. Anisocoria greater in the dark indicates a sympathetic (Horner) lesion on the side of the smaller pupil; greater in the light, a parasympathetic lesion on the side of the larger pupil; equal in both, physiologic.

html.definition: Unequal pupils. Anisocoria greater in the dark indicates a sympathetic (Horner) lesion on the side of the smaller pupil; greater in the light, a parasympathetic lesion on the side of the larger pupil; equal in both, physiologic.

g-anosognosia.definition: Unawareness or denial of a deficit, classically of a left hemiplegia after a right parietal stroke or of blindness in Anton syndrome; it prevents the patient from reporting the problem and from engaging in rehabilitation.

html.definition: Unawareness or denial of a deficit, classically of a left hemiplegia after a right parietal stroke or of blindness in Anton syndrome; it prevents the patient from reporting the problem and from engaging in rehabilitation.

g-anticholinergic-toxicity.definition: Delirium with dilated pupils, dry skin, urinary retention, tachycardia and hyperthermia from muscarinic blockade; a common reversible cause of confusion in the elderly on bladder, sleep and allergy drugs.

html.definition: Delirium with dilated pupils, dry skin, urinary retention, tachycardia and hyperthermia from muscarinic blockade; a common reversible cause of confusion in the elderly on bladder, sleep and allergy drugs.

g-aphasia.definition: A disorder of language, not of speech mechanics, from a lesion of the dominant (usually left) hemisphere. Classified by fluency, comprehension and repetition: Broca (non-fluent, comprehension preserved), Wernicke (fluent, comprehension impaired), conduction (repetition impaired), global and transcortical (repetition preserved).

html.definition: A disorder of language, not of speech mechanics, from a lesion of the dominant (usually left) hemisphere. Classified by fluency, comprehension and repetition: Broca (non-fluent, comprehension preserved), Wernicke (fluent, comprehension impaired), conduction (repetition impaired), global and transcortical (repetition preserved).

g-apperceptive-agnosia.definition: Failure to recognize objects because their shape cannot be assembled from the visual input; the patient cannot copy or match the object. Lesions lie in the lateral occipital and occipito-temporal cortex, often bilateral after hypoxia.

html.definition: Failure to recognize objects because their shape cannot be assembled from the visual input; the patient cannot copy or match the object. Lesions lie in the lateral occipital and occipito-temporal cortex, often bilateral after hypoxia.

g-apraxia-of-speech.definition: Impaired planning and sequencing of the articulatory movements of speech with groping, inconsistent errors and effortful output, despite normal strength of the muscles; a sign of left inferior frontal, insular or opercular lesions and of the non-fluent variant of primary progressive aphasia.

html.definition: Impaired planning and sequencing of the articulatory movements of speech with groping, inconsistent errors and effortful output, despite normal strength of the muscles; a sign of left inferior frontal, insular or opercular lesions and of the non-fluent variant of primary progressive aphasia.

g-apraxia.definition: Inability to perform a learned skilled movement on command despite intact strength, sensation and comprehension, from a lesion of the dominant parietal lobe or its connections to the premotor cortex.

html.definition: Inability to perform a learned skilled movement on command despite intact strength, sensation and comprehension, from a lesion of the dominant parietal lobe or its connections to the premotor cortex.

g-aprosodia.definition: Loss of the melody, rhythm and emotional intonation of speech (expressive) or of the ability to understand it (receptive), from right hemisphere lesions homologous to the left language areas. The words are correct but sound flat, and irony and anger are missed.

html.definition: Loss of the melody, rhythm and emotional intonation of speech (expressive) or of the ability to understand it (receptive), from right hemisphere lesions homologous to the left language areas. The words are correct but sound flat, and irony and anger are missed.

g-arterial-territory.definition: The region of brain supplied by one artery. Infarct patterns follow territories, and the territory maps shown on the MRI slices in this atlas are population averages that vary between individuals, especially at the borders.

html.definition: The region of brain supplied by one artery. Infarct patterns follow territories, and the territory maps shown on the MRI slices in this atlas are population averages that vary between individuals, especially at the borders.

g-artery-of-percheron.definition: A variant in which a single paramedian thalamic artery from one P1 segment supplies both medial thalami and the rostral midbrain; its occlusion produces bilateral paramedian thalamic infarcts with sudden coma or hypersomnolence, vertical gaze palsy and amnesia.

html.definition: A variant in which a single paramedian thalamic artery from one P1 segment supplies both medial thalami and the rostral midbrain; its occlusion produces bilateral paramedian thalamic infarcts with sudden coma or hypersomnolence, vertical gaze palsy and amnesia.

g-ascending-arousal-system.definition: The cholinergic, monoaminergic, orexinergic and glutamatergic projections from the upper brainstem and hypothalamus to the thalamus and cortex that maintain wakefulness; damage to the paramedian upper pons and midbrain, or bilateral thalamic damage, produces coma.

html.definition: The cholinergic, monoaminergic, orexinergic and glutamatergic projections from the upper brainstem and hypothalamus to the thalamus and cortex that maintain wakefulness; damage to the paramedian upper pons and midbrain, or bilateral thalamic damage, produces coma.

g-asomatognosia.definition: Failure to recognize a limb as one's own, typically the left arm after a right posterior parietal lesion; the patient may attribute it to someone else or complain that a stranger's arm is in the bed.

html.definition: Failure to recognize a limb as one's own, typically the left arm after a right posterior parietal lesion; the patient may attribute it to someone else or complain that a stranger's arm is in the bed.

g-aspects.definition: The Alberta Stroke Program Early CT Score: ten regions of the MCA territory on two CT levels, one point deducted for each region with early ischemic change; low scores predict poor outcome and hemorrhage after reperfusion.

html.definition: The Alberta Stroke Program Early CT Score: ten regions of the MCA territory on two CT levels, one point deducted for each region with early ischemic change; low scores predict poor outcome and hemorrhage after reperfusion.

g-association-fibers.definition: White-matter axons connecting cortical areas within one hemisphere: short U-fibers between neighboring gyri and the long fasciculi (arcuate and superior longitudinal, inferior longitudinal, inferior fronto-occipital, uncinate, cingulum) that link the lobes into networks.

html.definition: White-matter axons connecting cortical areas within one hemisphere: short U-fibers between neighboring gyri and the long fasciculi (arcuate and superior longitudinal, inferior longitudinal, inferior fronto-occipital, uncinate, cingulum) that link the lobes into networks.

g-associative-agnosia.definition: Failure to recognize an object whose form is perceived normally: the patient can copy and match it but cannot say what it is or how it is used. It reflects disconnection of the visual form areas from the semantic system in the anterior temporal lobe.

html.definition: Failure to recognize an object whose form is perceived normally: the patient can copy and match it but cannot say what it is or how it is used. It reflects disconnection of the visual form areas from the semantic system in the anterior temporal lobe.

g-ataxia.definition: Incoordination of movement: cerebellar ataxia (dysmetria, intention tremor, dysdiadochokinesia, not worse with eyes closed) or sensory ataxia from loss of proprioception (worse with eyes closed, Romberg positive).

html.definition: Incoordination of movement: cerebellar ataxia (dysmetria, intention tremor, dysdiadochokinesia, not worse with eyes closed) or sensory ataxia from loss of proprioception (worse with eyes closed, Romberg positive).

g-aura.definition: The first subjective symptom of a focal seizure, produced by discharge in the cortex of onset and therefore the best localizing feature: epigastric rising and fear for the medial temporal lobe, colored shapes for the occipital lobe, tingling for the parietal lobe. Migraine aura is a spreading cortical event of minutes rather than seconds.

html.definition: The first subjective symptom of a focal seizure, produced by discharge in the cortex of onset and therefore the best localizing feature: epigastric rising and fear for the medial temporal lobe, colored shapes for the occipital lobe, tingling for the parietal lobe. Migraine aura is a spreading cortical event of minutes rather than seconds.

g-autonomic-dysreflexia.definition: Paroxysmal hypertension with headache, sweating and bradycardia triggered by a noxious stimulus (typically bladder distension) below a spinal cord lesion above T6, from unmodulated sympathetic discharge.

html.definition: Paroxysmal hypertension with headache, sweating and bradycardia triggered by a noxious stimulus (typically bladder distension) below a spinal cord lesion above T6, from unmodulated sympathetic discharge.

g-axonotmesis.definition: Nerve injury in which axons are interrupted but the connective tissue tubes remain, so that Wallerian degeneration is followed by regeneration along the tubes at about a millimeter a day; typical of traction and crush injuries.

html.definition: Nerve injury in which axons are interrupted but the connective tissue tubes remain, so that Wallerian degeneration is followed by regeneration along the tubes at about a millimeter a day; typical of traction and crush injuries.

g-babinski-sign.definition: Extension of the big toe with fanning of the other toes when the lateral sole is stroked, indicating a corticospinal (upper motor neuron) lesion. Normal in infants before myelination of the corticospinal tract.

html.definition: Extension of the big toe with fanning of the other toes when the lateral sole is stroked, indicating a corticospinal (upper motor neuron) lesion. Normal in infants before myelination of the corticospinal tract.

g-ballismus.definition: Violent, large-amplitude flinging movements of the proximal limbs, usually on one side (hemiballismus), from a lesion of the contralateral subthalamic nucleus.

html.definition: Violent, large-amplitude flinging movements of the proximal limbs, usually on one side (hemiballismus), from a lesion of the contralateral subthalamic nucleus.

g-blood-brain-barrier.definition: The tight-junctioned capillary endothelium with its astrocyte end-feet and pericytes that excludes proteins, most drugs and hydrophilic molecules from the brain; it is absent in the circumventricular organs and breaks down in tumor, infection, inflammation and infarction, which is what contrast enhancement shows.

html.definition: The tight-junctioned capillary endothelium with its astrocyte end-feet and pericytes that excludes proteins, most drugs and hydrophilic molecules from the brain; it is absent in the circumventricular organs and breaks down in tumor, infection, inflammation and infarction, which is what contrast enhancement shows.

g-bradykinesia.definition: Slowness and progressive reduction in the amplitude of repetitive movements, the cardinal sign of parkinsonism, reflecting under-activation of the motor cortex by the basal ganglia–thalamic loop.

html.definition: Slowness and progressive reduction in the amplitude of repetitive movements, the cardinal sign of parkinsonism, reflecting under-activation of the motor cortex by the basal ganglia–thalamic loop.

g-brain-death.definition: Irreversible loss of all brainstem function: deep coma of known irreversible cause without confounders, absent pupillary, corneal, oculocephalic, caloric, gag and cough reflexes, no cranial motor response and apnea on a formal test; spinal reflexes may persist.

html.definition: Irreversible loss of all brainstem function: deep coma of known irreversible cause without confounders, absent pupillary, corneal, oculocephalic, caloric, gag and cough reflexes, no cranial motor response and apnea on a formal test; spinal reflexes may persist.

g-burst-suppression.definition: An EEG pattern of bursts of activity alternating with periods of flat suppression, seen with deep anesthesia, hypothermia and severe anoxic injury; a poor prognostic sign after cardiac arrest.

html.definition: An EEG pattern of bursts of activity alternating with periods of flat suppression, seen with deep anesthesia, hypothermia and severe anoxic injury; a poor prognostic sign after cardiac arrest.

g-butterfly-glioma.definition: A glioblastoma (or lymphoma) that crosses the corpus callosum to involve both frontal lobes in a butterfly shape.

html.definition: A glioblastoma (or lymphoma) that crosses the corpus callosum to involve both frontal lobes in a butterfly shape.

g-cataplexy.definition: Sudden loss of muscle tone triggered by emotion, especially laughter, with preserved consciousness; the intrusion of REM sleep atonia into wakefulness, pathognomonic of narcolepsy with orexin deficiency.

html.definition: Sudden loss of muscle tone triggered by emotion, especially laughter, with preserved consciousness; the intrusion of REM sleep atonia into wakefulness, pathognomonic of narcolepsy with orexin deficiency.

g-cauda-equina.definition: The bundle of lumbar and sacral nerve roots descending in the lumbar cistern below the conus medullaris (L1–L2). Compression produces a lower motor neuron, radicular picture with saddle anesthesia and late sphincter loss: a surgical emergency.

html.definition: The bundle of lumbar and sacral nerve roots descending in the lumbar cistern below the conus medullaris (L1–L2). Compression produces a lower motor neuron, radicular picture with saddle anesthesia and late sphincter loss: a surgical emergency.

g-charcot-bouchard-aneurysm.definition: Small dilatation of a perforating artery (lenticulostriate, thalamoperforating, pontine) weakened by chronic hypertension; its rupture produces the deep hypertensive hemorrhages of the putamen, thalamus, pons and cerebellum.

html.definition: Small dilatation of a perforating artery (lenticulostriate, thalamoperforating, pontine) weakened by chronic hypertension; its rupture produces the deep hypertensive hemorrhages of the putamen, thalamus, pons and cerebellum.

g-cheyne-stokes-respiration.definition: A crescendo-decrescendo breathing pattern with apneic pauses, from bilateral hemispheric or diencephalic dysfunction or from heart failure; central neurogenic hyperventilation, apneustic and ataxic breathing mark progressively lower brainstem levels.

html.definition: A crescendo-decrescendo breathing pattern with apneic pauses, from bilateral hemispheric or diencephalic dysfunction or from heart failure; central neurogenic hyperventilation, apneustic and ataxic breathing mark progressively lower brainstem levels.

g-chorea.definition: Irregular, flowing, unpredictable involuntary movements that flit from one body part to another, from dysfunction of the striatum and the indirect pathway (Huntington disease, Sydenham chorea, drugs).

html.definition: Irregular, flowing, unpredictable involuntary movements that flit from one body part to another, from dysfunction of the striatum and the indirect pathway (Huntington disease, Sydenham chorea, drugs).

g-chromatolysis.definition: The reaction of a neuron whose axon has been cut: swelling of the cell body, dispersal of Nissl substance and displacement of the nucleus to the periphery as the cell switches from transmission to regeneration.

html.definition: The reaction of a neuron whose axon has been cut: swelling of the cell body, dispersal of Nissl substance and displacement of the nucleus to the periphery as the cell switches from transmission to regeneration.

g-circumventricular-organs.definition: Midline structures around the ventricles that lack a blood-brain barrier and sense or secrete into the blood: the area postrema, median eminence, organum vasculosum, subfornical organ, pineal gland and posterior pituitary. They enhance normally after contrast.

html.definition: Midline structures around the ventricles that lack a blood-brain barrier and sense or secrete into the blood: the area postrema, median eminence, organum vasculosum, subfornical organ, pineal gland and posterior pituitary. They enhance normally after contrast.

g-clonus.definition: Rhythmic involuntary contractions elicited by a sudden sustained stretch, typically at the ankle, indicating hyperexcitable stretch reflexes after an upper motor neuron lesion. More than a few beats is abnormal.

html.definition: Rhythmic involuntary contractions elicited by a sudden sustained stretch, typically at the ankle, indicating hyperexcitable stretch reflexes after an upper motor neuron lesion. More than a few beats is abnormal.

g-commissural-fibers.definition: Axons crossing between the hemispheres: the corpus callosum, the anterior commissure (temporal and olfactory), the hippocampal commissure and the posterior commissure (pretectal and vertical gaze fibers).

html.definition: Axons crossing between the hemispheres: the corpus callosum, the anterior commissure (temporal and olfactory), the hippocampal commissure and the posterior commissure (pretectal and vertical gaze fibers).

g-conduction-aphasia.definition: Fluent speech with preserved comprehension but disproportionately impaired repetition and phonemic paraphasias that the patient notices and tries to correct, from a lesion of the arcuate fasciculus or the supramarginal gyrus that disconnects the posterior temporal from the frontal speech areas.

html.definition: Fluent speech with preserved comprehension but disproportionately impaired repetition and phonemic paraphasias that the patient notices and tries to correct, from a lesion of the arcuate fasciculus or the supramarginal gyrus that disconnects the posterior temporal from the frontal speech areas.

g-confabulation.definition: Production of false memories and answers without intent to deceive, filling gaps in memory; characteristic of diencephalic and basal forebrain amnesia (Korsakoff syndrome, anterior communicating aneurysm rupture) and of frontal lobe dysfunction rather than of pure hippocampal amnesia.

html.definition: Production of false memories and answers without intent to deceive, filling gaps in memory; characteristic of diencephalic and basal forebrain amnesia (Korsakoff syndrome, anterior communicating aneurysm rupture) and of frontal lobe dysfunction rather than of pure hippocampal amnesia.

g-contralateral.definition: On the opposite side of the body from the lesion. Corticospinal weakness, spinothalamic pain loss and cortical sensory loss are contralateral to lesions above the level at which their fibers cross.

html.definition: On the opposite side of the body from the lesion. Corticospinal weakness, spinothalamic pain loss and cortical sensory loss are contralateral to lesions above the level at which their fibers cross.

g-conus-medullaris.definition: The tapered end of the spinal cord at L1–L2 containing the sacral segments; lesions produce early symmetric saddle anesthesia and sphincter failure with little leg weakness.

html.definition: The tapered end of the spinal cord at L1–L2 containing the sacral segments; lesions produce early symmetric saddle anesthesia and sphincter failure with little leg weakness.

g-core-penumbra-mismatch.definition: The difference between the irreversibly infarcted core (low blood volume or restricted diffusion) and the larger hypoperfused but viable penumbra on perfusion imaging; a large mismatch identifies patients who benefit from late thrombectomy.

html.definition: The difference between the irreversibly infarcted core (low blood volume or restricted diffusion) and the larger hypoperfused but viable penumbra on perfusion imaging; a large mismatch identifies patients who benefit from late thrombectomy.

g-cortical-magnification.definition: The disproportionate area of visual cortex devoted to the central few degrees of the visual field, mapped to the occipital pole; it explains why macular vision survives partial calcarine lesions and why the macula is represented at the pole where two arteries meet.

html.definition: The disproportionate area of visual cortex devoted to the central few degrees of the visual field, mapped to the occipital pole; it explains why macular vision survives partial calcarine lesions and why the macula is represented at the pole where two arteries meet.

g-cortical-ribbon-sign.definition: Gyriform restricted diffusion or T2 hyperintensity of the cortex, seen in prion disease, after hypoxia (laminar necrosis), in status epilepticus and in some encephalitides.

html.definition: Gyriform restricted diffusion or T2 hyperintensity of the cortex, seen in prion disease, after hypoxia (laminar necrosis), in status epilepticus and in some encephalitides.

g-cortical-spreading-depression.definition: A slowly propagating wave of neuronal depolarization followed by silence that travels across the cortex at a few millimeters a minute; the mechanism of the migraine aura, whose scintillations march across the visual field over twenty minutes.

html.definition: A slowly propagating wave of neuronal depolarization followed by silence that travels across the cortex at a few millimeters a minute; the mechanism of the migraine aura, whose scintillations march across the visual field over twenty minutes.

g-corticobasal-syndrome.definition: Asymmetric parkinsonism with limb apraxia, dystonia, myoclonus, cortical sensory loss and an alien limb, from asymmetric frontoparietal and basal ganglia degeneration (corticobasal degeneration or Alzheimer pathology).

html.definition: Asymmetric parkinsonism with limb apraxia, dystonia, myoclonus, cortical sensory loss and an alien limb, from asymmetric frontoparietal and basal ganglia degeneration (corticobasal degeneration or Alzheimer pathology).

g-cremasteric-reflex.definition: Elevation of the testis when the medial thigh is stroked; the afferent runs in the ilioinguinal nerve and the efferent in the genitofemoral nerve (L1-L2). Lost in L1-L2 lesions and in corticospinal lesions above them.

html.definition: Elevation of the testis when the medial thigh is stroked; the afferent runs in the ilioinguinal nerve and the efferent in the genitofemoral nerve (L1-L2). Lost in L1-L2 lesions and in corticospinal lesions above them.

g-crossed-cerebellar-diaschisis.definition: Reduced metabolism and blood flow of the cerebellar hemisphere opposite a large cerebral lesion, from loss of corticopontocerebellar input, seen on PET and perfusion imaging; not an infarct.

html.definition: Reduced metabolism and blood flow of the cerebellar hemisphere opposite a large cerebral lesion, from loss of corticopontocerebellar input, seen on PET and perfusion imaging; not an infarct.

g-crossed-syndrome.definition: A cranial nerve palsy on one side with long tract signs (weakness or sensory loss) on the opposite side of the body, produced by a single brainstem lesion that involves an uncrossed cranial nerve nucleus or fascicle together with corticospinal or sensory fibers that cross elsewhere. The cranial nerve names the level: III for the midbrain, VI or VII for the pons, XII for the medulla.

html.definition: A cranial nerve palsy on one side with long tract signs (weakness or sensory loss) on the opposite side of the body, produced by a single brainstem lesion that involves an uncrossed cranial nerve nucleus or fascicle together with corticospinal or sensory fibers that cross elsewhere. The cranial nerve names the level: III for the midbrain, VI or VII for the pons, XII for the medulla.

g-cushing-response.definition: Hypertension with bradycardia and irregular breathing produced by medullary ischemia when intracranial pressure approaches arterial pressure, a sign of impending brainstem compression.

html.definition: Hypertension with bradycardia and irregular breathing produced by medullary ischemia when intracranial pressure approaches arterial pressure, a sign of impending brainstem compression.

g-dandy-walker-malformation.definition: Cystic dilatation of the fourth ventricle with hypoplasia and upward rotation of the cerebellar vermis and an enlarged posterior fossa, presenting with hydrocephalus and ataxia.

html.definition: Cystic dilatation of the fourth ventricle with hypoplasia and upward rotation of the cerebellar vermis and an enlarged posterior fossa, presenting with hydrocephalus and ataxia.

g-dawson-fingers.definition: Ovoid demyelinating lesions oriented perpendicular to the lateral ventricles along the deep medullary veins, seen on sagittal FLAIR in multiple sclerosis; a discriminating feature against vascular white-matter disease.

html.definition: Ovoid demyelinating lesions oriented perpendicular to the lateral ventricles along the deep medullary veins, seen on sagittal FLAIR in multiple sclerosis; a discriminating feature against vascular white-matter disease.

g-decerebrate-posturing.definition: Extension and internal rotation of the arms and extension of the legs in response to pain, indicating damage between the red nucleus and the vestibular nuclei (midbrain-pons), where unopposed vestibulospinal and pontine reticulospinal tone drives the extensors; a worse sign than decorticate posturing.

html.definition: Extension and internal rotation of the arms and extension of the legs in response to pain, indicating damage between the red nucleus and the vestibular nuclei (midbrain-pons), where unopposed vestibulospinal and pontine reticulospinal tone drives the extensors; a worse sign than decorticate posturing.

g-decorticate-posturing.definition: Flexion of the arms with extension of the legs in response to pain, indicating dysfunction above the red nucleus (hemispheres, diencephalon) with intact rubrospinal tone.

html.definition: Flexion of the arms with extension of the legs in response to pain, indicating dysfunction above the red nucleus (hemispheres, diencephalon) with intact rubrospinal tone.

g-decussation.definition: A crossing of fibers from one side of the neuraxis to the other. The main decussations are the pyramidal (corticospinal, cervicomedullary junction), the sensory (medial lemniscus, lower medulla), the spinothalamic (anterior white commissure, within the cord), the optic chiasm and the superior cerebellar peduncle (midbrain). Where a pathway crosses determines whether a lesion produces ipsilateral or contralateral signs.

html.definition: A crossing of fibers from one side of the neuraxis to the other. The main decussations are the pyramidal (corticospinal, cervicomedullary junction), the sensory (medial lemniscus, lower medulla), the spinothalamic (anterior white commissure, within the cord), the optic chiasm and the superior cerebellar peduncle (midbrain). Where a pathway crosses determines whether a lesion produces ipsilateral or contralateral signs.

g-default-mode-network.definition: The set of regions (medial prefrontal cortex, posterior cingulate and precuneus, angular gyri, hippocampal formation) that is most active at rest and during self-referential thought and memory retrieval and deactivates during attention-demanding tasks; its posterior hub is the first to lose metabolism in Alzheimer disease.

html.definition: The set of regions (medial prefrontal cortex, posterior cingulate and precuneus, angular gyri, hippocampal formation) that is most active at rest and during self-referential thought and memory retrieval and deactivates during attention-demanding tasks; its posterior hub is the first to lose metabolism in Alzheimer disease.

g-dermatome.definition: The strip of skin supplied by the sensory fibers of one spinal nerve root. Key landmarks: C6 thumb, C7 middle finger, C8 little finger, T4 nipple, T10 umbilicus, L4 medial leg, L5 dorsum of the foot and big toe, S1 lateral foot.

html.definition: The strip of skin supplied by the sensory fibers of one spinal nerve root. Key landmarks: C6 thumb, C7 middle finger, C8 little finger, T4 nipple, T10 umbilicus, L4 medial leg, L5 dorsum of the foot and big toe, S1 lateral foot.

g-disconnection-syndrome.definition: A deficit produced by interrupting the white-matter connection between two intact cortical areas rather than by destroying either: conduction aphasia (arcuate fasciculus), alexia without agraphia (splenium), left-hand apraxia and agraphia (callosal body), and the split-brain syndrome after callosotomy.

html.definition: A deficit produced by interrupting the white-matter connection between two intact cortical areas rather than by destroying either: conduction aphasia (arcuate fasciculus), alexia without agraphia (splenium), left-hand apraxia and agraphia (callosal body), and the split-brain syndrome after callosotomy.

g-dissociated-sensory-loss.definition: Loss of pain and temperature with preservation of touch, vibration and position sense, or the reverse. It shows that the spinothalamic and lemniscal pathways, which travel separately in the cord and brainstem, have been affected differently, and points to a cord or lateral brainstem lesion rather than a nerve, thalamic or cortical one.

html.definition: Loss of pain and temperature with preservation of touch, vibration and position sense, or the reverse. It shows that the spinothalamic and lemniscal pathways, which travel separately in the cord and brainstem, have been affected differently, and points to a cord or lateral brainstem lesion rather than a nerve, thalamic or cortical one.

g-dopamine-transporter-imaging.definition: SPECT imaging of the presynaptic dopamine transporter in the striatum; reduced, asymmetric putaminal uptake indicates nigrostriatal degeneration (Parkinson disease, Lewy body dementia, atypical parkinsonism) and is normal in essential tremor and drug-induced parkinsonism.

html.definition: SPECT imaging of the presynaptic dopamine transporter in the striatum; reduced, asymmetric putaminal uptake indicates nigrostriatal degeneration (Parkinson disease, Lewy body dementia, atypical parkinsonism) and is normal in essential tremor and drug-induced parkinsonism.

g-dorsal-stream.definition: The occipito-parietal pathway that computes where objects are and how to act on them (location, motion, reaching, attention); lesions produce optic ataxia, simultanagnosia, akinetopsia and neglect. The 'where' or 'how' pathway.

html.definition: The occipito-parietal pathway that computes where objects are and how to act on them (location, motion, reaching, attention); lesions produce optic ataxia, simultanagnosia, akinetopsia and neglect. The 'where' or 'how' pathway.

g-dural-tail.definition: A tapering strip of enhancing dura extending from the margin of an extra-axial mass, typical of meningioma.

html.definition: A tapering strip of enhancing dura extending from the margin of an extra-axial mass, typical of meningioma.

g-duret-hemorrhage.definition: Linear or flame-shaped hemorrhages in the midline of the pons and midbrain caused by stretching of perforating arteries during downward transtentorial herniation; a sign of a usually fatal stage.

html.definition: Linear or flame-shaped hemorrhages in the midline of the pons and midbrain caused by stretching of perforating arteries during downward transtentorial herniation; a sign of a usually fatal stage.

g-dwi.definition: An MRI sequence sensitive to the restricted diffusion of water in cytotoxic edema, which shows acute infarcts as bright areas within minutes of onset, well before CT or conventional MRI change; also bright in abscess, epidermoid and highly cellular tumors.

html.definition: An MRI sequence sensitive to the restricted diffusion of water in cytotoxic edema, which shows acute infarcts as bright areas within minutes of onset, well before CT or conventional MRI change; also bright in abscess, epidermoid and highly cellular tumors.

g-dysarthria.definition: Impaired articulation of speech with intact language, from weakness or incoordination of the muscles of speech: spastic (pseudobulbar), flaccid (bulbar), ataxic (cerebellar) or hypokinetic (parkinsonian).

html.definition: Impaired articulation of speech with intact language, from weakness or incoordination of the muscles of speech: spastic (pseudobulbar), flaccid (bulbar), ataxic (cerebellar) or hypokinetic (parkinsonian).

g-dysexecutive-syndrome.definition: Impairment of planning, initiation, set shifting, inhibition and monitoring with preserved basic language and memory, from dorsolateral prefrontal lesions or their subcortical circuits; tested by fluency, Luria sequences, go/no-go and trail making, and missed by screening tests of memory.

html.definition: Impairment of planning, initiation, set shifting, inhibition and monitoring with preserved basic language and memory, from dorsolateral prefrontal lesions or their subcortical circuits; tested by fluency, Luria sequences, go/no-go and trail making, and missed by screening tests of memory.

g-dysmetria.definition: Overshooting or undershooting a target during a reaching movement, seen in the finger-nose and heel-shin tests, a sign of cerebellar hemisphere dysfunction ipsilateral to the lesion.

html.definition: Overshooting or undershooting a target during a reaching movement, seen in the finger-nose and heel-shin tests, a sign of cerebellar hemisphere dysfunction ipsilateral to the lesion.

g-dystonia.definition: Sustained or intermittent muscle contractions producing twisting movements and abnormal postures, from disordered basal ganglia output; may be focal, segmental or generalized.

html.definition: Sustained or intermittent muscle contractions producing twisting movements and abnormal postures, from disordered basal ganglia output; may be focal, segmental or generalized.

g-empty-delta-sign.definition: A filling defect in the enhancing superior sagittal sinus on contrast CT or MRI, marking thrombus within the sinus in cerebral venous thrombosis.

html.definition: A filling defect in the enhancing superior sagittal sinus on contrast CT or MRI, marking thrombus within the sinus in cerebral venous thrombosis.

g-excitotoxicity.definition: Neuronal death caused by excessive glutamate acting on NMDA receptors, flooding the cell with calcium; the mechanism of neuronal loss in ischemia, status epilepticus, hypoglycemia and trauma.

html.definition: Neuronal death caused by excessive glutamate acting on NMDA receptors, flooding the cell with calcium; the mechanism of neuronal loss in ischemia, status epilepticus, hypoglycemia and trauma.

g-extinction.definition: Failure to perceive a stimulus on one side when a competing stimulus is presented simultaneously on the other, although each is perceived alone; the mildest form of neglect, tested with double simultaneous touch, sounds or visual stimuli after right parietal lesions.

html.definition: Failure to perceive a stimulus on one side when a competing stimulus is presented simultaneously on the other, although each is perceived alone; the mildest form of neglect, tested with double simultaneous touch, sounds or visual stimuli after right parietal lesions.

g-eye-of-the-tiger-sign.definition: Central T2 hyperintensity within a hypointense globus pallidus on MRI, from iron accumulation with central gliosis, characteristic of pantothenate kinase-associated neurodegeneration.

html.definition: Central T2 hyperintensity within a hypointense globus pallidus on MRI, from iron accumulation with central gliosis, characteristic of pantothenate kinase-associated neurodegeneration.

g-false-localizing-sign.definition: A deficit that suggests a lesion at a site other than the true one, produced by displacement or generalized pressure: a sixth nerve palsy from raised intracranial pressure, or hemiparesis on the side of a mass from compression of the opposite cerebral peduncle against the tentorium (Kernohan notch).

html.definition: A deficit that suggests a lesion at a site other than the true one, produced by displacement or generalized pressure: a sixth nerve palsy from raised intracranial pressure, or hemiparesis on the side of a mass from compression of the opposite cerebral peduncle against the tentorium (Kernohan notch).

g-fasciculation.definition: A visible twitch of a group of muscle fibers produced by spontaneous discharge of a single motor unit, a sign of lower motor neuron irritability or degeneration, most significant when combined with wasting and weakness.

html.definition: A visible twitch of a group of muscle fibers produced by spontaneous discharge of a single motor unit, a sign of lower motor neuron irritability or degeneration, most significant when combined with wasting and weakness.

g-febrile-seizure.definition: A generalized seizure with fever in a neurologically normal child between six months and five years, usually brief and benign; complex features (focal, prolonged, repeated) raise the risk of later epilepsy and require evaluation.

html.definition: A generalized seizure with fever in a neurologically normal child between six months and five years, usually brief and benign; complex features (focal, prolonged, repeated) raise the risk of later epilepsy and require evaluation.

g-flair.definition: Fluid-attenuated inversion recovery: a T2-weighted MRI sequence with the CSF signal suppressed, making periventricular and cortical lesions such as demyelinating plaques, edema and gliosis conspicuous.

html.definition: Fluid-attenuated inversion recovery: a T2-weighted MRI sequence with the CSF signal suppressed, making periventricular and cortical lesions such as demyelinating plaques, edema and gliosis conspicuous.

g-floppy-infant.definition: An infant with hypotonia; if weak with absent reflexes and tongue fasciculation the cause is a lower motor neuron disorder (spinal muscular atrophy, congenital myopathy, neuromuscular junction), if strong with brisk reflexes a central cause (hypoxic injury, chromosomal or metabolic disease).

html.definition: An infant with hypotonia; if weak with absent reflexes and tongue fasciculation the cause is a lower motor neuron disorder (spinal muscular atrophy, congenital myopathy, neuromuscular junction), if strong with brisk reflexes a central cause (hypoxic injury, chromosomal or metabolic disease).

g-focal-cortical-dysplasia.definition: A localized malformation of cortical development with disorganized layers, dysmorphic neurons and balloon cells, seen on MRI as cortical thickening, blurred gray-white junction and a transmantle FLAIR band; a leading cause of surgically treatable epilepsy.

html.definition: A localized malformation of cortical development with disorganized layers, dysmorphic neurons and balloon cells, seen on MRI as cortical thickening, blurred gray-white junction and a transmantle FLAIR band; a leading cause of surgically treatable epilepsy.

g-forehead-sparing.definition: Preservation of forehead movement in a facial weakness, indicating an upper motor neuron (central) lesion, because the upper facial nucleus receives bilateral cortical input. A lower motor neuron lesion paralyzes the whole side of the face.

html.definition: Preservation of forehead movement in a facial weakness, indicating an upper motor neuron (central) lesion, because the upper facial nucleus receives bilateral cortical input. A lower motor neuron lesion paralyzes the whole side of the face.

g-frontal-release-signs.definition: Primitive reflexes that reappear with frontal or diffuse cerebral damage: the grasp, palmomental, snout, rooting and glabellar tap responses. Individually nonspecific, together they suggest frontal disinhibition.

html.definition: Primitive reflexes that reappear with frontal or diffuse cerebral damage: the grasp, palmomental, snout, rooting and glabellar tap responses. Individually nonspecific, together they suggest frontal disinhibition.

g-fusiform-face-area.definition: A region of the right posterior fusiform gyrus that responds selectively to faces and extracts the configuration that identifies an individual; its damage produces prosopagnosia.

html.definition: A region of the right posterior fusiform gyrus that responds selectively to faces and extracts the configuration that identifies an individual; its damage produces prosopagnosia.

g-glasgow-coma-scale.definition: A 3-15 point scale of eye opening (1-4), verbal response (1-5) and motor response (1-6) that grades the level of consciousness; 8 or less defines coma. The FOUR score adds brainstem reflexes and breathing.

html.definition: A 3-15 point scale of eye opening (1-4), verbal response (1-5) and motor response (1-6) that grades the level of consciousness; 8 or less defines coma. The FOUR score adds brainstem reflexes and breathing.

g-glymphatic-system.definition: The perivascular pathway along which CSF flows into the brain and interstitial fluid and solutes are cleared to the venous and lymphatic drainage, most active during sleep; implicated in the clearance of amyloid.

html.definition: The perivascular pathway along which CSF flows into the brain and interstitial fluid and solutes are cleared to the venous and lymphatic drainage, most active during sleep; implicated in the clearance of amyloid.

g-herniation.definition: Displacement of brain from one intracranial compartment to another under pressure: subfalcine (cingulate under the falx), uncal (medial temporal lobe through the tentorial notch), central (diencephalon downward), tonsillar (cerebellar tonsils through the foramen magnum) and upward (cerebellum through the notch).

html.definition: Displacement of brain from one intracranial compartment to another under pressure: subfalcine (cingulate under the falx), uncal (medial temporal lobe through the tentorial notch), central (diencephalon downward), tonsillar (cerebellar tonsils through the foramen magnum) and upward (cerebellum through the notch).

g-heteroplasmy.definition: The coexistence of normal and mutant mitochondrial DNA within a cell, varying between tissues and relatives, which explains the variable expression and maternal inheritance of mitochondrial disorders such as MELAS.

html.definition: The coexistence of normal and mutant mitochondrial DNA within a cell, varying between tissues and relatives, which explains the variable expression and maternal inheritance of mitochondrial disorders such as MELAS.

g-heterotopia.definition: Gray matter in the wrong place, along the ventricular wall (periventricular nodular) or as a band within the white matter, because neurons stopped migrating; it follows gray matter signal on all MRI sequences, does not enhance, and is a common cause of epilepsy.

html.definition: Gray matter in the wrong place, along the ventricular wall (periventricular nodular) or as a band within the white matter, because neurons stopped migrating; it follows gray matter signal on all MRI sequences, does not enhance, and is a common cause of epilepsy.

g-hints.definition: Three bedside tests (Head Impulse, Nystagmus pattern, Test of Skew) that distinguish a peripheral from a central cause of acute vertigo; a normal head impulse, direction-changing nystagmus or skew deviation indicates a central lesion.

html.definition: Three bedside tests (Head Impulse, Nystagmus pattern, Test of Skew) that distinguish a peripheral from a central cause of acute vertigo; a normal head impulse, direction-changing nystagmus or skew deviation indicates a central lesion.

g-holmes-tremor.definition: A slow, coarse tremor present at rest and worsening with posture and action, appearing weeks to months after a lesion of the midbrain or thalamus that damages both the cerebellothalamic and nigrostriatal pathways.

html.definition: A slow, coarse tremor present at rest and worsening with posture and action, appearing weeks to months after a lesion of the midbrain or thalamus that damages both the cerebellothalamic and nigrostriatal pathways.

g-holoprosencephaly.definition: Failure of the forebrain to divide into two hemispheres, from alobar (a single ventricle, cyclopia) to lobar (fused frontal lobes, absent septum pellucidum), associated with midline facial defects, sonic hedgehog pathway mutations and trisomy 13.

html.definition: Failure of the forebrain to divide into two hemispheres, from alobar (a single ventricle, cyclopia) to lobar (fused frontal lobes, absent septum pellucidum), associated with midline facial defects, sonic hedgehog pathway mutations and trisomy 13.

g-homonymous-hemianopia.definition: Loss of the same half of the visual field in both eyes, produced by a lesion behind the optic chiasm on the opposite side. Congruity increases and pupillary involvement disappears as the lesion moves from the optic tract to the occipital cortex.

html.definition: Loss of the same half of the visual field in both eyes, produced by a lesion behind the optic chiasm on the opposite side. Congruity increases and pupillary involvement disappears as the lesion moves from the optic tract to the occipital cortex.

g-homunculus.definition: The distorted map of the body on the primary motor and somatosensory cortex, with the leg on the medial surface (anterior cerebral territory), the trunk at the vertex and the arm, hand and face on the lateral convexity (middle cerebral territory). It explains why anterior cerebral infarcts weaken the leg and middle cerebral infarcts the face and arm.

html.definition: The distorted map of the body on the primary motor and somatosensory cortex, with the leg on the medial surface (anterior cerebral territory), the trunk at the vertex and the arm, hand and face on the lateral convexity (middle cerebral territory). It explains why anterior cerebral infarcts weaken the leg and middle cerebral infarcts the face and arm.

g-hoover-sign.definition: In functional leg weakness, the 'weak' leg extends at the hip involuntarily when the patient flexes the other hip against resistance; a positive sign of functional weakness, not merely an absence of organic findings.

html.definition: In functional leg weakness, the 'weak' leg extends at the hip involuntarily when the patient flexes the other hip against resistance; a positive sign of functional weakness, not merely an absence of organic findings.

g-horner-syndrome.definition: Miosis, mild ptosis and, with central or preganglionic lesions, facial anhidrosis, from interruption of the uncrossed three-neuron sympathetic pathway to the eye anywhere from the hypothalamus to the carotid artery.

html.definition: Miosis, mild ptosis and, with central or preganglionic lesions, facial anhidrosis, from interruption of the uncrossed three-neuron sympathetic pathway to the eye anywhere from the hypothalamus to the carotid artery.

g-hot-cross-bun-sign.definition: A cruciform T2 hyperintensity in the pons from degeneration of the transverse pontocerebellar fibers and the raphe, seen in the cerebellar type of multiple system atrophy.

html.definition: A cruciform T2 hyperintensity in the pons from degeneration of the transverse pontocerebellar fibers and the raphe, seen in the cerebellar type of multiple system atrophy.

g-hummingbird-sign.definition: The silhouette of the atrophic midbrain with a preserved pons on midline sagittal MRI in progressive supranuclear palsy, resembling a hummingbird's head and beak.

html.definition: The silhouette of the atrophic midbrain with a preserved pons on midline sagittal MRI in progressive supranuclear palsy, resembling a hummingbird's head and beak.

g-hydrocephalus.definition: Enlargement of the ventricles from obstruction of CSF flow (obstructive, non-communicating) or impaired absorption (communicating). The pattern of ventricular dilatation locates the block; obstructive hydrocephalus contraindicates lumbar puncture.

html.definition: Enlargement of the ventricles from obstruction of CSF flow (obstructive, non-communicating) or impaired absorption (communicating). The pattern of ventricular dilatation locates the block; obstructive hydrocephalus contraindicates lumbar puncture.

g-hyperdense-artery-sign.definition: Increased density of an occluded artery on non-contrast CT (the hyperdense MCA or basilar sign) from the fresh thrombus within it; an early marker of large vessel occlusion.

html.definition: Increased density of an occluded artery on non-contrast CT (the hyperdense MCA or basilar sign) from the fresh thrombus within it; an early marker of large vessel occlusion.

g-hypsarrhythmia.definition: The chaotic, high-amplitude, multifocal spike-and-slow-wave EEG pattern of infantile spasms.

html.definition: The chaotic, high-amplitude, multifocal spike-and-slow-wave EEG pattern of infantile spasms.

g-ideomotor-apraxia.definition: Inability to perform a learned skilled movement to command or by imitation (pantomime tool use, wave goodbye) despite intact strength, sensation and comprehension; from left inferior parietal or premotor lesions, and affecting both hands because the right hemisphere receives its movement formulas through the corpus callosum.

html.definition: Inability to perform a learned skilled movement to command or by imitation (pantomime tool use, wave goodbye) despite intact strength, sensation and comprehension; from left inferior parietal or premotor lesions, and affecting both hands because the right hemisphere receives its movement formulas through the corpus callosum.

g-infantile-spasms.definition: Clusters of brief flexor or extensor jerks in infancy with a chaotic high-voltage EEG (hypsarrhythmia) and developmental regression, signaling a serious underlying cause such as tuberous sclerosis or a malformation and demanding urgent treatment.

html.definition: Clusters of brief flexor or extensor jerks in infancy with a chaotic high-voltage EEG (hypsarrhythmia) and developmental regression, signaling a serious underlying cause such as tuberous sclerosis or a malformation and demanding urgent treatment.

g-insular-ribbon-sign.definition: Loss of the gray-white distinction of the insular cortex on non-contrast CT within hours of a middle cerebral artery occlusion; the insula is the most distal perforator territory and the first to fail.

html.definition: Loss of the gray-white distinction of the insular cortex on non-contrast CT within hours of a middle cerebral artery occlusion; the insula is the most distal perforator territory and the first to fail.

g-internal-capsule.definition: The compact band of projection fibers between the caudate and thalamus medially and the lentiform nucleus laterally, with an anterior limb (frontopontine and anterior thalamic radiation), a genu (corticobulbar), a posterior limb (corticospinal and sensory thalamocortical fibers), and retrolenticular and sublenticular parts (optic and acoustic radiations). Lacunes here produce pure motor or sensorimotor stroke.

html.definition: The compact band of projection fibers between the caudate and thalamus medially and the lentiform nucleus laterally, with an anterior limb (frontopontine and anterior thalamic radiation), a genu (corticobulbar), a posterior limb (corticospinal and sensory thalamocortical fibers), and retrolenticular and sublenticular parts (optic and acoustic radiations). Lacunes here produce pure motor or sensorimotor stroke.

g-internuclear-ophthalmoplegia.definition: Failure of adduction of one eye on lateral gaze with nystagmus of the abducting eye, with preserved convergence, from a lesion of the medial longitudinal fasciculus on the side of the eye that fails to adduct.

html.definition: Failure of adduction of one eye on lateral gaze with nystagmus of the abducting eye, with preserved convergence, from a lesion of the medial longitudinal fasciculus on the side of the eye that fails to adduct.

g-ipsilateral.definition: On the same side of the body as the lesion or the structure being discussed. Cerebellar signs, lower motor neuron cranial nerve palsies and Horner syndrome are ipsilateral to their lesion.

html.definition: On the same side of the body as the lesion or the structure being discussed. Cerebellar signs, lower motor neuron cranial nerve palsies and Horner syndrome are ipsilateral to their lesion.

g-jacksonian-march.definition: Spread of clonic jerking from one body part to adjacent parts (thumb to hand to arm to face) as a seizure discharge moves along the motor homunculus of the precentral gyrus.

html.definition: Spread of clonic jerking from one body part to adjacent parts (thumb to hand to arm to face) as a seizure discharge moves along the motor homunculus of the precentral gyrus.

g-kernicterus.definition: Bilirubin toxicity of the neonatal brain, selectively damaging the globus pallidus, subthalamic nucleus, hippocampus and brainstem nuclei and producing dyskinetic cerebral palsy, deafness and upgaze palsy; the immature blood-brain barrier lets unconjugated bilirubin in.

html.definition: Bilirubin toxicity of the neonatal brain, selectively damaging the globus pallidus, subthalamic nucleus, hippocampus and brainstem nuclei and producing dyskinetic cerebral palsy, deafness and upgaze palsy; the immature blood-brain barrier lets unconjugated bilirubin in.

g-kernohan-notch.definition: Compression of the contralateral cerebral peduncle against the opposite tentorial edge during uncal herniation, producing a hemiparesis on the same side as the mass, a false localizing sign.

html.definition: Compression of the contralateral cerebral peduncle against the opposite tentorial edge during uncal herniation, producing a hemiparesis on the same side as the mass, a false localizing sign.

g-lacune.definition: A small deep infarct (under 15 mm) from occlusion of a single penetrating artery, most often in the internal capsule, thalamus, basal ganglia or pons, producing one of the classical lacunar syndromes without cortical signs.

html.definition: A small deep infarct (under 15 mm) from occlusion of a single penetrating artery, most often in the internal capsule, thalamus, basal ganglia or pons, producing one of the classical lacunar syndromes without cortical signs.

g-leukodystrophy.definition: A genetic disorder of myelin formation or maintenance producing symmetric, confluent white-matter disease with progressive spasticity, ataxia and cognitive decline; the regional pattern on MRI (parieto-occipital, frontal, periventricular) and associated features point to the gene.

html.definition: A genetic disorder of myelin formation or maintenance producing symmetric, confluent white-matter disease with progressive spasticity, ataxia and cognitive decline; the regional pattern on MRI (parieto-occipital, frontal, periventricular) and associated features point to the gene.

g-lewy-body.definition: Intraneuronal inclusion of alpha-synuclein found in the substantia nigra, brainstem nuclei and cortex in Parkinson disease and dementia with Lewy bodies; the pathology spreads from the olfactory bulb and vagal nucleus upward.

html.definition: Intraneuronal inclusion of alpha-synuclein found in the substantia nigra, brainstem nuclei and cortex in Parkinson disease and dementia with Lewy bodies; the pathology spreads from the olfactory bulb and vagal nucleus upward.

g-lhermitte-sign.definition: An electric shock sensation down the spine and limbs on neck flexion, indicating a lesion of the cervical posterior columns, classically demyelination, also seen in B12 deficiency and cervical spondylosis.

html.definition: An electric shock sensation down the spine and limbs on neck flexion, indicating a lesion of the cervical posterior columns, classically demyelination, also seen in B12 deficiency and cervical spondylosis.

g-light-near-dissociation.definition: Pupils that fail to constrict to light but constrict to a near target, produced by lesions of the pretectum (Parinaud, Argyll Robertson) or by aberrant regeneration in the ciliary ganglion (Adie).

html.definition: Pupils that fail to constrict to light but constrict to a near target, produced by lesions of the pretectum (Parinaud, Argyll Robertson) or by aberrant regeneration in the ciliary ganglion (Adie).

g-lissencephaly.definition: A smooth brain with absent or shallow sulci and a thick, abnormally layered cortex from arrested neuronal migration (LIS1, DCX and other genes), presenting with severe developmental delay and epilepsy.

html.definition: A smooth brain with absent or shallow sulci and a thick, abnormally layered cortex from arrested neuronal migration (LIS1, DCX and other genes), presenting with severe developmental delay and epilepsy.

g-locked-in-state.definition: Complete paralysis of the limbs and lower cranial nerves with preserved consciousness and vertical eye movements, from a lesion of the ventral pons that spares the tegmentum; must be distinguished from coma by asking for a blink or upward gaze.

html.definition: Complete paralysis of the limbs and lower cranial nerves with preserved consciousness and vertical eye movements, from a lesion of the ventral pons that spares the tegmentum; must be distinguished from coma by asking for a blink or upward gaze.

g-logopenic-aphasia.definition: Progressive word-finding pauses and impaired sentence repetition with preserved grammar and single-word comprehension, from left temporo-parietal atrophy, usually caused by Alzheimer pathology.

html.definition: Progressive word-finding pauses and impaired sentence repetition with preserved grammar and single-word comprehension, from left temporo-parietal atrophy, usually caused by Alzheimer pathology.

g-long-term-potentiation.definition: A lasting increase in synaptic strength after brief high-frequency activity, best studied at the CA3-CA1 synapse of the hippocampus and dependent on NMDA receptors; the cellular model of memory storage.

html.definition: A lasting increase in synaptic strength after brief high-frequency activity, best studied at the CA3-CA1 synapse of the hippocampus and dependent on NMDA receptors; the cellular model of memory storage.

g-lower-motor-neuron.definition: The anterior horn cell or cranial nerve motor neuron and its axon to the muscle. Lesions cause flaccid weakness, wasting, fasciculation, hypotonia and loss of the tendon reflex whose arc it forms.

html.definition: The anterior horn cell or cranial nerve motor neuron and its axon to the muscle. Lesions cause flaccid weakness, wasting, fasciculation, hypotonia and loss of the tendon reflex whose arc it forms.

g-macular-sparing.definition: Preservation of the central few degrees of vision in a homonymous hemianopia, characteristic of occipital infarcts because the macular cortex at the occipital pole receives collateral supply from the middle cerebral artery.

html.definition: Preservation of the central few degrees of vision in a homonymous hemianopia, characteristic of occipital infarcts because the macular cortex at the occipital pole receives collateral supply from the middle cerebral artery.

g-malignant-mca-infarct.definition: Infarction of most of the MCA territory with cytotoxic edema that peaks at 2-4 days and produces midline shift and herniation; decompressive hemicraniectomy within 48 hours improves survival, especially in patients under 60.

html.definition: Infarction of most of the MCA territory with cytotoxic edema that peaks at 2-4 days and produces midline shift and herniation; decompressive hemicraniectomy within 48 hours improves survival, especially in patients under 60.

g-mesolimbic-pathway.definition: Dopaminergic projections from the ventral tegmental area to the nucleus accumbens, amygdala and hippocampus (mesolimbic: reward, motivation, addiction, psychosis) and to the prefrontal cortex (mesocortical: working memory, motivation).

html.definition: Dopaminergic projections from the ventral tegmental area to the nucleus accumbens, amygdala and hippocampus (mesolimbic: reward, motivation, addiction, psychosis) and to the prefrontal cortex (mesocortical: working memory, motivation).

g-meyer-loop.definition: The anterior sweep of the inferior fibers of the optic radiation over the temporal horn before they turn back to the lower calcarine cortex; it carries the contralateral upper visual field and is cut by anterior temporal lobectomy, producing a superior quadrantanopia.

html.definition: The anterior sweep of the inferior fibers of the optic radiation over the temporal horn before they turn back to the lower calcarine cortex; it carries the contralateral upper visual field and is cut by anterior temporal lobectomy, producing a superior quadrantanopia.

g-mni-space.definition: A standard stereotaxic coordinate system based on averaged MRI templates from the Montreal Neurological Institute, with x (left–right), y (posterior–anterior) and z (inferior–superior) in millimeters from the anterior commissure. This atlas uses the MNI152NLin2009cAsym template; all meshes and slice positions are expressed in its RAS millimeter coordinates.

html.definition: A standard stereotaxic coordinate system based on averaged MRI templates from the Montreal Neurological Institute, with x (left–right), y (posterior–anterior) and z (inferior–superior) in millimeters from the anterior commissure. This atlas uses the MNI152NLin2009cAsym template; all meshes and slice positions are expressed in its RAS millimeter coordinates.

g-mononeuropathy.definition: Disease of a single peripheral nerve, usually from compression at a known site (carpal tunnel, ulnar groove, fibular head), producing sensory and motor deficits in the nerve's territory only.

html.definition: Disease of a single peripheral nerve, usually from compression at a known site (carpal tunnel, ulnar groove, fibular head), producing sensory and motor deficits in the nerve's territory only.

g-monro-kellie-doctrine.definition: Within the rigid skull the volumes of brain, blood and CSF are constant, so an added volume (mass, edema, hematoma) must displace CSF or venous blood; when that compensation is exhausted, intracranial pressure rises steeply and herniation follows.

html.definition: Within the rigid skull the volumes of brain, blood and CSF are constant, so an added volume (mass, edema, hematoma) must displace CSF or venous blood; when that compensation is exhausted, intracranial pressure rises steeply and herniation follows.

g-motor-unit.definition: One lower motor neuron and all the muscle fibers it innervates. Denervation and reinnervation change the size and shape of motor unit potentials on EMG: large in reinnervation, small and polyphasic in myopathy.

html.definition: One lower motor neuron and all the muscle fibers it innervates. Denervation and reinnervation change the size and shape of motor unit potentials on EMG: large in reinnervation, small and polyphasic in myopathy.

g-myotome.definition: The group of muscles supplied by one spinal root. Root weakness crosses peripheral nerve territories (C7: triceps and wrist flexors), whereas nerve weakness crosses root territories.

html.definition: The group of muscles supplied by one spinal root. Root weakness crosses peripheral nerve territories (C7: triceps and wrist flexors), whereas nerve weakness crosses root territories.

g-neglect.definition: Failure to attend to or respond to stimuli on one side of space, usually the left after a right parietal lesion, with extinction on double simultaneous stimulation and often anosognosia. It is a disorder of attention, not of sensation.

html.definition: Failure to attend to or respond to stimuli on one side of space, usually the left after a right parietal lesion, with extinction on double simultaneous stimulation and often anosognosia. It is a disorder of attention, not of sensation.

g-neurapraxia.definition: The mildest nerve injury: a focal conduction block from demyelination or ischemia without axonal loss, recovering in days to weeks; the Saturday night radial palsy and a tourniquet palsy are examples. Distal nerve conduction is preserved.

html.definition: The mildest nerve injury: a focal conduction block from demyelination or ischemia without axonal loss, recovering in days to weeks; the Saturday night radial palsy and a tourniquet palsy are examples. Distal nerve conduction is preserved.

g-neurofibrillary-tangle.definition: Intraneuronal aggregate of hyperphosphorylated tau protein that appears first in the entorhinal cortex and spreads to the hippocampus and association cortex in Alzheimer disease; tangle stage tracks the cognitive decline better than amyloid plaques.

html.definition: Intraneuronal aggregate of hyperphosphorylated tau protein that appears first in the entorhinal cortex and spreads to the hippocampus and association cortex in Alzheimer disease; tangle stage tracks the cognitive decline better than amyloid plaques.

g-neurotmesis.definition: Complete transection of a nerve including its connective tissue sheaths; regeneration fails or forms a neuroma unless the nerve is surgically repaired or grafted.

html.definition: Complete transection of a nerve including its connective tissue sheaths; regeneration fails or forms a neuroma unless the nerve is surgically repaired or grafted.

g-neurulation.definition: Folding and closure of the neural plate into the neural tube during the third and fourth weeks; failure at the anterior neuropore produces anencephaly and at the posterior neuropore spina bifida.

html.definition: Folding and closure of the neural plate into the neural tube during the third and fourth weeks; failure at the anterior neuropore produces anencephaly and at the posterior neuropore spina bifida.

g-nigrostriatal-pathway.definition: The dopaminergic projection from the substantia nigra pars compacta to the putamen and caudate that sets the gain of the basal ganglia loops; its degeneration causes Parkinson disease and its blockade drug-induced parkinsonism.

html.definition: The dopaminergic projection from the substantia nigra pars compacta to the putamen and caudate that sets the gain of the basal ganglia loops; its degeneration causes Parkinson disease and its blockade drug-induced parkinsonism.

g-nmda-receptor.definition: A glutamate receptor that opens only when glutamate binds and the membrane is depolarized, admitting calcium; the coincidence detector of long-term potentiation and the mediator of excitotoxicity, blocked by ketamine and targeted by the antibodies of anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis.

html.definition: A glutamate receptor that opens only when glutamate binds and the membrane is depolarized, admitting calcium; the coincidence detector of long-term potentiation and the mediator of excitotoxicity, blocked by ketamine and targeted by the antibodies of anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis.

g-nystagmus.definition: Rhythmic involuntary oscillation of the eyes, named by the direction of the fast phase. Peripheral vestibular nystagmus is unidirectional, horizontal-torsional and suppressed by fixation; central nystagmus changes direction with gaze, may be vertical or purely torsional and is not suppressed.

html.definition: Rhythmic involuntary oscillation of the eyes, named by the direction of the fast phase. Peripheral vestibular nystagmus is unidirectional, horizontal-torsional and suppressed by fixation; central nystagmus changes direction with gaze, may be vertical or purely torsional and is not suppressed.

g-oligoclonal-bands.definition: Discrete immunoglobulin bands on CSF electrophoresis that are absent from the serum, indicating intrathecal antibody synthesis; present in most patients with multiple sclerosis and in chronic CNS infections.

html.definition: Discrete immunoglobulin bands on CSF electrophoresis that are absent from the serum, indicating intrathecal antibody synthesis; present in most patients with multiple sclerosis and in chronic CNS infections.

g-optic-ataxia.definition: Misreaching for an object under visual guidance despite normal strength, sensation and cerebellar function, from disconnection of the parietal visuomotor cortex from the premotor cortex. Part of Balint syndrome with simultanagnosia and ocular apraxia.

html.definition: Misreaching for an object under visual guidance despite normal strength, sensation and cerebellar function, from disconnection of the parietal visuomotor cortex from the premotor cortex. Part of Balint syndrome with simultanagnosia and ocular apraxia.

g-orexin.definition: A peptide made by lateral hypothalamic neurons that stabilizes wakefulness by exciting the arousal nuclei; loss of these neurons causes narcolepsy type 1 with cataplexy and low CSF hypocretin.

html.definition: A peptide made by lateral hypothalamic neurons that stabilizes wakefulness by exciting the arousal nuclei; loss of these neurons causes narcolepsy type 1 with cataplexy and low CSF hypocretin.

g-pancoast-tumor.definition: An apical lung tumor invading the lower trunk of the brachial plexus (C8-T1) and the stellate ganglion, producing shoulder and medial arm pain, hand wasting and a Horner syndrome.

html.definition: An apical lung tumor invading the lower trunk of the brachial plexus (C8-T1) and the stellate ganglion, producing shoulder and medial arm pain, hand wasting and a Horner syndrome.

g-papez-circuit.definition: The limbic loop of memory: hippocampus and subiculum, fornix, mammillary body, mammillothalamic tract, anterior thalamic nuclei, cingulate gyrus and cingulum, entorhinal cortex and back to the hippocampus. Interruption at any point produces anterograde amnesia.

html.definition: The limbic loop of memory: hippocampus and subiculum, fornix, mammillary body, mammillothalamic tract, anterior thalamic nuclei, cingulate gyrus and cingulum, entorhinal cortex and back to the hippocampus. Interruption at any point produces anterograde amnesia.

g-papilledema.definition: Swelling of both optic discs from raised intracranial pressure transmitted along the optic nerve sheaths. Vision is preserved until late, in contrast to the early visual loss of optic neuritis, and the blind spots are enlarged.

html.definition: Swelling of both optic discs from raised intracranial pressure transmitted along the optic nerve sheaths. Vision is preserved until late, in contrast to the early visual loss of optic neuritis, and the blind spots are enlarged.

g-paraphasia.definition: Substitution of an incorrect sound (phonemic: 'tencil' for pencil) or word (semantic: 'fork' for spoon) during speech; a marker of aphasia. Phonemic errors point to the posterior perisylvian and arcuate region, semantic errors to the temporal semantic system and the ventral stream.

html.definition: Substitution of an incorrect sound (phonemic: 'tencil' for pencil) or word (semantic: 'fork' for spoon) during speech; a marker of aphasia. Phonemic errors point to the posterior perisylvian and arcuate region, semantic errors to the temporal semantic system and the ventral stream.

g-penumbra.definition: Brain tissue around an infarct core that is hypoperfused and non-functioning but still viable, and can be saved by reperfusion within a limited time; its extent is estimated by perfusion imaging or the mismatch between clinical deficit and infarct core.

html.definition: Brain tissue around an infarct core that is hypoperfused and non-functioning but still viable, and can be saved by reperfusion within a limited time; its extent is estimated by perfusion imaging or the mismatch between clinical deficit and infarct core.

g-periodic-discharges.definition: Repetitive epileptiform complexes at regular intervals on the EEG: lateralized (PLEDs) over an acute cortical injury such as herpes encephalitis or stroke, generalized in prion disease and after anoxia.

html.definition: Repetitive epileptiform complexes at regular intervals on the EEG: lateralized (PLEDs) over an acute cortical injury such as herpes encephalitis or stroke, generalized in prion disease and after anoxia.

g-periventricular-leukomalacia.definition: Ischemic necrosis of the periventricular white matter of the premature brain, injuring the leg fibers of the corticospinal tract and the optic radiation and producing spastic diplegia and visual perceptual deficits; seen as periventricular white-matter loss and irregular ventricular margins.

html.definition: Ischemic necrosis of the periventricular white matter of the premature brain, injuring the leg fibers of the corticospinal tract and the optic radiation and producing spastic diplegia and visual perceptual deficits; seen as periventricular white-matter loss and irregular ventricular margins.

g-plexopathy.definition: A lesion of the brachial or lumbosacral plexus, between the roots and the peripheral nerves, producing deficits broader than one nerve and not confined to one root, with reduced sensory nerve action potentials because the lesion is distal to the dorsal root ganglion.

html.definition: A lesion of the brachial or lumbosacral plexus, between the roots and the peripheral nerves, producing deficits broader than one nerve and not confined to one root, with reduced sensory nerve action potentials because the lesion is distal to the dorsal root ganglion.

g-polymicrogyria.definition: An excess of small, fused gyri with a thick irregular cortex from abnormal late cortical organization, often perisylvian and bilateral, producing pseudobulbar palsy, epilepsy and developmental delay.

html.definition: An excess of small, fused gyri with a thick irregular cortex from abnormal late cortical organization, often perisylvian and bilateral, producing pseudobulbar palsy, epilepsy and developmental delay.

g-polyneuropathy.definition: Generalized disease of the peripheral nerves. Length-dependent axonal neuropathies begin symmetrically in the toes and ascend in a stocking-glove pattern; demyelinating neuropathies produce proximal and distal weakness with areflexia and slowed conduction.

html.definition: Generalized disease of the peripheral nerves. Length-dependent axonal neuropathies begin symmetrically in the toes and ascend in a stocking-glove pattern; demyelinating neuropathies produce proximal and distal weakness with areflexia and slowed conduction.

g-posterior-cortical-atrophy.definition: A visual variant of Alzheimer disease beginning in the occipito-parietal and occipito-temporal cortex with simultanagnosia, optic ataxia, alexia and visual agnosia while memory is relatively preserved.

html.definition: A visual variant of Alzheimer disease beginning in the occipito-parietal and occipito-temporal cortex with simultanagnosia, optic ataxia, alexia and visual agnosia while memory is relatively preserved.

g-projection-fibers.definition: Axons connecting the cortex with subcortical structures, brainstem and spinal cord: corticospinal, corticobulbar, corticopontine and corticostriatal fibers descending, and thalamocortical radiations ascending, gathered in the corona radiata and internal capsule.

html.definition: Axons connecting the cortex with subcortical structures, brainstem and spinal cord: corticospinal, corticobulbar, corticopontine and corticostriatal fibers descending, and thalamocortical radiations ascending, gathered in the corona radiata and internal capsule.

g-prosopagnosia.definition: Inability to recognize familiar faces despite intact vision and intact recognition by voice or gait, from damage to the right (or bilateral) fusiform face area and its connections to the anterior temporal lobe. Patients often deny it and rely on hair, glasses or voice.

html.definition: Inability to recognize familiar faces despite intact vision and intact recognition by voice or gait, from damage to the right (or bilateral) fusiform face area and its connections to the anterior temporal lobe. Patients often deny it and rely on hair, glasses or voice.

g-pseudobulbar-palsy.definition: Spastic weakness of the muscles of speech and swallowing with a brisk jaw jerk and emotional lability, from bilateral upper motor neuron (corticobulbar) lesions, in contrast to the flaccid, wasted bulbar palsy of lower motor neuron disease.

html.definition: Spastic weakness of the muscles of speech and swallowing with a brisk jaw jerk and emotional lability, from bilateral upper motor neuron (corticobulbar) lesions, in contrast to the flaccid, wasted bulbar palsy of lower motor neuron disease.

g-quadrantanopia.definition: Loss of one quadrant of the visual field in both eyes: a superior quadrantanopia follows lesions of Meyer's loop in the temporal lobe or the lower calcarine bank; an inferior quadrantanopia follows lesions of the parietal optic radiation or the upper calcarine bank.

html.definition: Loss of one quadrant of the visual field in both eyes: a superior quadrantanopia follows lesions of Meyer's loop in the temporal lobe or the lower calcarine bank; an inferior quadrantanopia follows lesions of the parietal optic radiation or the upper calcarine bank.

g-radiculopathy.definition: Disease of a spinal nerve root, typically from disc herniation or foraminal stenosis, producing pain, sensory loss and weakness in the dermatome and myotome of that root with loss of its reflex.
