html.definition: Disease of a spinal nerve root, typically from disc herniation or foraminal stenosis, producing pain, sensory loss and weakness in the dermatome and myotome of that root with loss of its reflex.

g-ragged-red-fibers.definition: Muscle fibers with subsarcolemmal accumulations of abnormal mitochondria that stain red with modified Gomori trichrome; the histological hallmark of mitochondrial myopathy.

html.definition: Muscle fibers with subsarcolemmal accumulations of abnormal mitochondria that stain red with modified Gomori trichrome; the histological hallmark of mitochondrial myopathy.

g-rapd.definition: Paradoxical dilation of one pupil when a light is swung onto it from the other eye, showing that the afferent light signal from that eye is weaker. It indicates an optic nerve, chiasmal or optic tract lesion and never causes anisocoria.

html.definition: Paradoxical dilation of one pupil when a light is swung onto it from the other eye, showing that the afferent light signal from that eye is weaker. It indicates an optic nerve, chiasmal or optic tract lesion and never causes anisocoria.

g-rem-sleep-behavior-disorder.definition: Loss of the normal atonia of REM sleep so that dreams are acted out, from dysfunction of the pontine REM circuits; it precedes Parkinson disease, Lewy body dementia and multiple system atrophy by years.

html.definition: Loss of the normal atonia of REM sleep so that dreams are acted out, from dysfunction of the pontine REM circuits; it precedes Parkinson disease, Lewy body dementia and multiple system atrophy by years.

g-retinotopy.definition: The orderly mapping of the retina, and hence the visual field, onto the visual pathway and cortex. Upper retinal (lower field) fibers stay superior in the radiation and cortex; the macula occupies the occipital pole.

html.definition: The orderly mapping of the retina, and hence the visual field, onto the visual pathway and cortex. Upper retinal (lower field) fibers stay superior in the radiation and cortex; the macula occupies the occipital pole.

g-rigidity.definition: Increased tone that is present throughout the range of passive movement and does not depend on velocity (lead-pipe), often with a ratchety cogwheel quality when tremor is superimposed. A sign of extrapyramidal disease, classically parkinsonism.

html.definition: Increased tone that is present throughout the range of passive movement and does not depend on velocity (lead-pipe), often with a ratchety cogwheel quality when tremor is superimposed. A sign of extrapyramidal disease, classically parkinsonism.

g-ring-enhancement.definition: A rim of contrast enhancement around a non-enhancing center, produced by a necrotic tumor (glioblastoma, metastasis), an abscess (thin smooth wall, central restricted diffusion), a resolving hematoma or tumefactive demyelination (incomplete ring); the wall, the diffusion and the time course separate them.

html.definition: A rim of contrast enhancement around a non-enhancing center, produced by a necrotic tumor (glioblastoma, metastasis), an abscess (thin smooth wall, central restricted diffusion), a resolving hematoma or tumefactive demyelination (incomplete ring); the wall, the diffusion and the time course separate them.

g-romberg-sign.definition: Marked worsening of balance when the eyes are closed while standing with the feet together, indicating loss of proprioceptive input (posterior columns or peripheral nerves) that vision was compensating for. It is not a cerebellar sign.

html.definition: Marked worsening of balance when the eyes are closed while standing with the feet together, indicating loss of proprioceptive input (posterior columns or peripheral nerves) that vision was compensating for. It is not a cerebellar sign.

g-semantic-dementia.definition: Progressive loss of the meaning of words and of knowledge about objects and people with fluent, empty speech, from asymmetric anterior temporal lobe atrophy; a variant of frontotemporal lobar degeneration.

html.definition: Progressive loss of the meaning of words and of knowledge about objects and people with fluent, empty speech, from asymmetric anterior temporal lobe atrophy; a variant of frontotemporal lobar degeneration.

g-sensory-level.definition: The dermatomal boundary below which sensation is impaired in a spinal cord lesion. The level for pin-prick lies one or two segments below the actual lesion because spinothalamic fibers cross obliquely over that distance.

html.definition: The dermatomal boundary below which sensation is impaired in a spinal cord lesion. The level for pin-prick lies one or two segments below the actual lesion because spinothalamic fibers cross obliquely over that distance.

g-serotonin-syndrome.definition: A toxic state from excess serotonergic activity (drug combinations) with agitation, clonus, hyperreflexia, tremor, sweating, diarrhea and hyperthermia; the clonus and rapid onset distinguish it from neuroleptic malignant syndrome.

html.definition: A toxic state from excess serotonergic activity (drug combinations) with agitation, clonus, hyperreflexia, tremor, sweating, diarrhea and hyperthermia; the clonus and rapid onset distinguish it from neuroleptic malignant syndrome.

g-simultanagnosia.definition: Inability to perceive more than one object at a time, so that a scene cannot be taken in as a whole; the patient reads single letters but not words and describes a picture item by item. A sign of bilateral parieto-occipital damage and a component of Balint syndrome.

html.definition: Inability to perceive more than one object at a time, so that a scene cannot be taken in as a whole; the patient reads single letters but not words and describes a picture item by item. A sign of bilateral parieto-occipital damage and a component of Balint syndrome.

g-sleep-spindle.definition: A brief 12-14 Hz burst on the EEG of stage N2 sleep generated by the thalamic reticular nucleus and thalamocortical loops; with K-complexes it marks light non-REM sleep.

html.definition: A brief 12-14 Hz burst on the EEG of stage N2 sleep generated by the thalamic reticular nucleus and thalamocortical loops; with K-complexes it marks light non-REM sleep.

g-somatotopy.definition: The orderly representation of body parts within a pathway or nucleus. In the corticospinal tract the arm fibers lie medial to the leg fibers in the cord, and in the posterior columns the leg fibers lie medially; such arrangements explain the order in which functions are lost by expanding lesions.

html.definition: The orderly representation of body parts within a pathway or nucleus. In the corticospinal tract the arm fibers lie medial to the leg fibers in the cord, and in the posterior columns the leg fibers lie medially; such arrangements explain the order in which functions are lost by expanding lesions.

g-spasticity.definition: Velocity-dependent increase in muscle tone with a clasp-knife release, resulting from loss of descending inhibition (largely reticulospinal) after upper motor neuron lesions. Distinguished from the lead-pipe or cogwheel rigidity of basal ganglia disease, which is present throughout the range and independent of speed.

html.definition: Velocity-dependent increase in muscle tone with a clasp-knife release, resulting from loss of descending inhibition (largely reticulospinal) after upper motor neuron lesions. Distinguished from the lead-pipe or cogwheel rigidity of basal ganglia disease, which is present throughout the range and independent of speed.

g-spinal-shock.definition: The transient loss of all reflex activity below an acute spinal cord lesion, with flaccidity, areflexia and an atonic bladder, lasting days to weeks before spasticity and hyperreflexia emerge.

html.definition: The transient loss of all reflex activity below an acute spinal cord lesion, with flaccidity, areflexia and an atonic bladder, lasting days to weeks before spasticity and hyperreflexia emerge.

g-spot-sign.definition: A focus of contrast extravasation within an acute intracerebral hematoma on CT angiography, predicting hematoma expansion and worse outcome.

html.definition: A focus of contrast extravasation within an acute intracerebral hematoma on CT angiography, predicting hematoma expansion and worse outcome.

g-status-epilepticus.definition: A seizure lasting more than five minutes or seizures recurring without recovery; a medical emergency treated with benzodiazepines then a loading antiepileptic, because prolonged seizures cause excitotoxic neuronal death. Non-convulsive status is an unrecognized cause of coma diagnosed only by EEG.

html.definition: A seizure lasting more than five minutes or seizures recurring without recovery; a medical emergency treated with benzodiazepines then a loading antiepileptic, because prolonged seizures cause excitotoxic neuronal death. Non-convulsive status is an unrecognized cause of coma diagnosed only by EEG.

g-swallow-tail-sign.definition: The normal hyperintense nigrosome-1 in the dorsolateral substantia nigra on susceptibility-weighted MRI, shaped like a swallow's tail; its loss supports Parkinson disease and other nigral degenerations.

html.definition: The normal hyperintense nigrosome-1 in the dorsolateral substantia nigra on susceptibility-weighted MRI, shaped like a swallow's tail; its loss supports Parkinson disease and other nigral degenerations.

g-synkinesis.definition: Involuntary movement accompanying a voluntary one because regenerating axons have reached the wrong targets, as when the eye closes on smiling after facial nerve recovery; crocodile tears (lacrimation on eating) are the autonomic form.

html.definition: Involuntary movement accompanying a voluntary one because regenerating axons have reached the wrong targets, as when the eye closes on smiling after facial nerve recovery; crocodile tears (lacrimation on eating) are the autonomic form.

g-syrinx.definition: A fluid cavity within the spinal cord, usually cervical and often associated with a Chiari malformation, that first destroys the pain fibers crossing in the anterior white commissure and produces a cape-like dissociated sensory loss.

html.definition: A fluid cavity within the spinal cord, usually cervical and often associated with a Chiari malformation, that first destroys the pain fibers crossing in the anterior white commissure and produces a cape-like dissociated sensory loss.

g-tethered-cord.definition: Abnormal fixation of the low-lying conus by a thick filum, lipoma or scar so that growth stretches the cord, producing progressive leg weakness, foot deformity, back pain and bladder dysfunction in childhood or adolescence.

html.definition: Abnormal fixation of the low-lying conus by a thick filum, lipoma or scar so that growth stretches the cord, producing progressive leg weakness, foot deformity, back pain and bladder dysfunction in childhood or adolescence.

g-thunderclap-headache.definition: A severe headache reaching maximum intensity within a minute; subarachnoid hemorrhage until proved otherwise by CT within six hours or lumbar puncture, with reversible vasoconstriction, dissection, venous thrombosis and pituitary apoplexy as the alternatives.

html.definition: A severe headache reaching maximum intensity within a minute; subarachnoid hemorrhage until proved otherwise by CT within six hours or lumbar puncture, with reversible vasoconstriction, dissection, venous thrombosis and pituitary apoplexy as the alternatives.

g-tinel-sign.definition: Tingling in the distribution of a nerve produced by tapping over it, marking a site of entrapment (carpal tunnel) or the advancing front of regenerating axons after injury.

html.definition: Tingling in the distribution of a nerve produced by tapping over it, marking a site of entrapment (carpal tunnel) or the advancing front of regenerating axons after injury.

g-todd-paresis.definition: Transient weakness of the body part involved in a focal motor seizure, lasting minutes to hours after it ends, from exhaustion of the motor cortex; it localizes the focus and can mimic a stroke.

html.definition: Transient weakness of the body part involved in a focal motor seizure, lasting minutes to hours after it ends, from exhaustion of the motor cortex; it localizes the focus and can mimic a stroke.

g-top-of-basilar-syndrome.definition: Embolic occlusion of the distal basilar artery infarcting the midbrain, thalami and occipital lobes: somnolence, vertical gaze and pupillary abnormalities, visual field loss or cortical blindness, hallucinations and amnesia, often without weakness.

html.definition: Embolic occlusion of the distal basilar artery infarcting the midbrain, thalami and occipital lobes: somnolence, vertical gaze and pupillary abnormalities, visual field loss or cortical blindness, hallucinations and amnesia, often without weakness.

g-transcortical-aphasia.definition: Aphasia with preserved repetition: the transcortical motor type (reduced fluency, preserved comprehension) follows medial or dorsolateral frontal lesions outside the perisylvian loop, the transcortical sensory type (fluent, impaired comprehension) follows temporo-parieto-occipital lesions, and the mixed type follows watershed infarcts that isolate the intact perisylvian cortex.

html.definition: Aphasia with preserved repetition: the transcortical motor type (reduced fluency, preserved comprehension) follows medial or dorsolateral frontal lesions outside the perisylvian loop, the transcortical sensory type (fluent, impaired comprehension) follows temporo-parieto-occipital lesions, and the mixed type follows watershed infarcts that isolate the intact perisylvian cortex.

g-transependymal-edema.definition: A halo of FLAIR hyperintensity around the ventricles in acute obstructive hydrocephalus, from CSF forced through the ependyma into the periventricular white matter.

html.definition: A halo of FLAIR hyperintensity around the ventricles in acute obstructive hydrocephalus, from CSF forced through the ependyma into the periventricular white matter.

g-tremor.definition: Rhythmic oscillation of a body part. Rest tremor (parkinsonism), postural and action tremor (essential tremor, physiological, thyrotoxic), intention tremor (cerebellar outflow) and Holmes tremor (rest, postural and intention combined, midbrain).

html.definition: Rhythmic oscillation of a body part. Rest tremor (parkinsonism), postural and action tremor (essential tremor, physiological, thyrotoxic), intention tremor (cerebellar outflow) and Holmes tremor (rest, postural and intention combined, midbrain).

g-trendelenburg-sign.definition: Dropping of the pelvis toward the swing leg when standing on one foot, from weakness of the gluteus medius and minimus; a sign of superior gluteal nerve injury, L5 root lesions or hip disease, producing a waddling gait when bilateral.

html.definition: Dropping of the pelvis toward the swing leg when standing on one foot, from weakness of the gluteus medius and minimus; a sign of superior gluteal nerve injury, L5 root lesions or hip disease, producing a waddling gait when bilateral.

g-trigeminal-autonomic-cephalalgia.definition: A group of strictly unilateral orbital headaches with ipsilateral lacrimation, nasal congestion, ptosis and miosis from parasympathetic activation and sympathetic deficit: cluster headache, paroxysmal hemicrania, SUNCT and hemicrania continua, distinguished by attack duration and treatment response.

html.definition: A group of strictly unilateral orbital headaches with ipsilateral lacrimation, nasal congestion, ptosis and miosis from parasympathetic activation and sympathetic deficit: cluster headache, paroxysmal hemicrania, SUNCT and hemicrania continua, distinguished by attack duration and treatment response.

g-trigeminocervical-complex.definition: The caudal spinal trigeminal nucleus and the C1-C3 dorsal horns, where afferents from the dura, the cranial vessels and the upper neck converge; it explains referral of head pain between the face, occiput and neck and is the relay of migraine and cervicogenic headache.

html.definition: The caudal spinal trigeminal nucleus and the C1-C3 dorsal horns, where afferents from the dura, the cranial vessels and the upper neck converge; it explains referral of head pain between the face, occiput and neck and is the relay of migraine and cervicogenic headache.

g-triphasic-waves.definition: Generalized, frontally predominant three-phase EEG waves seen in metabolic encephalopathies, classically hepatic and uremic; nonspecific but suggestive when the EEG is diffusely slow.

html.definition: Generalized, frontally predominant three-phase EEG waves seen in metabolic encephalopathies, classically hepatic and uremic; nonspecific but suggestive when the EEG is diffusely slow.

g-u-fibers.definition: Short subcortical association fibers that arch beneath a sulcus to connect adjacent gyri; their sparing (metachromatic leukodystrophy, small vessel disease) or involvement (Canavan disease, some toxic leukoencephalopathies) helps classify white-matter disease on MRI.

html.definition: Short subcortical association fibers that arch beneath a sulcus to connect adjacent gyri; their sparing (metachromatic leukodystrophy, small vessel disease) or involvement (Canavan disease, some toxic leukoencephalopathies) helps classify white-matter disease on MRI.

g-uhthoff-phenomenon.definition: Transient worsening of neurological symptoms, typically vision, with a rise in body temperature, because demyelinated fibers fail to conduct when warmed. Characteristic of multiple sclerosis.

html.definition: Transient worsening of neurological symptoms, typically vision, with a rise in body temperature, because demyelinated fibers fail to conduct when warmed. Characteristic of multiple sclerosis.

g-upper-motor-neuron.definition: The neuron of the motor cortex or brainstem whose axon descends in the corticospinal, corticobulbar or other descending tracts to influence the lower motor neuron. Upper motor neuron lesions cause weakness with spasticity, hyperreflexia, clonus and an extensor plantar response, with little wasting.

html.definition: The neuron of the motor cortex or brainstem whose axon descends in the corticospinal, corticobulbar or other descending tracts to influence the lower motor neuron. Upper motor neuron lesions cause weakness with spasticity, hyperreflexia, clonus and an extensor plantar response, with little wasting.

g-vasogenic-edema.definition: Extracellular fluid leaking through a broken blood-brain barrier and spreading through the white matter around tumors, abscesses and hemorrhages, sparing the cortex and responding to dexamethasone; contrasted with cytotoxic edema, the cell swelling of infarction that involves gray and white matter and restricts diffusion.

html.definition: Extracellular fluid leaking through a broken blood-brain barrier and spreading through the white matter around tumors, abscesses and hemorrhages, sparing the cortex and responding to dexamethasone; contrasted with cytotoxic edema, the cell swelling of infarction that involves gray and white matter and restricts diffusion.

g-vegetative-state.definition: Wakefulness with sleep-wake cycles, open eyes and reflex movements but no evidence of awareness, after diffuse cortical or thalamic damage with a preserved brainstem; the minimally conscious state shows inconsistent but reproducible signs of awareness.

html.definition: Wakefulness with sleep-wake cycles, open eyes and reflex movements but no evidence of awareness, after diffuse cortical or thalamic damage with a preserved brainstem; the minimally conscious state shows inconsistent but reproducible signs of awareness.

g-ventral-stream.definition: The occipito-temporal pathway that identifies what is seen (shape, color, faces, words, objects), running from the primary visual cortex through the fusiform and inferior temporal cortex to the anterior temporal lobe; lesions produce agnosia, prosopagnosia, achromatopsia and alexia.

html.definition: The occipito-temporal pathway that identifies what is seen (shape, color, faces, words, objects), running from the primary visual cortex through the fusiform and inferior temporal cortex to the anterior temporal lobe; lesions produce agnosia, prosopagnosia, achromatopsia and alexia.

g-vestibulo-ocular-reflex.definition: The three-neuron reflex that moves the eyes opposite to head rotation to keep gaze stable, tested at the bedside by the head impulse and oculocephalic maneuvers. Loss on one side (a corrective saccade after a head impulse) indicates a peripheral vestibular lesion.

html.definition: The three-neuron reflex that moves the eyes opposite to head rotation to keep gaze stable, tested at the bedside by the head impulse and oculocephalic maneuvers. Loss on one side (a corrective saccade after a head impulse) indicates a peripheral vestibular lesion.

g-visual-word-form-area.definition: A region of the left posterior fusiform gyrus that learns to recognize letter strings and familiar words as visual wholes; its damage produces pure alexia with letter-by-letter reading whose time grows with word length.

html.definition: A region of the left posterior fusiform gyrus that learns to recognize letter strings and familiar words as visual wholes; its damage produces pure alexia with letter-by-letter reading whose time grows with word length.

g-wallerian-degeneration.definition: Breakdown of the axon and its myelin distal to an injury, with Schwann cell tubes persisting in the peripheral nerve to guide regeneration; in the central nervous system it is visible on MRI as signal change and atrophy of a tract (the cerebral peduncle after a capsular stroke) months later.

html.definition: Breakdown of the axon and its myelin distal to an injury, with Schwann cell tubes persisting in the peripheral nerve to guide regeneration; in the central nervous system it is visible on MRI as signal change and atrophy of a tract (the cerebral peduncle after a capsular stroke) months later.

g-wartenberg-syndrome.definition: Entrapment of the superficial branch of the radial nerve where it pierces the forearm fascia or under a tight wrist band or handcuff, producing pain and paresthesias of the dorsolateral hand and thumb without weakness.

html.definition: Entrapment of the superficial branch of the radial nerve where it pierces the forearm fascia or under a tight wrist band or handcuff, producing pain and paresthesias of the dorsolateral hand and thumb without weakness.

g-watershed.definition: The territory at the boundary between two arterial supplies, where perfusion pressure is lowest and infarction occurs first during hypotension or upstream stenosis: between ACA and MCA on the superior frontal convexity, between MCA and PCA in the parieto-occipital region, and in the deep white matter.

html.definition: The territory at the boundary between two arterial supplies, where perfusion pressure is lowest and infarction occurs first during hypotension or upstream stenosis: between ACA and MCA on the superior frontal convexity, between MCA and PCA in the parieto-occipital region, and in the deep white matter.

g-xanthochromia.definition: Yellow discoloration of the CSF supernatant from bilirubin, appearing about twelve hours after subarachnoid hemorrhage and persisting for two weeks; it distinguishes true hemorrhage from a traumatic tap.

html.definition: Yellow discoloration of the CSF supernatant from bilirubin, appearing about twelve hours after subarachnoid hemorrhage and persisting for two weeks; it distinguishes true hemorrhage from a traumatic tap.

qz-01.vignette: A 68-year-old man with atrial fibrillation is found slumped at breakfast. He does not speak or follow commands, his eyes are turned to the left, the right side of his face droops below the eye and his right arm and leg do not move. He does not blink to a threat from the right.

options.text: Left middle cerebral artery stem territory

qz-01.explanation: Global aphasia, gaze deviation toward the lesion, right hemianopia and a face-arm-leg hemiplegia together require the whole left MCA territory: the language cortex, the frontal eye field, the optic radiation and the capsule. A capsular lacune gives no aphasia or field defect; a pontine lesion would turn the eyes away from the lesion and add a peripheral facial palsy.

html.vignette: A 68-year-old man with atrial fibrillation is found slumped at breakfast. He does not speak or follow commands, his eyes are turned to the left, the right side of his face droops below the eye and his right arm and leg do not move. He does not blink to a threat from the right.
html.explanation: Global aphasia, gaze deviation toward the lesion, right hemianopia and a face-arm-leg hemiplegia together require the whole left MCA territory: the language cortex, the frontal eye field, the optic radiation and the capsule. A capsular lacune gives no aphasia or field defect; a pontine lesion would turn the eyes away from the lesion and add a peripheral facial palsy.

qz-02.vignette: A 55-year-old woman with sudden vertigo and vomiting has hoarseness and cannot swallow her saliva. Her right eyelid droops slightly and the right pupil is smaller. Pin-prick is dull on the right side of her face and on the left arm and leg. Strength is normal everywhere.
qz-02.stem: Which single lesion explains all the findings?
qz-02.explanation: Ipsilateral facial pain loss (spinal trigeminal tract), contralateral body pain loss (crossed spinothalamic tract), ipsilateral Horner syndrome and ipsilateral bulbar palsy with preserved strength is the lateral medullary syndrome on the side of the facial signs. The lateral pons would add facial weakness and deafness.

html.vignette: A 55-year-old woman with sudden vertigo and vomiting has hoarseness and cannot swallow her saliva. Her right eyelid droops slightly and the right pupil is smaller. Pin-prick is dull on the right side of her face and on the left arm and leg. Strength is normal everywhere.
html.explanation: Ipsilateral facial pain loss (spinal trigeminal tract), contralateral body pain loss (crossed spinothalamic tract), ipsilateral Horner syndrome and ipsilateral bulbar palsy with preserved strength is the lateral medullary syndrome on the side of the facial signs. The lateral pons would add facial weakness and deafness.

qz-03.vignette: A 30-year-old man is stabbed in the back at the level of the lower thoracic spine. He has weakness of the right leg with a brisk knee jerk and an upgoing toe, cannot feel a tuning fork on the right ankle, and cannot feel a pin on the left leg below the groin.
qz-03.stem: Which pathway accounts for the left-sided finding?
qz-03.explanation: Pain and temperature fibers cross in the anterior white commissure within a segment or two of entry, so the right spinothalamic tract carries pain from the left leg; a right hemicord lesion therefore gives left pain loss with right weakness and right proprioceptive loss (Brown-Séquard).

html.vignette: A 30-year-old man is stabbed in the back at the level of the lower thoracic spine. He has weakness of the right leg with a brisk knee jerk and an upgoing toe, cannot feel a tuning fork on the right ankle, and cannot feel a pin on the left leg below the groin.
html.explanation: Pain and temperature fibers cross in the anterior white commissure within a segment or two of entry, so the right spinothalamic tract carries pain from the left leg; a right hemicord lesion therefore gives left pain loss with right weakness and right proprioceptive loss (Brown-Séquard).

qz-04.vignette: A 72-year-old hypertensive woman wakes with weakness of the left face, arm and leg that are all equally affected. Sensation, visual fields, speech and awareness are normal. CT is normal.
qz-04.stem: The most likely site of the lesion is:

options.text: Right posterior limb of the internal capsule

qz-04.explanation: A pure motor hemiparesis involving face, arm and leg equally without any cortical or sensory sign is a lacunar infarct in the posterior limb of the internal capsule (or basis pontis), where the corticospinal and corticobulbar fibers are packed together and the sensory fibers lie just behind.

html.vignette: A 72-year-old hypertensive woman wakes with weakness of the left face, arm and leg that are all equally affected. Sensation, visual fields, speech and awareness are normal. CT is normal.
html.explanation: A pure motor hemiparesis involving face, arm and leg equally without any cortical or sensory sign is a lacunar infarct in the posterior limb of the internal capsule (or basis pontis), where the corticospinal and corticobulbar fibers are packed together and the sensory fibers lie just behind.

qz-05.vignette: A 45-year-old woman notices that when she looks to the right, her left eye stays in the middle while the right eye moves fully and jerks. When a pencil is brought toward her nose both eyes converge normally.
qz-05.explanation: Failure of adduction of the left eye on right gaze with abducting nystagmus of the right eye and preserved convergence is a left internuclear ophthalmoplegia: the left MLF carries the crossed interneuron axons from the right abducens nucleus to the left medial rectus subnucleus.

html.vignette: A 45-year-old woman notices that when she looks to the right, her left eye stays in the middle while the right eye moves fully and jerks. When a pencil is brought toward her nose both eyes converge normally.
html.explanation: Failure of adduction of the left eye on right gaze with abducting nystagmus of the right eye and preserved convergence is a left internuclear ophthalmoplegia: the left MLF carries the crossed interneuron axons from the right abducens nucleus to the left medial rectus subnucleus.

qz-06.vignette: A 60-year-old man has a complete ptosis of the right eye. When the lid is lifted the eye is turned down and out, and the pupil is 7 mm and unreactive. He has a severe headache.
qz-06.stem: What is the most urgent diagnosis to exclude?
qz-06.explanation: A painful third nerve palsy with a dilated fixed pupil means compression of the superficially placed pupillary fibers, classically by a posterior communicating aneurysm; a microvascular palsy usually spares the pupil. Emergency CTA is required.

html.vignette: A 60-year-old man has a complete ptosis of the right eye. When the lid is lifted the eye is turned down and out, and the pupil is 7 mm and unreactive. He has a severe headache.
html.explanation: A painful third nerve palsy with a dilated fixed pupil means compression of the superficially placed pupillary fibers, classically by a posterior communicating aneurysm; a microvascular palsy usually spares the pupil. Emergency CTA is required.

qz-07.vignette: A 25-year-old woman has had blurred vision in the left eye for three days with pain on moving the eye. Acuity is 6/36 on the left, colors look washed out, and the left pupil dilates when the light is swung onto it from the right eye. The fundus is normal.
qz-07.explanation: Monocular visual loss with color desaturation, pain on eye movement, a relative afferent pupillary defect and a normal disc is retrobulbar optic neuritis of that nerve. Chiasmal and retrochiasmal lesions produce bilateral or homonymous field defects.

html.vignette: A 25-year-old woman has had blurred vision in the left eye for three days with pain on moving the eye. Acuity is 6/36 on the left, colors look washed out, and the left pupil dilates when the light is swung onto it from the right eye. The fundus is normal.
html.explanation: Monocular visual loss with color desaturation, pain on eye movement, a relative afferent pupillary defect and a normal disc is retrobulbar optic neuritis of that nerve. Chiasmal and retrochiasmal lesions produce bilateral or homonymous field defects.

qz-08.vignette: A 40-year-old man walks into door frames on both sides and has stopped driving. Confrontation testing shows that he cannot see the examiner's fingers in the temporal half of the field of each eye. His acuity is normal and he has recently noticed enlarged hands and a change in his face.
qz-08.explanation: Bitemporal hemianopia is the signature of a chiasmal lesion, where the crossing nasal retinal fibers from both eyes are interrupted; the acromegalic features point to a pituitary macroadenoma compressing the chiasm from below.

html.vignette: A 40-year-old man walks into door frames on both sides and has stopped driving. Confrontation testing shows that he cannot see the examiner's fingers in the temporal half of the field of each eye. His acuity is normal and he has recently noticed enlarged hands and a change in his face.
html.explanation: Bitemporal hemianopia is the signature of a chiasmal lesion, where the crossing nasal retinal fibers from both eyes are interrupted; the acromegalic features point to a pituitary macroadenoma compressing the chiasm from below.

qz-09.vignette: A 70-year-old man's daughter reports that he ignores food on the left side of his plate, shaves only the right side of his face and denies that his left arm is weak although he cannot lift it. He draws all the numbers of a clock on the right side.
qz-09.stem: The lesion is most likely in the:
qz-09.explanation: Left hemispatial neglect with anosognosia is the hallmark of a right inferior parietal lesion; the right hemisphere attends to both sides of space, so its loss leaves the left side unattended. A field defect would not produce denial or the clock drawing pattern.

html.vignette: A 70-year-old man's daughter reports that he ignores food on the left side of his plate, shaves only the right side of his face and denies that his left arm is weak although he cannot lift it. He draws all the numbers of a clock on the right side.
html.explanation: Left hemispatial neglect with anosognosia is the hallmark of a right inferior parietal lesion; the right hemisphere attends to both sides of space, so its loss leaves the left side unattended. A field defect would not produce denial or the clock drawing pattern.

qz-10.vignette: A 50-year-old woman with a large right frontal tumor becomes drowsy over an hour. Her right pupil is dilated and unreactive. Her right arm and leg are weak with an upgoing toe.
qz-10.stem: Why is the weakness on the same side as the tumor?

options.text: The tumor has spread to the left hemisphere
The right cerebral peduncle is compressed by the uncus
The left cerebral peduncle is compressed against the tentorial edge
The corticospinal tract has not crossed at this level

qz-10.explanation: Uncal herniation normally compresses the ipsilateral peduncle and weakens the contralateral limbs; when the midbrain is pushed across so that the opposite peduncle is notched against the tentorium (Kernohan notch), the weakness appears on the side of the mass. The dilated pupil, not the weakness, indicates the side of the lesion.

qz-11.vignette: A 35-year-old woman has a drooping right eyelid that is only 1–2 mm lower than the left, a right pupil that is smaller than the left, and the difference is greater when the lights are dimmed. She has had right-sided neck pain since a yoga class two days ago.
qz-11.stem: What is the most important next step?

options.text: MRI of the brain for a pituitary tumor
CT angiography of the neck for carotid dissection
Chest X-ray for an apical tumor

qz-11.explanation: A Horner syndrome (anisocoria greater in the dark, mild ptosis) with new neck pain is an internal carotid dissection until proven otherwise; the sympathetic plexus runs on the carotid wall. Vessel imaging of the neck is urgent because of the stroke risk.

qz-12.vignette: A 62-year-old man has weakness of the right arm and leg that spares the face and loss of vibration and position sense in the same limbs. On protrusion his tongue deviates to the left and the left half of the tongue is wasted.
qz-12.explanation: A lower motor neuron tongue palsy (deviation toward the lesion, wasting) with contralateral limb weakness and proprioceptive loss and a spared face is the medial medullary syndrome on the side of the tongue palsy: the pyramid and medial lemniscus serve the opposite side while the hypoglossal nucleus is ipsilateral.

qz-13.vignette: A 20-year-old motorcyclist has an arm that hangs at his side, rotated inward with the elbow straight, after a crash in which his shoulder hit the road. He can move his fingers normally. Sensation is reduced over the outer shoulder and forearm.
qz-13.explanation: The waiter's tip posture with preserved hand function and lateral arm sensory loss is an upper brachial plexus (Erb) palsy from traction on C5–C6: shoulder abductors, external rotators, elbow flexors and supinator are lost.

qz-14.vignette: A 58-year-old woman trips over her right foot. She cannot dorsiflex or evert the right foot, but inversion and plantar flexion are strong and the ankle jerk is normal. Sensation is reduced over the dorsum of the foot. She recently lost 15 kg.

options.text: Common peroneal nerve at the fibular neck

qz-14.explanation: Foot drop with weak eversion but preserved inversion (tibialis posterior, L5 via the tibial nerve) and a normal ankle reflex is a common peroneal neuropathy; an L5 radiculopathy would weaken inversion and hip abduction as well. Weight loss removes the fat protecting the nerve at the fibular neck.

qz-15.vignette: A 45-year-old alcoholic is admitted confused and unsteady. He cannot abduct either eye and has coarse nystagmus. A junior doctor gives intravenous glucose and he becomes more drowsy.
qz-15.stem: What should have been given first, and which structures are being damaged?

options.text: Thiamine; the mammillary bodies and periaqueductal region

qz-15.explanation: Confusion, ophthalmoplegia and ataxia in a malnourished alcoholic is Wernicke encephalopathy, a thiamine-dependent injury of the periventricular structures around the third and fourth ventricles and aqueduct; glucose without thiamine precipitates or worsens it, and the mammillary body damage leaves Korsakoff amnesia.

qz-16.vignette: A 66-year-old man describes electric shocks in his right cheek and jaw lasting a second, set off by chewing and by touching a spot beside his nose. Between attacks he has no pain and the examination, including the corneal reflex, is normal.
qz-16.stem: Which nerve divisions are involved and what is the usual cause?

options.text: V2 and V3; vascular compression of the trigeminal root

qz-16.explanation: Paroxysmal lancinating pain with trigger zones in the maxillary and mandibular territories and a normal examination is classic trigeminal neuralgia, usually from compression of the root entry zone by a loop of the superior cerebellar artery.

qz-17.vignette: A 55-year-old woman has a spastic gait, a small stiff tongue that she cannot protrude, slow strangled speech and cries uncontrollably when asked about her family. Her jaw jerk is very brisk. There is no wasting or fasciculation of the tongue.

options.text: Bilateral lower motor neuron lesions of IX–XII (bulbar palsy)

qz-17.explanation: Spastic dysarthria, a spastic tongue without wasting, a brisk jaw jerk and emotional lability are the features of pseudobulbar palsy from bilateral upper motor neuron (corticobulbar) lesions; bulbar palsy would show a wasted, fasciculating tongue and an absent jaw jerk.

qz-18.vignette: A 78-year-old woman on warfarin has become confused and unsteady over three weeks and now has a mild left hemiparesis. CT shows a crescent-shaped collection over the right hemisphere that is slightly darker than brain and crosses the coronal suture.
qz-18.explanation: A crescentic, hypodense extra-axial collection that crosses sutures in an elderly anticoagulated patient with a subacute course is a chronic subdural hematoma from torn bridging veins; an epidural hematoma is biconvex, hyperdense and does not cross sutures.

qz-19.vignette: A 30-year-old woman has an unsteady gait with a wide base and cannot tandem walk, but the finger-nose and heel-shin tests are almost normal when she is lying down. She has headaches in the morning and vomits. Her discs are swollen.
qz-19.stem: Which part of the cerebellum is most likely involved?
qz-19.explanation: Severe truncal and gait ataxia with relatively spared limb coordination is a midline (vermian) syndrome; a midline mass over the fourth ventricle also obstructs CSF flow, explaining the headache, vomiting and papilledema.

qz-20.vignette: A 64-year-old man develops a right hemianopia. He can write a sentence but cannot read it back a minute later, although he can spell words aloud and recognizes words spelled to him. He cannot name colors but matches them correctly.

options.text: Left angular gyrus and Wernicke's area
Left calcarine cortex and splenium of the corpus callosum
Right calcarine cortex and left angular gyrus
Left optic tract and lateral geniculate body

qz-20.explanation: Alexia without agraphia arises when a left occipital infarct blinds the right hemifield and the accompanying splenial lesion disconnects the seeing right occipital cortex from the left angular gyrus; writing, which needs no visual input, survives.

qz-21.vignette: A 28-year-old woman notices double vision and drooping eyelids by evening that are better in the morning. Her pupils are normal. Chewing tires her halfway through a meal. Reflexes and sensation are normal.
qz-21.stem: What is the site of the disorder?
qz-21.explanation: Fatigable ptosis, diplopia that fits no nerve and bulbar fatigue with spared pupils, reflexes and sensation is myasthenia gravis, a postsynaptic acetylcholine receptor disorder; Lambert–Eaton (presynaptic) causes proximal leg weakness with areflexia and autonomic symptoms.

qz-22.vignette: A 40-year-old man has burned his fingers several times without feeling it. Pin-prick and temperature sensation are absent over both shoulders, arms and the upper chest, but he feels a tuning fork and joint movement normally there. The small muscles of his hands are wasted and the arm reflexes are absent.

options.text: Posterior columns of the cervical cord

qz-22.explanation: Bilateral cape-like dissociated loss of pain and temperature with preserved proprioception, plus lower motor neuron signs in the arms, is a central cervical cord lesion destroying the crossing spinothalamic fibers and the anterior horns: syringomyelia.

qz-23.vignette: A 70-year-old woman with a spinning sensation and vomiting for six hours has nystagmus that beats to the right when she looks right and to the left when she looks left. Rapid head turning to either side produces no corrective eye movement. She cannot stand without support.
qz-23.explanation: Direction-changing (gaze-evoked) nystagmus, a normal head impulse test and inability to stand are central features of the HINTS examination; a peripheral lesion gives unidirectional nystagmus with an abnormal head impulse toward the affected ear.

qz-24.vignette: A 45-year-old woman has developed a slowly worsening hearing loss in the left ear over two years with tinnitus. Speech discrimination in that ear is much worse than the pure-tone loss predicts. The left corneal reflex is absent and there is mild left facial weakness.
qz-24.stem: The most likely lesion is a:
qz-24.explanation: Progressive retrocochlear unilateral hearing loss followed by trigeminal and then facial involvement is the sequence of a cerebellopontine angle mass, usually a vestibular schwannoma, stretching the neighboring nerves as it grows.

qz-25.vignette: A 22-year-old man is quadriplegic after a diving injury at C5. On the third day a nurse finds him flushed and sweating above the neck with a headache and a blood pressure of 220/120 and a pulse of 48. His bladder is distended.
qz-25.explanation: A noxious stimulus below a lesion above T6 triggers massive sympathetic discharge from the disconnected splanchnic outflow, producing hypertension with reflex bradycardia and flushing above the lesion: autonomic dysreflexia. Emptying the bladder is the treatment.

qz-26.vignette: A 60-year-old man develops a resting tremor of the right hand that disappears when he reaches for a cup, with small handwriting and reduced arm swing on the right. His face is expressionless.
qz-26.stem: Which structure has degenerated, and on which side?
qz-26.explanation: Asymmetric parkinsonism reflects dopamine loss in the substantia nigra contralateral to the affected limbs, because each basal ganglia loop acts on the opposite body through the crossed corticospinal projection.

qz-27.vignette: A 50-year-old woman has the worst headache of her life, reaching its peak within seconds, with vomiting and neck stiffness. CT within two hours is reported as normal.

options.text: Lumbar puncture at 12 hours looking for xanthochromia

qz-27.explanation: A thunderclap headache requires exclusion of subarachnoid hemorrhage; CT is very sensitive within six hours, but a negative early CT in a typical history is followed by lumbar puncture at 12 hours to detect the bilirubin of xanthochromia, and then vessel imaging if positive.

html.vignette: A 50-year-old woman has the worst headache of her life, reaching its peak within seconds, with vomiting and neck stiffness. CT within two hours is reported as normal.

qz-28.vignette: A 35-year-old woman reports numb, tingling hands that wake her at night and that she shakes to relieve. The thumb, index and middle fingers are affected, the little finger is spared, and the thenar muscles are slightly wasted. Sensation over the base of the thumb on the palm is normal.

options.text: Median nerve in the carpal tunnel
Lower trunk of the brachial plexus

qz-28.explanation: Nocturnal paresthesias in the lateral three and a half digits with thenar weakness and sparing of the thenar palm (palmar cutaneous branch leaves above the tunnel) is carpal tunnel syndrome; a C6 root lesion would involve the forearm and reflexes.

qz-29.vignette: A 58-year-old man cannot look up. His pupils are large and do not react to light but constrict when he looks at his nose, and when he tries to look up his eyes jerk inward and retract. He has had headaches for a month.
qz-29.explanation: Up-gaze palsy, light-near dissociation, lid retraction and convergence-retraction nystagmus form the dorsal midbrain (Parinaud) syndrome, from compression of the pretectum and posterior commissure, typically by a pineal tumor or hydrocephalus.

qz-30.vignette: A 66-year-old woman is brought in with sudden weakness of the right leg, much worse than the arm, with the face spared. She is slow to respond, has a grasp reflex in the right hand and is incontinent of urine. Speech is preserved.

options.text: Left middle cerebral artery, superior division

qz-30.explanation: Leg-predominant contralateral weakness with abulia, a grasp reflex and incontinence follows infarction of the medial frontal lobe and paracentral lobule, the territory of the anterior cerebral artery, where the leg is represented on the homunculus.

qz-31.vignette: A 62-year-old right-handed woman speaks fluently but her sentences are full of wrong words she does not notice, she cannot follow a two-step command, and when asked to repeat 'no ifs, ands or buts' she produces nonsense. Her strength is normal. Finger counting is missed in the right upper quadrant.
qz-31.explanation: Fluent paraphasic speech with impaired comprehension and repetition is Wernicke aphasia, from the posterior superior temporal gyrus of the dominant hemisphere; the superior quadrantanopia comes from Meyer's loop in the temporal white matter beneath it, and normal strength shows the precentral gyrus of the superior division is spared.

qz-32.vignette: A 70-year-old man is brought by his wife because he no longer recognizes her or their children by their faces, though he knows them at once by voice. He reads normally, names objects and has a left upper quadrant field defect.
qz-32.explanation: Prosopagnosia with preserved reading and object naming points to the right fusiform face area; the left upper quadrant defect places the lesion in the right occipito-temporal region where the lower calcarine bank and the optic radiation lie nearby. A left fusiform lesion would impair reading (pure alexia) rather than faces.

html.vignette: A 70-year-old man is brought by his wife because he no longer recognizes her or their children by their faces, though he knows them at once by voice. He reads normally, names objects and has a left upper quadrant field defect.

qz-33.vignette: A 58-year-old right-handed woman has a small stroke. Her strength and sensation are normal, but when asked to show how she would use a key or brush her teeth she cannot do it with either hand, and she cannot copy meaningless hand postures. She understands the instructions and can describe the actions in words.
qz-33.explanation: Ideomotor apraxia of both hands with intact comprehension and strength is a lesion of the dominant left inferior parietal lobule, which stores the movement formulas that the right hemisphere receives through the corpus callosum; a callosal lesion would spare the right hand, and a right parietal lesion would produce neglect rather than apraxia.

qz-34.vignette: A 66-year-old man wakes unable to read the newspaper, although he can write a note to his wife, which he then cannot read back. He names objects and speaks normally. He has a right homonymous hemianopia.
qz-34.stem: Which two structures are damaged together?

options.text: Left angular gyrus and left arcuate fasciculus
Left calcarine cortex and the splenium of the corpus callosum
Left pars triangularis and left insula
Right calcarine cortex and the genu of the corpus callosum
Left planum temporale and left Heschl's gyrus

qz-34.explanation: Alexia without agraphia is a disconnection: the left visual cortex is destroyed (right hemianopia) and the splenial fibers that would bring the surviving right visual cortex's information to the left language cortex are cut, so words are seen but cannot be read; writing, driven from the intact language areas, is preserved.

html.vignette: A 66-year-old man wakes unable to read the newspaper, although he can write a note to his wife, which he then cannot read back. He names objects and speaks normally. He has a right homonymous hemianopia.

qz-35.vignette: A 74-year-old woman after cardiac arrest can read single letters but not words, reaches past objects she looks at, and describes a picture of a kitchen one item at a time without grasping the scene. Acuity is normal.
qz-35.explanation: Simultanagnosia, optic ataxia and ocular apraxia form Balint syndrome, from bilateral dorsal parieto-occipital damage; after cardiac arrest the lesions lie in the border zones between the middle and posterior cerebral arteries, the superior lateral occipital and superior parietal cortex.

qz-36.vignette: A 55-year-old man has sudden weakness of the left leg with a normal arm and face. He is apathetic and answers slowly, and his wife says he has been incontinent since the event. A grasp reflex is present on the left.

options.text: Right middle cerebral artery, superior division

qz-36.explanation: Leg-predominant weakness with abulia, incontinence and a grasp reflex is the anterior cerebral artery territory: the paracentral lobule (leg), the medial frontal micturition and motivation areas and the cingulate cortex. An MCA lesion would weaken the face and arm.

html.vignette: A 55-year-old man has sudden weakness of the left leg with a normal arm and face. He is apathetic and answers slowly, and his wife says he has been incontinent since the event. A grasp reflex is present on the left.

qz-37.vignette: A 48-year-old woman has had brief nocturnal attacks for years: she sits up suddenly, her right arm rises abducted and her head turns toward it, she makes a loud noise, and it is over in twenty seconds. She remembers the attacks. Two EEGs have been normal and she was told the attacks are psychological.
qz-37.explanation: A brief nocturnal tonic seizure with a fencing posture (contralateral arm abducted, head turned toward it), vocalization and preserved awareness is the signature of the supplementary motor area; the focus is interhemispheric, so the scalp EEG is often normal, and the posture points to the left SMA. Medial temporal seizures begin with an epigastric aura and impair awareness.

qz-38.vignette: A 30-year-old woman with epilepsy describes each seizure beginning with a rising feeling in her stomach and a sense that everything has happened before, followed by lip smacking and fumbling with her right hand while her left hand assumes a fixed clawed posture. She is confused for ten minutes afterward and has difficulty speaking.
qz-38.explanation: The epigastric aura and deja vu come from the medial temporal lobe; the dystonic posture of the left hand points to the contralateral (left) hemisphere, the automatisms are ipsilateral to the focus, and postictal aphasia marks the language-dominant side. Left mesial temporal epilepsy is the answer.

html.vignette: A 30-year-old woman with epilepsy describes each seizure beginning with a rising feeling in her stomach and a sense that everything has happened before, followed by lip smacking and fumbling with her right hand while her left hand assumes a fixed clawed posture. She is confused for ten minutes afterward and has difficulty speaking.
html.explanation: The epigastric aura and deja vu come from the medial temporal lobe; the dystonic posture of the left hand points to the contralateral (left) hemisphere, the automatisms are ipsilateral to the focus, and postictal aphasia marks the language-dominant side. Left mesial temporal epilepsy is the answer.

qz-39.vignette: A 45-year-old man has drug-resistant seizures of the type described above. Coronal FLAIR MRI shows a small bright left hippocampus with loss of its internal architecture and a dilated left temporal horn.
qz-39.explanation: A small hippocampus with increased FLAIR signal, loss of the internal digitations and an enlarged temporal horn is mesial temporal sclerosis, the commonest surgically curable epilepsy; a tumor would expand rather than shrink the hippocampus and herpes would be acute with fever.

qz-40.vignette: A 68-year-old woman is admitted with sudden deep sleepiness. When roused she cannot look up, has no memory of the morning and drifts off again. Her pupils are sluggish. Strength and sensation are normal.
qz-40.explanation: Hypersomnolence with vertical gaze palsy and amnesia and no long-tract signs is bilateral paramedian thalamic and rostral midbrain infarction, the territory of a single artery of Percheron arising from one P1 segment.

qz-41.vignette: A 60-year-old man develops weakness of the right face, arm and leg, loss of all sensation on the right side and a right homonymous hemianopia within an hour. He speaks normally, follows commands and is aware of his deficits. CT shows no cortical change.
qz-41.stem: Which artery is most likely occluded?
qz-41.explanation: Hemiparesis, hemisensory loss and hemianopia without aphasia or neglect is the triad of the anterior choroidal artery, which supplies the posterior limb of the internal capsule (motor and sensory fibers) and the optic tract and geniculate; an MCA stem occlusion would add cortical signs, and a lenticulostriate lacune would spare the fields.

qz-42.vignette: A 72-year-old hypertensive man has sudden weakness of the left arm and leg with ataxia of the same limbs out of proportion to the weakness; sensation, speech and vision are normal.
qz-42.stem: Which structure best explains the combination?

options.text: Right posterior limb of the internal capsule with corticopontine fibers

qz-42.explanation: Ataxic hemiparesis is a lacune of the posterior limb (or basis pontis) interrupting the corticospinal tract and the corticopontine fibers together; the corticopontine input crosses in the pons and the cerebellar output crosses back, so ataxia lands on the weak side. A cerebellar lesion would give ipsilateral ataxia without weakness.

qz-43.vignette: A 35-year-old man is found to have a small infarct of the right supramarginal gyrus after a cardiac embolus. Which of the following is the most likely persistent deficit?
qz-43.explanation: The right inferior parietal lobule is the ventral attention hub; its lesion produces left neglect and extinction, often lasting because the superior longitudinal fasciculus II beneath it is interrupted. Aphasia and bilateral apraxia are left-hemisphere signs.

qz-44.vignette: A 54-year-old woman has a fall and afterward cannot smell coffee. Over months her family notes that she has become tactless, makes crude jokes and spends impulsively. She scores normally on a memory test.
qz-44.stem: Which region should be imaged first?
qz-44.explanation: Anosmia with disinhibition and preserved memory is the orbitofrontal syndrome: the gyri recti and orbital cortex sit on the anterior fossa floor beside the olfactory tracts and are bruised in falls (or compressed by an olfactory groove meningioma). The dorsolateral cortex would give a dysexecutive picture without anosmia.

qz-45.vignette: A 63-year-old man is brought by his daughter because he has become apathetic, sits all day and answers in monosyllables since a stroke two weeks ago. He is fully oriented and has no weakness. MRI shows a small infarct in the head of the caudate nucleus and the anterior limb of the internal capsule.

options.text: Anterior thalamic radiation and prefrontal-striatal loop

qz-45.explanation: The anterior limb carries the anterior thalamic radiation between the mediodorsal and anterior thalamus and the prefrontal cortex, and the caudate head is the striatal station of the prefrontal loop; their interruption produces abulia without weakness, the frontal picture of a medial lenticulostriate (Heubner) infarct.

qz-46.vignette: A 58-year-old man with atrial fibrillation has a stroke and afterward cannot repeat sentences, although he speaks fluently and understands everything; his speech contains sound substitutions that he corrects. MRI shows a small infarct in the left supramarginal white matter.
qz-46.explanation: Conduction aphasia (fluent, comprehending, unable to repeat, self-corrected phonemic errors) is a disconnection of the posterior temporal from the frontal language cortex through the arcuate fasciculus, which runs beneath the supramarginal gyrus.

qz-47.vignette: After removal of a medial frontal tumor a 40-year-old woman is mute and does not move her right arm for a week, then recovers fully over the following month. Repetition, when she began to speak, was normal from the start.

options.text: Broca aphasia from the pars opercularis
Supplementary motor area syndrome with frontal aslant tract disconnection
Anterior cerebral artery infarct of the paracentral lobule

qz-47.explanation: Transient mutism and contralateral akinesia after medial frontal surgery, with preserved repetition and full recovery in weeks, is the supplementary motor area syndrome: the SMA and its frontal aslant connection to the inferior frontal gyrus initiate speech and movement, and the lateral cortex takes over as they recover.

qz-48.vignette: A 70-year-old man has a stroke leaving him unable to see anything in his right visual field, but he can still recognize faces and read slowly. His pupils react normally. On fields, a small island of central vision survives on the right.
qz-48.stem: Where is the lesion and why is the center spared?

options.text: Right optic tract; the macula has bilateral representation
Left calcarine cortex; the occipital pole receives middle cerebral artery collateral supply
Left optic radiation; macular fibers run separately
Left lateral geniculate; the macula projects to the pulvinar
Right calcarine cortex; the field defect is functional

qz-48.explanation: A congruous right hemianopia with normal pupils is a left calcarine (PCA) infarct, and the spared central island is macular sparing, because the macular cortex at the occipital pole is also supplied by terminal middle cerebral artery branches.

html.vignette: A 70-year-old man has a stroke leaving him unable to see anything in his right visual field, but he can still recognize faces and read slowly. His pupils react normally. On fields, a small island of central vision survives on the right.

qz-49.vignette: A 52-year-old woman notices that the left half of the room looks washed out, as if in black and white, while the right half is colored. Acuity is normal and she has a subtle left upper quadrant defect.

options.text: Right ventral occipito-temporal cortex (lingual and fusiform gyri)

qz-49.explanation: Hemiachromatopsia in the left hemifield with an upper quadrant defect places the lesion in the right ventral occipito-temporal cortex below the calcarine sulcus, where the color-processing V4 region on the lingual and fusiform gyri lies next to the lower calcarine bank that represents the upper field.

qz-50.vignette: A 45-year-old man has progressive right-sided hearing loss and tinnitus, then numbness of the right face and, later, unsteadiness with a right-sided intention tremor. MRI shows a mass in the right cerebellopontine angle extending into the internal auditory canal.
qz-50.stem: Which cerebellar structure accounts for the last symptoms?

options.text: Right flocculus and cerebellar hemisphere (lobule VI, Crus I)

qz-50.explanation: A vestibular schwannoma compresses the eighth nerve first, then the trigeminal nerve, then the flocculus and the anterior cerebellar hemisphere beside the middle cerebellar peduncle, producing ipsilateral limb ataxia and gaze-evoked nystagmus; cerebellar signs are ipsilateral because the outflow crosses twice.

qz-51.vignette: A 66-year-old man with hypertension has sudden vertigo and vomiting and cannot stand. Head impulse testing is normal, there is direction-changing nystagmus, and there is no weakness, hearing loss or facial numbness.
qz-51.stem: Which arterial territory is most likely involved?

options.text: Medial branch of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (nodulus and uvula)

qz-51.explanation: Acute vertigo with a normal head impulse test, direction-changing nystagmus and inability to stand is a central vestibular lesion, most often a medial PICA infarct of the nodulus and uvula (lobules IX-X); AICA infarcts add deafness and facial weakness, and lateral medullary involvement adds crossed sensory loss.

qz-52.vignette: A 60-year-old woman has a stroke in the right cerebellum. Her examination is remarkable only for mild gait unsteadiness, but her husband reports that she has become disorganized, cannot plan the day and answers questions in a flat, disinhibited way.
qz-52.stem: Which lobules are most likely infarcted?

options.text: Crus I and Crus II of the posterior lobe

qz-52.explanation: A cerebellar lesion with executive and affective change and little motor deficit involves the posterior lobe hemispheres (Crus I and II), the cognitive cerebellum connected to the prefrontal cortex; the anterior lobe and lobule VIII carry the body maps and would produce ataxia.

qz-53.vignette: A 25-year-old woman has a slow, coarse tremor of the right arm that is present at rest, worsens when she holds the arm out and becomes wild when she reaches for a cup. It began three months after a midbrain hemorrhage.

options.text: Left dentatorubrothalamic tract with the nigrostriatal fibers in the midbrain

qz-53.explanation: A delayed rest-postural-intention tremor after a midbrain lesion is Holmes (rubral) tremor, from combined damage to the cerebellothalamic fibers passing through the red nucleus and to the nigrostriatal fibers; the lesion is contralateral (left midbrain) because the dentatorubrothalamic tract has already crossed.

qz-54.vignette: A 78-year-old woman with a recent large left putaminal hemorrhage has a transient right hemiparesis. Which anatomical fact explains why hypertensive hemorrhages favor this site?

options.text: The putamen has the richest cortical blood supply
The lateral lenticulostriate arteries are end-arteries arising directly from the high-pressure M1 segment
The putamen lies in a watershed between two territories
The internal capsule has no blood-brain barrier
The putamen is drained by the great cerebral vein

qz-54.explanation: The lateral lenticulostriate perforators leave the M1 segment at right angles and take its full pressure without collateral support, so chronic hypertension produces lipohyalinosis and Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms there; their rupture is the putaminal hemorrhage and their occlusion the capsular lacune.

qz-55.vignette: A 33-year-old woman develops weakness of hip abduction and foot dorsiflexion on the right with numbness of the dorsum of the foot after a prolonged labor. The ankle jerk is preserved. Nerve conduction studies show a normal superficial peroneal sensory response.

options.text: Common peroneal nerve at the fibular neck

qz-55.explanation: Foot drop with weak hip abduction (superior gluteal nerve) cannot be a peroneal palsy, and a normal superficial peroneal sensory potential despite a numb dorsum means the lesion is proximal to the dorsal root ganglion or in the plexus close to it: the L5 root or lumbosacral trunk compressed by the fetal head. The sciatic nerve would reduce the sensory potential and spare hip abduction.

qz-56.vignette: A 40-year-old man who fell asleep with his arm over a chair wakes with wrist and finger drop. The triceps is strong, the brachioradialis is weak, and sensation is lost over the dorsum of the hand and the back of the forearm.
qz-56.stem: At which level is the radial nerve injured?
qz-56.explanation: A spared triceps with weak brachioradialis and wrist extensors places the lesion at the spiral groove, below the triceps branches; numbness of the posterior forearm shows the posterior antebrachial cutaneous branch, which leaves in the groove, is involved, excluding a lesion below the elbow, where only the dorsal hand would be numb or, in a posterior interosseous lesion, nothing at all.

qz-57.vignette: A 50-year-old woman has numbness of the little finger, wasting of the hand muscles and numbness of the medial forearm up to the elbow. The nerve conduction study shows an absent medial antebrachial cutaneous sensory response.

options.text: Lower trunk or medial cord of the brachial plexus
Median nerve at the carpal tunnel

qz-57.explanation: The ulnar nerve supplies no forearm skin; numbness of the medial forearm with an absent medial antebrachial cutaneous potential proves the lesion is in the medial cord or lower trunk (thoracic outlet syndrome, Pancoast tumor, Klumpke injury), not at the elbow.

qz-58.vignette: A 19-year-old man has a shoulder injury in rugby. Afterward he cannot abduct the shoulder or flex the elbow, sensation is reduced over the lateral arm and forearm, and the scapula wings laterally when he braces his shoulders back. EMG shows denervation of the rhomboids.
qz-58.stem: Which is the most likely site of injury?

options.text: Upper trunk of the brachial plexus

qz-58.explanation: The pattern is an Erb-type upper plexus picture, but rhomboid denervation means the dorsal scapular nerve, which leaves the C5 root before the trunk forms, is involved, placing the lesion at the roots; a preganglionic root avulsion carries a poor prognosis and changes the surgical plan.

qz-59.vignette: A 4-month-old ex-premature infant has stiff legs that scissor when held upright, with relatively normal arms. Cranial ultrasound in the neonatal period showed periventricular cysts.
qz-59.stem: Why are the legs affected more than the arms?

options.text: The leg area of the motor cortex is supplied by the anterior cerebral artery
The corticospinal fibers for the legs run closest to the lateral ventricles and are injured by periventricular leukomalacia
The spinal cord is more vulnerable in prematurity
The arm fibers cross earlier in the medulla

qz-59.explanation: Spastic diplegia of prematurity is periventricular leukomalacia: the corticospinal fibers for the legs descend through the periventricular white matter nearest the ventricles, in the border zone of the immature brain's perfusion, while the arm and face fibers run more laterally and are spared.

qz-60.vignette: A 24-year-old woman with a two-week history of headache worse on lying down and transient visual obscurations has papilledema and a sixth nerve palsy. CT of the brain is normal. MR venography shows an absent flow signal in the right transverse sinus.
qz-60.stem: What is the diagnosis and the mechanism of the sixth nerve palsy?

options.text: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension; the nerve is compressed in the cavernous sinus
Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis with raised pressure; the sixth nerve is stretched over the petrous ridge as a false localizing sign
Pontine glioma; the abducens nucleus is infiltrated
Migraine; the palsy is ophthalmoplegic migraine
Meningitis; the nerve is inflamed in the subarachnoid space

qz-60.explanation: Headache, papilledema and a sixth nerve palsy with a normal CT mean raised intracranial pressure, and the absent transverse sinus flow makes the cause venous sinus thrombosis; the long intracranial course of the abducens nerve over the petrous apex makes it the nerve stretched by pressure, a false localizing sign that does not indicate a pontine lesion.

topic-brain-tumor-localization.name: Brain tumors: localization and patterns
topic-brain-tumor-localization.summary: Intracranial tumors present through three mechanisms, focal deficit or seizure from the cortex or tract they invade or compress, raised intracranial pressure from their mass and edema or from the hydrocephalus they cause, and endocrine or cranial nerve syndromes from their position at the skull base, so the presentation localizes the tumor and the location predicts the histology: gliomas infiltrate the white matter of the hemispheres, meningiomas sit on the dura, metastases lodge at the gray-white junction, pituitary adenomas and craniopharyngiomas occupy the sella and suprasellar cistern, vestibular schwannomas fill the cerebellopontine angle, and medulloblastomas and ependymomas fill the fourth ventricle in children. Imaging pattern, age and the atlas position narrow the diagnosis before the biopsy.

sections.heading: Hemispheric tumors
sections.body: Diffuse gliomas (astrocytomas and oligodendrogliomas, graded by IDH and 1p/19q status and histology) infiltrate the frontal and temporal white matter, presenting with seizures when low grade and with progressive focal deficit, headache and personality change when high grade; glioblastoma enhances irregularly around necrosis and crosses the corpus callosum as a butterfly lesion. Metastases (lung, breast, melanoma, kidney, colon) lodge at the gray-white junction where the arterioles narrow, are often multiple and round with disproportionate edema, and present with seizures or deficits appropriate to the cortex they occupy. Primary CNS lymphoma sits in the deep periventricular white matter and the corpus callosum, enhances homogeneously and restricts diffusion, and melts with steroids. Meningiomas compress rather than invade, arising from the convexity, the falx and parasagittal dura (leg weakness and seizures), the sphenoid wing (proptosis and optic neuropathy), the olfactory groove (anosmia and frontal change) and the tuberculum sellae (chiasmal syndrome). Functional localization follows the atlas: precentral tumors cause focal motor seizures and weakness, dominant temporal tumors aphasia, occipital tumors field defects, and frontal tumors personality change with late focal signs.

sections.heading: Sellar, suprasellar and skull-base tumors
sections.body: Pituitary adenomas cause hormone excess (prolactin, growth hormone, ACTH) or hypopituitarism and, as they rise through the diaphragm, a bitemporal hemianopia from the chiasm and cavernous sinus syndromes from lateral extension; apoplexy into an adenoma produces thunderclap headache, visual loss and ophthalmoplegia. Craniopharyngiomas in children and adults are cystic, calcified suprasellar masses that compress the chiasm and the hypothalamus, producing visual loss, growth failure, diabetes insipidus and obesity. Germinomas of the pineal and suprasellar region cause Parinaud syndrome, hydrocephalus and diabetes insipidus. Skull-base tumors present as cranial nerve syndromes named by the foramen: cavernous sinus (III, IV, VI, V1), superior orbital fissure, orbital apex (with II), petrous apex (VI and V), cerebellopontine angle (VIII, then VII and V, then cerebellar signs, for vestibular schwannoma and meningioma), jugular foramen (IX, X, XI for glomus tumors and schwannomas) and clivus (chordoma with VI palsy). Optic pathway gliomas belong to neurofibromatosis type 1.

sections.heading: Posterior fossa and intraventricular tumors
sections.body: In children the posterior fossa is the commonest site: medulloblastoma arises in the vermis and fills the fourth ventricle with truncal ataxia, vomiting and hydrocephalus and seeds the CSF; pilocytic astrocytoma is a cystic hemispheric mass with a mural nodule and limb ataxia; ependymoma grows from the floor of the fourth ventricle through the foramina; and diffuse midline glioma of the pons produces cranial nerve palsies, long-tract signs and ataxia with a fatal course. In adults, hemangioblastoma (with von Hippel-Lindau disease), metastases and cerebellar gliomas occur. Intraventricular tumors (colloid cyst of the third ventricle with positional headache and sudden death from acute hydrocephalus, central neurocytoma and subependymoma of the lateral ventricle, choroid plexus papilloma) present with obstructive hydrocephalus. Brainstem tumors show the level-specific crossed syndromes of the brainstem entries.

sections.heading: Mass effect, edema and the treatment logic
sections.body: Vasogenic edema spreads through the white matter around tumors because their vessels lack a blood-brain barrier and it responds to dexamethasone; the mass and edema raise pressure and, as the atlas herniation entries describe, displace the cingulate under the falx, the uncus through the incisura and the tonsils through the foramen magnum. Headache that is worse in the morning and on lying, vomiting, papilledema and a sixth nerve palsy are the pressure signs, and a false localizing sixth nerve palsy must not be attributed to a pontine tumor. Seizures accompany cortical tumors and are treated with antiepileptics but not prophylactically in their absence. A bitemporal hemianopia is a sellar mass until the MRI is done; a cerebellopontine angle tumor starts with hearing
Morning headache, vomiting and a sixth nerve palsy are pressure, not localization
Multiple round lesions with big edema at the gray-white junction are metastases; find the primary in the lung or breast

pathology.finding: Irregular ring enhancement around central necrosis, extensive FLAIR infiltration crossing the callosum, elevated perfusion and no central restricted diffusion.

Homogeneously enhancing extra-axial dural mass with a dural tail, CSF cleft and hyperostosis; calcified and dense on CT.
Multiple round enhancing lesions at the gray-white junction with disproportionate edema; hemorrhagic in melanoma, kidney and choriocarcinoma.
Sellar mass with suprasellar extension waisted by the diaphragm (snowman shape) elevating the chiasm; the normal gland is displaced and the stalk deviated.
Enhancing cerebellopontine angle mass extending into the internal auditory canal (ice-cream cone), with widening of the canal.

pearls: Steroids before a biopsy can erase a lymphoma; image first, treat second when lymphoma is possible
The child with a head tilt and morning vomiting has a posterior fossa tumor until proved otherwise
Tractography turns the atlas bundles into surgical boundaries
pitfalls: Ring enhancement is shared by glioblastoma, metastasis, abscess, lymphoma and tumefactive demyelination; diffusion, the wall and the clinical course separate them

html.summary: Intracranial tumors present through three mechanisms, focal deficit or seizure from the cortex or tract they invade or compress, raised intracranial pressure from their mass and edema or from the hydrocephalus they cause, and endocrine or cranial nerve syndromes from their position at the skull base, so the presentation localizes the tumor and the location predicts the histology: gliomas infiltrate the white matter of the hemispheres, meningiomas sit on the dura, metastases lodge at the gray-white junction, pituitary adenomas and craniopharyngiomas occupy the sella and suprasellar cistern, vestibular schwannomas fill the cerebellopontine angle, and medulloblastomas and ependymomas fill the fourth ventricle in children. ","
