topic-cns-infections-localization.name: CNS infections by compartment
topic-cns-infections-localization.summary: Infections of the nervous system are localized by the compartment they occupy: the subarachnoid space and meninges (meningitis), the brain parenchyma (encephalitis and abscess), the epidural and subdural spaces (empyema and spinal epidural abscess), the ventricles (ventriculitis), the cord (myelitis) and the roots and nerves (radiculitis, neuritis). Each compartment has a clinical signature (meningism, altered consciousness with seizures and focal signs, a mass syndrome, back pain with a cord level), a route of entry (blood, contiguous sinus or ear, direct inoculation, retrograde along nerves) and an imaging and CSF pattern, and the pathogen is predicted by age, immune status, exposure and the compartment. Time matters most in bacterial meningitis and herpes encephalitis, where treatment precedes the confirmation.

sections.heading: Meningitis: the subarachnoid compartment
sections.body: Bacterial meningitis (pneumococcus, meningococcus, Listeria in the elderly and immunosuppressed, group B streptococcus and E. coli in neonates) produces fever, headache, neck stiffness, photophobia and declining consciousness within hours, with a purulent CSF (neutrophils, low glucose, high protein) and complications from the inflamed basal cisterns: cranial nerve palsies, hydrocephalus, vasculitic infarcts and cerebral edema; antibiotics and dexamethasone are given before the lumbar puncture when the puncture will be delayed, and a CT precedes the puncture when there is a focal deficit, papilledema, seizures or coma. Viral meningitis (enteroviruses, herpes simplex type 2, mumps) is self-limited with a lymphocytic CSF and normal glucose. Tuberculous and fungal (cryptococcal) meningitis are subacute basal meningitides with lymphocytes, low glucose and high protein, cranial nerve palsies, hydrocephalus and infarcts, and neoplastic meningitis mimics them. Rash and shock point to meningococcus; a recent sinus or ear infection points to pneumococcus and to a contiguous abscess.

sections.heading: Encephalitis and abscess: the parenchymal compartment
sections.body: Herpes simplex encephalitis attacks the medial temporal lobes, the insula and the orbitofrontal cortex, usually asymmetrically, producing fever, confusion, aphasia, seizures and memory loss, with a lymphocytic CSF, a positive PCR, temporal FLAIR change and periodic lateralized discharges on EEG; acyclovir is started at suspicion. Arboviral and enteroviral encephalitides involve the thalamus, basal ganglia and brainstem (Japanese and West Nile), rabies ascends the nerves to the brainstem and limbic system, and autoimmune encephalitis mimics all of these. A brain abscess follows contiguous spread from the sinuses (frontal lobe), the ear (temporal lobe and cerebellum) or hematogenous seeding (gray-white junction, multiple), producing a mass syndrome with headache, focal signs and seizures, often without fever; it enhances in a ring with central restricted diffusion and needs drainage and antibiotics. Toxoplasmosis (multiple ring lesions in the basal ganglia), progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (non-enhancing white-matter lesions) and cryptococcoma are the lesions of the immunosuppressed, and neurocysticercosis is the commonest cause of seizures worldwide.

sections.heading: Empyema, spinal infections and the roots
sections.body: Subdural empyema, usually from frontal sinusitis, is a surgical emergency with headache, fever, seizures and rapid deterioration and a thin enhancing collection over the convexity or along the falx; epidural abscess is slower. Spinal epidural abscess (staphylococcus from bacteremia, injection or surgery) produces back pain, fever, a radicular then a cord syndrome, and an enhancing epidural collection on MRI that compresses the cord and must be decompressed before paralysis; vertebral osteomyelitis and discitis accompany it. Infectious myelitis (enteroviruses, herpes viruses, HIV, syphilis, tuberculosis) produces a cord syndrome with CSF pleocytosis; poliomyelitis and its modern mimics attack the anterior horn with flaccid asymmetric paralysis. Radiculitis and neuritis follow herpes zoster (dermatomal pain and vesicles, with facial palsy in Ramsay Hunt), Lyme disease (facial palsy, painful radiculitis, meningitis), leprosy (thickened nerves with anesthetic patches), HIV and cytomegalovirus.

sections.heading: Chronic and treatable mimics
sections.body: Neurosyphilis (meningovascular stroke in the young, tabes dorsalis with lightning pains and Argyll Robertson pupils, general paresis with dementia) and tuberculosis are the great imitators and are treatable; HIV produces a meningitis at seroconversion, a subcortical dementia, a vacuolar myelopathy, neuropathies and the opportunistic infections; prion disease is a transmissible but not infectious mimic of rapid dementia; and Whipple disease, Lyme neuroborreliosis and fungal infections present as chronic meningitis or encephalopathy. Every chronic meningitis therefore has a CSF sent for mycobacterial culture, cryptococcal antigen, syphilis serology and cytology, and every unexplained encephalopathy has an HIV test. The compartmental logic, meninges versus parenchyma versus epidural space versus roots, remains the fastest route to the right test and the right drug.

keyPoints: Meningism means the subarachnoid space; confusion with seizures and focal signs means the parenchyma; back pain with a cord level means the epidural space
Neutrophils and low glucose is bacterial; lymphocytes with low glucose is tuberculosis, fungus or cancer; lymphocytes with normal glucose is viral
Herpes encephalitis lives in the medial temporal lobe and the insula and spares the putamen; start acyclovir before the PCR returns
An abscess enhances in a ring with restricted diffusion in the center and is drained, not biopsied
Spinal epidural abscess is back pain, fever and a rising deficit: MRI and surgery the same day

imaging.normalAppearance: Contrast MRI is the study for every compartment: leptomeningeal enhancement and cisternal exudate in meningitis, temporal and insular FLAIR change in herpes, ring enhancement with restricted diffusion in abscess, extra-axial enhancing collections in empyema, and epidural enhancing collections with cord compression in the spine; CT precedes lumbar puncture when mass effect is possible.

pathology.finding: Leptomeningeal enhancement over the convexity and in the basal cisterns with FLAIR-bright sulcal exudate; hydrocephalus and infarcts in complicated cases.
Asymmetric medial temporal, insular and orbitofrontal FLAIR hyperintensity with cortical restricted diffusion and petechial hemorrhage; the putamen is spared.
pathology.timing: Changes are present within 48 hours; CT is often normal

pathology.finding: Ring-enhancing lesion with a thin, smooth capsule and central restricted diffusion; satellite lesions and surrounding edema.
Thick basal cisternal enhancement, hydrocephalus, infarcts of the perforator territories and tuberculomas.
Enhancing epidural collection with cord compression, adjacent discitis and vertebral marrow edema on STIR.

pearls: Give the antibiotic before the scan when meningitis is likely and the scan will take an hour
A ring lesion in an immunosuppressed patient is toxoplasmosis, lymphoma or abscess; the diffusion and the response to treatment separate them
Facial palsy with a rash in the ear or a summer tick bite is not Bell palsy
pitfalls: A normal CSF glucose does not exclude bacterial meningitis early or after antibiotics; treat the picture
Temporal lobe signal change with fever is herpes until the PCR says otherwise; autoimmune encephalitis is the next thought

topic-consciousness-coma-brain-death.name: Consciousness, coma and brain death
topic-consciousness-coma-brain-death.summary: Consciousness has two components, arousal, maintained by the ascending reticular activating system of the upper brainstem, hypothalamus and thalamus, and awareness, generated by the cerebral cortex and its thalamic connections, and impaired consciousness follows from a lesion of the paramedian upper brainstem, from bilateral thalamic or diffuse hemispheric dysfunction, or from a unilateral mass that compresses the brainstem by herniation. The examination of the comatose patient reads the brainstem level by level through the pupils, eye movements, corneal and gag reflexes, motor responses and breathing pattern, separates structural from metabolic coma, detects herniation in time to act, distinguishes coma from the locked-in state, the vegetative and minimally conscious states and psychogenic unresponsiveness, and, when all brainstem function is irreversibly lost, establishes brain death.

sections.heading: The anatomy of arousal
sections.body: Cholinergic, monoaminergic and glutamatergic neurons of the pontine and midbrain tegmentum project through the intralaminar thalamus and directly to the cortex and, with the orexin and histamine systems of the hypothalamus and the basal forebrain, keep the cortex awake; a lesion of the paramedian midbrain and upper pons, of both thalami, or of both hemispheres (diffuse injury, metabolic encephalopathy, drugs, seizures) produces coma, whereas a lesion of one hemisphere does so only by herniating. Awareness requires the cortex and its thalamocortical loops: the vegetative state (unresponsive wakefulness) has an intact brainstem with sleep-wake cycles, open eyes and reflex movements but no awareness after diffuse cortical or thalamic damage; the minimally conscious state shows inconsistent but reproducible signs of awareness; and the locked-in state, from a ventral pontine lesion, has full awareness with only vertical eye movements and blinking, and must never be mistaken for coma.

sections.heading: The examination of the comatose patient
sections.body: The level of consciousness is graded (Glasgow Coma Scale or FOUR score) and the brainstem is examined from top to bottom: pupils (equal and reactive in metabolic coma; a unilateral fixed dilated pupil in uncal herniation; midposition fixed in midbrain damage; pinpoint reactive in pontine damage or opioids; large and fixed in anticholinergic poisoning or death), eye position and the oculocephalic and caloric responses (intact in metabolic coma, absent with pontine damage, dysconjugate with brainstem lesions), corneal reflexes (pons), gag and cough (medulla), the motor response to pain (localizing, withdrawal, decorticate flexion from lesions above the red nucleus, decerebrate extension from midbrain-pontine lesions, none) and the breathing pattern (Cheyne-Stokes with bilateral hemispheric or diencephalic dysfunction, central hyperventilation with midbrain, apneustic and ataxic breathing with pontomedullary damage). Asymmetry means a structural lesion; preserved brainstem reflexes with deep coma mean a metabolic or toxic cause; and fundoscopy, neck stiffness and a skin and breath examination add the systemic clues.

sections.heading: Herniation and the rostrocaudal march
sections.body: A supratentorial mass raises pressure and displaces the brain: subfalcine herniation of the cingulate gyrus compresses the anterior cerebral artery; uncal herniation compresses the third nerve (dilated pupil), the posterior cerebral artery and the midbrain (contralateral then ipsilateral hemiplegia through Kernohan's notch), and central transtentorial herniation pushes the diencephalon and brainstem downward in a sequence of diencephalic (small reactive pupils, Cheyne-Stokes, decorticate posturing), midbrain (midposition fixed pupils, decerebrate posturing, hyperventilation), pontine (pinpoint pupils, absent oculocephalics, ataxic breathing) and medullary (apnea, cardiovascular collapse) stages; a posterior fossa mass produces upward or tonsillar herniation with medullary compression, apnea and death. Recognizing the stage, treating pressure (head elevation, osmotherapy, hyperventilation briefly, ventricular drainage, decompressive surgery) and removing the mass before the midbrain stage is the emergency of neurology.

sections.heading: Prognosis, disorders of consciousness and brain death
sections.body: After cardiac arrest, absent pupillary and corneal reflexes at 72 hours, absent cortical somatosensory evoked potentials, a malignant EEG, high neuron-specific enolase and diffuse cortical and basal ganglia diffusion change predict a poor outcome; after traumatic and other causes the trajectory is less certain and the vegetative state can evolve to minimal consciousness over months, so decisions are staged and functional imaging and careful behavioral scales are used. Brain death is the irreversible loss of all brainstem function: a known irreversible cause, no confounding drugs, hypothermia or metabolic derangement, deep coma with absent pupillary, corneal, oculocephalic, caloric, gag and cough reflexes, no motor response of cranial nerve origin, and apnea on a formal test; ancillary tests (EEG, angiography, perfusion scintigraphy) support the diagnosis when the examination is incomplete. Spinal reflexes and the Lazarus sign can persist and do not contradict it.

keyPoints: Coma needs the paramedian upper brainstem, both thalami or both hemispheres; one hemisphere causes coma only by herniation
Reactive pupils with deep coma mean metabolic or toxic; an asymmetric or fixed pupil means structural
Decorticate flexion is above the red nucleus, decerebrate extension below it; the change marks the march of herniation
Locked-in patients are awake: ask for a blink or an upward gaze before calling anyone comatose
Brain death is a clinical diagnosis of the brainstem, made only when the cause is known and the confounders excluded

imaging.normalAppearance: CT identifies mass lesions, hemorrhage, hydrocephalus and the cisternal effacement of herniation; MRI with DWI shows diffuse hypoxic injury, brainstem lesions and the paramedian thalamic infarcts of Percheron; EEG separates non-convulsive status and encephalopathy; perfusion studies support brain death.

pathology.finding: Effacement of the suprasellar and perimesencephalic cisterns, medial temporal displacement over the tentorial edge, midline shift and later Duret hemorrhages in the brainstem.
Bilateral cortical ribbon, basal ganglia, thalamic and hippocampal restricted diffusion with loss of gray-white differentiation on CT after cardiac arrest.
pathology.timing: DWI change peaks at 2-5 days

pathology.finding: Bilateral medial thalamic restricted diffusion with or without a midbrain lesion in a patient with sudden coma or hypersomnolence.
Absent intracranial arterial filling with opacification of the external carotid branches; radionuclide perfusion shows the hollow skull sign.

pearls: Examine the pupils every fifteen minutes in a patient with a mass: the pupil warns before the breathing stops
Naloxone, glucose and thiamine cost nothing and reverse three comas that look structural
The Glasgow score records the level; the brainstem reflexes record the site
pitfalls: Non-convulsive status epilepticus is a common unrecognized cause of coma with a normal CT; the EEG is part of the coma examination
A patient with a ventral pontine stroke who does not move is locked in, not unconscious, until proved otherwise

topic-cortical-layers-organization.name: Cortical layers, columns and functional areas
topic-cortical-layers-organization.summary: The cerebral cortex is a sheet of gray matter two to four millimeters thick, folded into gyri to fit the skull, and organized in six layers whose relative thickness varies with function: granular sensory cortex has a thick input layer IV, agranular motor cortex has giant output cells in layer V and almost no layer IV, and association cortex is intermediate; the layers are crossed by vertical columns of neurons that share a receptive field or a feature, and the columns are grouped into the Brodmann areas that the atlas parcellation approximates. Knowing the layers explains why some diseases pick out particular cortical types (Alzheimer tangles in layers III and V of association cortex, laminar necrosis after hypoxia in layer III, cortical dysplasia with disorganized layers) and why the EEG, evoked potentials and cortical stimulation read the cortex as they do.

sections.heading: The six layers and the two cell types
sections.body: Layer I (molecular) contains dendritic tufts and horizontal fibers; layer II (external granular) small pyramidal and stellate cells; layer III (external pyramidal) medium pyramidal cells whose axons form the association and commissural fibers to other cortex; layer IV (internal granular) the stellate cells that receive the specific thalamic input; layer V (internal pyramidal) the large pyramidal cells, including the giant Betz cells of the motor cortex, whose axons descend to the brainstem, spinal cord and striatum; and layer VI (multiform) the cells that project back to the thalamus. Pyramidal cells are the excitatory glutamatergic projection neurons, oriented perpendicular to the surface so that their summed dendritic currents generate the EEG; interneurons, mostly GABAergic, shape their activity and their loss produces hyperexcitability. Radial glia guide the neurons into place during development and the U-fibers beneath layer VI connect adjacent gyri.

sections.heading: Cortical types and functional areas
sections.body: Primary sensory cortices (somatosensory area 3, visual area 17 with its stria of Gennari, auditory areas 41 and 42) are koniocortex with a thick granular layer IV for thalamic input; primary motor cortex (area 4) is agranular with its Betz cells; premotor and association cortices (areas 6, 9, 46, 39, 40, 22) are homotypical, with balanced layers; and the limbic allocortex (hippocampus with three layers) and periallocortex (entorhinal, cingulate) are older and simpler. The Brodmann map of about fifty cytoarchitectonic areas underlies the functional localization the atlas uses: motor and premotor areas 4 and 6, the frontal eye field in area 8, Broca's areas 44 and 45, somatosensory areas 3, 1 and 2, the parietal association areas 5, 7, 39 and 40, the visual areas 17, 18 and 19, the auditory areas 41, 42 and Wernicke's area 22, and the prefrontal areas 9, 10, 11 and 46; the Harvard-Oxford and other atlases parcellate the same sheet by gyral anatomy.

sections.heading: Columns, maps and plasticity
sections.body: Neurons stacked vertically through the layers respond to the same stimulus feature (a whisker, an orientation, an ocular dominance, a sound frequency) and form columns half a millimeter wide, so each area is a mosaic of feature maps laid over a topographic map of the receptor surface: the homunculi of the motor and sensory strips, the retinotopy of the visual cortex with its cortical magnification of the macula, and the tonotopy of Heschl's gyrus. These maps are plastic: they expand with use (the reading finger of Braille readers), shrink with disuse, invade deafferented territory (the phantom limb whose face region has taken over the hand area), and reorganize after stroke as the basis of rehabilitation. Acetylcholine, noradrenaline and dopamine from the modulatory systems permit this plasticity, and the excitatory-inhibitory balance within each column sets the threshold for seizures.

sections.heading: Clinical correlates of cortical architecture
sections.body: Hypoxia kills the most metabolically active layers first, producing laminar necrosis of layer III visible as cortical ribbon signal on MRI; Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease and status epilepticus also show ribboning; Alzheimer tangles concentrate in the large pyramidal cells of layers III and V that form the association fibers, disconnecting the cortical networks; focal cortical dysplasia disorganizes the layers with dysmorphic neurons and balloon cells and is a common cause of refractory epilepsy; polymicrogyria and lissencephaly are failures of lamination; and cortical stimulation during awake surgery maps the functional areas onto the patient's gyri because the Brodmann boundaries do not follow the sulci exactly. The EEG records layer III and V pyramidal cell currents, evoked potentials record the arrival of thalamic input in layer IV, and transcranial magnetic stimulation excites the layer V output of the motor cortex, each a window on one part of the architecture.

keyPoints: Granular cortex receives (layer IV), agranular cortex sends (layer V): sensory areas are granular, motor areas are agranular
Layer III projects to other cortex, layer V to the brainstem and cord, layer VI back to the thalamus
Columns share a feature; areas share a map; the homunculus is the map of the central gyri
Laminar necrosis, Alzheimer tangles and cortical dysplasia each pick out particular layers
The maps move: plasticity after injury is the reason rehabilitation works and phantom limbs hurt

imaging.normalAppearance: High-resolution T1 and T2 images show cortical thickness, the gray-white junction and the stria of Gennari; DWI shows cortical ribbon injury; FLAIR shows dysplasia and polymicrogyria; functional MRI and magnetoencephalography map the functional areas onto the individual's gyri.

pathology.finding: Gyriform cortical restricted diffusion in the acute phase and T1 hyperintensity of the cortex weeks after global hypoxia, hypoglycemia or prolonged seizures.
Focal cortical thickening, blurring of the gray-white junction and a transmantle FLAIR band pointing at the ventricle.
Thickened, irregular cortex with many small gyri and shallow sulci, often perisylvian, with a bumpy gray-white junction.
Regional cortical thinning on surface-based analysis in the pattern of the disease (temporo-parietal in Alzheimer, frontotemporal in FTD), used as a research and increasingly a clinical biomarker.

pearls: The stria of Gennari is visible with the naked eye and on high-resolution MRI: it marks the primary visual cortex
Cortical ribbon signal on DWI means the gray matter is dying layer by layer: hypoxia, seizures or prions
Brodmann areas are cytoarchitecture; the gyri are folds; the two only approximately coincide
pitfalls: Gyral anatomy is a proxy for cytoarchitecture; the central sulcus locates the motor strip reliably, but language areas vary and must be mapped in the individual

topic-csf-physiology-blood-brain-barrier.name: CSF physiology and the blood–brain barrier
topic-csf-physiology-blood-brain-barrier.summary: Cerebrospinal fluid is secreted by the choroid plexus of the ventricles at about half a milliliter a minute, flows through the ventricular system into the subarachnoid space by the foramina of the fourth ventricle, and is absorbed into the venous sinuses through the arachnoid granulations and along the cranial and spinal nerve sheaths; the whole volume of about 150 ml turns over three or four times a day. The blood–brain barrier of tight-junctioned capillary endothelium and the blood–CSF barrier of the choroid epithelium keep the extracellular fluid of the brain constant and exclude most drugs and proteins, and both are breached by inflammation, tumor and infarction. These systems explain hydrocephalus, intracranial hypertension, the composition of a normal and an abnormal spinal fluid, and why contrast enhancement means disease.

sections.heading: Production, circulation and absorption
sections.body: The choroid plexus in the lateral, third and fourth ventricles secretes CSF actively, driven by carbonic anhydrase and the sodium pump of the choroid epithelium (the target of acetazolamide), at a rate that is largely independent of pressure; the fluid passes through the interventricular foramina, the third ventricle, the aqueduct and the fourth ventricle, and leaves through the median foramen of Magendie and the lateral foramina of Luschka into the cisterna magna and the basal cisterns. It flows over the convexity to the arachnoid granulations, where a pressure gradient of a few centimeters of water moves it into the superior sagittal sinus, and along the olfactory and spinal nerve roots to lymphatics; a glymphatic route along perivascular spaces clears interstitial solutes during sleep. Absorption rises with pressure, so a fixed increase in production produces only a modest rise in pressure; obstruction of flow or absorption produces hydrocephalus.

sections.heading: Hydrocephalus and intracranial pressure
sections.body: Obstruction within the ventricles or at the fourth ventricular outlets (tumor, aqueductal stenosis, hemorrhage, Chiari) produces non-communicating hydrocephalus with enlargement of the ventricles above the block; impaired absorption at the granulations after subarachnoid hemorrhage, meningitis or venous sinus thrombosis produces communicating hydrocephalus in which all ventricles dilate. Normal-pressure hydrocephalus of the elderly combines ventriculomegaly with a triad of gait apraxia, incontinence and dementia and improves with shunting when a large-volume tap improves the gait. Intracranial pressure is normally below 15 mmHg; because the skull is closed, the Monro-Kellie principle means that any added volume of blood, CSF, edema or mass must displace another, and when compensation fails pressure rises steeply and herniation follows. Idiopathic intracranial hypertension raises CSF pressure without a mass or ventricular enlargement and threatens vision through papilledema.

sections.heading: Composition and lumbar puncture
sections.body: Normal CSF is clear, with fewer than five lymphocytes per microliter, protein below 0.45 g/L, glucose about two-thirds of the plasma value and an opening pressure of 10 to 20 cm of water in the lateral position. Neutrophils, low glucose and high protein mean bacterial meningitis; lymphocytes with normal glucose mean viral meningitis or encephalitis; lymphocytes with low glucose mean tuberculosis, fungi or carcinomatosis; red cells that do not clear between the first and last tube, with xanthochromia after twelve hours, mean subarachnoid hemorrhage; and oligoclonal bands present in CSF but not serum mean intrathecal immunoglobulin synthesis, the laboratory signature of multiple sclerosis. The puncture is made below the conus, at L3-L4 or L4-L5, and is dangerous when a mass or obstructive hydrocephalus creates a pressure gradient across the tentorium or the foramen magnum.

sections.heading: The barriers and their failure
sections.body: Brain capillaries have continuous tight junctions, few vesicles and a sheath of astrocyte end-feet and pericytes, so lipid-soluble molecules, gases and substances with transporters (glucose, amino acids, levodopa) enter while proteins, most antibiotics, dopamine and many drugs do not; the choroid plexus epithelium forms the blood–CSF barrier with the same selectivity. The circumventricular organs (area postrema, median eminence, organum vasculosum, subfornical organ, pineal and posterior pituitary) have fenestrated capillaries and sense or secrete into the blood. The barrier opens in inflammation, tumor, infarction and hypertensive crisis, which is why gadolinium and iodinated contrast enhance those lesions, why vasogenic edema spreads through the white matter around them, why antibiotics reach the CSF only when the meninges are inflamed and why osmotic agents such as mannitol shrink the normal brain more than the injured part. Immature barriers in the neonate let bilirubin reach the basal ganglia in kernicterus.

keyPoints: CSF is made at 0.5 ml per minute and turned over three to four times a day; absorption, not production, sets the pressure
Non-communicating hydrocephalus blocks the ventricles; communicating hydrocephalus blocks the granulations; both enlarge the temporal horns first
Contrast enhancement means the blood–brain barrier is open: tumor, inflammation, infection or subacute infarction
Neutrophils and low glucose in CSF mean bacterial meningitis; lymphocytes with low glucose mean tuberculosis, fungus or cancer
The Monro-Kellie doctrine makes every added milliliter in the skull someone else's problem

imaging.normalAppearance: Ventricular size relative to the sulci and the temporal horns distinguishes hydrocephalus from atrophy; CSF flow studies show aqueductal flow; contrast enhancement maps barrier breakdown.

pathology.finding: Dilated lateral and third ventricles with a normal fourth ventricle in aqueductal stenosis; periventricular FLAIR halo of transependymal CSF in acute cases.
Ventriculomegaly out of proportion to sulcal atrophy with tight high-convexity sulci and an enlarged Sylvian fissure (DESH pattern).
Empty sella, flattened posterior globes, distended optic nerve sheaths and transverse sinus stenosis on MRV, with normal ventricles.
Ring or solid enhancement after gadolinium with finger-like FLAIR edema spreading through the white matter around a tumor or abscess.

pearls: Measure the opening pressure at every lumbar puncture; a normal CSF with high pressure is idiopathic intracranial hypertension or venous thrombosis
Never puncture below an obstruction you have not imaged
Acetazolamide works on the choroid plexus, which is why it treats intracranial hypertension
pitfalls: Ventricles enlarge with atrophy too; hydrocephalus needs the temporal horns rounded and the sulci tight, not just big ventricles

topic-dementia-patterns.name: Dementia: anatomical patterns of cognitive decline
topic-dementia-patterns.summary: Each degenerative dementia attacks a network in a characteristic order, so the first symptoms and the pattern of atrophy on MRI localize the disease before any biomarker: Alzheimer disease begins in the entorhinal cortex and hippocampus and spreads to the posterior cingulate and parietal association cortex, producing amnesia first; frontotemporal degeneration begins in the orbitofrontal and anterior temporal cortex, producing behavioral change or semantic loss; Lewy body disease affects the brainstem, the basal forebrain and the visual association cortex, producing fluctuations, visual hallucinations and parkinsonism; and vascular cognitive impairment reflects the frontal-subcortical circuits disconnected by small vessel disease. The examination should therefore ask which cognitive domain failed first and map it onto the atlas.

sections.heading: Alzheimer disease: the medial temporal and parietal pattern
sections.body: Tau tangles appear first in the transentorhinal and entorhinal cortex, spread to the hippocampus and then to the temporal, parietal and frontal association cortex, while amyloid accumulates diffusely in the neocortex years before symptoms; the earliest deficit is therefore anterograde episodic memory (rapid forgetting, repeated questions, failure of delayed recall that cueing does not rescue), followed by word finding, visuospatial disorientation and executive decline. MRI shows medial temporal atrophy graded on coronal images, then parietal atrophy, and FDG-PET shows posterior cingulate and precuneus hypometabolism; CSF shows low amyloid-beta 42 and high phosphorylated tau, and amyloid and tau PET confirm the pathology. Atypical variants attack the same pathology to different networks: posterior cortical atrophy (visual), logopenic aphasia (left temporo-parietal) and the frontal variant. Cholinesterase inhibitors address the basal forebrain cholinergic loss.

sections.heading: Frontotemporal lobar degeneration: the anterior pattern
sections.body: The behavioral variant begins with disinhibition, apathy, loss of empathy, compulsive or ritualistic behavior, hyperorality and dietary change and executive failure with relatively preserved memory and visuospatial function, reflecting orbitofrontal, anterior cingulate, insular and anterior temporal degeneration (tau or TDP-43); MRI shows frontal and anterior temporal atrophy, often asymmetric, with knife-edge gyri. Semantic dementia is asymmetric anterior temporal atrophy with fluent speech empty of meaning, loss of word comprehension and of knowledge about objects and people; progressive non-fluent aphasia is left inferior frontal and insular atrophy with effortful, agrammatic speech and apraxia of speech. Motor neuron disease, progressive supranuclear palsy and corticobasal degeneration overlap with these syndromes, and onset before 65 with a family history suggests a genetic cause.

sections.heading: Lewy body disease and vascular cognitive impairment
sections.body: Dementia with Lewy bodies produces fluctuating attention and alertness, recurrent well-formed visual hallucinations, REM sleep behavior disorder and parkinsonism, with visuospatial and executive deficits more than amnesia early on; alpha-synuclein spreads from the brainstem and olfactory bulb to the limbic and neocortical regions, the basal forebrain cholinergic loss is severe, and MRI shows relative preservation of the medial temporal lobes while dopamine transporter imaging shows nigrostriatal loss. Neuroleptic sensitivity is dangerous. Vascular cognitive impairment presents with slowed processing, executive dysfunction, gait apraxia, urinary urgency and emotional lability from confluent white-matter disease, lacunes and microbleeds disconnecting the frontal-subcortical circuits, or with a stepwise course after strategic infarcts of the thalamus, caudate or angular gyrus; it coexists with Alzheimer pathology in most elderly patients.

sections.heading: Rapidly progressive and treatable dementias
sections.body: A dementia evolving over weeks to months is a different disease: Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (myoclonus, cortical ribboning and basal ganglia restricted diffusion on MRI, periodic sharp waves on EEG, positive real-time quaking-induced conversion in CSF), autoimmune encephalitis (limbic seizures and psychiatric change with antibodies against neuronal surface antigens), Wernicke encephalopathy, and infections such as HIV, syphilis and Whipple disease. Treatable contributors to any dementia include normal-pressure hydrocephalus (gait first, then incontinence, then cognition), hypothyroidism, vitamin B12 deficiency, depression, sleep apnea, subdural hematoma and, above all, drugs with anticholinergic and sedative action. The workup of every dementia therefore includes imaging, thyroid function, B12, a drug review and a mood assessment, and a rapidly progressive course adds CSF, EEG and autoimmune serology.

keyPoints: Ask which domain failed first: memory (Alzheimer), behavior or language (frontotemporal), attention and vision with hallucinations (Lewy), speed and gait (vascular)
Medial temporal atrophy on coronal MRI is the structural signature of Alzheimer disease; frontal and anterior temporal atrophy of frontotemporal degeneration
Cueing rescues retrieval in subcortical and frontal dementias but not the storage failure of Alzheimer disease
Dementia with Lewy bodies fluctuates, hallucinates and moves badly; do not give it a neuroleptic
Weeks-to-months dementia is prion, autoimmune or metabolic until proved otherwise

imaging.normalAppearance: Volumetric T1 for regional atrophy (medial temporal, parietal, frontal, anterior temporal), FLAIR for vascular burden, SWI for microbleeds, DWI for prion disease, FDG-PET for the metabolic pattern and amyloid or tau PET and CSF biomarkers for Alzheimer pathology; dopamine transporter SPECT for Lewy body disease.

pathology.finding: Bilateral hippocampal and entorhinal atrophy with widened temporal horns and parietal atrophy; FDG-PET hypometabolism of the posterior cingulate, precuneus and temporo-parietal cortex.
Frontal and anterior temporal atrophy, often asymmetric, with relative sparing of the posterior cortex; FDG-PET frontal hypometabolism.
Reduced striatal dopamine transporter uptake with relatively preserved medial temporal volume; FDG-PET occipital hypometabolism with the cingulate island sign.
Cortical ribbon and striatal restricted diffusion, sometimes thalamic (pulvinar sign in variant disease), with periodic sharp-wave complexes on EEG.
Confluent periventricular and deep white-matter hyperintensities, lacunes, microbleeds and strategic infarcts of the thalamus or caudate.

pearls: A dementia workup that omits the drug list misses the commonest reversible cause
Gait before memory means normal-pressure hydrocephalus; test with a large-volume tap
Semantic dementia patients ask what a word means; Alzheimer patients ask the same question twice
pitfalls: Depression in the elderly impairs attention and retrieval and mimics dementia; treat it and retest before labeling
Anticholinergic burden from bladder, sleep and allergy drugs produces a reversible dementia that no scan will show

topic-epilepsy-localization.name: Epilepsy: seizure semiology and localization
topic-epilepsy-localization.summary: A seizure is a transient burst of abnormally synchronized cortical activity, and its clinical expression is a map of the cortex it passes through: the first symptom (the aura) names the site of onset, the sequence of later symptoms traces the spread, and the postictal deficits mark the cortex that was exhausted. Focal seizures arise in one region and may spread to both hemispheres; generalized seizures begin in bilateral thalamocortical networks. The atlas structures involved, the medial temporal lobe, the frontal motor and supplementary motor areas, the insula, the occipital lobe and the thalamus, each produce a recognizable semiology, and the interictal and ictal EEG, the MRI and the neuropsychology converge on the epileptogenic zone that surgery can remove.

sections.heading: Temporal lobe seizures
sections.body: Medial temporal seizures, the commonest focal epilepsy of adults, begin with a rising epigastric sensation, fear, deja vu or an olfactory or gustatory hallucination from the amygdala, hippocampus and uncus, then impair awareness with a motionless stare, oral automatisms (lip smacking, chewing) and hand automatisms ipsilateral to the focus with dystonic posturing of the contralateral hand; they last one to three minutes and are followed by confusion and, with dominant-side onset, postictal aphasia. Lateral temporal seizures begin with auditory hallucinations, vertigo or complex visual scenes. The substrate is usually hippocampal sclerosis, a dysembryoplastic tumor, a cavernoma or a dysplasia, and anterior temporal lobectomy renders most patients seizure-free when MRI, EEG and neuropsychology agree.

sections.heading: Frontal lobe seizures
sections.body: Frontal seizures are brief, frequent, nocturnal and often bizarre: supplementary motor area seizures produce sudden asymmetric tonic posturing with the contralateral arm abducted and the head turned toward it (the fencing posture) and vocalization with preserved awareness; primary motor cortex seizures produce clonic jerking that marches along the homunculus (the Jacksonian march) and leave a Todd paresis; frontal eye field seizures turn the head and eyes away from the focus; prefrontal and cingulate seizures produce hypermotor thrashing, pedaling, screaming and fear; opercular seizures produce salivation, throat sensations and speech arrest. Scalp EEG is often normal or obscured by movement, and these seizures are frequently misdiagnosed as parasomnias or psychogenic attacks until video-EEG shows their stereotypy.

sections.heading: Parietal, occipital and insular seizures, and generalized epilepsies
sections.body: Parietal seizures begin with contralateral tingling, pain, a sense of a missing or moving limb or vertigo; occipital seizures begin with elementary colored visual hallucinations in the contralateral field, ictal blindness or eye deviation, and spread forward to temporal or parietal semiology; insular seizures produce laryngeal constriction, paresthesias and autonomic changes and mimic temporal seizures. Generalized epilepsies (absence, myoclonic, generalized tonic-clonic) begin in thalamocortical circuits with generalized spike-wave discharges: absence seizures are brief stares with 3 Hz spike-wave, juvenile myoclonic epilepsy adds morning jerks and photosensitivity, and the choice of drug differs from focal epilepsy, some sodium channel blockers worsening absence and myoclonus. Status epilepticus, a seizure over five minutes or repeated without recovery, is a medical emergency treated with benzodiazepines then a loading antiepileptic.

sections.heading: Localizing the focus for treatment
sections.body: The history establishes the aura and the spread; interictal EEG shows spikes over the focus (anterior temporal spikes in medial temporal epilepsy, obscured or midline spikes in frontal epilepsy); MRI with thin coronal FLAIR and T1 through the hippocampi finds sclerosis, dysplasia and tumors; FDG-PET shows interictal hypometabolism of the focus, and ictal SPECT shows hyperperfusion; neuropsychology lateralizes memory and language; and when these disagree, intracranial recording with depth electrodes maps the onset. Lateralizing signs during the seizure include ipsilateral automatisms with contralateral dystonia, head version away from the focus at the start of a bilateral tonic-clonic seizure, postictal aphasia (dominant) and postictal nose wiping with the ipsilateral hand. The treatment ladder runs from drugs to resective surgery, laser ablation, vagus nerve or responsive stimulation and thalamic stimulation.

keyPoints: The aura is the address: epigastric and fear for the medial temporal lobe, colored shapes for the occipital lobe, a tonic fencing posture for the supplementary motor area
Dystonic posturing of a hand during a seizure points to the opposite hemisphere; automatisms with it point to the same side
Frontal seizures are short, nocturnal and strange, and the EEG is often normal
Hippocampal sclerosis is the commonest surgically curable epilepsy; look at the hippocampi on coronal FLAIR
Absence and myoclonic epilepsies are generalized and are worsened by some drugs that help focal seizures

imaging.normalAppearance: An epilepsy MRI protocol includes thin coronal T2/FLAIR and volumetric T1 perpendicular to the hippocampal axis, T2* or SWI for cavernomas and hemosiderin, and post-contrast images when a tumor is possible; FDG-PET and ictal SPECT add localizing evidence.

pathology.finding: Small hippocampus with loss of internal architecture and increased FLAIR signal, often with ipsilateral fornix and mammillary body atrophy and a dilated temporal horn.
Cortical thickening, blurred gray-white junction and a transmantle band of FLAIR signal tapering toward the ventricle; often subtle and missed without thin slices.
Cortically based multicystic or bubbly T2-bright lesion of the temporal lobe with little edema and little or no enhancement.
Popcorn-like lesion with a hemosiderin rim on T2 and blooming on SWI, without edema unless recently bled.

pearls: A first seizure after 25 is focal until proved otherwise: image the brain
Ask the witness what happened first, not what happened most
Todd paresis after a seizure localizes the motor cortex and can mimic a stroke for hours
pitfalls: Convulsive syncope with a few jerks is not epilepsy; the setting, the prodrome and the rapid recovery separate them
Psychogenic attacks coexist with epilepsy in a fifth of patients; video-EEG, not the story, decides

Focal seizures arise in one region and may spread to both hemispheres; generalized seizures begin in bilateral thalamocortical networks. The atlas structures involved, the medial temporal lobe, the frontal motor and supplementary motor areas, the insula, the occipital lobe and the thalamus, each produce a recognizable semiology, and the interictal and ictal EEG, the MRI and the neuropsychology converge on the epileptogenic zone that surgery can remove.

topic-headache-localization.name: Headache: pain-sensitive structures and localization
topic-headache-localization.summary: The brain itself has no pain receptors; headache arises from the dura and its arteries, the venous sinuses, the large arteries at the base, the periosteum, the scalp and the cervical structures, all innervated by the trigeminal nerve above the tentorium and the upper cervical roots below it, converging on the trigeminocervical complex in the caudal medulla and upper cord. Primary headaches (migraine, tension-type, cluster and the other trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias) are disorders of this system's activation and modulation by the brainstem and hypothalamus; secondary headaches are its irritation by hemorrhage, meningitis, raised or low pressure, dissection, venous thrombosis, giant cell arteritis or mass, and recognizing the red flags that point to them is the main clinical task.

sections.heading: Anatomy of head pain
sections.body: The supratentorial dura, the falx and the cerebral arteries are supplied by the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve (with maxillary and mandibular contributions to the middle meningeal region), so supratentorial pain is referred to the eye, forehead and temple; the posterior fossa dura and the tentorium are supplied by the upper cervical roots and the recurrent tentorial branch, so infratentorial pain is referred to the occiput and neck. Both inputs converge in the trigeminocervical complex (the spinal trigeminal nucleus and the C1-C3 dorsal horns), which explains why occipital pain accompanies migraine and why neck disease causes frontal pain. The trigeminovascular reflex releases calcitonin gene-related peptide from trigeminal terminals around the meningeal vessels, the target of modern migraine drugs, and the pain is modulated by the periaqueductal gray, the raphe and the locus coeruleus, the reason serotonergic and noradrenergic drugs prevent headache.

sections.heading: Primary headaches and their generators
sections.body: Migraine begins with hypothalamic and brainstem activation (premonitory yawning, hunger, mood change), sometimes an aura of cortical spreading depression that marches across the visual cortex over twenty minutes, then a throbbing unilateral headache with nausea, photophobia and phonophobia from sensitization of the trigeminovascular system and the thalamus, lasting hours to days. Cluster headache is a strictly unilateral orbital pain of 15 to 180 minutes with ipsilateral lacrimation, nasal congestion, ptosis and miosis from parasympathetic activation through the superior salivatory nucleus and sympathetic deficit, recurring at the same time of day in bouts and timed by the posterior hypothalamus; paroxysmal hemicrania and SUNCT are shorter versions with distinct treatment responses. Tension-type headache is bilateral, pressing and without autonomic features, and medication-overuse headache follows frequent analgesic use in any primary headache.

sections.heading: Secondary headaches and the red flags
sections.body: A thunderclap headache reaching maximum within a minute is subarachnoid hemorrhage until CT and, if negative after six hours, lumbar puncture prove otherwise, and its mimics (reversible cerebral vasoconstriction, dissection, pituitary apoplexy, venous thrombosis) need vascular imaging. A headache worse on lying, waking the patient, with vomiting, papilledema or a sixth nerve palsy means raised pressure from a mass, hydrocephalus, venous thrombosis or idiopathic intracranial hypertension; a headache that appears on standing and resolves lying down means low pressure from a CSF leak. Fever with neck stiffness means meningitis; a new headache after 50 with jaw claudication and a high sedimentation rate means giant cell arteritis and demands steroids before the biopsy; neck pain with Horner syndrome means carotid dissection; and any headache with a new focal sign, seizure or change in pattern needs imaging.

sections.heading: Localizing pain to a structure
sections.body: Pain around the eye with a sixth nerve palsy or ophthalmoplegia points to the cavernous sinus, the superior orbital fissure or the orbit; pain at the vertex or behind the eye with visual loss points to the pituitary region; occipital pain with neck stiffness points to the posterior fossa or the meninges; unilateral neck pain radiating to the face with a small pupil points to the carotid; trigeminal neuralgia is a brief electric pain in one division triggered by touch, usually from vascular compression at the root entry zone; occipital neuralgia is a shooting pain in the C2 distribution. Post-traumatic and cervicogenic headaches reflect the trigeminocervical convergence, and the location of a mass rarely matches the site of the pain except when it involves the dura directly.

keyPoints: The brain does not hurt; the dura, the vessels and the neck do, all through the trigeminocervical complex
Supratentorial pain is referred to the eye and forehead, infratentorial pain to the occiput and neck
Thunderclap means subarachnoid hemorrhage until proved otherwise; the six-hour CT rule applies
Cluster headache keeps hypothalamic time and comes with a wet, red eye and a droopy lid
A new headache after 50 with a high sedimentation rate is giant cell arteritis; treat before the biopsy

imaging.normalAppearance: Primary headaches have normal imaging; imaging is for red flags: non-contrast CT for hemorrhage, CTA or MRA for aneurysm, dissection and vasoconstriction, MRV for venous thrombosis, MRI with contrast for meningeal disease, low pressure and masses.

pathology.finding: Hyperdense blood in the basal cisterns and Sylvian fissures within six hours of a thunderclap headache; CTA finds the aneurysm.
pathology.timing: CT sensitivity falls after 6 hours; lumbar puncture for xanthochromia beyond 12 hours

pathology.finding: Diffuse smooth pachymeningeal enhancement, brain sagging with a low-lying brainstem and tonsils, subdural collections and pituitary enlargement in a patient with orthostatic headache.
Absent flow in a sinus with the empty delta sign on contrast CT or MRI and venous infarcts that do not respect arterial territories.
Intramural hematoma crescent on fat-saturated T1 and tapered stenosis of the internal carotid or vertebral artery in a patient with neck pain and headache.

pearls: Ask how fast the headache reached its peak before asking where it hurts
Positional headache means pressure: worse lying means high, worse standing means low
Migraine with aura is a cortical event; the aura marches, the visual disturbance of a TIA does not
pitfalls: A normal CT does not exclude subarachnoid hemorrhage after six hours; the lumbar puncture does
The worst headache of a chronic migraineur can still be a hemorrhage: judge the onset, not the patient

topic-leukodystrophies-mitochondrial.name: Leukodystrophies and mitochondrial disorders
topic-leukodystrophies-mitochondrial.summary: Leukodystrophies are genetic disorders of myelin formation or maintenance that produce symmetric, confluent white-matter disease with progressive spasticity, ataxia, visual loss and cognitive decline, in contrast to the patchy asymmetric lesions of multiple sclerosis and vascular disease; the distribution on MRI (parieto-occipital, frontal, periventricular with or without the U-fibers, with or without the cerebellum and brainstem), the age of onset and the associated features (adrenal failure, peripheral neuropathy, macrocephaly, cataract) point to the enzyme or gene. Mitochondrial disorders, from defects of oxidative phosphorylation, attack the tissues with the highest energy demand and produce a different pattern: stroke-like cortical lesions that ignore arterial territories, deep gray matter necrosis, myopathy, neuropathy, deafness, diabetes and lactic acidosis, often with maternal inheritance.

sections.heading: The main leukodystrophies
sections.body: X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy (ABCD1, very long chain fatty acids) produces in boys a parieto-occipital demyelination advancing forward with an enhancing rim, behavioral change, visual and auditory agnosia and adrenal failure, and in adult men a spastic paraparesis with neuropathy (adrenomyeloneuropathy); metachromatic leukodystrophy (arylsulfatase A) gives a symmetric periventricular disease sparing the U-fibers with a tigroid pattern, a demyelinating neuropathy and a childhood or adult onset with psychiatric change; Krabbe disease (galactocerebrosidase) gives infantile irritability, spasticity, optic atrophy and neuropathy with dense thalami and corticospinal involvement; Alexander disease (GFAP) gives frontal-predominant white-matter disease with macrocephaly; Canavan disease (aspartoacylase) gives diffuse subcortical disease with macrocephaly and an elevated N-acetylaspartate peak; Pelizaeus-Merzbacher disease (PLP1) gives nystagmus and hypomyelination from infancy; vanishing white matter disease shows white matter turning to CSF signal with episodes provoked by fever; and the adult-onset forms (cerebrotendinous xanthomatosis with cataracts and tendon xanthomas, CADASIL with anterior temporal and external capsule lesions, adult polyglucosan body disease) are treatable or at least diagnosable causes of spastic paraparesis and dementia.

sections.heading: Reading the white matter pattern
sections.body: The questions are: is the disease hypomyelinating (persistently immature myelin signal on T1 and T2) or demyelinating (loss of formed myelin with T2 hyperintensity); which region leads (parieto-occipital in adrenoleukodystrophy, frontal in Alexander, periventricular sparing U-fibers in metachromatic, diffuse with U-fibers in Canavan); is there contrast enhancement at the advancing edge (adrenoleukodystrophy); are the cerebellum, brainstem, corticospinal tracts, corpus callosum or thalami involved; is the head large (Alexander, Canavan) or small; are cysts present (vanishing white matter, megalencephalic leukoencephalopathy); and is there a neuropathy (metachromatic, Krabbe, adrenomyeloneuropathy). Toxic leukoencephalopathies (methotrexate, heroin inhalation, carbon monoxide, chemotherapy) and metabolic ones (hypertensive PRES, osmotic demyelination) can mimic the symmetric pattern and are excluded by the history; the age-related and vascular patterns are asymmetric and patchy.

sections.heading: Mitochondrial disorders
sections.body: Mitochondrial DNA is maternally inherited and heteroplasmic, so the same mutation produces different syndromes in different tissues and relatives: MELAS (mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis and stroke-like episodes; m.3243A>G) gives stroke-like cortical lesions that cross arterial territories, favor the parieto-occipital cortex and shift over time, with seizures, migraine, deafness, diabetes and short stature; MERRF gives myoclonic epilepsy with ragged red fibers; Leigh syndrome gives infantile regression with symmetric necrotic lesions of the basal ganglia, brainstem and periaqueductal gray; Kearns-Sayre syndrome gives progressive external ophthalmoplegia, retinal pigmentation and heart block from large deletions; Leber hereditary optic neuropathy gives sequential painless central visual loss in young men; and nuclear-encoded disorders of mitochondrial maintenance (POLG) give epilepsy, ataxia, neuropathy and liver failure precipitated by valproate. Lactate is raised in blood and CSF and on spectroscopy, muscle biopsy shows ragged red and cytochrome-oxidase-negative fibers, and genetic testing of blood, urine or muscle confirms the mutation.

sections.heading: Clinical approach and treatment
sections.body: Progressive symmetric spasticity, ataxia or cognitive decline with a symmetric white-matter MRI pattern demands a leukodystrophy workup: very long chain fatty acids and adrenal function, arylsulfatase A, galactocerebrosidase, lysosomal enzymes, plasma sterols, nerve conduction studies and, increasingly, a gene panel or exome; cerebrotendinous xanthomatosis is treated with chenodeoxycholic acid, adrenoleukodystrophy with early stem cell transplantation or gene therapy, and metachromatic leukodystrophy with enzyme replacement or gene therapy in the presymptomatic stage, so recognition matters. Multisystem disease with encephalopathy, myopathy, deafness, diabetes, short stature and maternal relatives affected demands lactate, muscle biopsy and mitochondrial genetics; treatment is supportive with avoidance of valproate and other mitochondrial toxins, arginine for MELAS episodes and management of the cardiac conduction defects. The atlas white-matter, basal ganglia and brainstem entries show the structures these diseases pick out.

keyPoints: Symmetric confluent white-matter disease is genetic, toxic or metabolic; patchy asymmetric disease is vascular or inflammatory
The region that leads names the leukodystrophy: parieto-occipital adrenoleukodystrophy, frontal Alexander, periventricular sparing U-fibers metachromatic
Stroke-like lesions that ignore arterial territories and migrate over time are MELAS
Maternal inheritance with deafness, diabetes, short stature and myopathy means mitochondrial disease
Several leukodystrophies are now treatable early: recognize the pattern before the deficit is fixed

imaging.normalAppearance: MRI with T2, FLAIR, DWI, contrast and spectroscopy characterizes the white-matter pattern and the mitochondrial lesions; the myelination timetable is the reference in children; serial imaging shows progression or migration.

pathology.finding: Symmetric parieto-occipital white-matter T2 hyperintensity spreading through the splenium with a thin enhancing leading edge; Loes score tracks progression.
Confluent periventricular and deep white-matter T2 hyperintensity sparing the U-fibers with radiating stripes (tigroid pattern) and later cerebellar and callosal involvement.
Cortical and subcortical T2/DWI hyperintensity in the parieto-occipital or temporal lobe that crosses arterial boundaries, with elevated lactate on spectroscopy and migration on follow-up.
Symmetric T2 hyperintensity of the putamen, caudate, thalamus, periaqueductal gray and brainstem tegmentum in an infant with regression and lactic acidosis.
Confluent white-matter hyperintensity with characteristic anterior temporal pole and external capsule involvement, lacunes and microbleeds in a young adult with migraine and strokes.

pearls: Check adrenal function in every boy with parieto-occipital white-matter disease and behavioral change
Valproate can kill a patient with a POLG mutation; ask about family history before prescribing it in unexplained epilepsy
A raised CSF lactate in a child with regression points to the mitochondria
pitfalls: Age-related white-matter hyperintensities and multiple sclerosis are asymmetric; do not call a symmetric confluent pattern vascular
A migrating cortical lesion with a normal angiogram in a young diabetic with deafness is MELAS, not vasculitis

topic-localization-approach-exam.name: Localization: the neurological examination as a map
topic-localization-approach-exam.summary: Neurological diagnosis answers two questions in order, where is the lesion and what is it, and the first is answered by the examination read against the anatomy: the level (cortex, subcortical white matter, basal ganglia, thalamus, brainstem, cerebellum, spinal cord, root, plexus, nerve, junction, muscle), the side (crossed or uncrossed pathways), and the number of lesions (one, multiple or diffuse). Each examination component tests a system whose anatomy this atlas shows, and combinations of findings that can only be explained by one site are the strongest evidence; the pattern of onset (sudden, stepwise, progressive, relapsing) then narrows the pathology. This entry summarizes the logic that the syndrome entries apply case by case.

sections.heading: Level: which floor of the building
sections.body: Cortical lesions add cortical signs (aphasia, neglect, apraxia, agnosia, field defects, seizures, cortical sensory loss) and produce weakness that favors one body part (face and arm or leg); subcortical capsular lesions produce equal face-arm-leg weakness without cortical signs; basal ganglia lesions produce movement disorders rather than weakness; thalamic lesions produce hemisensory loss of all modalities including the face; brainstem lesions produce crossed signs (a cranial nerve on one side with long-tract signs on the other), vertigo, diplopia and dysarthria; cerebellar lesions produce ipsilateral ataxia without weakness; cord lesions produce a sensory level, bilateral signs below the lesion, sphincter change and dissociated sensory loss; and peripheral lesions produce lower motor neuron signs in the distribution of a root, plexus, nerve or a length-dependent pattern with sensory loss. The upper versus lower motor neuron distinction (tone, reflexes, plantar responses, wasting, fasciculation) is the first branch of the tree.

sections.heading: Side: the crossings
sections.body: The corticospinal tract crosses at the pyramidal decussation, the dorsal column pathway in the lower medulla, the spinothalamic tract within the cord one or two segments above entry, the trigeminal pathways in the pons and medulla, the optic pathway partially at the chiasm, the cerebellar outflow in the superior cerebellar peduncle (so cerebellar signs are ipsilateral), and the cranial nerve nuclei project to the same side; therefore weakness contralateral to a facial palsy that includes the forehead means a pontine lesion, pain loss on one side of the face and the other side of the body means a lateral medullary lesion, and weakness with proprioceptive loss on one side and pain loss on the other means a hemicord lesion. Gaze deviation toward the weak side means a pontine lesion, away from it a hemispheric one. Sensory levels for pin lie one or two segments below the lesion, and a Horner syndrome is ipsilateral to any lesion of the sympathetic pathway.

sections.heading: Number and time course
sections.body: A single lesion is sought first; when findings cannot be explained by one site (optic neuritis plus a cord level, or a facial palsy plus a foot drop), the process is multifocal (multiple sclerosis, vasculitis, metastases, emboli) or diffuse (encephalopathy, polyneuropathy, myopathy). The tempo names the pathology: seconds to minutes and maximal at onset is vascular (ischemia, hemorrhage) or a seizure; minutes to hours with spread is migraine or seizure; hours to days is inflammatory, infectious or toxic-metabolic; weeks to months is neoplastic or subacute degenerative; months to years is degenerative or genetic; and relapsing-remitting is demyelinating, vascular or paroxysmal. Age, risk factors and the systemic examination (fever, rash, lymphadenopathy, murmurs, skin stigmata) complete the differential before any test.

sections.heading: The examination as a system check
sections.body: Mental status tests the cortex and its networks (attention, language, memory, visuospatial, executive); the cranial nerves test the brainstem level by level (II and III midbrain, V-VIII pons, IX-XII medulla) and the special senses; the motor examination tests tone, power by segment, reflexes and the plantar response; the sensory examination tests the two ascending systems separately (pin and temperature for the spinothalamic, vibration and position for the dorsal columns) and the cortical modalities; coordination tests the cerebellum and its inputs; and gait integrates everything (hemiparetic, spastic, ataxic, parkinsonian, steppage, waddling, apraxic and functional gaits each have a site). A focused examination driven by the history takes ten minutes, and the atlas's syndrome entries show how each pattern is assembled from these findings.

keyPoints: Where before what: level, side and number, then tempo
Cortical signs place the lesion in the cortex; equal face-arm-leg weakness without them places it in the capsule
Crossed findings mean brainstem; a sensory level means cord; ipsilateral ataxia means cerebellum
Sudden and maximal at onset is vascular; progressive over weeks is a mass; relapsing is demyelination
If one lesion cannot explain everything, look for a multifocal or diffuse process

imaging.normalAppearance: Imaging is chosen by the localization: MRI with DWI for brain and brainstem, MRI of the appropriate spinal level for cord and root, CT for acute hemorrhage and bone, vascular imaging when the tempo is vascular, and electrophysiology for the peripheral levels.

pathology.finding: A small deep restricted-diffusion lesion in the posterior limb explains face-arm-leg weakness without cortical signs; a cortical lesion explains aphasia or neglect with partial weakness.
Paramedian or lateral brainstem lesion at the level named by the cranial nerve; DWI may lag the examination by a day.

pathology.pathology: Spinal cord lesion with a sensory level
pathology.finding: Intramedullary signal change or extrinsic compression at or above the clinical level, imaged with sagittal T2 and STIR of the whole cord when the level is uncertain.

pearls: Examine the gait first: it screens the whole nervous system in ten steps
The forehead decides the facial palsy, the pupil decides the third nerve, the plantar decides the motor neuron
Never let imaging replace the examination in the brainstem, where the first scan is often normal
pitfalls: Functional (non-organic) weakness is a diagnosis of positive signs (Hoover sign, give-way weakness, inconsistency), not of a normal scan

html.summary: Neurological diagnosis answers two questions in order, where is the lesion and what is it, and the first is answered by the examination read against the anatomy: the level (cortex, subcortical white matter, basal ganglia, thalamus, brainstem, cerebellum, spinal cord, root, plexus, nerve, junction, muscle), the side (crossed or uncrossed pathways), and the number of lesions (one, multiple or diffuse). Each examination component tests a system whose anatomy this atlas shows, and combinations of findings that can only be explained by one site are the strongest evidence; the pattern of onset (sudden, stepwise, progressive, relapsing) then narrows the pathology. This entry summarizes the logic that the syndrome entries apply case by case.

topic-movement-disorder-circuits.name: Movement disorders and the basal ganglia circuits
topic-movement-disorder-circuits.summary: Movement disorders are disorders of the basal ganglia and cerebellar circuits rather than of the corticospinal tract, so they produce too little movement (parkinsonism) or too much (tremor, chorea, ballism, dystonia, myoclonus, tics) without weakness. The basal ganglia loops from cortex through striatum, pallidum, subthalamic nucleus and substantia nigra to the thalamus and back select and scale movement under dopaminergic control; their pathology maps onto the phenomenology, nigral dopamine loss to parkinsonism, striatal degeneration to chorea, subthalamic damage to ballism, pallidal and striatal dysfunction to dystonia, and the cerebellothalamic outflow to action tremor. This entry ties the phenomenology to the circuits and to the treatments that act on them.

sections.heading: The loops and their pharmacology
sections.body: The motor loop runs from the sensorimotor cortex to the putamen, where medium spiny neurons of the direct pathway (D1 receptors) inhibit the internal pallidum and substantia nigra pars reticulata to release movement, and neurons of the indirect pathway (D2 receptors) inhibit the external pallidum, disinhibiting the subthalamic nucleus, which excites the output nuclei to suppress competing movements; dopamine from the pars compacta facilitates the direct and inhibits the indirect pathway, so its loss tilts the balance toward inhibition and akinesia, and its excess or receptor supersensitivity toward involuntary movement. Parallel oculomotor, associative and limbic loops explain the saccadic, cognitive and psychiatric features of basal ganglia disease. Acetylcholine from striatal interneurons opposes dopamine (the basis of anticholinergic treatment of tremor), glutamate from the subthalamic nucleus drives the output nuclei (the target of subthalamic stimulation), and GABA is the transmitter of every projection neuron in the loop.

sections.heading: Hypokinetic disorders
sections.body: Parkinson disease is asymmetric bradykinesia with rest tremor and rigidity, beginning after alpha-synuclein has spread from the olfactory bulb and the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus (hyposmia, constipation, REM sleep behavior disorder) to the substantia nigra, and later to the cortex (dementia); levodopa restores striatal dopamine, dopamine agonists act on the receptors, and subthalamic or pallidal stimulation corrects the abnormal output when fluctuations and dyskinesias appear. Atypical parkinsonism is symmetric and levodopa-resistant: progressive supranuclear palsy adds early falls, vertical gaze palsy and midbrain atrophy; multiple system atrophy adds autonomic failure and cerebellar signs with pontine and putaminal change; corticobasal syndrome adds asymmetric apraxia, dystonia and alien limb with parietal atrophy; and dementia with Lewy bodies puts cognition first. Drug-induced parkinsonism from dopamine antagonists, vascular parkinsonism of the legs from small vessel disease, and normal-pressure hydrocephalus are the mimics with a normal dopamine transporter scan.

sections.heading: Hyperkinetic disorders
sections.body: Tremor is classified by when it occurs: rest tremor is nigrostriatal (parkinsonism), postural and kinetic tremor of the hands and head is essential tremor arising in the cerebellothalamic circuit and treated with propranolol, primidone or thalamic stimulation, and intention tremor is cerebellar. Chorea is a random flowing movement from striatal indirect-pathway loss (Huntington disease with caudate atrophy, Sydenham chorea, levodopa dyskinesia, tardive dyskinesia); hemiballism is violent proximal flinging from a contralateral subthalamic lesion; dystonia is sustained co-contraction producing twisting postures, generalized in genetic childhood forms (DYT1), focal in adults (cervical dystonia, blepharospasm, writer's cramp) and treated with botulinum toxin or pallidal stimulation; myoclonus is a brief shock-like jerk of cortical, subcortical, brainstem or spinal origin (post-anoxic, metabolic, epileptic, prion); tics are suppressible stereotyped movements and sounds of Tourette syndrome, a disorder of the limbic and motor loops. Wilson disease (copper, Kayser-Fleischer rings, liver disease) can produce any of these in the young and is treatable.

sections.heading: Examination and localization of movement disorders
sections.body: Observe at rest, on posture and on action; look for slowness with decrement on finger tapping (bradykinesia), lead-pipe or cogwheel rigidity, and asymmetry (Parkinson disease); test vertical saccades and the pull test (progressive supranuclear palsy); check orthostatic pressure (multiple system atrophy); look at the eyes for Kayser-Fleischer rings and the tongue for chorea; test praxis and cortical sensation (corticobasal syndrome); and ask about drugs, family history and psychiatric symptoms. The site follows the phenomenology: unilateral chorea or ballism is a contralateral striatal or subthalamic lesion; hemidystonia is a contralateral striatal, pallidal or thalamic lesion; unilateral action tremor is an ipsilateral cerebellar or contralateral thalamic-midbrain lesion (Holmes tremor); and bilateral, symmetric disorders are degenerative, metabolic or drug-induced. Imaging shows the caudate atrophy of Huntington disease, the hummingbird midbrain of progressive supranuclear palsy, the hot-cross-bun pons of multiple system atrophy, the eye-of-the-tiger pallidum of iron disease and the symmetric basal ganglia change of Wilson disease.

keyPoints: Too little movement is nigral dopamine loss; too much is striatal, subthalamic or pallidal disinhibition; weakness is neither
Asymmetric onset with rest tremor and a levodopa response is Parkinson disease; symmetric, falls, gaze palsy or autonomic failure means an atypical syndrome
Hemiballism is a contralateral subthalamic lesion; hemichorea and hemidystonia are contralateral striatal or pallidal lesions
Essential tremor is a cerebellothalamic disorder and the ventral intermediate thalamus is its surgical target
Any movement disorder under 40 with liver disease is Wilson disease until the copper is measured

imaging.normalAppearance: Structural MRI is normal in Parkinson disease and essential tremor and is used to find mimics and atypical patterns; dopamine transporter SPECT confirms nigrostriatal loss; SWI and neuromelanin imaging show nigral change; copper studies and slit-lamp examination find Wilson disease.

pathology.finding: Caudate head atrophy with boxcar frontal horns and putaminal atrophy; frontal atrophy later.
Midbrain atrophy with a concave upper border (hummingbird sign on sagittal images, Mickey Mouse on axial) and a low midbrain-to-pons ratio.
Pontine and cerebellar atrophy with the hot-cross-bun sign (MSA-C) or putaminal atrophy with a lateral hyperintense rim (MSA-P).
Symmetric T2 hyperintensity of the putamen, caudate, thalamus and midbrain (face of the giant panda) with Kayser-Fleischer rings on slit lamp.
Asymmetric loss of putaminal uptake (comma to dot) with preserved caudate early; normal in essential tremor and drug-induced parkinsonism.

pearls: Watch the patient walk into the room: arm swing, stride and turning make the diagnosis before the handshake
Dopamine blockers cause parkinsonism, akathisia, dystonia and tardive dyskinesia: read the drug list first
REM sleep behavior disorder, hyposmia and constipation precede the tremor by years
pitfalls: Bradykinesia is slowness with decrement, not simple slowness; without decrement, think of depression, hypothyroidism or vascular slowing
