topic-nerve-injury-regeneration.name: Peripheral nerve injury, degeneration and regeneration
topic-nerve-injury-regeneration.summary: A peripheral nerve is a bundle of axons with their Schwann cell sheaths, organized into fascicles by the perineurium and held in the epineurium, and its response to injury follows fixed rules: distal to a cut the axon and its myelin degenerate over days (Wallerian degeneration) while the Schwann cells survive, proliferate and form tubes that guide regenerating sprouts from the proximal stump at about a millimeter a day; the cell body swells and turns its metabolism to growth (chromatolysis); and recovery depends on whether the connective tissue tubes remain intact. The classification of injuries into neurapraxia, axonotmesis and neurotmesis predicts recovery, the electrophysiology dates the injury, and the same rules explain why the central nervous system, whose oligodendrocytes and glial scar block regrowth, does not recover in the same way.

sections.heading: Structure of the nerve and types of injury
sections.body: Myelinated axons, wrapped by one Schwann cell per internode with nodes of Ranvier for saltatory conduction, carry motor, large sensory and some autonomic signals, whereas unmyelinated axons in Remak bundles carry pain, temperature and postganglionic autonomic signals; fascicles are separated by the perineurium, which is the blood-nerve barrier, and the epineurium carries the vasa nervorum. Neurapraxia is a conduction block from focal demyelination or ischemia without axonal loss (the Saturday night radial palsy, a tourniquet palsy), recovering over days to weeks; axonotmesis is axonal interruption with intact connective tissue (traction, crush), recovering by regeneration along the preserved tubes at about one millimeter a day; neurotmesis is complete transection with loss of the tubes, in which regeneration fails or produces a neuroma unless the nerve is repaired. Compression at entrapment sites produces first demyelination and then axonal loss, and ischemia from vasculitis produces infarction of nerve segments.

sections.heading: Degeneration and the cell body response
sections.body: Within days of axonal interruption the distal segment fragments and its myelin is cleared by Schwann cells and macrophages, so the distal nerve stops conducting after about a week (the reason a nerve conduction study is normal in the first days after a transection and must be repeated); the muscle it supplied atrophies, develops fibrillations and positive sharp waves on EMG after two to three weeks and loses its motor end plates over months. The neuron reacts by chromatolysis, swelling with dispersal of Nissl substance and displacement of the nucleus, switching from transmission to regeneration; neurons whose axons are cut close to the cell body may die. In the central nervous system the same degeneration occurs (Wallerian degeneration of the corticospinal tract is visible on MRI after a capsular stroke), but oligodendrocytes do not support regrowth, myelin debris and the astrocytic scar inhibit it, and functional recovery depends on plasticity and sprouting of surviving connections rather than regeneration.

sections.heading: Regeneration, reinnervation and their errors
sections.body: Sprouts from the proximal stump enter the Schwann cell tubes (bands of Bungner), which express growth-promoting molecules, and grow at one to three millimeters a day, so the time to recovery is estimated from the distance to the muscle; the advancing front can be followed by Tinel sign (tingling on percussion over the regenerating axons) and by the sequence of muscle recovery from proximal to distal. Reinnervation restores function only if axons reach the right targets: misdirection after facial nerve injury produces synkinesis (eye closure with smiling) and crocodile tears, and after limb nerve injury produces co-contraction and poor sensory localization. Surviving motor neurons also sprout collaterals to adopt denervated muscle fibers, producing the large motor units of chronic denervation on EMG and the giant motor units of old poliomyelitis. Regeneration slows with age and distance, and muscle that stays denervated for more than a year or two cannot be recovered, which sets the timing of nerve repair and transfer surgery.

sections.heading: Clinical and electrophysiological assessment
sections.body: The examination localizes the lesion by the pattern of motor and sensory loss and by Tinel sign; nerve conduction studies after a week distinguish conduction block (preserved distal response, absent proximal-to-distal conduction) from axonal loss (reduced or absent distal response), and EMG after three weeks shows denervation and, months later, reinnervation; MRI neurography and ultrasound show the site of entrapment, transection or neuroma. Management follows the injury type: observation and splinting for neurapraxia, serial examination with EMG for axonotmesis, and exploration with repair or grafting within weeks for neurotmesis, with nerve transfers when the distance to the muscle is too great. Entrapment neuropathies are relieved by decompression before axonal loss is severe. The same biology underlies the neuropathies: demyelinating ones (Guillain-Barre, CIDP) block conduction and recover quickly, whereas axonal ones (diabetes, vasculitis, toxins) recover slowly by regeneration and sprouting.

keyPoints: Neurapraxia conducts distally and recovers in weeks; axonotmesis regenerates at a millimeter a day; neurotmesis needs a surgeon
Nerve conduction studies are normal in the first days after a transection: repeat them after a week, and EMG after three
Tinel sign marks the front of regeneration; count the millimeters to the muscle
Misdirected regeneration produces synkinesis and crocodile tears after facial nerve injury
The central nervous system degenerates the same way but does not regenerate: plasticity, not regrowth, is its recovery

imaging.normalAppearance: Ultrasound and MR neurography show nerve caliber, fascicular architecture, entrapment, neuroma and transection; MRI of muscle shows denervation edema early and fatty atrophy late; electrophysiology remains the main measure of injury type and recovery.

pathology.finding: Focal enlargement and loss of fascicular pattern of the nerve proximal to the compression site (carpal tunnel, cubital tunnel, fibular neck), with flattening under the retinaculum.
Discontinuity of the nerve with a bulbous enhancing stump neuroma on MR neurography; distal muscle denervation edema on STIR.
Diffuse STIR hyperintensity of the muscles in the nerve's territory within weeks of injury, replaced by fatty atrophy on T1 after months.

pathology.pathology: Wallerian degeneration of the corticospinal tract
pathology.finding: T2 hyperintensity and atrophy of the ipsilateral cerebral peduncle and pyramid months after a capsular infarct.

pearls: Do not tell a patient with a transected nerve to wait and see: the tubes close and the muscle dies within two years
A normal distal nerve response in a paralyzed limb one week after injury is good news: the axons are intact
Fibrillations on EMG are the muscle's complaint that its nerve is gone
pitfalls: Early nerve conduction studies underestimate axonal injury; the distal response persists for a week after transection

topic-neural-development-malformations.name: Neural development and malformations
topic-neural-development-malformations.summary: The nervous system forms from the neural plate by neurulation, segmentation of the neural tube into the primary and secondary brain vesicles, proliferation of neurons in the ventricular zone, radial migration to build the cortex, and the late events of synapse formation and myelination that continue into adult life. Each step has a characteristic failure: a defect of closure gives spina bifida or anencephaly, a defect of prosencephalic cleavage gives holoprosencephaly, a defect of proliferation gives microcephaly, a defect of migration gives lissencephaly, heterotopia and polymicrogyria, and a defect of the posterior fossa gives Chiari and Dandy-Walker malformations. Knowing the timetable turns a malformation into a date of injury.

sections.heading: Neurulation and the neural tube
sections.body: The neural plate folds during the third and fourth weeks and closes first in the cervical region, then zips toward the anterior neuropore (closing around day 25) and the posterior neuropore (day 27). Failure at the anterior end produces anencephaly and encephalocele; failure at the posterior end produces the spectrum of spina bifida from occulta to myelomeningocele, in which the open cord is exposed on the back and almost always accompanied by a Chiari II malformation and hydrocephalus. Folate before conception reduces the risk, and maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein and second-trimester ultrasound detect the open defects. The neural crest, which separates from the closing tube, gives rise to the dorsal root and autonomic ganglia, Schwann cells, the adrenal medulla and the meninges of the cord, so crest disorders combine peripheral nerve, pigment and craniofacial findings.

sections.heading: Vesicles, flexures and the ventricular system
sections.body: The rostral tube expands into the prosencephalon, mesencephalon and rhombencephalon, then into the telencephalon and diencephalon, the midbrain, and the metencephalon (pons and cerebellum) and myelencephalon (medulla); the lumen of the tube becomes the ventricles and the aqueduct, and the flexures bend the axis so that the cerebral hemispheres come to lie above the brainstem. Failure of the prosencephalon to divide into two hemispheres is holoprosencephaly, ranging from a single ventricle with cyclopia to a mild form with only a missing septum pellucidum and midline facial change, associated with sonic hedgehog pathway defects and trisomy 13. Aqueductal stenosis, from malformation or infection, is the commonest cause of congenital hydrocephalus.

sections.heading: Proliferation and migration of cortical neurons
sections.body: Neurons are born in the ventricular and subventricular zones between the seventh and sixteenth weeks and migrate along radial glia to the cortical plate, the later-born neurons passing the earlier ones to form the six layers inside-out; interneurons arrive tangentially from the ganglionic eminences. Reduced proliferation yields microcephaly (genetic, or from congenital infection, alcohol or radiation); arrested migration yields lissencephaly with a thick, smooth four-layered cortex (LIS1, DCX), band and periventricular nodular heterotopia in which neurons stop in the white matter or beside the ventricle (FLNA), and abnormal late organization yields polymicrogyria and focal cortical dysplasia, the commonest structural causes of childhood epilepsy. The timing of the insult, not its nature, decides the pattern.

sections.heading: Posterior fossa, spinal cord and myelination
sections.body: The cerebellum forms from the rhombic lips of the metencephalon and the vermis fuses in the midline late in the first trimester; failure gives the Dandy-Walker malformation with a cystic fourth ventricle and vermian hypoplasia, and a small posterior fossa crowds the tonsils downward as the Chiari malformations. The spinal cord ends at the level of the third lumbar vertebra at birth and rises to L1-L2 by adulthood because the vertebral column grows faster; failure of the filum to lengthen tethers the cord and produces progressive leg and bladder symptoms in childhood. Myelination proceeds from the brainstem outward and from sensory to motor systems, finishing in the frontal association areas in the third decade, which is why an infant's Babinski sign is normal and why white-matter diseases of childhood are staged by the myelination that should have occurred.

keyPoints: Neural tube closure fails in the fourth week: anencephaly at the front, spina bifida at the back, both reduced by preconception folate
The pattern of a malformation dates the insult: proliferation (microcephaly) before migration (lissencephaly, heterotopia) before organization (polymicrogyria)
Holoprosencephaly is a failure of midline cleavage and is often paired with midline facial defects
Chiari II accompanies myelomeningocele; Chiari I is an adult finding with a small posterior fossa
Tethered cord presents with growth: leg weakness, foot deformity and bladder symptoms appear as the child lengthens

imaging.normalAppearance: Fetal and neonatal ultrasound and MRI stage the malformation; in children and adults T1 and T2 volumetric MRI show gyral pattern, cortical thickness, gray matter in the wrong place (heterotopia) and posterior fossa anatomy.

pathology.finding: Smooth cortex with few shallow sulci, thick cortical band and a figure-of-eight hemispheric shape; band heterotopia shows a second layer of gray matter beneath a thin cortex.
Nodules isointense to gray matter lining the lateral ventricles, often bilateral, in a patient with seizures beginning in adolescence.
Small posterior fossa with the vermis and medulla displaced below the foramen magnum, tectal beaking, hydrocephalus and a lumbosacral spinal defect.
Cystic dilatation of the fourth ventricle with hypoplasia and upward rotation of the vermis and an enlarged posterior fossa.

pearls: A newborn with an open back has a brain problem too: hydrocephalus and Chiari II are part of the package
Migration disorders are epilepsy disorders; look for them on the MRI of every child with refractory seizures
The cord ends at L1-L2 in the adult and L3 in the newborn: choose the puncture level accordingly
pitfalls: Gray matter in the white matter on MRI is heterotopia, not tumor; it follows gray matter signal on every sequence and does not enhance

html.summary: The nervous system forms from the neural plate by neurulation, segmentation of the neural tube into the primary and secondary brain vesicles, proliferation of neurons in the ventricular zone, radial migration to build the cortex, and the late events of synapse formation and myelination that continue into adult life. Each step has a characteristic failure: a defect of closure gives spina bifida or anencephaly, a defect of prosencephalic cleavage gives holoprosencephaly, a defect of proliferation gives microcephaly, a defect of migration gives lissencephaly, heterotopia and polymicrogyria, and a defect of the posterior fossa gives Chiari and Dandy-Walker malformations. Knowing the timetable turns a malformation into a date of injury.

topic-neuroimaging-basics.name: Neuroimaging basics: reading CT and MRI against the atlas
topic-neuroimaging-basics.summary: Computed tomography maps X-ray attenuation, so bone and acute blood are bright and edema, infarction and air are dark, and it answers the emergency questions of hemorrhage, mass effect, hydrocephalus and fracture in minutes; magnetic resonance imaging maps proton signal under different weightings, so it separates gray from white matter, shows edema and demyelination on T2 and FLAIR, restricted diffusion in acute infarction and abscess on DWI, blood products on gradient and susceptibility images, and barrier breakdown after gadolinium. Each sequence is a question, and the atlas's MRI slices, which use the T1 and T2 templates, are the normal against which every abnormal study is compared; the arterial and venous meshes give the vascular map for CT and MR angiography.

sections.heading: CT: density and the acute questions
sections.body: Hyperdensity means blood (acute hemorrhage, a thrombosed vessel, a hyperdense MCA sign), calcification, dense tumor or contrast; hypodensity means edema, infarction older than a few hours, old blood, fat or air. The early signs of ischemic stroke are subtle: loss of the insular ribbon, obscuration of the lentiform nucleus and effacement of sulci, graded by the ASPECTS score; a hemorrhage is obvious and its site (putamen, thalamus, pons, cerebellum for hypertension; lobar for amyloid angiopathy and malformations; basal cisterns for aneurysmal subarachnoid) names its cause. Mass effect shows as sulcal effacement, ventricular compression, midline shift and cisternal effacement in that order, and the temporal horns round early in hydrocephalus. CT angiography shows occlusions, aneurysms and dissections; CT perfusion separates the infarct core from the penumbra. CT is the test for trauma, for the first hours of stroke and for patients who cannot have MRI.

sections.heading: MRI: sequences as questions
sections.body: T1 shows anatomy with white matter bright and CSF dark, and fat, subacute blood, melanin, protein and gadolinium bright; T2 shows CSF and edema bright; FLAIR suppresses CSF so that periventricular and cortical lesions, subarachnoid blood and meningeal disease stand out; DWI with the ADC map shows restricted diffusion in acute infarction (bright DWI, dark ADC, for about ten days), abscess pus, dense tumors such as lymphoma and medulloblastoma, prion disease and status epilepticus; SWI and gradient echo show hemosiderin, microbleeds, cavernomas, calcification and venous structures; STIR suppresses fat for the spine and orbits; and gadolinium enhancement marks barrier breakdown in tumor, infection, inflammation, subacute infarction and demyelination. MRA and MRV image the arteries and veins without contrast. Contraindications are ferromagnetic implants and some devices; gadolinium is avoided in severe renal failure.

sections.heading: Patterns that localize the pathology
sections.body: An arterial infarct respects a territory and has a wedge shape; a venous infarct crosses territories, is often hemorrhagic and lies near a thrombosed sinus; a watershed infarct is linear along a border zone. Demyelination produces ovoid periventricular lesions perpendicular to the ventricles, juxtacortical, callosal, brainstem and cord lesions, some enhancing; small vessel disease produces patchy deep and periventricular hyperintensities with lacunes and microbleeds. Ring enhancement with central restricted diffusion is an abscess; ring enhancement without it is a necrotic tumor or, with a thin rim, a demyelinating lesion; multiple enhancing lesions at the gray-white junction are metastases; a dural-based enhancing mass with a tail is a meningioma; and leptomeningeal enhancement is infection, carcinomatosis or sarcoidosis. Symmetric deep gray matter signal change points to toxic, metabolic, hypoxic or prion disease; symmetric white-matter disease points to a leukodystrophy or toxic leukoencephalopathy.

sections.heading: The spine, the vessels and the pitfalls
sections.body: Spinal MRI uses sagittal T2 and STIR to find cord signal change, compression and the level, axial images to define foraminal and canal stenosis, and contrast for tumor, infection and inflammation; CT shows bone. Vascular imaging (CTA, MRA, DSA) is read against the atlas arteries: the site of an occlusion predicts the infarct, the branch point predicts the aneurysm, and the tapered stenosis with intramural hematoma is the dissection. Pitfalls include the normal bright posterior limb on FLAIR, ependymitis granularis at the frontal horns, the incompletely myelinated white matter of infants, the prominent flocculus and choroid plexus that mimic masses, flow artifacts in the sinuses that mimic thrombosis, and the age-related white-matter hyperintensities that are not multiple sclerosis; and every study must be read with the clinical localization in hand, because an incidental finding will otherwise become the diagnosis.

keyPoints: CT for blood, bone and the first hour; MRI for everything else
DWI is the sequence of the acute stroke and the abscess; FLAIR of demyelination and the periventricular lesion; SWI of blood and calcium; gadolinium of the open barrier
Arterial infarcts respect territories; venous infarcts, tumors and infections do not
Ring enhancement with restricted diffusion in the center is an abscess; with a thin, open ring it is demyelination
Read the scan after the examination, not instead of it

imaging.normalAppearance: The atlas MRI slices are the MNI T1 and T2 templates at 1 mm; the T1 shows white matter bright and the T2 shows CSF bright, and the label overlays name every structure at the cursor.

pathology.finding: Bright on DWI with dark ADC within minutes, FLAIR-bright after 4-6 hours, T2-bright by 24 hours; enhancement in the subacute phase; encephalomalacia later.
Hyperdense mass with surrounding hypodense edema; on MRI the signal evolves with the blood products (hyperacute T2-bright, acute T2-dark, subacute T1-bright, chronic hemosiderin rim).
Ring-enhancing lesion with central restricted diffusion and a smooth thin capsule that is T2-dark; the ring is thinner toward the ventricle.
Ovoid periventricular, juxtacortical, infratentorial and spinal cord lesions on FLAIR and T2; some enhance; central veins on SWI.
Irregular ring-enhancing mass with central necrosis, surrounding FLAIR infiltration and elevated perfusion; no central restricted diffusion.

pearls: Compare every lesion with the atlas slice at the same coordinates: the normal is the best contrast agent
A normal early DWI does not exclude a small brainstem or lacunar infarct; repeat it
Symmetry on MRI means metabolic, toxic, hypoxic or genetic; asymmetry means vascular, neoplastic or inflammatory
pitfalls: The scan cannot tell you which lesion is symptomatic; the examination does
Contrast enhancement in a subacute infarct mimics a tumor; the clinical time course and the vascular territory decide

topic-neuromuscular-patterns.name: Neuromuscular patterns: nerve, root, plexus, junction and muscle
topic-neuromuscular-patterns.summary: Weakness with a normal brain and cord comes from one of five levels, the anterior horn cell, the root or plexus, the peripheral nerve, the neuromuscular junction and the muscle, and each level has a signature in the distribution of weakness, the presence or absence of sensory loss, the reflexes, the pattern of wasting and fasciculation, the fatigability and the electrophysiology. Motor neuron disease combines lower motor neuron signs with upper motor neuron signs and spares sensation; neuropathy is length-dependent and sensory; radiculopathy follows a root and its reflex; junction disease fluctuates and spares reflexes and sensation; and myopathy is proximal, symmetric and painless with normal sensation. Nerve conduction studies and electromyography then confirm the level and separate axonal from demyelinating disease.

sections.heading: Anterior horn cell and root
sections.body: Motor neuron disease produces asymmetric wasting, fasciculation and weakness beginning in one limb or the bulbar muscles, with brisk reflexes in wasted muscles and extensor plantars from the accompanying upper motor neuron degeneration, and no sensory loss; a split hand with wasting of the thenar side, a brisk jaw jerk and a wasted fasciculating tongue are characteristic, and EMG shows widespread denervation and reinnervation in three regions. Radiculopathy produces pain radiating along a dermatome, weakness in a myotome that crosses several nerves (C7 weakens triceps, wrist flexors and finger extensors), sensory loss in the dermatome and loss of the corresponding reflex (C5-6 biceps and brachioradialis, C7 triceps, L3-4 knee, S1 ankle); the sensory nerve action potential is normal because the lesion is proximal to the dorsal root ganglion, the finding that separates a root from a plexus lesion.

sections.heading: Plexus and peripheral nerve
sections.body: Plexopathy produces weakness and sensory loss in the territory of several nerves and several roots at once (the upper trunk: C5-6 muscles of the shoulder and elbow flexion; the lower trunk: intrinsic hand muscles and the medial forearm), with reduced sensory potentials because the lesion is distal to the ganglion; trauma, tumor infiltration, radiation and the inflammatory neuralgic amyotrophy are the causes. Mononeuropathies follow one nerve's territory and are usually entrapments at known sites (median at the carpal tunnel, ulnar at the elbow, radial at the spiral groove, peroneal at the fibular neck), and mononeuritis multiplex from vasculitis picks off nerves one by one. Polyneuropathy is length-dependent and symmetric, beginning in the feet with sensory loss, absent ankle jerks and later weakness; axonal neuropathies (diabetes, alcohol, drugs) reduce amplitudes, whereas demyelinating neuropathies (Guillain-Barre, CIDP, hereditary) slow conduction and block it, and a rapidly ascending paralysis with areflexia is Guillain-Barre until proved otherwise.

sections.heading: Neuromuscular junction and muscle
sections.body: Myasthenia gravis produces fatigable weakness of the eyelids, extraocular muscles, face, bulbar muscles and proximal limbs that worsens through the day and with exercise and improves with rest, with normal reflexes and sensation; acetylcholine receptor or MuSK antibodies, decrement on repetitive stimulation and jitter on single-fiber EMG confirm it, and a thymoma must be sought. Lambert-Eaton syndrome is the presynaptic mirror image: proximal weakness that improves briefly with exercise, absent reflexes that return after contraction, dry mouth and an underlying small cell lung cancer, with increment on high-frequency stimulation. Botulism descends from the cranial nerves with dilated pupils. Myopathies produce symmetric proximal weakness (difficulty rising from a chair, climbing stairs, lifting the arms) with preserved reflexes until late, normal sensation, sometimes myalgia, a raised creatine kinase and small polyphasic motor units on EMG; inflammatory, toxic (statins), endocrine, dystrophic and metabolic causes are separated by distribution, rash, family history and biopsy.

sections.heading: The examination and the electrophysiology
sections.body: The bedside sequence is: is the weakness upper or lower motor neuron; if lower, is there sensory loss (nerve, root, plexus) or not (anterior horn, junction, muscle); is the distribution distal and symmetric (polyneuropathy), proximal and symmetric (myopathy or junction), in one nerve or root, or multifocal; are reflexes lost early (neuropathy, Lambert-Eaton, Guillain-Barre) or preserved (myopathy, myasthenia, motor neuron disease early); and does it fatigue or fluctuate (junction). Nerve conduction studies separate axonal loss (small amplitudes) from demyelination (slow velocities, prolonged distal latencies and F waves, conduction block) and localize entrapments; EMG separates neurogenic (large, reduced-recruitment units with fibrillations) from myopathic (small, early-recruiting units) patterns and finds subclinical denervation in motor neuron disease. Creatine kinase, antibody panels, genetic testing, nerve or muscle biopsy and imaging of the root or plexus complete the localization.

keyPoints: Sensory loss excludes anterior horn cell, junction and muscle; its absence with lower motor neuron signs points to them
A normal sensory nerve action potential in a numb dermatome means the lesion is at the root, proximal to the ganglion
Fatigable ptosis and diplopia with normal reflexes is myasthenia; proximal weakness that improves with exercise and returns reflexes is Lambert-Eaton
Length-dependent symmetric sensory loss with absent ankle jerks is polyneuropathy; asymmetric wasting with brisk reflexes is motor neuron disease
Proximal, symmetric, painless weakness with normal sensation and a raised creatine kinase is muscle

imaging.normalAppearance: Imaging is reserved for the root and plexus: MRI of the spine for radiculopathy, MR neurography or ultrasound of the plexus and entrapment sites, chest CT for thymoma and lung cancer, and muscle MRI for the pattern of edema and fatty replacement in myopathy; the main tests are electrophysiological.

pathology.finding: Disc protrusion or foraminal stenosis compressing the root at the level predicted by the dermatome and reflex; asymptomatic degenerative change is common, so the clinical level rules.
Thickening and T2 hyperintensity of the trunks or cords with enhancement in inflammatory or infiltrative disease; ultrasound shows hourglass constrictions in neuralgic amyotrophy.
Symmetric muscle edema on STIR in the thighs with fatty replacement in chronic disease; guides the biopsy site.
Anterior mediastinal mass on chest CT in a patient with acetylcholine receptor antibodies.

pearls: Look at the tongue, the hands and the gait before touching the reflex hammer: fasciculation, split hand and foot drop tell the level
Ascending weakness with lost reflexes is Guillain-Barre: measure the vital capacity, not just the strength
Do not stop a statin without a creatine kinase, and do not blame the statin without one
pitfalls: Myasthenia has normal reflexes and no wasting; a wasted hand with brisk reflexes is motor neuron disease, however fatigable the patient feels

topic-neurotransmitter-systems.name: Neurotransmitter systems
topic-neurotransmitter-systems.summary: The brain uses a small number of transmitters in two organizations: the point-to-point synapses of glutamate (excitatory) and GABA and glycine (inhibitory) that carry the signals of every pathway in this atlas, and the diffuse modulatory systems of dopamine, noradrenaline, serotonin, acetylcholine and histamine that arise from small brainstem and basal forebrain nuclei and set the state of the whole brain. Peptides, purines and endocannabinoids modulate both. Clinical neurology is largely the pharmacology of these systems: parkinsonism is dopamine loss, myasthenia is a cholinergic synapse under attack, epilepsy is an excess of glutamate over GABA, anticholinergic delirium and serotonin syndrome are drug effects on the modulatory nuclei, and antidepressants, antipsychotics, anesthetics and antiepileptics are all transmitter drugs.

sections.heading: Fast transmission: glutamate, GABA and glycine
sections.body: Glutamate is the transmitter of the corticospinal tract, the thalamocortical and corticocortical projections, the sensory afferents and the cerebellar mossy and climbing fibers; it acts through AMPA receptors for fast depolarization and NMDA receptors that require depolarization and glutamate together and let calcium in, the coincidence detector of synaptic plasticity and the mediator of excitotoxic death in stroke, status epilepticus and hypoglycemia. GABA is released by cortical interneurons, striatal and pallidal projection neurons, Purkinje cells and the reticular thalamic nucleus, opening chloride channels (GABA-A, the site of benzodiazepines, barbiturates and most anesthetics) or potassium channels (GABA-B, the site of baclofen). Glycine is the inhibitory transmitter of the spinal cord and brainstem; its blockade by strychnine or tetanus toxin and its receptor mutations in hyperekplexia produce rigidity and exaggerated startle. Seizures are a failure of the balance between these systems.

sections.heading: Dopamine and noradrenaline
sections.body: Dopamine neurons of the substantia nigra pars compacta project to the striatum (nigrostriatal), and those of the ventral tegmental area to the accumbens, amygdala and prefrontal cortex (mesolimbic and mesocortical); the tuberoinfundibular neurons of the hypothalamus inhibit prolactin. Loss of the nigrostriatal system produces parkinsonism, excess mesolimbic activity produces psychosis and addiction, and dopamine antagonists produce parkinsonism, dystonia, akathisia, tardive dyskinesia and hyperprolactinemia, while agonists produce hallucinations and impulse control disorders. Noradrenaline arises almost entirely from the locus coeruleus and drives arousal, attention, the stress response and the descending inhibition of pain; its loss contributes to the sleep and autonomic symptoms of Parkinson disease, and drugs that raise it (stimulants, some antidepressants) improve attention and raise blood pressure. Peripheral noradrenaline is the sympathetic transmitter, and dopamine-beta-hydroxylase deficiency abolishes it.

sections.heading: Serotonin, acetylcholine and histamine
sections.body: Serotonin from the raphe nuclei modulates mood, anxiety, appetite, sleep, pain and the trigeminovascular system, which is why triptans and reuptake inhibitors act where they do and why combining serotonergic drugs produces the clonus, hyperthermia and agitation of serotonin syndrome. Acetylcholine is the transmitter of motor neurons at the neuromuscular junction (nicotinic receptors, the target of myasthenia antibodies, curare and botulinum toxin), of all preganglionic and parasympathetic postganglionic autonomic neurons (nicotinic and muscarinic), of the basal forebrain projection to the cortex and hippocampus that sustains attention and memory (lost in Alzheimer and Lewy body disease), and of the pedunculopontine and striatal interneuron systems; anticholinergic drugs cause delirium, and cholinesterase inhibitors treat both myasthenia and dementia. Histamine from the tuberomammillary nucleus promotes wakefulness, the reason sedating antihistamines sedate.

sections.heading: Transmitter disorders at the bedside
sections.body: A transmitter system can be recognized by its clinical signature: excess dopamine gives psychosis and chorea, deficiency gives parkinsonism; excess cholinergic activity gives salivation, lacrimation, urination, diarrhea, bronchospasm and fasciculations (organophosphates), deficiency gives dry mouth, dilated pupils, urinary retention and delirium; excess serotonin gives clonus and hyperthermia; loss of GABA gives seizures and the withdrawal syndrome of alcohol and benzodiazepines; and NMDA receptor antibodies give psychosis, seizures, dyskinesia and autonomic instability in anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis. Neuromuscular junction disorders divide by the synapse: presynaptic (Lambert-Eaton, botulism) versus postsynaptic (myasthenia gravis). Drug histories should be read as a list of transmitter manipulations.

keyPoints: Glutamate and GABA carry the signal; the monoamines and acetylcholine set the state
Parkinsonism is dopamine loss, psychosis is dopamine excess, and the same drugs move patients between the two
Anticholinergic delirium, serotonin syndrome and neuroleptic malignant syndrome are transmitter emergencies that mimic infection
The neuromuscular junction is the most accessible synapse: presynaptic calcium channels (Lambert-Eaton), vesicle release (botulism), postsynaptic receptors (myasthenia)
NMDA receptors couple depolarization to calcium entry: plasticity when brief, cell death when prolonged

imaging.normalAppearance: Transmitter systems are imaged functionally: dopamine transporter SPECT for the nigrostriatal pathway, neuromelanin MRI for the nigra and locus coeruleus, PET ligands for cholinergic and serotonergic terminals.

pathology.finding: Reduced dopamine transporter uptake in the putamen, asymmetric and posterior-predominant, in Parkinson disease and Lewy body dementia; normal in essential tremor and drug-induced parkinsonism.
Loss of neuromelanin signal in the locus coeruleus and substantia nigra pars compacta on neuromelanin-sensitive T1 images.
Often normal or with subtle medial temporal FLAIR change despite severe psychiatric, seizure and autonomic disturbance; CSF antibodies make the diagnosis.

pearls: Read every drug list as a transmitter list before blaming the brain
Cholinesterase inhibitors help attention more than memory because the nucleus basalis dies first
A patient on two serotonergic drugs with clonus and fever has serotonin syndrome, not sepsis, until proved otherwise
pitfalls: A normal dopamine transporter scan in a parkinsonian patient means the problem is downstream (drug-induced, vascular or functional), not in the nigra

html.summary: The brain uses a small number of transmitters in two organizations: the point-to-point synapses of glutamate (excitatory) and GABA and glycine (inhibitory) that carry the signals of every pathway in this atlas, and the diffuse modulatory systems of dopamine, noradrenaline, serotonin, acetylcholine and histamine that arise from small brainstem and basal forebrain nuclei and set the state of the whole brain. Peptides, purines and endocannabinoids modulate both. Clinical neurology is largely the pharmacology of these systems: parkinsonism is dopamine loss, myasthenia is a cholinergic synapse under attack, epilepsy is an excess of glutamate over GABA, anticholinergic delirium and serotonin syndrome are drug effects on the modulatory nuclei, and antidepressants, antipsychotics, anesthetics and antiepileptics are all transmitter drugs.

topic-pediatric-neurological-syndromes.name: Pediatric neurological syndromes
topic-pediatric-neurological-syndromes.summary: The child's nervous system differs from the adult's in its unfinished myelination, its open sutures, its immature reflexes and its dependence on developmental milestones as the measure of function, so the same anatomy produces different clinical pictures: a hemispheric lesion produces hemiplegic cerebral palsy rather than a stroke syndrome, raised pressure produces a bulging fontanelle and a big head rather than papilledema, and a metabolic disease produces regression of milestones rather than dementia. The commonest pediatric syndromes, cerebral palsy, hydrocephalus and Chiari, febrile and epileptic seizures, neurocutaneous disorders, posterior fossa tumors, floppy infant syndromes and the leukodystrophies, are each anchored to atlas structures and a developmental timetable.

sections.heading: The developing examination
sections.body: Primitive reflexes (Moro, grasp, asymmetric tonic neck, stepping) are present at birth and disappear by six months as the corticospinal tract myelinates; their persistence or asymmetry is the earliest sign of an upper motor neuron lesion, and the Babinski sign is normal until walking begins. Tone evolves from the flexor hypertonia of the newborn to the hypotonia of early infancy and then to adult tone; a floppy infant with weakness has a lower motor neuron disorder (spinal muscular atrophy with tongue fasciculation and absent reflexes, congenital myopathy, myasthenia, botulism), whereas a floppy infant with preserved strength and brisk reflexes has a central cause (hypoxic injury, chromosomal disorder, metabolic disease). Milestones (social smile at 6 weeks, sitting at 6 to 8 months, walking at 12 to 18 months, words at 12 months, sentences at 2 years) are the functional examination, and their loss, regression, is the hallmark of a degenerative or metabolic disease and must never be attributed to behavior.

sections.heading: Cerebral palsy, hydrocephalus and the posterior fossa
sections.body: Cerebral palsy is a non-progressive motor disorder from injury to the developing brain: spastic diplegia from periventricular leukomalacia of prematurity (the leg fibers of the corticospinal tract lie closest to the ventricle), spastic hemiplegia from perinatal middle cerebral artery stroke, spastic quadriplegia from diffuse hypoxic-ischemic injury, dyskinetic palsy from basal ganglia and thalamic injury in term asphyxia or kernicterus, and ataxic palsy from cerebellar malformation. Infant hydrocephalus presents with an enlarging head, a tense fontanelle, splayed sutures, sunsetting eyes from posterior commissure compression and irritability; aqueductal stenosis, Chiari II with myelomeningocele, post-hemorrhagic hydrocephalus of prematurity and posterior fossa tumors are the causes. Posterior fossa tumors (medulloblastoma of the vermis, pilocytic astrocytoma of the hemisphere, ependymoma of the fourth ventricle, diffuse pontine glioma) present with morning vomiting, ataxia, head tilt and cranial nerve palsies.

sections.heading: Seizures and neurocutaneous syndromes
sections.body: Febrile seizures are brief generalized seizures with fever between six months and five years in a neurologically normal child and carry a small risk of later epilepsy; complex febrile seizures (focal, prolonged, repeated) and a first afebrile seizure need more evaluation. Infantile spasms (flexor jerks in clusters with hypsarrhythmia on EEG) signal a serious cause such as tuberous sclerosis or a malformation and regress development unless treated; childhood absence epilepsy, benign epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes and juvenile myoclonic epilepsy are the common age-related syndromes with characteristic EEGs. The neurocutaneous disorders link skin to brain: neurofibromatosis type 1 (cafe-au-lait spots, optic pathway gliomas, learning difficulty), tuberous sclerosis (hypomelanotic macules, cortical tubers, subependymal nodules and giant cell astrocytomas, infantile spasms), Sturge-Weber (facial port-wine stain with leptomeningeal angioma, seizures and hemiparesis) and neurofibromatosis type 2 (bilateral vestibular schwannomas).

sections.heading: Metabolic, degenerative and acquired disorders
sections.body: Inborn errors present with encephalopathy, seizures and regression, often precipitated by fasting or illness: urea cycle and organic acid disorders in the newborn, mitochondrial disorders with stroke-like episodes and lactic acidosis (MELAS), lysosomal storage diseases with hepatosplenomegaly and cherry-red spots, and the leukodystrophies (metachromatic, Krabbe, adrenoleukodystrophy) with progressive spasticity and white-matter change on MRI. Acquired disorders include bacterial meningitis (group B streptococcus and E. coli in neonates, pneumococcus and meningococcus later), herpes encephalitis, acute disseminated encephalomyelitis after infection, Guillain-Barre syndrome, and non-accidental injury, which must be considered in any infant with subdural hemorrhage, retinal hemorrhages and fractures. Neonatal hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy affects the watershed cortex in mild and the deep gray matter in severe insults, and its grading determines cooling and prognosis.

keyPoints: Regression of milestones is never behavioral: it is metabolic, degenerative or epileptic until proved otherwise
A floppy infant who is weak has a lower motor neuron disease; a floppy infant who is strong has a brain disease
Spastic diplegia is the signature of prematurity because the leg fibers run beside the ventricles
Sunset eyes in an infant are Parinaud syndrome from hydrocephalus stretching the posterior commissure
Infantile spasms need an EEG and a skin examination under Wood's lamp today, not next month

imaging.normalAppearance: Cranial ultrasound through the fontanelle for hemorrhage and ventricular size in infants, MRI for malformations, injury patterns and white-matter disease staged against the myelination timetable, and CT only for acute trauma or shunt failure.

pathology.finding: Loss of periventricular white matter with irregular ventricular margins and thinning of the posterior corpus callosum in an ex-premature child with spastic diplegia.
Restricted diffusion and T1 hyperintensity of the posterior putamen, ventrolateral thalamus and perirolandic cortex in severe insults; watershed cortex in partial prolonged insults.
pathology.timing: DWI peaks at 3-5 days; T1 changes appear after a week

pathology.finding: Enhancing midline vermian mass filling the fourth ventricle with restricted diffusion and hydrocephalus; spine imaging for drop metastases.
Cortical tubers (FLAIR-bright expanded gyri), subependymal nodules along the ventricles and a subependymal giant cell astrocytoma at the foramen of Monro.
Subdural hematomas of different ages, interhemispheric blood and hypoxic injury with retinal hemorrhages and skeletal fractures.

pearls: Measure the head circumference at every visit; the curve is the child's intracranial pressure record
Morning vomiting with a head tilt in a child is a posterior fossa tumor until the MRI is done
Retinal hemorrhages plus subdural blood in an infant means abuse until a rigorous alternative is proven
pitfalls: Unmyelinated white matter in an infant is bright on T2 and must not be called edema or leukodystrophy; compare with the myelination expected for age

topic-sleep-eeg-basics.name: Sleep, arousal and EEG basics
topic-sleep-eeg-basics.summary: Wakefulness is maintained by the ascending arousal system of the brainstem and hypothalamus, cholinergic, monoaminergic and orexinergic, which drives the thalamus and cortex, and sleep is imposed by the preoptic hypothalamus, which switches those systems off, with the REM state generated in the pons. The electroencephalogram records the summed synaptic currents of cortical pyramidal cells, paced by thalamocortical loops, and its rhythms map these states: alpha in relaxed wakefulness, theta and spindles in light sleep, delta in deep sleep, low-voltage fast activity with eye movements and atonia in REM. Disorders of this machinery, narcolepsy, REM behavior disorder, insomnia after hypothalamic lesions, coma from brainstem damage and the encephalopathies that slow the EEG, are read directly from the physiology.

sections.heading: The ascending arousal system
sections.body: Cholinergic neurons of the pedunculopontine and laterodorsal tegmental nuclei activate the thalamus, and monoaminergic neurons of the locus coeruleus (noradrenaline), the raphe (serotonin), the tuberomammillary nucleus (histamine) and the ventral tegmental area (dopamine) together with the basal forebrain cholinergic neurons activate the cortex directly; the orexin neurons of the lateral hypothalamus stabilize the whole system in the waking state. Damage to the paramedian upper pons and midbrain, where these pathways converge, produces coma, and bilateral paramedian thalamic infarction produces hypersomnolence, whereas hemispheric lesions cause coma only when they compress the brainstem. Loss of the orexin neurons produces narcolepsy, in which the wake state collapses into sleep and REM intrudes into waking as cataplexy, sleep paralysis and hypnagogic hallucinations.

sections.heading: The sleep switch and the sleep cycle
sections.body: The ventrolateral and median preoptic nuclei inhibit every arousal nucleus with GABA and galanin at sleep onset and are inhibited by them during waking, a mutually inhibitory flip-flop that gives sharp transitions and is biased by the homeostatic pressure of adenosine (blocked by caffeine) and the circadian signal from the suprachiasmatic nucleus through the dorsomedial hypothalamus. Non-REM sleep deepens through stages N1 to N3 as thalamic neurons hyperpolarize and generate spindles and then delta waves; REM sleep is generated by the sublaterodorsal nucleus of the pons, which produces cortical activation, rapid eye movements and, through the medullary reticular formation, the atonia of skeletal muscle. Cycles of 90 minutes repeat four to six times, with REM lengthening toward morning. Loss of REM atonia produces dream enactment, the REM sleep behavior disorder that precedes synucleinopathies by years.

sections.heading: Reading the EEG
sections.body: Scalp electrodes record 10 to 100 microvolt fluctuations produced by synchronous postsynaptic potentials in the apical dendrites of cortical pyramidal cells; the rhythms depend on thalamocortical pacing and cortical health. Normal waking shows a posterior alpha rhythm of 8 to 13 Hz that attenuates with eye opening, drowsiness shows theta, N2 sleep shows sleep spindles and K-complexes, and N3 shows high-amplitude delta; REM shows low-voltage fast activity with sawtooth waves. Diffuse slowing indicates encephalopathy of any cause, triphasic waves suggest metabolic or hepatic encephalopathy, focal slowing indicates a structural lesion, periodic lateralized discharges indicate an acute cortical injury such as herpes encephalitis or stroke, generalized periodic complexes in a demented patient suggest Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, and burst suppression or electrocerebral silence indicate deep anesthesia or catastrophic injury. Epileptiform spikes and sharp waves are the subject of the epilepsy entry.

sections.heading: Clinical disorders of sleep and arousal
sections.body: Narcolepsy type 1 is orexin deficiency with cataplexy and low CSF hypocretin; idiopathic hypersomnia and sleep apnea are the other causes of daytime sleepiness, and the multiple sleep latency test with a preceding polysomnogram separates them. REM sleep behavior disorder is a pontine sign and predicts Parkinson disease, Lewy body dementia or multiple system atrophy. Insomnia follows preoptic and anterior hypothalamic lesions; circadian disorders follow suprachiasmatic damage and blindness. Coma reflects damage to the arousal system or bilateral hemispheric dysfunction, and its grading, the brainstem reflexes and the EEG pattern determine prognosis; the persistent vegetative state retains sleep-wake cycles without awareness, and the locked-in state retains both. Sedative and antihistamine drugs act on these same nuclei, which is why they cause both sleep and delirium.

keyPoints: Coma needs a lesion of the paramedian upper brainstem or of both hemispheres; a single hemisphere cannot produce it without herniation
Narcolepsy is orexin loss: sleep attacks, cataplexy and REM intrusions
REM sleep behavior disorder is a pontine sign that predicts synuclein disease years before parkinsonism
The posterior alpha rhythm that blocks with eye opening is the first thing to find on a normal EEG
Triphasic waves, periodic lateralized discharges and burst suppression each tell a different story: metabolic, focal cortical injury, catastrophic

imaging.normalAppearance: Sleep disorders are diagnosed by polysomnography and the multiple sleep latency test; MRI is reserved for secondary causes (hypothalamic, pontine and thalamic lesions) and coma.

pathology.pathology: Paramedian thalamic and midbrain infarct with hypersomnolence
pathology.finding: Bilateral paramedian thalamic restricted diffusion with or without a midbrain lesion (artery of Percheron).

pathology.pathology: Pontine tegmental lesion with REM disturbance
pathology.finding: Lesion of the dorsolateral pontine tegmentum (infarct, demyelination, tumor) in a patient with new dream enactment or cataplexy.

pathology.pathology: Hypothalamic lesion with narcolepsy or insomnia
pathology.finding: Mass, inflammation or infarct of the lateral or anterior hypothalamus with secondary narcolepsy or loss of sleep.

pearls: Ask about dream enactment in every patient with parkinsonism or dementia: the answer dates the disease
A slow EEG says encephalopathy, not which one; the history and the metabolic screen say which
Sedatives and antihistamines act on the same nuclei that produce delirium in the elderly
pitfalls: Daytime sleepiness in a snorer is sleep apnea until a sleep study says otherwise; do not label it narcolepsy

topic-stroke-mechanisms-hemorrhage.name: Stroke mechanisms and intracranial hemorrhage
topic-stroke-mechanisms-hemorrhage.summary: A stroke is a sudden focal neurological deficit from a vascular cause, ischemic in about four-fifths and hemorrhagic in the rest, and its mechanism determines both the pattern of injury and the treatment: large artery atherosclerosis, cardioembolism, small vessel disease, dissection and rarer causes produce ischemic infarcts in the territories shown in this atlas, whereas hypertension, amyloid angiopathy, aneurysms, vascular malformations, venous thrombosis and anticoagulation produce hemorrhage into the parenchyma, the subarachnoid space or the subdural and epidural compartments. Localization gives the territory, the territory gives the artery, and the artery and the patient give the mechanism; recanalization within hours saves ischemic tissue, and the site and volume of a hemorrhage decide its danger.

sections.heading: Ischemic mechanisms and their imaging signatures
sections.body: Cardioembolism (atrial fibrillation, valve disease, recent infarction, endocarditis) sends clots to the large intracranial arteries and produces cortical infarcts in several territories or ages, often with hemorrhagic transformation; large artery atherosclerosis of the carotid bifurcation or the intracranial vessels produces territorial infarcts by artery-to-artery embolism and border-zone infarcts by hypoperfusion; small vessel lipohyalinosis of the lenticulostriate, thalamoperforating and pontine perforators produces lacunes with the classic lacunar syndromes; dissection of the carotid or vertebral artery in young patients produces neck pain, Horner syndrome and embolic infarcts; and rarer mechanisms include vasculitis, reversible vasoconstriction, hypercoagulable states, sickle cell disease, moyamoya and paradoxical embolism through a patent foramen ovale. The evaluation therefore includes vascular imaging from the aortic arch to the circle of Willis, cardiac rhythm monitoring and echocardiography, and the lipid and glucose profile that drives secondary prevention with antiplatelets or anticoagulants, statins and blood pressure control.

sections.heading: Acute ischemic stroke: time, core and penumbra
sections.body: Ischemic tissue dies at a rate that depends on collateral flow: the core is infarcted within minutes at the center of the territory, while the penumbra survives on leptomeningeal collaterals for hours and is the target of treatment. Intravenous thrombolysis within four and a half hours and mechanical thrombectomy for large vessel occlusion within six hours, or up to twenty-four hours when perfusion imaging shows a small core and a large penumbra, restore flow; the deficit, the NIH stroke scale, the CT ASPECTS score and the CTA occlusion site guide the decision, and hemorrhage, recent surgery and anticoagulation are the main contraindications. After reperfusion or without it, the infarct swells for three days, and malignant middle cerebral or cerebellar infarcts need decompressive surgery before herniation. Transient ischemic attacks carry a high early stroke risk and are investigated with the same urgency.

sections.heading: Intracerebral and subarachnoid hemorrhage
sections.body: Hypertensive hemorrhage arises from Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms of the perforating arteries and strikes the putamen, thalamus, pons and cerebellum; cerebral amyloid angiopathy of the elderly produces lobar hemorrhages at the cortical surface with microbleeds and superficial siderosis; arteriovenous malformations and cavernomas bleed in the young; anticoagulants, thrombolysis, tumors and venous thrombosis cause the rest. The hematoma expands in the first hours (the spot sign on CTA predicts it), and outcome depends on volume, location (brainstem and large deep hemorrhages are worst), ventricular extension and the level of consciousness; treatment is blood pressure lowering, reversal of anticoagulation and surgery for cerebellar hemorrhages over three centimeters or with brainstem compression. Aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage presents with a thunderclap headache, meningism and often a third nerve palsy from a posterior communicating aneurysm; it is complicated by rebleeding, vasospasm and delayed ischemia between days four and fourteen, hydrocephalus and hyponatremia, and is treated by coiling or clipping the aneurysm within a day.

sections.heading: Venous thrombosis and the extra-axial hemorrhages
sections.body: Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, from hypercoagulable states, pregnancy, infection and dehydration, raises pressure and produces headache, seizures and venous infarcts that cross arterial boundaries and often bleed; the superior sagittal sinus gives bilateral parasagittal lesions and the transverse sinus temporal lesions; MRV shows the absent flow and anticoagulation is the treatment despite the hemorrhage. Epidural hematoma from a middle meningeal artery tear under a temporal fracture produces a lucid interval and a lens-shaped clot that does not cross sutures; subdural hematoma from torn bridging veins produces a crescent that crosses sutures, acute in trauma and chronic in the elderly and anticoagulated, with fluctuating confusion and headache; both are surgical when they compress the brain. The atlas's venous meshes and the dural layers show why each collection has its shape.

keyPoints: The territory names the artery; the patient names the mechanism; the mechanism chooses the prevention
Cortical infarcts in more than one territory are embolic until proved otherwise; deep small infarcts are small vessel disease
The penumbra is a collateral phenomenon: good collaterals buy time for thrombectomy
Hypertension bleeds deep (putamen, thalamus, pons, cerebellum); amyloid bleeds lobar; aneurysms bleed into the cisterns
Venous infarcts cross arterial territories and bleed, and their treatment is anticoagulation

imaging.normalAppearance: Non-contrast CT first (hemorrhage, early ischemic signs, ASPECTS), then CTA of the arch-to-vertex vessels and CT perfusion or MRI with DWI for the core and penumbra; MRV for venous thrombosis; SWI for microbleeds and amyloid angiopathy; DSA for aneurysms and malformations.

pathology.finding: Small core (low cerebral blood volume) with a larger area of prolonged time-to-peak; the mismatch is the tissue thrombectomy can save.
Hyperdense hematoma in the putamen extending into the capsule and ventricle; a spot sign on CTA predicts expansion.
pathology.timing: Repeat CT at 6 hours for expansion

pathology.finding: Lobar hemorrhage with multiple cortical microbleeds and cortical superficial siderosis on SWI in an elderly patient.
Cisternal blood on CT, an aneurysm on CTA, and on days 4-14 narrowing of the proximal arteries with new perfusion deficits.
Absent flow in the sagittal or transverse sinus with parasagittal or temporal hemorrhagic venous infarcts.

pearls: Time is brain: every minute of a large vessel occlusion costs nearly two million neurons
A thunderclap headache with a third nerve palsy is a posterior communicating aneurysm until the CTA is done
A cerebellar hemorrhage over three centimeters goes to the operating theater, not the ward
pitfalls: A stroke in a young patient with neck pain is a dissection; do not attribute it to migraine
Lobar hemorrhage in the elderly needs SWI for microbleeds before anticoagulation is ever considered again

html.summary: A stroke is a sudden focal neurological deficit from a vascular cause, ischemic in about four-fifths and hemorrhagic in the rest, and its mechanism determines both the pattern of injury and the treatment: large artery atherosclerosis, cardioembolism, small vessel disease, dissection and rarer causes produce ischemic infarcts in the territories shown in this atlas, whereas hypertension, amyloid angiopathy, aneurysms, vascular malformations, venous thrombosis and anticoagulation produce hemorrhage into the parenchyma, the subarachnoid space or the subdural and epidural compartments. Localization gives the territory, the territory gives the artery, and the artery and the patient give the mechanism; recanalization within hours saves ischemic tissue, and the site and volume of a hemorrhage decide its danger.
